Title: Speech during the Signing of the Memorandum of Understanding on Data Sharing between the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas and the Department of Labor and Employment
Occasion: Signing of the Memorandum of Understanding on Data Sharing between the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas and the Department of Labor and Employment
Speaker: BSP Governor Eli M. Remolona Jr.
Transcription:
​

[Labor] Secretary Benny [Bienvenido] Laguesma, Undersecretary Carmela [Torres], colleagues from the Department of Labor and Employment (DOLE) and the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP), magandang umaga po sa ating lahat. 

Today's signing is more than just a formal agreement. It is a shared commitment to share data and shape policies. 

This reminds me of Arthur Okun—who introduced the misery index. This index is the sum of inflation and unemployment. I say it captures something really powerful—it captures economic hardship, which is felt when prices are high and jobs are scarce. 

At the BSP, we closely monitor inflation. But to see the full picture, we also need labor statistics. Employment and wage trends help us understand where the economy is going. 

The MOU (memorandum of understanding) that we are about to sign strengthens our ability to see the whole picture. With secure and timely data sharing, we can respond faster and smarter. 

For the BSP, it means clearer insights into price shocks and their impact on incomes.

For DOLE, it means more targeted support for our workers. Together, we can align our policies to serve the Filipino people better. I am excited for what this partnership will bring. 

Good data lead to good policy—and good policy leads to good progress.

Maraming salamat po. ​

Title: Statement during the Monetary Policy Press Briefing, August 2025
Occasion: Monetary Policy Press Briefing
Speaker: BSP Governor Eli M. Remolona Jr.
Transcription:
​

Good afternoon. I hope you like the new format for our Monetary Policy announcement.

As you know earlier today, the Monetary Board decided to reduce its key policy interest rate. The target RRP (reverse repurchase) rate will now be reduced by 25 basis points to 5 percent.

Based on the latest data, I think this puts us at our sweet spot for both inflation and output.

The projected inflation rate over the next year or so is where we want it to be. Output is moving to where we think our capacity is. The policy rate itself is at our Goldilocks rate – neither too high nor too low.

I would characterize this as still dovish, but slightly less so than before in terms of the forward guidance. 

We came to this decision after weighing many different scenarios. We looked at a central scenario, a relatively hawkish scenario, and a relatively dovish scenario, for both inflation and output. 

In the end, we chose the central scenario for both. We had to look at so many scenarios because there is still a lot of uncertainty.

Overall, we see the inflation outlook to be very manageable and inflation expectations to be well-anchored. But we still see more significant risks to the inflation outlook than to the output outlook. 

Thank you.​

Title: Speech during the Manila Tech Summit
Occasion: Manila Tech Summit
Speaker: BSP Governor Eli M. Remolona, Jr.
Transcription:
​

Your Excellency President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., Fintech Alliance Chairman Lito Villanueva, colleagues from government and BSP (Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas), magandang umaga po sa inyong lahat.

Our theme today is essentially about future-proofing finance. One way to think about this is through network effects.

As the best experts say, a system grows stronger as more people participate in it. Like a phone network, it works best when everyone is connected. Then amazing things happen and the social good escalates.

To us, future-proofing finance looks like this.

First, inclusion makes the system stronger. Our QR Ph and Paleng-QR Ph allow tricycle drivers, sari-sari stores, and small businesses to take digital payments. Every new user adds value to the network.

Second, security instills trust in the network. Our Cyber Resilience Plan and AFASA (Anti-Financial Account Scamming Act) guard against fraud and cyber-attacks. Without trust, the system cannot grow.

Third, innovation keeps the system relevant. We continue to champion smart technologies, open finance—including tools like the Personal Equity Retirement Account or PERA. Many of you joined us when we launched this joint pilot earlier this month.

At the BSP, we like to keep things simple. We like smart innovations that solve real problems. We like simple solutions that people can easily use. And we like secure systems that can withstand shocks and attacks. This is how we connect inclusion, security, and innovation.

The BSP cannot be the only game in town. The Fintech Alliance plays a vital role. You are the builders, the connectors, [and] the innovators.

We need your help to future-proof our financial system.

Maraming salamat po at mabuhay tayong lahat. ​

Title: Exhibit Opening of Kultura. Kapital. Kasalukuyan. Contemporary Art from the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas
Occasion: Exhibit Opening of Kultura. Kapital. Kasalukuyan. Contemporary Art from the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas
Speaker: BSP Governor Eli M. Remolona, Jr.
Transcription:
​

Magandang hapon po.

Thank you, Chairman [Andoni] Aboitiz, Director [-General Jeremy] Barns, MBMs (Monetary Board Members) Romy [Romeo Bernardo], Walter [Wassmer], [Jose] Jojo [Querubin], DG (Deputy Governor) Berna [Romulo-Puyat], DG Elmore [Capule], Tess Espenilla, and all our esteemed guests [colleagues from Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas].

We are grateful to the National Museum for this partnership. We have shared 103 artworks from our Spanish colonial collection across the museum's exhibits.

More recently, we still have the Edades you mentioned, Jimmy [Jaime Laya]. We now have it back in the Davao branch.

So, this has been a wonderful, wonderful collaboration. It occurs to me that artists and central bank economists are not all that different. Both build new worlds, maybe imagined worlds. Both challenge norms and both imagine the future.

The artist constructs these worlds through brushstrokes or found objects, such as a toilet seat—like Marcel Duchamp. Economists will do it through complicated equations or mathematical models. This is why I love both. I love both art and economics.

When I became Governor, I was so happy to find in my office—Say (Amando) Tetangco (Jr.'s) office, Jimmy  Laya's office—there was a Joya, there was a Malang, there was an Antonio, and there was a Belleza.

I do not know if that Joya is the same Joya you mentioned, Jimmy—the one from Mapa High School. But I have a good one in my office.

Chairman Aboitiz, you are welcome to visit my office anytime.

My wife and I, Marie and I, always made time to visit museums wherever we went. In New York, our favorite is the MoMa—[Museum of] Modern Art, and the Whitney [Museum]. In Switzerland, our favorite is the Beyeler [Foundation Museum], and we have seen the Prado [Museum].

We have seen the other museums in the neighborhood, and I have tended to rope in my colleagues to go with me. They walk with me and visit the same museums. So, I am very excited about today's exhibit.

The works on display are not just for viewing. It tells stories of our identity, our struggles, and our hope. They remind us that building a nation takes both economic strength and cultural depth.

So, on behalf of all of us here and the Filipino people, thank you to the leaders of contemporary art in the Philippines. Thank you for inspiring us with your dedication and your creativity.

Maraming salamat at mabuhay tayong lahat.

###​

Title: In the Last Mile, We Faced Unusual Headwinds
Occasion: Economic Journalists Association of the Philippines Economic Forum
Speaker: BSP Governor Eli M. Remolona, Jr.
Transcription:
​

I would like to echo [Department of Finance] Secretary Ralph [Recto] in thanking you for helping us communicate economic policies. I know this is a tough job. Economics is always hard to communicate, but I think you have been successful in doing it. So, maraming salamat.

Let me start with global policy uncertainty. This has been mentioned by Secretary Ralph.

The most difficult part of the uncertainty has been the one about trade policy uncertainty. I do not have to describe what happened, but when we measure it, we construct a dictionary of words that are related to policy uncertainty, and then we count the number of times those words are mentioned in the media, and so on.

It spiked, especially in April 2025, at the time of the Liberation Day [when] tariffs were announced.

It was not just about trade policy. Policy uncertainty, in general, also spiked. It also spiked around the same time that trade policy uncertainty spiked.

That had serious economic consequences. When you have uncertainty about the economy, what happens is you postpone your investments. You postpone your big-ticket consumption items.

And that is what we saw. We saw that globally, and we saw that in the Philippines. For this, we look at what we call soft data.

Normally, when we model the economy, we only use hard data. But for this kind of phenomenon, which is very hard to understand, we use soft data. We use data on business confidence, for example.

This is collected regularly by the Institute of Supply Management. This has tended to be reliable.

This is a measure of business confidence. The numbers fell in June and July, and that has showed up in the slowing growth of our economy.

Nonetheless, as you have seen before, as you have seen in the earlier presentations, when we look at the outlook for growth, we are doing very well actually, compared with other emerging markets.

We are doing 5.5 percent, as Secretary Ralph has mentioned, which is pretty good. Much better than other emerging markets. This is IMF (International Monetary Fund) data, by the way, so it is not just ours.

And then advanced economies are projected to grow at 1.3 percent. So, considering the circumstances, we are doing very well.

In terms of inflation, we think we will hit 2.0 percent in 2025. That is much better than other emerging markets [EMs]. They [EMs] would hit 3.1 percent, and other advanced economies, I think, would hit 3.3 percent. So [the Philippines has] lower inflation than both advanced economies and emerging markets.

So, that is the broad picture. When we look at inflation more carefully, we show the dynamics of inflation.

As has been mentioned before, there was the start of the Russia-Ukraine war early in 2022 that led to a spike in energy prices that boosted or raised our inflation rate.

Food prices also went up. What happened was Russia cut off the supply of natural gas to Europe that affected other sources of energy, especially oil. So, that caused our inflation rate to reach 8.7 percent in January 2023.

In the beginning, it was mostly energy that was causing the rise in inflation, but food prices also went up. The big event was in July 2023 when India banned the export of basmati rice that affected the prices of rice exports of other countries. It affected the prices of our rice imports. And since 2023, the main driver of our high inflation has been food inflation.

In the last few months, food inflation went negative. And so that brought our inflation rate down to 0.9 percent as of July. The core inflation rate [was] down to 2.3 percent.

We are actually now below our target band. Core inflation is the part of the inflation that is affected by monetary policy. [Energy and food] are the parts of inflation that tend to be driven by supply factors. Core inflation is driven by demand factors, which is the part of inflation that the central bank can affect.

We also look at inflation for the bottom 30 percent of households. Food is 51 percent of the consumer basket of the bottom 30 percent of households. That is mainly rice, fish, and vegetables.

Similar to the picture for headline inflation, the recent inflation numbers have been driven largely by food prices. In fact, food prices started coming down from negative inflation in the last several months, so that for the bottom 30 percent, inflation in July was negative 0.8 percent.

We think that is a good outcome, and we hope that inflation will continue to be very helpful to the bottom 30 percent of Filipinos.

So, that is the dynamics of inflation. As you know, [on] June 10, Israel attacked Iran and started bombing Iran. We were so scared, not about the war itself, but because we thought the Strait of Hormuz would be closed and that would cause oil prices to spike.

As you can see, oil prices have been a major driver of inflation in the Philippines. We were standing and looking at this in June. We were looking at futures prices of oil. At the time of the war in June, futures prices were rising.

The ceasefire came very quickly, and oil prices dropped, and futures prices also dropped.

So, that helped us project lower inflation rates for the Philippines. If you look at our forecasts, we see our inflation target remaining within reach.

I think we still have work to do, but we are looking at 2027 headline inflation of 3.3 percent, core inflation of 3.1 percent. Both are within our target.

We are hoping we can achieve that because I think that would help stabilize the economy, and that would help support investment, support lending by our banks.

But as I said, we have work to do. So, that is my story. I hope you guys can help us communicate that story, as well as the stories that have been told by [Department of Economy, Planning, and Development] Secretary Arsi (Arsenio Balisacan), Secretary Ralph, [Department of Budget and Management] Assistant Secretary Romy (Romeo Matthew Balanquit).

Maraming salamat po.

​###​

Title: Digital Pathways to Financial Security
Occasion: Ceremonial Signing and Go-Live for Project OFxPERA
Speaker: BSP Governor Eli M. Remolona, Jr.
Transcription:
​
To our partners in the financial sector, colleagues in government, ladies and gentlemen, Magandang araw po sa inyong lahat.

Today’s event is more than a launch. It is a shift in how we think about banking. Your bank account should give you easy access to all sorts of other financial services. 

That is what is called open finance. At its core, it is about connection. Your customer’s consent, banks, and third-party providers of financial services can securely share financial data through application programming interfaces or APIs. 

This makes insurance, investments, and other financial services simpler, smarter, and more personalized.
 
We actually borrowed this idea from Brazil. Banco Central do Brasil embedded open finance into Pix. Pix is their real-time payments system.

Today, around 49 million Brazilians consented to their data being shared—allowing them to send money, switch banks, and access credit with ease. This is what happens when systems connect, and users are empowered. 

This brings us to open finance or PERA. 

The Personal Equity and Retirement Account or PERA was introduced in 2016 to help Filipinos save for the long term. It is voluntary, tax-advantaged, and open to everyone. 

But uptake has been slow—with just 6,100 accounts as of June 2025. 

We know the appetite for financial health is there. So, what is missing? 

Sometimes, the challenge is not always the product. Sometimes, it is the pathway. By making PERA the starting point for open finance, we build this pathway. PERA now becomes part of a seamless digital ecosystem, making saving and investment simpler for everyone. 

At the same time, the project also allows us to jumpstart open finance from concept to practice. 

So, now users can explore their options more clearly, thanks to consent-driven data sharing via the account information services. Users can save more easily with the payment initiation services that automate contributions. 

This is more than innovation. It is financial health. We are part of builders with banks, asset managers, regulators, and civil society. 

The success of PERA and open finance depends on how closely aligned we are in systems and in purpose. 

Maraming salamat po at mabuhay tayong lahat.

Title: A Tale of Two Externalities
Occasion: BSP Forum on National ID: Building Trust and Synergy in Digital Identity for an Inclusive and Secure Financial System
Speaker: BSP Governor Eli M. Remolona, Jr.
Transcription:
​

MBM (Monetary Board Member) [Rosalia] Lea [De Leon], MBM [Jose] Jojo [Querubin], DG (Deputy Governor) Berna [Romulo-Puyat], DG Zeno [Abenoja], [Philippine Statistics Authority] Assistant Secretary [Rosalinda] Rose [Bautista], Assistant Secretary [Kristine] Joy [Diaz-Teston], colleagues from the government, partners from the private sector, ladies and gentlemen, good morning!

Thank you for taking part in this forum.

The National ID tells a powerful story of inclusion and network effects.

The more people we onboard, the more valuable the National ID becomes. As its usefulness grows, so does the social good.

Here is what that looks like:

In 2022, 5.8 million unbanked Filipinos opened their first transaction accounts through PhilSys registration. Partnering with Landbank, the Philippine Statistics Authority enabled onsite account creation using only the National ID. No extra paperwork, no long forms to fill. For many, it was their first step into formal financial inclusion.

Economists call this network externalities.

Every new enrollee strengthens the old system. Like a phone network, it works best when everyone is connected. And once they are, amazing things happen.

Then you have the positive externalities of inclusion as the benefits ripple across sectors:

  • A vendor saves up for her kids.
  • A father uses one ID to access PhilHealth.
  • A tricycle driver receives his pension with ease.
  • A family gets ayuda after a storm, fast and fuss-free.

Each success story is more than convenience. It is access to financial and public services. It is a system working as it should.

Getting here was not easy. This reform is complex technically, logistically, and even politically. Agencies must align and systems must talk to each other. It demands active collaboration among a diverse set of stakeholders.

But still, we push forward. Because we know what is at stake. What we are building is bigger than a database. We are building trust.

We are building a Philippines where your identity is no longer a barrier, but a bridge.

So, let us keep going. Every Filipino we onboard make the whole system stronger.

Maraming salamat. I am excited about the discussions ahead.

###​

Title: Speech during the 32nd Anniversary of the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas
Occasion: 32nd Anniversary of the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas
Speaker: BSP Governor Eli M. Remolona, Jr.
Transcription:
​

Magandang umaga! Happy anniversary.

Our theme today is digital, sustainable, inclusive. These are not just buzzwords. They are principles that shape the way we think, we work, and the way we serve.

But the center of it all is digitalization. It is everywhere.  Now with artificial intelligence (AI), it is impossible to ignore. The growing conversation around AI is still evolving and so are the expectations.

Goldman Sachs says there will be a significant 7-percent annual boost to GDP (gross domestic product) over the next 10 years. By contrast, Nobel Laureate, Daron Acemoglu sees a more modest gain of 1 percent a year.  He  cautioned that without thoughtful design AI would deepen inequality and centralize power. The truth likely lies somewhere in this region. This reminds me of Yogi Berra—the baseball player and coach. He said, when you come to a fork on the road, take it.

We are now at that fork. The real question is not whether to adopt AI, it is about how we use it, to empower rather than to displace.

To this end, we made some progress. In monetary policy we are leveraging generative AI to extract insights from non-traditional, unstructured high-frequency data.

These are especially helpful during periods of befuddling uncertainty.

In banking supervision, SupTech and RegTech are helping us streamline reporting and assess risks faster. These are essential as banks become more complex and interconnected.

In cybersecurity, we have launched ASTERisC*, rolled out the Financial Services Cyber Resilience Plan, and implementing the Anti-Financial Account Scamming Act. This will enhance the BSP's (Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas) ability to combat cybercrimes. 
In payments, digital transactions have surpassed our 50 percent target. QR Ph was expanded to 178 local government units—encouraging broader adoption among small merchants and accelerating financial inclusion.

Likewise, Bills Pay PH has simplified payments for recurring bills like utilities and credit cards.

We have also made important strides for BSP. After all, technology is only as good as the people who use it.

As of this week, our refreshed website offers a faster and more responsive experience.

At 32, we are not just marking time, we are charting our direction. One, powered by innovation and rooted in sustainability and inclusion.

So, as we stand at this fork, let us not hesitate. Let us take it together with purpose and with target. Happy anniversary. Magandang umaga po!

###

Title: Welcome Remarks at the Presidential and National Anti-Money Laundering, Counter-Terrorism Financing, Counter Proliferation Financing Coordinating Committee (NACC) Recognition Ceremony
Occasion: Presidential and National Anti-Money Laundering, Counter-Terrorism Financing, Counter Proliferation Financing Coordinating Committee Recognition Ceremony
Speaker: BSP Governor Eli M. Remolona, Jr.
Transcription:
​​​

Intro​duction

Colleagues from the government, partners in the private sector, esteemed guests, good afternoon. Magandang hapon po.

I am pleased to welcome you to this recognition ceremony where we honor the champions behind our exit from the FATF grey list. Our sincere thanks to the Office of the President for hosting this occasion in the revered halls of Malacañang.
 
Over a decade of challenge

We were placed on the grey list in 2021. But the real story stretches back 10 years before that. Starting in 2010, global banks were already doing something called de-risking—where they started cutting off their relationships with our banks. 

This means, this exit ends not just three years on the grey list, but more than a decade of doing business with a handicap. We spent more than a decade wandering in the wilderness. 

A study of grey-listed countries shows that grey listing results in deep declines in foreign direct investments, capital inflows, inward payments, and external loans. This reduced our access to global markets, which limited our growth potential.

Grey listing imposed enhanced monitoring while we address gaps on anti-money laundering, counterterrorism and proliferation financing frameworks.
 
That is real pressure because failure will mean something much worse. It could mean going to the blacklist. We had three years to work on it, but we came together, we made our way out of the wilderness. 

Getting off the grey list was not easy. It was critical that the President (Ferdinand R.) Marcos (Jr.) made it a priority and Executive Secretary (Lucas) Bersamin steered our efforts. 

Through concerted reforms, government agencies fortified our financial system and reaffirmed our commitment to combating financial crimes. 

Closing

Today, we honor our public and private sector champions who made this happen. Many of you work quietly behind the scenes but today, we give you the recognition and gratitude you deserve. 

Maraming salamat sa inyong lahat. Mabuhay tayong lahat!

###


​​​

Title: Going Digital: Changing the Digital Finance Narrative
Occasion: 4th Digital Financial Inclusion Awards
Speaker: BSP Governor Eli. M. Remolona, Jr.
Transcription:
​

Introduction

Good afternoon, everyone. Good afternoon, [Microfinance Council of the Philippines, Inc. Chairperson] Gilbert [Maramba]. Good afternoon, [Citi Philippines CEO] Paul [Favila]. Good afternoon, Teodoro [Lamang Jr.]. Thank you for your inspiring testimony. 

Thank you all for joining us in this media launch for the Digital Financial Inclusion Awards. It is something that we do every year that recognized microentrepreneurs leading the way in digital finance. 

Shift in focus

Going digital is not always easy. Part of the challenge is what psychologists Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman described as the availability bias, which is our tendency to focus more on dramatic events rather than the common ones. 

In digitalization, we hear a lot about online fraud and scams because they tend to be dramatic events. We do not talk about the boring benefits, faster transactions, better financial access, and new opportunities. 

This makes small businessowners hesitant, “Ang hirap pumasok sa digital” or “Baka maloko pa kami d’yan.” While these concerns are valid, they should not hold us back. 

This is why we are here. To help shift the focus to the real success stories. The BSP and its partner agencies are working to make the digital landscape more secure, simpler, and more accessible. 

First is safer digital space. The Anti-Financial Account Scamming Act or AFASA was actually enacted to fight fake accounts, fraud, and scams. The implementing rules and regulations are in the works. 

Second is simpler digital banking. The QRPh and the new Standard Business Loan Application Form or SBLAF streamlined payments and credit application. Launched last December, the SBLAF is short, user-friendly, and fully digital. 

Third, is broader digital access. The moratorium on digital banking license application was lifted, which means more digital banks helping small businesses in opening accounts, applying for loans, and transacting seamlessly. 

With these measures, digital finance is becoming more secure, more efficient, and more inclusive. The entrepreneurs we are honoring here are proof of that. 

Take Shanie Lou, who scaled her baking business through social media platforms and e-wallets. Or Ligaya, who used e-commerce to expand the market for her hand-woven bags. 

Closing

To our friends in the media, we ask you to share these stories and help shift the narrative. Let us show every Juan and Maria that digital finance is not something to fear—it is something to embrace. 

Maraming salamat po at mabuhay tayong lahat!​​​

Title: Getting Out of the Grey List--And Staying Out
Occasion: Tuesday Club Meeting
Speaker: BSP Governor Eli M. Remolona, Jr.
Transcription:
​

Good morning, Tuesday Club!

Thank you once again for having me here. Special thanks to Marichu for adjusting the schedule--it was for an important reason, which I’ll be sharing today.

Two weeks ago, I went to Paris to appear before the Financial Action Task Force (FATF) Plenary Meeting. I was joined by Executive Secretary Bersamin, Securities and Exchange Commission Chairperson Aquino, and Insurance Commissioner Reynaldo Regalado. It was the culmination of our country’s efforts to be stricken off from the FATF greylist.

What exactly is FATF and what is the greylist? The FATF was established in 1989 by the G-7 group of countries. The mandate of FATF is to develop international standards to combat money laundering. But over time, that mandate has expanded to include countering terrorism financing and proliferation financing.

What the FATF does to carry out its mandate is to evaluate countries, [under] what is called a Mutual Evaluation, to see if they meet FATF standards. Countries that have deficiencies are placed on a List of Jurisdictions Under Increased Monitoring, that is the official name for the greylist. That means we have some deficiencies in terms of compliance with anti-money laundering rules and anti-terrorism financing rules. The thing about being on the greylist is that [it] places on your correspondent banks—or banks abroad that are dealing with us—a heavy burden in terms of compliance against money laundering. In fact, you may remember 2012, I think. One major global bank was caught violating its compliance measures and it was fined something like $1.9 billion. So, that is what comes with being on the greylist. Your banks have to be very careful [because of] the very strict compliance procedures– [and] heavy fines [for non-compliance].

In 2021, the Philippines was placed on the greylist. That means the FATF gives us recommendations on things that we should do so we ourselves would comply with anti-money laundering measures. It is easier for the banks if we do a lot of the compliance part ourselves. That is the advantage of FATF greylist, if you are not complying, they tell you how to comply. So, they give you a list of what are called action items. In 2018, they gave us 18 action items that will help us figure out how to comply with money laundering processes.

These action items included oversight of money service businesses, oversight of casino junkets, oversight of designated non-financial businesses or professions (DNFBPs)— in other words, list the lawyers and the bankers involved in these things—and also non-profit organizations to make sure that even non-profit organizations comply with the items on the list. Law enforcement agencies were tasked to improve the confiscation of proceeds of crimes, and the prosecution of money laundering and terrorism financing cases. 

For context on what happened in 2021… Even 10 years before that, banks were already doing something called de-risking: they were already starting to cut off relationships with our banks. The correspondent banks abroad were cutting relationships with our banks here, which meant it was hard to send money here, it was hard to open accounts abroad, especially the smaller banks. The bigger banks somehow maintained the relationships with our banks because they could afford it. They could afford the compliance measures.

Then, in 2016 we had the Bangladesh heist. So, that brought us extra unwanted global attention. Actually, it was the 2016 Bangladesh heist that I think led to the greylist of 2021. So, we already suffered from measures that were being imposed on us even before the greylist. The greylist just made it official, and it allowed FATF to give us 18 items to get out of the greylist.

The good news from last month was not the end of a four-year ordeal; it was actually the end of a nine-year ordeal if you count from 2016.

So, we were told actually in 2021 [that] to get off the greylist by 2025 was too ambitious. We have consultants who were working with us. That was too ambitious, but we have to try. And so, under the leadership of President Marcos, the National Anti-Money Laundering and Counter Terrorism Financing Coordinating Committee (NACC) was reorganized in 2023, a scorecard system [was implemented] to hold the member agencies accountable for their deliverables. The Executive Secretary has been the chairman of NACC. I have been the vice chairman of NACC.

The directive of the President and the collaboration of national agencies in the NACC exemplifies the "whole-of-government" approach. This worked very well.

FATF also wanted to see high-level commitment. It was not just complying with 18 action items. They wanted to see evidence that there was commitment at the highest level. So, the banning of POGOs was a demonstration of that high-level commitment. That [banning POGOs] was not on the [FATF’s] list [of action items for the Philippines]. Nonetheless, I think it was important in getting us off the greylist.

By October 2024, the FATF determined that the Philippines had satisfied the action plan. So, when it was not enough for the FATF to determine based on our reports on the action plan, they had to send a team to conduct an onsite assessment to validate what we have reported to them.

So, the team came here in January. That onsite team said, yes it is true, the Philippines has satisfied the action plan and then in February, there was a big meeting in Paris, which I attended. I gave one intervention and the executive secretary gave another intervention, and then after that, FATF decided that we are okay, we had met the expectations of FATF. There were no objections at all. So, it was a unanimous decision by FATF [for the Philippines to be removed from the greylist].

In fact, we are recognized for good behavior. [The Philippines is seen as] a regional leader in tackling money laundering and terrorism financing, so they [FATF] asked us to provide evaluators for the other countries in Asia that are still on greylist.

So, the official statement as you know came out on February 21, 5 pm Paris time, 12 midnight here. It was a weekend. But, if you looked at what happened to the peso before that weekend and after that weekend, I think it was anticipation of more investments coming into the Philippines.

Now, just because we are off the greylist does not mean that we are done. We have to make sure we do not get back into the greylist. In the past, we go in, we go out. This time, we are determined to stay out of the greylist. So, part of that means looking at our risks again. We call that national risk assessment.

So, we look at the whole economy to figure out what else can lead to risks of money laundering, what else can lead to terrorism financing and so on.

The next [FATF] evaluation [of the Philippines] will be in 2027. We want to make sure that we pass that evaluation.

In the meantime, we can reap the benefits of our delisting from the FATF greylist.

That delisting renews investor confidence. It paves the way for the restoration of correspondent bank relationships. So, it helps our OFWs, but it is more than that. It helps convince foreign investors to come in. Makes it easier for foreign banks to deal with our banks. So, I hope we can stay out of the greylist. We are determined to stay out of the greylist.

I think that is all I have for now. I am happy to take questions.

###

Title: Speech for the National AML/CTF/CPF Coordinating Committee – Supervision of Financial Institutions Sub-Committee Stakeholder Appreciation Program
Speaker: BSP Governor Eli. M. Remolona, Jr.
Transcription:
​

Good morning, everyone! Magandang umaga po.

First, let me express my gratitude to all of you—our partners across BSP-supervised sectors, industry associations, and colleagues from the government. 

The Philippines, as we know, was included in the FATF Grey List in 2021. We knew then that we had a tough road ahead of us. However, we recognized the challenges and took decisive actions. We addressed the gaps in our anti-money laundering and counter terrorism and proliferation financing framework. These reforms reinforced the integrity of our financial system and strengthened our fight against financial crimes.  These efforts were recognized by the FATF, and that’s how we got out of the greylist. Parang tayong nabunutan ng tinik.

This achievement would not have been possible without your commitment. To our financial institutions and industry associations, thank you for faithfully discharging your responsibilities to combat money laundering, terrorism financing and proliferation financing. You played an indispensable role in addressing the key strategic deficiencies identified by the FATF. Salamat sa tulong n’yo, sa onsite meeting 'nung January.

To our partners in the Supervision of Financial Institutions Sub-Committee or the SFISC, including the AMLC, SEC, Insurance Commission, BSP, and DILG—your dedication to adopt and implement sustainable reforms and targeted strategies was essential in meeting the FATF action plan.

Our work does not stop here. Hindi pa tapos ang laban. Building on the lessons we have learned from our experience on the FATF Grey List, we must continue to strengthen our AML/CTPF regime. We must be vigilant in addressing emerging risks to ensure a resilient financial system.

Let’s keep moving forward, maintain the momentum, and stay united in our fight against financial crimes.

Maraming salamat. Mabuhay tayong lahat!​

Title: Keynote Message for the Annual Reception for the Banking Community
Occasion: 2025 Annual Reception for the Banking Community
Speaker: BSP Governor Eli M. Remolona, Jr.
Transcription:
​

Good evening, everyone. 

Former central bank governors, members of the Monetary Board, partners from the banking and diplomatic community, government officials, friends from the media, ladies and gentlemen, happy new year!

First of all, congratulations to all of you and thank you for a milestone-filled 2024. 

It has been a remarkable year and I am truly grateful for the hard work that each one of us has put in. Indeed, we have much to celebrate. 

We received from S&P (Global) an upgrade in our credit rating outlook. With your help, we launched the peso IRS (interest rate swap) market, and we took significant steps to expand the government repo (repurchase) market. We also rolled out the Financial Services Cyber Resilience Plan and helped pass the Anti Financial Account Scamming Act.

In the midst of all these, we also began circulating the new smarter, cleaner, and stronger polymer banknotes.

The year 2024 also happens to be the 75th anniversary of central banking in the Philippines. Please join me in applauding the services of BSP employees, the current ones, as well as those who served before them, some of them are here with us today.

We also have some new faces among us, including two members of the Monetary Board, Walter Wassmer and Jose Querubin. Their perspectives have already proven to be very helpful.

As we look ahead to 2025 and beyond, I am thrilled to continue working with you to build on our shared successes. Let us continue working together on digitalization and financial inclusion. Let us also intensify our efforts on Open Finance to ensure that people can choose financial services that best suit their needs.

Having worked with many of you over the years, I know that we share the same goal, and we share the same drive to make the banking industry a stronger engine for jobs and growth for the Filipino people.

Let me now call on my fellow members of the Monetary Board to join me on stage for the ceremonial toast.​

Title: Welcome Message for the 3rd Digital Financial Inclusion Awards
Occasion: 3rd Digital Financial Inclusion Awards
Speaker: BSP Governor Eli M. Remolona, Jr.
Transcription:
​

Introduction

Citi Philippines CEO Paul Favila, Microfinance Council Chairperson Gilbert Maramba, fellow members of the selection committee—who had to work so hard to pick the winners, outstanding microentrepreneurs, tireless microfinance institutions, and our dear guests—good morning and welcome!

As most of you know, these awards started 22 years ago. It was called the Microentrepreneurship of the Year Awards. Three years ago, and not because microentrepreneurship is so hard to pronounce, we decided to call it the Digital Financial Inclusion Awards (DFIA), and this is for both microentrepreneurs and the microfinance institutions that help them.

When we kicked off the 3rd DFIA, when we did it last March, I called digitalization the “secret sauce” of financial inclusion. It is just like bagoong in kare-kare. 

Digitalization

Today, we celebrate 16 microentrepreneurs as Paul has mentioned, and six microfinance institutions. For the microentrepreneurs, I like the description in this event’s brochure: From trade fairs to Facebook posts. You have turned pocket-change businesses into your own gold mines.

And while B2C (business to consumer) gets most of the attention, some of you maximized technology to transact with your suppliers and, for one of you, even your resellers.

Meanwhile, the microfinance institutions are stepping up their game with apps for loan management, cash flow management, and other financial processes along with mobile apps to make it easier for your customers.

You have all shown how digitalization can unlock huge inclusion opportunities. 

You actually also helped the BSP (Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas). Thanks to your work, the BSP’s Digital Payments Roadmap and the National Strategy for Financial Inclusion are not just checklists—they are living, thriving achievements.

Your efforts help build a future where financial inclusion is not just a buzzword but a reality for everyone. Seventy-one percent of households now have a deposit or e-money account. Fifty-two percent of all payments are now digital.

Closing

Of course, there is more work to do. Because for many Filipinos, microenterprises and microfinance are not just businesses—they are steppingstones to a better life. It is about sending kids to school, securing their future, and maybe even buying that dream house. 

So, when it comes to digital financial inclusion, let us bring more Filipinos to the table, and share this feast—including the kare-kare!

A big shoutout to our partners from Citi, MCPI (Microfinance Council of the Philippines), and the selection committee. Again, to this year’s winners—congratulations! Maraming salamat po!

###

Title: Understanding Interconnectedness: Conglomerate Risks and its Impact on Financial Stability
Occasion: 41st Environmental Scanning Exercise
Speaker: BSP Governor Eli M. Remolona, Jr.
Transcription:
​

Members of the Monetary Board, BSP (Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas) colleagues, guests, ladies and gentlemen, good afternoon.

Welcome to the 41st Environmental Scanning Exercise. This one is about the issue of conglomerate risk.

When a bank is part of a conglomerate, the basic principle of regulation is simple. It is to ensure that the conglomerate is a source of strength to the bank rather than a source of weakness. 

In general, conglomerate risk arises when a bank lends to a seemingly healthy company, but that company gets dragged down by problems at one of its affiliates within the conglomerate. Such a scenario happens if these different companies are interconnected through shareholdings, loans, or even supply contracts. 

This means we can’t just look at the borrower. We also need to consider the companies to which it is connected.

I am looking forward to this discussion because conglomerates play a big role in our economy, much like in many Asian countries. 

At the same time, large banks have significant exposures to these conglomerates. It is important to understand the accompanying risks. 

For example, in the Philippine Stock Exchange, the composite index consists of 30 companies—12 of those are part of conglomerates. Together, they control 90 percent of total market capitalization. The top five alone control 74 percent of the total market capitalization.

Many banks are also part of conglomerates. Seven out of the 10 largest banks in this country are part of a conglomerate. They represent 60 percent of the banking system’s assets as of 2021. 

If any of the firms in the conglomerate get into trouble, banks and even the economy, may be in for an unpleasant surprise.

Today, our goal is to better understand the extent of risks of conglomerate activity and find solutions, including best regulatory practices from abroad, that can help us manage these risks. 

We already have regulations that monitor banks’ large exposures, but identifying potential risks remains a challenge.

I look forward to hearing your thoughts and exchanging ideas with you.

Maraming salamat.

Title: Expanding Financial Inclusion through Islamic Finance
Occasion: Philippine Islamic Finance Roadshow
Speaker: BSP Governor Eli M. Remolona, Jr.
Transcription:
​

Introduction

His Excellency Dato’ Abdul Malik Melvin Castelino, Ambassador of Malaysia to the Philippines; His Excellency Agus Widjojo, Ambassador of Indonesia to the Philippines; fellow members of the Monetary Board — Ms. Rosalia V. De Leon, Mr. Romeo L. Bernardo, Mr. Walter C. Wassmer, and Mr. Jose L. Querubin; distinguished guests; colleagues and partners from the ADB (Asian Development Bank) and banking industry, good morning.

Today’s Islamic finance roadshow marks a significant step in the Philippines’ remarkable journey toward building a dynamic, inclusive, and globally competitive Islamic finance ecosystem. This event highlights the government’s deep commitment to expanding financial inclusion and providing opportunities for market players and investors in this very promising sector.

Vast potential of Islamic finance 

Since the enactment of the Islamic Banking Law in 2019, the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP), with support from the Asian Development Bank, has been fostering a regulatory environment conducive to the growth of the Islamic finance sector in the Philippines.

A recent market study underscores the sector’s vast untapped potential, particularly among underserved Muslim communities seeking Shari’ah-compliant financial services. Since the opening of the first Islamic bank in the country in 1973, the BSP has aspired to integrate Islamic banking into the broader financial system.

The last few years saw a frenzy of activity, and significant progress has been made. We now have tax neutrality regulations. We now have takaful guidelines. We now have Shari’ah-compliant deposit insurance. We now have the country’s first sovereign US dollar sukuk, and we look forward to peso sukuks and corporate peso sukuks. 

We now have the establishment of the Shari’ah Supervisory Board in the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao. We now have one Islamic bank licenses for two new Islamic banking windows and for two takaful operators. 

That is quite an achievement. Congratulations for a job well done. But we still have more work to do.

Our vision goes beyond inclusion. We see Islamic finance as a driver of sustainable economic growth. Moving forward, the BSP, in partnership with the ADB and other stakeholders, will continue to strengthen the ecosystem through education, capacity building, and infrastructure development.

Closing

In closing, all these milestones reaffirm our commitment to a competitive and sustainable Islamic finance ecosystem built on transparency, fairness, and collaboration. Together, we can make Islamic finance a transformative force that benefits more and more Filipinos and strengthens the national economy.

Maraming salamat po at mabuhay po kayo!
###

Title: Welcome Remarks for the 2024 BSP-IMF Systemic Risk Dialogue
Place: Crimson Resort and Spa Mactan, Cebu
Occasion: 2024 Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas-International Monetary Fund Systemic Risk Dialogue
Speaker: BSP Governor Eli M. Remolona, Jr.
Transcription:
​

Introduction

Maayong buntag!​

Senior officials from the region, my colleagues at the Monetary Board of the BSP (Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas), our partners from the private sector, global and local financial market practitioners, ranking officials from the IMF (International Monetary Fund) and other multilateral agencies, friends from the media, good morning.

It's my pleasure to welcome​​​​ all of you to Mactan Island in Cebu for this third systemic risk dialogue. This conference has traditionally been hosted by the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas and by the International Monetary Fund. It has always been our desire to be more inclusive, not only about the ideas we exchange, but also for the commitment of our region to engage and hold this event globally.

So, I would like to acknowledge the active participation of the Bank Indonesia in preparing for this year’s dialogue. We thank Governor Perry of the Bank Indonesia for agreeing to host the 2025 conference in Indonesia. We look forward to that.

Inclusivity and commitment in addressing systemic risk

We first came together for this conference in 2019. The intention was to shine light on systemic risk, and to talk about macroprudential policy. It still remains a frontier field. It’s nuanced because, borrowing from Aristotle, the whole is different from the sum of its parts. This year, we come together again to explore the many facets of systemic risk and its attendant macroprudential policy.

The non-bank financial sector has noticeably grown since the GFC (Global Financial Crisis). On one hand, this is welcome news because it addresses some of the concentration risks that arise from relying too much on the banking industry. On the other hand, financial markets are never an “either- or.” There is much diversity within non-bank financial institutions, just as there are inter linkages with non-banks and banks. In exchanging interlinkages, its opportunities and risks should be of great interest to regulators and practitioners.

Then there is technology. There is generative AI (Artificial Intelligence). It is an enabler for the non-bank financial market. It is something that banks have embraced. It is redefining the demands of the consumer.

Closing

To everyone in the panel of this dialogue, thank you very much for sharing with us your time. The organizers are grateful. We look forward to your insights and taking away the nuggets to drive us forward.

To our participants, we look forward to an engaging discussion. The expertise of our panelists speak for themselves. We should take full advantage of that, but it will be all better if you share your own thoughts on the issues. This is after all, a dialogue.

Thank you to the organizers from the IMF, the Bank Indonesia, and the BSP. I thank you for working through the many challenges. The fact that we are here in Mactan having this dialogue is a testament of your efforts and commitment. Maraming salamat po.

To all of us who have come all this way, some from Washington, DC, some from Sri Lanka, thank you for investing a part of yourselves to be here. I have been told there are about 170 individuals in this conference today. There's still a number of parties who wanted to join but we got to close the registration because of space limitations. 

With this record number of participants, how this dialogue will turn out—it really depends on our interaction. This is because this dialogue is itself a measure of the systemic and global nature of the financial system.

I look forward to the engaging discussions. Last night's dinner is a guide, and there's certainly much that lies ahead. 

Maraming salamat po at mabuhay tayong lahat.


###



​

Title: Enhancing Yield Curve Benchmarks
Occasion: Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas-Bankers Association of the Philippines Event on Enhancing Benchmarks for the Yield Curve
Speaker: BSP Governor Eli M. Remolona, Jr.
Transcription:
​

Introduction

TG Limcaoco, Paul Favila, other leaders of the banking community, BSP (Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas) colleagues, ladies and gentlemen, good afternoon. Magandang hapon po. 

Today marks a significant milestone in the development of the Philippine capital markets. As TG and Paul have explained, we are addressing the gaps--the devil in the details--in achieving a benchmark yield curve, the kind of curve that we need for a modern capital market. 

This has been quite a challenge but our bankers, BSP colleagues, and regulators are rising to the challenge.

Better transmission

For the BSP, a good benchmark yield curve will enhance the transmission of the monetary policy, particularly through the expectations channel. 

Our monetary policy now puts some emphasis on forward guidance. We try to convey to the markets what we think we are likely going to do moving forward, subject as always to new data. 

We also try to convey our sense of uncertainty surrounding the data and our own actions. The point of forward guidance is to guide market expectations of future interest rates and for these expectations to form a yield curve.

A benchmark yield curve is one that reflects through trading and hedging, a consensus of market participants. It can then serve as reliable basis for pricing loans, for investment strategies and fundraising. 

If this works, we will have strengthened the transmission mechanism for monetary policy.

Enhanced peso interest rate swap

So, congratulations to the Bankers Association of the Philippines for developing the enhanced Peso Interest Rate Swap. The BSP’s launch of the Variable Overnight Reverse Repurchase Rate will help lay the foundation for these swaps. 

I thank the 15 banks that are committing to make markets in these swaps and the five additional banks that will actively participate.

Why focus on interest rate swaps? As you know, the last few decades have seen roadmap after roadmap for developing the Philippine bond market. These roadmaps focused largely on the cash market for bonds. 

Unfortunately, they have failed to fully work. We were left with what I have characterized as a choppy yield curve with uneven liquidity, a yield curve that does not quite do its job of reconciling the different expectations of market participants.

This time we are focusing on a derivatives market—that of interest rate swaps. I am optimistic that this new strategy will work. 

This optimism stems partly from the experience of Europe. As you know, the Eurozone adopted a common currency in 2000. This meant a fragmented bond market, with separate German, Italian, and French bond markets. It was the euro interest rate swap that came to the rescue, providing a benchmark curve for the Eurozone as a whole. 

Closing

Indeed, globally, the turnover in interest swaps is now about three times the turnover in bond markets.  We look forward to joining this global transformation.

Once again, thank you to everyone who helped in these efforts. Your work inspires us to continue advancing capital market development for the benefit of Philippine banks, businesses, and Filipino families.

Maraming salamat po.

Title: Exploring the Bright Spots in Deepening Capital Markets
Place: Asian Development Bank Headquarters, Mandaluyong City
Occasion: Deepening Capital Markets through Expanding MSME Financing and Corporate Bonds for Small Issuers
Speaker: BSP Governor Eli M. Remolona, Jr.
Transcription:
​

I braved the traffic to come here because the topic is close to my heart. I have long expressed a desire to deepen our capital markets in the Philippines. I think Justine (Diokno-Sicat) has already explained the main issues relating to deepening capital markets. 

In the case of the central bank, it is driven by two of our mandates. We have the mandate for price stability and for financial stability. 

When it comes to price stability, deeper capital markets strengthen our transmission mechanism. Right now, when we move the policy rate, it takes about a year for the rate to have an effect. 

We want to do better than that. It helps to have a decent yield curve. 

When it comes to financial stability, as Justine explained, we want some kind of an Alan Greenspan “spare tire” when the banking system gets into trouble. We want investments that have access to some other sources of funds, and that would be the corporate bond market and the stock market. 

Now, I have good news and bad news. 

The good news is on Monday, we are going to launch the interest rate swap market, and the bankers here are all part of that. The interest rate swap market, we hope, will provide a good yield curve that will help in the pricing of bonds and even of mortgages-like instruments. 

In Europe, that was the case. When the eurozone switched to the euro, it left its way to a fragmented bond market. What emerged in Europe was a swaps market, which became the benchmark. And in time, the swap market served to enhance the whole market. It fosters the development of a yield curve. 

Right now, the best we have is the Bval (Bloomberg Valuation Service) curve, which is useful and relies on data, but it is still not good enough. It is a choppy curve and not really ideal for pricing.

I think good things will come out of the Monday launch. I am very optimistic about that. 

The bad news is we are still at the loss as what to do in the corporate bond market.

Let me describe the corporate bond market as it stands. 

It is kind of a Lake Wobegon market. Lake Wobegon is a fictional town in Minnesota where all the women are strong, all the men are good-looking, and all the children are above average. 

In our corporate bond market, most of the bonds are triple A. There are a few double A issues, but I think it helps to compare our market to Thailand. I looked up the new data as of August. The Philippine bond market is US$15 billion in outstanding amount of corporate bonds, while the Thai bond market is US$92 billion in outstanding. So, it is six times bigger than our corporate bond market.

More importantly, in our bond market, 95.8 percent of the issues are triple A, and there is 4 percent double A. So that is a place where all the men are good looking, and all the women are strong, I think. 

In Thailand, double A is 32 percent and single A is 55 percent. The bulk of the issues in Thailand are single A and a lot of triple B issues at 17 percent. Thailand makes us look bad. In fact, I think in November, the Bank of Thailand is sending us a team to explain to us how they were able to deepen their corporate bond market. 

I hope in this discussion today, we get better ideas for actionable policies to help deepen our capital markets. This will help us in our transmission mechanism and in our financial stability as well. 

Thank you very much. I look forward to the discussion.

###

​

Title: Message for the Outstanding BSP Stakeholders Appreciation Ceremonies
Place: MassKara Function Room, Citadines, Bacolod City
Occasion: Outstanding BSP Stakeholders Appreciation Ceremonies
Speaker: BSP Governor Eli M. Remolona, Jr.
