Title: The challenges we face at Bangko Sentral
Occasion: General Membership Meeting of the Financial Executives Institute of the Philippines
Speaker: BSP Governor Eli M. Remolona, Jr.
Transcription:
​

I want to talk today about the challenges we face at the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP) and begin with what is going on in our economy.

Economic prospects remain firm

We saw in 2023, a 5.6-percent GDP [gross domestic product] growth. That is pretty good. We are still the fastest-growing economy in the fastest-growing region of the world.

As you know, Europe basically had zero growth, the US [United States] maybe 3.0 percent, which is remarkably strong, stronger than expected. China, our next biggest trading partner, perhaps maybe at 5.0 percent. It looks strong, but that is very low compared to what used to be 9.7 percent over 15 years. So, China is a very different economy now from what it used to be.

Unemployment is down to 3.1 percent, which is also pretty good. So, thanks to our economic managers, I think we are doing well.

On the monetary side, we have raised the monetary policy rate by 450 basis points in the face of a very high inflation rate. And that seems to have worked.

Our inflation rate peaked at 8.7 percent in January 2023 and is now down to 3.4 percent, which is within our target range for inflation. I think those are good, reassuring numbers. But I would say it is still too soon to declare victory.

If you look at our forecast for inflation for this year, the average is hovering near the edge of our forecast range, around 3.9 percent. We hope it will drop to 3.5 percent next year.

So, 3.9 percent is just within our target range. But there are upside risks. If you look at what we consider to be the average probability of our inflation rate exceeding our target range for 2024, the probability is over 50 percent. That is not good enough.

The upside risks are mainly electricity rates, transport charges, and higher oil prices. There are some downside risks, but the government is making strenuous efforts to mitigate the impact of El Niño mainly through drought-resistant seeds.

So, we are hoping that will work.

That is what is going on in the inflation front. Our number one mandate is to stabilize prices, keeping inflation within the target range of two to four percent.

The good news is that our banks are doing well. Suppose you look at the regulatory numbers. Our what we call the capital adequacy ratio is at 16.4 percent. The regulatory standard or the regulatory floor is 10 percent. So, we are well above the regulatory floor regarding capital.

When it comes to liquidity, 183 percent. The liquidity we are measuring here is the LCR or the liquidity coverage ratio. The regulatory standard is 100 percent. Loans have been growing briskly, 9.8 percent, and the NPL [non-performing loans] is manageable at 3.2 percent.

So, the banks are okay. So, the banks should be able to finance growth.

So, that is where we stand.

Let me now go on to talk about what challenges we face.

Conducting monetary policy in a supply-shock economy

We are facing the challenge of monetary policy in what has become a supply-shock economy. Our economy has been subject to more supply shocks than in the past, which is very unusual.

We also aspire to help digitalize the banking and payment system. We will talk about that in a little bit. We also aspire to help deepen the capital markets with your help.

So, I hope to discuss some issues related to deepening the capital market.

Let me say about how we are doing monetary policy these days. As you know, we got hit by oil price shocks, food price shocks, and fertilizer price shocks.

Globally, inflation peaked in 2022. Our inflation rate peaked in January 2023 at 8.7 percent—the highest in 14 years. As I have said, we are down to 3.4 percent, partly because of the monetary policy.

The difference between the economy we now have and the economy we used to have is the dominance of supply shocks hitting us. What happens, I think, in our analysis of the supply shocks is that supply shocks lead to inflation expectations. The oil price goes up, people think other prices will also go up because oil, of course, is an input to the production of many things, and so prices go up for those other things.

We call those things second-round effects.

So, the main effect is oil price shock, which leads to  second-round effects. The thing about  second-round effects is that they are asymmetric. So, the oil price will come down, but the second-round effects do not. They are sticky downwards, so it is asymmetric. And that is what we worry about.​

This means we cannot just look through supply shocks. We have to worry about supply shocks because of the asymmetry of second-round effects.

What helps us is our framework for inflation targeting. We decided to target inflation so it stays within two to four percent. We made ourselves an inflation-targeting central bank.

That helps because it anchors expectations. So, when you have supply shocks, inflation expectations do not go crazy. They are kind of sticky as well. That anchoring has been a big help to our monetary policy.

Once you have a well-anchored inflation, you can more easily manage second-round effects.

We worry about whether inflation will remain well-anchored. So, we have estimates of the risks of the anchoring and worry about them de-anchoring every time we meet as a Monetary Board.  

So, that is the new monetary policy strategy or the new monetary policy framework that we follow.​

Digitalizing the banking and payments system

We also aspire to digitalize the financial system. We have four initiatives or four pathways to that end.

One is called the Open Finance Framework. If you are a well-established bank, you would be participating in this. If you are BPI [Bank of the Philippine Islands], BDO, or Metrobank, you will be part of the Open Finance Framework.

Open finance means working with application programming interfaces (APIs). These platforms connect you to other financial services and connect your customers to other financial services. Then, you have to figure out how to integrate that platform into your system.

But banks now are working with 50 [to] 100 APIs doing many different things.

Our role here is to make sure that when you use your customers' data, you use it with their permission. They still own the data; you do not own that data. Your customers own their data and want to ensure that when you use that data with APIs or other platforms, you get their permission first, and then you can do whatever you like.

You could also do digital banking. This means you raise deposits online and make loans online. The first part is easy; the second part is not so easy. In our culture, apparently, you need a human being to collect on loans, but nonetheless, we are hoping digital banks can figure this out. And a couple of them are figuring it out.

They are six now. We are limiting the number of digital banks to six licenses, but we are looking very closely at the industry and are going to decide if we are going to open it up again. Maybe we can attract different business models and make the industry more exciting.

We also have a regulatory sandbox. The regulatory sandbox means you try your innovation, do a proof of concept, and do a pilot, but when you do that, you work with a regulator.

The regulator is there to help you and tell you what the regulatory implications might be if you succeed. We are not there to judge whether you will succeed or not. We are just there to help you. If you grow, you know what you are getting into regarding regulations. It is about minimizing regulatory uncertainty. If you have a new idea, enter a sandbox. We will assign you a regulator. We will scold you, oh bawal 'yan, but that is for your own good.

Then, of course, there is generative AI [artificial intelligence]. That is inevitable.

If you have used ChatGPT, you know how irresistible it is.

So, we do not even have to encourage it. You guys will do it without any encouragement, but of course, we have to think of guard rails for generative AI.

As you know, generative AI leads to what we call hallucinations; it imagines things that never happened. It leads to herding; it gives the same answer to different questions.

So, we think that, for now, at least, when using generative AI, a human being should work with it and look at the answers before you decide. Apparently, it is not so hard to tell whether the answers are wrong.

If you teach at Ateneo or SMU and take a take-home exam, you are almost sure the student will use AI. A student who does not use AI is not a good student.

But apparently, it is easy to tell. When the homework comes in, you look at it, and you will know whether AI is used. The point is to use AI so that you will have reasonable answers, good answers, not just ones generated by the computer.

So, that is what we are trying to do with digitalizing the economy and the financial system.

On top of these things, we are promoting a digital payment system that serves the unbanked.

So, here, you can start with an e-wallet or a basic deposit account. A simplified deposit account is supposed to be easy to open for anyone.

We hope this will lead to people joining the formal financial system. They will have access to bank credit, other financial services, and eventually the whole financial ecosystem—access to investment instruments, access to the right kind of insurance, and so on.

That, in general, is what we are doing, and the guy in charge of that is [BSP] Deputy Governor Mert Tangonan. So, he is the guy to ask questions about digital payments.

One thing we are doing regarding cross-border retail digital payments is the Project Nexus. It is a project by the ASEAN [Association of Southeast Asian Nations] central banks. If you have a fast payment system like InstaPay, you can connect to Nexus, which is the case for ASEAN. Singapore has it, Indonesia has it, and Malaysia has it. ASEAN central banks or economies will all be connected to Nexus. We think Nexus will be operational in 2026, and this will allow remittances to come to the Philippines at no more than 3.0 percent. The nice thing about Nexus is it is designed to be completely scalable. In other words, you can connect to a country with a fast payment system.

Unfortunately, the US [United States] does not have a fast payment system yet, so hindi pa konektado ang US, but once they have it, they can connect. Brazil can connect now, and India can connect now. And I think other countries can soon connect.

Deepening the capital markets

Let me now turn to capital markets.

As you know, we have a lot to do in capital markets. But I thought as a central bank, we could focus on just three things.

First, an excellent, reliable benchmark yield curve. If you look at the existing yield curve, the BVAL [Bloomberg Valuation Service] curve, it is a choppy yield curve.

As you know, there are kinks in the curve, and the kinks are very strange because if there is a kink, it is so easy to arbitrage. You take positions on both sides of the kink, and then an arbitrage trade makes you money very quickly. But somehow, the kinks do not go away.

There may be a lack of liquidity in the yield curve. Maybe because we have been too ambitious, we designate market makers at several maturities. I think five maturities are where market makers should provide a reasonable bid-ask spread. That has not worked; bid-ask spreads have remained very wide, reflecting the lack of liquidity.

I think my proposal – and I would like to discuss with you - is do what Europe did. In Europe, when the eurozone was starting, government markets were fragmented. So, without any government initiative and without any central bank taking the lead, the swaps curve emerged as the benchmark curve.

Maybe that is the way to do it now. Use the swaps curve. You are not as exposed to price changes as you would be if you were holding government securities because swaps, as you know, are just net payments between the fixed rate and the floating rate.

If we have a swaps curve, maybe you need to make markets, perhaps in just one maturity, the five-year. Maybe that will be good enough. Somehow, this has not happened; the short end still seems problematic. We do not have a good repo [repurchase] market to tie down the short end.

I do not understand what the reason is because we have the GMRA [Global Master Repurchase Agreement], which is supposed to be so simple and so acceptable that the whole world will use it. Somehow, it has not worked here

So, I would like to revive the swaps market, the IRS [interest rate swaps] market, and insist on the market making at least the five-year maturity—which is the sweet spot for fixed-income securities, corporate bonds, and derivative contracts.​

So, maybe that will work. I welcome your advice on this.

Then, we have what I call our Lake Wobegon corporate bond market. Those of you who are old enough might have heard of Garrison Keillor. Lake Wobegon is a fictional town in Minnesota, and he said in Lake Wobegon, all the women are strong, all the men are good-looking, and all the children are above average. That sounds like a good description of our corporate bond market. All the issues are triple-A. A few double A issues but no single A, no triple B. How come it becomes so hard to be an issuer of single A or triple B?

Other countries have done it. In Thailand, the median issue is single-A. So, I do not know why it is so hard for a potentially lower issuer to join the corporate bond market.

And finally, we have our missing portfolio flows. We used to fear portfolio flows because we saw them as hot money. They come in and leave at the first sign of trouble.

But these days, they are not so scary. In the first place, they are so negligible these days; they can come in and out, and it will not matter.

But the big thing is the game has changed; the intent is not into active investment anymore; it is in passive investment. Passive means you buy the index. At least at the core of your portfolio, you need an index. Maybe you can play around on the sides of your portfolio, but the core has to be an index.

Huge trillions of dollars are now flowing into the major equity indices, global equity indices, and the major primary bond indices. I think we are in a few indices. We talked to Vanguard, and they said we are about 0.1 percent of their bond index.

But we are not in any major equity indices, BlackRock or State Street. We do not know why; people say it is our withholding taxes, but we are not sure what is going on.

Bakit hindi tayo kasali? The smaller markets are in these indices. Colombia is in that index. Etsepuwera tayo, hindi tayo kasali. I do not know why they do not like us.​

So, there it is. Those are my questions.

So, I have three wishes for the capital market: Build a benchmark curve, maybe using the swaps curve. Let us open the corporate bond market—single A, triple B, all investment grade onshore. Then, join the global shift to equity index in emerging market bond ETF [exchange-traded funds].

By the way, the indices are actively traded as exchange-traded funds. So, those are my three wishes, and I hope you guys can help us.

Maraming salamat po!

Title: Message during the Release of the 2023 Financial Stability Report
Occasion: Release of the 2023 Financial Stability Report
Speaker: BSP Governor Eli M. Remolona, Jr.
Transcription:
​Introduction

Magandang umaga sa inyong lahat!

I thank everyone for making time to join us here in the BSP [Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas] on a Tuesday morning.

Tomorrow is Valentine’s Day, and we will speak about love and roses!

But today, let me talk about the danger of rosy scenarios.

Today, we present to you our 2023 Financial Stability Report (FSR)—an FSCC [Financial Stability Coordination Council] communication tool for managing systemic risk. 

What is our FSR? It is a report published at least annually, pieced together from the collective wisdom of the FSCC, from suggestions by the BSP’s Monetary Board and the FSCC agency-offices, and from inputs from other participants of our financial system.

The reason for the FSR is that we want to communicate to participants of the financial system to help them make better-informed decisions, and maybe tell us what we may have missed. 

The challenge is that systemic risk is inherently difficult to comprehend. Markets are fluid, and things can change very quickly. Some risks arise from our own markets and some risks in foreign markets can spill over onto our shores.

The risks that are of the biggest concern are those that are brewing in out-of-sight vulnerabilities, risks that turn out to be contagious and to lead to broader dislocations.

You have heard of "black swans" indicating highly unlikely surprises or "the butterfly effect" to describe how small things can lead to far-reaching consequences. 

These are the things we worry about.

Indeed, financial market participants often make risky investments based on rosy scenarios.

The more widely shared the scenario, the more dangerous it is. When something goes wrong in these scenarios, it sometimes leads to mass panic. There is a rush for the exits, causing massive investments to collapse.

This is no idle theory.

In 1993, the World Bank published a volume called The East Asian Miracle. It told a rosy scenario about our neighbors, including Indonesia, Malaysia, Thailand, and South Korea.

International investors bought the story. They bought it lock, stock and barrel. 

The World Bank was nice enough not to include the Philippines in its East Asian Miracle. Yet, somehow, we did not escape the rosy scenario, Nadamay pa rin tayo. 

In 1995, the Metro Pacific Group, along with a consortium of international investors, submitted the winning bid for Fort Bonifacio. The bid was US$1.6 billion. It was called "the property deal of the decade."

We all know what happened next. In July 1997, we saw the sudden onset of the Asian crisis. All around the region, currencies and stock markets plunged. Massive loans went unpaid, property prices collapsed, and tall buildings languished unfinished. The whole region went into recession.

We remember the crisis, but we often forget the rosy scenario that led to it. This FSR is about reminding us about the dangers of the rosy scenario and identifying the possible channels of contagion. 

We purposely wrote our FSR so that it is not a technical report crowded with fancy equations.  Instead, we wrote it as a thematic narrative that tries to unearth the risks beneath the rosy scenarios. We provide a view of the macroeconomy and the financial markets from the perspective of systemic risk. We present the headline numbers and how they might interact with one another. 

This particular FSR takes a very institutional-level focus and makes an assessment of how capital markets may play a greater role in the resilience of the Philippine economy. 

So, I invite everyone to download a copy and parse through the pages of the 2023 Financial Stability Report. Read about the risks we see and our planned courses of action. 

Let us know what you think, and we are more than happy to engage.

Join us in navigating the financial stability journey together.

Marami pong salamat at mabuhay tayong lahat!

Title: Message for the Ceremonial Signing of Revised Memorandum of Agreement on Information Exchange
Occasion: Ceremonial Signing of Revised Memorandum of Agreement on Information Exchange
Speaker: BSP Governor Eli M. Remolona, Jr.
Transcription:
​

Introduction​

Magandang hapon po.

This is a very important occasion, and I am pleased to be part of it.

We are here to celebrate the conclusion of the revised Memorandum of Agreement or MOA on Information Exchange between the BSP [Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas] and PDIC [Philippine Deposit Insurance Corporation].

This is important because the deposit contract is a very strange contract.

If you are a depositor, you either get your money back or you do not.

This means the biggest risk for banks is the deposit run. And our biggest tool against that risk is deposit insurance.

Now, over the years, things have changed. The environment has changed for deposits.

The last amendment to this agreement took place in 2004. I think we are still recovering from the Asian [financial] crisis. This was followed by the global [financial] crisis in 2008.

And these crises are reasons for change. So, it is timely that we revise our [agreement on] information exchange.

When I say things have changed, one thing that has changed was in 2014 [when] we adopted Basel III. Now we have capital adequacy ratios [and] liquidity coverage ratios. ​

But more than that, I think the culture has changed in terms of regulation, both by the PDIC and the BSP.

We have moved from a very prescriptive examination and supervision style to a more risk-based and more principles-based approach.

We do not tell banks specifically what to do. We tell banks to take risks seriously, and that is the reason for all these regulatory standards.

Because of these changes, we need a new kind of agreement for information exchange.

I extend my gratitude to all those who worked hard in the development of this agreement.

I appreciate the thoughtful deliberation made by the team to ensure that this agreement is comprehensive and that all the information that needs to be shared falls within the revised MOA.

The MOA also covers information that supports other functional departments of the BSP such as legal services, economic statistics, as well as loans and credit.​​

As we move forward, let us remember that the success of this collaboration will depend on the effective information [and] implementation of this agreement.

I enjoin everyone as stewards of this revised MOA who have joined us today to follow through on your commitments to keeping the revised MOA updated, relevant, and operational in pursuit of our primary objective of promoting financial system stability.

Mabuhay po tayong lahat!

Title: Capital Market Development
Place: Manila Golf and Country Club, Makati City
Occasion: Fellows Meeting of the Foundation for Economic Freedom
Speaker: BSP Governor Eli M. Remolona, Jr.
Transcription:
​

Magandang gabi sa inyong lahat.

 
Thank you, Vaughn, for that generous introduction. The secrets that he revealed, I deny them all.

It is wonderful to be here. I think I am still a member of FEF [Foundation for Economic Freedom]. I follow your discussions on Viber. So, I decided maybe I will talk about something I have not seen on Viber, and maybe I can get some help from you guys.

A deeper capital market

I want to talk about deepening capital markets.

As you know, over the years, there have been roadmap after roadmap, on how to deepen our capital markets.

In the 1990s, the IMF would borrow me from the New York Fed [Federal Reserve of New York]. I would come here to see how to deepen capital markets.

But so far, there is still much to be done. So, maybe we could try harder.

From the point of view of the central bank—there are two reasons why we would care about capital markets.

First, we need the capital markets to strengthen the transmission mechanism of monetary policy. I will explain a little bit about that.

And then, there is also the Greenspan reason, which is to diversify the sources of financing for our economy, for our investment, and for our businesses.

So, let me start with the transmission mechanism.

As you know, the policy rate that we have, the overnight RRP (reverse repurchase rate), is an overnight rate.

An overnight rate does not affect too many economic decisions. Maybe a one-year rate that would affect credit and consumer decisions. A five-year rate might affect mortgages and other business investments.

The way it works now is we have a policy rate, and then that vaguely affects expectations of what the policy rate might be in the future.

These vague expectations would lead to maybe changes in asset prices, but we do not know the mechanism exactly because we do not see it.

What has happened in the last few years — especially since 2008 and when we had a global fund crisis - the emphasis has become forward guidance instead of just the policy rate itself.

The nice thing about forward guidance is it directly affects expectations. You can actually see it happen. You give the forward guidance today—2:00, [at] 2:15, you will see the yield curve move. So, it is a very strong mechanism.

In fact, it is a stronger mechanism than just the policy rate. The forward guidance itself is a very powerful tool.

We would like to have the same tool in the Philippines. And what we want to affect especially is the yield curve, but it would affect other asset prices.

Spare tire

When it comes to the risk management of the financial system as a whole, let me quote from Alan Greenspan. In the wake of the Asian Crisis he said, “This leads one to wonder how severe East Asia's problems would have been…had those economies not relied so heavily on banks as their means of financial intermediation…Had a functioning capital market existed, the outcome might well have been far more benign."

In academic circles, this is called the Greenspan's spare tire. You need a spare tire for the banking system, and that spare tire would be the capital market.

Regional picture

Our neighbors have taken this to heart, and they have developed their capital markets. And we are still here with the same capital market that we had 30 years ago.

Let me divide this up. If you look at stock markets as a percent of GDP [gross domestic product], you can see Thailand, South Korea, and Malaysia have bigger markets than us in terms of ratio to GDP.

Corporate bond markets are the same thing. South Korea, Malaysia, [and] Thailand have bigger bond markets than we do.

So here are the questions. I would like to talk a little bit about our choppy yield curve and then talk about what I call our Lake Wobegon corporate bond market, and then finally talk about our missing portfolio flows.

Let me start with the yield curve and how we would build a benchmark yield curve. The yield curve that we use now is called BVAL [Bloomberg Valuation Service]; it is constructed for us by Bloomberg, doing the best it can with the data that is available.  

The orange line is what the BVAL curve looks like as of [January] 26th.

As you notice, the curve kinks. If it were a liquid market, there would be no kicks because it is so easy, I think, [for] most of you guys, especially the bankers among you, to take positions in two neighboring maturities, and then you will make money just by selling the one with the maturity with the spike and then buy the neighboring bonds.

So, I have to think that the bankers among you can do something similar.

You would use the smoother curve that you get when you do the right kind of arbitrage. But then, if that is what you do, you do not know how well our transmission mechanism is working.

 

Interest rate swaps

But I think we can think about… using the swaps curve. This is the experience in the Euro area, around 2000-2010.

Because of a fragmented market, they turned to the swaps market. And interest rate swaps are so easy. This contract is by far the largest over-the-counter derivative contract in the world.

When we last looked at it, it was US$440 trillion. It is so easy to use that one wonders why it is not well used in the Philippines.

Some people say it is the contracts—the master agreements that we have. You know the GMRA [Global Master Repurchase Agreement] contract, or the short end of the curve, the repo [repurchase] contract was designed to be so simple and so easy to use.

The swaps contract itself is the master agreement. Again, it is very simple, designed to be widely accepted, but somehow, not in the Philippines.

What I propose—please let me know what you think—is we use the 5-year swaps contract. It is the sweet spot for interest rates: one benchmark, one maturity using the swaps contract.

Japan, for example, has only one benchmark, the 10-year JGB [Japanese Government Bond]. So, I think, especially for a market like ours, one maturity should be enough.

So, I would like comments on that.

The next issue for me is what I call our Lake Wobegon corporate bond market. Those of you who are old enough might remember Garrison Keillor. He used to talk about Lake Wobegon—a fictional town in Minnesota, and he said, “All the women are strong, all the men are good-looking, and all the children are above average."

I think that applies to our corporate bond market. In our corporate bond market, virtually all of the issues are AAA. A few issues are AA but no A, no BBB.

Now, if you look at the graph, the pie chart on the left is the Philippines, the blue slice is the triple A, and the gray slice is AA.

So, very highly rated bonds.

If you look at the Thai corporate bond market, the brown slice is A, and then the yellow slice is BBB.

So, their market gives access to lower-rated issuers, which we seek not to be able to manage. Maybe, PhilGuarantee can help with this.

As you know, in the 1980s, there was a dude named Michael Milken who was known as the “junk bond king."

In the 1980s, he worked with Drexel Burnham Lambert to put together a large network of investors in high-yield bonds. This allowed him to raise vast amounts of money for leveraged buyout firms.

And today, because of Michael Milken, the median bond issue in the United States corporate bond market is non-investment grade, it is BB.

So that is quite an achievement I think, for Michael Milken. Eventually, he went to jail for fraud, but that is not part of his life we can learn from.

Hot money

The third issue I think I would like to bring to you is portfolio inflows.

We are scared of portfolio inflows because it is hot money.

This is from a newspaper just last Monday, US$247 million leaving the Philippines, mainly portfolio outflows. It looks like a scary headline, but US$247 million is nothing. It is negligible relative to things like remittances, things like BPO [business process outsourcing] revenues.

If you look at the data, here I will show you the data for our neighbors including ourselves. This is relative to GDP. Blue is the Philippines, yellow is Malaysia, gray is Thailand, orange is South Korea, and green is Indonesia.

As you can see, we have some of the smaller portfolio inflows. There is still something like hot money; they come in and out, but it is very small for the Philippines.

The good news is that the investing game has changed. It is now all about passive investing. 

A long time ago in the 1960s, two other dudes, Harry Markowitz and William Sharpe, wrote papers that said, what you must do is diversify. Buy the whole market, buy the market portfolio.

Of course, these days, you want your core portfolio to be the market portfolio, and then you can play around, if you are smart enough, to play around with the stock-taking. But your core portfolio must be the diversified market portfolio.

Around 2008, investors finally saw the insights of William Sharpe and Harry Markowitz, 20 years after they won the Nobel prize for this.

So, passive investing became the mode for investing in capital markets. These days, the way you do passive investing is to buy an index. An index of the market, or you buy an index of a sector of the market.

Bonds, equities, you do the same thing. You do passive investing.

Exchange-traded fund

Now, the world has introduced index funds that are traded as ETF [exchange traded fund], global ETF.

When an ETF invests in the Philippines, it is not hot money because it is the whole index. To get out of the Philippines, you have to sell the whole index. So, it is not hot money.

The big three are Vanguard, BlackRock, and State Street. As you know, they manage the biggest exchange-traded funds.

In fact, between the three of them, they owned 90 percent of the S&P 500.

We are not included in these ETFs. We are not part of the index. We are excluded from the index. But other countries are in the index: Colombia, India, you name it.

Bakit wala tayo? Bakit hindi tayo makasali? What is wrong with us? Why do they not like us?

The top three emerging market bond funds for ETFs are managed by JP Morgan, Barclays, and Invesco.

Again, we are not in their indices. We are just not included. I do not know why.

And you know, there are smaller markets than us, and yet those markets are included, and we are not.

So, let me end by saying, by the way, Larry Fink—the CEO [chief executive officer] of BlackRock, is a friendly dude, so some of you should talk to him and ask how come we are not in the BlackRock index?

So, I have three wishes. We want to build a good benchmark yield curve. Then, we want to open the corporate bond market to A and BBB borrowers. And then, we want to join that global shift to equity index and emerging market bond ETFs.

Maraming salamat po.

Title: Opening Remarks for the Workshop on Nature, Macroeconomy, and Finance
Occasion: Workshop on Nature, Macroeconomy, and Finance
Speaker: BSP Governor Eli M. Remolona, Jr.
Transcription:
​

Introduction

Good morning, everyone. ​

In a larger sense, this morning has been too nice. I took my usual walk this morning, and I said to myself, ang sarap naman, hindi mainit. There was a nice cool breeze. Just perfect for a morning walk. And it was misleadingly perfect because I think it allows us to be complacent about climate change.

In 2015, when Mark Carney was still governor of the Bank of England, he warned about the tragedy over the horizon. He said, once climate change becomes a defining issue for financial stability, it may already be too late.

Climate change

At some point, maybe in the 2030s, we might reach tipping points. There are thresholds where the effects of climate change, accelerate and become irreversible.

At those points, there might be very little we can do. These tipping points include the melting of the ice sheets near the North Pole, the melting of the ice sheets near the South Pole, the melting of the permafrost—the frozen layers near the surface of the earth, the destruction of coral reefs in the warmer parts of the ocean, and the collapse of ocean currents in the North Atlantic.

So, workshops like this are a matter of urgency. I welcome this two-day international workshop on nature, macroeconomy, and finance.

Thank you to our co-organizers, the London School of Economics and Political Science (LSE), the Grantham Research Institute on Climate Change and the Environment, [and the] International Network for Sustainable International Policy Insights, Research, and Exchange (INSPIRE).

We are pleased to host this event in the BSP [Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas], following similar workshops in Singapore, Indonesia, and Malaysia.

The objective of this workshop is to understand the impact and dependencies of nature and ecosystem services on the macroeconomy and financial sector.

We will discuss the opportunities, financial risks, and policy challenges from the perspective of emerging market economies.

Today, the global economy faces urgent risks due to the degradation of nature, particularly through economic activities such as deforestation and land use change. These will have significant macroeconomic implications.

In 2009, we saw the destruction brought by Ondoy. In climate change, we might expect more and more typhoons like Ondoy.

For our part, our mandate is to contribute to the stability of the financial system. We have to monitor the buildup of environmental risks through our supervised financial institutions.

We are working with other member agencies, regional counterparts, and international networks to help us create a network for the financial system to manage environment-related opportunities.

We are constructing a taxonomy that will apply to the activities and assets of financial institutions. ​

This taxonomy will be the framework for classification and can be the basis for initially disclosure, and potentially for incentives like the assignment of risk weights and, eventually, a basis for a carbon trading. So, we are working on that.

Preliminary research on environment-related risks shows that big banks face international risks, primarily for extreme weather events, through their exposure to the agricultural sector and residential mortgages.

As a result, we have been building our capacity to conduct analysis and research, introduce nature-related risks, and how they will affect the structure of the economy and their implications for financial stability.

Conclusion

So, let me thank the speakers who took the time to share their expertise in this field, participants from different departments of the BSP, our partner and government agencies, and supervised banks.

Thank you again to the LSE group, Dr. Simon Dikau, Elena Almeida, and Thessa Vasudhevan, the World Wildlife Fund, and the INSPIRE group for bringing this workshop to the BSP and contributing to the current discussions on nature and biodiversity laws.

As we delve deeper into this topic, it is useful to keep in mind the words of John Muir, a Scottish-born nationalist. He said, “When you try to pick out anything by itself, we find it hitched to everything else in the universe."

This means working together to understand better the dynamics and solutions that benefit our economies and planet. ​

Thank you, maraming salamat po, mabuhay tayong lahat.

Title: Message for the Annual Reception for the Banking Community
Occasion: Annual Reception for the Banking Community
Speaker: BSP Governor Eli M. Remolona, Jr.
Transcription:
​Introduction

Magandang gabi.

I am so glad the weather cooperated.

Former central bank governors, members of the Monetary Board, colleagues and friends from the banking and diplomatic community, fellow government officers, ladies and gentlemen, a pleasant good evening to all of you. 

On behalf of the Monetary Board, I'd like to thank you all for gracing the 2024 annual reception for the banking community within these walls of Fort San Antonio Abad.

I am especially delighted to join you in this yearly tradition because tonight's celebration is a very special one. This year marks 75 years of central banking in the Philippines. 

It is fitting that we gather here at Fort Antonio Abad. This fort, together with Intramuros, was designated a national cultural treasure by the National Museum of the Philippines.

It played a significant part of the history of Manila and similar to this fort, the BSP [Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas] has come a long way as a central bank from its inauguration on January 3, 1949. 

Due to the leadership of visionaries who recognized that the BSP must change with the times and the painstaking efforts of the men and women of the BSP who made this happen, we are all here today.

The BSP started as a central monetary authority in 1949. It later assumed the responsibility for regulating the financial system.

And then in 2019, we were able to inscribe in our charter our three fundamental mandates, maintaining price stability; financial stability; and a safe and efficient payments and settlement system. 

Through all these years, the BSP has managed to be a source of stability for the economy.

We are not resting on our accomplishments. We deeply feel that we still have work to do.

Indeed, we have outlined a reform agenda. It is an ambitious agenda, and we will need your help for most of it.

Four goals

Let me just mention four goals in this agenda.

First, we want to further enhance our monetary policy framework by sharpening our research, our model, and non-monetary tools. 

We want these to be more responsive to inflation pressures, particularly during periods of unusual and large supply shocks. 

So far, the BSP managed to anchor inflation expectations and thus, effectively control second-round effects. 

Through our inflation-targeting framework, headline inflation has gone down to 3.9 percent as of December 2023, from a high of 8.7 percent in January 2023.

Second, we will strengthen the way we conduct systemic risk oversight. You saw what happened in March 2023 with Silicon Valley Bank and Credit Suisse. We don't want this to happen to us. 

And for now, the banking system remains healthy, characterized by strong balance sheets, profitable operations, and sound performance indicators. 

The banking system likewise stood firm and proved its true resilience through the pandemic and through the international disruptions of March 2023. 

Third, the BSP financial stability mandates also carry with it the responsibility to deepen our capital markets. 

This is meant to diversify the sources of funds in our financial system so that our businesses and our investments do not have to rely entirely on the banking system in case there is a credit crunch.

Fourth, we will strive to make the BSP sustainability initiative more meaningful by infusing it with an inclusion perspective. 

We want to ensure that the entire financial system supports an inclusive adaptation program so that the burden of transition does not fall on the most vulnerable segments of our society. 

Parallel to this, the BSP is harnessing digital technology to empower sectors which have been traditionally underbanked. 

We think our open financial framework will unlock opportunities for consumers. 

The BSP has been relentless in bringing our Paleng-QR Ph Plus Program to various parts of the country, giving market vendors, public transport drivers, and other merchants a more convenient way of accepting e-payments for their transactions.

Conclusion

So, the BSP has accomplished a lot in the last 75 years. 

None of these would have happened without the help of various stakeholders present here today. 

To the past members of the BSP Monetary Board and BSP officers, we salute you for helping shape the BSP into the world-class organization that it is today.

Meanwhile, I hope that through the initiatives which we will put into play in collaboration with the banking industry, the BSP will be able to contribute to a brighter and better future for our countrymen. 

To officially cap this evening, let me now call on my fellow Monetary Board Members (MBM) to please join me on stage for the ceremonial toast, MBM Bruce Tolentino, MBM Anita Aquino, MBM. Rosalia de Leon. MBM. Romeo Bernardo, and MBM Benjamin Diokno.

Mabuhay po tayong lahat and enjoy the evening.

Title: Remarks for the 22nd Weekly Membership Meeting of the Rotary Club of Manila and Makati
Occasion: 22nd Weekly Membership Meeting of the Rotary Club of Manila and Makati
Speaker: BSP Governor Eli M. Remolona, Jr.
Transcription:
​I am very happy to be here. I just realized from the beginning of the program that it will be very hard for me to become a member of the Rotary Club because, as it is well known in the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP), the Governor is sintunado.

Three challenges
 
I will talk about three challenges that we face in the Bangko Sentral. I do not know if you can show the slides, but we have three things over which we do things in the Bangko Sentral. The first thing is how to conduct monetary policy in what we call a “supply-shock economy." As you know, the world was hit by an unusual combination of supply shocks, especially in 2022.

We, ourselves, we are hit by those things. In fact, we are the harder-hit economies when it comes to supply shocks.
So, I will talk about that—how you do monetary policy in the face of those kinds of shocks. And then, I want to talk about digitalizing the banking system. One of our mandates is to maintain financial stability, but I feel—and the BSP feels—that part of maintaining stability is also to keep up with technological trends, especially within the banking system.

And then, I want to talk about the payments system. The challenge in the payments system for us now is how to use [it] as a gateway for financial inclusion so that we get more and more kababayans to become part of the formal financial system.

So, those are the three things I would like to talk about, and I would welcome any questions on these things.

Supply shocks

As I said, we were hit by supply shocks, the likes of which we have never seen before. There are shocks in oil; they were in food; they were in fertilizer; and they were not just large shocks, but they came with a high degree of frequency. This part of it is unusual.

Globally, inflation rates rose to levels that have not been seen in decades. In our case, the inflation rates that we face reached their highest peak in 14 years in January of 2023. So, the inflation rate at that time was 8.7 percent. Since then, we have brought it down to 4.1 percent. So, my discussion is how we did that.

Now, among observers, we are told that the supply shocks, you can just ignore it. You can just look through it and pretend it was not there because anyway, those shocks will dissipate. If the price goes up, it will come down. So, why bother tightening the monetary policy?

That is actually a debate in academic circles, but among central banks, we have settled the debate. We know what to do in the face of those supply shocks. I will show you the graph of inflation.

Blue is the headline inflation; this includes everything. And then, orange is core inflation; this is when you take food and energy out of the CPI [consumer price index]. The difference between the two is the consequence of supply shocks. I do not know if you notice, but when supply shocks go up, even the core goes up.

And then, when supply shocks dissipate, the core stays up for a while. That is very important to know because that means you cannot just look through supply shocks.

What happens in our experience from our statistical work is that supply shocks lead to a kind of inflation expectation that leads to second-round effects.

So, other things go up; wages go up; transportation fares go up; and then, some of the things that go up with supply shocks do not come down.

So, the supply shocks come down; the price of oil comes down; and the price of food comes down; but then, the second-round effects do not come down. Monetary policy has to do something about that, and that is the reason we have to tighten the monetary policy in the face of supply shocks.

This is challenging because this is a new phenomenon. We have models. We have statistics that are not calibrated to this phenomenon. So, we use the models, but we use a lot of judgment. And, I think, somehow, things have worked.

So, supply shocks lead to inflation expectations that lead to second-round effects. What we do in the face of that phenomenon is rely on our inflation target.

It is fortunate that we are a central bank that is an inflation-targeting central bank. That means we say, we announce to everybody that we target inflation rates so that they stay within 2.0 percent and 4.0 percent.

That is a big help. Because of those targets, we are able to anchor expectations. Otherwise, expectations may get out of control, and you get very large second-round effects.

By being able to anchor inflation expectations, we are able to manage the second-round effects. So, that is our strategy. That is monetary policy strategy in what we call a “supply-shock economy." So, that seems to be working. On Friday, the next inflation number will come out, and we are crossing our fingers that it will be a good number. But that is where we are.

By the way, people say that we are tightening too much. That is a very difficult challenge because we want to make sure that we do not tighten unnecessarily. We do not want to cause a loss of output that is not necessary.

Sometimes, we make a mistake, and we tighten too much. But even when we make a mistake and we tighten too much, the loss of output tends to be temporary. So far, I think, we have been okay. We have been doing just the right amount of tightening.

If you look at our GDP [gross domestic product] growth in 2023, [it is] 5.5 percent. That does not look so high compared to 2021 for example. But 5.5 percent is the highest growth rate within the fastest-growing region, Southeast Asia. China is doing 5.2 [percent], and we are doing 5.5 [percent]. So, that is not so bad.

There are more jobs with that kind of growth rate. The unemployment rate is down to 4.2 percent. The underemployment rate is down to 11 percent; it used to be 14 percent.

So, in terms of growth, in terms of employment, we seem to be managing reasonably well in the face of supply shock.

Strong banking system
 
The banking system, I think, is in good shape unlike in previous crises. Many of us remember in the 1980s, our banking system got into trouble in the 1980s along with Latin American countries. In fact, we call that the Latin American debt crisis. We were part of it.

And so, when we tried to recover around 1989 from the Latin American debt crisis, the banks were part of the problem; they were not part of the solution. The banks had to repair their balance sheets.

The same thing happened in 1997–1998. The banks got into trouble. They had to repair their balance sheets. And so, they were part of the problem.

This time around, they were part of the solution. They went through the pandemic with very healthy balance sheets.

If you look at, for example, their capital adequacy ratios (CARs)—we call them “capital buffers"—banks, on average, have a 16-percent CAR. That is capital divided by risk-weighted assets.

The international standard is 10 percent. They are well above the standard for capital adequacy.

When it comes to liquidity, we are at 183 percent. The technical word for this is the liquidity coverage ratio, [which we are at] 183 percent. The international standard is 100 percent. So, our banks are very liquid.

Banks have more than adequate capital, which means they can still support our growth. In fact, loan growth has been 8.3 percent—that is quite healthy. And then, our non-performing loan (NPL) ratio, the ratio of NPLs to loans, is at 3.4 percent. That is pretty good. Coming out of the pandemic, it was nearly 5 percent.

During the Asian [financial] crisis, it had reached 12 percent. 3.4 percent is not so bad. We want to bring it down to 2.0 percent. 1.5 percent—that is what you get during good times.

So, the banks, as I have said, have been part of the solution rather than part of the problem.
 
Digital efforts

But we want to do better for the banks. And so, we are encouraging them to digitalize. I think that is inevitable.

They have to digitalize, and there are four approaches to doing that. We have something called the Open Finance Framework.

This is what they are doing in Europe for example. Banks these days, they are connected to something called APIs, or application programming interfaces.

They are connected to each other. They are connected to other institutions through these APIs that allow them to do business that involves consolidating customer balance sheets, doing investments for customers, and doing data analytics for customers.

In fact, for compliance purposes, APIs are going to be used to help banks satisfy their compliance requirement with the central bank. This is the jargon in the field; this is called “reg tech" [regulatory technology].

The BSP itself is using technology to oversee regulations and compliance of banks; that is called “sup tech" [supervisory technology].

Apart from the Open Finance Framework, we have what we call “regulatory sandboxes." What this means is that if you are a fintech [financial technology] and you have a very promising innovation, then you can come to the BSP, and we will give you a regulator.

So, you can work with that regulator—you can test your idea, you can discuss the proof of concept, you can pilot your idea—and your regulator will be next to you to get your side, to tell you what might be the regulatory consequences if you bring your idea to the market.

So, it is not about judging whether you really have a good idea and whether you will succeed. It is about minimizing regulatory uncertainty so when you actually put your project into place, you will have a very good idea of what the regulations will be.

A very special case of that is our digital banking framework. We have now given licenses to six digital banks. They are doing well on the deposits side. They are able to get deposits online.

A digital bank is not supposed to have any physical, no brick-and-mortar presence. So, everything has to be done online. And our digital banks have been very successful in raising deposits online. They are, to be honest, still struggling to make loans online. And it seems to be very hard to collect on loans online.

In the Philippines, it seems that you need a human being to collect [loan payments]—but, maybe, there is a way to overcome that—and that is why we only have six licenses so far. Some are more successful than others, and there is experience in other countries that digital banks are successful in making good loans.

So, that is a special case of a regulatory sandbox.

Finally, of course, we have generative AI [artificial intelligence]. As you know, this is inevitable. Everybody will be doing generative AI. ​So, what we are doing is looking at risks. There are many risks to generative AI, and we want to understand those risks. For example, generative AI tends to be prone to hallucinations. They tend to imagine things that never happened. They are prone to herding. They tend to make the same recommendations to different institutions regardless of specific circumstances.

So, those are some of the dangers, but we think that generative AI will still be used. They are just irresistible to banks and to ourselves. If you used ChatGPT, you know how irresistible that is.

Serving the unbanked
 
And then, finally, we want to make use of the digital payment system to serve the unbanked. We have two strategies in this regard. We have a local strategy in which we are using e-wallets [electronic wallets]—you know, your GCash or your PayMaya—and what we call basic deposit accounts (BDAs), which are deposit accounts that allow you to open an account in the bank in a very simplified way.

Together, in these two things, the e-wallets and the BDAs, we have found some successes that will lead to bank credit and other forms of financial services, including investments.

Our efforts where we should get the unbanked to be part of the formal financial ecosystem—that is our domestic strategy. ​​We have an international strategy. The one we do with our neighbors, the ASEAN [Association of Southeast Asian Nations] central banks, Singapore, Thailand, Malaysia, and Indonesia. We are working on a project called Nexus. This is to connect the fast payment systems of each individual central bank for each individual country.

We have a fast payment system ourselves; it is called InstaPay. Other countries have their own fast payment systems, and Nexus is designed to connect all those fast payment systems.

So, we can go from pesos into baht, baht into ringgit, almost instantaneously. Maybe, it will take 0.5 seconds but not so bad.

The goal is, when this is in place, to transfer money not costing more than 2.0 percent. The G20 goal is 3.0 percent; our own goal is 2.0 percent.

And the nice thing about Nexus is that it is designed to be very scalable. It is going to be easy to add more participants as long as they have a fast payment system.

The United States (US) is not ready. The US does not really have a fast payment system like InstaPay. They have the Fed [US Federal Reserve] now, but it is not the same as InstaPay. Brazil is ready; India is ready; and they have been asking to join. So, we will welcome them to the system.

Of course, we want the US and Europe to join the system. And once they are ready, it will be very easy.

So, that is my discussion. We want to enhance our monetary policy framework so we can deal more effectively with supply shocks. We want to digitalize our banks. And then, we want to get the unbanked to be included in the formal financial system—not only locally but also internationally.

Title: An Environment of Stability that Fosters Inclusive Growth
Occasion: Philippine Economic Briefing
Speaker: BSP Governor Eli M. Remolona, Jr.
Transcription:
​

Maayong umaga sa tanan. Nalipay ako, naari ako, subong sa Iloilo. Namit ang pagkaon; matahum ang esplanade.

Cabinet secretaries and Mr. Speaker, it is my pleasure to give the opening remarks.

I will talk about the role of the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP) in fostering economic growth, and that role is largely to provide an environment of stability—stability in prices and stability in the banking system.

In describing that role, I would also like to present the three challenges that we face as we try not just to provide stability, but also to strengthen sustainable growth and to strengthen inclusive growth.

So, these challenges are three things. We are doing monetary policy in what is essentially a supply-side economy. We are being hit by supply shocks all the time.

This is something new to the globe and to our economy. And then, to make the banking system even stronger, we want to digitalize the banking system.

Finally, to make growth more inclusive, we are trying to fashion a payment system that serves the unbanked.

Monetary policy

So, let me start with the supply shocks. We have been hit by supply shocks, not just us but the whole world. The kinds of shocks, the likes of which we have never really seen before. We had shocks in oil, and we had shocks in food—those are not unusual. But we had shocks in semiconductors, and we had shocks in fertilizer—those supply shocks pushed inflation rates up.

If you look at the graph, the blue line is headline inflation. That is our whole basket of food, energy, and services. That blue line went up to as high as 8.7 percent in January this year. What was pushing it up mainly was supply shocks.

The difference between the blue line and the orange line, the orange line is core inflation—that is when we take out food and energy. But the difference is supply shocks. You can see the orange line was pushing up the blue line. This is true for the whole world, not just us. But we were harder hit than most.

Finally, with the right kind of monetary policy, we have been bringing down inflation. As of November, the inflation rate was 4.1 percent, and I will explain what we have been doing to do that.

Our dilemma is that, in some cases, when there are supply shocks, you just look through supply shocks; you ignore the supply shocks. Like what my mother used to say, “'Wag mo nang kamutin ang sugat mo, gagaling din 'yan."

The thing with supply shocks is if they are large enough, if they are frequent enough, they affect expectations. And then, you get second-round effects—you get increases in wages; you get increases in services.

The interesting thing about this other price is they go up, but they do not come down. The goods prices go up, and they come down. These other things, they go up, and they stay up. And so, that is the kind of inflation we have to manage somehow.

And, I think, we have the advantage that in 2002, we instituted this thing called inflation targeting framework. In other words, we announce our target inflation rate. The target is now 2.0 [percent] to 4.0 percent. We announced that many years ago, and we are trying to stick to that target.

If we are credible, the target serves to anchor inflation expectations. It tends to minimize the second-round effects.

So, that is what we have been doing with monetary policy. We have been watching expectations closely. We have been making forward guidance. We have been telling the market that this is what we are going to do in the next few meetings, and that seems to help anchor expectations and reduce second-round effects. So, that is monetary policy.

 

Robust banking system

Now, thankfully, in our banking system, our banks have remained strong even through the pandemic.

In the past when we had a crisis, the banks became part of the problem rather than part of the solution; they had to repair their balance sheets. This time, they remained very strong and very supportive of growth.

The international standard for capital is 10 percent. So, we have been following that. But our banks are at 16 percent. They are more capitalized than the international standard.

In terms of liquidity, the international standard is 100 percent. Our banks are at 183 percent—a lot of liquidity.

So, liquidity, even with the monetary policy tightening, is very available, and the banks are strong enough to continue to lend.

I say they are strong enough, but we want them to be even stronger, which is why we go to our program for digitalizing banks.

 

Digitalizing banks

There are four approaches. We have an Open Finance Framework—this is the thing that connects banks together. They share information of customers and so on. But we want to make sure that in this framework, the customers' data is only used with the consent of the customer.

Of course, we also worry about cyber risk and all that. But the basic principle for the Open Finance Framework is when banks use all these new digital platforms, they use consumer data, and they make sure they first ask permission when they want to use that data.

And then, we have this thing called “regulatory sandbox." This is where if you have a new innovation, you want to play around, you want to test it, you want to prove that it works, but we assign a regulator to you.

So, the regulator helps you to minimize regulatory risk. This is not about predicting whether you will be successful or not, it is predicting whether you can obey important regulations.

Digital banking is one of those things that are in a sandbox. We issued six digital licenses. These guys are able, actually very successful, to collect deposits just online. They do not have offices; it is all online.

They are still struggling with figuring out how to make loans. That is the hard part, that is why they are still in a sandbox.

And then, of course, we have generative AI [artificial intelligence]. This is a new thing for us, but, as you know, it is inevitable.

So, even now, we have to examine the risks. So, when they become more widely used, we know how to regulate generative AI.

Finally, we want a digital payment system that serves the unbanked.

This is our strategy for helping the government with inclusive growth.

We have two strategies actually. We have the local strategy in which we have e-wallets [electronic wallets], or we have the basic deposit account. That leads to bank credit for the unbanked and to other financial services so that the unbanked become part of the whole financial ecosystem. That is on the domestic side.

On the international side, we have an exciting collaboration with our neighbors in the ASEAN [Association of Southeast Asian Nations].

For the neighbors that have digital fast payment [systems]—in our case, InstaPay is our digital fast payment system—we are collaborating on a platform. So, this will avoid going into dollars; this will avoid corresponding banks.

We go to a platform where the peso can be easily exchanged for baht, ringgit, or rupiah. And then, it is going to be efficient, and the cost will come down. We hope—this is our goal in two years—to [reduce cost up to] 1.0 percent of the transfer. The G20 goal is 3.0 percent; our goal is 1.0 percent for moving money.

And this thing is very scalable. It is going to be easy to include other countries. The United States, of course, they are not ready yet; they do not have the kind of fast payment [system] that we have.

The countries that seem to be ready to be part of this are Brazil and India. This is very scalable, and the network effects are very powerful.

Let me say a little bit more of what is happening domestically.

We feel good that when you look at the share of digital payments to total transactions, we are seeing a shift from cash to digital payments.

As of 2022, 42 percent of transactions have been digital. We are hoping that by this year, we do not have the numbers yet for 2023, it will reach 50 percent.

Now, what has this done? It has brought people into the formal financial system.

As of 2021, 56 percent of Filipino grownups have formal financial accounts. And we hope that by this year, it will be 70 percent so we are reassured that we are able to make progress.

Conclusion

So, to summarize, we are doing monetary policy in a supply-shock economy, and this is about understanding inflation expectations and anchoring those inflation expectations.

We are also trying to digitalize the banking system. And here, we offer the Open Finance Framework, digital banking, a regulatory sandbox, and regulated generative AI.

When it comes to inclusion, we are trying to fashion a payment system that offers a gateway into the banking system for the unbanked and an efficient cross-border payment system.

Madamo gid nga salamat!

Title: Message for the First Ateneo Economics and Management Alumni Homecoming
Occasion: First Ateneo Economics and Management Alumni Homecoming
Speaker: BSP Governor Eli. M. Remolona, Jr.
Transcription:
​

Magandang gabi sa inyong lahat!

How about we talk about monetary policy in a supply-shock economy?

In 2022, the world was hit by supply shocks, the likes of which we had not seen before. We saw these shocks in food, in oil, in semiconductors, and in fertilizer.

As a consequence, global inflation rates went through the roof. In our case, in the Philippines, headline inflation rose to 8.7 percent last January, the highest in 14 years.

In these circumstances, what is monetary policy to do?

In the old-school Keynesian world, inflation is inflation regardless of the source. In the face of inflationary supply shocks, the central bank should tighten, as it would in the face of inflationary demand shocks. Of course, monetary policy works with a lag, while the impact of supply shocks tends to be immediate. You can do the math.

On the other hand, if you lived in the make-believe world of so-called rational expectations, what you would do is you would look through the supply shocks. No need to do anything. Anyway, the shocks will dissipate. “'Wag mong kamutin ang sugat mo," my mother would say. “Gagaling din 'yan."

Second-round effects

Unfortunately, the real world is more complicated. In the real world, if supply shocks are large enough and frequent enough, they give rise to the kind of inflation expectations that lead to second-round inflationary effects.

These second-round effects tend to be sticky downwards. Once wages go up because of supply shocks, they do not come down after the shocks dissipate. In general, with supply shocks, goods prices go up and then come down. In their wake, however, the prices of services go up and stay up. In other words, second-round effects are asymmetric.

In this world of asymmetric second-round effects, inflation expectations become crucial.

In this world of expectations, it helps enormously that in 2002, the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas adopted an inflation targeting framework. We now have a target range for inflation of between 2.0 [percent] and 4.0 percent. When monetary policy is credible, that target serves to anchor inflation expectations.

In November, the inflation rate was 4.1 percent. That is within striking distance of our target. Yes, it is too soon to declare victory. But much of the credit for the decline in inflation is the fact that our inflation expectations have remained well-anchored and second-round effects have remained manageable.

I guess that is enough economics for an alumni homecoming.

Conclusion

So, let me close with a few words of wisdom: Basta ang inflation rate ay bumaba ng todo, hindi na baleng si Gov. Eli ay sintunado!

Noong Marso, pumutok ang SVB [Silicon Valley Bank] at Credit Suisse, buti na lang naiwasan natin ang global crisis!

Ang masaklap lang, si KathNiel hindi na raw nagki-kiss!

Maraming, maraming salamat po!
