Title: The ADB as the Philippines’ Trusted Partner in Nation-Building
Occasion: Opening remarks for the Business Session at the 56th ADB Annual Meeting in Incheon
Speaker: BSP Governor Felipe M. Medalla
Transcription:
​

Let me start by expressing our appreciation to the ADB (Asian Development Bank) and the Republic of Korea for hosting this meeting. By the way, I walked around a lot since I arrived, and I am very impressed by Incheon’s parks and buffers between vehicular noise in the highways and residential areas. I would like to thank the officials of Incheon and its people for their hospitality.

Bright growth prospects for the Philippines and developing economies

The theme, “Rebounding Asia: Recover, Reconnect, and Reform” is the best way to summarize what Asian economies must do in the coming years. 

Recent forecasts of various international and multilateral institutions, including the ADB, highlight the strong recovery of developing Asian economies.

The Philippines, for instance, grew by 7.6 percent last year. We expect GDP (gross domestic product) to grow by 6.0-7.0 percent this year and 6.5-8.0 percent in 2024 to 2028.

With regards to inflation, the latest outturns are still high, but we are quite confident that inflation – although it remains elevated – will revert towards the mid-point of our target by next year. 

Nevertheless, the risk to inflation, especially because of possible global shocks and tensions, maybe even the El Niño, continue to lean toward the upside for 2023 and 2024. Therefore, going forward, the central bank remains vigilant against inflation risk over the policy horizon.

Policy priorities for sustained economic development

In line with the Philippine Development Plan (PDP), the strategies of the Philippine government will focus on modernizing agriculture, expanding agribusiness, encouraging private sector participation in infrastructure development, promoting digital transformation, and enhancing the competitiveness of local industries, among others.

The ADB as a partner in nation-building

We acknowledge that the ADB has been relentless in its efforts to alleviate poverty and social inequality, tackle climate change, enhance resilience and sustainability, and foster growth across the Asia-Pacific region. 

For that, we thank the ADB for its continuous support to the Philippines.

In particular, the ADB has been a strong partner in the pursuit of the Philippines development agenda. Recently, the ADB held a consultation with our national government to present the Bank’s proposed themes for new country partnerships focusing on intensifying climate action, which the Philippines needs, because we will no longer build new [coal-fired] power plants. In this regard, the ADB’s energy transition mechanism is very important.

Second, it is investing in climate-smart transportation and digital transformation.

Third, of course is investing in Filipinos.

These clearly are well-within and quite consistent with ADB’s policies and agenda.

Prudent fiscal management 

While the contributions of the ADB provide tremendous financing support, for our part, it is imperative that strong fiscal consolidation strategies be undertaken. This fiscal consolidation strategy will bring down our debt-to-GDP ratio from the current 63.5 percent to less than 60 percent by 2025 and cut the deficit-to-GDP ratio from the current 6.4 percent to 3.0 percent by 2028.

At the same time, the government will Build Better More as it remains committed to the goal of ramping up spending on public infrastructure and completing on schedule especially ongoing projects in all parts of the country within the next six years. 

With target infrastructure disbursements carefully recalibrated in consideratio​​n of the available fiscal space, government spending in the [infrastructure] sector is expected to reach pre-pandemic levels by the end of the term of the current president. Coupled with the tighter fiscal program, this is expected to signal stronger economic growth in the medium-term.

Multilateral cooperation and concessional funding and assistance given to developing member countries will remain to be the most effective tools in ensuring a sustainable and inclusive recovery. We commend the ADB efforts in exploring initiatives that will increase its lending capacity.

Taking a whole-of-government and whole-of-society approach to public issues

Climate action and navigating policy issues surrounding it require a whole-of-society approach. The ADB needs to find ways to seamlessly restructure finance in such a way that it will be a greater enabler for greener and more resilient growth for its member countries.

As we continue to see developments in this dynamic region, we will continue to see member countries [meet their] evolving needs. Let us continue to work together in envisioning our own path of development and ushering improved social and economic well-being for our people. ​

Thank you very much.

Title: Navigating Global Uncertainties through a Whole-of-System Perspective
Occasion: Special Financial Stability Coordination Council Briefing on Emerging Systemic Risk Scenarios and its Implications to the Philippines
Speaker: BSP Governor Felipe M. Medalla
Transcription:
​

First of all, I am so glad to see many friends that I have not seen physically for a long time. Thank you for coming. Our topic for today is “Emerging systemic risk scenarios and its implications to the Philippines.” 

When stability belies brewing instability

As an economist, our background is, sometimes, too much of many good things [that] may actually result in stressful situations. 

A very good example is the economist Hyman Minsky who was known for saying, “The root of instability is stability.” For instance, during a period of very stable growth in real estate prices, people begin to have a feeling that real estate is [an] extremely safe [investment]. Indeed, this [view] is confirmed by the fact that there are no defaults [around that time]. But when we look back, the reason there were no defaults, then, was that real estate prices [were] steadily rising. If the buyer, for some reason, suffers a financial problem, all he had to do was sell the property to pay. Therefore, [we saw] no defaults [at the beginning].

So, you can have a period of long stability that can actually cause the buildup of stress [over time]. Eventually, when a real shock comes and real estate prices start falling, then it is likely too late. The buildup of stress has become too large that a crash ensues.

Now, you have the opposite [situation]. With real estate prices falling, people cannot pay their debt. Since they cannot pay their debt, then the banks are in trouble. And since the banks are in trouble, the economy is in trouble. When the economy is in trouble, government collections go down. All sorts of terrible things could happen when there is seeming strength and stability [on the surface].

When regulatory actions aimed at stability become the very cause of instability

One of the lessons learned from the Asian financial crisis was that it seemed that central banks were guaranteeing the exchange rate because they intervened to keep it stable, and they were capable of doing so because there were so much [foreign exchange (forex)] inflows. 

Then, people, seeing that the central bank has high forex reserves, become overconfident. So, they borrow in their own currency. 

Without intending to, the central bank had an implied put on the exchange rate and encouraged behavior that, later on, was not sustainable.

When the bubble pops and the music stops: what now? 

Of course, the other question is, given this buildup of stress, what would later be the trigger? In this case [Asian financial crisis], the trigger was something that happened in Thailand, which eventually affected Indonesia. 

For those of us who are old enough to remember, if you look at that period, it was clearly a very stressful period [for the banks]. But when you do look back, the contraction of the economy from 1997 to 1998 was just 0.5 percent. 

On the other hand, COVID caused the economy to contract by almost 17 percent in Q2 2020, relative to Q2 2019. For the whole year [of 2020], there was almost a 10-percent contraction of the economy, yet there was no sense of buildup of stress [in the financial system]. The question is why? Of course, one answer is that the banks were better-capitalized [now than in 1997].

In addition, in my own view, COVID might have actually prevented the next real estate crisis. It brought everything back to “normal.” The misalignment of [property] prices became less serious.

The point is, the exercises that we have to do, the other part [of it] is looking at what could possibly trigger these emerging systemic risk scenarios. In particular, a very interesting question is: How could monetary, fiscal, and banking policies in these countries [in the region] affect us [in the Philippines]?

Financial stability as a shared responsibility 

Three government agencies are largely mandated to promote financial stability.

By the way, the central bank’s original mandate was banking stability. Now, the [expanded] mandate is financial stability. Clearly, we have to work together with regulators from other parts of the capital markets, namely the Securities and Exchange Commission and the Insurance Commission.

But as you can see, [under the current market structure], what happens in the banking sector is clearly more important for two reasons: One, it is a very big part of the economy. The last time I looked, total bank assets is about equal to GDP [gross domestic product].  Of course, you can say that the fixed assets of the economy are four, five times its production. Therefore, banks are financing only one-fourth of all the fixed assets because, remember, these fixed assets do not count in one year. In that sense, the share of banks in what is being financed is quite large.

The other problem, of course, is that the banks are more interconnected. The banks themselves are a central part of the payment system.

Scenario generation and planning as useful exercises in systemic risk management

That is why I am so glad you are all here so that we can discuss these issues in a less formal way, [engage in] the exercise of developing systemic risk scenarios, and ask questions on its implications on the Philippines.

In addition to that, we do other scenario-generating activities, like: What would happen if one big conglomerate fails? We do not know what the cause could be. 

For instance, [suppose] there is a mistake in contracting. A power supplier guarantees the price of power regardless of the price of fuel. In return, he gets a premium. What happens if the price of fuel goes way beyond any imagined scenario? What happens to the firm? What happens to the power supply and so on and so forth? In this particular scenario, the worst thing that could happen, in a sense, [is that] the courts could say, “The company is no longer responsible for [maintaining] the fixed price because of the unusually high increase in world prices.” The sad thing is that if a crisis like that happens, the impact of the stress is distributed to consumers [through higher energy bills].

The importance of clear and careful communication for policymakers 

But there is a problem with these discussions. When we are talking about these scenarios, merely discussing them could be misinterpreted by the media. It could have unintended effects. “Dini-discuss pala ng Bangko Sentral kung paano [ang] mangyayari kung babagsak si ganito.” Then, people, all of a sudden, will start thinking, “Aba, babagsak si ganito!”

Clearly, the discussion has to be open, but at the same time, we have to make sure that we know [and communicate to the public that] these are scenario-generating exercises. We have to be very careful what we say to the public because what we do could be misinterpreted.

At any rate, I am so glad you are all here. The only way to learn, as a society, to prepare for these scenarios and actually make [generate] these scenarios so that we can better plan [for them] is to have these discussions and do it in an open way—probably, with quite a bit of carefulness about what we say and what we communicate to the media and the public.

With that, I open this briefing on emerging systemic risk scenarios and their implications for the Philippines. 

I thank you in advance for your contributions to improving our knowledge about how these scenario-generating exercises can be useful. Thank you very much. Maraming salamat.​

Title: Growth amid Headwinds: Balancing Inflation and Economic Growth in the Philippines
Occasion: First General Membership Meeting of the Money Market Association of the Philippines
Speaker: BSP Governor Felipe M. Medalla
Transcription:
​

To the BSP’s [Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas] partners from the Money Market Association of the Philippines (MART), ladies and gentlemen, magandang gabi sa inyong lahat. 

Before I start, let me share with you a conversation I was having on my table. Where is the letter ‘T’ in [the acronym of the] Money Market Association of the Philippines? There is one at the end of the word “market.” So, we were wondering why your acronym is “MART.” 

The important point, though, is that it works. You may not know the exact meaning of the acronym, but you know exactly what it represents. In a sense, the Philippine economy is like that. It is not the most conventional economy. Indeed, it is an economy where the services sector became very large before there was any full-blown industrialization—one case of many unique things about the country. 

Thank you for inviting me to be your guest of honor and speaker at your First General Membership Meeting. As always, we value these conversations with you—various associations—where we are interested in the same things but not necessarily seeing them in the same way or from the same point of view or mindset. Putting these together, these different mindsets give us a better grasp of policy. 

Navigating the delicate balance between controlling inflation and keeping output loss to a minimum

The theme for this presentation is balancing inflation and economic growth. I should say that there are times when there is nothing to balance. For instance, if the cause of inflation is excess demand, then [the act of postponing addressing inflation [through policy rate adjustments] does not have any sacrifice [in terms of output loss] and does not result in any gain in output. All you do is postpone the pain of adjustment [later on]. 

There is no tradeoff. It is either you take the pain now [or later]. The tradeoff is when you take the pain of output loss now to control inflation or take the pain of output loss later to contain inflation. As in most businesses, postponing treatment makes [administering] the cure more painful. Worse, it makes the probability of a successful cure lower. 

Fortunately, in the case of the Philippines, the cause of [above-target] inflation is not excess demand. That is the advantage of having an independent central bank, which I will discuss later. 

When supply-side pressures warrant a decisive monetary response

In this case, there has to be some tradeoffs, which is—to the extent that the inflation is [driven by] supply shocks—the fear that supply shocks can morph into self-fulfilling higher inflation. Supply shocks cause prices to rise. Rising prices increase inflationary expectations, which, in turn, can cause higher inflation. Therefore, we are afraid that second-order effects make a very hard choice of using higher interest rates to address supply shocks. That is, if you do not raise interest rates to respond to supply shocks, then you may have a bigger problem later. 

On the other hand, if it turns out that the supply shocks are like viruses that could cure themselves, then, maybe, [we can] just try staying at home, wrapping ourselves in a very thick kumot (blanket) and wait for the fever to go down by itself. That is the problem. There is a possibility that it is self-curing, and you do not have to do anything. 

Of course, you do not know. So, you can make two mistakes: One is that it [supply-side driven inflation] is self-curing, and you tried to cure it, then there is output loss. The other mistake is that it is not self-curing, and it can become a spiral. If you have postponed addressing it, inflation expectations become so deeply embedded that getting rid of it becomes harder. It is like if you did not treat the disease, it is now [spreading] all over your body; therefore, the medicine that has to be given will [have to] be more powerful. 

In that sense, there is a balancing act.  The balancing act is really the result of economics—like a medicine [from] 200, 300 years ago where your doctor is more likely to kill you than cure you. Precisely, the balancing is the result of great uncertainty on what is really needed. 

On top of that, [there is] the great uncertainty about how [inflationary] expectations are formed and the extent to which the central bank is capable of changing how people form expectations when it really matters.  Clearly, then—and this is how I look at it as an economist, even predominantly supply shock-caused inflation must require some form of monetary response. 

That is where I will start. Faced with a challenging macroeconomic environment, I hope that this presentation will shed light on the BSP’s policy actions, which are anchored on three pillars and, in turn, contribute to sustaining economic recovery. 

Central bank independence and inflation-targeting: The Philippine experience

As I already said, the Philippine central bank has the benefit of being an independent central bank. It has used this period of independence to establish its [inflation-targeting] credibility, and it also has used this period of independence not to follow the textbook [definition]. 

The textbook says: An inflation-targeting central bank should not care too much about the exchange rate. If we had followed that, we would have let the peso appreciate to ₱35 [against the dollar] when the US Fed [United States Federal Reserve] started quantitative easing and negative interest rates. Then [BSP] Governor [Amando] Tetangco [Jr.] thought that that was not the case. If you allowed excessive appreciation, the result later will be excessive depreciation. Excessive appreciation will cause an output loss because wages will not go down when the currency is appreciating. That is when wages are “downward rigid.” So, excessive appreciation is harmful. 

To his credit, he [former Governor Tetangco] used that period to prevent the peso from appreciating too much [by building up the BSP’s foreign exchange (forex) reserves]. International reserves went from US$45 billion to over US$90 billion in a very brief period of less than four years, but that resulted in another problem. As we buy dollars, we either borrow or print pesos to buy them. 

To make matters worse, the law prevented us from buying from the public. Every time we buy dollars, we either print pesos or borrow money from banks. The problem is that the banks can always change their mind and lend the money. The liquidity that we created is [what] we owe the banks, but the banks can change their minds and say, “Wait a minute. I no longer want to deposit my money with the BSP.”

When I was on the Monetary Board, we had special deposit accounts that reached ₱2.3 trillion. It is not surprising because forex reserves went from US$45 billion to US$90 billion. We were thinking that if the banks changed their minds and started withdrawing and lending that money, we will have problems on our hands. 

Fortunately, we now have the power to borrow from the public. That is one thing we learned. We owe money from the public that will not become loans. If we owed money from banks and the banks decide to withdraw the money and lend, you will now have what is called the “money multiplier process gone wild.”

Significant and one-way changes in the exchange rate posed risks to price stability 

The other side of it is when the peso depreciates too much, our fear is that the translation of peso depreciation [exchange rate pass-through] to inflation, which is [usually] very low, will become high. 

Our measurement shows that during the inflation-targeting period, a ₱1 change [depreciation] in the exchange rate will increase inflation by 0.076 ppt [percentage point] in the short run.1 

This means that when the exchange rate goes up and down—[or] is not going in any particular direction—and all the changes are very small, people do not bother to change prices because changing the price is also “expensive,” especially if after you raise it, you have to bring it down again. If you raise prices and by the next month, you have to reduce them again, you will just confuse your buyers.

Now, what happened was quite different. In just nine months, from January 2022 to October 2022, the peso-dollar rate moved [depreciated] by [a peak of] 13 percent. 

As you can see in the chart, our first mandate is price stability, and we were not sure that the translation of the changes in exchange rate to inflation will remain small. In the words of macroeconomists, the translation of changes in the exchange rate to inflationary expectations has changed.

If you look at countries in Latin America, that is a problem. [A significant] change in the exchange rate [results in] higher prices. Higher prices [beget] changes in the exchange rates with very little gain—because what really matters is the exchange rate, divided by the price, right? If the exchange rate has doubled but the price has [also] doubled, the real terms of the exchange rate did not make it more competitive. These are the concerns we have. 

My main topic would be the first pillar, but I will not be giving a good picture without discussing the two other pillars.

The third pillar: Bringing the benefits of digital payments within and among countries

The third pillar—a safe, secure, and efficient payments and settlements system—used to be a boring topic. You have the PhilPaSS [Philippine Payment and Settlement System], then you have the oldest technology, which is printing coins. You actually see that in the Bible when Christ was asked who should be [featured] in the coin. Christ said, “It should be Ceasar.” Not him, not God. After all, the king will hang you if you print money, which is his sole monopoly.

It [payments and settlements] is becoming exciting because of the rise in digital payments. You can see this in the two forms of payments [systems] that we have: [First is] InstaPay, which is almost instantaneous. InstaPay is what we call our fast payment system. It has different names in different countries. In another country [Singapore], it is called PayNow. In our case, it is InstaPay. Of course, [the other is] PESONet, which settles only twice a day. What you do before 12 o’clock gets settled in the mid-afternoon. What you do before 5 o’clock gets settled between around 6:00 p.m. and 7:00 p.m. Of course, the second one allows for [transfers of] greater amounts and can be a substitute for checks.

It [InstaPay transaction volumes] already exceeded ATM [automated teller machine] transactions. PESONet [transactions], sooner or later, will overtake [the volume of] checks.

In addition, we have great dreams of making the system even better. We have our so-called Paleng-QR. The goal is [for] merchants and even transportation [operators] to be paid by means of a QR [quick response] code. A tricycle driver? QR code. A market vendor? QR code. If you want to give money to a beggar, here is a QR code. 

The vision is, you can do this wherever you are in the ASEAN [Association of Southeast Asian Nations]. That one is a little further away because you have the exchange rate. Cross-border payments are generally far more complex, but that dream will probably be true in two to three years. At least five countries in the ASEAN-5 [are working on this project], [including] Singapore, Indonesia, Malaysia, Thailand, and the Philippines. We will [aim to] have a single QR for the entire system, or at least in the case of ASEAN, you have different QR systems, but they have enough commonalities to be interoperable.

The second pillar: Philippine banks remain a pillar of strength amid global banking turmoil

The second pillar is financial stability. Clearly, the financial sector is much more than the banks, but the banks are the largest [component]. For instance, long-term money is more with the insurance companies.

Now, on our second pillar—and this is very important, our banks are strong. The biggest worry, after [the collapse of] Silicon Valley Bank, is: What if, as we raise policy rates to control inflation, that will cause a huge drop in some bond and asset prices? To the extent that the banks carry those assets, you can severely reduce the capitalization of banks—or to the extent that borrowers from banks lose from the falling asset prices. Remember, in finance, higher discount rates mean lower present value. Everybody here knows that higher interest rates generally mean lower bond prices or even lower stock prices. 

If that [policy rate adjustment] itself can cause financial instability, then the policymaker is in a bind. His tools or his medicine causes side effects. [So,] he is now reluctant to use it on the main disease. 

Higher inflation [is usually addressed through] higher interest rates. What if the higher interest rate endangers banks and endangers the financial system? [Can policymakers decide to] just let inflation go rather than cause the side effect?

Financial stability gives free rein to preserve price stability

Fortunately, that is not the case with us. Why is it that “the worry that the tool for curing inflation will not be used because of fear of side effects” is not true in the Philippines? 

Now, we have several explanations for this. The first explanation is that our policy rate is not starting from zero. Indeed, it looks like it is starting from 2.0 percent, but it was at 2.0 percent for a very short period—only as a response to COVID-19. In contrast, in the US and Europe, it was zero for a long time.

What is the problem with low interest rates? The best way to think about this is to think of perpetual bonds. You buy the bond, and you will never pay the principal. You will just get interest payments annually. To make it simple, suppose you have 1.0 percent in long-term equilibrium interest rates. If you have a [bond worth] ₱100, it will earn 1.0 percent [in interest]. What if, all of a sudden, the interest rate becomes 2.0 percent? How much money do you need now to earn 2.0 percent? That is ₱50. So, a new bond [of] ₱50 will give you 2.0 [percent]. The old bond, that [one worth] ₱100, gives you 1.0 [percent]. What will happen to the price of the old bond? It will fall by half. 

In other words, a mere increase [in the policy rate] from 1.0 percent to 2.0 percent is cutting the price of the bond by half. Of course, that is not true because the maturity will be 10 years, but the direction is the same. The point is: The smaller the starting point, the greater [it is] percentage-wise. In other words, 1.0 ppt is 100 percent of 1. If you are starting from higher interest rates, then in relation to the base, the increase is lower. That is the other thing that is going for the Philippines.

The other thing that is going for the Philippines is that our banks are well-capitalized. They lose money [because] the mark-to-market losses of the banks from the higher interest rates are large, but their gains from the higher rates more than offset it. 

In that sense, a comforting thought is that our main tool for fighting inflation does not have unwanted side effects. It will not bring about financial instability. We are, in a way, unconstrained to use our tools.

Expanded toolkit proves adequate to put out the fire

In addition, we have decided to use two tools. Because we were accumulating forex during “unconventional monetary policy times,” then we can use forex intervention.

By the way, the peso is not really over-depreciating relative to other currencies. It is only the US dollar that was really appreciating. But then, who cares? To the extent that the dollar is [the global currency of choice] because most global transactions are [carried out] in dollars, therefore, it [the depreciation] really hurts.

We are lucky, then, that we have sufficient forex buffers to use two tools. There was a time, for four straight policy meetings, [when the US Fed raised the policy rate by] 75 basis points (bps). In just four policy meetings, they have increased their policy rate by 300 bps, which is quite unheard of. They have made large increases in the past but not as quickly as 300 bps in just four meetings.

In short, we have the tools for addressing the US policy pivot [to rapid and unprecedented tightening]: a combination of forex intervention and policy rate changes to address excessive depreciation. 

Indeed, from January to October last year, the peso depreciated by 13 percent. That [depreciation] got reversed after October [2022], but [it was] also because the market sensed that there will be no more jumbo increases [in the Fed funds rate].

As a result, inflation is expected to revert to within target by year-end after months of exceeding the target 

Our forecast now is—by the way, this forecast will be revised downward. There are 12 headline inflation [prints] every year. That [average], divided by 12 [months], we thought it will be 6.0 percent this year, but, I think, our forecast will be revised. This could be [revised downward] because of very low month-on-month (m-o-m) inflation prints in February and March [2023].

As you can see in this chart, we expect inflation to correct to within target or [revert to] below 4.0 percent by November or December this year. 

But, again, with the new [within target m-o-m inflation] prints, it [the normalization in inflation] may come a little bit earlier, like October or September. But even if it happens in September, it is 18 straight months of inflation being higher than 4.0 percent, which is [the upper band of] our target. [Again, that is] 18 straight months of above-target inflation. 

The good thing, though, is we have not lost credibility [as an inflation-targeting central bank] because everyone knows it is [inflation is driven by] supply-side [pressures]. Everyone knows we have clearly addressed it quite aggressively. 

This is the source of our optimism: the fact that the markets do agree that we will address it [above-target inflation] and that we will not have an inflationary spiral. Indeed, our forecast is what you can see there—inflation going down to below 4.0 percent. Depending on which forecast, I think, the next forecast that we have is that it will be going down to below 4.0 percent and [settle] within target already by October or even September. By next year, inflation is expected to average very close to 3.0 percent.

The way to get there was painful—17, 18 straight months [of above-target inflation] in the best-case scenarios. By the way, the worst streak [on record before the current elevated inflation] was 15 straight months. In other words, [after experiencing] a series of four shocks, eventually, the system absorbs it within the end of a 12-month period after the last or fourth shock. 

The problem, of course, is that the inflation expectations of the private sector are now down but are still higher than our own [at the central bank]. But this is not something to worry about; this has always been the case. 

[When] we [at the central bank] adjust our [inflation] forecast downwards, the private sector also adjusts theirs but not as much as we do. If we wait long enough and they see the evidence, they will eventually begin to follow ours. That is what our regression shows.

Recent month-on-month inflation figures paint an encouraging picture of easing price pressures

An encouraging part of the picture is the [recent] m-o-m [inflation figures]. The period from March 2022 to January 2023—it is hard to find a period as bad as that. In other words, within that 13-month period, only one month was [inflation] consistent with our target. 

If course, the worst month was last January. [Non-seasonally adjusted inflation for] January 2023 was 1.7 percent higher than [inflation in] December 2022. Annualized, that is [inflation of] almost 20 percent, right? Of course, if you remove the seasonal effects because January is usually a high month for inflation, it [January 2023 seasonally adjusted inflation] is still high at 1.0 percent. 

We had too much of that [consecutive supply shocks]. My analogy is wrestling. There is a tag team, then the other team is cheating. The first wrestler is beating up the good guys. Because they are honest, the other guys cannot tap in, but the bad guys all come to the ring at the same time and take turns beating him up. These [back-to-back supply-side pressures driving inflation] are happening over a 12-month period.

The picture, though, is that that is over. On a seasonally adjusted basis, m-o-m inflation in March 2023 was zero. As you can see from the chart, without seasonal adjustments because January [inflation] was very high, it [m-o-m inflation in March] is actually negative [at minus 0.2 percent]. If you did not do any seasonal adjustments, we actually had a change from one month to the next, where the price index is actually lower than the previous month. We think that this will be the trend if we go by our model and previous experience.

A similar story holds for core inflation, which went down from 0.5 percent [in February 2023] to 0.4 percent [in March 2023]. Core food inflation is down to 0.2 percent [over the same period], which is consistent with the 2.0–4.0 percent inflation [target]. Non-food core inflation is just 0.3 percent [over the same period], which is also consistent with our target. 

If the deceleration in inflation continues, barring any further shocks coming from the supply side, we project that inflation will begin to revert back to target. Indeed, the average inflation for 2024 would be much closer or slightly below 3.0 percent than to 4.0 percent.

Non-monetary interventions by the national government complement decisive monetary response

Now, one of the reasons this [deceleration in inflation] is working very fast is that the government finally decided that balancing [the interests of consumers and farmers should tilt in favor of the consumers]. The general tendency is to be protective of farmers, and there is a good reason for that. The reason for protecting the farmers is that foreign suppliers are fair-weather friends. When domestic supply in the country that supplies us food goes down, what will be their first act? Ban exports [to importing countries, like the Philippines]. So, the goods are not there when they are in trouble. Therefore, we would rather have a little bit more expensive domestic supply, which is guaranteed. 

The other reason for wanting to protect agriculture is that our farmers are poorer than the average. 

But with the very high inflation in food, the President has decided that: “Well, this time, we will import.” An interagency committee has been assigned to spot the [agricultural] shortages so that the imports will be adequate and timely. 

In other words, both monetary policy and non-monetary policy of the government are now addressing inflation.

And as I already talked about, as you can see in the inflation picture, the exchange rate picture, the threat of a continuously weakening peso disanchoring inflation expectations are, more or less, gone. 

Robust forex inflows provide a cushion against external shocks and lend support to the peso

In addition, structural receipts, forex inflows from remittances, forex inflows from BPOs [business process outsourcing], and even forex inflows from direct investments are actually countering the effects of a large balance of trade deficit. 

This is shown by the fact that the GIR [gross international reserves] has recovered from US$92 billion to US$100 billion now.

The BSP’s actions summarized

To summarize, this is what we [at the central bank] did. We raised the policy rate by 425 bps because it was just 200 bps before July 2021. 

You can see that no other country did [raised their policy rate] as much as we did—although, as I said, this exaggerates it because [bringing the policy rate to] 200 bps was just a temporary anti-COVID response. Without that, the policy rate would have been around 3.25 to 3.50 percent. So, we are much closer to South Korea [that raised by a cumulative 300 bps] than it looks. 

Of course, we also had changes in the exchange rate, which is really a great way of adjusting to a large deficit due to imports exceeding exports. 

We also sold forex reserves. As you can see, we are quite similar on the change in the international reserves. We sold 6.7 percent [of forex reserves]; South Korea, 8.0 percent; and India, 11.0 percent. The outliers are Vietnam, which sold much more than we all did [at 20.8 percent], as well as Indonesia and Malaysia, which hardly sold anything. Of course, Indonesia and Malaysia were actually beneficiaries of the commodity boom that is related to the Ukraine war. 

That is the main picture. The central bank has sufficient tools to address inflation, without those tools having unacceptable side effects on financial stability.

We combined the use of two tools, which are interest rates and forex intervention. In addition, we always explain to the people why we are doing what we are doing. 

Economy on the mend, room for growth despite policy normalization

As you can see, we have recovered from a very deep contraction of the economy caused by COVID. [During] the worst quarter [in Q2 2020], it contracted by nearly 17 percent. 

But if you were measuring GDP [gross domestic product] weekly, the 0.7 percent contraction of Q1 2020 is also quite bad. Because remember, COVID struck with just two weeks remaining in the first quarter.

We had very good GDP numbers last year, averaging 7.6 percent growth. Our own forecasts show that GDP growth will fall but will not fall below 6.0 percent—and if it does, not very much. 

The main [growth] driver is from pent-up demand or what people call “revenge spending.” That this hotel hall is full of people is anecdotal evidence. Year-on-year (y-o-y) spending on hotels and restaurants rose by 24 percent [in Q4 2022]. Thanks to MART, no? 

Y-o-y car sales increased by 31 percent in 2022. Of course, why would you buy a car during the lockdowns? It will be depreciating and rotting in your garage. So, you postpone buying. But if you postponed buying a car for three years, you will be buying cars soon—[that is,] if you were planning to buy before the pandemic. 

Unemployment remains low.

And, now, international tourism is recovering. 

That is why as I said, we still have room for growth despite the large increases in the policy rate.

Closing message

In closing, I would say that the BSP is able to address both price and financial stability because its main tool for price stability—the interest rate—has not been constrained by financial stability concerns.

We remain steadfast in providing an enabling regulatory landscape through progressive reforms aimed at future-proofing the financial system.

Finally, we invite the MART and market players to continue supporting the government’s efforts in sustaining the growth momentum of the Philippines. In particular, the creation of more and better-quality jobs, the promotion of green and sustainable investments, and innovations in financial digitalization will create opportunities for development for the whole country.

Thank you very much for your patience and attention.


###

____________________________________________

[1] Corrected figures for the short-run exchange rate pass-through. Over the long run, a ₱1 depreciation will increase inflation by 0.116 ppt.​

Title: Financial Stability: Steering the Boat through Strong Waves
Occasion: Opening of the Financial Stability Exhibit
Speaker: BSP Governor Felipe M. Medalla
Transcription:
​

Guests, ladies and gentlemen, magandang umaga. It is my pleasure to welcome all of you to the opening of the exhibit that has to do with financial stability, themed “Executive Insights on Systemic Risks: Its Nuances and Challenges.” The title alone is very nuanced and challenging. This exhibit has been put together by our Office of Systemic Risk Management (OSRM) to better understand systemic risks.

Economic stability and growth as a shared mission

I will start by citing the mandates of the BSP [Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas]: to maintain and promote price stability, financial stability, and a stable and efficient payments system. 

If I were to complete it [the central bank’s mission statement], [it is] “in pursuit of sustainable and inclusive growth.” When you include everything, especially inclusivity and sustainability, it is [involved in] the business of the entire society because it is not just [working toward] a stable or growing economy, it must be inclusive and sustainable as well. 

Clearly, the BSP is an important player, but it has to deal with many other parts of society—let us say, in the case of banking stability, the banks and, of course, the rest of the government. 

For instance, the current [elevated] inflation is not just due to excess money but due to shortages of many agricultural and food products and, of course, the Ukraine war that caused fuel [prices] to rise.

It is very hard to define stability and, in fact, sometimes, it is easier to define its absence. 

How crises impact the Philippine economy and banking sector

How many of you were already born in 1997? If you recall, there was the Asian financial crisis, which—from the point of view of many bankers in the Philippines—was also a banking crisis. And yet, the economy contracted by only 0.5 percent in 1998 [despite the crisis]. 

On the other hand, with COVID, the economy actually contracted nearly 10 percent [in 2020]. And yet, the impact on the banking system has not been the same [as that of the Asian Financial Crisis of 1997].   

Not just the size of the waves, but the strength of the boat and how well it is managed

So, if I were to use that analogy, what matters is not just the size of the waves, but the strength of the boat. 

I can personally speak about this because when I was a college student at a university nearby, I spent two months in a Navy boat because ‘yun ang ROTC [Reserve Officers' Training Corps] namin. Ang dami dami kong demerits. So, I chose [to spend] two months in a Navy boat rather than repeating ROTC. There were waves that were so strong that people who were not used to it were vomiting. And yet, the boat remained stable. 

The key, then, is not just the size of the waves, but how strong the boat is and, I suppose, how well-steered the boat is. Maybe, a large wave could sink the boat if it strikes the boat from the side and could, therefore, upend it. So, the way the boat is navigated [also matters].

Financial stability as a shared responsibility, but bank regulation remains key in “bank-centric” financial system

Therefore, we must work together with all our partners in government. In particular, the most important regulatory agencies are the Securities and Exchange Commission, the Insurance Commission, the Philippine Deposit Insurance Corporation, and the Department of Finance—who, collectively, form the Financial Stability Coordination Council or the FSCC.

Of course, the central bank regulates banks and not the entire capital market, but we play a very important role because the Philippine economy is so-called “bank-centric.” I was looking at the recent balance sheet of banks. All the assets of all the banks that we regulate, it is about ₱23 trillion. And then, I look at GDP [gross domestic product], it was also roughly ₱22 trillion. 

By the way, this overstates the importance of the BSP because the assets of an economy are greater than its annual GDP. If the usual ratio is fixed capital is four times the output, then you can say that the banking system has financed one-fourth of the fixed capital of the economy. That is a lot!

Therefore, making sure that the banks are well-capitalized, highly liquid, well-managed, and well-governed is extremely important. 

Mismatches sowing instability 

If you go back to [the] 1997 [crisis], there were plenty of mismatches. Again, you could attribute instability to mismatches. There were a lot of businesses that borrowed in dollars, but their revenues were in pesos. So, when the peso depreciated because of the crisis that started in Thailand, clearly, the debt has grown very much and very high. Then, if your assets are real estate, they are falling [in value]. Clearly, a lot of people are in trouble. That is the first thing.

The other problem, of course, is banks are engaged in maturity transformation. They finance loans that take time to be paid [with deposits], but the depositor can change his mind and withdraw his money quickly or in a few days. Clearly, the issues have to do with the governance of banks: how well-capitalized they are, how liquid they are, and how exposed they are.

Philippine banks remain strong and stable amid global banking developments 

Of course, Philippine banks are not as badly affected by the [recent banking] crisis in the United States (US) [where the proximate cause was the interest rate increases of the US Federal Reserve (US Fed) in response to domestic inflation]. As it [the US Fed] increased interest rates, bond prices fell, and some banks were in trouble. 

In the Philippines, that does not seem to be the case because of two reasons: First, we were not starting from a zero interest rate; we were starting from [a policy rate of] 2.0 percent [in November 2020]. The second reason, our [policy rate of] 2.0 percent was there for less than a year [from November 2020 to May 2022], whereas it was zero in the US for a long time. And, as I already said, our banks are well-capitalized.

The task ahead

The point is, spotting financial instability and when it could happen is not easy because it is a combination of many things: What is the source of the crisis? Is it a crisis from abroad that is spreading contagion? How many imbalances and mismatches are there in the major economic players? 

What to expect from the financial stability exhibit

I guess, this is what we have to keep understanding because it is so complex. Many factors have to come together—some domestic, some foreign. We must watch out for anything that we can imagine is relevant.

Therefore, this exhibit [is important]. In this exhibit, you will hear from our Monetary Board Members about why a failed bank is not necessarily going to create a crisis for the system. Of course, we have our own terminologies. Some banks are called “domestically systemically important banks.” If they fail, the central bank is under even greater pressure to help it rather than just close it.  

In closing, let me thank OSRM for mounting this exhibit and our colleagues who made this possible. 

This exhibit is a collective step forward on the new frontier of developing and increasing our ability in spotting potential crises, potential instability, and therefore, prevent them from happening. 

I urge everyone to take advantage of the available information, listen to the videos, read the boards, and join us in managing the challenges ahead. 

By the way, when I was going through the exhibit, my first impression is how photogenic most of my colleagues are on the Monetary Board. Maraming salamat po, and I hope you will enjoy watching the exhibit.  


###

Title: From ‘Nowhere’ to ‘Now Here’: The CRD as a Step Toward a Vibrant Financing Ecosystem for SMEs
Occasion: Credit Risk Database Scoring Model Launch
Speaker: BSP Governor Felipe M. Medalla
Transcription:
​

Ambassador Koshikawa Kazuhiko; JICA [Japan International Cooperation Agency] Chief Representative Sakamoto Takema; the Credit Risk Database (CRD) Japan expert team; representatives of participating banks, especially my friend, [Rizal Commercial Banking Corporation Chief Executive Officer] Eugene [Acevedo]; and, of course, the three [industry] associations that we are all familiar with—the association of banks [Bankers Association of the Philippines], thrift banks [Chamber of Thrift Banks], and rural banks [Rural Bankers Association of the Philippines]—to whom I have given two or three speeches in the course of the past year. So, they are probably bored seeing me. Of course, to all our friends and to all BSPers, konnichiwa! 

It is my honor to join you all today for the launch of the CRD scoring model. We have heard from our esteemed guests, the previous speakers, about the promise of this approach and look forward to the many exciting possibilities. 

How myopic policies sometimes start with good intentions

Now, I am going extemporaneous. One of the reasons that I strongly believe in this [program] is that from the premise that MSMEs [micro, small, and medium enterprises] are important come very bad policies [to support them], like “Banks must lend X percent of their loans to SMEs [small and medium enterprises].” The problem is that it becomes a one-size-fits-all policy. 

One example of that, for instance, is a highly specialized Japanese bank—with less than a hundred employees and focused on lending to Japanese firms in the Philippines—is being told to lend to MSMEs and agriculture. Most of them end up saying, “We must just pay the fines [for non-compliance].” It is a terrible thing. It is a tax on foreign investors who want to help the Philippine economy—this one-size-fits-all policy.

Another terrible example is, rural banks are being penalized for not lending enough to MSMEs when, in fact, some medium-scale industries are bigger than some rural banks. You can see that, sometimes, good intentions lead to bad policies. 

The last time that I went to Malacañang to join a meeting with the President and his Cabinet, they realized that 70 percent of bank lending is mandated by one law or the other. For that reason, my friend, Eugene, will become a bureaucrat. He will just be following those [loan] allocations.

In other words, a better way of doing things must be done. And as with many things, sometimes, little changes could mean a lot. 

That is why I like [JICA Chief Representative] Sakamoto-san’s way of putting it: “Nowhere” can become “now here” just by putting the letter ‘w’ from the second word to the first. Of course, many changes are not like that where one change changes everything, from “nowhere” to “now here.” I wish many things can become better just by moving one letter, but this is about as close to it as we can get. In the general order of expenditures, it is not a lot but a very big beginning.

SMEs turn to families as a way to raise funds 

The other side of it is my personal experience. I look at my friends who are successful businessmen. Many of them started by borrowing from relatives. If your relatives cannot trust you [to lend you money], who will, right? The worst part is when you have to borrow from your father-in-law. Some of my friends did that; they must have really wanted to go into business to do that. 

Unfortunately, that is probably worse than collateral-based lending. Not all of us have collateral; not all of us have fathers-in-law who are willing to lend us money. We really have to move away from that.

Although there is such a thing as graduation, I noticed that some of these friends of mine [who started by borrowing from relatives] got a good start and have very good financial statements now. After 10 to 20 years [of being in business], they have become very bankable. Banks are fighting over each other to lend them money.

But, precisely, the reliance on these things [family relationships] to develop credit will, of course, bypass many people in the economy. 

What happens if you do not have a father-in-law to lend you money? What happens if you do not have collateral?

Shifting to data-driven lending through an analysis of anonymized firm data

Clearly, an approach [to lending] that uses [anonymized] data [is key]. A very important word is “anonymous.” There is no such thing as an “anonymous father-in-law,” for instance. 

As a graduate student of economics, that has always been a holy grail: Knowing the characteristics of a firm, hopefully, predicts where it will locate and so on and so forth.

I think, not only will the CRD scoring model contribute to bridging the funding gap for our SMEs, but it will also enhance the credit risk management of financial institutions. 

From ‘nowhere’ to ‘now here’

If I may, we have a similar related program called the Paleng-QR Ph Plus initiative, which is also driven by the same motivation. That is, if a lot of transactions are done in QR [quick response] payments, this will generate a trail of financial information, which may also improve the quality of lending. 

Many of these things put together will reduce the temptation of legislators to follow one-size-fits-all policies that are very well-intentioned but have a lot of unintended side effects, as I mentioned earlier.

I am very optimistic that “nowhere” will become “now here.” With the help of all our partners, I have no reason to think otherwise. 

Japan as a reliable partner

Before I end, let me thank the government of Japan and JICA for their contributions to the CRD project and their unwavering support of our development efforts. 

In my previous life, I was NEDA [National Economic and Development Authority] director-general. During this time, when the credit risk [between United States and Philippine sovereign debt] was 600 basis points, no other institution was more important to us and no other country was more important to us than JICA and Japan. They have always been with us when we needed them the most.

We thank JICA for extending its technical assistance to the Bangko Sentral for another year, until 31 March 2024. 

Of course, I also thank our 32 CRD participating banks as well as our partner industry associations, government agencies, and academic and research institutions for making this project possible.  

Closing message

We look forward to continued partnership with all of you to keep the CRD project ever-relevant and responsive to the evolving needs of the financial community. As we move forward, let us keep aflame this shared commitment for the benefit of the SME sector in particular and the Filipino people in general. 

Arigatou gozaimasu! Maraming salamat po, at mabuhay tayong lahat! 


###

Title: Carrying the Digital Financial Inclusion Mission Forward
Occasion: 2023 Digital Financial Inclusion Awards Media Launch
Speaker: BSP Governor Felipe M. Medalla
Transcription:
​

Mr. Paul Favila of Citi Philippines; Mr. Gilbert Maramba of the Microfinance Council of the Philippines (MCPI); Mr. Paolo Honrado, president of the Rural Bank of Guinobatan; Ms. Lorie Almazora, our Digital Champions–Microentrepreneur Awardee from the first DFIA [Digital Financial Inclusion Awards]; and, of course, to my fellow advocates for financial inclusion, magandang hapon.

It is an honor to celebrate the second year of the DFIA with you. The DFIA program is very much aligned with our National Strategy for Financial Inclusion (NSFI), which aims to promote inclusive digital finance. 

Nurturing digital-ready entrepreneurs

As the chair of the interagency Financial Inclusion Steering Committee that implements the NSFI 2022–2028, the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP) remains steadfast in leading digitalization efforts and programs to support MSMEs [micro, small, and medium enterprises] and the microfinance sector. 

Let me cite some of the BSP’s initiatives in this area. 

First, our Paleng-QR Ph Plus program maximizes the QR [quick response] Ph initiative and its use in wet markets, local transportation, and business establishments. 

To date, 13 local government units (LGUs) have issued ordinances in support of this program, and we have launched it in seven cities—Baguio, Davao, Tagbilaran, Naga, Lapu-Lapu, Pasig, and Bacolod—and I am glad to share that several other LGUs are considering respective rollouts.

We also actively support the implementation of our national ID [identification] system, PhilSys. By the way, the importance of this ID is very clear: Without e-money [electronic money], the number of people who have formal banking accounts will be less than half of what it is now. In addition, we continue to promote technical assistance for the digitalization initiatives of the microfinance sector.  

With the NSFI 2022–2028 as our guide, we hope to cover more ground with our partners and stakeholders.

Call to join DFIA 2023

This awards program gives us the venue to highlight our inclusive digital finance agenda and microfinance advocacy—not to mention all the inspiring stories that we saw and heard when the awards were given.

We encourage everyone to submit nominations for this year’s DFIA. Last year, we received a total of 53 nominees—47 of which are microentrepreneurs and six are micro-finance institutions. With your help, we hope to receive more this year.  

In closing, let me express our sincere gratitude and appreciation to Citi Philippines and MCPI. I hope that we can continue to build on this fruitful collaboration as we carry our digital financial inclusion mission forward. 

Thank you very much, and good afternoon.

Title: Beyond the Numbers: The Central Bank’s Policy Actions During and Beyond the Pandemic
Occasion: JPMorgan Investor Seminar at the sidelines of the International Monetary Fund-World Bank Spring Meetings
Speaker: BSP Governor Felipe M. Medalla
Transcription:
​

Thanks very much, Mr. Aziz. Should I call you Jahangir? To your team and clients, thank you for the opportunity to present to you, and magandang umaga, which is “good morning” in our language. 

You are right. We were badly hit by the pandemic. We probably had the longest and strictest lockdown in the world. The worst quarter was [in Q2 2020 when there was] a nearly 17-percent [economic] contraction, relative to the same quarter last year. That was where we are coming from, and both the central bank and fiscal authorities, of course, did everything in their power to reduce the impact [of the pandemic] on the economy.

Imagine, if we had not done what we did, maybe, it would have been a 25-percent contraction. The problem was, of course, if the vaccine came late. The reaction was to lock everybody down. 

Taking decisive action on the monetary front 

So, our response [at the central bank] was extraordinary. For the first time, the central bank lent money directly to the government. Under our system, this requires Congressional approval. Of course, the loan has been paid back already.

In addition, because people were panicking and moving to cash, [in order] to prevent bond prices from falling too much, we also bought government securities. Because normally as the Philippine economy needs more money, we purchase foreign exchange (forex), which supplies more money to the economy.

In this particular time and space, the central bank not only lent money directly to the government, but it also bought government securities and cut the policy rates to 200 basis points (bps). 

Growth surprised on the upside

When the vaccine came and hospitalization rates fell drastically, there was normalization, which just happened last year. 

Because of all the things that we have done to prevent the economy from going down and all the stimulus that came in, the economy turned out very, very strong last year, surprising everyone. I think, the World Bank [2022 gross domestic product (GDP)] forecast was 6.0 percent, and the [forecast of the] IMF [International Monetary Fund] was even lower, but the actual growth [for 2022] was 7.6 percent. That [recovery] was largely due to revenge spending and pent-up demand. 

Exit strategy to unwind extraordinary support measures that were already in place

When we cut the policy rates by 400 bps, we already had an exit plan. As soon as the economy recovers—no matter what the inflation is—we will go to a more normal policy rate. The more normal policy rate is higher than the midpoint of our [2.0–4.0 percent] inflation target. If our [midpoint of the] target inflation is 3.0 percent, the policy rate should be higher than 3.0 percent. In other words, we were starting from a policy rate that was quite abnormal, to begin with.

We would have raised it [the policy rate] from 2.0 percent to 3.5 percent even if there was no problem because that was our plan from the very beginning. Once the pandemic is no longer a problem for the economy, there is no need for all these things [accommodative measures]. That was the plan—a gradual exit. 

Global developments pushed the carefully crafted exit plan ahead of schedule

Of course, Uncle Sam changed all of that. We never thought that the US Fed [United States Federal Reserve] will do four 75 bps [hikes] in a row at that time. The exit was a lot faster and sooner than we thought. 

The other thing is the [Ukraine-Russia] war, which made the [prices of] gasoline and flour very expensive. This was the first supply shock. And these two together forced the BSP [Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas] to be very aggressive. As you can see, inflation in the Philippines hit 8.7 percent at the peak [in January 2023].

Month-on-month inflation rose as supply shocks bite

To me, the more telling numbers are the green bars [referring to month-on-month (m-o-m) inflation]. You can see, by March [2022], there is the Ukraine war. [So, m-o-m inflation was] 0.9 percent. Annualized, that is more than 10 percent. By April [2022], [we experienced] another 0.9 percent [in m-o-m inflation]. 

We have not seen this number of shocks in a 10-month period. I looked back at our record as an inflation-targeting central bank. The typical [supply] shock is half as big and half as long as this. That is why in the past, when we have supply shocks, inflation will exceed the inflation target. And, maybe, the longest [streak] is 15 months in a row. This time, we think, it [inflation] will exceed it [the target for] 19–20 months. 

In fact, we thought that in December 2022, it [the peak] was already happening because the m-o-m [inflation] normalized. But then, we were hit by another shock. After the fuel shock, of course, in the Philippines, the cause was onions. We had [one of] the most expensive onions in the world.

In other words, it looks like inflation is sticky. In reality, we were just unlucky. [There was] a series of punches coming. 

The other one was the African Swine Flu. [Since] Asians do not like frozen meat, importing meat is not an option. Then, the supply of vegetables and fruits was destroyed by the very bad weather. 

All of these gave us a 1.0-percent increase in m-o-m [inflation] in January [2023]. Annualized, that is 12 percent. Actually, the number is even more shocking if you do not remove seasonal effects. The m-o-m [inflation in January 2023] was 1.7 percent. 

Above-target consumer price index items increase, crowding out within and below-target items, and demand-side pressures emerge

Then, you can see this. The proportion of [consumer price index (CPI)] items above 4.0 percent [upper end of the inflation target] became very, very high. 

Inflation in the services sector that does not directly use the products that are “under shock” also increased because, of course, they [employees] will ask for higher wages and so on and so forth.

Thankfully, recent inflation prints show signs of e​asing as monetary and non-monetary measures kick in

Now, we are beginning to see, finally, that it [the path of inflation] is normalizing. In fact, the price index in March [2023] is actually slightly lower than the January [2023] price index. So, we have two good m-o-m [inflation prints for] February and March. 

What is happening, of course, is that the policies that we undertook, which I will explain later, plus the imports [worked].

What is holding back inflation is the supply shocks that began to have second-order effects. That is why you can see core inflation, the red line, is actually quite high.

Of course, we revised our inflation forecast, and this was much lower before. Our inflation forecast [for 2023] now is 6.0 percent, but the private sector’s forecast is 6.1 percent. 

By the way, the way we calculate it [full-year inflation forecast] is the average of the 12 [months of] year-on-year headline inflation. 

Note that the [inflation] expectations for next year [by the] private sector is that it [2024 inflation] is now going to be below 4.0 percent, although it is still higher than our forecast. Our own forecast is that it [2024 inflation] is going to be slightly below 3.0 percent next year because we revised downward from the previous policy meeting [in February 2022], when we thought it was going to be 3.1 percent. 

In other words, unless new shocks come in, the direction of the m-o-m changes, and our models say that inflation will be below 4.0 percent starting November or December this year, and [it] will average close to 3.0 percent next year. 

A part of the actions [to stem inflation] are not just monetary. [We have] the importation of key commodities, safety nets for those who are poor, and medium-term strategies to enhance farm productivity. 

JPMorgan Emerging Market Economics Head Jahangir Aziz: The Rice Institute was put together in the 1950s, and we have been waiting for a miracle rice variety since then.

Yeah, [we have th​e] same story about our two countries there. But, I think, the importation helped very much, and now, we are seeing negative [growth in] food prices. Because the [elevated] inflation was largely [driven by] supply shocks, the [tightening] monetary policy settings prevented the supply shocks from being overly magnified. That is the story. 

The other thing that complicated the story was that even at 2.0 percent, our [former] policy rate [during the pandemic] was still significantly higher than the US policy rate. 

But when the US raised the policy rate and the difference [between the two policy rates] became around 1.0 percent, the peso weakened significantly, especially on the back of rising current account deficits. The current account deficit was about US$5.0 billion in 2021 and became US$17.0 billion in 2022.

JPMorgan: Governor, before we move on to the Fed, can I steer it back to core inflation?

Core inflation, in our case, generally—with a lag—starts following the headline [figures]. 

By the way, we are also seeing the m-o-m core going down. For most of the [CPI] items, with a few exceptions, it [inflation] is below 0.3 percent. So, even core [inflation] is going down from the m-o-m [perspective]. 

JPMorgan: And with China normalizing supply [chains], are import prices also coming off that? 

Yes. In addition, when Chinese demand is rising, it is very good for the Philippine economy. The first beneficiary will be tourism because as you can see [in] the size of the two countries, one is 10 times the other. If a small percentage of a billion [people] goes to you, that is a lot of tourists. My other joke there is if every Chinese ate half a banana, that is a big boost to the Philippine banana industry.

The other good news is that the Fed—this is your market saying so—seems to be no longer going to do a big rate adjustment. And, probably, [there will be] just a few more [hikes], right?

JPMorgan: The market has [priced in] this one more rate hike for May, and then, it is a pause. Then, the market’s pricing in the second half [of the year], a significant cut. We [at JPMorgan] do not buy the cut, but we do buy the pause.

At any rate, it is important to us [at the central bank] because when the policy rate difference between us and the US is less than 1.0 percent, the currency weakens. 

It is actually a very simple fact. I asked Filipinos a question: “If the interest rate on a peso instrument is equal to the interest rate of a dollar instrument, which would you prefer?” I have yet to meet a Filipino who likes the peso. I think, in every country, that is true. If the dollar is so special, you must always have a premium over it.

JPMorgan: In terms of the way you think about interest rates, you spoke about real rates at the beginning, right? You wanted real rates to be positive, slightly above the real rate. At the same time, as you rightly pointed out, there is—like every other emerging market—there is a differential that you need to maintain compared to the Fed funds rate. 

Unless you want your currency to depreciate.

JPMorgan: I am guessing you do not want that, and it is one stable exchange. So, all of us in this room are waiting for the Fed to pause for inflation to come down at various speeds across different countries. And central banks in emerging markets, basically, [are] starting an easing cycle. All of us are looking at the same thing: Where and how much can these rates go? So, we are trying to gauge that. 

You talked about benchmarking your interest rates in terms of a positive real rate. Does that positive real rate take into account where the Fed funds [rate] is going to be? Or is that something that—in your heads, at least—you should add to whatever the real rate [is] that you are thinking of?

That is a very nice question. Let us say, our forecast [is] that everyone is certain [that] a pause will happen. So, the real rate will soon be—if we do not do anything—[it] will soon be 6.25 percent, minus 3.0. That is a very high real rate. It is not a very high real rate now, but it will be. It will be a tragedy for us [the peso] if the US policy rate is higher than 3.5 percent. For instance, if the US policy rate is 5.0 percent.

So, what can we do? I think, we will be forced to have a much higher policy rate than you otherwise think.

JPMorgan: That is exactly my question. Suppose you believe the Fed, and the Fed is saying that “We will go on a prolonged pause at, let us say, 5.25, 5.50.” 

Then, it will be very hard for [emerging market] countries. That is why I always keep saying to Philippine markets, “I need just a few data points to know when to pause. I need more data points when to cut.” 

When we will cut is the greatest uncertainty of all. When will we pause? 

JPMorgan: That is fine. But, as you rightly pointed out, if inflation goes down to what your expectations are at 3.0 percent, you are going to open up very, very, very tight monetary conditions, and you might be forced to keep that tightness simply because the Fed does not move.

Yeah. By the way, it has happened before. Their [the US] interest rate was so low that we were forced to have a lower interest rate, too. We were forced to buy a lot of dollars to prevent the peso from appreciating.

So, we are just seeing the other [side of the coin]. Another way to view it is that our reserves went from US$45.0 billion to US$95.0 billion in less than four years. What we are seeing now is the other side of it. Your Q [GDP] and your R [interest rate] are clearly affected by what happens to those rates [in the US]. 

So, that is why I am completely silent on when we will cut. I am more vocal about when, we think, we will pause.

JPMorgan: But will not there be pressure coming from the domestic side of the economy, given the fact that you are keeping rates too tight and growth slows down?

You are right there. So, the question is: “How much depreciation can society tolerate?” By the way, it [changes in the exchange rate] is very distributive. Some people like it [depreciation] because their relatives are sending money [in dollars] home. The employees of the BSP, whose salaries are based in pesos, do not like it. That is why it is a very, very strong distributive issue. 

I think, what will happen there is that we will be at a midpoint. In some cases, we will accept some depreciation. In some cases, the extent of the depreciation will disanchor inflationary expectations, then you will have to have a tight monetary policy.

JPMorgan: Governor, would I be wrong if I summarize what you just said that in the event the Fed keeps rates or pause for a long enough time, if inflation starts rolling off, then you will be easing but easing cautiously?

Yes, we are watching how fast the Fed will adjust rates. But, I think, we have already learned our lesson. A policy rate difference of 75 bps or 50 bps is a formula for a perpetually depreciating peso. By the way, you will see this in the next chart. You can see the peak [depreciation] of this chart is in October [2022] when year-to-date, from January 2022 to October 2022, [depreciation] was at 13 percent. 

By the way, when something like that happens, people will forget the central bank’s inflation target. Nobody will believe you. 

Now, what did we do? Of course, we raised policy rates. We raised it more than other people, and we sold forex.  

But you will notice that our selling of forex reserves is aligned with the actions of other central banks in the region. We sold about 7.9 percent of our forex reserves [from end-2021 to end-2022]. Korea sold 8.0 percent, and India [sold] 11 percent [over the same period]. The outliers are Indonesia [which added 0.2 percent] and Malaysia [which sold 1.2 percent] because they actually benefit from the oil boom. The other outlier is Vietnam, [which sold] 19.9 percent. But everyone, more or less, is in that 8.0–9.0 percent [range]. 

By the way, we were not comparing notes. We just ended up doing the same thing. 

JPMorgan: For those who are here for the session on Indonesia, I asked the same question. The question was the fact that three Asian countries, India, Indonesia, and the Philippines—all three of them, use multiple instruments in basically doing flexible inflation-targeting—I am using that euphemism— which has a lot of trade-offs between a lot of variables: higher flexibility, what happens to government bond yields, what happens to interest rates, what happens to inflation, and what happens to growth. Does that framework allow you to deliver better outcomes than, let us say, [if] your hands were tied by a central bank act that said that you have to meet this target and you can only use interest rates as an instrument?

Yes, I think. For instance, if we had not accumulated forex, our output would have been much lower. Because our finding is that when the currency is appreciating, the translation [exchange rate pass-through to inflation] to lower prices is lower than when it is depreciating. 

This means that your competitiveness will fall if your currency is appreciating and prices are not falling. ‘E’ divided by ‘p’ is falling. By ‘E,’ I mean the number of pesos per dollar. It will destroy not just your export industry but your import-substituting [and] manufacturing. All of those things will fall. 

Therefore, the central bank that prevents the currency from appreciating does better during this period. But because it also did that, it now has the weapons [forex reserves] to intervene when the other thing [depreciation] is going on.

JPMorgan: I am sure the Treasury really liked the fact that you have a lot of profits to be given to them this year.

No, it cannot be given to them. This is the nice thing about the Philippines. The losses cannot be declared as dividends because they are unrealized. 

Taking a regional perspective: Examining the Philippine central bank’s actions against its peers

You noticed that, of course, we did [raise the policy rate by] three 25 bps. If we had not had abnormally low policy rates because of the pandemic, we would be more like South Korea [which raised their policy rate by a cumulative 300 bps]. [A policy rate of] 200 bps was really too low, to begin with. 

We are more like South Korea and India. We are not that different either. It is just that we were more aggressive during the pandemic because our lockdowns were longer and more painful. There is an explanation for why we were different, but it is really amazing how similarly [we acted]. Either we are all stupid or we are all smart, right? 

JPMorgan: I mean, if you assess inflation, you may find that inflationary outcomes in all of these countries are also very similar.

[That is] right, although the differences, again, will be the [per country] peculiarities. In the case of the Philippines, [it was] overprotection of agriculture and bad weather [that pushed up inflation]. 

You can see it: The economy contracted by nearly 17 percent in Q2 2020. What is scarier was the 0.7-percent [contraction in Q1 2020] because there was a lockdown for only one-eighth of the quarter. So, if you multiply it by eight, you will see how it was already very bad during the last week of the first quarter. 

But, as you can see, there is a very strong recovery. As I already said, the [full-year] recovery last year surprised most of us, including us—most analysts, including us, although we are less surprised than others. 

Now, we expect the economy to grow by about 6.0 percent. The range there is the government’s target, but, I think, our forecast [at the central bank] is 6.0 percent next year.

JPMorgan: Does that 6.0 percent forecast that you are looking forward to now, when you think about this year, the global economy, [and] what the Fed will be doing—we are all talking about recession risks happening somewhere down the road—when you think about that 6.0 percent, do you think that you will be needing major cuts to reap that 6.0 percent if the Fed allows you? Or do you think that the export sector of the Philippines will remain robust in order for you to be able to deliver 6.0–7.0 percent because China will be delivering a much stronger growth rate?

By the way, the upside risk of our [GDP] forecast is that China ends up being stronger [than forecasted]. 

JPMorgan: But the linkages of the Philippines are stronger with China than the US?

Yes. Right now, our biggest export market is China. 

The other difference is that our great dependence on the West is, as it turns out, not as sensitive to Western economic growth. For instance, we noticed that there is a long pattern when remittances are not very sensitive to US recession. And that is because, I guess, they really need the nurses [from the Philippines] no matter what. 

Then, BPOs [business process outsourcing revenues] also turn out to be quite resilient because, I think, the difference between Filipino [labor] cost and the US cost is quite high. 

That is the difference. Our forex receipts are a lot more resilient because they are not goods.

JPMorgan: We were talking about this in the India session. Typically, when the US goes into recession to cut down costs even more, the outsourcing demand—

[It] actually increases. In other words, the countries that are more dependent on goods exports are more vulnerable. 

I think, more or less, [I] have covered the picture. But my point was that the reason we are quite confident that the m-o-m [inflation] figures will eventually bring us very quickly to normal inflation is that we are quite aggressive in our policy rate changes. 

One of the reasons we are aggressive is that we are confident that high policy rates will not destabilize our banks. When you look at their balance sheets, they actually hold some government securities.
