It is clear that they will take a loss [due to tightening financial conditions], but their gain from the higher interest rate will offset that.

Actually, if there is anything that should scare us, [it] is a rise in non-performing loans. But that will happen only if we have a very weak economy. It has happened in 1997 when overpriced assets plunged.

JPMorgan: Related to your banking sector, one of the reasons as to why I am guessing you are confident to address this is because you also have a very high reserve requirement.

Yes, but we actually cut it from 20 percent to 12 percent. If not for the fact that we are raising policy rates, the reserve requirement will now be either 9.0 or 10 percent.

JPMorgan: Because it is still much higher than in the region, when we look toward easing monetary conditions—generally, if you are not able to because of the interest rate differential with the US, if you are not able to cut policy rates as much because you have to consider what has happened—

We can cut the reserve requirement. We have one more ace. By the way, it [the high reserve requirement] is not something that you like to keep anyway because what you will find is that there will be regulatory arbitrage. It turns out that it is a blessing that despite the high reserve requirement, there was not much arbitrage. The reason that we want to cut it, even if it is not needed by the economy, is that we were afraid that we will be killing the institutions that can be regulated and making money move to institutions that cannot be regulated. 

That is the picture. The fact that we have a high reserve requirement actually turns out to be an accidental plus, which we are already planning to cut anyway.

Financial stability as a pillar of strength

As I said, the banks are strong. Lending growth has recovered to 10 percent in February, although there is some slowdown in real estate, it probably is a good thing. This is really always the sector that causes us troubles later on. 

By the way, one of the reasons the real estate [sector] slowed down is one of the biggest reasons for the increase in real estate demand. [It] was [that] online gaming from China was being housed in the Philippines—POGOs [Philippine Offshore Gaming Operators], as we call it. The Chinese government does not like it. So, we decided that it is too much trouble. So, we are also probably phasing it out. That is the other reason that real estate loans have slowed down. 

This is the reason the Philippine banking system is strong: limited exposure to banks in the US that closed, generally lower balance sheet vulnerabilities, then, of course, sufficient capital. 

And [banks are] quite liquid because as we were reducing the reserve requirements, we were introducing liquidity regulations. The two most important ones are the liquidity coverage ratio and the net stable funding ratio. We were afraid that if a bank is too dependent on large depositors, when those large depositors run [to withdraw], they are in trouble. So, we have regulations around that. 

Digital payments on the rise

These are the other stories. We are becoming more digital. We have two [payment] systems: one is PESONet, which operates a batch processing system. You can use your phone to make transfers and transfer larger amounts, but it is [processed via] batch. If you enter your request by 8:00 a.m., it will probably be transferred between 11:30 a.m. and 12:00 p.m. If you do it after 12:00 p.m., it is probably transferred between 4:30 p.m. and 5:30 p.m. As you can see, in a short time, I think, it will overtake checks. By the way, the checks are not such a big problem either because what is happening now is you can scan the check with your phone, then it is [the cash] deposited. 

And then, [we have transactions via the fast payment system] InstaPay, where the limit of transactions is about ₱50,000 or less than a thousand [dollars], [which] is also growing. 

We are really more ambitious here. ASEAN [Association of Southeast Asian Nations] has a program where cross-border payments will be used by phone, using “Nexus”—the platform developed by the Bank for International Settlements. 

In addition, we want to standardize our QR [quick response] system so that even the operators of the tricycle, tuk-tuk, and jeepney should be able to receive QR payments.

The Philippines can and has safeguarded both price and financial stability 

This is essentially the message. Our main focus is price and financial stability. Thank God, the tools we need for price stability have not been restricted by financial stability. 

We have a regulatory landscape that, I think, remains sound, stable, and supportive of economic growth.

I forgot to say that our independence is embedded in the Constitution. 

Guided by three pillars, we continue to adapt to the changing needs and evolving economic landscape. Then, sometimes, we are just lucky, like you said, we have high reserve requirements. So, if we cannot cut policy rates because of US inflation, we can actually just reduce the reserve requirements.

Title: Responding to a “Tag Team” of Inflationary Pressures
Occasion: Barclays’ Emerging Markets Roundtable at the sidelines of the International Monetary Fund-World Bank Spring Meetings
Speaker: BSP Governor Felipe M. Medalla
Transcription:
​

Good morning and thank you, [Barclays Managing Director and Head of Emerging Asia Economics Research] Rahul Bajoria, the Barclays team, and your clients. As they say in the Philippines, magandang umaga. 

Central bank independence and the three pillars

I will start by saying that we are an independent central bank, and our independence is enshrined in our Constitution. It was rewritten in 1987, and the law that implemented the requirements of the Constitution for our independence was done [passed] three or four years later. 

Later on, 10 or 12 years later, we decided to be an inflation-targeting central bank, after New Zealand and Australia. That turned out to be very consistent with our mandate, which you can see in the next slide—price stability. We define price stability as [an inflation target of] 2.0–4.0 percent, but we always say [that our target is] 3.0 percent ± 1.0 [percentage point (ppt)].

Financial stability is our second pillar, although we [at the central bank] only regulate banks. Other agencies regulate the private bonds and the stock market—that is the [purview of the] Securities and Exchange Commission. Then, longer-term capital insurance is regulated by another agency called the Insurance Commission. The three of us [together with the Department of Finance], we are what is called the Financial Stability Coordination Council. But the Philippines is very bank-centric because our capital markets are less developed. In that sense, much of the action that comes with the Fed’s [United States Federal Reserve] response to financial stability is undertaken by the central bank.

Finally, we have a third objective, which is a safe, secure, and efficient payments system. This used to be boring until it became exciting because of digital payments. I will talk mostly very little about the two [pillars] and spend more time on the first [pillar] because all the problems are in the first.

Headline and core inflation remain elevated but month-on-month figures point to signs of easing

The next slide shows you the problem. Inflation is high whenever you look at the headline or core [figures]. The good news is that it seems to have peaked in January [2023]. We thought, initially, that it will peak in November [2022], but there are several supply shocks that postponed the peak. 

The easier way to understand inflation and its momentum is the little bars below: These are the month-on-month (m-o-m) inflation [numbers]. The reason we do not explain that too much to the public is that we have to adjust it for seasonality. For instance, 1.7 percent m-o-m inflation in January translates to what? 18 or 19 percent [in annualized inflation] if that had continued for 12 months. 

It turns out that since January is price adjustment month, if you adjust for seasonality, that 1.7 percent [on a non-seasonally adjusted basis] is just 1.0 percent [on a seasonally adjusted basis]. But it is still large, right? 

Last January, we had the biggest [m-o-m] inflation in just one month. Adjusted for the seasonality, the January price index is 1.0 percent higher. If that [trend in m-o-m inflation] were to continue, we will have 12 percent [annualized] inflation. 

Fortunately, our view is that [it is] not the case. We initially thought that it already peaked because it [m-o-m inflation] fell to 0.3 percent [in November 2022]; but then, it rose to 1.0 percent [in January 2023]. So, now, we are seeing a more consistent [downward] pattern, and the new price index in March [2023] is actually slightly lower than the January price index.

Of course, that [downward trend] cannot continue. [Otherwise], we will have a period of negative inflation. Of course, we will adjust for seasonality. It is just that—the two-month period of zero m-o-m inflation. That is the reason we are confident. [That is] because the factors that cause much of the inflation are largely supply shocks. Unless there are new supply shocks, we are on our way toward our target of 2.0–4.0 percent.

Identifying the “tag team” of back-to-back supply shocks

Historically, the supply shocks [driving inflation] will go on for many months. The longest period where we have about 4.0 percent [above-target] inflation was 15 months. As you can see, though, in this particular period, nearly every month is a “shock” month.

The way I see it—for those of you who watched wrestling when you were young—it is like having a tag team. When the bad guys are beating up the good guys and he gets tired, he calls the other guy to beat him up. Then, they take turns beating him. Eventually, the good guys win, but it does go on for quite a long time. 

So, what was our tag team? Nearly everything! Initially, the Ukraine-Russia war made fuel expensive. Our price watcher watches the cost of operating a private vehicle. Many people go to work either on a motorcycle or [a] car, and those [prices] spiked a lot. 

On top of that, food and flour prices went up—that is the first spike. Then, just as we thought it was beginning to wane, another set [of supply shocks hit]. We had a sugar shortage. The price of sugar nearly doubled. Between July and December last year, it increased by nearly 50 percent in six months. 

Later on, we had a meat problem because of the African Swine Fever. We had to slaughter nearly all our pigs because we did not want it [the disease] to spread. Unfortunately, in this case, there is a very strong preference for fresh meat so importing does not help very much. 

Later on, we had bad weather that hit [the supply of] vegetables. We call it—if we are using a Spanish word—the sibuyas problem, which is onions [once translated]. We probably had the most expensive onions in the world because we have a very protectionist policy for farmers. “Oh, our farmers are poor. We should not import.” In this case, we should import because it [the price] was really very high. Unfortunately, the import was delayed, precisely, because of this fear of hurting farmers. 

Then, later on, you had [supply shocks from] fruits and vegetables.

Demand-side pressures on inflation starting to manifest

Because the economy was very strong, we were expecting it to grow 6.5 percent last year, but it ended up growing 7.6 percent [in 2023]. 

In the latter part of the year, we had a little bit of demand [pressures] in inflation [in addition to supply-side pressures]. We are seeing that in higher rentals. 

Path of inflation already target-consistent

Our forecast, essentially, is that the average year-on-year inflation over the last 12 months of this year will be around 6.0 percent, although we will most likely revise this downward. 

As you can see, the path of inflation that we see is that by November or December this year and by next year, inflation will already be below 4.0 percent. 

Non-monetary interventions already coming online to ease supply-side pressures

I already talked about the commodities that we started to import. It was the first time that politicians have said, “Maybe this time, the farmers are not going to complain too much if we import.” This is what is bringing down a lot of the prices. 

This time, politics swung in favor of the consumer. But generally, the politics is pro-farmer. “Oh, these poor farmers.” “Oh, we should not import rice because people who supply rice, when they have shortages [in their home countries], they ban exports.” By the way, a lot of other countries have done that. But if the price is too high, then clearly, that does not make sense anymore. 

So, the government responded this time and said, “Under extraordinary times, we will be importing.” That is why food inflation actually became negative in the last three months [of 2023]—January, February, and March. 

On the Fed and the exchange rate

Of course, what the Fed does also affects us. In the past, our policy rate was comfortably higher than the Fed policy rate. 

The problem was, after the last increases in the Fed policy rates, the differential between our policy rate and the Fed actually became about 1.0 percent. We found out that at that range, people put a premium on the dollar [since] the dollar is supposed to be a safe haven. The moment you have a differential smaller than that [1.0–1.25 ppts], the peso starts to depreciate. 

Normally, we do not react to the exchange rate, [except to smoothen excessive volatility], but [it is different], given that inflation is very high and given that the depreciation of the peso was large and continuous. From January to October last year, the peso depreciated by 14 percent. 

With these two factors together, we [at the central bank] had two responses: We significantly raised the policy rate, and the other one was we sold foreign exchange (forex). 

And you can see, it starts to work. The moment we started doing that [tightening policy], the peso started to appreciate. In fact, since January [to 4 April 2023], it actually appreciated by about 2.0 percent. The exchange rate is no longer a driver of inflation. 

In addition, our current account improved because remittances and BPO [business process outsourcing] earnings started to support the peso. 

As a result, after our forex reserves declined because we sold [forex reserves] to support the peso, our reserves started to recover. It went as low as US$90 billion. Now, it is back to a hundred billion dollars [as of end-March 2023].

Maximizing expanded use of the inflation-fighting toolkit

This is what we did. You note that the Philippines increased the policy rate much more than any country in that table. We are the most aggressive central bank in responding to both the weak dollar and the high inflation. 

Some have criticized me and said, “It is a supply shock. Why are you responding with interest rates?” The answer is simple. If we do not do anything, inflation will start migrating to other products, which we were already seeing. 

In addition, as I have already said, we sold forex. As you can see in the chart, we are not very different from South Korea, Thailand, and India. The outlier there is Vietnam; it sold 19.9 percent of its forex reserves. The other outliers, on the other side, are Indonesia and Malaysia that hardly sold anything [from their forex reserves]. Of course, those two countries actually benefited from the high commodity prices, and they have no reason to do so.  

In summary, the toolbox is very simple: interest rates to address inflation and forex intervention to address excessive depreciation of the currency, although the increasing interest rates already partially address the depreciating currency.

Managing expectations through forward guidance 

While we are doing all of this, we are constantly telling the public why we are doing what we are doing. 

By the way, the best sign of that is: Every time we have a policy meeting, 90 percent of the analysts predict exactly what we [at the central bank] will do. Maybe they joke among themselves that, maybe, the guy who makes a mistake should be fired. 

Pent-up demand driving the economy forward

The other thing I can say is that the economy remains strong in spite of all of these. Indeed, as I said, the economy grew by 7.6 percent last year. And this year, it is expected to grow by nearly 6.0–6.5 percent, although the World Bank (WB) and the IMF [International Monetary Fund] are saying [that it will grow at a slightly slower pace of] 5.5 percent. 

The head of the WB in the Philippines and the region was in our economic briefing, and he was the commentator. He said, “We think we are right [in forecasting future gross domestic product growth], but we are praying we are wrong.”

Why is the economy strong? Part of it is pent-up demand. During the pandemic, people postponed purchases for years. Why buy a car when you are not allowed to use it? You did not want to go anywhere because you might contract the virus. Some people did not go to restaurants. Some people even postponed weddings. 

Finally, [pent-up demand surged] when people saw that infections were going down and the hospitalization rate was extremely low. By the way, we keep track of infection rates in the Bangko Sentral [ng Pilipinas (BSP)]. All our hospitalizations were prior to vaccination.

This resulted in a strong recovery of the economy. They called it “revenge spending” or “pent-up demand.” You can see this in tourism. You can see that in restaurants—by the way, restaurants contributed partially to inflation because they raised prices. What happened was some of the restaurants closed [due to the pandemic], and the ones that stayed alive are struggling.

Unemployment actually went down, and there is a very quick recovery of domestic tourism. The kids of my neighbors decided to get married in Boracay.

Financial stability: a pillar of strength

Let me proceed with the topics that I do not want to spend any time on because there are hardly any problems there. 

[On] financial stability: Our banks are very strong. Indeed, when we raise interest rates, their holdings of government securities, the price went down. But their gain from the higher profits from the higher interest rates more than wiped out the loss from their government securities holdings.  The reason they are very strong is that they are quite liquid because we have regulations on liquidity. The two most important [liquidity] ratios are liquidity coverage ratio and net stable funding ratio. 

Right now, they [the banks] decided to place much of their liquidity with us [at the central bank] because, under the new law, we are now allowed to not just borrow from banks, but we can also borrow from the public. That is the other news: The tools that we have to do what we have to do are much stronger now than before. 

During the recovery [of the economy], loans also recovered quickly. We also adopted Basel [capitalization] standards very quickly a long time ago. 

The third pillar: no less important

The last item [pillar] is digital payments. We have two systems [clearinghouses]—one is PESONet. PESONet is a substitute for checks. It is a batch process. For instance, you use your phone to make a transfer. Anything that you do before 12 o’clock, the transfer will happen at around 1 o’clock. Anything that you do after 12 o’clock, the money will be transferred before 6 o’clock. Even the physical checks, you no longer have to physically [go to the bank]. You can take a picture of your check or scan it, and the bank will accept it as a deposit. 

In addition, we have a fast payment system called InstaPay, and transactions there are growing very, very fast. Our goal is a QR [quick response] payment system that even small merchants and taxi drivers can scan [using] a QR code.

Preserving price and financial stability

In summary, the BSP is able to address both price and financial stability because its main tool for price stability, the interest rate, is unconstrained because we have very strong banks. 

We will continue, of course, to make sure that banks remain sound and that domestic systematically important banks (DSIBs), they’re required [to put up] more capital than the average bank. 

Despite the fact that our inflation is much higher than what we are used to, we are confident that we have taken sufficient monetary action to pull it down, and the government, in turn, has loosened protectionism and temporarily relaxed restrictions on imports of food. That means the supply side [pressures on inflation] are also addressed.

Thank you very much for your patience, and we are eager to listen and answer your questions.

Title: The Central Bank’s Inflation-Fighting Playbook
Occasion: Bank of America Small Talks Symposium at the sidelines of the 2023 International Monetary Fund-World Bank Spring Meetings in Washington
Speaker: BSP Governor Felipe M. Medalla
Transcription:
​

We [at the central bank] have three pillars: price stability, financial stability—on financial stability, we have to work with two other regulatory bodies [the Securities and Exchange Commission and the Insurance Commission]—and then, of course, the payments and settlements system. I will not talk much about the last two [pillars] because the problems are not there. 

Payments digitalization on the rise

All I can say about the payment system is, it used to be boring; now, it is one of the most exciting due to digital payments. The principal contribution is [because of] the two systems: [The first is] PESONet, which does batch processing and allows large transfers. Then, we have the fast payment system that we call InstaPay, where it is almost real-time. Both are doing very well. 

Financial stability: a pillar of strength

On the other hand, what I can say about [financial] stability is that banks in the Philippines are strong. They are well capitalized.

Because of that [strength], it is not a constraint on how high we can raise the policy rate. The usual concern [following the collapse of Silicon Valley Bank] is that if you [the central bank] raise the policy rate too much, the banks themselves that hold a lot of government securities would take a loss, and, therefore, the higher policy rate becomes a threat to financial stability. In the Philippines, that is not the case. Effectively, we have what is called the “Tinbergen rule”: tools for price stability, tools for financial stability, and, of course, tools for payments system.

We Filipinos call it “lifting your own bench” when you are praising yourself. I am doing a little bench lifting [when I say that] because of that, we [at the central bank] are able to do quite well in responding to the challenges.

Narrowing interest rate differential weighed on the peso, which, in turn, added to inflationary pressures

Now, the challenges. Of course, loose monetary policy itself became a challenge. In the past, we cared very little about the effect of US [United States] policy rate changes because the gap between our policy rate and their policy rate was high.

But then, as the two policy rates became close, Philippine markets think that the peso should depreciate if the policy rate differential is too small. They think that there should be a premium for the dollar. So, as the US policy rate rose, the peso weakened.

Normally, we [at the central bank] did not care too much about it because the exchange rate changes were not large. Under normal times, changes in the exchange rate do not translate much to inflation for two reasons: [First,] the changes are not large, and [second,] the changes can go both ways.

Of course, the problem is, as the US policy rate rose, the peso fell. It also happened when the current account is large because of the high price of imports.

From January last year to October last year, the peso depreciated. It was depreciating every week, every month. So, we were afraid that if we let that happen continuously, nobody would believe our inflation targets anymore. Inflationary expectations will be disanchored.

Now, all of these were happening with the Ukraine-Russia war, which raised transportation costs. By the way, our statistical office estimates how much gasoline a person with a motorcycle uses per day and how much gasoline a person who drives to work [uses] every day. They generate a big part of the inflation number from that. Then, of course, the cost of fertilizer and flour [rose]. So, the result is very high inflation that is accompanied by a rapidly deteriorating exchange rate.

Taking action appropriate for an unprecedented time

So, we had to act. By the way, I am an accidental Governor. The reason I became the Governor is that the President wanted the [former] Governor [Ben Diokno] to be the secretary of finance. I was on the Monetary Board for 11 years, and I was the logical person to continue what he was doing.

The first central bank governor [whose term I am serving] died. There are actually three governors serving the same term because the [Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas] Governor gets a six-year term. I got the last year of the term, and I ended up raising policy rates more than the first two governors. This was from 200 basis points (bps) to 625 bps. 

But in spite of that, there are still pressures on the currency to depreciate. We sold 9.0–10.0 percent of our forex [foreign exchange] reserves. It did work. The peso, starting in October, recovered some of its losses. Year-to-date [from 1 January to 4 April 2023], it has appreciated [by] 2.0 percent.

Supply-side pressures add to the inflation problem

To complicate things, there were shortages that arose from supply shocks to agriculture. In an economy that can freely import agricultural goods, this would not have been a serious problem.

The problem is, because of politics, policies are designed to heavily protect the farmers [and restrict imports] so shortages have [caused] very large spikes in [the prices of] sugar, vegetables, fruits, [and] meat. These came in a sequence.

Month-on-month inflation on the rise

You can see this in the chart. The green bars below are month-on-month (m-o-m) inflation. What you will see there is, if you look at 12 months that ended in March this year, all the m-o-m changes in the price index—every number, except for two [months]—were much higher than what is consistent with our target.

The first bad month was March [2022]. It [seasonally adjusted m-o-m inflation] was 0.9 percent in just one month, followed by another 0.9 percent [in April 2022], and this was caused by the Ukraine war. As that was fading, we got another 0.9 percent [m-o-m inflation] in October [2022]. These are [caused by] agriculture [shortages, such as] sugar, the price of which increased by 50 percent in the last six months of last year. Later on, [we had] bad weather [that affected key agricultural items].

The worst one was January 2023, when it [m-o-m inflation] was 1.7 percent. But if we adjust it for seasonality, we end up with 1.0 percent.

Bank of America (BofA) Global Research Managing Director and Co-Head for Asia Foreign Exchange and Rates Strategy Claudio Piron: But I see you got a zero?

Yes.

BofA: So, is it mission accomplished?

It seems. But as they say, two birds do not make a spring. By the way, we thought the first 0.3 percent [m-o-m inflation in December 2022] was it [the peak] already because 0.3 times 12 [is within our target]. We thought that the supply shocks—because of our aggressive policy [rate] changes, because we were able to see the peso start to appreciate—we thought we have killed it [elevated inflation] already, and then, another big shock [in January 2023].

By the way, it became a joke because what happened was, the thing that became most expensive were onions. It became almost like jewelry now. But then, there was a swing in public opinion. “While we support the farmers, we think, it is about time we start importing again.” That is why we are now beginning to see negative m-o-m [inflation].

On the other hand, the pure momentum—what we call “knock-on effects”—from the first three major groups of shocks is still there. You have negative food [inflation] now, and, in addition, there are other things that are idiosyncratic, like we periodically raise the tax on cigarettes, what we call “sin taxes.” So, at the beginning of the year, there is a spike in tobacco and alcoholic products.

Mission accomplished? Inflation expected to settle within target by end-2023

But at the same time, our forecast is with what we have done. Of course, we probably slowed down the economy a bit. The fact that the peso is now much stronger, we cannot see inflation having its own momentum without new shocks.

Then, our forecast is in the absence of shocks. We expect inflation to fall below 4.0 percent by November, December [2023].

Indeed, we have a little anomaly, which is when we hit January next year, because of the very high base, inflation will actually be below 2.0 percent.

BofA: So, there is some suggestion that you are considering a pause?

Yes. I myself said that if the next month, April, is another below 0.3 percent [m-o-m inflation month], then we have a little more confidence that the trend, the decline in inflation [is more apparent], and the supply shocks have finally completely waned.

By the way, the way we report it, the inflation number for the year is the average of the 12 headline [inflation numbers]. So, if you have 8.0 percent inflation in January and 4.0 percent at the end of the year, the [full-year] average is, more or less, 6.0 percent.

By the way, this pattern is observed many times in the past. The longest streak of above 4.0 percent inflation that we have is about 15 months.

But these [current] shocks are particularly long and enlarged so we may have 19 or 20 months of above-target inflation. The good news is that people think that it is not the fault of the central bank because everybody knows that these are supply shocks.

By the way, this is one importance of our communication. We do not guarantee. We tell the people that monetary policy cannot stop supply shocks. All it can do is prevent second-order effects, making supply shocks turn into a much longer period.

BofA: And you can substantiate this? What about inflation expectations?

Yes. That is the other chart. Despite the high inflation in 2022 and 2023, inflation expectations for 2024 and 2025 are now within target. What we found is, they [the private sector] follow ours [central bank inflation forecasts], with a lag. So, if we are wrong, then we are wrong. And, of course, we will be wrong if there are supply shocks.

Private [sector inflation] forecasts are 3.7 percent [for 2024], but as you can see, ours is 2.9 percent. But we are not too worried about this. This happens every time we have high inflation. It takes time, a couple of months, for private-sector forecasts to converge with ours.

BofA: Is there a better way of coordinating [with fiscal authorities] or timing the cigarette price hikes, for instance?

That is hard to do. The problem if you postpone a tax, the temporary becomes permanent. It is dangerous to play with tax rates.

Actually, the coordination should have been [focused on] to allow imports faster. But again, the politics there is to protect the farmers. The other reason they want to protect the farmers is, the countries that supply us will stop exporting when they have shortages. It is better to have our own farmers even if they are more expensive. At least, they will always be supplying to us. Again, as an economist, I tell them, the solution to that is stocking [building inventories]. But economists never win debates when you have this very emotional [issue].

As shown in the next slide, the measures taken by the government are beginning to work [on easing supply-side pressures on inflation].

Waning pressure to match the Fed step by step

In addition, our forecast is that there will no longer be jumbo policy rate adjustments by the US [Federal Reserve (US Fed)].

In fact, when you look at the yield curve, it shows that eventually, the markets expect them [the Fed] to cut. In that setting, the big pressure for us to raise rates, we think, is no longer there. That is why I suggested that, maybe, this time, we can pause.

When we will start cutting is harder to predict. We need more very low or normal data points. Second, even if inflation becomes lower, it is hard for our policy rate to be lower than the US. Consider this scenario: The US keeps their policy rate where it is now, at 5.0, then inflation goes down, too.

BofA: Does the same apply on the way down? If the Fed is going to start cutting, you will automatically follow the rule and start cutting with the Fed?

Not if our inflation numbers are bad. When the interest rate differential issue is not important, inflation targeting is not an exchange rate issue. The normal situation is, when changes in the exchange rate are two-way and not large, it is not even a factor in our inflation targeting.

In other words, it becomes several instruments for each objective. The main weapon against inflation is interest rates.

BofA: Will you cut even if the Fed cannot cut?

I think, in this case, if the peso has appreciated, maybe. But at any rate, we will not be cutting very soon because we are still waiting for three or four more good data points. We have been burned before.

Robust external accounts provide strong external cushion

The other thing is, we are quite fortunate that remittances, net foreign direct investments, and robust business processing outsourcing (BPOs) supported [the peso].

What happened was that we had a very large increase in the current account deficit from 2021. Two-thirds of it [the increase in the current account deficit] was due to higher [import] prices. [The remaining] one-third was [due to] higher volume. We are very import-dependent on fuel. With the price of fuel normalizing, our current account is also improving, and remittance is forecast to grow 3.0 percent, BPO revenues at 9.0 percent this year. Actually, the current account relative to GDP [gross domestic product] will shrink from 4.4 percent of GDP last year to 4.0 percent this year.

Drawing from the Asian central bank playbook

By the way, one of the reasons for the large change in policy rate is that we had an abnormally low policy rate.

If you look at this chart, where you have a table on policy rate changes by country, you will see that Asian countries have three things in common: They, more or less, allowed the exchange rate to be a shock absorber. The idea is, if your current account deficit is rising, the best way to reduce that is to encourage people to substitute local goods for imports or encourage people to export more. The problem is, if the change in the exchange rate is too large, it will not move relative prices.

So, we [central banks in the region] all sold forex. And you will notice that the Philippines, South Korea, India, and Thailand sold, more or less, a similar level of forex to help mitigate the depreciation in their currency.

The outliers on the high side are Vietnam, which sold almost 19 percent [of its forex reserves], and on the low side, Taiwan, whose perennial problem is preventing appreciation, as well as Malaysia and Indonesia, which benefitted from the high prices of commodities.

Clearly, the Asian economies have one thing in common: part of their toolkit is forex intervention.

The other part is, of course, the interest rate weapon. When you see the Philippines, it is 425 [bps in cumulative policy rate adjustments], but the next highest is South Korea and India at 300 bps and 250 bps, respectively.

But that exaggerates what we did because we were among the hardest hit by the lockdowns. We had, probably, the longest and most strict lockdowns of any country I know, and economies shrank by 17 percent in the early stages of the lockdown [in Q2 2020].

Then, our response was to cut the policy rate to below our target. [It was] quite unusual: Our target [mid-point] is 3.0 percent, and the policy rate is 2.0 percent. This was because we are reacting to the shock.

The good news is that the banks seemed able to easily weather the impact of COVID [and lend]. And then, the stimulus that this provided allowed us [the economy] to recover, especially as the pent-up demand became very strong and as fewer people became infected by COVID-19 went to the hospitals. The strong economy that resulted from that [pandemic] is the other factor. The economy can actually take it [the impact of our rate hikes].

Calibrating all available policy levers

To summarize, the Philippines is fortunate to have the capacity to use the interest rate tool for controlling inflation because we are very, very far from a situation where high-interest rates are a threat to financial stability.

In addition, in the case of a situation where we cannot reduce policy rates because we are too close to the US policy rates, under that scenario, fortunately, our reserve requirements are quite high. So, there is room to cut.

We started out with a reserve requirement of 20 percent, and we pay zero to the banks. This started because when the US did QE [quantitative easing], there was literally a flood of money that would have caused the peso to over-appreciate. So, we bought forex and raised the reserve requirement. The first act, of course, increases money supply; the second one reduces it. It [adjusting the reserve requirement] worked, but the problem with that, in the long run, [is that] it will distort the financial system. Finance will move to areas where we cannot impose reserve requirements. So, we told ourselves, “This is a nice tool, but if we keep using this tool, we will distort the financial sector.”

Now, we decided to continuously reduce the reserve requirements. At the same time, we introduced liquidity regulations. We introduced the liquidity coverage ratio and the net stable funding ratio.

In other words, it turns out, the regulations of banks, capital regulations, liquidity regulations, and even the countercyclical buffer enabled us to have the freedom to make the interest rate whatever is necessary to be a successful inflation-targeting central bank.

I will end there. Thank you.

Title: View from Manila: Outlook for 2023 and 2024
Occasion: Philippine Economic Briefing in Washington, D.C., United States
Speaker: BSP Governor Felipe M. Medalla
Transcription:
Friends of the Philippines, ladies, and gentlemen, as they say in the Philippines, magandang umaga.

I will start by saying that the Philippine Constitution required the central bank to be an independent central bank. Of course, it took three or four years to pass a law after the Constitution was written to put that law down more precisely. The most important feature of that [law] is only one member of the Cabinet is a member of the Monetary Board (MB). The rest are people, like me, who have a fixed tenure, and the others are drawn from the private sector. Sometimes, the [representatives from the] private sector are former bankers—like my friend here, [MB Member] Tony Abacan, who was the former president of Metrobank. And, sometimes, they get academics, like me, who do not understand banking but eventually learn after being there for nearly 12 years.

BSP's three pillars: guiding principles of central banking

Our mandates, or our so-called three pillars, are price stability; financial stability; and a safe, secure, and efficient payments and settlements system.

On the payments and settlements system: transforming the way governments, businesses, and households pay

By the way, the third one [pillar] used to be boring. We print money and [provide] clearing [and settlement services]. Now, it is more exciting because—together with the government—we are promoting digital payments. Of course, the goal is that tax payments will be done digitally. And one vision that we have—that I share with [Finance] Secretary [Benjamin] Diokno—is when the Philippines imports goods, the customs duties are already computed properly while the ship is halfway to the Philippines. So, no more negotiations. Things become faster out of the port, right? So, all the payments to the government will also be easily tracked, including payments to local governments. This is getting very exciting.

In addition, of course, we want more and more people to have formal bank accounts, and that a lot of payments will be done digitally. That is exactly what is happening right now. We have [automated clearing houses], one is called InstaPay, and a bigger and bigger part of the payments are now digital. And then, we have PESONet, which is the equivalent of checks but is also electronic. So, we are moving fast on the digital side.

On financial stability: regulators work in tandem

Now, let me go back to the second one—financial stability.  Clearly, we do not regulate the stock market. We do not regulate the issuance of private bonds. We do not regulate insurance.

Financial stability is done by a committee chaired by me, and the other members of the committee are the chairman of the Securities and Exchange Commission and the chairman of the Insurance Commission.

On price stability: month-on-month inflation figures paint an encouraging picture

[Let us go] back to price stability. Well, if you look at that next picture, it seems alarming, right? Headline inflation is 8.6 percent [in February 2023], which eventually fell to 7.6 [percent in March]. If you take out the extreme price changes—what you would call core inflation—it is also quite high [at 8.0 percent in March].

But to me, the numbers that mean a lot more are the little bars below [month-on-month (m-o-m) inflation]. If you multiply that by 12, that is the implied inflation rate for the year if everything is the same. For instance, that first figure there, 0.9 percent [m-o-m inflation] in March 2022, that is terrible. That is 0.9 percent times 12 [months]. If that had continued for 12 months, the implied inflation is more than 10 percent.

On the other hand, if you look at the other end, there are two 0.3 percent [m-o-m inflation prints] there [in December 2022 and February 2023]. The first 0.3 percent [in December 2022], we celebrated too early and said, “Oh, we are there already!" 0.3 percent times 12 [months] is 3.6 percent [in annualized inflation, which is well within the inflation target band]. And then, we got hit by 1.0 percent [in January 2023], which is 12 percent [once annualized], right?

Of course, we are now seeing what, we think, will really be the trend next time, which is 0.3 percent from January to February [2023] and zero inflation from February to March. We think we are on our way toward our [inflation] target of 2.0 percent to 4.0 percent. And that is what is shown in the next chart.

Inflation forecasts may be revised downwards but subject to global forces

For the [current] year, of course, it is impossible to hit 4.0 percent [inflation target]. We will need negative inflation [during] the remaining part of the year to hit the 4.0 percent. By the way, we are revising this [forecast] with the newer numbers. [2023 full-year] inflation will probably be around below 6.0 percent in the revised numbers.

But, as you can see, for 2024, we are confident that we are going to be very close to the midpoint of our target [at 3.0 percent].

Of course, a lot of things can happen. Historically, when there was global deflation, inflation was actually below 2.0 percent for two years. Of course, nobody complained [then].

The point is, global forces can actually be the main driver of [domestic] inflation, and we have already experienced importing globally low prices. Now, of course, we are seeing the other side. We are probably importing high inflation globally.

Private sector inflation forecasts converging with the central bank's, reflecting inflation-targeting credibility

At any rate, the private sector forecasts [of inflation] are, more or less, very close to ours, except that [these] are slightly higher than ours for 2024 and 2025. [For 2023], the private sector says [that inflation will be] 3.7 percent; we [at the central bank] say around 3.0 percent.

By the way, this usually happens. The private sector eventually adjusts its forecast with a one or two-month lag from ours. I think this shows you how credible the central bank is [at inflation targeting]. It can make mistakes, just like any other central bank, but, clearly, it has been given the mandate and the powers to make sure that when there is inflation, it is not due to excess demand. It is not due to the fact that the central bank is printing money to finance the government. In fact, when you look at the rise of our balance sheet, it is largely because we purchased foreign exchange. The only time we purchased Philippine government bonds was because of COVID.

​​Fed actions: always relevant but less of a concern in policy-making

Of course, we are affected by what happens with the Fed [United States (US) Federal Reserve]. But, in general, our inflation policy is largely driven by Philippine inflation. What was unique about this year is that the US policy rate changes were so large—four 75 basis points (bps) [hikes] in a row—to the point where the Philippine policy rate became too close to the US policy rate. And, as you know, since the dollar is the global currency, people would prefer the dollar to the peso if the policy rates are the same.

We are now at that stage where we are watching that [differential]. We want to make sure that our policy rate is not lower and should be around 1.0 to 1.25 percentage points higher than the Fed's. That is what the markets are saying.

And, as shown in the next slide, when you have very, very narrow differentials between the Fed policy rate and ours, you have a weak peso. As you can see, it [the peso] has appreciated lately.

Taking decisive monetary action

And one of the reasons [behind the appreciation] is we have acted very aggressively. We increased the policy rate from 200 bps to 425 bps, more than any central bank in Asia. The only central bank that comes close is South Korea.

Now, we are probably near the end [of our tightening cycle]. We are probably [considering] pausing at the next meeting because the [m-o-m] inflation prints are very good. If April turns out to be another very low inflation month—so, that is three good points in a row—then we are in a position to pause.

How the central bank creates the conditions conducive to growth and supports economic development

​Let me wrap up and say, we [at the central bank] use all our powers, and we have enough of them to make sure that we support our three pillars. This has been very good for us but also quite good for the Philippine government itself.

And we are very, very fortunate that every Finance Secretary that the Philippines has ever had—that I can remember—has always been very fiscally responsible because they know that they can finance a big part of the debt of the government by issuing peso-denominated bonds. Indeed, around 80 percent of our debt is domestic debt, and much of that is longer than two years.

In summary, what you have is the financial and banking conditions of the Philippines that are consistent with long-term growth. No shortcuts. No boom and bust. We try to keep growth as steady as possible and to make sure that the banks are strong so that the economy will be supported by price stability, financial stability, and the payment system that we support. Thank you very much.

Title: Preserving Price and Financial Stability in the Philippines
Occasion: Meeting with Fitch Ratings at the sidelines of the 2023 International Monetary Fund–World Bank Spring Meetings
Speaker: BSP Governor Felipe M. Medalla
Transcription:
​

The headline [inflation] numbers are high. Even the core [inflation] numbers are high. But what must be seen is [inflation] in relation to month-on-month (m-o-m) changes. Unless there are new shocks, we are already moving toward an inflation path of below 4.0 percent by October or November [2023].

The reason for this is that the price index in March [2023] is actually slightly lower than the price index in January. One way to look at it is: Year-on-year [inflation] is the average of 12 m-o-m [inflation prints]. And if you have 10 very high [months of elevated inflation] and two [months of] very low [inflation], as soon as the higher months are bumped off by two months [of within-target inflation], then the inflation number is going back very quickly to below 4.0 percent [which is the upper end of the inflation target].

That is why we are confident that, in the absence of new shocks, average inflation will be within-target, possibly below 3.0 percent.

Supply-side pressures ease with the relaxation of import restrictions; looking to rice as a lesson

Because of base effects, because of very high inflation in January 2023, [m-o-m inflation for] last January was terrible. Without adjusting for seasonality, the January 2023 price index was 1.7 percent higher than December 2022. Anything terrible can happen [that can drive inflation, such as] Swine flu, meat shortage, [as well as increases on the prices of] vegetables, fruits, and sugar—all those little things.

What is notable is that rice is not there [in the items driving inflation]. The reason rice is not there is that the restrictions on imports were replaced with tariffs. 

In a sense, what caused the [elevated] inflation was that the government was restraining imports. But that is now being addressed. There was a survey [which revealed] that the issue that most people are concerned about is inflation. 

In other words, all of these are working to relax the speed of the importation process. The President is already on this. That is why I am quite confident that we will be back to normal inflation next year.

No tradeoffs between price and financial stability 

The other reason that this is the case is that we [at the central bank] essentially prevented knock-on effects from supply shocks because we were aggressive. We increased the policy rate from 200 basis points (bps) to 625 bps in just nine months. 

We were able to do that because we knew that bank balance sheets could take it [the impact of the rate hikes]. With high policy rates—while they [the banks] could have [incur] losses on their holdings of government securities—but with the higher interest rates, they earn more money. 

On the whole, because the banks have very strong balance sheets, financial stability was never a constraint in our use of the policy rate to quell inflation.

On the narrowing interest rate differential and the weakening exchange rate 

The other reason we did that [raise the policy rate] is, as the US [United States] increased its policy rate, its policy rate became very close to ours. 

If you asked people a hypothetical question, “If the interest rate on the peso instrument is the same as the interest rate on a dollar instrument, which instrument would you choose?” Even Filipinos would choose the dollar because of all the advantages of the king dollar. 

That is the other reason. The differential between our policy rate and the US policy rate, if it narrowed too much, could cause a very large fall in the peso.

However, this [depreciation] is also partly reflecting fundamentals since the current account deficit increased, and the deprecation of the peso last year was clearly not good for trade numbers. 

As foreign exchange pressures wane, the central bank can dedicate full resources and focus on fighting inflation

It [the depreciation] was due to the differential and the fact that people look at the exchange rate and say, “All the corporations that borrow abroad wanted to buy their dollar needs for debt servicing.” So, the moment we give [delivered] the 425 bps [in cumulative] policy rate increase, the peso appreciated. After a long series of policy rate adjustments, year-to-date [from 1 January to 4 April 2023], the peso actually appreciated by 2.0 percent. 

In other words, the exchange rate is no longer adding to the inflation problem.  

That is the situation. The policy rate [adjustment] addressed two issues: First, it prevented the knock-on effects of supply shocks from spreading too much. Second, it made the peso stronger, which also significantly reduced inflationary expectations. And, as I said, we did it without any risk that financial stability is reduced.

Title: What Sticky Inflation Means for Monetary Policy in Emerging Asia
Occasion: Governors Talks at the International Monetary Fund–World Bank 2023 Spring Meetings
Speaker: BSP Governor Felipe M. Medalla
Transcription:
​

First of all, thank you for inviting me. It is a privilege to be here as the representative of Asia’s [central bank] governors, although, as you said, [inflation in] the Philippines is quite different from the rest of Asia. 

Defining ‘sticky’ inflation

I would first like to qualify what is meant by “sticky.” Sticky inflation really is a lot of shocks. It is like the old wrestling days with a tag team. When one guy gets tired of beating the other guy, his partner comes in and replaces him. 

In this case, it is really a tag team [of supply shocks]. You had the Ukraine-Russia war. Then, later on, a lot of agricultural shocks. It started with sugar, later on, vegetables, meat, and fruits, partly because of very protectionist [agricultural] policies. Of course, farmers are poor; therefore, there were a lot of restrictions on imports, and there was a delay in issuing import permits. 

What happened is when you look at the 12 months, starting from March last year to February [this year], only one month1 was the month-on-month (m-o-m) inflation [within or] lower than 4.0 percent, divided by 12 [months in a year]. 4.0 percent is the high end of our [inflation] target because of all the shocks coming together.

Clearly, when you have high inflation because of all the supply shocks, this will eventually travel to the services sector. If food is expensive, you have to pay higher wages. If fuel is expensive, you have to pay higher wages. So, with a six-month lag, service sector inflation went up as well.

Deploying all weapons in expanded toolkit

We [the central bank] decided to use all our possible weapons. First, we let the market move the exchange rate, which is still [a] textbook [response]. The other one is we raised the policy rate, which is also textbook. The other one is we intervened [in the foreign exchange (forex) markets] because the exchange rate was moving too much because of United States (US) monetary policy.

What happened was, we ended up increasing policy rates from 200 basis points (bps) to 625 bps. This exaggerates the movement because the 200 bps [policy rate during the pandemic] was quite abnormal, to begin with. The normal policy rate in the Philippines is more like 3.5 percent, but because of COVID, we brought it down to 200 bps.

In addition, our balance sheet expanded by nearly 20 percent because we purchased a lot of government securities. Because of COVID, a lot of people were fleeing to cash, selling bonds. We did not like bond prices to fall too much. So, we bought bonds. This is the context. 

We ended up intervening [in the forex market] quite a bit. I will not say when and how much. We used to call it “foreign exchange participation,” but after a time, we already began to use “intervention” to more appropriately characterize our actions.

Results of decisive monetary action seen in easing m-o-m inflation and strengthening currency 

It [the mix of policy actions] worked. With the high policy rates, from January to October last year, the peso depreciated by about 13 percent against the US dollar. By October, because of the policy rate increases, it appreciated [on a year-to-date basis]. 

The last two prints of [m-o-m] inflation are quite encouraging. The March price index is actually slightly lower than the January price index. With seasonal adjustments, they are just about the same. Technically, we had zero inflation for two months. 

As you know, year-on-year is the sum of 12 m-o-m [figures], divided by 12 [months]. The last two [months] were good, but the first ten [months] were terrible. If we have more of this [within or below 0.3 percent m-o-m inflation], we should be back to below 4.0 percent by November or December [2023].

Strong prudential regulation, good governance cast the Philippines in a different boat from the US in navigating tradeoff between price and financial stability

The question that I am often asked is: “Why have the high policy rates not been a cause of worry for financial stability?” Because, as you know, if interest rates rise, bond prices fall, and the holders of the bond will take a loss.

In our case, because to begin with, we were starting [with a policy rate] from 2.0 percent—or even 3.5 percent if you take a normal view—unlike the US, Europe, and Japan, who were starting with zero [percent policy rate]. Therefore, the loss in bond prices is much higher.

Also, our more typical [bond] issue is five years and ten years. So, the loss in [bond] value due to changing interest rates is smaller. In the US, they have 30-year bonds.

The other thing is our regulation of banks. We have capital adequacy ratios. We have liquidity coverage ratios, net stable funding ratios. The banks, by and large, have very strong balance sheets. 

With me is Monetary Board Member Tony Abacan, who used to be the president of [one of] the biggest bank[s] in the Philippines, Metrobank. Our banks are run by people who have a very long memory of [the] 1997 [financial crisis].  They [have learned to] hate mismatches, even without us [at the central bank] telling them. 

We were able to raise policy rates. The banks took a loss in their holdings of government securities, but their profits [as a whole] increased because of the higher lending rate. By and large, the banks are very stable [despite tightening financial conditions].

In summary, if you use all your weapons, your primary weapon for inflation can be used to its full potential. The primary weapon is still interest rates, but this must be supported by good prudential regulation and buffers because foreign exchange markets can go crazy, and the currency issuer of the world [the US] is driven by very domestic concerns, [like] what happens to Iowa. Clearly, the policy rates in the US, they do not care what happens to the world in general. They are very targeted to what is happening in the US. You have to be ready. Therefore, having buffers is very important. 

International Monetary Fund (IMF) Asia-Pacific Department Director Krishna Srinivasan: You are saying that financial stability risks are less of a concern right now, compared to other countries in the region. You said that banks have already taken the loss on this. So, you are less concerned about the financial stability risk? In that sense, do you not see a tradeoff between financial stability and inflation in the Philippines? 

Yes. I am old enough to remember LIBOR [London interbank offered rate] going 20 percent. We are nowhere near that. With [former US Federal Reserve Chair Paul] Volcker, inflation was so high. He raised interest rates, and effectively, many countries started changing [their] monetary policy. The impact on the world was so huge. 

That is the other difference: Central bankers in Asia do remember 1997. The regulators do remember 1997, and our regulations, therefore, [reflect that]. 

IMF: Assuming that the tightening cycle is coming to an end, given the fact that [m-o-m] inflation in the last two months is coming down, what role does communication play here?

It is very important that the public knows why the central bank is doing what it is doing. Therefore, people say, “Of course, interest rates have to be high because the [elevated] inflation has to be controlled.” People have to also understand that some degree of exchange rate volatility is actually quite useful, and they trust the central bank enough to know when it is too much.

They realize that the fiscal authorities themselves must be doing the[ir part of the] job. The perception of the risk that the Philippines will default is quite low because, again, I am old enough to remember when the spread [between the Philippine and the US sovereign debt] was 600 [bps]. Imagine, the rate of the US Treasury is 600, and when we borrow abroad, we pay 600 plus 600 [in premium]. These are the other things that people must remember. It is very important to have your macroeconomic and monetary policy be very prudent and actually follow time-tested policies.  

IMF: In the context of inflation being very high for the last 8–10 months, what role has fiscal policy played in trying to protect the poor from the impact of inflation?

Two things: First, we actually have a conditional cash transfer [system] for families with young children to make sure that they will be kept in school.  We call it “4Ps: Pantawid Pamilyang Pilipino Program,” which [translated] is “bridges for families.” 

[Second], during the pandemic, we had a registry of people in need who were, [in turn], given cash after the lockdowns prevented them from working. 

The problem was cash collections were down and expenses were up. Fortunately, the perception of risk that the Philippines will default seems not to have changed despite the fact that our deficit-to-GDP [gross domestic product] ratio had gone from 3.0 percent to about 7.0 percent. I give credit to our Ministry of Finance. They actually publicly announced that the goal is to bring it [the deficit-to-GDP ratio] down to 3.0 percent by the end of the [term of the] current president. So, the government must actually show that it is behaving responsibly [when it comes to fiscal matters] and that the central bank is regulating banks without any political intervention, and that it is a truly committed inflation-targeting central bank. 

IMF: In some sense, the fiscal support provided is very targeted to people who are hit hardest by inflation?

And by the virus. Remember, a lot of people could not work because they were not allowed to leave their homes or, at least, their neighborhoods. Many of them have very little savings. It [the cash assistance] may look small. It could be, let us say, ₱5,000, which is around a hundred dollars, but that is the difference between them going hungry and not going hungry.

IMF: [In] the need for coordination between central banks and the fiscal authorities in the context of the pandemic and the latest shocks we have had, was there any explicit framework that you had? 

That is a good question. The first thing we did was lend ₱600 billion [in provisional advances], interest-free, to the government. It required an act of Congress—that is why it is so transparent. In other words, you do not like a few people telling the central bank what to do; it has to be the entire Congress. By the way, they [the national government] paid it back already.

The other thing we did, as people were panicking, fleeing to cash—now, one advantage of being an inflation-targeting central bank—is they were fleeing to the peso, not to the dollar.

IMF: What explains that?

Because they believe that the central bank is doing its best to meet the [inflation] target of 2.0 to 4.0 percent, and that when we do miss the target, it is due to supply shocks and not due to excessive monetary creation, not to excessive fiscal deficits.

IMF: And did you actually go and communicate that to the public at large—why they are having this kind of inflation?

Yes. Of course, they [the consumers] know. They know that the price of oil has increased right after the war. They know that flour became more expensive. The joke is that the price of bread did not go up, but the bread got smaller. 

I think, they also know when they are being [price] gouged, where there are monopolies. Indeed, where there are monopolies, prices are regulated. That explains later why inflation has a lag—because it could take six months before the regulator will accept the adjustment for water and electricity. Right after all the forces of inflation seem to have gone, [in] another six months, oil and water [prices] go up. But then, people know that they [these industries] are regulated and, I think, that the regulators have done a relatively credible job of balancing between keeping the firms healthy and protecting the public. 

IMF: You have done monetary policy tightening. You have intervened to make sure that the exchange rate works through in addressing inflation. [Did] you also get good coordination with the fiscal [authorities]?

Yes. We actually did help them. Otherwise, bond spreads would have risen if they had to borrow ₱600 billion [in] additional [funding]. If we had not bought ₱1.0 trillion pesos of bonds, bond yields would have risen. But it is not habit-forming. The last thing you want is for them to want more next time.

IMF: How do you protect against that? 

The independence of the central bank is actually [enshrined] in the Constitution. What is harder is to make the planning agency [National Economic and Development Authority] an independent agency, like the central bank. That is why they are unable to pass a law creating an independent planning agency, because it is almost a contradiction that the planning agency is equally loyal to Congress and the President. They have not solved that yet.

But carving out an independent central bank is easily doable because we have just three pillars: price stability, financial stability, and an efficient and safe payments system. That is the advantage of central bankers. The job can be carved out. All the politicians have to do is observe them, and if they notice that they are doing their jobs, let them be. 

So far, I owe it to my predecessors. They have done a good job. The public seems to understand that. Results of the survey show that the trust [in the central bank] is very high. We are able to answer the problem, in particular, the huge turnaround in US monetary policy from very, very low to [raising the policy rate by] four 75 bps in a row. Therefore, we had to respond.

IMF: So, inflation is coming down. You are not so worried about financial stability because you think banks have already taken a loss. What keeps you awake at night?

If a large conglomerate fails because they are so large and because of the single borrowers limit, they are probably borrowing from 20 banks. It turns out, from our own exercise, [the failure of] one large conglomerate is not enough to bring down the system.

Now, it is both a good and a bad thing that they [the conglomerates] are very stable. It is good for financial stability, but it is bad because that means [that] there is not enough competition because the conglomerates have particular advantages. 

Sometimes, that is the complaint. When GDP goes up, the typical person does not feel it. That is always a very common complaint, not just in the Philippines. When people learn that I am a central bank governor, they ask me, “Our economy grew by 7.5 percent, but I did not feel it.” Two out of three people I talk to think that way, and, I think, they are right.

IMF: And what is your response?

Pray for better things, but also, the grass is always greener on the other side. In many ways, the Philippine bureaucracy, the central bank, and politicians are far from perfect, but, by and large, they have done their job.

IMF: The Philippines does use a lot of capacity development support from the Fund. How do you see the role of the Fund in monetary stability, financial stability? What role does the Fund play and what role can it play going forward?

The last thing a central bank wants to do is reinvent the wheel. So, we ask, “What are other central banks doing? How do you make monetary policy more effective?” We started out with just a simple policy rate; we ended up with a[n interest rate] corridor, which is the policy rate plus 50 bps is the overnight lending rate and the policy rate minus 50 bps is the standing deposit rate. [We receive] the advice on the size of the auctions. The fact that the IMF has seen the other central banks [is valuable]. 

Of course, we do get advice as well from the Bank for International Settlements (BIS). Sometimes, the advice is not the same. I think that the BIS is a lot more approving of forex intervention and, I think, the IMF is moving toward that. Sometimes, you do learn from us, and we learn from you. 

In that sense, I think, the design of [monetary] tools and operations [is where the Fund can provide some insights]. If the Philippine central bank has not done it before but eventually has to do it, the question is: “How did other countries do it? What were the tools? What were the exact instruments?” 

For instance, our policy rate is not a real market rate because we ration the overnight rate when there is too much demand. So, we have to make a transition through an auction. Again, [this is where we hope to receive] advice from the IMF. What happens to countries where their policy rate is not a real market rate but, eventually, became based on auction? What should the size of the auctions be? And so on and so forth. Because you have seen how the other central banks have done it, where it is working and where it is not. Clearly, the advice that you, the IMF, have given to us has been very, very useful.

IMF: How much peer-to-peer learning is there in the region?

We [in the region] compare notes. I remember, a country said, “Be careful about the use of temporary tax cuts because we temporarily cut our VAT [value-added tax] by 3.0 percent, and, after 30 years, the “temporary cut” is still there.” We compare notes. We learn from each other. Do not cut your taxes unless you really mean to cut. “Temporary” tax cuts for temporary relief often end in disasters. Some of the lessons [from other countries] are negative, like Malaysia and Indonesia, [which] subsidized fuel very heavily. Maybe, they end up spending more on the subsidy than on education. When you look at who benefits [from the fuel subsidy], that is the top 25 percent. Some of the lessons are negative. Do not do this. They themselves tell us, “Do not do it. The moment you do it, you cannot undo it.”

This is the thing, especially with ASEAN [Association of Southeast Asian Nations] central banks. We see each other a lot. We compare notes and we learn from each other. ​
