Title: Trust: Evolving Amidst Challenging Times
Occasion: Trust Officers Association of the Philippines (TOAP) Summit
Speaker: BSP Governor Felipe M. Medalla
Transcription:
To the directors, officers, and members of the Trust Officers Association of the Philippines—or TOAP—ladies and gentlemen, good day.

Thank you for inviting me to be your keynote speaker for this year’s TOAP Summit and for the opportunity to share with you our view on issues facing the trust industry, especially during this trying time.
 
We at the BSP have always believed in engaging the industry through fora such as this to help you better appreciate our regulatory and supervisory approaches and understand why we do what we do.

Providing Context to Policy

Let me start with the economy to provide some context [to our policy actions].
 
Over the past ten years, the Philippine economy has been on a strong growth path. The expansion was both robust and inclusive: more than 6 percent growth, and poverty incidence was on the decline. 

COVID, however, put an end to this period of strong and inclusive growth.  

So we at the BSP got to work and took measures to support the nation through this crisis:

• First, we cut the policy rate to a record low of 2 percent
• Then, we lent ₱600 to the national government – interest-free

• Lastly, we bought a trillion pesos in government securities

Fortunately, it appears that the economy is on the mend. The economy grew by 5.7 percent last year, and we expect it to grow by 6.5-7.5 percent this year.

Even before the pandemic, the BSP had an exit strategy in place. The initial plan was a gradual, careful, and deliberate exit. We were considering increasing rates sometime in Q3 or Q4 2022, and the plan was gradual. Then, as the securities we bought matured, we would slowly decrease our holdings.  

That was the plan, but as they say, “The plans of mice and men often go awry.” What happened? The sudden pivot of US monetary policy and the Ukraine-Russia conflict strengthened the case for more aggressive tightening.

So it was important that we had to act sooner and take bigger actions.

As of our August policy meeting, we have raised the policy rate by a cumulative 175 basis points. We started with two 25 bps, followed by an off-cycle 75 bps, then a follow-through 50 bps. As you hear this speech, the Board will have a policy meeting. Of course, we will do whatever is necessary to achieve a target-consistent inflation path.

The national government has also paid back its provisional advance—ahead of schedule.

And we scaled down our government securities holdings and shifted the GS window into a normal liquidity facility.  

Now, with regard to inflation…

Based on our August policy meeting – and we will revisit these numbers at today’s meeting – inflation is forecasted to exceed our 2 to 4 percent target this year.  

Since a large part of inflation is largely driven by supply-side pressures, our monetary tools, which are aimed at stimulating or reducing demand, may not be as effective in responding to current inflation dynamics.

Moreover, it’s known that monetary policy acts with a lag. Our tools take about 6-18 months to kick into full effect. 

That’s why we support targeted interventions by the national government to reduce the impact of inflation on the most vulnerable groups – from transport groups to the agri-sector.
 
That said, we are confident that we will revert to a target-consistent inflation path. What does that mean? While inflation may exceed our target this year, it will start hitting close to the midpoint of the target by the middle of next year.  

Based on our August meeting, inflation is expected to average 4 percent in 2023 and slow down to 3.2 percent in 2024. 

Hopefully, we can put the worst behind us, but there’s no way to say that with full certainty.  
 
To put things into context, this situation of elevated inflation is not unique to the Philippines.

The latest inflation prints are much higher than the average for the last ten years and, for most countries, higher than the target. So inflation is high, but relative to other countries, the increase in our inflation rate is relatively low. 
 
We believe that our credibility as an inflation-targeting central bank has helped in this regard, and it will help again in the coming years as we work to bring inflation back to a target-consistent path.

As you can see from the previous chart, the US is one of the countries facing inflation much higher than the Philippines.

That’s why the Fed had to act as aggressively as it did to bring inflation under control.

As a small, open economy, the Philippines deemed it prudent to act and adjust its monetary policy settings, especially given the impact of the Fed’s actions and tightening global financial conditions on the exchange rate. We are monitoring these external developments closely in relation to how they affect the growth and inflation outlook. 

As always, our monetary policy decisions will continue to be guided by data.  

Zeroing in on the Trust Industry

Now against this backdrop, how has the trust industry fared?

We are pleased to hear that the trust industry has performed strongly, with assets under management (AUM) growing by a steady 3.4 percent in June. 

• When industry assets are broken down, we can see that recovery appears to be taking place despite the pandemic: Investment management accounts, or IMA, which represent almost half of trust assets, grew by 18.4 percent from pre-pandemic levels.

• Unit investment trust funds, or UITFs, which represent a quarter of trust assets, grew by a remarkable 47.9 percent between December 2019 and June 2022.

Let me discuss UITFs in more detail. For us at the BSP, UITFs are valuable in the promotion of financial inclusion and investment literacy since barriers to entry are lower compared to other investment alternatives.   

We are pleased to note that the number of UITF participants more than tripled to 2.2 million in 2021 from 657,500 in 2019. Much of this growth may have been driven by the accessibility of UITFs through digital platforms.  

Recognizing the potential of digital innovations, the BSP digitized PERA in 2020 to make it more accessible to the investing public. Two years since the launch, we are already seeing considerable progress, with the number of contributors tripling by the end of May 2022.

We thank our partners from TOAP and the BSP PERA Technical Working Group for their work on the information drive and public awareness campaign for the digital PERA. You can rest assured that the BSP will continue to work to promote awareness and encourage even more Filipinos to consider investing in the digital PERA to build their nest egg and prepare for retirement.   

In addition to the digital PERA, we recognize several initiatives by TOAP as part of ongoing efforts to develop the market, preserve the interests of the investing public, and bring it in line with international standards. You can rest assured that the BSP will continue to engage the industry in conversation on how we can do better. Your feedback is very important to us in this regard.   

One thing that may rank high on your agenda is access to BSP Securities. After receiving a request from the TOAP for access to BSP Securities, the BSP issued Circular No. 1130 dated 23 November 2021.

Said circular allows UITFs of eligible trusts to invest in the BSP Securities Facility via the secondary market starting December 2021. In the same circular, we allowed digital banks to participate in BSP monetary operations.  

What do we hope to achieve with this circular?  

• First, we aim to help develop the [capital] market; 
• Second, we envision this will help mop up excess liquidity from the system, especially after the BSP injected about ₱2 trillion into the financial system, equivalent to about 12 percent of nominal GDP during the pandemic;
• Third, this is part of operational refinements to the interest rate corridor.

While we do not allow investments funded by non-residents into the BSP securities facility, you might be pleased to hear that we are contemplating a relaxation of the implementation guidelines. Specifically, UITFs with a minimal share of funds from non-residents may be invested in BSP securities, subject to periodic monitoring and review.

Why did we prohibit these in the first place? We sought to prevent opportunistic investment activities by non-residents.

However, discussions are still ongoing on how we can operationalize this policy amendment. Rest assured that we are in talks with the industry for feedback on how we plan to implement this once the necessary approvals are in place.

We anticipate increased participation of trust entities in the BSP Securities Facility when this facility amendment is implemented.  

We expect the role of trusts to significantly improve the effectiveness of our monetary operations. As you know, we sometimes purchase foreign exchange and government securities, but we do not want this to result in excessive growth of the money supply. And the best way to do this is for the BSP to sell short-term central bank (CB) securities, such as the 28-day CB bills.

If the trusts are the main buyers of CB bills rather than the banks, we are more confident that our purchases of foreign exchange and government securities in the secondary market would not result in excessive growth of bank lending.

Another initiative by TOAP that we commend is the UITF Certification Program or the UCP for UITF marketing personnel. This certification program will help ensure that personnel selling UITFs are equipped to help investors understand what they’re buying based on their risk profiles and risk appetites. 

The certification requirement for UITF marketing personnel will be fully implemented by 2023 after having the transition period extended for one year. The BSP supports efforts of the TOAP and individual trust entities to raise the UCP completion rate by year-end.

As you know, the BSP takes consumer protection very seriously, especially with the enactment of the Financial Products and Services Consumer Protection Act or FCPA.

Lastly, we acknowledge the trust industry’s initiatives to digitalize its offerings and to provide access to a wider array of investment outlets to retail clients through feeder funds and funds-of-funds.  

Let me end by saying that the BSP recognizes the trust industry’s pivotal role in the deepening of the country’s financial markets. 

We look forward to the TOAP’s continued partnership in promoting the growth of the trust business while prioritizing consumer welfare. I wish you all a productive TOAP Summit.  

Thank you very much and Mabuhay!

Title: Onto a Sustainable Growth Path: The BSP’s Role in Helping the Philippine Economy Navigate a Challenging Environment
Occasion: HSBC Global Emerging Markets Forum
Speaker: BSP Governor Felipe M. Medalla
Transcription:
​

Good morning, everyone.  

Let me start by thanking HSBC for inviting me to speak at today’s Global Emerging Markets Forum.  

We, at the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP), have always been ready and glad that we can have this opportunity to converse with you so that you can understand us better and understand why we are doing what we are doing.  

I always say that our three pillars are constant: 

  1. Price stability: inflation that is both low and predictable. It is hard to overemphasize [the importance of] that. There are so many [difficult] possibilities when there is a long-run increase in prices. For instance, it would be very hard to issue fixed-rate bonds. If the bond buyer thinks that inflation will be 20.0 percent, it is very hard to sell him a bond that yields only 6.0 percent. I remember a time when the T-bills [Treasury bills] accounted for more than 60.0 percent of government bond issuances. Now, fast forward after inflation-targeting [regime of the central bank], the share of T-bills in total bond issuance is, I think, down to less than 10.0 percent. In other words, the government is able to borrow long-term and fixed-rate because people think that the inflation target of the central bank is likely to be achieved or if it is not achieved—there will be years where we exceed or [fall] below [target]—the midpoint of the inflation target is a good average over the long run. 
  2. Financial stability is also important. We know from past history that when banks become weak, they become shy about lending, and when that happens, you get years…of low growth. In addition, we like to look at environmental sustainability, not necessarily just for the country but for the banks to be very conscious of the risks involved that they must factor in.  
  3. Our last pillar is an efficient payments and settlements system. Now, because of fintech [financial technology], it is now quite an important topic as well. 

So, our three pillars are constant; what changes are the global conditions and, in the case of the payment and settlements system, the technology.  

If you use a ship as an analogy, the ship and what makes the ship strong remain the same. But, sometimes, the currents, waves, and winds change. As they change, piloting the ship will, of course, change.  

Of course, we were hard-hit by the pandemic, but we are now recovering very strongly—7.8-percent growth for H1 2022.  

What got us there, in part, was the very accommodative monetary policy by the central bank: 

  • For instance, we cut the policy rate to a record low of 2.0 percent.  
  • We bought one trillion pesos worth—this is unprecedented—of government bonds in the secondary market.  
  • In addition, we lent more than ₱600 billion to the government, interest-free. ​​

To give you a sense of proportion, at that time, the balance sheet of the central bank was ₱4.5 trillion. In other words, the central bank expanded its balance sheet by a third to help the economy. 

Now, like any measure to get the economy out of a deep slump like the pandemic, we, of course—from the very beginning—had an exit plan. We thought we would be exiting gradually; as the economy grew, we would make our exit plan. The plan was a gradual liftoff of rates and a gradual runoff of assets as the government securities that we held matured.  

But to be very frank, the exit plan became obsolete very quickly. As they say, “The plans of mice and men often go awry.”  

What were the unexpected developments? High commodity prices, slow global growth from the Ukraine-Russia conflict, and, of course, the pivot of the US Fed [US Federal Reserve]—from an attitude that viewed inflation as low and transitory to [viewing it as] high and persistent, which resulted in a much more aggressive tightening by the US Fed. As a result, the BSP had to take bigger and bolder actions: 

  • From two 25 basis points (bps) each [hike in the policy rate] in May and June when we still thought that the exit should be a gradual one, we followed it up with a surprise off-cycle 75 bps [hike], a follow-through 50 bps [hike], and then another 50 bps [hike] just last week. So, we raised our policy rate from 2.0 percent to 4.25 percent in just five months. 
  • The National Government also paid back its debt. 
  • And we scaled down our securities holdings. 

Now, let me go back to our most important pillar: price stability. As you know, we will probably exceed the 2.0–4.0 percent [inflation] target by quite a bit this year. The average [inflation] for this year will be 5.6 percent, way above [the upper band of our target] 4.0 percent. 

The question there is: are our policy responses working? We think they are. For instance, although by H1 2023, it [inflation] will still be quite high; by Q3 or Q4 2023, inflation will be closer to 3.0 percent than to 4.0 percent. As you can see in our forecasts, we expect inflation to be 4.1 percent in 2023 and 3.0 percent in 2024. This is what we call a target-consistent inflation path. 

The other way to look at it is that much of the inflation is due to supply-side [pressures], and these supply-side [pressures] are largely in turn due to external shocks. The impetus to inflation about which policy rates do not have very much effect. To begin with, changes in policy rates take 6–18 months before they work. Second, they are meant to reduce [or stimulate] demand and cannot address supply shocks. 

So, why did we raise rates? What we are trying to prevent is these supply shocks will create so much momentum that the following years will also be high-inflation years. Of course, our forecasts can be wrong, but if our forecasts are right, then what we have done is to prevent this high momentum of inflation—of 5.6 percent in 2022—from being carried over to the next two years. In other words, what we do not want is that inflation is high because inflation is high. What we do not want is a wage-price spiral. The worst case is prices are high and changes in the exchange rate are large, [so] prices are high. These are the things we are trying to prevent. 

So far, we think we have done what is necessary. The reason I say “so far” is there may be more coming from the US Fed.  

The other way to look at this is to look at core inflation. Core inflation used to be below 4.0 percent; now, it is higher than 4.0 percent. The right side of the chart will give the same picture. The share of core inflation to total inflation is rising. Therefore, we had to act. 

I think we acted on time. Although core inflation has now exceeded 4.0 percent, this has started to go down, and this is why we are forecasting a target-consistent path where much of the effect [of our rate hikes] will be felt in Q3 or Q4 2023 and 2024. 

Inflation, if left unchecked, could result in inflation gaining even more momentum. Higher prices beget higher prices, or what we call second-order effects. Our policy rate changes are not meant to address supply shocks, because supply shocks clearly cannot be addressed by reducing demand but [are aimed at] addressing second-order effects. 

We already see wage and transport hike petitions happening. The good sign is that they are not in excess of what we think will happen. 

You will see that in comparison to the United States, which has done 300 bps [in cumulative rate adjustments] since March, we at the BSP, since May, did 225 bps.  

If you were to compare what we have done with other Asian countries, we did the biggest policy rate changes, [followed by] Korea at 150 bps and India at 140 bps.  

The adjustment that we are doing has three components: 

  1. Allow the currency to adjust or respond to the exchange rate and be the natural shock absorber. If import prices are rising, dollars will be scarce. If dollars are scarce, the exchange rate will go up, and the correct response is… Imported goods will become more expensive so people will buy less. But we cannot rely completely on this response because too much of that [depreciation] could disanchor inflationary expectations. 
  2. We are also doing changes in the policy rate largely because the smaller [interest] difference with the US Fed is; the more attractive the US dollar becomes against the peso. Normally, we do not pay much attention to the exchange rate, but when you have very large changes in the exchange rate, even if the pass-through is only 10.0 percent, if the currency has depreciated 12.0 percent, the pass-through will be larger.  
  3. The other thing that we did was sell some reserves and participated in the forex [foreign exchange] market. As you can see, only Thailand has a percentage of reserves [sold] more than us.  

So, clearly, we now have to deploy all these three measures almost to the fullest. I say “almost” because we still have room to absorb and use these tools depending on what happens and what the US Fed does. 

You may ask: why is Indonesia not doing as much? The price changes are actually favorable [to them] since they export coal, which we [the Philippines] import. On the other hand, why is Thailand only doing 25 bps, whereas the Philippines did 225 bps [in terms of cumulative policy rate adjustments]? First, the Philippine economy has recovered more than Thailand. Second, Thailand has much bigger forex reserves than we do.  

But relying completely on these three tools is not enough. When much of the inflation is due to expensive food, the easiest thing to do…is reduce trade restrictions. The best example is sugar. When the sugar shortage threatens the food processing industries, the correct response, in the long run, is to improve [agricultural] productivity, but in the short run, import more. This is what we are hoping the government can do to address supply-side pressures, which, in effect, reduce the momentum of current inflation dynamics.  

As I already said, as an inflation-targeting central bank, we view adjustments in the exchange rate as healthy since they send the right signals. However, during times like these when there is a very strong dollar and most of our imports are dollar-denominated, the exchange rate becomes a cause for concern. 

We do not target a particular level or trend of the exchange rate, but we participate [in the forex market]. Because, at a certain point, if inflation gets too high and we let depreciation add to that further, clearly, the political preference for lower inflation will begin to dominate.  

Hence, in deciding on the appropriate stance of monetary policy under the current environment, while the BSP does prioritize bringing inflation back within the target band, it is also mindful of exogenous factors and now, in particular, much more mindful of the exchange rate. 

That said, we will continue to monitor the movements and the volatility of the peso, so these remain broadly aligned with the fluctuations of other regional currencies. If you take a longer view, the peso is the middle of the pack—not the most nor the least depreciated.  

The next question is: did we sacrifice too much growth because of what we did to protect our first pillar? So far, the answer is no. To begin with, the 2.0 percent [policy rate] that we are coming from is very low, which is really an extraordinary response to the pandemic. A big part of it [policy rate adjustment] would have happened anyway even if inflation is within the 2.0–4.0 percent target range. 

The projected inflation is not much lower than the policy rate. If our forecasts are correct, the inflation by Q3–Q4 2023 will be closer to 3.0 percent than to 4.0 percent. If the policy rate is 4.0 percent, then our real policy rate is only 1.0 percent or 1.25 percent. In real terms, the cost of money is still not very high.  

But what if the US Fed keeps doing more 75 bps? We cannot not react, but we do not have to match the US Fed point by point either, because our inflation problem is clearly very different from theirs. 

Indeed, one of the reasons we are having problems with the exchange rate is that the yen, euro, and pound are so weak, and the US dollar is so strong. The peso will…more probably gravitate toward the yen, pound, and won than the dollar. The reason being is the price of our imports has gone up so much.  

Our current account deficit, which used to be US$5 billion, is now projected to be US$20 billion. Most remittances tend to come in by the last part of the year. Our forecast is that the current account deficit in the last part of the year will be around US$20 billion because some of the [dollar] inflows will come as we approach Christmas, by Q4.  

Now, onto our second pillar: financial stability. ​This is the best way to describe our banking system: very high capital buffers, domestic liquidity is ample, sufficient reserves for non-performing loans, growing deposits and assets, and lending has now recovered. In other words, our banks are growing without sacrificing the stability of the financial system and without posing much danger to depositors. 

In other words, we have the basis for a strong recovery from the point of view of the banking system. This is very different to what happened during the Asian Financial Crisis when the banks were weakened, and as a result, it took four or even five years before lending started to normalize. 

As soon as demand improves, banks are more likely to lend while managing their risks. Banks are actively lending to productive sectors of the economy, and this is indicative of a recovering economy. 

Let me now go to our sustainability finance framework. 

As regulator, we are trying to play an important role in mainstreaming the environmental and sustainability agenda in the banks’ management of risks.  

While we are a rounding error when it comes to global greenhouse gas emissions, we have to recognize that climate change could create new risks for banks. I was just talking to a banker who said that some of their loans went bad because the property that was covered by their loans got affected by flooding. So, these are the factors that banks now must take into greater account when they evaluate their risk. Some bankers said, “Some banks may not have the capability to do that; they have to hire experts to make the environmental assessments.” In other words, some banks and their staff do not have that kind of people. So, they have to hire experts who could be quite expensive. That is one feedback we got.  

I suppose it is all worth it to the extent that they are able to quantify risk and price when they make loans. The worst possible scenario is you make a loan, and the interest rate is not high…but when the dreaded event happens, it turns out you will not make money because you did not factor in the risk of default when you made the loan.  

We are also trying to help in the development of financial instruments that reward green issuers of bonds and other forms of credit.  

However, this is easier said than done because what is to prevent an issuer from calling his bonds green [when it is not]? So, we have to have a taxonomy and a way of determining that you are not just financing what they call “greenwashing.”  

We want to improve the taxonomy because it is easy to just label anything as green even if it is just superficially so.  

We are working with other agencies and trying to use the same taxonomy as our ASEAN neighbors and put in clear definitions. 

Here are some measures to incentivize the financing of green or sustainable projects: 

  • First, we increased the single borrower’s limit from 25.0 percent to 30.0 percent. 
  • We are also hoping we can get the necessary revisions in the Agri-Agra Law [Agriculture, Fisheries, and Rural Development Financing Enhancement Act of 2022] so that sustainable finance can form part of compliance with mandatory credit to the agriculture sector. The BSP will soon release the exposure draft circular implementing said law.  

Now, onto our third pillar: a safe and efficient payments and settlements system.​ Our goal here is to digitalize the payments system. But it is hard to do that if people do not have accounts, because a typical digital payment uses an account to make a digital transfer.  

Fortunately, because of e-money, the number of accounts has increased significantly. We think that as a result of both increases in basic deposit accounts (BDA)—the banks are working with us to create BDAs that have zero fees and no maintenance level—together with the rapid increase in e-money, 70.0 percent of Filipino adults should be financially included by next year, up from 56.0 percent in 2021.  

In relation to this, we want 50.0 percent of retail payments to be digital. In 2021, it was 30.0 percent and in 2020, just 20.0 percent. So, this should be very doable. In other words, we are moving to a cash-lite economy. 

It is another dream that a citizen of any ASEAN country should be able to use his cellphone to make payments [to a citizen] in another ASEAN country.  

The Philippines already has an agreement with Singapore. The BSP and the Monetary Authority of Singapore have signed an agreement in November 2021 to decide on use-cases and identify interested participants by Q4 2022. 

We are in the process of getting an MOU [memorandum of understanding] with Bank Negara Malaysia signed by Q4 2022. 

The BSP is assessing a business case to connect India’s UPI [Unified Payments Interface] with InstaPay.  

If we are able to use a platform that has been developed by the Bank for International Settlements, we can actually have a multilateral [system] rather than bilateral agreements. We will not need bilateral agreements anymore. The dream of being able to use your mobile phone to make payments regardless of where you are in ASEAN, provided you are a citizen of an ASEAN country, will hopefully be realized sooner rather than later.  

On the local front, we want payments to government agencies to be digitalized—whether national or local. A friend from [the] Customs [Bureau] says that if payments for duties and taxes on imported goods can be digitalized while the ship is halfway through the point of origin and the Philippines, it will reduce negotiation, reduce corruption, and significantly reduce the cost of doing business. Instead of your goods staying so long in the ports, they will be released quickly as they arrive. 

The dream as well is that you can use your cellphone to pay for transport fares, the tricycle driver, and also in the marketplace. We are already doing this pilot program, Paleng-QR, in Baguio. I was personally there, and I bought taho using my cellphone.  

Equally important is when you take the bus, train, jeepney, or tricycle, you should be able to use your cellphone as well or at least [have] a card for making those payments.  

In closing, let me reiterate our key messages: 

  • The BSP stands ready to employ all necessary policy actions to bring inflation toward a target-consistent path over the medium term. Future monetary policy actions by the BSP will continue to be data-dependent and guided by evolving domestic and international developments. 
  • Domestic growth is expected to be robust and to be sustained over the medium term due to rising consumption and investment.  
  • We will continue to foster an enabling environment for the financial institutions under our supervision. 
  • Lastly, we advocate for the increased role of digital platforms in achieving greater efficiency and financial inclusion, while maintaining and enhancing a safe and efficient payment system.  

Maraming salamat at magandang umaga sa inyong lahat.  [Thank you very much and good morning, everyone.​]

###

Title: Banking regulation in the era of accelerated digital transformation and post-pandemic economic recovery
Occasion: The Asian Banker – Finance Philippines 2022
Speaker: BSP Governor Felipe M. Medalla
Transcription:
Good morning everyone. Let me start by thanking “The Asian Banker” for the opportunity to share insights on the BSP’s role in regulating banks during an era of accelerated digital transformation and post-pandemic recovery.

We at the BSP have always believed in engaging the industry through fora such as this to help you better appreciate BSP’s point of view and understand why we do what we do.  

As you may know, we have three pillars in the BSP: price stability, financial stability, and a safe, secure, and efficient payments and settlements system. The BSP makes sure to respond to developments in the economy and the financial sector, mindful of these core mandates.

Our first pillar of price stability – where prices grow at a stable and predictable rate – provides a conducive environment for banks to do business and support growth. 

Given the theme of this event, the discussion will focus more on our second and third pillars, which define our role as a financial supervisor and overseer of the payments and settlements system.  

In my presentation, I will address two questions:  

• First, how does the BSP provide a conducive environment for banking through our three pillars? 
• And second, how do we design our regulatory and supervisory approaches in an era of accelerated digital transformation?  

Let me begin by sharing our economic narrative to provide context for our discussion.
 
The economy grew by an average of 6 percent for a period of ten years before the pandemic put a very rapid end to this period of growth.

Fortunately, as restrictions on mobility were relaxed, the economy grew by 5.7 percent in 2021 and by 7.8 percent in the first half of 2022, giving us confidence that the economy is well on its way to recovery.

Let me share what the BSP has done to support the economy through this crisis:

• We brought the policy rate to a record low of 2 percent,
• We also extended ₱600 billion in provisional advances to the National Government—interest-free, 
• And lastly, we purchased ₱1 trillion in government securities in the secondary market.

But we knew, from the very beginning, that we had to exit from these ultra-accommodative policies. Our initial plan was a gradual and careful one. But as you know, powerful global forces – from the pivot in the US monetary policy to the Ukraine-Russia conflict – changed our plans.

So instead of the gradual approach, we had to exit sooner and take bigger and bolder actions:  

• As of our August policy meeting, we have raised the policy rate by a cumulative 175 basis points. We started with two 25 bps, followed by an off-cycle 75 bps, then a follow-through 50 bps. And as you hear this speech, the Board will have a policy meeting. Of course, we will do what is necessary to achieve a target-consistent inflation path.
• Then, the National Government paid the provisional advances ahead of the actual maturity date.
• Lastly, we scaled down our government securities holdings. 

Despite the normalization of policy settings, our policy rate is still accommodative. Remember: we're coming from 4 percent pre-pandemic [policy rate]. As you can see in this chart, our policy rate is still lower than it used to be. ​ If you compare the policy rate to inflation, the real rate is still negative.  

Achieving a target-consistent path of inflation is of great importance to us. Respectable growth is still possible under these terms, but for the BSP, price stability, one of our pillars, is the primary concern. ​

On the financial sector…

​Let me summarize this slide by saying that our banks are growing without sacrificing the stability of the financial system and the interest of depositors. We can see this reflected in all these positive statistics: growing assets, recovering loan growth, increasing deposits, and sustained profitability while remaining sufficiently capitalized and liquid.

According to the BSP’s banking sector outlook survey, bank leaders maintain optimistic views on the economy’s growth prospects.

Having said that, banks face several risks.

According to our Banking Sector Outlook Survey for the second semester of 2021, our banks have identified credit risk, cybersecurity risk, and environment-related risk as top risks.

For the BSP’s part, financial stability, our second BSP pillar, calls for us to also closely monitor these risks and craft relevant regulations.

Based on our surveillance toolkit, our banks remain on stable footing. So far, banks have been able to manage risks at the institutional level. 

As of July 2022, the gross NPL ratio remains single digit at 3.57 percent from 3.60 percent a year ago. This was matched by ample NPL coverage ratio of 99.2 percent.

Cybersecurity risk is another cause for concern.

To counter cybersecurity threats while at the same time promoting digital innovation, the BSP has developed a Cybersecurity Roadmap to institutionalize cyber-resilience in the financial services industry.  

Now, onto digitalization…

Our policy agenda on digitalization will not only make the financial system more inclusive but also more efficient.

As you may know, we have welcomed the entry of digital banks into the system. These are new industry players that would further push the digital transformation of finance.​ To ensure that these banks safely operate, the BSP is about to issue the second set of rules that will clarify the prudential requirements applicable to digital banks.

A digital financial marketplace model is being developed, which will set forth, among others, the criteria for the grant of authority to engage in digital marketplace operations and the related supervisory expectations. The model builds on the open finance framework.

To be well positioned to respond to emerging risks and challenges, BSP also leverages supervisory technology or “Suptech” in our operations.

Suptech applications support faster and more flexible data capture compared to the traditional template-based approach. In turn, this allows for earlier detection of potential risks and improved supervision.

Related to this, the BSP has rolled out our regulatory sandbox framework to better understand and supervise emerging technologies and business models. Through the framework, BSP is able to ensure that financial innovations are scrutinized prior to deployment to the public. 

The banking regulations are accompanied by initiatives that aim to shift our country from a cash-heavy to a cash-lite economy.  These programs fall under the BSP’s third pillar of safe and efficient payments and settlements system.​

The BSP's overarching strategy is embodied in the Digital Payments Transformation Roadmap 2020 – 2023. The Roadmap has the twin objectives of converting at least 50 percent of the total retail transactions volume into digital form and 70 percent of Filipino adults onboarded to the financial system by 2023.

There has been accelerated growth in the adoption of digital payments. For 2021, the share of digital payment transactions to total transactions grew to 30.3 percent. Meanwhile, the value of digital payments increased to 44.1 percent.

We have several initiatives to further broaden digital payments adoption across several use cases.

Last but not the least, we recognize the importance of sustainable finance. While we are a rounding error when it comes to greenhouse gas emissions, we have to recognize that climate change could create new risks for banks. So we tell banks to factor the environment and climate risk into their lending and credit decisions.

The more industrialized countries that are contributing more to global warming are actively discouraging banks from lending to greenhouse gas-emitting industries. But our focus is more on how it may affect default rates.

Moving forward, the BSP will adopt guidelines on climate stress testing and sustainable finance taxonomy, enhance disclosure requirements and prudential reports, and look into regulatory incentives to incentivize financing toward green or sustainable projects.

In closing, regulating banks amid an accelerated digital transformation and post-pandemic recovery is very tricky. But with our three pillars guiding our actions, we are ready to face the challenge.  

Rest assured that the BSP will continue to foster an enabling environment that allows the financial institutions under our supervision to contribute to our three pillars of price stability, financial stability, and safe, secure, and efficient payments and settlements system while supporting economic growth.

Thank you for your attention. Our Assistant Governor Lyn Javier will represent the BSP in the Q&A.

Title: Keynote Speech for Philippine Payments Management Inc. (PPMI) Annual Membership Meeting
Occasion: Philippine Payments Management Inc. (PPMI) Annual Membership Meeting
Speaker: BSP Governor Felipe M. Medalla
Transcription:
​

To the officers and members of the Philippine Payments Management Inc., our partners in payments digitalization, good day. Thank you for inviting the BSP to your annual membership meeting. 

As a member of the Monetary Board for the past decade and now as BSP Governor, I could not help but reminisce and reflect on how far our collaborative partnership has come. It has been five years since we jointly built the National Retail Payment System Framework, which gave rise to PESONet and InstaPay. We have made significant progress since then, and we have you to thank for these milestones. 

With your support, we were able to significantly grow the share of digital payments from 10 percent in 2018 to 20.1 percent in 2020 and 30.3 percent in 2021. 

Fortunately, digitalization and financial inclusion go hand-in-hand. About 56 percent of adults in the country now own transaction accounts. This is equivalent to an additional 22 million Filipinos we had onboarded in the formal financial system, up from 2019, when only 29 percent of adult Filipinos had transaction accounts. 

What is more promising is that e-money accounts are now the most owned accounts. The proportion of Filipinos that own e-money accounts rose fourfold from just 8 percent in 2019 to 36 percent as of 2021.

The rise in digital payments adoption was mainly supported by the sustained growth in PESONet and InstaPay, and QR Ph P2P payments, which were, in turn, driven by the broader participation of diverse financial institutions in the NRPS.

The growth in the number of participants expanded the access points for more Filipinos to be onboarded in the digital payment ecosystem and benefit from digital financial services. 

We have continued to roll out more digital payment innovations. Allow me to go over two of them:

First, the QR Ph Person-to-Merchant (P2M), which we rolled out in October 2021 to digitalize merchant payments.

To promote the broader adoption of the QR Ph P2M facility, the BSP engaged with the Department of the Interior and Local Government for the Paleng-QR Ph program. We launched Paleng-QR in Baguio last month to allow consumers to pay at wet markets and tricycle hubs using contactless methods.

Second, we have the PESONet Multiple Batch Settlement (MBS) in January 2022, which increases the daily batch settlement to two cycles within a banking day. Through MBS, PESONet users can now receive funds at an earlier time than the usual end of the banking day, enabling users to settle large value payments faster, and consequently increasing PESONet’s viability as an alternative to checks.

Despite our achievements, we know that there are still many opportunities to bring the benefits of these innovations closer to more Filipinos. 

For instance, it is crucial for us to digitalize more business payments which account for 24.1 percent of total monthly retail payments in the country. While supplier payments made up about 89.98 percent of business payments in 2021, only less than four percent of these payments were in digital form. Business owners still have a strong preference for checks and are constrained by the current requirements for paper trails. 

Recognizing such concern, the BSP looks forward to further collaboration with the PPMI in rolling out more innovative digital payment streams that would successfully address these gaps in our payments digitalization agenda.  

We have three initiatives in the pipeline: 

• First, we will be able to launch Bills Pay within the year to help unify the currently fragmented payment mechanism we have today. It will also support the digitization of government collections as mandated by EO 170 or the Adoption of Digital Payments for Government Disbursements and Collections. By the way, the IRR of EO 170 is about to be issued. 

• Similarly, the Request to Pay and Direct Debit facilities will provide greater efficiency in carrying out person-to-business, or P2B, and business-to-business, or B2B, payments, such as payments for goods, services, bills, and utilities. 

• Another key initiative lined up is the enhancement of our cross-border payment corridors, wherein the BSP is working with PPMI members to establish bilateral payment linkages with our ASEAN peers. 

Our shared commitment towards digital transformation has immensely helped our fellow Filipinos experience the benefits of cashless payments. However, our greatest innovations still lie ahead of us. 

Let us continue to lay the strong foundations for an innovative, safe, and efficient national payment system in order to lift every Filipino’s capability to participate in the gains of the growing digital Philippine economy.

Maraming salamat at mabuhay po tayong lahat!

Title: Keynote Message of BSP Governor Felipe M. Medalla Appreciation Cocktails for “Cool Minds, Brave Hearts”
Occasion: Appreciation Cocktails for “Cool Minds, Brave Hearts”
Speaker: BSP Governor Felipe M. Medalla
Transcription:
For me, this is a really wonderful afternoon to see former governors, colleagues, and former co-members of the Monetary Board – I’m happy to see so many familiar faces in today's event to celebrate the success of our coffee table book "Cool Minds, Brave Hearts: The People of the Central Bank,” which was recently awarded the “Best Book on Professions” at the 39th National Book Awards by the National Book Development Board and the Manila Critics Circle last July 30.

This book is actually part of a four-book project in celebration of the 70th year of Philippine central banking in 2019. These four books are first, “The Story of Philippine Central Banking: Stability and Strength at Seventy”; second, “No One Left Behind”; third, “Yaman”, and the award-winning fourth, “Cool Minds, Brave Hearts.” By the way, “Stability and Strength” and “Yaman” were also recognized as finalists of the National Book Awards in the history category.

This last book documents how the BSP consistently instituted needed reforms, adapted to the challenges and opportunities of the times and remained steadfast in its commitment to its mandate.

The book project series was conceptualized in the last quarter of 2018 and was approved by the late Governor Nesting Espenilla. With so many production speedbumps and, of course, the pandemic, the last book in this series, Cool Minds, Brave Hearts, was finally printed in the second quarter of 2021. Let me give credit to my predecessor and now Finance Secretary Ben Diokno for pushing for the completion of this project despite the challenges brought on by the pandemic.

Of the four books in the series, I expect that many of us here can relate to Cool Minds, Brave Hearts the most because this is our story. We are the actors here. We are the men and women who are part of the seven decades of central banking in the Philippines.

As the book showcases the BSP's tapestry of trials and triumphs, we aim to bring into the consciousness of every Filipino our inspiring journey that shaped and sharpened the contours of the Philippine economy and financial system over the years.

Let the pages remind us of our shared experiences as an institution—the milestones marked by the past central bank governors, the immense wisdom contributed by the central bank’s monetary board members, and the unwavering dedication and hard work of BSPers over the years.

At this point, let me congratulate the people behind this brilliant publication and the authors, whose cool minds and brave hearts deserve our praise and respect.

First of all, let me acknowledge the author, Roel Landingin, who covered me way back during my NEDA days in the late ’90s.

I would like to thank Studio 5, our partner in several award-winning BSP publications, for their steadfast efforts, despite the production limitations during the pandemic.

I would also like to recognize the role of Ms. Fe dela Cruz, our former CORAO director, and long-time consultant. Her direction spelled the difference and made this award-winning book into what it is. Salamat, Fe!

Last but not least, I would like to thank all our colleagues for their contributions to building a reliable and trustworthy central bank for the country.

The reason we have to celebrate is that a lot of good things were accomplished. And as this is a continuing story, I hope the young and future crop of BSPers will learn, emulate, and take inspiration from our esteemed colleagues, as chronicled in our award-winning book. Mabuhay ang BSP.

Mabuhay ang ating bansang Pilpinas. Maraming salamat.

Title: Enabling Sustainable Growth: The BSP’s Blueprint Toward a Post-COVID Economy
Occasion: Citi “Perspectives” Forum
Speaker: BSP Governor Felipe M. Medalla
Transcription:
​

Good afternoon to everyone. Thank you, Citi, for inviting me to your event. 

Let me begin by giving you the macroeconomic picture and close with some key messages.  

I will start by saying that we take our three pillars very seriously. Those three pillars are price stability, which is operationalized in our inflation targeting [framework]; financial stability, a big part of which is we closely watch the capitalization of banks. They must have sufficient capital relative to the risks that they take on—whether they took it on voluntarily or accidentally. Of course, [our third pillar that has become] very important recently is the efficient payment and settlements system. The key to this is digitalization and more and more cashless, cash-lite payment systems. 

We do care about economic growth although it is not explicitly a part of any one of the three pillars. We believe that when we deliver on these three pillars, that is the best way we can contribute to economic growth if one takes a longer view. 

Over the past 10 years, we did very well until COVID came. We had both high and inclusive growth. Growth was more than 6.0 percent, and poverty incidence was falling. 

COVID, however, put an end to this period of strong and inclusive growth.  

Fortunately, in our view, I think due partially to the extraordinary measures we [at the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP)] have taken, we are seeing a nascent and, most likely, durable recovery. The economy grew by 5.7 percent last year, and we expect it to grow by at least 6.5 [percent in 2022] as shown in [projections of the] DBCC [Development Budget Coordination Committee], where the BSP is a resource institution.  

What brought about this nascent and strong recovery? There were hardly any lockdowns, unlike at the start of the pandemic when the lockdowns were so crippling that the economy contracted by nearly 17.0 percent in Q2 2020. Our reaction to this was:  

  • To bring down the policy rate to a record low of 2.0 percent. Knowing full well that inflation will be between 2.0–4.0 percent, we had a policy rate of 2.0 percent.  

  • We also lent ₱600 billion, interest-free, to the National Government. To their credit, they have paid this back already. 

  • Then, we purchased one trillion pesos of government securities in the secondary market. 

To give you a sense of proportion, at that time, the balance sheet of the BSP was ₱4.5 trillion. So, effectively lending ₱600 billion and [buying] one trillion pesos in government securities are increasing the balance sheet by more than a third.  

Naturally, in the absence of lockdowns, this should stimulate the economy, especially in light of the fact that there is so much pent-up demand. 

From the very beginning, we were already preparing for an exit. The exit that we planned was going to be a gradual increase in policy rates—no 50s, no 75s—and that it would start [by] Q3. Unfortunately, as a Scottish poet once said, “The best laid plans of mice and men often go awry.”  

What happened?

  • First, there was the Ukraine-Russia conflict, which resulted in very high oil and non-oil imports. 

  • In addition, there was what was largely an unanticipated pivot in US monetary policy. With very large changes in US interest rates and the dollar as a safe haven, naturally, a smaller differential between peso policy rates and US policy rates will make the dollar much more attractive.  ​

There was a sort of double whammy: the higher growth of the economy relative to trading partners means our imports will grow faster than exports; second, higher prices of imports would increase demand for dollars. Our estimate is that two-thirds of the increase in the current account deficit was due to higher [import] prices and only a third is due to growth.  

The large increases [in the US Federal Reserve’s (US Fed) rate hikes] meant there was quite a bit of pressure on the peso to depreciate compared to other countries that were having fewer problems with the increase in import prices. We import nearly all of our oil and import quite a bit of our food. The impact on the demand for dollars increases [is] naturally resulting in a weaker peso. On top of that, the narrowing differential between the Philippine and US policy rates added further to the weaker peso. 

To summarize, these caused us to increase our policy rate sooner and by a larger amount compared to the initial plan. Now our policy rate is 3.75 percent compared to 2.0 percent in just four months. 

With regard to inflation, when we took these measures, we thought that whatever we do, we will miss our inflation targets in 2022 for the simple fact that our policy instru​​​ments are not very effective against this kind of inflation. To begin with, inflation is largely a supply shock, and to add to that, our policy instruments take 6–18 months before they take full effect. 

The outturn of new information meant we had to revise the inflation forecast even further. For instance, we revised our forecast from 5.0 percent to 5.4 percent between the June and our last August meeting. For 2023, partly because of the policy rate increases, we revised our average inflation forecast from 4.2 percent to 4.0 percent, but this does not yet take into account the 50-basis points (bps) [increase] we just did. We are quite confident that, absent new shocks, inflation will be very close to the midpoint of our targets to 3.2 percent.  

In other words, we are moving toward a target-consistent path. It is above target [now], but the path is target consistent over the next year. There is still some chance that we may exceed 4.0 percent next year. Then [in 2024], it will be closer to 3.0 [percent] than 4.0 [percent]. 

The good news is private sector economists seem to take our forecasts very seriously. Our studies show that when we revise our forecasts, private forecasts tend to follow.  

The other thing that is noteworthy is despite high inflation in 2022, inflationary expectations are closer to 4.0 percent than 5.0 percent. In 2024, it is [private sector forecasts that are] below 4.0 percent, although it is higher than our own forecast. We think that private sector economists will revise their forecast downwards as we revise ours and take into account the effects of our policy rate changes, and we expect that the commodity prices will be kinder to Philippine inflation in the next year. 

One of the reasons we acted aggressively is we were afraid of what is called second-order effects. It is not very strong: wages are increasing but not [to the extent that we are] worried about a wage-price spiral; we are also seeing an increase in transport fares. 

In our base forecast, the second-order effects should not prevent us from hitting near the mid-point of our target in 2024.  

Although the inflation rate next year will be closer to 4.0 percent than 3.0 percent, it is largely because of [lower figures in] the first half [of the year]. In the second half of the year, we should already see headline inflation closer to 3.0 percent than 4.0 percent. Of course, knowing that these are forecasts and we have been wrong before.  

One of the things that we now worry about is the exchange rate. In the past, we largely ignored the exchange rate because we saw it as a healthy reaction of the market to fundamentals. Naturally, if imported goods are expensive, demand for dollars will rise and the peso depreciates. The markets are signaling that people should buy less imported goods, and domestic suppliers should be more competitive with imports in the local markets. 

However, there are times when we worry that the changes in the exchange rate do not just change relative prices between tradables and non-tradables but may also potentially become the anchor of new inflationary expectations rather than our forecasts.  

That is why we had to move quite aggressively.  

The point is we are in a global period of very high inflation. The situation has been reversed: it is the rich countries that have very high inflation. The most recent inflation prints are much higher than the average for the last 10 years and, for most countries, higher than target. 

The other way to look at it is to look at the ratio of the most recent inflation prints to the average of the last 10 years, and you could see that the Philippine ratio is second lowest, after China.  

So, inflation is high, but relative to other countries, the increase in our inflation is relatively low.  

In that sense, we think that our credibility as an inflation-targeting central bank has helped, and it will help again in the coming years. That is why we take our first pillar very seriously. 

If you compare the Philippines with the US Fed, you can see that they had done 225 bps [in cumulative rate adjustments], and we have done 175 bps. The reason is that our inflation problem is not as big as the US, but at the same time, we are worried that if we did not act aggressively, it may be harder to control inflation if we act too late.  

The question we always hear is: does this [policy normalization] take away or kill the nascent recovery that we are now observing?  

We believe that the 175-bps [increase]—or even 25 bps or 50 bps more—will not be a major factor in reducing growth. 

Before the pandemic, the typical policy rate was around 4.0 percent, which was the case as of January 2020. If you compare policy rates to inflation, the real rate is, in fact, still negative. 

Another way to look at it is to see the Philippines through three metrics:  

  • how much we [the peso] depreciated relative to other countries; 

  • how much we increased the policy rate; and 

  • how much our [gross] international reserves were reduced. 

There are three responses to the current situation: (i) let the currency depreciate as a response to fundamentals, (ii) raise the policy rates, and (iii) intervene in the forex [foreign exchange] markets. 

  • In terms of policy rate, we had the largest increase, the second being South Korea. 

  • In terms of depreciation, we are very close to Thailand but lower than Korea. 

  • In terms of percent reduction in reserves, although not all of these are interventions, we did not make the biggest intervention nor the smallest. 

In other words, we are using all the conventional tools at our disposal to address the problem. We are addressing it just like other central banks do. Maybe because we have very different situations, that explains why our responses were [of] different magnitudes. 

The good news is this is not like the Asian Financial Crisis. Our reserves are much larger. They are comfortable but not excessive. 

Now, let me go onto our second pillar: financial stability. ​ 

Our banks are adequately capitalized. They have [ample] non-performing loan coverage. There is ample liquidity. Deposits are growing; lending and assets continue to grow. 

So, you have a banking system that is growing without sacrificing the safety of deposits as well as the stability of the financial system.  

The BSP, as regulator of banks, is trying to play an important role in mainstreaming the sustainability agenda. We would like lending institutions to factor in the default risk that climate change would bring about. If these [extreme weather events] happened on a large scale, this would affect default rates, and we tell banks to factor this into their assessment of lending and credit risk. 

In addition, we want to help in the development of financial instruments that reward green issuers of bonds and other forms of credit.  

We want to improve the taxonomy because it is so easy to just label anything as green when, in fact, it is not—this is what we call “greenwashing.” We are working with other agencies and trying to use the same taxonomy as our ASEAN neighbors and put in clear definitions. 

We are also looking at measures to incentivize the financing of green or sustainable projects. One plan is to raise the single borrower’s limit for sustainable lending. The other one is we allow them to be used as part of alternative modes of compliance with reserve requirements. We are also considering the potential use of preferential rediscount rates or allowing higher valuation for loan purposes. 

Now, finally our third pillar—a safe and efficient payments system.​ The most important development here is the role of digitalization and fintech [financial technology] that will both improve financial inclusion and efficiency of the payments system.  

We noticed, for instance, a large increase in the number of Filipinos that are financially included, and this could not have happened without the large rise in the share of telcos [telecommunications companies] and e-wallets. 

E-money accounts increased from 8.0 percent [in 2019] to 36.0 percent [in 2021], whereas bank accounts increased from 12.0 percent to 23.0 percent [over the same period]. E-money was the most common type of account among adults in the middle class, low-income population, and those aged 15–49. In other words, without e-money, [expanding] financial inclusion would have been much slower.  

We are also beginning to see some form of credit being done through fintech, although there are some concerns, like unethical ways of [debt] collection. We think that should not be done and should remain illegal. 

The BSP is also collaborating with the Philippine Payments Management, Inc. in rolling out more digital payments. The use of fast payment systems has expanded the role of electronic payment systems.  

Locally, we have the Paleng-QR where [in] public markets and public transportation, everyday commerce, people can use their phones to make payments using QR codes.  

In addition, we are working with some of our ASEAN partners to make this possible cross-border. We have an agreement with Singapore, Malaysia, and Indonesia. The long-term vision is that all these countries can use a common platform as the ones coming from the Bank for International Settlements so that this will be a multilateral rather than a bilateral system. 

On the local front, we are also encouraging the use of e-payments for payments to government agencies: 

  • I just visited yesterday the launch of an Automated Fare Collection System which we are doing in collaboration with the Department of Transportation and other government agencies.  

  • Then, there is the use of electronic payments by the Bureau of Internal Revenue, which will not only make it easier for taxpayers to make payments but will probably also make it easier [for the government] to raise revenue. 

In closing, let me reiterate our key messages: ​

  • Domestic growth is expected to be robust and to be sustained over the medium term, providing scope for the BSP to roll back its pandemic stimulus—although faster than we initially planned. 

  • The BSP stands ready to employ all necessary policy actions to bring inflation toward a target-consistent path over the medium term, consistent with our primary objective of price stability.  

  • We will continue to foster an enabling environment for the financial institutions under our supervision. 

  • Finally, we advocate for the increased role of digital platforms in achieving greater efficiency and financial inclusion, while maintaining and enhancing a safe and efficient payment system.  

On my final point, I urge Citi to continue espousing its sustainability and financial inclusion agenda and be our partner in nation-building.  

Maraming salamat. [Thank you]  

###

Title: Transforming Transport by Digitalizing Payments
Occasion: Automated Fare Collection System (AFCS) EMV Contactless Pilot Launch
Speaker: BSP Governor Felipe M. Medalla
Transcription:
​

Fellow workers in government, especially officials from the Department of Transportation (DOTr), good day.  

By the way, I was expecting to see [Transport] Secretary [Jaime] Bautista here.  

The reason is, when I took my oath, katabi ko siya. Ang tagal naming nagkwentuhan. It turns out, kaibigan niya ‘yung kapatid ko. Napakaliit talaga ng mundo.  

[The reason is, when I took my oath, I was seated next to him. We talked for a long time. It turns out, he was a friend of my sibling. The world is small indeed.] 

And I was impressed by how much he is thinking about how to improve transportation, especially for people who cannot afford private transportation.   

Let me also greet fellow bankers, President and CEO of the Land Bank of the Philippines Cecile Borromeo and Vice President of Digital Banking Randolph Montesa. 

Ang bansag ng mga ekonomista sa Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP) ay “macro,” hindi micro. Puro macro ang tinitingnan.  Ang major counterparty namin, o ang ka-deal namin, ay  mga bangko.  

[Economists refer to the BSP as “macro,” not micro—solely looking at the macro perspective. Our major counterparty, or those we deal with, are banks.] 

Nakakalula ‘yung dami ng zero. Halimbawa, nangungutang kami sa bangko para ma-regulate ang money supply. Kunyari, ang utang namin sa inyo, Cecile [Land Bank], maari nating sabihing ₱2.3 trillion. In other words, number “2” na may kasunod na 12 na zeroes. 

[The number of zeroes is overwhelming. For example, we borrow from the bank to regulate the money supply. For instance, our debt from Land Bank, we can say that it is at ₱2.3 trillion. In other words, it is a number "2,” followed by 12 zeroes.] 

Ngayon, ang mahirap sa isang macro na organisasyon na may napakalaking pananaw, dahil sa napakalaki ng ekonomiya, baka makalimutan nila ang napakaraming tao [na bumubuo sa pananaw na iyon].  In other words, ‘wag kakalimutan ang mga tao dahil lang sa statistics.  

[Now, the difficult thing about a macro-organization that has a vast perspective, because of the expanse of the economy, is that they may tend to forget the many people that form that perspective. In other words, let us not forget the people just because of statistics.] 

This will show my age. Noong ako ay estudyante, later a junior instructor sa UP [University of the Philippines]—noong araw kasi may junior instructor sa UP—sumasakay ako ng bus galing Batangas. Ang bus noong araw, walang aisle kasi ‘yung side niya sa sidewalk, doon lahat lalabas. [‘Yung mga pasahero sa] bawat silya, doon ang kanilang labas.  Ang advantage ng walang aisle, may dagdag na isang pasahero [bawat hilera].  

[This will show my age. When I was still a student, later a junior instructor in UP—there was a junior instructor in UP before—I would ride a bus from Batangas. Buses back then did not have an aisle because its side, the one facing the sidewalk, served as the entryway. Passengers from each row pass through that side. The advantage of not having an aisle is an extra passenger for every row.] 

Pero napakahirap noon para sa mga kundoktor kasi ang kundoktor nakabitin sa labas. At saka, bibilib ka sa kundoktor kasi kahit nakabitin siya sa labas, tatanungin niya isa-isa ang pasahero, “Saan ka pupunta?” Ibig sabihin, mine-memorize niya [kung] saan nanggaling yung pasahero at saan bababa. At papaano kung wala siyang panukli? Ang gagawin niya, kokolektahin niya lahat ng pera, mauupo siya sa likod, tapos bubutasin niya yung ticket, isa-isa. Tapos memorize niya kung sino pa ang kanyang susuklian. Babalikan niya ‘yan [nang isahan] kasi alangang balikan pa niya pa-isa isa—medyo delikado yung paganun-ganun ka sa bus.  

[But it was hard for conductors back then, as they must hang from the outside. You would be amazed at the conductors because, despite their position, they would ask the passengers, one by one, “Where are you going?” It means they memorize where the passengers came from and where they are headed. And what happens when conductors do not have loose change? They would collect all the payments of the passengers, sit at the back, and mark each ticket. Then, they memorize who among the passengers do they still need to provide change to. The conductors would return to them all at once—as it would be dangerous to move from one aisle to another while hanging from the outside.] 

Sabi ko sa sarili ko, kapag naging konduktor ka ng bus, baka pwede ka nang mag-PhD [Doctor of Philosophy] sa economics. Biruin mo, tatandaan mo lahat ‘yun. Pero the point is ‘yung sistema, masyadong nagre-require ng full attention and focus.  

[I told myself, once you become a conductor, you might already be able to gain a PhD in economics. Come to think of it, you have to memorize all of those things. But the point is that the system requires too much, even full, attention and focus.] 

Of course, gusto nating umunlad tayo. Makakalagpas tayo doon. At yung mga bansa na nauna na sa atin…sometimes, mas mahirap ‘yung nauna ka… Wala ‘yung mga features na dinescribe ninyo. Of course, cashless na sila, pero wala ‘yung open, interoperable [system]. 

[Of course, we want to develop. We will get through this. And to the countries that are ahead of us...sometimes, it is more difficult when you came first...  They do not have the features that you described. Of course, they are cashless, but they do not have an open, interoperable system.] 

At saka, ‘yung dinescribe niyo kaninang napakagandang [palagay] na: “Paano magme-maintain ng balance para sa aking [pambayad sa] transportation, eh hirap na hirap na nga ako sa isang kahig, isang tuka? Wala na nga akong pera, ilalagay ko pa sa card? Paano ang pambili ko ng pagkain?” Kaya talagang, noong araw, lahat ng bagay ay hiwa-hiwalay.  

[Also, you raised a good sentiment earlier on: “How will I maintain a balance in my payment for transportation when I am already having a hard time earning enough money for food? I already lack funds. Why should I place what I have on a card? How about my budget for food?” That is why, back then, everything was dispersed.] 

Fortunately, ang teknolohiya ay nag-improve, at pwede nang paghaluhin ‘yung pera na pambili ng sardinas at saka pamasahe. At ito ay isang napaka-importanteng punto—multi-modal siya.  

[Fortunately, technology improved, and now, we can put our money for food and transportation in one place. And a very important point is—it is multi-modal.] 

In other words, malaking increase in efficiency at ginhawa. Na-solve ‘yung problema na kawawa naman ang mahirap na tao—na kakaunti na nga ang pera niya, ‘yung balanse pa ay natutulog sa kanyang card.  

[In other words, there was a huge increase in efficiency and ease. The problem of poor people—that they only have a small amount of money, yet the balance had to remain on their card—was solved.] 

Kami, ang lalaki ng mga tinitingnan namin [sa BSP]. Meron kaming three pillars:  

  • Ang first pillar namin ay price stability. Napakalaki noon kasi ‘yun ay kung ano ang average na price ng binibili ng lahat ng mga Filipino.  

  • Ang pangalawa ay banking stability. ‘Yung mga bangko nga na aming counterparty at mga nire-regulate, ‘yung iba [sa kanila] sobrang pagka-laki-laki, katulad niyang bangko ni Cecile [Land Bank].  

  • Ang pangatlo naming pillar ay payments [and settlements] system. ‘Yung payments system na ‘yan ay mayroong [kakayahang mag-proseso ng] malalaking payments. Halimbawa, noong araw ay [gumagamit ng] tseke; ngayon, PESONet na. Of course, maghihintay ka lang nang kaunti. Kung nag-transfer ka ng pera ng alas otso ng umaga, mare-reflect lang sa kabila ng mga alas dose. Kung trinansfer mo after 12 o’clock, mare-reflect lang…pero hindi mo na kailangan ng tseke. Of course, dumami nang dumami yung cashless payments sa pamamagitan ng InstaPay. Pero kulang ‘yan kung hindi nararamdaman ng mga tao araw-araw.  

[For us, we look at big things at the BSP. We have three pillars: 

  • Our first pillar is price stability. This one is vast because it covers the average price of the goods that all Filipinos purchase. 

  • Our second pillar is banking stability. The banks that are our counterparty and those that we regulate, some of them are really massive, like Land Bank. 

  • Our third pillar is payments and settlements system. The payments system has the capacity to process huge payments. For example, back then, people used cheques; now, they use PESONet. Of course, one would have to wait a little while. If you transferred money at 8 o’clock in the morning, it would be reflected on the receiver’s end by around 12 o’clock. If you transferred after 12 o’clock, it will be reflected by… But you no longer need a cheque. Of course, the number of cashless payments kept on increasing due to InstaPay. But that is not enough if the people would not feel its impact everyday.] 

Kaya I am really very grateful to all the people who worked together to get this pilot going: ‘yung mga samahan ng jeepney drivers, ang ating LTFRB [Land Transportation Franchising and Regulatory Board], ang ating mga kapwa empleyado ng gobyerno sa DOTr, at ang ating mga kasama sa Land Bank. Nangyari ito dahil lahat ay nagtulungan.  

[That is why I am really very grateful to all the people who worked together to get this pilot going: the association of jeepney drivers, our LTFRB, our fellow government employees from DOTr, and our partners from Land Bank. This became possible because everyone worked hand-in-hand.] 

At ang aking tingin…sana lumaki ito at dumami nang dumami ang [ating] kasama. Ang ating bisyon ay ang Land Bank card mo—of course, pwede namang ibang bangko pero baka magsimula sa Land Bank—‘yung Land Bank card mo ay pwede [ng gamitin] sa lahat. ‘Yun ang maganda dito—ang pag-expand nito sa transportation. Hindi lang transportation ang ma-i-improve, lahat ng aspeto ng buhay, tulad na nga ‘yung kung pupunta ka sa McDonald’s...at the same time. So, ‘yun ang ating bisyon.  

[And in my view...I hope that this program expands and that our partners increase. Our vision is that your Land Bank card—of course, it could be other banks, but we may start with Land Bank—your Land Bank card can be used for every transaction. The great thing about this is its expansion into transportation. It improved not only transportation but also all aspects of life, like if you would go to McDonald’s... at the same time. So, that is our vision.] 

So, maraming salamat sa inyong lahat [thank you to everyone], and I congratulate all of you in advance. I am so optimistic about what this project can do.  

Of course, medyo OA ako kung minsan [I may seem over acting sometimes], [but] I will use the analogy of the man who first landed on the moon, Neil Armstrong: “One step for a man, a giant step for mankind.”  

Maraming salamat at magandang hapon sa lahat.  [Thank you very much and good afternoon, everyone.]
