Title: Opening Message for S&P Annual Review
Occasion: S&P Annual Review
Speaker: BSP Governor Felipe M. Medalla
Transcription:
​

First of all, I’d like to thank the members of S&P for coming over here. Let me explain our actions in the central bank and our overall conduct of monetary policy.

I have been a member of the Monetary Board since 2011 – first appointed by President Aquino, reappointed by President Duterte, and more recently, appointed by President Marcos to be Governor. I guess I represent continuity.

We’re often asked what the central bank does and whether it grapples with the classic tradeoff between growth and inflation. Before I tell you that, let me share that the Taylor rule is part of our analytical tool kit. For those who are not familiar, it’s a very simple equation where the adjustment in the policy rate [is examined against] some weighted sum between the deviation of actual inflation to target and deviation of output growth from natural growth rate capacity.
 
In other words, high inflation means higher policy rate; low output means lower policy rate. I cannot remember a day in any Monetary Board meeting where we haven’t used the Taylor Rule. In other words, we’re a lot more focused on inflation than, let’s say, the Fed. There’s a very simple reason for that: as a small, open economy, a lot of our inflation actually has little to do with the tightness of labor markets.

The other reason [why we’re focused on inflation] is that the inflation that we fail to fight now will be the inflation that we will fight tomorrow. It’s not a good idea to wait till tomorrow. Procrastination is the worst formula you can ever have because postponing fighting inflation is like postponing fighting a disease. When it gets stronger, you will need stronger medicine. If you take a little bit longer than a year, there’s very little conflict between stable prices and economic growth. Indeed, if you wait too long, inflation is so high your output loss would be greater later on. It’s really a tradeoff between fighting it now, when the output loss is smaller, and fighting it later, when the output loss could already be bigger. This is especially the case when postponing tightening means lost credibility. To [re]gain credibility, you have to show action later, and that will cost you dearly, as we’re beginning to see in the US. They [the Fed] have to be more aggressive now. That is essentially the way the BSP had behaved even before I joined.

However, when the pandemic came, we became “unconventional”: we cut the policy rate to 2 percent. For a central bank whose target is 2-4 percent, that really means if you hit the midpoint of the target, that is a -1 percent policy rate.

In addition, markets were panicking, fleeing to cash, and people were selling bonds. In an area where secondary markets were not as developed as the United States, and you were seeing higher bond prices as people were fleeing to cash, we knew that was a wrong behavior of the market because the pandemic is supposed to reduce capex. On the other hand, it will make people want to save more. The correct direction of interest rates was to fall from a fundamental standpoint, but it was actually rising. Which was why we started buying bonds in the secondary markets.

That, together with the special assistance we gave to the government, P600 billion [in provisional advances], was a P1.6 trillion increase in our balance sheet. It was around P4.5 trillion [in total].    

But from the very beginning, we had an exit plan. From our [initial] plan, as we recovered from the pandemic, we would gradually raise interest rates back to the normal levels.

But, as they say, “The plans of mice and men often go awry.” In this case, it was what happened in the US: US monetary policy becoming so aggressive and, of course, the very large increase in our import prices. Our own calculation showed that only one-third of the increase in our current account deficit was due to economic growth; the remaining two-thirds was due to high oil and non-oil prices.

Therefore, it was very clear that we had to exit sooner and faster than planned. Initially, we were making a gradual exit: 25 [bps in May], 25 [bps in June]. Then, we saw inflation was getting worse; we raised the policy rate by 75 bps in a [July] meeting that was not scheduled. And then in the following regular meeting, we raised by another 50 bps [in August].

Of course, how exactly we will raise the rates in the coming three meetings for the year is anybody’s guess. Like it or not, what the US does will be the main driver because our inflation is lower than the US, but we cannot afford to have such a small interest rate differential between the peso debt and dollar debt. If the differential is zero, nobody would like the peso. That’s the way the global architecture of finance goes.

The other reason is we allowed the depreciation of the peso because we saw it working as the market intended. If the prices of imports are rising, then the market should signal that maybe we should buy fewer imported goods. However, but if, in addition to relative scarcity, you have the Fed jacking up rates, you can get to the point where the depreciating peso, caused by the Fed actions, could disanchor inflationary expectations. The last thing we wanted was that people’s expectations about inflation would be driven by what’s going on in the exchange rate than what we announced as our [inflation] targets. That is essentially how I would describe monetary policy. Wherever we’re going in the next three meetings will be very data-dependent.

The question, of course, that we ask ourselves is, have we killed growth? Looking at the market, we are quite confident that what we call the nascent recovery is still there. Maybe it’s now hard[er] to think of [achieving] it. Personally, I think it’s hard to think of 7.5 percent, but I think the lower end of the targets, as mentioned in the DBCC, is quite doable,

The other thing that we see is that the quality of employment is rising. What happened was the wage and salaried employment were the most affected by the pandemic. In an economy with a very little safety net from the government [for unemployment], the most common way to help yourself is self-employment. We’re beginning to see wage employment recovering.

The other advantage of the Philippines is that we notice it’s fairly easy for monetary policy to stimulate demand. I guess that has to do with a rather optimistic population, and a young one at that.

The other thing that causes me to be optimistic is that the policy rate is still below its pre-pandemic level. There is still some room to rise. Nevertheless, we do admit that there may be some loss in output in the near-term. But if we take a longer view, there is very little loss of output. If you postpone fighting inflation, you’re going to lose output sooner or later. Better to lose it now when inflation is still relatively easy [to control].

Our own forecast is that this year, average inflation will be way above our 2-4 percent target. Next year, without factoring in the effects of our policy rate, the midpoint of our forecast for next year is 4 percent. But because of the recent actions that we have taken, I think it’s now below 4 percent, better than a 50/50 bet that we will meet our target. That is the way it looks. Our forecast for 2024 is very, very close to the midpoint of our target.

Now, of course, the future is very hard to predict, but if we look at our track record, there are very, very few occasions where we were above our target for more than two years in a row. Equally, there are periods where we were below targets; I remember 2015-2016. We do miss the target every now and then, but a great part of the reason why we miss our targets are global and domestic supply shocks, about which monetary policy is not very effective in the short run.

I look forward to a comprehensive and constructive discussion with all of you, especially on the things in the central bank’s toolkit. Thank you.

Title: Acceptance Message:  Hosting of the 2023 AFI Global Policy Forum
Occasion: Country Hosting of Alliance for Financial Inclusion (AFI) 2023 Global Policy Forum
Speaker: BSP Governor Felipe M. Medalla
Transcription:
​

The Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas is most honored to have been chosen to host the Global Policy Forum in 2023.

Title: Microfinance: Thriving through Uncertainties
Occasion: Microfinance Council of the Philippines, Inc. (MCPI) 2022 Annual Conference
Speaker: BSP Governor Felipe M. Medalla
Transcription:
​

Good morning. 

Thank you, Aris, Ed, and all the officers and directors of the Microfinance Council of the Philippines—both outgoing and incoming. I am glad to hear that you consider the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP) as your number one ally. From our point of view, you are also a very important ally of the BSP. It is hard to think of financial inclusion without looking at microfinance. Thank you for inviting me to speak on behalf of the BSP at your annual conference. 

This year, the theme is “Microfinance: Thriving through Uncertainties.” This speaks of the key role of microfinance institutions—or MFIs—in expanding financial inclusion. 

Despite the challenges of the pandemic, you were able to continue serving the entrepreneurial poor, reinforcing your position as last-mile providers. 

Of course, the pandemic has hit you very hard just like the rest of the economy. From very high [loan] growth rates until 2019—averaging more than 20.0 percent—there was a contraction of 2.5 percent in 2020. Indeed, whether you look at the value of loans or the number of borrowers, you have not yet come back from pre-pandemic levels. 

Thank God, the trends are encouraging. Recovery is on the horizon. With all the dedicated people in microfinance, especially in your council, I am confident that by this year or the next, you will have more than fully recovered. For instance, in Q4 2021, you already had a growth rate of 4.1 percent [in microfinance loans]. Although repayment fell to a low of 56.5 percent in Q2 2020 from a more normal 98.9 percent before the pandemic, it has now gone back to 84.0 percent in February 2021.

So, things are looking up. Hopefully, as the economy reopens, so will the activities and the success of the sector.

It is very important because, for us, MFIs are reliable partners in our push for financial inclusion. 

MFIs are present in 80.0 percent of municipalities and cities and are located at the heart of communities.

According to the BSP Financial Inclusion Survey, 9.0 percent of the adult population maintains an account with MFIs, making MFIs the third choice for account maintenance, next only to e-money issuers and banks.  

Tellingly, the same survey showed that 23.0 percent of Filipino borrowers secured loans from MFIs, compared to only 12.0 percent from government institutions, 8.0 percent from cooperatives, and 7.0 percent from lending-financing institutions, making MFIs the most favored formal sector loan provider in 2021. 

Let me emphasize the words, “formal sector.” You are the most important bridge from the unorganized or informal sector to the formal sector.

Who are the providers of these microfinancing solutions?

• There are 139 banks offering microfinance loans. There is CARD [Bank] for one. 

• Then, you have microfinance NGOs [non-governmental organizations] which have an outstanding portfolio of ₱50.4 billion and 6.2 million clients as of 2020.

• Cooperatives, on the other hand, had an outstanding loan portfolio of ₱288 billion and 8.8 million members as of 2020.

​​In short, MFIs are a key component in achieving our financial inclusion goals, especially in reaching the most vulnerable. 

When traditional banks cannot grant loans to microentrepreneurs—due to various reasons, be it lack of collateral or lack of documents—microfinance institutions provide loans with simple requirements and zero collateral.

Of course, loans may be smaller in value than extended by banks, but when one looks at them from the ground level, [they are] no less important. It is how many parents could have missed tuition payments; how many businesses could have missed buying their inventory. In other words…even though the loans are smaller, they are not of lower strategic value. 

Through microfinance, microentrepreneurs have been empowered, which allowed their modest businesses to grow into promising ventures. Indeed, some of them have “graduated” and are now regular borrowers of banks.

Given your resilience, the theme of this event, “Microfinance: Thriving through Uncertainties,” resonates with every Filipino—umuunlad bagamat nagkaroon ng krisis.

We want to honor that and help you along the path to growth, hopefully, as regulators, by creating the conditions for an enabling regulatory environment, [by observing] as [the late Governor] Nesting Espenilla calls it “proportionality,” in our regulations through:​

• ​First, expanding access to credit; and

• Second, promoting digitalization. 

Under the refreshed National Strategy for Financial Inclusion, or NSFI, the BSP supports initiatives to enhance the financing ecosystem for micro, small, and medium enterprises (MSMEs) and the agriculture sector. 

We have several initiatives to enhance credit access.

One is expanding the PhilGuarantee’s [Philippine Guarantee Corporation] MSME Credit Guarantee Program. This is very important because many MSMEs have been hurt by the pandemic, and maybe the only way they can return to creditworthiness is if they are given another chance by having access to guarantees.

Also helping with the collateral problem is the long-standing goal of the Credit Surety Fund, which was pioneered by the BSP.

It is also important to expand alternative financing options for MSMEs. Oftentimes, the source of the solution is supply-side. They are better, more productive, more efficient, and more profitable—and therefore will have better access to credit. 

Digitalization is quite important. Here, we can improve the relative position of small lenders relative to the big ones. I should mention:​

• Paleng-QR Ph – This program taps LGUs’ [local government units] policy championship in promoting the use of QR Ph payments among small merchants. I was just in Baguio, and we launched it together with Mayor [Benjamin] Magalong. I actually bought taho using my e-wallet;

• Basic deposit accounts;

• Facilitation of technical assistance and matching grants supporting the digital transformation of rural financial institutions and other last-mile providers; and

• Promoting internet connectivity in underserved areas. There are lots of beautiful stories here. During the last typhoon that hit Siargao, it was a rural bank that remained open—Cantilan Bank. When all the big banks were unable to provide services, here was a rural bank that had access to satellite [technology] and made people, some of them stranded, much better off. Here, our partners are DOST [Department of Science and Technology] and PhilSA [Philippine Space Agency]. There are two rural banks participating [in testing satellite technology via satellite internet service provider]: Progressive Bank of Malvar and Rural Bank of Cuenca. 

With your vast network and reach, your members are effective agents not only of financial inclusion but also of digital transformation and progress. You, the microfinance community, have made it possible to provide much-needed financial services, especially to those whose livelihoods were affected by stringent mobility and health restrictions. We thank you for helping keep our countrymen afloat during these difficult times, and we trust that you will stay true to that commitment. 

Rest assured of the BSP’s support. We appreciate and like what you are doing [to support MFIs], and we would be extremely dense if we do not realize that [your key role in development]. As they say, we rise together by lifting others. 

Maraming salamat at magandang umaga.

Title: Opening Message for BSP North and Central Luzon Regional Macroeconomic Conference Series (RMCS)
Occasion: BSP North and Central Luzon Regional Macroeconomic Conference Series (RMCS)
Speaker: BSP Governor Felipe M. Medalla
Transcription:
​

Colleagues from the government, partners from the private sector, members of the academe, friends from the media, ladies, and gentlemen, naimbag nga bigat kadatayo amin.

I am pleased to welcome everyone from the North and Central Luzon Regions to the third Regional Macroeconomic Conference Series, or RMCS. After I was appointed to the Monetary Board, I attended many of these RMCS, and I know how interested people in the regions are, judging by their active participation in the discussions and the open forum.

This current series builds on the conference series already held in Central Visayas, Davao, and SOCCSKSARGEN – which were all done virtually. While we initially planned the next RMCS to be face-to-face, we opted to hold it virtually in light of the COVID-19 situation. Nonetheless, we hope that this one – although it’s online – would be as enriching and as engaging as if we were meeting in person.

Today’s presentations will focus on recent economic developments and general banking system developments with a focus on the condition and performance of the North Luzon area. These were your top concerns based on the pre-conference survey.

One would say that the main role of the regions is largely in our third pillar [safe, secure, and efficient payments and settlement system]. But as you know, our third pillar is extremely important, especially now with digitalization. Many things that happen at the regional level also inform us on [our first and second pillars of] inflation and financial stability, and we would love to hear your insights and experiences which are closer to what’s going on in the ground, to validate, or maybe in some cases, make us change our view on highly aggregated data that we use in our models.

I have said this before: while we are probably the best institution in this country for taking a macroeconomic view at the country level, we are, of course, very focused on GDP, price index, and capital formation at the national level – all very highly aggregated levels, But we should never ever forget to look at the regional-level data to inform our decisions and policy actions. For instance, given that inflation is highest for food items, clearly, these issues are more serious in some regions than in others. To ignore regional differences will be a big mistake.

Thank you for your attention, and I hope you will have a very productive morning. Agyamanak unay! Mabuhay po tayong lahat!

Title: Opening Message for Moody’s Credit Rating Review
Occasion: Moody’s Credit Rating Review
Speaker: BSP Governor Felipe M. Medalla
Transcription:
​

Dr. Diokno already described the economy. What I will now explain is why we have raised policy rates by 175 bps. Does the central bank even care about growth? The answer is it does care about growth, but it cares even more about its inflation-targeting mandate. In the long run, it’s actually good for the government since you can issue longer-term bonds if everybody believes in the inflation forecast.

The overall belief in the Philippines is that inflation targets are missed in the Philippines because of external and supply shocks, for which policy rates are not the most effective tools. So why did we raise rates?

The first answer to that question is we would have raised it anyway as part of our normalization. When the economy was recovering, we were very aggressive in making sure that the pandemic did not [cause the economy to] contract more than [what could have been] generated by the lockdowns.

We brought down the policy rate to 2 percent. I’ve been with Monetary Board for 11 years; 3.5 percent is, more or less, the normal policy rate. That’s not surprising since the midpoint of our inflation target is 3 percent, so it’s only logical that we have a positive, real policy rate.

Of course, the pandemic changed everything – we went to a 2 percent policy rate, lent P600 billion to the national government interest-free, and then, we saw markets panicking and fleeing to cash because of the uncertainty. In other words, markets were going in the “wrong” direction. The pandemic is expected to reduce capex and make people want to save more. The “correct” reaction of the market should have been to lower interest rates, but they were fleeing to cash because of the sense of uncertainty, To ease further upward pressure on interest rates, we purchased a trillion pesos of bonds from the secondary market. In relation to our balance sheet of P4.5 trillion, that’s quite big.

All along, we had an exit plan. It was [supposed] to be a gradual liftoff of rates – probably starting the last three months of the year. [But] we were surprised by developments in the US. We were surprised by the movements in commodity prices due to the Ukraine war. These were not part of our forecast. Thus, our exit came sooner and bigger [than expected]. We started with two 25 bps, an off-cycle 75 bps, and then another 50 bps. If you compare us with Thailand and Indonesia, we are among the central banks in Southeast Asia that was the most aggressive. Why? If you look at it relative to the original exit plan, we would have done at least 100 bps anyway, but [we] could have done it in the last half of the year.

In reality, the policy rate is still quite supportive of growth. Indeed, this is happening when there are no lockdowns. When you look at Google Mobility indices, you can see [the improvement]. In the BSP, our COVID numbers, we noticed, and this is exactly the same [trend] as the rest of the nation: low hospitalization.

Our source of confidence that growth will take place is, first, that people have learned to live with the virus, and second, vaccinations and previous infections make them more resilient. The fact that the virus affects the upper respiratory tract rather than the lower makes it more transmissible but less deadly. In that context, we are quite optimistic that [economic] growth is taking place.

Why the surprise [slower-than-expected growth] in Q2 2022? I was personally expecting 8 percent; what happened was much lower. If you look at growth from a seasonally adjusted quarter-on-quarter basis, we’re on a slight reduction. The answer has nothing to do with the virus; it has to do with the fact that when people are spending lots more of their money on transportation and electricity, they have less money for other things. That is what the data shows. When you take out essentials from consumption, what remains is non-essential. The growth of non-essentials already expanded to pre-pandemic levels and is now low again compared to pre-pandemic levels.

The slower growth is not due to monetary policy; it’s due to the fact that between driving less, using less electricity, being less likely to go to restaurants [as people have less to spend after spending for non-discretionary items], the economy would slow down. The slow economy is due to the high cost of imports and, unluckily, the high cost of some local agricultural products, [which] has reduced money for discretionary spending.

This, together with the policy rate increases, give us an even more chance of seeing below 4 percent inflation next year. Our policy rates are not in response to the current inflation per se; they are forward-looking because we take very seriously our inflation-targeting mandate.

If inflation is high next year, this would not be due to external supply shocks anymore but due to second-order effects. We notice, for instance, that wages are rising and transport fare petitions. There’s very little we can do about this. But absent other shocks, we expect inflation to be below 4 percent next year and closer to 3 percent than to 4 thereafter.

My point is we did not take away growth [with our tightening]. What we did was create bigger growth opportunities next year and the next. The other way to look at it is: we might have lost a little bit of output this year, but if we had postponed our actions, we would have lost more in the following years because the pressure to raise rates would have been even greater if we had not acted on inflation this year. In Tagalog, mas mabuti ang maaga kaysa magaling. Don’t see our moves as being anti-growth. We’re actually laying the groundwork for better growth in the coming years.

Another point: our banks are in a good position to absorb losses: there’s enough provisioning, and capitalization is quite high – much higher than what’s required. Not all non-financial corporates are healthy, but that’s the very nature of capitalism. In any distribution of firms in any capitalist economy, some will be doing much better or worse than average, but on average, [the banks are] quite strong.

In my experience with the Monetary Board, never were we told by the government that our policy rate was too high. Never were we told by the government to be gentle to a bank. The independence of the central bank is well understood by authorities, most of all by the current Secretary of Finance. Thank you

Title: A Call to Action toward Sustainable Growth
Occasion: European Business Community (EBC) 7th Economic Briefing
Speaker: BSP Governor Felipe M. Medalla
Transcription:
​

Good afternoon, everyone. Let me thank the European Business Community (EBC) for the opportunity to share the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas’ (BSP) insights on safeguarding price and financial stability amid challenging times.

Today’s event highlights the importance of our collaborations domestically and abroad. Europe has been an important economic partner of the Philippines, and we invite the EBC to continue their investment and projects in our country.

Our existing trade arrangements with Europe have partly contributed to the Philippines’ greater market access to Europe. For instance, under the EU Generalized System of Preferences Plus (GSP+), more than 6,000 Philippine exports to EU member states enter duty-free. Since the Philippines’ application to the GSP+ in 2014, exports to the EU have increased to US$8.5 billion in 2021 from just US$6.7 billion in 2014. 

So, I am often asked, how can the BSP contribute to the government’s growth and poverty reduction goals? In what way can the BSP support the national government achieve these ambitious growth targets? 

The answer is in by doing our job—our three pillars, as we call them—and doing them well.

While it is not part of our direct mandates, the central bank contributes to growth by working toward our three pillars.

When we deliver on our core mandates, we help promote an environment and create the conditions conducive to growth. So, growth is a natural by-product of making sure we do our jobs well. 

Let me go over how we do just that. 

Our first pillar is price stability, about which I will say more later.

Our second pillar is financial stability. As you can see in this slide, banks are growing without sacrificing the stability of the system while preserving depositor interest—growing assets and profitability while remaining sufficiently capitalized and liquid. Banks are actively lending to productive sectors of the economy, indicative of recovering economic activity. When banks are strong, people are encouraged to save. These savings are lent out to support households, businesses, and communities.

The third pillar is a safe and efficient payments and settlements system. Under our Digital Payments Transformation Roadmap 2020–2023, we aim to shift from a cash-heavy to a cash-lite economy. So, how does this pillar contribute to growth? Think of our role as plumbers. Good plumbing work would ensure smooth flow of water, same as having a safe and efficient payment system that ensures that transactions are settled and closed. It also strengthens confidence in the system.

Now back to our first pillar: price stability. Let me backtrack to show you where we are coming from. At yesterday’s meeting, the Monetary Board raised the policy rate by 50 basis points (bps), bringing the overnight reverse repurchase rate to 3.75 percent. 

What was the Board responding to? Inflation rose to 6.4 percent in July, owing mainly to faster price increases of key food items like meat, fish, and sugar. 

As you can see from this slide, the latest baseline inflation forecasts suggest that inflation could remain elevated in 2022 and 2023. Based on our August 18 assessment, inflation is expected to average 5.4 percent for 2022, before slowing to 4.0 percent in 2023, and finally decelerating to within the target range at 3.2 percent for 2024. 

What we are worried about is that inflation gains momentum. Higher prices beget higher prices. Inflation results in more inflation—or what we call second-order effects.

We have seen further second-round effects by way of wage and transport fare hike petitions, which strengthen the case for ongoing tightening by the BSP.

That said, the Philippines is not alone in experiencing above-target inflation. This is clearly not unique to the Philippines. A growing number of countries—from advanced economies to emerging economies—are grappling with high prices. 

In response to higher-than-expected inflation in the US, we have seen the US Federal Reserve (US Fed) pivoting from initially seeing inflation as something transitory to making inflation their priority concern. 

So, the US Fed hiked by 225 bps year-to-date in a bid to control US inflation. The interest differentials between the Philippines and the US began to move in favor of the US dollar, which could lead to depreciation pressures on the peso.

Given the magnitude of the US Fed’s policy actions, the Philippines could not not react. That is why we took action. But we do not have to move in complete lockstep with the US Fed and match their actions one for one.

As an inflation-targeting central bank, we believe changes in the exchange rate are healthy and work in the correct direction.

The BSP does not normally react to movements in the exchange rate in keeping with our market-determined exchange rate policy. But in recent periods, the peso depreciation, while remaining with regional peers, has been adding significantly to the build-up of inflationary pressures. 

I have already said, on separate occasions, that the BSP is ready to take more steps to bring inflation back to a target-consistent path. 

As shown in this chart, there are broadening pressures on inflation as denoted by the 12-month moving average (red line). 

While we have hiked by a cumulative 175 bps, our policy settings are still accommodative. Remember: we are coming from a 4.0-percent pre-pandemic policy rate, which was in January 2020. As you can see in the chart, our policy rate is still lower than it used to be. Achieving a target-consistent path of inflation is of great importance to us. Respectable growth is still possible under those terms, but for the BSP, price stability is the primary concern. 

In closing, we invite the members of the EBC to work toward the BSP’s vision of a stronger, more digitalized, and more inclusive Philippine economy. In particular, the creation of better-quality jobs and the promotion of green and sustainable investments will create opportunities for development. 

I trust that we can count on your support as we move toward these objectives and goals for the nation. Thank you for your attention.

###

Title: Effective Central Bank Independence: Essential Element to Economic Stability
Occasion: Management Association of the Philippines (MAP) 2nd Face-to-Face Economic Briefing
Speaker: BSP Governor Felipe M. Medalla
Transcription:
​

Good afternoon, everyone.  

I would like to thank the Management Association of the Philippines (MAP) for the opportunity to share my insights. I have heard the presentation of my good friend [National Economic and Development Authority (NEDA) Secretary] Arci [Balisacan]. So, what I will share is the role of the central bank in all of these.  

These are the most important things to us: stable prices, as defined now as inflation between 2.0–4.0 percent; a stable and strong financial system; and a secure, safe, and efficient payment system. 

But why are these things important [to us]? The best example of this is our response to the pandemic: 

We bought a trillion pesos of bonds in the secondary market. By the way, one trillion is a lot because, at that time, our balance sheet was about ₱4 trillion. 

Of course, we also lent ₱600 billion to the government, interest-free. 

That stabilized the situation. In other words, the collapse of the economy by almost -9.0 percent [in 2020] could have been much worse. 

Of course, the question you ask is: where did we get the power to do that? The answer is our independence. During all those years, we never “printed” money to support the government. We bought a lot of foreign currency, mostly dollars. Because our independence was respected [by] government after government, as the economy needed more money, we produced the money by buying foreign assets. So, when the time came—when COVID came—we had more than enough resources to shore things up.  

In addition, because inflation was stable [then], the share of longer-term bonds in government debt was rising. This is the kind of environment we want: price stability so that fixed-rate loans are possible.  

We are very glad that the government and the Constitution itself created central bank independence and a law was written to make it independent. So far, in my entire 11 years on the Monetary Board, not once were we told by the government, “We like this interest rate. Keep this interest rate. Do this. Do that. Do not close that bank. Be nice to this bank.” This is the kind of environment we are in. 

That was, at the same time, accompanied by very good fiscal management.  

The man you are honoring, [former MAP member, the late] President [Fidel] Ramos said, “Oil price stabilization? Abolish that because it does not work in Philippine politics.” The entire idea of oil price stabilization is when international [oil] prices are rising, [the government would partially] subsidize it, and [it will] get the money to subsidize it when prices are falling. If you let politicians manage it [the fund], they will follow it only when the prices are rising. So, the subsidy will be unfunded. Ramos said, “The Philippines must be educated. Fuel prices are driven by international forces. The government has no business trying to stabilize it.”  

Then, [former President] Gloria Arroyo increased the value-added tax (VAT) from 10.0 to 12.0 percent and included fuel to VAT—a very unpopular decision.  

Later on, in the case of [former Department of Finance] Sec. [Carlos] Dominguez, he said “Let us cut personal income tax, raise fuel taxes, raise taxes on cigarettes, and raise taxes on sugary goods.”  

Our country, in other words, has a long history of good fiscal and monetary policy.  

The worst thing for a central banker is what they call fiscal dominance. You print more money than you should because you are saving the world. That is a very big dilemma. Your choice is letting it [the government] default or printing the money to save it. So, the second is the lesser of two evils. This is one [good] thing about the country. In spite of all the things we were quarreling about, we were able to agree. We were able to agree that the time called for a higher VAT and a VAT that would cover small things.  

We were quickly rewarded by capital markets [for this move]. When I was in NEDA, the spread between the 10-year dollar bond of the Philippine government and the 10-year dollar bond of the US government was 600 basis points (bps). The only difference was the borrower. Why were we paying 6.0 percent more? Because they thought we would default… After VAT, now, it is what? 100 bps? The [pain from] VAT alone is small compared to all the savings that came from [more affordable] loans. 

These [reforms] produced a fantastic period of [pre-pandemic] growth: 6.5-percent growth, 3.0 percent inflation, and falling poverty. We were also gifted by millions of Filipinos that attracted BPOs [business process outsourcing] and exported a lot of workers. The quality of the labor force and the excellent fiscal and monetary management produced a wonderful period. The question is: can we replicate this [after the pandemic]? 

Before I go to the topic, let me say that the banking system is strong: very well capitalized and they make provisions for losses. If a bank behaves badly, we tell them to raise capital. We have strong banks. You can see that in the recovery of lending growth. [Having] strong banks is good news. 

The rescue package we had for the government during the pandemic was so large that the IMF [International Monetary Fund] noticed and said, “Why is your balance sheet now ₱7 trillion from ₱4.5 trillion?” And they called it “unconventional.” We told them, “It is not unconventional because it is in our Charter.” But they said [in response], “It is unconventional because you have never done it before.” 

The key is: [if] the central bank, during good times, accumulates assets because the economy is growing, it can issue more money. Because of their faith in the currency, people want to hold the currency. These are the good things that are going for us. 

Of course, any rescue plan must have an exit. No central bank should ever rescue the economy and then ask, “Now that we have done this, how do we get out of this?” That is the big question in rich countries that have done a lot of QE [quantitative easing]. In our case, we said we will exit as the economy recovers. We will gradually lift the rates and then, we will let the securities that we bought mature gradually. 

But as they say, “The plans of mice and men often go awry.” The surprises came [in the form of the] US interest rate [liftoff]. The question is, what is next? When you have that, of course, the exit has to be more rapid. 

We are exiting much faster. The government already paid us back their advances. We are allowing the one trillion [in government securities] to run off our balance sheet. Maybe in the next two years, ₱200 billion of that will mature. And then, our interest rate increases were a lot harder [larger] than expected.  

Nonetheless, I am quite optimistic that the economy remains strong and can actually absorb the rate increases. Of course, whether the last one, yesterday’s 50 bps [hike] is the last one, nobody knows. The answer is: we will look at the data. 

This is our fan chart before the [August policy] meeting. Inflation will fall to 4.0 percent [in 2023]. The only reason August inflation is 5.4 percent is [because] we are averaging, and the first three months were low. So, 5.4 percent is the average of low numbers from January–March and the high numbers from the last three, four months. Some people are saying this will [still] rise because it has not peaked yet. My personal forecast is that the peak will come by September–October. And after that, as global prices start to fall and partly because people are expecting a US recession, then we will have lower inflation. In techno-speak, we are moving to a target-consistent inflation path.  

Most central banks would say, “Be as vague as you want.” But that was the old philosophy before [former US Federal Reserve (US Fed) Chair Ben] Bernanke. Then, when more and more academics went into central banking, he said, “We will tell you exactly what we think is going to happen and that is what we are going to do.” Of course, that is called forward guidance.  

It is no longer going to be 4.0 percent [average inflation in 2023] because we hiked by 50 bps [in our latest move]. The revisions downward are partly because we expect commodity prices to start easing but also because we expect our policy rate hikes to eventually bite. It takes 6–12 months before it [rate hike] takes effect. There is nothing we can do about the current high inflation from a monetary standpoint.  

The thing to do [to reduce inflation] is not to let bureaucrats and politicians know when and how much to import. Get the bureaucrats and the politicians out of import decisions. The best way to do that is if you want high protection, impose high tariffs. If you want low protection, impose low tariffs. The debate should be on how high the tariffs should be. It [the current setup] creates a lot of room for rent-seeking [because] he [a person or a small group of persons] gets permits to import instead of the government getting the difference between the Philippine price and foreign price. [What is] worse [is] if we give quotas to few people who connive. The best lesson on how to do it was when Sec. Dominguez tariff-ied rice. 

This is one of the reasons we raised rates. The red bar is the proportion of items below 2.0 percent [inflation]; you can see how quickly it is shrinking when it used to be the predominant item. Some items are resistant to demand pressures, but you notice that those items are getting fewer. On the other hand, the items in purple, which is above [the 4.0 percent] target, are growing.  

That means inflation is beginning to creep throughout the system and we had to act. The inflation you are seeing now compared to the inflation you were seeing before is the reaction of markets to the high imported inflation, or second-order effects, which we have to stop. We are beginning to see these as well [in the form of] minimum wage adjustments and transport fares.  

The other way to look at it is the comparison of the weighted median (grey line), which removes all the volatile items that are going up a lot, and the headline inflation (blue line), which covers everything. The blue line is skyrocketing. More alarming, even if you take out those big-ticket items that are going up, the grey line is inching up closer and closer to 4.0 percent. So, we had to act. 

This compares the US-Philippines in terms of the number of [cumulative] adjustments in their [respective] policy rates. They [the US Fed] did 225 bps; we did 125 bps.  

We had no choice: we had to respond to the US Fed, but we do not have to match every point that they do because their inflation is higher. In the US, it [inflation] is 8.5 percent. In the Philippines, it is 6.4 percent [at the latest reading].  

An even better way to look at this is to look at the ratio of the inflation of the ten-year average for all the countries to the current [inflation]. Which country has one of the lowest ratios? The Philippines and China. In other words, this is a global phenomenon—this [period of high] inflation—and relative to others, we are doing better. In Europe, it is 7.4 times; in UK, it is 5.2 times; and in US, it is 4.5 times. In other words, inflation in the US is 4.5 times higher than it used to be. In the case of the Philippines, inflation is 2.3 times [higher than the ten-year average]. And in China, it is only 1.3 times. 

The policy rate is 3.75 percent now, but relative to inflation, it is still low. By and large, our monetary policy is still accommodative.  

The point is: a foreigner is not looking at the gap [between the policy rate and inflation]; they are looking at the nominal gap between our interest rate and the US interest rate. Imagine a world where our policy rate is the same as the US. Clearly, where would the money go? So, we had no choice but to respond. It is called the impossible trinity. 

The other side of it, aside from monetary policy, is we are very concerned about digitalization and inclusion. Fortunately, they go together. Because without the telcos [telecommunications companies], the number of people without [access to] a bank will be much lower. Brick-and-mortar is a very expensive way to reach depositors. 

My final point: let us avoid fiscal dominance at all costs. The central bank is put in a position with two very undesirable choices: finance the government or let it default. So, will economic growth solve the debt problem? The current numbers for this year suggest yes. Even if we grow at only 6.0 percent, inflation is already 5 ½ percent. So, nominally, the economy is already growing at 11.0 percent. The average interest rate is less than 5.0 percent so we will outgrow the debt.  

Of course, the more difficult problem is what if growth is 3.0 percent and inflation is back to 3.0 percent? That is not true anymore. When that time comes, and I hope it does not come, we will have [to have] a very, very objective discussion on how we can solve the problem. That problem cannot be solved unless we all agree. If it turns out, in a year or two from now, we were over-optimistic about economic growth, then we have to go to Plan B: which is how we increase tax revenue. That is my message. 

Maraming salamat.  ​

Title: Taking steps to improve coin recirculation in the Philippines
Occasion: MOA signing with Participating Retailers for the Coin Deposit Machine Project
Speaker: BSP Governor Felipe M. Medalla
Transcription:
​

SM Retail Inc. Controllership and Financial Planning Senior Vice President Jonathan H. Ng, Filinvest Land Inc. Deputy Chief Finance Officer Janeth De los Reyes, and Robinsons Retail Holdings Inc. – Robinsons Supermarket Managing Director Stanley Co.; fellow BSPers, partners, ladies and gentlemen, good afternoon.

The phrase “barya lang po sa umaga” – suggests there’s really a shortage of coins. I remember when I was growing up, as a 15-year-old first-year student in a school nearby, I would take the bus from Lipa to La Salle Taft, where my boarding house was nearby. I would wonder about the skill of the conductor. During those times, the buses did not have aisles; they had continuous seats all the way to the side. In other words, one side of the bus is completely closed, and the other side is completely open. The conductor has no change. What he does is he swings from outside the bus, literally like an acrobat, moving from one side to the other, asking everybody where they’re going. After having asked that, he punches all the tickets. Alam niya kung ilan ang Lipa, ilan ang Batangas City, ilan ang Malvar. Fantastic memory. And then he will collect all the payments. A lot of people overpay because they don’t have exact change. In the end, he will now get all the coins, and somehow, he’s able to remember who to give the money back to. So, in other words, to solve the coin problem, you need a very smart bus conductor.

We seem to have the same problem now: the problem of recirculating coins. When I look at this project, everyone is benefitting: us [at the BSP], we’re going to save a lot of money on the cost of minting. Let me give a small lecture on seigniorage: it’s nicer to print P1000 [banknote] because the P6 gives you P1000. If the P1000 earns a little bit of interest, you recover the P6. That’s called positive seigniorage. On the other hand, the coins have a small face value, yet the cost of production is so high. So you’re helping us solve this problem.

But you’re also helping the public because there’s a sense of fairness. Ayaw ng mga tao ng sukli ay kendi. This is solving problems for everyone.

The only question I want to ask myself is, with something as good as this, why did it just come only now? The question is why and the reason is somebody has to think of it. And thank God, enough people thought about it, and now people came together and talked about it, and here we have it!

We in the BSP think that [with] our investment in the machines plus the creativity of our partners, everyone will benefit. In other words, partial ideas put together can become full-blown ideas that work.

I’m very, very optimistic that after a two-year pilot run, we will be able to deploy these machines, and hopefully, I’m quite confident that the benefits will be realized.

The lesson from this is: what other things here in BSP could follow this model? And I’m thinking, what about the fact that we are so “dependent” on the P1000 bill because the ATM is the best way to distribute currency? Banks don’t like to put P100 bills in ATMs because it’s very expensive, right? Such that the P100 bill tends to just keep circulating [in the informal economy] even if it’s no longer fit. So, another version of this [model]: maybe we will have fitter notes that would use the very principle we used here [in the coin deposit project] and find the very same partners we have here.

When we think this way and work together this way, we, together, can do a lot of things. Thank you very much, and good afternoon.

Title: The Road Ahead: Priorities for the Next Six Years
Occasion: Economic Journalists Association of the Philippines (EJAP) Virtual Forum
Speaker: BSP Governor Felipe M. Medalla
Transcription:
​

Good morning.  

[Your theme] “The Road Ahead: Priorities for the Next Six Years” is a very easy question to answer for a central banker because we have our three pillars: price stability, financial stability, and an efficient and secure payments and settlements system. Those three pillars do not change; what does change is the environment and in the case of the payment system, the technology. In that sense, though our pillars are constant, the dynamic of the policies of the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP) is very fluid.  

As you can see in the chart—note that these numbers are old data and do not reflect the latest data that we will use [at our policy meeting] tomorrow. That said, for this year, we will clearly miss our 2.0–4.0 percent inflation target. Due to the fact that the last two headline inflation numbers are higher than expected, you would expect an upward revision [to our forecast for the year]. However, it can also go the other way.  

Indeed, the actions we take are all meant to bring the current forecasts of 4.2 percent [for 2023] below 4.0 percent and 3.3 percent [forecast for 2024], closer to 3.0 percent. Of course, it is easier said than done. And if we focus too much on that [inflation] and ignore the effects on output, the output loss of our actions can be very large. That is why we call it flexible inflation-targeting. That is why it is a band—2.0–4.0 percent. If you are too focused [on hitting] the midpoint of the target, you will sacrifice a lot of GDP [gross domestic product].  

I can already say that we should aim for a point lower than 4.0 percent next year and closer to 3.0 percent the following year. The rest of the term of the current president should be within 2.0–4.0 percent. Forecasting anything beyond 18 months is really futile. The normal distribution is about 95.0 percent probability, and that standard deviation gets larger and larger as the forecast policy horizon goes further.  

To give you an example, we were pleasantly surprised in 2016–2017 when inflation was lower than target. Why? Because the global environment was deflationary.  

So, these are the forecasts of private sector economists—they are not very far from ours. We ran a regression between our forecasts as the independent variable and private sector forecasts as the dependent variable, [and we found that] BSP forecasts influence private sector forecasts. 

It is our role to influence inflationary expectations. Our role is to tell the public: we will use everything in our toolkit to bring inflation to within the target band, in this case, 2.0–4.0 percent. It is just that there are times when supply shocks and global shocks are just too powerful.  

Of course, as shown by the sugar incident, both natural [factors] and [man-made] policy could affect prices—bad weather, expensive fertilizer, reduced sugar supply, etc. I keep saying that bureaucrats saying how [much] to import is always a formula for disaster because so many things [data] are needed that you end up with too much or too little imports.  

You can see that the latest inflation prints suggest intensifying inflationary pressures—whether you look at the year-on-year or the 12-month moving average, all the lines are going up. 

Even more alarming is that the share of items [within the inflation target] is getting smaller, whereas the share in purple [items above target] is rising. This is the current challenge that we are facing.  

We are also beginning to see what we call second-round effects. Naturally, if the inflation rate is high, people will ask for more adjustments in wages. Naturally, if fuels get more expensive, transport groups will ask for price adjustments. So, second-round effects are already being seen. 

The other way to look at this is to look at core inflation, which takes out volatile items. But even if you take out the volatile items, as you can see, the grey line is [still] going up and is closer to 4.0 percent than to 3.0 percent.  

To make things even more difficult, the peso has depreciated quite a bit. Of course, as you can see in the graph, we are in the company of many: in other words, it is a strong dollar, not a weak peso. But for the consumer, [most] things are getting expensive because imports are largely denominated in dollars. As the Americans say, “The dollar is our currency, [but] it is your problem.” 

Normally, we do not care too much about the exchange rate movements because they are healthy adjustments. But there are times, if it is [depreciation] too much, it might actually disanchor inflationary expectations.  

For instance, in the experience of Latin America during the bad old days, depreciation has actually contributed to a balance of payments deficit because every time the currency depreciates, inflation goes up by an equivalent amount. If you look at the ratio of the exchange rate and the price index, every time the numerator goes up, the denominator goes up, too. So, the ratio does not change. If that happens, you can even have hyperinflation—inflation causing exchange rate changes and exchange rate changes causing inflation. And to make things worse, debt is dollar-denominated, bankruptcies [can happen], and so on and so forth. You do not want to get there.  

Fortunately, we have the capacity, the forex reserves and, I hope, the confidence of the public to make sure we will succeed in achieving price stability. 

This chart shows that, relative to target, most countries are missing their inflation targets. The biggest miss is the UK, [which has a] target of 2.0 percent, but inflation is 9.4 percent. Europe [has a] target of 2.0 percent, but inflation is 8.9. Even USA… These countries have lower targets than us but [are experiencing] higher inflation than us. 

This is not misery loves company nor an excuse-making. All I am trying to show is that the tools of the central bank cannot move these things. It is like using a needle to push a cannonball.  

You will see that we have changed policy rates by [a cumulative] 125 basis points (bps), including the surprise 75 bps [rate hike]. The 75 bps [move] was a surprise in two ways: [first] it was not scheduled, and [second] it was 75 bps.  

The US Federal Reserve (US Fed) has actually done 225 bps [in cumulative rate adjustments]. From the picture I just showed previously, their actual inflation is much, much higher than target, so they are much more aggressive than us. [We may] expect the US Fed to be less aggressive than before, but we cannot rule out 50 bps [moves]—which, in central bank language, are [considered] large adjustments.  

[While] we do not discount what the US Fed is doing, the question becomes the extent to which we do have to respond, taking into account the exchange rate effect. If the exchange rate changes are already so large, you do not want that to add further to the already high inflation rate. 

In spite of the increases, what I would like to emphasize is that…while we increased the policy rate—it was at 200 bps for a long time—the yellow line is much lower than the red and blue lines. 

In other words, policy [settings] is still quite accommodative. The reason is that COVID forced us to be very aggressive in supporting the economy:  

  • We cut the policy rate to 2.0 percent, which we have never done before. 
  • We bought over a trillion pesos of government securities in the secondary market. 
  • We also lent ₱600 billion, interest-free, to the government. 

It is working and that is what we call a nascent, strong economic recovery. 

Even with the global problem, we already had an exit plan. Of course, the exit came sooner and faster than expected, given what is happening outside the Philippines. 

You can see there was a large contraction of the economy because of lockdowns; the economy contracted by almost 17.0 percent [in Q2 2020].  

Fortunately, we were able to bounce back [with] vaccination and also because it seems that the current strain of COVID is not sending as many people to the hospital as the previous one. We can see that [trend] as well in our own statistics of our employees. 

Therefore, in that sense, I am optimistic that given the current [COVID] strain has not sent too many people to the hospital, we are less likely to lock [the economy] down. If we do have lockdowns, they will likely be limited. 

The other source of my optimism is that the services sector has already seen a quite strong recovery. What is lagging behind is agriculture. In particular, [agricultural] production could not keep up as demand for sugar increased, which is quite related to GDP growth because [it is found in] soft drinks, restaurants, ice cream—all of these things.  

For our second pillar, financial stability, you see a lot of strength. The pictures show that by and large, banks are strong, loans are recovering, and banks have sufficient provision in capital to take a hit from defaults due to COVID. This is the picture for loan demand, also quite encouraging.  

Of course, the downward revision by the IMF [International Monetary Fund] of global growth is the downside to growth, but it is also a downside to inflation.  

Indeed, what we are seeing now is oil prices are now going down because people are expecting demand to fall due to a slowdown in the US economy.  

Most people say, including Jamie Dimon of JPMorgan, that a [US] recession is inevitable. [They say that] the economy is not like a plane that you can land all the time; sometimes, it crashes, and sometimes, the landing is not very good. Exactly… To what extent to which all these policies by the US Fed, which are meant to control inflation, could now result in a hard landing is something we cannot guess. The best experts could be wrong, like Paul Krugman.  

Global commodity prices are easing. All these factors will contribute to growth, to a stronger Philippine economy because we are a net importer of all these things. 

But who can forecast what will happen? What I am saying is that forecasting things at this point is a very dicey thing. 

Amidst all of these, of course, there are things that we must do. Technology is changing the payments system, and we must adapt to it. New firms and new types of banks will rise. We now have six digital banks, and the regulators must learn how to regulate. 

These are the issues that we are looking at:  

  • Corporate and risk governance of banks 
  • Sustainable finance – We tell the banks to include climate change in their calculation of default and risk. In other countries, banks are being told to reduce lending to polluting industries or activities. We are not doing that because we are a rounding error in the production of greenhouse gases.  
  • Digital transformation 

As part of our Digital Payments Transformation Roadmap, we aim to digitalize at least half of retail payments and ensure at least 70.0 percent of Filipino adults have transaction accounts because if you do not have accounts, you cannot be a part of the financial system. You may have heard the news of the Paleng-QR [launch in Baguio] where I bought taho from a vendor using a QR code. 

In closing, in line with the theme of this forum, “The Road Ahead: Priorities for the Next Six Years,” the BSP's policy priorities for the next six years will remain anchored on our mandates, on our three pillars: promoting price stability, financial stability, and a safe and efficient payment and settlements system. 

On price stability: we stand ready to take the necessary policy actions and focus our efforts on anchoring inflation expectations and bringing inflation back to target as soon as possible, considering the tradeoff between speed [on which we normalize policy] and output loss. 

On financial stability: the BSP will continue to foster an enabling environment for the financial institutions under our supervision and, as I said, our supervision and rules adjust to the changing times and technology. 

Lastly, the BSP recognizes and advocates for the increased role of digital platforms in achieving greater efficiency in the country's payment system and financial inclusion. That is why getting everyone a [national] ID, whether digital or physical, is a priority for the President because many services of the government would become more efficient if we had a way of identifying everybody, especially providing targeted assistance to the poor.  

Thank you very much for your attention.
