Title: Speech for BSP Young Professionals Program (YPP) Batch 1 Graduation
Occasion: BSP Young Professionals Program (YPP) Batch 1 Graduation
Speaker: BSP Governor Felipe M. Medalla
Transcription:
​

Magandang hapon sa inyong lahat. This brings me back to my UP days when I used to enjoy graduation ceremonies. BSP colleagues, guests, ladies, and gentlemen, of course, most importantly, our dear graduates.

Let me start by congratulating this pioneering batch of the BSP YPP – or Young Professionals Program – for successfully completing the program.

Today, we celebrate and honor you for what you have accomplished – completing what I see is a really hard, rigorous 18 months that most likely forced all of you to immerse yourselves in different areas of central banking and see it from the point of view of various departments in the bank. You were able to successfully complete two projects, I was told, with your sponsoring departments, which I am sure will contribute to our processes, systems, and knowledge base here in the BSP.

So the next question is: what now or now what? Dear graduates, it’s time for you to build your own career not just as central bankers but as public servants in the truest sense of the word. You’ll be lucky to be in an institution that, in our view, serves the people because of the importance of its three pillars. As you help BSP achieve them and improve the performance of the economy through its three pillars, you have also served the country.

Of course, there are other ways of serving the country, like being a good brother to your younger siblings or, just like me, being a good husband and father to my children. But there’s nothing like working for an institution whose mandates are so clearly defined and whose tools are largely in its own hands.

Of course, there are things beyond our control, like any other institution that has to deal with a very complex environment, but it’s very clear what the metrics are. If you’re a BSPer, you will have a methodology for removing what we call exogenous variables. Which of the nice things that happen are due to us? Which of the nice things that happen is pure luck? But it could also go the other way: which of the bad things that happen are just pure bad luck? And which of the bad things are things that suggest that we should get better?

I’m certain that there’s more to come — more opportunities to learn and grow, to contribute, and to add value.

By the way, do not use NBA metrics. In NBA, you know exactly what the performance of a team is when you’re in or out of the game. They call this the plus-minus statistics, ‘we without you.’ Some players are plus 10; some players are minus 30, meaning every time they’re in, the game is losing badly. Even in that particular case, it need not be your fault, meaning you’re a young player, and you’re used only when the team is losing. Even in that particular case, where pluses and minuses are so easy to compute, how much it is when you’re in or out of the game, nothing can really be measured for certain. That’s why values, beliefs, vision, and dreams are important because pluses and minuses cannot be your true being.

What is it then that [you need] in this journey where measuring your output is so hard? This entire field of economics [is] where you can measure the output of the thing but never measure the output of the members of the team. Sometimes, it could be frustrating; sometimes, it could be exciting because your team did very well, and you knew you contributed. What are these things that you need?

Of course, you must have self-discipline. We often confuse this with zest and enthusiasm. Why? Much of the work is not like reading a book, then it turns out to be boring, so you put it down. Or you might join a weight-loss program and then give up, saying, ‘I’ll make up later,’ or enrolling in a new course and backing off midway when your interest wanes. In other words, don’t be ningas-kugon. True commitment demands from us the self-discipline to finish what we started and, most of all, to complete it without sacrificing quality.

Now, the second quality is perseverance, but I don’t have to explain this too much. The fact that you’re here. You finished the program. You have this.

The third is loyalty. Loyalty does not mean big, heroic actions because sometimes that may be the requirement. We’ve seen that happen to our employees when despite great disasters, they’re able to [keep things running and] prevent the branch from elements disabling [it]. You don’t need to be heroic all of the time, sometimes it calls for you to just show up when expected and do the needful: be punctual in your appointments, make time for people, especially the members of your own team, and, of course, keep your word. These acts of loyalty will make you important men and women of honor and important assets of the BSP.

Mahal kayo ng BSP. Mahalin niyo ang BSP. The adjective “mahal” has at least two different meanings. Mahal is an adjective for beloved. The other one is pricey or expensive or high value. But they’re not contradictory. When you say, dahil mahal niyo ang BSP, binibigay niyo ang lahat mahahalagang bagay para sa kanya.

After this, you will go back to your respective offices and do what you have to do, finish the task that you have to finish. But I hope that you will go home with a renewed sense of commitment to finish strong in everything that you do and be committed to doing work that you will be proud of because you always deliver quality work. As they say, “Para sa Pilipino, para sa bayan at ang BSP ay para sa bayan.”

Before I end, let me thank DG Ed Bobier, YPP Chairperson Lou Sicat, and YPP Vice Chairperson Jayzle Ravelo for putting this excellent program together.

Once again, to Batch 1 of the BSP Young Professionals Program, congratulations, and we look forward to many great things from all of you. Maraming Salamat.

Title: Bringing Paleng-QR PH Plus to Baguio
Occasion: Paleng-QR PH Launch in Baguio
Speaker: BSP Governor Felipe M. Medalla
Transcription:
​

Good morning everyone. Like Mayor Benjie, I’d like to skip the formal introduction… Mayor Benjamin Magalong, I’d like to thank you for a beautiful conversation yesterday evening. Of course, I’d like to greet Congressman Mark Go. It is extremely important that the correct legislation that supports digitalization all happen, and we will need your support. And all the other partners - I have to greet the representative of DILG Regional Director Araceli San Jose - and all our private sector partners; this cannot happen without the private sector.

As you know, procurement in government is very difficult. Buying anything takes months, but with the private sector, which has its own system, has a great advantage over us in this respect, and that’s why we need them very much. I noticed people from both Maya, Globe, and GCash. I was thinking of what quotation I will use to start this speech. And I was initially thinking of Neil Armstrong. When he landed on the moon, he said, “One small step for man, giant step for mankind.” Of course, they never went back to the moon because it was very expensive.

But nonetheless, a lot of lessons were learned. Indeed, until now, they left behind a metal disk that can be detected and targeted by a laser beam to the moon, and now we have very precise measures of how far the moon is because of that device. And there are many things they have learned by going to the moon that can also be applied elsewhere.

But that kind of quotation is not really appropriate for this project because it turns out Baguio has not taken one step, it already has taken many steps. So, we started Paleng-QR in the right city. Of course, we are hoping and praying that it will spread throughout the Philippines and it will reach the sidewalk vendor, the tricycle driver, and the jeepney driver. By the way, the jeepney driver is very important. When I used to take the jeepney, I would notice sometimes the wife was seated in front. Sabi ko, “That’s not too wise.” They lose one revenue [with the] seat [taken], right? Then I found out the wife is auditing the revenue of the husband. Now with Paleng-QR, hindi na niya kailangang sumakay ng jeep, tingnan niya na lang ang transaction record ng asawa niya.

Now, of course, that also creates new risks. Like what if all these information gets in the wrong hands? That’s why the Data Privacy Law is extremely important, but at the same time, the implications in the future are staggering. Can you imagine if every merchant that was willing to waive his right tells the bank, “You can look at my records.” The bank will see his transaction, and without asking for collateral, can already make an assessment of how much loan can be granted to that merchant.

By the way, this is not a very distant future, and BSP already started on the project with JICA on a credit scoring system. If you look at all the data that you have on anyone, you can already calculate a credit score. And imagine a world where you no longer need collateral. Because the biggest thing that holds back the poor is a chicken-egg question: wala kang property kaya hindi ka maka-utang, pero kaya hindi ka makautang dahil wala kang property. So [Paleng-QR Ph] will break it – that really very bad, negative circle. But we want our positive circles.

I’m really so impressed with Baguio. This is the place where the positive circles are happening. Of course, I will not mention any more what the Baguio App is already doing - I am very impressed - for instance when somebody needs assistance, all he has to do is tap one icon there, and the location device of your cellphone turns on…and it already knows where you are. If it happens that there is a camera in that place, the city will actually see you. So, if there is any place where we want to start [Paleng-QR Ph], we picked the right place.

Of course, success is not automatic. As the Chinese say, “cross the river by feeling the stones.” Kasi malalim yung river. Pero kung maraming bato ka na pwedeng tungtungan at palukso-lukso ka sa bawat bato, kahit pa gaano kalalim yung river, mako-cross mo. Eh paano kung sa gitna wala ka nang makitang bato? Atras, diba? And tweak. I also heard that word ‘tweak’ so many times.

So, I’m so optimistic. We are truly excited to roll out the Paleng-QR Ph here in Baguio City, and we look forward to everyone’s support for the successful implementation of this program, not just in Baguio but everywhere in the Philippines. Maraming salamat at magandang umaga sa inyong lahat.

Title: Towards the Path to Recovery
Occasion: Rural Bankers Association of the Philippines (RBAP) Meeting
Speaker: BSP Governor Felipe M. Medalla
Transcription:
​


When I was growing up in Lipa City, there was only one bank in Lipa and that was a rural bank—that is the Malarayat Rural Bank. They are still around. Eventually, PNB [Philippine National Bank] came. Only much, much later did we see commercial banks. So, my point is, you have PNB but that was there upon government orders. No particular individual really chose Lipa. On the other hand, the commercial banks came when Lipa was already a large and successful city—when it was possible to send mail and just give the street without the number, and the mail will still reach you. 

My point is: rural banks were there long before the city was progressing. That is why I have always said to myself: I may have studied macroeconomics. I may have studied what people call price theory, which is how the price system, by equating demand and supply, is actually allocating resources efficiently. Those are very abstract concepts. The tendency is to look at large numbers or summaries: total assets, total loans, or some not-very-good statistics, like non-performing loans, but never looking at the detail. I am glad to tell you all my friends here that, in the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP), we may be good at the macro, but we will never forget the micro. We will never say, “Oh, this sector accounts only for 3.0 percent of total assets,” and a very simple reason for that, [which] I already described, [is] the days when I was growing up. 

These numbers that are aggregated hide a lot of important details. For instance, if you look closely at commercial banks, the branches are more deposit-gatherers than loan-granters and decision-makers. If a loan is big, it has to be decided at the head office. When you look at the fund flows, literally, the commercial banking system is gathering savings from all over the country to finance the government—[via their purchases of Treasury bills]—and, of course, to finance really big undertakings. This is not bad. What we learned from Japan and Korea is that largeness, if it is dynamic, can be an economic miracle. So, when you see all those big stories of success, conglomerates, of course, that is very important for global competitiveness and that is one reason, I guess, that Japan and Korea are very successful: their zaibatsus and chaebols conquered the world. 

But there is another side to human progress which is what is happening at the individual level, what is happening to individual places. My hometown of Lipa, at that time, was a small place but, clearly, towns like that did matter. So, for that reason, the rural banks are very important to us. 

Of course, you also have to have some form of standards and goals. Sometimes, certain things do not pass, and certain things pass. I am glad to hear from your presentation that you have a PCA [Prompt Corrective Action] Academy. [I am] glad to know that you are actually saying, “Maybe we can learn from each other.” 

There has to be a way of going around so that banks can learn from each other. Maybe a way of doing [that is] case writing, maybe changing the numbers a little bit. The success stories are being documented and the failures, too, are being documented. 

So, I think of the role of doing something about the third generation because it is a very common failure. A very well-run bank that has been around for 30, 40 years is in trouble because the grandfather was passionate about the bank and so was the son, and the son actually learned from the father. However, the third generation is a bit spoiled and no longer interested in [running] the bank. 

One solution is learning how to transition from being a family-run bank to being a professionally-run bank. But I suppose that is not easy, because we see that transition from the family-run, taipan-centered [organizations], and you can see that the transition is very disorderly. 

The Macroeconomy & BSP’s Policy Actions to Maintain Price Stability 

Let me start with the macroeconomy. 

If you make this graph longer in the left direction, you will see very tall positive bars—more than 10 years of very high growth averaging 6.5 percent [before the pandemic]. Then, a big crash [in 2020]. The pandemic ended more than 10 years of very high growth. The economy shrank by almost 10.0 percent [in 2020]. 

The economy has started to recover, and we take a little bit of credit for that. We saw how bad the pandemic was to the economy and decided to take very aggressive action: 

We cut the policy rate to a record low of 2.0 percent. 

Not only that, we also noticed that people were panicking. People were fleeing to cash. This is one lesson from history: when people do not know what is going on, they flee to cash. Economic theory says that if the people are panicking, the pandemic will actually make interest rates fall because it will reduce demand for CaPex [capital expenditure]. The motive to save is even stronger. More savings, less CaPex = low interest rates. But exactly the opposite happened. The lesson is that markets can go crazy. The central bank is not just the lender of last resort; it is the market-maker of last resort. The central bank starts buying government securities; we bought a trillion pesos worth. On top of that, we lent ₱600 billion, interest-free, to the government. That calmed the market and interest rates went in the right direction. Low CaPex should mean low interest rates; that is exactly what happened. If we had not intervened, then markets would have gone crazy, and the exact opposite should have happened. ​

But we know that what we did is something not normally done—things that you do only under abnormal times. The IMF [International Monetary Fund] called it an “unconventional” monetary policy. If this continues for too long, this could sow the seeds of a bubble or may threaten financial stability. So, we must have an exit plan. When you have a speeding car, you do not suddenly step on the brakes; you decline gradually to a nice stop. The passenger who is sleeping should not be woken up. 

But of course, that is not what happened—big, big surprises. Even Nobel Prize economists were totally wrong about US inflation. They were saying, US inflation is low and transitory. What you are seeing instead is high and somewhat persistent. What does the US Federal Reserve do when that happens? It tries to regain credibility by having unusually large and frequent interest rate changes. 

What happens when the global currency has higher interest rates? That global currency will actually be the safe haven because these are disturbed times. By itself, money will be moving to the safe haven. Tapos, mataas pa ‘yung interest ng safe haven. [Then, the interest rate of the safe haven is high.] So, you have falling currencies. That is why I keep saying it is a strong dollar, not a weak peso. 

The problem is mahal pa rin ang imports. [The problem is that imports are still expensive.] On top of that, even if the exchange rate did not change, mahal pa rin [it is still expensive]. We are calculating that not only did imports go up by almost 50.0 percent, of course, oil went up even more. If you add 50.0 percent plus a 10.0-percent deprecation of currency, that is quite a shock for many products. Fortunately, many other prices are not responding. Any central banker is afraid that as the other products respond too, you will have a spiral. Prices are high because prices are high. Wages are high. Prices are high. Before you know it, you have inflation out of control. 

Even if it is not popular, we will do what we have to do so that higher inflation does not beget higher inflation. The last thing you want is prices are high because prices are high. That will be a never-ending spiral. 

From the beginning, we were thinking of exiting [from these policies]. But because of high prices, the Ukraine war, and the sudden and unpredicted change in US monetary policy, we were afraid of what we called second-order effects. 

Of course, you do not see it everywhere. My favorite example of how rising imported prices does not affect local prices is that the cost of a haircut remains the same. The point is you still see a lot of products that are not responding. We look at that by taking out the outliers and using statistical methods, we take out the things that are rising or falling too much [to arrive at] core inflation. 

There are two measures of inflation: this month vs. 12 months ago. July 2022 vs. July 2021 is 6.4 percent, whereas June 2022 vs. June 2021 is 6.1 [percent], whereas January 2022 vs. January 2021 is below 4.0 percent. You can see the acceleration. 

So, our response, therefore, is, “This situation is different from what we initially expected. We did not anticipate the Ukraine war, that the US will experience this kind of inflation.” Therefore, our response was two 25 bps.  

Initially, we were sticking to the gradualist story. But then, the peso was falling rapidly. Normally, we do not react to the exchange rate because it is [small exchange rate fluctuations] actually a healthy thing. What that means is that high import prices are causing a dollar shortage. And what is the best way to reduce a shortage? Make the things scarcer and pricier, therefore less people will buy. The market works because it changes what we call relative prices. The imported goods become more expensive compared to domestic goods. Hopefully, the reaction of people is to shift away from imported goods, which is healthy. 

The problem is the moment inflation has second-order effects; it affects not just the ratio, but all the levels. 

In other words, changing prices that do not include the efficiency of the economy for allocation only causes inflation. That is why we had to act. 

You can see here that the Philippine peso depreciated, but there are currencies that depreciated even more. 

You can now look at the summary and see that in terms of depreciation, we are second to South Korea, taking out Europe and Japan. We are also the same as South Korea in terms of increase in policy rate. 

Notice that Indonesia has hardly moved [their policy rate] because they have oil—so, they are not as hit [by high oil prices]. 

Malaysia also has oil, and I just learned from a conference in Seoul that the reason their inflation is not so high is because they are subsidizing. But they, themselves, admit that it is [fuel subsidies] not sustainable. 

[In addition to policy rate adjustments], the Philippines sold reserves. The decline in our reserves is almost 10.0 percent. 

[In comparison], Thailand relied less on interest rate adjustments. They relied more on selling reserves, selling US$36 billion. The reason they are so reluctant [to increase rates] is their economy is so weak because of falling tourism figures. They are much harder hit than we are. 

That is the balancing act. It is a combination of many tools: letting your currency depreciate to the extent that we have adequate reserves, and we can offset some. It is like having bullets: when you shoot, you want to hit something. That is the balance that we sought. 

Fortunately, we have comfortable reserves but not excessive. 

The Banking Sector and BSP initiatives 

A story about the banking system: if I have to summarize this graph, what you have is growing deposits, growing loans, without sacrificing safety [of the system] and without having to run to the BSP for emergency loans—you have liquidity. Those are the numbers: growing assets, loan growth, deposit growth, profit growth, and, as far as we can see, adequately capitalized. 

Yesterday, we decided on an environmental sustainability [framework], meaning we tell the banks, “You must now incorporate climate-related risk in your assessment of risk.” 

In other countries that are contributing more to global warming, they are actually trying to discourage lending to greenhouse gas-emitting industries. But that is not our problem. We are almost a rounding error in terms of contribution to pollution. Our main problem is we must now be ready for rising default rates. We already knew this with agriculture: pests and drought—but now, we are thinking of other climate-related risks. 

A Focus on the Rural Banks 

Now, about you: there are about 389 rural banks. When I joined the Monetary Board, there was about double that number. Part of the reason is good—mergers. Some of the other reasons are because banks that are in PCA for a long period eventually went under. 

This is what I mean when I talk of Lipa, and there are many Lipas everywhere. Let us not look at percentages; let us look at how important rural banks are as institutions that do not just gather deposits to bring the money to Manila but recycle it, [and] the savings get redirected to where the savings are coming from. 

We support a regulatory environment for growth. We have a Rural Bank Strengthening Program (RBSP), which you are mirroring in your own programs. 

[Through the RBSP], we are going for safe and sound banks that are well-capitalized, and we must realize that there are economies of scale. Imagine a small nuclear plant [of] the size of a motorcycle engine. That is scale economies. 

The other economy is economy of scope. There are advantages of bigness because sometimes your activities fluctuate. If you have many activities and one activity is down, another activity is up. Then, you are able to use your resources more efficiently. 

The opposite of that are banks that are too small that they can barely afford the overhead. Imagine a bank with ₱20 million in capital, with leverage of 5 times, an interest margin of 4.0 percent, ₱4 million. What is the salary [you are paying to your employees]? Ubos na agad [capital] sa salary at kuryente. [The capital was already spent for payment of employees' salaries and electric consumption.]​ One bad loan and it is dead. This level of operation is so small that its overhead is eating into the interest margin. So, you have to reach a certain size to be stable. But we are reasonable. We are not saying, “Do it [right away].” 

We looked at the numbers and saw that the average bank [capitalization] is ₱100 million. We do not want all of you to hit the average, but maybe ₱20 million is too small. What we are saying now is [the minimum capital requirement is] ₱50 million. 

There are lots of good news. You are actively using InstaPay and PESONet. 

When there was a really big typhoon in Siargao, who was alive and open? Rural banks. 

The lesson from Cantilan is that rural banks can upscale in the use of technology and the cloud. We are thinking that this is not our function—this is fiscal— but [part of] our advocacy is to…help provide assistance to upscale the local bank and, maybe, explore a fund to guarantee MSMEs [micro, small, and medium enterprises]. I am glad to tell you that our newest Deputy Governor is the former Tourism Secretary who was the Undersecretary of Agriculture, who was managing the Agricultural Guarantee Fund [Pool]. 

Now, in closing, the story from your AVP [audio-visual presentation] shows that the small store can become large, [and] you [rural banks] can be the enabler of that. 

On the part of the BSP, rest assured that we do not aggregate numbers, but we look closely at the details.  

Maraming salamat at magandang gabi sa inyong lahat. [Thank you very much and good evening, everyone.]

###

Title: Sustaining the Philippine Economic Growth Story: The Role of the Central Bank in a Challenging Global Environment
Occasion: Federation of Filipino-Chinese Chambers of Commerce and Industry, Inc. (FFCCCI) Forum
Speaker: BSP Governor Felipe M. Medalla
Transcription:
​

Good afternoon.  

To all the members of the Federation, especially your president, Dr. Henry [Lim Bon Liong], I very much welcome this opportunity to be able to talk to you and make a short presentation. 

The Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP) appreciates these opportunities that allow us: 

First, to share our perspectives on the economy and our outlook and the central bank’s responses to these developments; and 

Second, to listen to the concerns and issues of those most affected by our policies. 

We have always believed that the BSP will be able to do a better job if the business community knows that we appreciate your point of view and you also understand why we do what we do. 

Let me first take us back to pre-pandemic time. At that time, the economy was humming along very nicely. On average, GDP [gross domestic product] grew by 6.5 percent for a period of 10 years before the pandemic. Moreover, it uplifted the lives of many Filipinos: poverty was reduced not just as the economy was growing but [also because] the government was improving tax collection and spent some of the money on pro-poor and pro-growth platforms. 

As you can see on the chart, the pandemic put a very rapid end to this beautiful period of growth. [In] Q2 2020, [there] was actually a 16.9-percent contraction. In Q1 2020, it [the economy] only shrank 0.7 percent, but the reason [why the contraction was not larger] is obvious: the lockdowns only started in the first two weeks of Q1. Two bad weeks outweighing 10 good weeks—that means that the last two weeks were even worse. If you calculate GDP weekly, the last two weeks of Q1 2020 were the worst. 

Fortunately, the decline of the economy became less and less. The explanation was simple: we learned to live with the virus. The lockdowns become more sensible, and more people got vaccinated. Now, we know better. 

There is a very large recovery starting from 2021, but do not be deceived by the numbers. The 12.1 percent [growth in Q2 2021] may look large, but it is 12.1 percent of something that is 10.0 percent smaller. The 12.1 percent [growth] is much, much smaller than the 11.6-percent contraction in Q3 2020. 

Fortunately, the strength continued. Despite the -3.8 percent [contraction] in Q1 2021, the overall growth in 2021 was 5.7 percent. The signs are very good because Q1 2022 was an expansion of 8.2 percent. If this [pace of growth] proceeds, we should have 7.0 percent annually in 2022. Let me explain what the BSP has done that has partially fueled this bounce back: 

  • We brought the policy rate to a record low of 2.0 percent. Considering that target inflation is 2.0–4.0 percent, it is actually lower than the lower of the midpoint of our inflation target; 
  • We also bought one trillion pesos in government securities; and 
  • [We] extended ₱600 billion in provisional advances to the National Government, interest-free. 

We knew all along that it would work, but we also knew that we had to exit from these very supportive monetary policies. The [exit] program aims to reverse a lot of these things: raise the policy rate, the government pays back its advances, and as the securities we bought matured, we will not buy new ones. The one trillion pesos [in government securities that we purchased] will gradually decline. 

That was the initial picture—a very gradual exit from ultra-accommodative monetary policies. Unfortunately, as Robert Burns said, “The best laid plans of mice and men often go awry.” That is exactly what happened. 

What were the surprises? 

  • The biggest surprise is that America was initially saying that inflation was low and transitory. We know now exactly the opposite happened. Naturally, the US Federal Reserve (US Fed) reacted very strongly. 
  • In addition, we had the Ukraine war, which caused the prices of oil and non-oil imports to go up significantly. The most important non-oil imports are fertilizer and flour. 

Because of US monetary policy, the dollar became king again. Everyone wants to go back to the dollar because it is the safe haven. If the interest on peso assets is the same as interest rates on US assets, the choice is clear: go for the US assets. This has resulted in many currencies, not just the peso, to depreciate. 

To sum up: we had an initial exit plan that said maybe we will start exiting in the last quarter of this year. Instead, we had to exit sooner. The [initial] exit would be gradual, maybe ​25 basis points (bps). But, as you know, we did two 25s in an unscheduled move, then we increased it by 75 bps—which is very unusual and very high for most central banks, especially ours. 

The first thing that I would like to tell you is that it worked. The peso stabilized. The intended effect of the increase in interest rate is to slay inflation, and one of the ways to do that is to stop the deprecation of the peso. Higher interest rates also reduce inflation because it will reduce demand. People are willing to buy less if it is costly to borrow. 

The unintended effect that we are afraid of is that the recovery I just described will be nipped in the bud. We call it a nascent economic recovery. 

Fortunately, our numbers show that these [rate] increases that we have done so far and maybe even what we plan on doing later will not prevent the economy from recovering. 

This graph shows that the lowest line—policy rate—is rising but is lower than the two lines above—the 12-month moving average and actual month-on-month headline inflation. Therefore, interest rates may have risen but they are lower than the increase in inflation. 

In other words, what we are doing is we are not going to kill off the recovery. 

As the economy recovers, imports are also recovering. But on top of that, prices are recovering. The current account deficit has been adjusted significantly. The forecast was adjusted by more than US$3 billion for 2023. When you combine that with the increases in 2022, that is a total demand for US$6 billion. 

Normally, the central bank will not respond to changes in the exchange rate. After all, they do signify healthy adjustments to what is going on. 

The market works because it makes scarce things more expensive. Therefore, people will have the incentive to use it carefully and try to produce more of it. Similarly, the things that are in excess supply, their price will go down. So, people will want to consume more of it and produce less of it and move their resources to products that have become more expensive. It changes relative prices by encouraging the production of things that are becoming more expensive and discouraging consumption of such things. 

Unfortunately, foreign exchange is not the usual good. What we found in the BSP is if the exchange rate is moving very fast, if the changes are small and can go in either direction, the changes in the price of the dollar do not affect the way people price their goods. But if the changes in the exchange rate are large and sure to go in one direction, it becomes another story. They [producers] begin to relate that maybe if the exchange rate is moving at 10.0 percent, [then] maybe we should raise our price depending on the import content [of our products]. 

This table shows the policy rate response of the BSP and the US Fed. In our case, we had two 25 bps and 75 bps, or [a cumulative] 125 bps. The US, on the other hand, raised by 225 bps [cumulatively]. As you can see, the gap between our respective policy rates has become narrower, plus the expectation that demand for the dollar will rise because of the current account, means that people will be buying their dollar needs ahead of time. 

The pivot of the US Fed from being unconcerned about inflation to being very concerned has resulted in large changes in US monetary policy. 

We cannot ignore that, but we do not have to match them one for one. We did 125 bps, and they did 225 bps. We have increased it [the policy rate] much less than them. My point is: we have a balancing act. We have to respond to what is going on outside the Philippines, but at the same time, we have to be very concerned that what we do does not kill the recovery that is just going on. 

What are we worried about? We are worried that all these that are happening will change the dynamic of prices. The most difficult situation: prices are rising because prices are rising. That is what we want to avoid. For instance, there are signs of adjustment in the minimum wage and transport fares. 

In sum, the BSP had to move sooner, faster, and bolder to avoid disanchoring inflation expectations. 

In plain terms, we want the people to believe in our inflation target rather than [use] the news of the changes in the exchange rate [as their basis] for making inflation forecasts. 

Of course, we are ready to take more action, if necessary, to make sure our inflation targets are credible. We might miss it because global forces are just too strong, but as soon as these global forces taper off, it will [normalize.] and not create a wage-price spiral. 

I think our policies thus far, judging by the stabilization of the exchange rate after our 75-bps policy hike, seem to be working. But as I said, global forces are so strong that they could overwhelm the effects of our interest rate hikes. In 2022, we will probably get an average inflation [rate] of 5.0 percent. Inflation next year will be 4.2 percent, but we are quite confident that in 2024, it will be below 4.0 percent. 

This is another way to look at it. The chart shows several variables: which country sold more reserves, and which increased its policy rate the most? Then, on the first column, which currency depreciated the most? Excluding Euro and Japan, the Philippines is second to [South] Korea in depreciation, tied with Korea in the increase in policy rate, and second to Thailand in terms of selling reserves. 

In short, the BSP is coping with what is happening by: 

Saying “Imports should be more expensive so let the exchange rate move”; 

But at the same time, we do not want too much of that [depreciation] so we raise the policy rate; and 

Then, we sold foreign exchange. 

Fortunately, our reserves are still comfortable, and I give credit to then BSP Governor Amando Tetangco for this who borrowed a humungous ₱2.3 trillion to buy dollars. 

Now that I have talked about the macroeconomic and foreign picture, let me proceed to our banks. 

If I were to summarize all these numbers in one sentence: the banking system is growing without sacrificing the safety of depositors and the stability of banks. 

In addition, let me share our other concerns: 

  • We are trying to improve the governance of some banks. Some banks are putting in more independent directors. 
  • We are also supporting the movement toward more sustainable finance because we know that climate change could create new risks for banks. 
  • We are also promoting digital transformation. Not only does it make the system more efficient, but it also makes it easier for people to be part of the banking system because they can do it through their phones. 

However, it has created a new problem called cybersecurity. These are the things that we are looking at, and we want to make sure that our financial sector is cyber-resilient. 

So far, we have been quite successful. A big part of the transactions is becoming digital rather than cash. 

In 2021, more than 3 out of 10 transactions do not involve physical cash. From 30.0 percent, we expect it to grow more. On our second goal…more than half or 56.0 percent of total adults own transaction accounts in Q3 2021, up from only 29.0 percent in 2019. 

Let me share my key takeaways: 

  • First of all, the central bank takes its role of [preserving] price stability very seriously. 
  • We will continue to foster an enabling environment such that the financial institutions under our supervision contribute to a safe and secure reliable payments system. 

That is why it is very important to me that I am able to address your Federation because I know for a fact that all of your members are involved in spheres of the economy that affect significantly all of these spheres. 

Thank you for your attention, and I would welcome questions.  ​

Title: Preserving Price Stability in a Challenging Global Environment
Occasion: UP School of Economics Alumni Association (UPSEAA) Forum
Speaker: BSP Governor Felipe M. Medalla
Transcription:
​

UP School of Economics Alumni Association (UPSEAA) President Jeffrey Ng, distinguished officers of the association, and fellow alumni, good afternoon. 

Let me start by saying that it is very important for the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP) that we are able to communicate with groups such as the UPSEAA. As you well know, the School right now is overrepresented in the Cabinet relative to its number of graduates—the Finance Secretary, the NEDA [National Economic and Development Authority] Director-General, and the Budget Secretary, so much so that my friends tell me that if the economy does badly under the current president, they will blame UPSE. But of course, that is not true; that is like blaming sociologists for a crime. 

Let me say that, as suggested by the title, we are indeed facing challenging times, probably harder to find anything comparable to this if one looks only at our post-war history. 

First, the pandemic caused the economy to shrink by almost 10.0 percent in 2020. If one looks only at Q2 2020, the damage done was even higher. Never in the history of our country did we experience this kind of contraction. 

The response of the BSP was, to use the word by the IMF [International Monetary Fund] in their dialogues with us, “unconventional” monetary policies. Deputy Governor [Francisco] Dakila, another UPSE alumnus, told the IMF that it is not unconventional; it is in the BSP Charter. What we did was legal. But the IMF said, to the extent that you have never used it before, it is unconventional. 

What did we do? 

First, we brought the policy rate to a record low of 2.0 percent.  

We extended ₱600 billion in provisional, interest-free advances to the National Government. 

Finally, we purchased one trillion pesos worth of government securities on the secondary market. 

And it worked. The economy actually grew very rapidly in Q1 2022, and we expect the Q2 2022 [performance] to be quite good also. 

Indeed, we were so sure that our policies would work that we were sure that we needed an exit strategy. Whether or not inflation was high, we would start raising rates. 

The exit already began: the government paid back the ₱600 billion in provisional advances. We were thinking that we will raise policy rates, even if inflation is normal, starting the first month of Q3. The word we used then was a “gradual” exit from the ultra-low interest rates we had then. 

But as you now know, a lot of things have changed since then: 

The Russian war on Ukraine made a lot of things we import, oil or non-oil, quite expensive. 

Inflation [in the US] turned out to be much higher and much more persistent than even the US Federal Reserve (US Fed) had anticipated as late as three months ago. Therefore, the US Fed had to pivot from not worrying about inflation to being very hawkish. If capital is mobile and the interest rate in one country is about the same as the US, since the US dollar is the safe haven during bad times, funds will flow out and move to the US and, therefore, add extra pressure on currencies such as the peso.  

In addition, our economic growth increased faster than our trading partners’. So, our imports increased much faster than our exports. Add to that the higher price of imports and we have a fairly large current account deficit, which by itself will already cause the peso to depreciate. If that was the only reason that the peso was depreciating, then it is a good thing—produce more of what is scarce and demand less of it. Unfortunately, the currency is not just any other commodity because if you have a consistently rising exchange rate, people may no longer believe our inflation target and instead anchor their inflation expectations on the changing [exchange] rate. 

Now, if inflation were low and exchange rate changes were small, that would not be a problem. For small changes in the exchange rate, the elasticity is less than 0.1. However, if the changes are large, the relationship becomes non-linear, and it will change inflationary expectations and cause what we call second-order effects. 

Therefore, we had to act sooner and bigger because that will prevent the need to act even bigger in the future. 

We do not have to match the interest rate changes of the US Fed, but we cannot afford not to act. 

The exchange rate itself is beginning to add to inflationary pressures and inflationary expectations, so we decided to act. 

And we decided to act very quickly. Our action [75-basis points (bps) off-cycle rate hike] was a surprise in two ways: first, it was off-cycle; and second, we seldom increased rates by more than 50 bps. 

Fortunately, the increase in the policy rate will not, in our view, kill or significantly slow down what we see as nascent economic growth. 

Our own analysis is that the economy can absorb the impact of the rate hike. The fact that the economy grew by 8.2 percent in Q1 2022 and that we expect it to grow even faster in Q2 2022, we are confident that the economy will [continue to] grow rapidly this year. 

But while there are encouraging signs of recovery, we can see that there are other things that complicate the situation. 

The current account deficit was significantly larger than what we initially forecasted. In this chart, we revised our forecast of the current account deficit significantly because of higher oil and non-oil prices. 

The question becomes very simple: how much of our reaction will be policy rate changes and how much will be sales of foreign exchange? Both have their advantages and disadvantages. 

First, if you sell forex, it might backfire because the markets see that your reserves are low and say that “All the more reason the peso will depreciate.” But we also know that high interest rates may have an unintended effect on growth. Moreover, banks hold quite a bit of government securities. If interest rates rise, the price of​​ bonds, which banks hold, will fall. Therefore, the banks lose money, they have less capital, and they may be less inclined to lend. Those are the things that we are now balancing. 

There are two barrels in our weapon. Which do we rely on more? In this chart, you can see the different reactions of different countries: 

South Korea and the Philippines increased their policy rate the most—125 bps. 

On the other hand, as a percentage of their reserves, Thailand sold the most. Thailand did not even change its policy rate. 

Indonesia is quite different: it sold less reserves and did not increase policy rates. The difference between Indonesia and the Philippines is that they are not as dependent on oil imports as we are. 

Different countries have different ways of reacting, and the Philippines [stood] at the higher end of the policy rate and [ranked] quite high relative to the percentage reduction of reserves. What explains that is we are more dependent on imports of things that have become more expensive. In addition, because our growth rate is higher, we were less afraid to raise the policy rate, unlike other countries. 

It is a balancing act between the two tools: forex interventions and raising policy rates. 

But there are interesting questions: why did we not sell more [dollars]? Could we have done less than 125 bps [in policy rate adjustments]? But in our mind, the policy rate increases, especially the surprise off-cycle 75 bps, were actually very powerful in changing expectations and have already resulted in a much more stable peso. We did what we had to do with the comfort that we may reduce growth—but not significantly that we can still grow rapidly. If we postpone the adjustments and wait for the inflation to be too high, policy rates, later on, would have to rise even more, and output loss in the future would be greater than what we took now.  

We are quite confident that the 125-bps increase will be quite effective in reducing inflation and reducing depreciation of the peso. 

The midpoint of our inflation forecast for 2023 is 4.2 percent. If you do nothing, the probability that we [inflation] will exceed 4.0 percent is much more than 50.0 percent. We expect to hit near the midpoint of the inflation target in 2024. 

From the point of view of an inflation-targeting central bank, it is better if the midpoint of the inflation target for next year is below 4.0 percent, which, in our estimates, is the case now that we have taken the necessary measures, like the 75-bps increase, but [also] for another reason. The high rate increases in the US will most likely cause a recession. And even if they do not, [these will] significantly slow down the growth of the US economy that demand for petroleum and other products will fall, which will contribute to lower inflation sooner than as shown in the chart now. 

In short, safeguarding price stability is not just an essential condition for preserving macroeconomic stability. If you take a longer view, especially when inflation is high, it is better to control inflation sooner than later. Because if you wait till later, the output loss will be greater. 

If you take a longer view, there is no conflict between price stability and economic growth. More so, if you take an even longer-term view—if the central bank is credible in its inflation targets—it is easier for the government to issue longer-term peso-denominated bonds. If you look backward, you can see when we were so dependent on T-bills [Treasury bills] because it was so hard to sell longer-term bonds, since there was so much uncertainty over the future inflation rate. 

Finally, I would like to make the point that it is better if people understand why the central bank does what it does. A predictable central bank would be more effective. If they know what we are doing, the signals we send are clear and the direction of the economy will be more certain. 

But in addition to that, there are other things that we have to do. We have to get better as a central bank. One of the things we did was [to launch] a research academy, which has strong ties with UPSE. We recently had a seminar series where both faculty members of UPSE and staff of BRAc [BSP Research Academy] made paper presentations. 

The other new thing is big data. You actually have data that are of greater frequency, which may hopefully be used in combination with more traditional data that economists use for us to have better analysis and forecasts. 

In closing, central banks should not only attend to immediate concerns but also keep one eye on our credibility, our skills, and our technological capacities so that we may be equal to the task—or what we call our three pillars: price stability; financial stability; and safe, secure, and efficient payments system. 

With that, I conclude my talk and thank you for your attention. I welcome questions from fellow alumni.

Title: Toward Sustainable Banking
Occasion: Bankers Institute of the Philippines (BAIPHIL) Induction Ceremony
Speaker: BSP Governor Felipe M. Medalla
Transcription:
​

To the newly inducted officers and members of the Bankers Institute of the Philippines (BAIPHIL), all the past officers, advisers, and members, it is my pleasure to be here this afternoon. It is also my pleasure to be able to communicate to you what the central bank is doing. 

When I heard your hymn, there was a very good phrase, “Serve your bank and the country.” It has two possible meanings: you serve your bank nine-to-five, and the rest of the time, you serve the country. But that is probably not the meaning of the phrase. For me, a very important interpretation [of the lyric] is that by serving your bank and making your bank better, you make the country better. It is not always the case that that coincidence of objectives maps together so well. 

So, I ask myself, why is it that the first meaning is the more common one? I serve my company, and on the other side of my life, I serve the country, my family, and my town. Why is it so different from banks? 

Then, I said to myself, that is exactly how I felt about being a faculty member of the University of the Philippines (UP). When I looked at my students, later on, I realized that no matter how I screwed up, they turned out well. I did not damage them enough, therefore, I served the country. Back when I was a young faculty member, I was a killer. I would flunk one-third of my class because I was too idealistic, and I did not see life from the point of view of the student. I did not realize there are other things they enjoyed doing other than studying. 

So, when I had four kids who went to college and went to UP, I realized that kawawa pala yung mga estudyante sa ginagawa ko [the students are unfortunate because of what I am doing]. Over time, I became more and more mellow and began to see things from the point of view of my children. 

I see that when I was a professor at UP. I also see that when I serve the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP). As I do my best at my job in the BSP, I am serving the country. So, what is it that makes the work for banks not the same? The interest, of course, is public interest. 

Bankers, because about 80.0 percent of the money you lend does not belong to shareholders, that is why you are very important. When you fail, so many people suffer. 

Anybody that is in government should also think that way: the best way to serve the country is to do your best for your agency. 

Your theme “Innovate! Train! Certify!”—these are very important things: bringing the best out of any organization. If you do not innovate, train, and certify, many things will not improve. So, I hope that you will succeed in realizing the objectives that bring about innovation, training, and certification. 

Our partnership with BAIPHIL goes many years back. Three years ago, we had a partnership on the Clean Note and Coin Policy. You helped us connect with transport groups, retailers, vendors, local governments, and other stakeholders. With your help, we were able to reduce the amount of unfit currency that remains in circulation. Indeed, I would like feedback from you on how to make this even better. 

For instance, when I look at the distribution of notes or paper currency by volume, the 1000-Piso represents an amazing 34.8 percent. In terms of value, the share of 1000-Piso is even bigger. On the other hand, the share of the 100-Piso, in terms of volume, is 20.5 percent. And yet, when you look at the average transactions that I personally make, I am more likely to use ₱100 than ₱1000. That is because I have credit cards. If it is a relatively large transaction, I will not be using the 1000-Piso bill or pay using QR. 

The question that comes to mind is since it [₱100] is relatively small in volume compared to ₱1000, the only conclusion is that the ₱100 makes up for its small value by having a faster “velocity,” meaning it changes hands more frequently. Anong ibig sabihin noon? Madali siyang magiging unfit. [What does that mean? It will quickly become unfit.]  

But then, it usually circulates in [informal] sectors that do not [often] use the banking system and, therefore, is unlikely to come back to us [at the central bank] for replacement. So, mas pudpod yung ₱100 kaysa ₱1000. [So, ₱100 is more worn out than ₱1000.] 

So, we are thinking, what can we do about that? Perhaps we can encourage the malls to encourage consumers to surrender their unfit ₱100 and, for every so many pieces of unfit ₱100 that one returns, one could get a raffle ticket. The other solution is to maybe replace it with a coin, but that may increase the likelihood of the bill being kept away in a jar. 

Maybe we could also test the polymer on the 100-Piso bill. This is just an idea.  

At any rate, we appeal to you that if ever, in the future, we decide to introduce the 100-Piso [polymer] as a test circulation, we will get your support and your feedback.  

We hope that in all our future endeavors and activities that make the payment system better, you will be there for us and give us feedback. 

At this point, let me give you a brief overview on our banking system. If I were to summarize this entire graph in one sentence: banks are growing without sacrificing the stability and safety of depositors. All those statistics: growing deposits, growing loans and yet very high capital adequacy, and more than sufficient liquidity. 

Having said that, you do face risks, and some of the risks are new; some of the risks are old. The newest, of course, is cybersecurity risk. 

Of course, the changing natural environment may also make some loans risky. All of those things are the ones that we have to think about to the extent to which the changing climate and temperature of the earth can actually affect your default rates. 

In addition, you face very old risks. This is where my field [macroeconomics] is very much short. Many economic textbooks ignore default or assume default can easily be calculated and, therefore, can be easily priced in. The typical macroeconomic textbook does not even have a section on the banks. The entire banking system became a little black box. That is what I learned when I went out to the real world: madaming hindi nagbabayad ng utang [a lot do not pay their debts]. That is the problem that the typical bank has to solve, plus interest rates, bond prices, and asset prices can fluctuate and hurt you. 

So, our message is: we hope that you are able to manage those risks. 

Of course, we will continue to monitor you. Thus far, we like what we see. Non-performing loans, loans that are behind, [are sufficiently covered] and to that, we say, “Well, maybe we learned a lot from the Asian Financial Crisis.” 

In addition, to address cybersecurity risk, the BSP has intensified cyber-surveillance efforts. Related to this, of course, is what happens when a depositor is complaining that his loss is due to the fault of the bank. He probably would need consumer protection and adjudication [services] as well, and these are the things that we are looking to improve. 

As I already stated, we recognize the importance of factoring in environment into your [risk] analysis because, in the future, it could become a major source of risk. 

For instance, the reason we will have to move to renewable energy is if you build a coal plant now, nobody will insure you because of the global action against coal-fired plants. 

The BSP will continue to build on its existing regulatory and supervisory frameworks. We will nurture the growth of digital innovations. In that sense, the pandemic was a major factor in speeding it [payments digitalization] up. We realize it is a very, very important path, especially since we found that electronic wallets (e-wallets) helped in [expanding] financial inclusion. The banks are just too far; [maintaining] branches are just too expensive. Digital will be very important for both cost-cutting and extending the reach of banks. 

If you will allow me, our kasambahay [house helper] who helped raise the children got married, but my wife keeps in touch.  

Because of the lockdowns, gutom na gutom na sila at hindi makapag-trabaho, pero ‘di pa dumadating ‘yung ayuda. Tinanong niya [Mrs. Medalla], “Paano kami makakapagpadala ng pera sa iyo?” Wala kasi siyang Gcash, Paymaya, o bank account. You know what saved the day? ‘Yung sari-sari store sa tabi niya, merong [e-wallet account]. Doon namin pinadala yung pera. 

[Because of the lockdowns, they were very hungry and unable to work, but the financial support from the government has not yet arrived. Mrs. Medalla asked, “How are we going to send you money?” Our helper does not have a Gcash, Paymaya, or bank account. You know what saved the day? The neighborhood sundry store beside their house; It has an e-wallet account. That is where we sent the money.] 

These are little things that get lost when you are too focused on macro. The BSP cares about [individual] welfare—whether they are represented in the largest of numbers or the smallest of numbers. We are not just a macro central bank; we are interested in the lives of the people. And what we have seen, thus far, is that these new ways of transferring money are actually, in some cases, life-saving, as with the case I gave you. 

We want you to be our partner in improving financial literacy. For some reason, we score lower than our neighbors [in knowledge and application of economic and financial concepts]. I have a few theories about that: the problem in the Philippines, as you learn concepts, you learn them with the language that it is used to teach in. So, if you are not good at English, you will not learn the thing that is being taught. This is an untested hypothesis of mine; I could be very well wrong. 

Before I end, let me describe what has happened [on the macroeconomic front]: we have the biggest shock to the economy after WWII [World War II]. In no time did the economy shrink by more than 10.0 percent in one year. Fortunately, that [contraction] did not continue. As we learned [how to live with the virus] and became vaccinated, the cost to the economy became lower and lower. That is why I expect a stronger year this year. My own [full-year growth] forecast is 7.0 percent. 

  • To support the economy through the pan​demic, the BSP took decisive action: 
  • We brought down policy rates to an unprecedented 2.0 percent, which is the lowest level of our inflation target. 
  • We also bought a trillion pesos in government securities from the secondary market because markets were panicking. How did we know they were panicking? In theory, the pandemic should reduce CapEx [capital expenditure], which should reduce interest rates because the desire to save will always be there, and the desire to invest will go down. But actually, the reverse was happening in the markets. Why? Fear. And when you are fearful, where do you go? Cash. If you are extremely afraid, not all cash is the same; the US dollar is king. 

From the very beginning, when we use these “unconventional”—according to the IMF [International Monetary Fund]—policies, we do not do that without an exit plan. From the very beginning, we had an exit plan. 

At a certain point, the 2.0 percent interest rate is just too low if the economy is strong. We must, as the economy becomes stronger, lift the rates. The advances to the government must also end. And maybe, we will taper off our holdings of government securities, but we will not be buying new securities as they mature. 

That was the plan: liftoff of interest rates, starting maybe by Q4 2022. But as you can see, we did two 25 basis points (bps) and a 75 bps [from May to July]. What changed? What happened to the [initial] strategy? 

As a Scottish poet, named Robert Burns, once said, “The best laid plans of mice and men often go awry.” But the plans did not go awry; the plans are still valid, but they needed bigger adjustments. The adjustment is we have to lift off interest rates sooner because of the huge pivot of US interest rates policy. Nobody thought that the US will do two 75 bps [hikes]. Everyone was surprised by how high and how persistent [US] inflation is, and the US Federal Reserve (US Fed) is busy stopping inflation and recovering its credibility. Unfortunately, the US keeps saying, “The dollar is our currency, but it is your problem.” Like it or not, we have to adjust. 

Of course, we will react but will not match every change. We cannot not react, but we do not have to chase it either. With the permission of my colleagues from the Monetary Board, I already signaled that we may do 25 bps or 50 bps. 

The reason we are so careful is we do not want to kill the nascent recovery. We are now more and more confident that the economy can take a little bit more [of our rate hikes]. How much more depends on the inflation picture. 

After all is said and done, we do care about economic growth, but economic growth is not in our three pillars while price stability is. If the economy completely sinks, then the banks will be in trouble. Extreme declines in economic growth threaten stability. Now that it is there, it is a question of timing, on how to exit. 

Where will you put your money if the rates on dollar paper securities are exactly the same as the interest rate in peso? “The dollar is the US currency, but it is our problem.” We must calibrate our policies to be able to achieve our objectives of price stability and economic stability, but we cannot ignore the dollar. 

Last message: we think that the path of inflation is now target-consistent. In the fan chart, the midpoint of our forecast is 4.2 percent. The global forces generating inflation are just too powerful. Fortunately, in our recent revisions, the midpoint [in 2024] is now below 4.0 percent. 

One thing that you will notice from the numbers is that the bond markets in the US are predicting a recession. Short-term rates are rising but nothing is happening to the 10-year rate. In fact, it might even decline slightly. One way to look at it is that the 10-year rate is the average of the short-term rates before it. So, if the early ones go up but the average does not, that means some other rates in the middle must fall to compensate for the higher short-term. What does that mean? They are forecasting a recession, which will force the US Fed to reduce interest rates. That is how I interpret the US bond market. 

But nonetheless, our [the Philippine] advantage is we have a simpler economy; it is a lot easier to understand. With your help and your support, we hope we understand it well enough to deliver on the three pillars.  

Maraming salamat at mabuhay tayong lahat. ​
