Title: Philippine Economic and Financial Updates
Occasion: Financial Executives Institute of the Philippines (FINEX) General Membership Meeting
Speaker: BSP Governor Felipe M. Medalla
Transcription:
Good day, everyone, mga kaibigan [friends].  

First of all, my last non-virtual public speech was with FINEX [Financial Executives Insitute of the Philippines] also. Then, my first public [on-site] speech [as the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP) Governor] is again with FINEX. I thank you for inviting me to share my view on the latest developments in the Philippine economy and, of course, from the point of view of a central banker. 

Let me start by saying that these are truly difficult times and quite unique for two reasons. We were starting with monetary policy that was meant to speed up the recovery of the economy from a nearly 10.0-percent contraction. If I can compute GDP [gross domestic product] per week, what would the contraction look like? The worst two weeks of the Philippine economy were the last two weeks of Q1 2020—because an economy that was initially growing at 6.0 percent contracted by 1.0 percent, when, in fact, there were only two weeks of lockdown. When you compute backward, the rate of contraction was actually 20.0 percent. If that had continued, the economy would have been 20.0 percent smaller. Fortunately, we learned [how to live with COVID] along the way. We found out that certain things hurt us more than the virus. We learned along the way and coped with it better and better. Then, we got vaccinated. 

You saw the contraction and are now seeing recovery. In Q1 2022, we grew by 8.2 percent. I think the Q2 2022 [GDP figures] will be great, too. If things go well, we will be returning to pre-pandemic growth. Those 10 years before the pandemic were quite exceptional: growth was both high and inclusive. The rate of growth of wage and salaried employment was strong. Meanwhile, [the share of] unpaid family workers was declining—a true sign of becoming a more market-oriented, formal sector economy. 

Here is what we did during the pandemic: 

  • [We reduced to] 2.0 percent policy rate. Never in the history of the Philippines, since we became an independent central bank, did we have a 2.0 percent policy rate. That is understandable, of course, since the mid-point of the inflation target is 3.0 percent.  

  • We bought one trillion pesos worth of government securities. Our balance sheet [before that] was ₱4.5 trillion. 

  • And we lent ₱600 billion to the National Government. 

But while we were doing all these [accommodative measures], we were already thinking of an exit plan. But as the Scottish poet Robert Burns said, “The best laid plans of mice and men often go awry.” They are not awry; they just have to be massively adjusted. The plan is still the same except it will be way ahead. The liftoff of the policy interest rate will be way ahead and the size—as shown by our 75-basis points (bps) off-cycle increase—is bigger.  

I thought that [our previous hike of] 25 bps and a surprise 75 bps is more dramatic than two 50 bps. Two 50 bps at our regular meetings is inferior to one 25 bps and a 75 bps that you did not expect. The market had to be jolted, too. This central bank is not staying idly by.  

Now, we had to exit from that. The plan was to exit maybe in the first month of Q4 [and do it] gradually: 25 bps. Then, we will gradually wean the government off this cheap money. 

Of course, the ongoing debate in the US about inflation: you had a team ‘Low and Transitory’ and a team ‘Large and not Transitory.’ By the way, Nobel Prize winner Paul Krugman was wrong [about US inflation], and he wrote a column trying to explain why he was wrong. 

Now, we had to speed up everything. Why did we do that? The textbook inflation-targeting central bank cares about the exchange rate only as inputs in the model to the inflation rate. Whatever interest you have on the exchange rate, it is because it affects inflation. The normal situation is when changes in the exchange rate are small and transitory, they hardly translate to inflation. However, if it is large and [it goes] in one direction, we have to compute longer-run elasticities. In the first case [where changes in the exchange rate are small], elasticity [to inflation] was 0.06 to 0.1. But we are not seeing small changes and, possibly, our elasticities are much higher. 

Unlike the textbook inflation-targeting central bank, we are an Asian inflation-targeting central bank. What does that mean? We do care about exchange rate volatility. We think we should have some because having none will [make the central bank] look like an insurance company. We like volatility but not excess volatility. Not only that, it gets to a point where we care about the [absolute] level: if the exchange rate moves to ₱35:$ [at the extreme level], that is going to be disastrous. Philippine products measured in dollars become more expensive. 

That is why we tend to accumulate reserves when the currency is appreciating. When I first entered the central bank, it took courage on the part of [former BSP Governor Amando] Tetangco to borrow ₱2.5 trillion to grow the reserves from US$45 billion. We lost money because our reserves were earning much less, but that was a fantastic decision from a longer-term standpoint. 

We also care a lot about the exchange rate when it is moving up too fast because who will believe our inflation targets? To use econ-speak, it will disanchor inflation expectations. These are all the reasons we have to consider. 

We have other things: we want to develop the relationship between the GS [government securities] markets and our policy rates. Fortunately, we were able to get amendments on our charter so we can borrow directly from the public. Historically, why was that removed from the powers of the central bank? It was the reaction to the “Jobo” Bills.  

For technical reasons, borrowing from the public is better than borrowing from the banks…because the people who are there to save the money and put it in securities are most likely going to roll it over; they have no intention of lending it to anybody. In other words, we have more permanent ways of sterilization. We have powers we did not have before.  

We are also asking for more powers: BSP supervisors should be able to look at the bank accounts of [officials] of banks. Bank supervisors should not be covered by deposit secrecy. We need your support there. Do not [let bank deposit secrecy] paralyze bank supervisors.  

The other way to look at things is to contrast us with Thailand. Thailand hardly moved its policy rates; we have already raised by 125 bps. Why? They have more dollars to spare. When you sell dollars, you are actually tightening monetary policy. Pesos are going back to the central bank. 

Our GIR [gross international reserves] level was about US$108 billion; now, it is about US$100 billion. If you look at Thailand, their dollar sales are much larger, [since] they have the luxury of bigger reserves. We, on the other hand, think our reserves are comfortable, not excessive, and this is not the time to waste our bullets. 

When you look at the yellow line, the policy rate, even after the increase, is still significantly lower than it used to be. It [policy rate increase] will not kill the economy. 

The policy rate is higher now, but the inflation rate is even higher. And, in fact, the midpoint of our forecast for next year is 4.2 percent. Relative to our own year-ahead forecast of what the inflation will be next year, the policy rate is still negative in real terms. So, we can afford to step on the brakes without killing the nascent economic growth. 

A lot of the inflation is [driven by] supply shocks. If you take out the extreme values and get the averages, that tells you what the more regular inflation is. The problem is oil and non-oil [items], which became very expensive. The hope is that these prices will normalize. 

We revised our current account deficit and you will notice that the revision was huge—from about US$5 billion to about US$20 billion. This is a question we are often asked: how do you finance that? My answer is: this is why some depreciation of the peso is healthy. People with Foreign Currency Deposit Unit (FCDU) accounts will change their minds and convert some of that to pesos. In a sense, we are lucky that we have the FCDU system. You can consider that our second-level reserves. 

If you look at our inflation forecast—and this will have to be revised [at the next meeting]—it is 4.2 percent for 2023. We will revise this with the new numbers. We have a better than 50/50 chance to do lower than 4.0 percent. That is why we may do 25 bps or 50 bps at the next meeting to make sure that there is enough follow-through for that to happen. We are quite confident that there is still sufficient momentum for growth. What if I am wrong? I still will not regret it because GDP growth is not one of our three pillars, and we believe that, in the long run, credible inflation targets result in higher growth. 

The other way to look at it is the moment inflation is out of control, unavoidably, large output has to be lost to kill it. The best memory of that is [former US Federal Reserve Chair Paul] Volcker. Unless you are willing to live with high inflation forever, high inflation will eventually result in lower output. The larger inflation is, the chances of bringing it down without bringing down growth are near zero. You can fly the plane, but you cannot land. This is the reason we are very firm about our three pillars, the first of which is price stability. 

You all know that we will definitely exceed 4.0 percent this year, and there is very little we could do about it. You have these powerful global forces, about which you can do little. It has also been said in the US that, “The dollar is our currency, but it is your problem.” 

If you look at the numbers, you will see that our depreciation is not exactly out of line. There are countries that are more depreciated and less depreciated than us. Before we did the 75 bps [off-cycle rate hike], we were neck and neck with the South Korean won. So, the 75 bps worked. But if a central banker does too many surprises, nobody will believe him anymore. This is my last surprise in my term. 

What is our view on the [peso-]dollar [exchange rate]? It is healthy most of the time. It sends the right signals if it changes relative prices. For things that are relatively expensive, consume less, produce more. For cheaper items, buy more, produce less. This is the classic invisible hand of Smith. 

But the problem with the exchange rate is, [it can be said] if you allow this kind of depreciation, why should we [the public] believe that you [the central bank] can achieve 2.0–4.0 percent [inflation target]? Is not that a logical question to ask? A central bank that does not care about 7.0–8.0 percent depreciation clearly cannot be serious about its 2.0–4.0 percent [inflation target]. Therefore, we have to act.  

If you look at studies done by the Bank for International Settlements, they say that the Asian way is correct—a central banker should have two tools: interest rate and intervention in markets. The other lesson from the Asian Financial Crisis is that capital can be volatile, and the IMF [International Monetary Fund] can be ruthless in telling you, “No more money is coming at a time when money is leaving.” Therefore, you have large contractions. Having reserves is a good form of being countercyclical with respect to the rest of the world. 

As you manage the exchange rate, there will be periods when it is close to the lower or upper end [of the range of market expectations]. When everybody is sure you are fighting appreciation, that is the best time to borrow money from abroad. 

We believe that one of the lessons from the Financial Crisis is we must be able to take care of ourselves when capital markets become unreliable. “Markets can remain irrational longer than you can stay liquid for so long.” It is costly, very low-return, when you see bad times like these, especially if you contrast the Philippines with Thailand. The problem is when you sell reserves, you are actually tightening monetary policy already. So, you might as well make it official. 

Our policy rates are still accommodative. As it goes up, it is not keeping up with the inflation. As inflation goes down, the real policy rate becomes less negative. 

We are providing support for the recovery, thus far, even with the increase that I say will happen in August and maybe the rest of the year. 

Of course, the banking system remains stable and resilient with capital adequacy ratio of 17.1 percent on a solo basis and 16.1 percent on a consolidated basis. 

We are continuing our own dialogue with the banks and the private sector about monitoring of large exposures. You must remember: We value your views. We will not always say, “We agree with you.” But oftentimes, when we hear your views, we do change our mind or modify our policies because, many times, your feedback is very useful. 

We are keen on continuing this dialogue with the industry. We will have a second package of regulations on environmental sustainability, providing granular expectations on the management of environmental and social risk in relation to credit and operational risk exposure. While we are not a big factor in global warming…at the same time, clearly, there will be risks involved in climate change. For example, it is very hard to finance coal fire plants because no international insurer will insure them. These are the things we have to adjust. 

Digital is extremely as important, and the BSP has developed a Cybersecurity Roadmap covering three key areas: namely, capacity building, collaborative engagements, and continuing policy framework and supervisory enhancements to institutionalize resilience to cyber-attacks. We are also lobbying [for] no more anonymous sim cards because they are a major tool for fooling people. 

We hope to digitalize at least half of all retail payments and ensure that at least 70.0 percent of Filipino adults should have transaction accounts. Our major tool there is, of course, the basic deposit account. 

What are my key takeaways? 

  • The BSP stands ready to employ all the necessary policy actions to bring inflation toward a target-consistent path over the medium term. In other words, we will try very hard to hit it next year or the year after. 

  • We will continue to foster an enabling environment for the financial institutions under our supervision. For instance, we are very keen on reducing the reserve requirement because those that we do not regulate do not have reserve requirements. The last thing we want to do is handicap those that we regulate. Of course, we have no choice because you are managing depositors’ money. If you look at every bank, at least 70.0 percent of your lending is not your money but the depositors’. It is our duty to make sure that depositors’ interests are protected. 

  • The BSP recognizes and advocates for the increasing role of digital platforms in achieving greater efficiency and financial inclusion.  

Let me tell you a personal story: During the pandemic, my wife got a text from the yaya [house helper] that brought up our youngest. They could not make work, and the promised ayuda [government support] had not yet come. My wife said, “How can we send money?” The yaya said, “There is a sari-sari store [neighborhood retail store] next to us; send the money to her GCash [account].”  

The money got there, and she only paid ₱100 [in transfer fees]. For them, that was a lifeline. To me, when I see all these examples—how people-to-people transfers are made easier, especially during the pandemic—this is more important than all macroeconomic numbers. After all, what good are the nice macroeconomic numbers if they are not felt by everyone? 

Thank you for your support for BSP initiatives. Salamat [Thank you] for this opportunity to address you.  ​

###

Title: BSP-DLSU Research Collaboration
Occasion: MOU Signing BSP-DLSU Research Collaboration
Speaker: Governor Felipe M. Medalla
Transcription:
Brother Bernard Oca, President of the De La Salle University, Dr. Raymond Girard Tan, Vice President for Research and Innovation of DLSU, Deputy Governor Francis Dakila, members of the BSP Research Expert Panel, officials, and colleagues, good afternoon. 

I speak to you from the perspective of a former professor of economics and a central banker. Having been both for quite some time – by the way, I’d like to add, I am an alumnus of De La Salle where I got my undergraduate degree in economics – I have long recognized the importance of connecting the theoretical and the empirical and in turn, the theoretical and the empirical with the operational and on-the-ground conditions. After all, academics and researchers provide valuable theoretical insights and empirical experience that inform how we carry out our core mandates – from the conduct of monetary policy to the crafting of bank regulations and the enhancement of the country’s payment system. Those three are what we call our three pillars.

It’s against this backdrop that I am proud to say that the BSP has always attached great value to interactions with the academe and research institutions, especially top institutions like De La Salle. 

An example is the BSP Sterling Chairs which has been in place since 2006.  The BSP Sterling Chairs aim to help maintain and promote a critical mass of productive research scholars in economics, statistics, business administration, finance, accounting, agriculture, and other related fields – which we do with the University of the Philippines. 

The BSP also conducts regular Environmental Scanning Exercises to foster open discussions on various critical and current issues. 

In 2021, we established the BSP Research Academy – or BRAc, for short – to strengthen our research capacity.  We hope that BRAc will help foster a thriving research culture in the BSP by promoting and conducting objective, rigorous, independent, and policy-relevant research. We hope to achieve the level of objectivity and rigor of academics and come up with evidence-based research that can inform policy formulation and decisions. We also intend to explore emerging issues and engage in blue skies research that can help the BSP become future-ready. And this is where collaboration is important.

Through this Memorandum of Understanding on research collaboration with De La Salle, the BSP affirms the importance of collaboration and intellectual exchange in research.

Under the MOU, we may explore sharing of information and resources, co-authorships, joint publications, and sponsorships of conferences and other research events.

Finally, I would like to express my gratitude to our research partner, my alma mater, DLSU, for participating in this valuable and noteworthy endeavor. May this mark the beginning of a long, productive, and collegial relationship toward building a body of high-quality research. Maraming salamat at mabuhay!

Title: Closing Remarks for APEC Webinar on Strategies and Initiatives on Digital Financial Inclusion: Lessons from Experiences of APEC Economies
Occasion: APEC Webinar on Strategies and Initiatives on Digital Financial Inclusion: Lessons from Experiences of APEC Economies
Speaker: Governor Felipe M. Medalla
Transcription:
To representatives of APEC member economies, esteemed speakers, and my colleagues at the BSP, ladies, and gentlemen, good afternoon.

Seven years ago, the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas set in motion the modernization of the retail payment system with the development of the National Retail Payment System (NRPS). Under the NRPS, we activated two Automated Clearing Houses, which we now call InstaPay and PESONet.

As you may have heard, we achieved several milestones since then.  By the end of 2021, nearly a third – or 30.3 percent - of total payment transactions were digital. To provide some perspective – in 2013, monthly digital payment transactions in the Philippines represented only 1.0 percent of total payment transactions. It rose to 20.1 percent by the end of 2020 as the pandemic accelerated digital payments adoption. By 2021, the share of digital payments, in terms of value, represented 44.1 percent of all retail payments.

At the core of this successful arrangement is the partnership between BSP and the payments industry.

What we learned from this experience is that by acting early, the BSP was able to put in place the infrastructure for digital payments. This proved to be essential in the event of the pandemic. Thus, digital payments, which was not originally construed for ensuring business continuity, provided an unexpected lifeline to struggling consumers and businesses navigating the Covid-19 pandemic.

Going forward, the BSP continues to implement the Digital Payments Transformation Roadmap and work towards its two key targets by 2023: first, transform half of the volume of retail payments into digital form. And from the figures I cited earlier, we are close to meeting our objective. Second, onboard 70 percent of adult Filipinos in the formal financial system through the opening of transaction accounts.

The BSP backs several initiatives to achieve the following goals: first, wider acceptance and use of digital payments services; second, increased digital payments adoption through better security, efficiency, and interoperability within the payments ecosystem; and lastly, financial stability and consumer protection through the issuance of cohesive regulatory and prudential standards.

Along with our regional peers, we will continue to advance digital inclusion via a conducive policy and operating environment that empowers the unserved and underserved segments of the economy to move up in life. We will continue to engage our stakeholders in the public and private sectors to foster innovation and promote efficiency and competition while preserving financial stability, financial consumer protection, and market integrity.

In closing, let me express my sincere appreciation to APEC for partnering with the BSP. I would also like to thank the moderators, panelists, and participants for sharing their ideas, insights, and experiences. I trust we can convert the rich insights from this webinar into actionable strategies and new campaigns as we continue our work. Salamat at mabuhay tayong lahat!

###

Title: Prospects for Financial Stability in the New Normal
Occasion: BSP-UPSE Distinguished Lecture Series 2022
Speaker: Governor Felipe M. Medalla
Transcription:
Good afternoon. It’s an honor to welcome Professor Thorsten Beck to deliver the first BSP-UPSE Distinguished Lecture, which has the theme “Prospect for Financial Stability in the New Normal.” It is also my great pleasure to acknowledge Monetary Board Member Anita Linda Aquino of the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas, Mr. Frederico Rafael Ocampo, Senior Vice-President of BDO Unibank and Chief Investment Officer of the BDO Trust and Investments Group, and Dr. Ramon Moreno, formerly of the Bank for International Settlements and currently a member of the BSP Research Experts Panel. On behalf of the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas and the UP School of Economics, where I used to serve as both Dean and Professor, I welcome all of you to this Lecture.

These are truly very challenging times even as we approach what seems to be the tail-end of this pandemic.  Policymakers have to contend with elevated inflation, policy normalization in advanced and emerging economies, geopolitical tensions, and financial market frictions that complicate their policy decisions. There is much scope to take stock, evaluate, and proactively manage the formation of systemic risk and exogenous shocks.

On the home front, we expect the Philippine economy to sustain its recovery. We note that quarterly private consumption expenditure levels have surpassed pre-pandemic levels already and continue to grow as the economy further opens up. In this respect, the employment picture improved significantly from pre-pandemic levels, thereby providing support for future economic growth.

In this context, the risks to the inflation and growth outlook come from domestic and external shocks. Supply disruptions have triggered a surge in global fuel and food commodity prices, raising import bills. These sustained price pressures have resulted in petitions for transport fare and wage hikes, posing further risks to inflation and exchange rate stability.
However, the greater risks emanate from policy spillovers as monetary authorities respond to inflationary pressures with hikes in policy interest rates.

Last week, we raised our policy rate by 75 basis points at a regular Monetary Board meeting, bringing the policy rate to 3.25 percent. By the way, don’t be misled by the term “regular.” It’s regular because the topics of the regular Monetary Board meeting are topics other than the policy rate. This was an off-cycle decision which we rarely do. We were not supposed to meet until August, but we recognize that such action was necessary to arrest the broadening of price pressures. By taking urgent action, we aim to anchor inflation expectations and temper mounting risks to the inflation outlook. At the same time, we back non-monetary efforts by the National Government to mitigate the impact of supply-side pressures on commodity prices.

Another pocket of risk is the possible reimposition of local COVID-19 restrictions amid an uptick in infections. The confluence of events poses challenges to risk pricing and market valuations of financial assets.

The BSP remains vigilant to the possible spikes in financial instability and stands ready to employ all the available tools to maintain the orderly conduct of transactions in our financial system and in the broader economy.

Amid this backdrop, we are privileged to have Professor Thorsten Beck of the Florence School of Banking and Finance and Professor of Financial Stability at the European University Institute to share his insights.

Ladies and gentlemen, let me now call on Deputy Governor and also newly appointed Head of the BSP Research Academy, Francisco Dakila, Jr., who incidentally is an alumnus of the UP School of Economics, to introduce our distinguished lecturer. DG Francis, please.

###

Title: Keynote Address for 2nd BSP International Research Fair
Occasion: 2nd  BSP International Research Fair
Speaker: Governor Felipe M. Medalla
Transcription:
Professor Athanasios Orphanides – who we all know was the former Governor of the Central Bank of Cyprus – Dr. Ozer Karagedikli of the Asia School of Business, members of the Monetary Board, esteemed speakers and discussants, my colleagues at the BSP, ladies, and gentlemen, good morning.

While many things that are now changing outside the Philippines are, to say the least, very challenging, especially to an inflation-targeting central bank like the BSP, I always like to remind myself that its core policymaking remains guided by forecasts of GDP growth and inflation rates, how our policies can affect them, and the lag between the policies and their effects.

We, of course, know that our forecasts can be wrong. To make myself feel better, let me recall two years when our forecasts were way off in the pleasant direction. In 2015 and 2016, we forecasted that inflation will be very close to the mid-point of our 2 to 4 percent target.  But the actual inflation was, in fact, 0.7 percent and 1.3 percent, while GDP growth was 6.3 and 7.1 percent, respectively. And GDE, the sum of consumption, investment, or expenditures, was growing even faster.

We told the public that we were wrong because import prices, which were inputs into our models, that is, to economists exogenous to our models, turned out to be much lower than expected. Of course, this is now happening in the opposite direction. The [deviation] in the inputs and our forecasts are way, way up.

And they were reassured when we told them that when we did runs that used the actual import prices, our forecasts of inflation turned out to be much closer to what actually happened.  The entire time that prices were below the target, people readily accepted our mantra: that monetary policies need not respond to transitory supply shocks. And they actually accepted that two years was transitory; that’s how kind they were to us. And never did we hear that we were behind the curve and that, from hindsight, they never said that monetary policy was too tight.  

Fast forward to the present, and the situation is, of course, much more difficult.  People don’t want to hear that our tools are not very good at addressing supply shocks.  They don’t care who; they want somebody to solve the problem. They, or at least the noisier part of the gallery, also want us to raise interest rates much more in response to what was initially unanticipated by US monetary policy hawkishness. In short, they don’t want us to be like the textbook version of an inflation-targeting central bank. So we need a lot of educating to do in making the markets accept volatility and live with it. We need to do more and more of that gradually over time. I asked some people, “What is the optimal volatility?” They always tell me, “More than what you had yesterday.”

The asymmetry of responses to good and bad supply shocks is, of course, not just a political phenomenon.  Clearly, in a country that has rarely experienced low inflation, the likelihood of a downward wage-price and exchange rate spiral is perceived to be close to zero.   On the other hand, the same spiral can be very powerful going upwards. Indeed, it was already in the textbooks for many decades now.  In modern jargon, we call it the disanchoring of inflationary expectations.  

Influencing inflation expectations is, therefore, half the battle, especially during episodes of high inflation when central banks cannot afford to look unconcerned or inattentive. Of course, we should be transparent to explain why when we are wrong.

When caught early enough, the appropriate policies could rein inflation expectations towards the inflation target. By the way, our studies show that private sector forecasts follow our forecasts with a lag – a very, very short lag. We do not want to lose that.

But we must admit that inflation expectations depend not just on monetary policy and even fiscal policy but on what happens outside the Philippines.

To repeat, safeguarding price stability is not just an essential condition for preserving macroeconomic stability; it can also contribute to higher economic growth. Of course, it is a pure coincidence that the inflation-targeting period of the BSP is also the highest growth rate [of the country]. For instance, the longer end of the Peso bond market is now much larger because of our IT credibility.

But to properly fulfill their mandates, it’s important that central banks reach their intended audience. Effective communication is key to credibly assure the markets that fundamentals are intact and that appropriate policy actions will be taken when needed in a pre-emptive fashion.  In this sense, it has been pointed out that “central bank communication can be used to manage expectations both by “creating news” and “reducing noise.”

Now, let me briefly touch on the final point. While global challenges,, like climate change and food security, are primarily within the remit of fiscal authorities, they affect our forecasts of the trajectories of variables of interest and their long-run values. This, of course, has implications for our policy decisions.

Thus, central banks might do well to be supportive of other things that are important in operations — like improving capacity in big data, and of course, developing our people, and providing avenues for regulated entities to participate in green funds.

In closing, while I believe central banks should attend to immediate concerns, we must also keep one eye on and devote resources to ensuring that we build our credibility, our skills, and our technological capacities to be equal to the task at measure.

I wish you a pleasant time at this conference. Be safe and Mabuhay!
###

Title: Speech for BSP’s 29th Anniversary: Opening Ceremonies
Occasion: BSP 29th Anniversary
Speaker: Governor Felipe M. Medalla
Transcription:
​

Magandang umaga sa inyong lahat. Today we celebrate the 29th year of the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas, and I wish everyone a Happy Anniversary.

First and foremost, let us take a moment to salute the outgoing Governor and incoming Finance Secretary, Dr. Ben Diokno, as he closed his three years, three months, and twenty-three days of outstanding work at the BSP. I cannot round off the 23 days because he was doing an excellent job as Governor to the very last day that he was Governor. Every day mattered.

To me, it's a great honor that he thought that I could fill his shoes, and, by the way, he was also filling the shoes of two Governors before him – Governor Tetangco and the late Governor Espenilla, whom I admire very much. We are truly lucky to have at least three excellent Governors.

To the general public, that he was “Global Central Banker of the Year” in 2022 speaks much of his brand of leadership amid the rough sailing of the past year [during] which the BSP was able to keep the economy and the financial system on even keel despite the pandemic. 

To us at the Monetary Board, he was an excellent central banker – global award or no global award. We didn’t need the global award to know he’s a good governor, but, of course, that was the icing on the cake.

Now, let me also thank in advance my fellow Monetary Board members for their future continuing wise counsel and collective wisdom, like what they gave to Gov Ben, which allowed us to support the economy without the slightest tarnishing of the credibility of the BSP in protecting and promoting the three pillars of central banking. Gov Ben, and I suppose me too, is lucky to work with a Board with a fantastic combination of speed and wisdom, and they know how to disagree without becoming disagreeable.

This is important since we are facing a very challenging economic environment.  We intend to devote the coming year to the continued pursuit of the BSP’s mandates and advocacies.

We did a lot in the past twelve months in pursuit of our mandates and functions amid serious challenges. Gov Ben already shared the highlights of BSP’s performance in his remarks.

We kept prices stable and inflation within our target.  Our banks have remained on solid footing, supported by continued growth in assets, deposits, stable capital and liquidity buffers, and ample loan reserves.

Our external position was very robust, given our international reserves. And the national payment system is safe and efficient, and we are now closer to our target of digitalizing half of the country’s retail payments transactions.

Even as we celebrate these accomplishments, we also gear ourselves for the challenging times ahead.

Amid signs of recovery from the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic, the global economy remains confronted by headwinds from Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, which can be expected to have continued uneven knock-on effects on domestic inflation and supply chain dynamics.

Moreover, the ongoing policy normalization among advanced economies is another clear challenge that could result in tighter global financial conditions, increased financial market volatility, and capital flow rebalancing across the globe, bringing with it heightened volatility in our foreign exchange rates and capital markets.  After all, both the EU and the US are not just raising policy rates, they are also winding down quantitative easing. This will be very challenging for us at the central bank.

The recent large policy rate hikes of the Fed in reaction to, what most would consider to be unanticipated, meaning wrongly forecasted, US inflation spike is causing nearly all currencies to significantly depreciate against the US dollar. This is certainly adding another layer of complication to our domestic inflation targeting and expectations.

This year, sad to say, the average inflation will, in all likelihood, breach the National Government’s target of 2-4 percent by quite a bit. Our current runs show that average inflation will remain elevated.

Given the size of the global supply shocks and the uncertainty when the Ukraine war will end, it will take more than a few months, many months, before the headline inflation, which is reported monthly by the PSA, to go down below 4 percent.

Times are indeed becoming increasingly challenging. While the headwinds confront the economy, our best policy stance is to remain focused.  We need to keep our pencils sharp, and we need to keep our ears closer to the ground.  BSP has ample policy space: our banks are well-capitalized, our foreign exchange reserves are robust, and BSP has embraced digital innovation wisely.  Equally importantly, we have a history of excellent coordination with our co-regulators and the other agencies of government.

As I count the tools in our policy toolbox, what gives me the confidence over and above all things I mentioned is the collective strength and unflagging dedication of BSPers – your strong commitment to the realization of the BSP’s goals, objectives, and advocacies. Not only are we favored by ample reserves, [but] we [also] have a great pool of highly skilled, dedicated, and patriotic BSPers.

I cannot be prouder to serve alongside all of you – from the Head Office, the Security Plant, our Regional Offices, and Branches.  The most professional government agency - bar none.

My fellow BSPers, I have been given the immense honor and privilege of being your new team captain. This is a role to which I will devote a large chunk of my time. I have plenty of waking hours; I don’t need much night sleep because I can catnap. So I appeal to all of you to continue your excellent work that has brought the BSP to where it is now.

While I am still taking stock of the full breadth of my responsibilities at the BSP, I am confident that this strong, professional, and well-respected organization will see me through the challenges of BSP governorship. Mabuhay ang BSP! Mabuhay ang ating mahal na bansang Pilipinas!
###

Title: Speech by Incoming BSP Governor Felipe M. Medalla Quarterly International Press Chat (IPC)
Occasion: Quarterly International Press Chat
Speaker: Felipe M. Medalla
Transcription:
​

I’d like to say good day to our friends from the regional and international media. Thank you for being our partners in delivering updates on the Philippines to the rest of the world.

I will start by saying that the most important thing to me is that the BSP is an inflation-targeting central bank, and that it will remain a very credible inflation-targeting central bank. We will continue strengthening the BSP’s reputation—pardon me for repeating the term—as an inflation-targeting central bank. We will remain vigilant over emerging price and output conditions and will undertake the necessary action to ensure that monetary policies remain appropriate.

Let me begin with the background which is, the pandemic brought us to unleash very accommodative monetary policy. The policy rate had never reached 200 basis points in the history of the Philippines. We had never lent ₱500 billion to the national government before. And we had never purchased ₱1 trillion of government securities in the secondary market. Those measures were necessary because of the pandemic, and from the very beginning, we had an exit plan, which is, we will begin raising rates as the economy becomes stronger, and we will control liquidity by sterilizing the possible effects of our quantitative measures on money supply.

Initially, we were thinking that the right time to raise policy rates was about the third or the fourth quarter of this year because that was the point where we estimate that demand and supply will become roughly, broadly balanced.

Of course, two things have happened to make us increase policy rates sooner. In May, we increased by 25 basis points and last week, we increased by another 25 basis points.

The reason for this, of course, is that number one, the economy turned out to be stronger than we forecasted—8.3 percent growth in the first quarter. Second, of course, is you have the world facing severe economic headwinds, which are contributing greatly to inflation.

The biggest source of inflation, in our case, is imported oil—nearly all of our oil is imported—and imported oil products have become expensive. Wheat has [also] become expensive because of the Ukraine-Russia war. Similarly, because a lot of fertilizer comes from Ukraine, that too has become expensive. So, for that reason, normalization of policy came one quarter sooner than we expected.

Moving forward, we will continue to be data-driven in deciding the timing of the succeeding policy normalization.

Everybody is trying to guess what we will do, and one analyst said every policy meeting from now on will be a policy increase until maybe the third meeting of next year. Well, we cannot rule that out, but since we are data-dependent, we know that many things can happen. That may mean that that’s too stringent, or it can [also] happen that that’s not enough. So, we will, at this point, say [for] every meeting, we will examine the conditions and decide what to do with policy rate.

Although I would say the last policy rate increase will not be the last one, exactly how many, I would rather not say because I don’t want to give forward guidance when there is so much uncertainty. We would be looking at broad-based data to look for opportunities for monetary policy actions to temper brewing demand-side pressures.

Of course, for what’s driving inflation, which are bad supply shocks, the tools that we have—which are essentially raising interest rates, reducing money supply to reduce demand—are not very effective. And then, at the same time, if the supply shocks could cause second-order effects on inflation, even in the case of supply shocks, we must respond by adjusting policy rate and tightening monetary policy.

Now, in this regard, some have suggested that we should have been more aggressive in tightening. Indeed, in the last policy meeting, the analysts were divided whether we will do 25 or 50 [bps hike]. Now, what I’d like to say is we don’t necessarily have to match the increases in the policy rate by the Fed. To begin with, they have a much higher inflation rate than the Philippines It has a very high demand relative to supply, and they’re really under great pressure to raise interest rates. We do not have the same problem.

Of course, it’s been argued that this will affect the exchange rate. The smaller the gap between our policy rate and [that of] the US, may mean the weaker the peso will be. But then, another thing that I’d like to emphasize is, that our policy, as an inflation-targeting central bank, we want the exchange rate to be market-determined as much as possible. Of course, that doesn’t mean we don’t care about it. And indeed, if it’s too far out of line, we normally sell some of our reserves to prevent overshooting. Now, there’s a good reason for that because, in a way, exchange rate adjustments are healthy adjustments if there is really, fundamentally, very strong demand for foreign exchange. Just like any commodity, the price will rise if there’s too much demand.

Of course, the moment it [exchange rate movement] gets in the way of our ability to maintain credibility about our inflation targets, we will take the necessary measures. Exactly when we’ll do that, of course, is to be determined by data. In other words, we allow the peso value to be broadly determined by the market… We find this policy prudent, given varying interests of different sectors of our economy, as far as the exchange rate is concerned.

Over the years, we have built external buffers to support the peso. Our gross international reserves are hefty, supported by steady influx of remittances, business process outsourcing receipts, and even [foreign] direct investments. In addition—and this is worth stressing—the 8.3 percent gross domestic product growth in the Philippines in the first quarter of this year makes it the fastest-growing economy in this part of the world, but our recovery is still nascent and needs to be nurtured.

So, the BSP will continue to strike the balance between, on the one hand, managing inflation without compromising economic growth, and on the other, sustaining economic recovery without causing inflationary expectations to be disanchored. So let me end here. I will be happy to answer your questions.

Title: PH Economy 2.0: Reinforcing Growth and Continuity
Occasion: Bloomberg Philippines NEXT Summit—Deciphering New Horizon
Speaker: BSP Governor Benjamin E. Diokno
Transcription:
​

Good afternoon.

It is an honor and a pleasure to share the latest developments in the Philippine economy.

The economy has grown by at least 6 percent annually until the pandemic stalled the momentum.

Now, we have bounced back and returned to our robust growth path.

Expansion in the first three months was broad-based. Agriculture, forestry, and fishing grew by 0.2 percent, industry rose by 10.4 percent, and services improved by 8.6 percent.

In addition, household consumption increased by 10.1 percent, while government consumption grew by 3.6 percent. 

Exports and imports also improved with 10.3 percent and 15.6 percent expansion, respectively.

With more relaxed restrictions, mobility indices improved from the levels seen at the height of the pandemic.

As of May 30, mobility trends for restaurants, cafes, shopping centers, theme parks, museums, libraries, and movie theaters continued to show improvement. 

Similarly, visits to transit stations likewise increased. 

Against this backdrop, the Philippine economy outperforms peers. Its 8.3 percent growth in the first quarter exceeded Malaysia, Indonesia, Vietnam, Singapore, and Thailand.

The employment picture has also significantly improved. From February to March 2022, 1.5 million jobs were created, bringing down the unemployment rate from the peak of 17.6 percent in April 2020. 

Foreign direct investments are soaring. After hitting a record high of 10.5 billion US dollars in 2021, net inflow of FDIs jumped by 8.0 percent to 1.71 billion US dollars in the first two months of this year.

Manufacturing conditions have likewise improved.

The S&P Global Philippines Manufacturing Purchasing Managers’ Index reached 54.1 in May this year, highest in over four years.

Consumer confidence is on an uptrend. Consumer sentiment is less pessimistic in Q1 2022 and more optimistic for the next 12 months at 30.4 percent. 

Similarly, the business confidence index rose to 59.7 percent for the second quarter of the year and to 69.8 percent for the next 12 months. 

The economic rebound may be credited in part to the crisis-response measures of the BSP. 

We deployed regulatory relief measures and extraordinary liquidity assistance to the National Government. We also moved to ensure adequate liquidity in the financial system to support credit activities.

The BSP extended provisional advances to the National Government worth 10.3 billion US dollars in 2020 and 2021, which was reduced to 5.7 billion US dollars in January 2022. The national government has fully paid these advances ahead of the maturity schedule on June 11, 2022. 

The BSP also provided big banks extra leg room to extend credit via a 200-basis points reduction in their reserve requirement ratio to just 12 percent. 

In total, the BSP infused to the financial system an amount equivalent to 11.3 percent of the GDP. 

We have also started the normalization process for our policy rate through a 25-basis point hike to 2.25 percent last May 19.

Also, as part of the policy normalization process, the BSP reconfigured its government securities purchasing window into a regular intraday facility.

The timing and conditions of our exit strategy continue to be data driven. It is a balancing act guided by several factors, such as inflation and growth outlook. 

A well-planned, well-calibrated, and well-communicated exit plan will prevent substantial market volatility, reduce potential spillovers, and sustain our recovery momentum. 

The Philippines is also determined to maintain fiscal discipline. After posting a higher debt-to-GDP ratio as a result of massive spending for COVID response, we are keen to return to our fiscal consolidation path. Based on the fiscal program, the national government’s debt should go down to 60.4 percent in 2024.

It is worth emphasizing that our current level of debt-to-GDP ratio is well below the figure for other economies, some of which have debts over 100 percent or even 200 percent of their GDP.

Our external accounts are also healthy. 

Our gross international reserves as of end-April this year stood at 106.8 billion US dollars, equivalent to 9.4 months’ worth of imports. The received doctrine is that three months of import cover is sufficient.

In line with the movement of other emerging market currencies, the Philippine peso depreciated by 2.62 percent to P52.37 as of May 31 from its end-2021 level.

The BSP keeps its market-determined exchange rate policy and intervenes only to ensure orderly market conditions and prevent excessive short-term volatility in the exchange rate. 

Moving on to the banking sector, banks continue to serve as a pillar of strength for the economy. 

Loan growth expanded at a faster rate of 10.1 percent year-on-year in April, up from 8.9 percent in March. 

Non-performing loans remained manageable at 4.1 percent of loan portfolio as of March this year.

Banks’ capital adequacy ratio of 17.4 percent remained above the threshold levels of 10 percent and 8 percent set by the BSP and the Bank for International Settlements, respectively. 

Moving on to our advocacies, two of the BSP’s strategic objectives are the transformation of at least 50 percent of all retail payments in the country into digital form and the onboarding of at least 70 percent of Filipino adults in the formal financial system.

With the enabling regulatory environment complemented by the pandemic that forced people to adopt modern payment systems, we are confident that we can achieve our twin targets by 2023. 

To further support our digitalization initiatives, the BSP has issued licenses to six digital banks.

On sustainable finance, the BSP is at the forefront of promoting sustainability principles in the financial sector.

We have issued regulations requiring banks to incorporate such principles into their operations. 

We are also among the early investors in the Bank for International Settlements’ Green Bond Fund and the Asia Green Bond Fund. 

The prospects for the Philippine economy are bright partly because of the strong fundamentals I have just mentioned and also because of the solid reform momentum. 

Even as the government was preoccupied with pandemic response, three landmark laws that further open the Philippines to foreign investors have been enacted. These are the amended Retail Trade Liberalization Act, Foreign Investments Act, and Public Services Act. 

During the last six years, the Duterte administration invested heavily in infrastructure under its Build, Build, Build program.

I call the period 2016-2021 as the Philippines’ Golden Age of Infrastructure, with infrastructure spending as percent of GDP hitting an average of 5.0 percent. In contrast, infra spending as a percent of GDP averaged 1.5 percent from 2001 to 2009 and 2.5 from 2010 to 2015.

The good news is that the incoming administration will inherit a better state of infrastructure to aid its development agenda.

A total of 88 infrastructure flagship projects for completion in 2023 and beyond will e up for the next administration to continue. 

With the economy on the mend from the COVID-19 crisis, macroeconomic prospects are bright. 

The International Monetary Fund shares the view about the Philippines’ favorable economic prospects vis-à-vis its peers. In its latest World Economic Outlook report, the IMF projects the Philippines to post the fastest growth in the region this year at 6.5 percent. 

But this outlook is not without risk. Taking into account the Russia-Ukraine conflict, the Development Budget Coordination Committee adjusted its full-year growth target to a range of 2.0 to 4.0 percent but is expected to ease back within the range in 2023. 

As has been announced, I have accepted the invitation by the newly elected President to lead the new economic team as finance secretary.

While changes come with a new set of challenges, I believe the country will significantly benefit from the policy continuity that the incoming administration is poised to observe.

I am confident that the transition in administration in the Philippines will pave the way for more economic gains for the Filipino people. 

Thank you for your attention.​​

Title: The Philippine Economy: Harnessing the Bright Spots
Occasion: Maybank Invest ASEAN 2022
Speaker: BSP Governor Benjamin E. Diokno
Transcription:
​

Good day. Thank you for inviting me to the Invest ASEAN Philippines Conference. It is my pleasure to join you today and share updates on the Philippine economy. 

The Philippines is on its way to full recovery.

After the pandemic-driven recession in 2020, the economy grew by 5.7 percent last year and sustained its robust momentum with an 8.3-percent growth in the first quarter of 2022. 

The employment picture is close to pre-pandemic level.

From a peak of 17.6 percent in April 2020, unemployment rate was down to just 5.8 percent in March this year. 

Moreover, foreign direct investments grew by 54.2 percent to an all-time high of 10.5 billion last year.

In the first two months of 2022, FDIs grew by 8.0 percent to USD1.7 billion. 

The purchasing managers’ index hit a four-year-high of 54.3 in April. 

Both business sentiment and consumer outlook have improved.

Our expectation surveys show broad improvements in outlook for the coming months. 

All these came on the back of a whole-of-government approach to recovery.

As we transition from one administration to another, the central bank will continue to deliver on its mandate and ensure macroeconomic management. On the whole, there are clear indications of continuity of key reforms under the new administration.

Following the government’s loan settlement with the BSP and the policy rate hike, the timing and conditions of the BSP's exit strategy will continue to be guided by the inflation and growth outlook over the medium term, the state of public health, and domestic and global risks to the economy.

Balancing the need to safeguard economic recovery and controlling inflation would be a key challenge for policymakers going forward. 

The balancing act requires a well-planned, well-calibrated, and well-communicated exit strategy.

Meantime, as we pursue policy normalization, the Monetary Board reconfigured the BSP’s government securities (GS) purchasing window from a crisis intervention measure into a regular liquidity facility. This will enhance our ability to manage domestic liquidity conditions.

We entered the pandemic with strong fundamentals.

Our healthy external accounts, marked by hefty gross international reserves, helped maintain relative order in the financial markets amid the crisis.

The government’s fiscal space allowed it to spend massively on COVID-19 response without incurring unmanageable debts.

We reformed the tax system. We simplified the tax structure, rationalized fiscal incentives, reduced personal and income tax rates, and increased taxes on oil, cigarettes, and sweetened beverages.

With the new tax system, the incoming administration will be in a better position to face the challenges of the post-pandemic economy.

At the IMF-World Bank Spring meetings in April, economies were encouraged to set longer-term goals that go beyond the immediate challenges of achieving full recovery from the pandemic and tempering the impact of the Russia-Ukraine conflict.

Such goals include reskilling and upskilling of workers, pushing for digital transformation, and promoting a more sustainable future. 

I am proud to share that we are making progress on these fronts. 

On reskilling and upskilling of labor, concerned government agencies in the Philippines have rolled out programs to help workers adapt to changing labor demands.

On digital transformation, the BSP’s policy agenda include digitalization of the country’s payments system. 

By 2023, we aim to digitalize at least half of retail payments and ensure at least 70 percent of Filipino adults have transaction accounts. 

Complementing this reform is the recently passed Financial Consumer Protection Act. The legislation provides regulators more power to act on and improves the resolution mechanisms for financial consumer complaints.

The BSP has also issued six digital banking licenses, in line with our Digital Payments Transformation Roadmap.

On sustainability, the BSP is at the forefront of promoting sustainability principles in the financial sector. 

We have issued regulations requiring banks to incorporate such principles into their operations. 

We are also among the early investors in the Bank for International Settlements’ Green Bond Fund and the Asian Green Bond Fund. 

All these initiatives advance global and regional cooperation efforts, with BSP putting a premium on the importance of international partnerships. 

In the recently concluded ASEAN and ASEAN+3 meetings, we actively discussed and promoted sustainable finance, payment connectivity, and trade facilitation.

The BSP also actively participates in the discussions and negotiations that enhance regional and bilateral safety nets, such as the Chiang Mai Initiative Multilateralization and the Bilateral Swap Arrangement with Japan.

We also engage with other central banks and financial services authorities in and out of the region to further strengthen bilateral ties through knowledge sharing and information exchange. The BSP has active memoranda of understanding with our counterparts in Indonesia, Mauritius, and Singapore in payments, banking, and sustainable finance.

Despite the challenges, regional cooperation continues to thrive with ongoing and new initiatives to further cement the groundwork for future aspirations. 

The Philippine government did not let the unprecedented crisis go to waste. Amid the pandemic, it continued to pursue game-changing reforms to make the Philippines a preferred investment destination. 

For instance, the Corporate Recovery and Tax Incentives for Enterprises or CREATE law cut corporate income tax and rationalizes the fiscal incentives system. 

In addition, three landmark laws were enacted to further open the Philippines to foreign investors. These include the amended Retail Trade Liberalization Act, the Foreign Investments Act, and the Public Services Act.

As you know, the government invested heavily in public infrastructure. The goal is to make up for past neglect, which made the Philippines one of the laggards in public infrastructure in the ASEAN region.

From 2018-2021, infrastructure spending as percent of GDP averaged 5.0 percent. In 2021, actual infrastructure spending reached PHP1.1 trillion or 5.8 percent of GDP.

These numbers tell the story of an administration that has succeeded to improve mobility and create a better investment climate.

As such, the next administration will inherit a potentially bigger and stronger economy owing largely to a better state of infrastructure.

The next administration will receive a long list of implementation-ready infrastructure projects. It ought to continue a total of 88 infrastructure projects for completion in 2023 and beyond.

The next administration must build on the gains of the past administration without compromising fiscal consolidation. This will come with strategic investments in select infrastructure projects, particularly those with high economic impact.

Considering this, we are optimistic that the Philippine economy will post an even better performance following a solid rebound last year. We expect the economy to grow by 7.0 to 8.0 percent this year, and by 6.0 to 7.0 percent next year.  

Having said this, like the rest of the world, the Philippines faces risks to its growth outlook, such as the prolonged Russia-Ukraine conflict. 

On the Russia-Ukraine conflict, its impact will be mainly through higher energy and oil prices. But we expect it to be manageable.

Based on latest estimates, inflation could settle within the revised government target range of 3.7 – 4.7 percent this year.

The BSP supports timely implementation of targeted non-monetary measures by the national government to prevent price pressures from broadening. 

For its part, the BSP continues to stand ready to take preemptive action when we see threats of disanchored inflation expectations.

In closing, the Philippines has rebounded solidly from the COVID-19 crisis. But we must all continue to work together to overcome current and emerging challenges.

Now more than ever, we must put a premium on stronger international cooperation to achieve our vision of a green, resilient, and inclusive global economy.

Thank you for your attention.​

Title: Philippines: Resilient Today, Economic Powerhouse Tomorrow
Occasion: UBS OneASEAN Conference
Speaker: BSP Governor Benjamin E. Diokno
Transcription:
​

Officers and staff of UBS, guests, ladies and gentlemen, good morning.

The theme of this conference— “Who has the Power?”—is quite thought-provoking.

This is a timely question, given than geopolitical tensions and elevated inflation are still happening as economies deal with the spillovers of the COVID-19 crisis. 

While no one is immune from the shocks, my proposition is that economies that have sound macroeconomic fundamentals and are reform-oriented have better chances of thriving. 

In the case of the Philippines and the rest of the ASEAN region, while the past two years of the pandemic have been difficult, strong fundamentals, and sound economic management have allowed us to bounce back.

Accelerated vaccination in the second half of the year allowed easing of mobility restrictions, thus speeding up economic recovery in the ASEAN. 

In the case of the Philippines, which is the region’s fastest-growing economy, the 8.3-percent growth in the first quarter of 2022 exceeded analysts’ forecasts.

Manufacturing activity in ASEAN region has been on expansion for eight consecutive months since the last quarter of 2021. The S&P Global Purchasing Managers’ Index for the region stood at 52.3 in May.

Meanwhile, the Philippines manufacturing sector continues to expand in May at 54.1. Looking ahead, firms remain confident that manufacturing output in the region will continue to recover.

Economic recovery came sooner than expected for the Philippines. 

With the 5.7 percent growth in 2021 and the 8.3 percent expansion in the first quarter of this year, we have returned to our pre-pandemic robust growth path, signaling the move to safely reopen the economy.

By allowing economic activities amid accelerated mass vaccination and observance of health protocols, we balance the need to support the economy on one hand and manage health risks on the other.

We expect growth to be even faster in the second quarter, which makes our full-year growth target of 7.0-8.0 percent for 2022 doable. 

The employment picture has improved. The unemployment rate dropped to 5.8 percent in March this year from the peak of 17.6 percent in April 2020. 

Foreign direct investments soared to an all-time-high of 10.5 billion US dollars last year. In the first two months of this year, FDIs jumped by 8.0 percent to 1.7 billion US dollars. 

This underscores investor confidence in the Philippines’ long-term growth prospects.

All these came on the back of a whole-of-government approach to pandemic recovery.

Complementing the national government’s recovery efforts, the central bank implemented its own COVID-response measures. 

We ensured adequate liquidity in the financial system and helped bolster domestic economic activity.

Through our various response measures, the central bank has injected approximately 41.9 billion US dollars into the financial system. That’s equivalent to about 11.3 percent of GDP.

The economy’s strong growth in the first quarter, together with the improved employment situation, provides scope for the BSP to scale back our pandemic response. 

We have thus begun the normalization process, guided by the inflation and growth outlook, state of public health, and domestic and global risks.

In normalizing, we are mindful of the need to safeguard economic recovery on one hand and to control inflation on the other.

Achieving that balance requires a well-calibrated and well-communicated exit strategy to avoid substantial market volatility, reduce spillovers, and continue the recovery momentum. 

Last May 19, we raised the key policy rate from a historic low of 2.0 percent to 2.25 percent.

Also last month, the National Government already paid in full its advances from the BSP worth 54O billion pesos or approximately 10 billion US dollars.

Before the pandemic, the Philippines’ debt-to-GDP ratio remains manageable and much lower compared to other economies.

The increase in our debt over the last two years was due in part to the massive cost of vaccination and healthcare, and also in part to the government’s infrastructure development agenda.

Under the “Build, Build, Build” program, big-ticket infrastructure projects were rolled out. These are worthwhile investments intended to increase the economy’s capacity and boost growth ahead.

If our economy continues to grow between 6 and 7 percent in the next few years, the Philippines can easily outgrow its public debt. 

Besides a manageable fiscal situation, another fundamental strength of the Philippines is its healthy external accounts. 

Our hefty gross international reserves acted as a buffer during the pandemic. 

A reliable source of foreign exchange is remittances from overseas Filipinos. 

With the reopening of economies, remittances grew by 5.1 percent in 2021 and 2.4 percent in the first quarter alone of this year. 

Another source of foreign exchange are receipts from business process outsourcing services. They grew by 9.5 percent last year.

In lien with the depreciation of other emerging market currencies due to the Ukraine-Russia conflict, the peso posted a manageable year-to-date depreciation of 2.6 percent to 52.37 pesos. 

The BSP observes a market-determined exchange rate policy. It intervenes only to ensure orderly market conditions and prevent excessive short-term volatility. 

Another strength of the Philippine economy is our sound and stable financial system, an offshoot of a long list of regulatory reforms since the Asian financial crisis. 

Prudent lending standards help banks keep their bad debts manageable while ample capitalization enables them to absorb shocks.

Credit rating agencies share the view of the Philippine economy’s resilience.

Amid a wave of credit rating downgrades globally resulting from the pandemic, the Philippines has managed to maintain all its investment-grade credit ratings. 

While policymakers were preoccupied with pandemic response, we did not lose focus on our vision of a stronger and more inclusive post-COVID economy. 

The BSP is contributing to this vision through its digital transformation agenda.

By 2023, BSP aims to digitalize at least half of retail payments and onboard at least 70 percent of Filipino adults to the formal financial system through transaction accounts. 

Complementing the agenda is the new Financial Products and Services Consumer Protection Act. The law improves the resolution mechanisms for financial consumer complaints, including those involving cybercrimes.

The BSP has also issued six digital banking licenses.

The COVID-19 pandemic emerged as a catalyst for digitalization. As a result of the pandemic, the volume and value of electronic payments in the country grew exponentially. 

The BSP also contributes to the vision of a stronger post-COVID Philippine economy through its sustainable finance agenda.

We have issued regulations requiring banks to incorporate sustainability principles into their operations. 

We are also among the early investors in the Bank for International Settlements’ Green Bond Fund and the Asian Green Bond Fund. 

We did not sit idly by as the virus raged. Congress approved three landmark laws that further open the Philippines to foreign investors. 

There are the amended Retail Trade Liberalization Act, the Foreign Investments Act, and the Public Services Act. 

By opening up more sectors of the economy, we anticipate an increase in job-creating investments moving forward. 

Infrastructure will also help the economy advance to its next stage of development. I call the period 2016-2021 as the Philippines’ Golden Age of Infrastructure, with infrastructure spending as a percent of GDP hitting an average of 5 percent. By contrast, infra spending as a percent of GDP averaged 1.5 percent from 2001-2009 and 2.5 percent from 2010 to 2018.

And that’s good news for the incoming administration as it will inherit a much-improved state of infrastructure to aid its development agenda. 

With all these positive developments, we are optimistic about the Philippine economy. We expect the economy to grow by 7.0 to 8.0 percent this year, and by 6.0 to 7.0 percent in the next six years. 

The IMF also has a positive outlook on the Philippines.

In April, the IMF raised its 2022 GDP growth projection for the Philippines from 6.3 to 6.5 percent, even as it downgraded its growth forecast for the global economy.

That said, like the rest of the world, the Philippines faces risks to its growth outlook. These include a possible deterioration in the COVID situation and a prolonged Ukraine-Russia conflict, which has led to elevated inflation. 

On the risk of a deteriorating COVID situation, the Philippines continues to do mass vaccination. In fact, nationwide second-booster inoculation has begun. 

On inflation, the BSP’s latest estimates show that inflation for the year will reach 4.6 percent, which is above the official target range of 2.0 to 4.0 percent.

Elevated inflation is seen to be temporary as estimates show this will slow down to 3.9 percent in 2023. 

The BSP continues to support non-monetary measures of the national government to manage inflation, including easing importation of certain food items, boosting farm productivity, and granting of direct subsidies to vulnerable citizens. 

We stand ready to make further adjustments in our policy settings, if deemed necessary, and we remain committed to our price stability mandate. 

Moving forward, the BSP’s actions and policy thrusts will continue to be anchored on its core mandates of promoting price and financial stability. Toward this end, the BSP will continue to pursue policy actions responsive to the needs of the time. 

On the financial sector, the BSP will intensify its monitoring and surveillance over its supervised institutions to ensure that they remain responsive to emerging risks and to promote the continued soundness, stability, resilience, and inclusivity of the banking system. 

Finally, on the external sector, the BSP will remain supportive of policies that will help strengthen the economy’s resilience to external shocks, including having a market-determined exchange rate, maintaining a comfortable level of reserves, and keeping the country’s external debt manageable. 

In closing, I would like to reiterate the proposition I made earlier in relation to the question “Who has the powers?”

Amid external headwinds, strong macroeconomic fundamentals help an economy weather storms in the short term, and sound policies and commitment to reform propel it to greater heights in the long run. 

Given its commitment to macroeconomic stability and unrelenting reform momentum, the Philippines is harnessing its potential to remain among the most resilient economies of today and become an economic powerhouse of tomorrow. Like our ASEAN peers, we trust that our sound decisions and policies have the power to stir our countries into better and stronger economies. ​​

Title: Speech during the FSCC Release of the Systemic Risk Crisis Management Framework
Occasion: FSCC Release of the Systemic Risk Crisis Management Framework
Speaker: BSP Governor Benjamin E. Diokno
Transcription:
​

Ladies and gentlemen, good morning.

The last three decades have seen significant developments in the financial market. Technology has practically eliminated physical divides, while financial engineering has allowed instruments to be specifically designed for certain stakeholders with certain needs at a certain point in time. As a result, financial markets today are complex and highly interlinked across national borders. This creates a value chain as much as it provides the channels for various spillovers. 

We have seen, over the past three decades, the Asian Financial Crisis, the Global Financial Crisis and, more recently, the COVID-induced global recession. Although these have happened at nearly a decade’s interval between them, regulators as well as the public do not take comfort when the unexpected happens. This is the nature of crises. They are unexpected but creates significant disruptions as they unfold. Someone will always bear the costs of the least disruptions, and invariably, it is the public. 

As we move forward towards full recovery, now is the opportune time to look ahead, recognizing lessons from the past while anticipating the possibilities of the future. This is why the Financial Stability Coordination Council put together this Systemic Risk Crisis Management Framework which we are releasing today.

Financial Stability, after all, is about systemic risks and the continuous task is to enhance the resilience of the financial system. Stability is, therefore, simply about risks and resilience, pre-emptively assessing the former while ensuring the latter by both avoiding shocks to the system as well as strengthening the ability to recover once those shocks occur. 

The SRCM is in keeping with the objective of managing systemic risks and strengthening the resilience of the system. It defines arrangements among the FSCC agencies that we will rely on in good times so that we are best organized under stressed conditions. 

The SRCM is a strategic document that highlights how ongoing tasks contribute to crisis management and identifying initiatives which we believe are needed moving forward. As we develop the tactical plans that underpin this strategic document, the SRCM is thus a living document that evolves with the market and the needs of its stakeholders. 

The Council fully understands the importance to the public of managing systemic risks and mitigating its disruptive effects. While financial stability is not about a forecast of the future, it is nonetheless all about considering all reasonable likely outcomes.

Some of you may know of the mantra of Hyman Minsky who once argued that it is in good times when instabilities are developed. This explains in part why crises are often a surprise. Sometimes, we see all the gains of better days, but we may be overlooking the underlying signs of vulnerabilities being built up. While it is virtually impossible to forecast the next crisis, its timing and its specific nature, this should not stop us from being prepared. This is the essence of the SRCM and it includes technical aspects, some of which the Secretariat may share in its presentation, as well as the critical element of communication. 

We have always believed that highly-aware stakeholders can make well-informed choices. As regulators, however, we also do recognize that system-level outcomes may turn out to be different from the sum of the behaviors of individual stakeholders. All these challenges simply mean that systemic risk crisis management, and invariably financial stability at large, is a collective effort.

Ladies and gentlemen, the ultimate objective is to improve the welfare of current and future generations. We do that through a well-functioning financial market, interlinked within its various components and collaborating with the rest of the real economy. This SRCM that we launched today can be many things at many times to many people, but it will always be about accruing the gains of financial markets, products and services to the Filipino people. This SRCM is a start, not the terminal goal. 

Thank you and good morning to everyone.​​
