Financial cooperation within the region has also intensified, especially on initiatives supporting the use of local currency, digitalization, payment interoperability, financial stability, and trade liberalization.

Regional central banks have mitigated the negative spillover effects of overreliance on the US dollar by holding large foreign exchange reserves. Swap arrangements with advanced economy central banks have also aided in ensuring dollar shortages are averted. 

To further mitigate this exposure, various initiatives have been undertaken to promote the use of local currencies within the region.

First, the Guidelines on ASEAN Local Currency Settlement Framework (LCSF) was finalized in October 2019 to encourage ASEAN Member States 

to consider establishing bilateral local currency settlement arrangements with other ASEAN member states.

Second, central banks have entered into local currency Bilateral Swap Agreements to promote bilateral trade and investment, maintain financial stability, and provide liquidity support to financial institutions. 

To further support the flow of goods, information, and movement of people across the region, the promotion of digital financial services and regional payment connectivity is one of the key priorities identified under the ASEAN Comprehensive Recovery Framework (ACRF).

The ASEAN Member States also agreed to adopt ISO20022 (ISO TWENTY OH 22) as a messaging and communication standard to prepare domestic payment systems for bilateral/multilateral linkages within ASEAN.

The ASEAN Payments Policy Framework was approved by ASEAN Finance Ministers and Central Bank Governors in April 2019. It provides guidance on the objectives, key principles, underlying rationale, and salient features of the interoperable real-time payments within ASEAN. 

The ASEAN Working Committee on Payment and Settlement Systems (WC-PSS) is currently working with the ASEAN Bankers Association (ABA) on the development of the ASEAN Interoperable QR Code Framework, including the development of guidelines to facilitate the future establishment of interoperable QR linkages across the region. 

There is also coordination with the BIS Innovation Hub on Project Nexus, a blueprint that outlines how countries can fully integrate their retail payment systems onto a single cross-border network.

To address the risks associated with financial integration, we are pursuing efforts to strengthen the region’s financial stability. 

In 2019, nine ASEAN Member States signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) on the ASEAN Cybersecurity Information Sharing Platform or CRISP, which took effect on February 1st 2021. Under CRISP, the Digital Technology Network was established to serve as a forum for information sharing on cybersecurity, mitigation actions, and policy recommendations.

Regional central banks also participate in other cyber risk information exchange platforms.

To broaden the policy toolkit in safeguarding the region against liquidity and financial market strains, and to demonstrate support in preserving regional financial stability, the ASEAN and ASEAN+3 central banks continue to participate in regional financial safety net arrangements such as the ASEAN Swap Arrangement (ASA) and Chiang Mai Initiative Multilateralization (CMIM). 

The ASA is a US$2 billion facility among the 10 ASEAN Member States which aims to provide short-term foreign exchange liquidity support for member countries experiencing balance of payments (BOP) difficulties.

The CMIM, on the other hand, is a US$240 billion multilateral currency swap arrangement among ASEAN+3 members, which aims to provide financial support to its members facing BOP and or short-term liquidity difficulties.

We also continue to pursue Regional Trade Agreements (RTAs) to reduce trade barriers and sustain the flow of goods and services. 

Developments on regional trade agreements have included the ASEAN-China Free Trade Area, the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership and the ASEAN Trade in Services Agreement.

As China further opens up its financial markets and extends the hand of financial cooperation, we take this as an opportunity to deepen our collaboration for shared prosperity of the region. 

Thank you for your attention and I wish for everyone’s good health.

Title: BSP Governor Benjamin E. Diokno's Message for the Philippine Sustainable Finance Roadmap & Guiding Principles Launch Event and Donors’ Forum
Occasion: Philippine Sustainable Finance Roadmap & Guiding Principles Launch Event and Donors’ Forum
Speaker: BSP Governor Benjamin E. Diokno
Transcription:
​

Her Majesty’s Ambassador to the Republic of the Philippines Laure Beaufils, Department of Finance Secretary Carlos G. Dominguez III, Ernst & Young Director Russell Marsh, our colleagues from the Green Force, guests, partners, and fellow sustainability champions, good afternoon!

Today marks a significant milestone in our sustainability journey as we launch “The Philippine Sustainable Finance Roadmap” and “The Sustainable Finance Guiding Principles”. 

The BSP is honored to be part of this milestone brought to life by the Green Force members with the support of the United Kingdom Government.

The BSP and the banking industry, consider the Roadmap and the Guiding Principles as key enablers in unlocking financing to sustainability projects and initiatives for three reasons. 

First, this will facilitate implementation of the Sustainable Finance Framework, which was issued in 2020 to mainstream sustainability principles in the banking sector in line with our national aspirations for sustainable development. 

While multiple efforts are underway to rethink and reset banking strategies to meet the expectations under the Framework, there is an undeniable need for a clear and strategic direction from the government side. 

The Sustainable Finance Roadmap will provide the necessary guideposts that will complement the objectives of the Sustainable Finance Framework. 

More importantly, it will harmonize future policy initiatives, regulatory interventions, and business strategies towards a genuinely sustainable and low-carbon transition. 

Second, this initiative will promote participation and strengthen the confidence of market players. The BSP recognizes the considerable progress in the adoption of green or sustainable finance among banks, as seen in the increase in green, social and sustainability bonds issuances by major banks. 

However, we can do more in for green or sustainability loans.  This type of financial product not only provides an opportunity for smaller banks to participate in sustainable financing, but also promotes inclusivity as it caters to a wide variety of borrowers including the unserved sector. 

Like the Roadmap, the Guiding Principles serve as a platform for the common understanding of varied stakeholders in identifying economic activities that are considered ‘sustainable.’ This will open up various opportunities and accelerate the mobilization and reallocation of capital towards green and sustainable activities. 

Third, this will steer the banks’ climate and environmental and social risk management. The Roadmap and the Guiding Principles serve as the green light for stakeholders to pursue priority areas which will contribute to low carbon transition. 

This will enable financial service providers, businesses, and investors to make parallel actions and optimal shifts in their capital allocations, thereby minimizing transition risks. At the same time, this will promote adequate and meaningful disclosures among market players, thereby supporting the stakeholders’ decision-making processes.

Ladies and gentlemen, while we celebrate these two key accomplishments of the Green Force, this is only the beginning.

We are set to release the second issuance on the Sustainable Finance Framework, which aims to provide granular expectations in managing environmental and social risks in relation to credit and operational risk areas. 

Likewise, we are completing our various initiatives under the Sustainable Central Banking Program, which aims to embed sustainability principles in the BSP’s operations and functions.

We are only a few weeks away from the 26th Conference of the Parties or COP26, which is a much-anticipated event for climate action around the globe. 

This is where the Philippines will prove its commitment to reduce carbon emissions and fight climate change. 

On this note, I would like to enjoin everyone – the policymakers, regulators, banking industry, business sectors, development agencies, and partners - to continue our collaboration and turn our ambitions into realizations for the future generation.

Thank you and Mabuhay!​

Title: Speech of  BSP Governor Benjamin E. Diokno for MUFG Insights 2021: Virtual Economic Briefing Session
Occasion: MUFG Insights 2021: Virtual Economic Briefing Session
Speaker: BSP Governor Benjamin E. Diokno
Transcription:
​

Good afternoon everyone. It is a pleasure to be with all of you in today’s virtual economic briefing session. 

Let me thank the MUFG Bank, led by Mr. Takeshi Hashida, the Country Head of the Manila Branch, for the invitation to be the guest speaker. 

Today, I will share with you some recent economic developments as well as government measures, including that of BSP’s, to help keep the economy afloat during this pandemic.

Like most emerging market economies, we recognize that it may take some time for the Philippine economy to go back to its original pre-pandemic growth trajectory. 

However, some key indicators suggest that it is on its way to recovery. 

In Q2 2021, the economy grew by 11.8 percent after five consecutive quarters of contraction.

The GDP growth in Q2 2021 was broad-based, with almost all sectors posting a rebound. 

It was led by manufacturing and construction on the production side and by investments and private consumption on the demand side. 

While this growth was partly due to base effects, it was also a result of the gradual reopening of the economy and the adoption of granular lockdowns in Metro Manila. 

The robust GDP outturn was also accompanied by improved labor conditions, with the unemployment rate at 8.1 percent in August 2021, half of the double-digit peak last year. 

These positive developments were accompanied by general improvements in both consumer and business sentiments.

On the monetary front, inflation remains manageable. 

Headline inflation eased slightly to 4.8 percent in September 2021, resulting in a year-to-date average of 4.5 percent. 

Meanwhile, core inflation, which excludes selected volatile food and energy items, was steady at 3.3 percent in the same month. 

We project full-year inflation is projected to be above the official target of 3.0 percent plus or minus 1.0 percentage point this year. 

But we expect it to settle close to the midpoint of the target range in 2022 and 2023, supported by the continued and timely implementation of non-monetary measures to address supply-side pressures on key food items. 

These include, among others, the temporary reduction in tariffs and the increase in the minimum access volume (MAV) for pork. 

The impact of which can already be seen as month-on-month meat inflation turned negative from May through September given the continued arrival of pork imports. 

The banking system remains resilient and stable. The banking sector’s total resources increased, while asset quality remained manageable. Its capital adequacy ratios stayed above the regulatory thresholds set by the BSP and the Bank for International Settlements. 

While bank lending remains subdued, latest data shows an improvement as total outstanding loans for production activities improved to 3.0 percent in August following a 0.8 percent growth in the previous month and a series of contractions since December last year.

Let me also add that we have achieved our target of reaching 20 percent of digital payments volume in 2020 – one of the silver linings of this pandemic, if I may say. 

The acceleration in digital payments was driven by person-to-merchant payments and person-to-person payments, including electronic fund transfers. 

Even before the pandemic, the BSP was able to lay out the critical foundations to an interoperable national retail payment system and enabling regulatory frameworks that allowed payment service providers to innovate and offer responsive digital payment products and services. These helped ease the burden of Filipinos given social mobility restrictions brought about by the health protocols.

Moving on to the external sector – it remains robust and provides a strong buffer against external headwinds. 

The country’s balance of payments (BOP) for the period January to August 2021 posted a deficit of US$253 million from a surplus of US$4.8 billion for the same period last year. 

This was partly attributed to a wider merchandise trade deficit and lower net foreign borrowings by the national government compared to the same period last year. 

Trade in goods deficit widened as imports of goods outgrew exports amid the resumption of international trade and recovery in global and domestic demand. 

Other structural sources of foreign exchange have also been resilient. 

Cash remittances grew 5.7 percent to US$20.4 billion in January to August of this year compared with the same period last year. 

For the same period, foreign direct investments rose 43.1 percent to US$5.6 billion compared with last year. 

Meanwhile, gross international reserves rose 6.7 percent to US$107.2 billion in September. At this level, it can cover 10.8 months’ worth of imports and is equivalent to 5 to 8 times of short-term external debt.

All these indicators point to improving economic activity. But significant risks remain. 

Economic prospects have diverged across countries, with the inequity in vaccine access emerging as a critical factor towards global recovery. 

Last week, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) revised its world economic outlook to 5.9 percent in 2021 and 4.9 percent in 2022, marginally lower by 0.1 percentage points than its July forecast.

This reflects a downgrade for advanced economies, in part due to supply disruptions and for low-income developing countries, largely due to worsening pandemic dynamics. 

It has also revised its GDP growth projections for the Philippines to 3.2 percent from 5.4 percent due mainly to the recent surge in infections and a weaker-than-expected recovery.

We feel that the IMF’s revised forecast is too pessimistic compared to the Development Budget Coordination Committee or DBCC’s revised forecast of 4 to 5 percent this year and 7 to 9 percent in 2022.

We continue to be cautiously optimistic on the near-term prospects of the Philippine economy given the ramped-up vaccine rollout, the relatively more successful granular lockdowns, and the sustained aggressive government measures to supports its economic recovery program. 

At the height of the pandemic, the government has passed several important reforms which could boost the country’s economic rebound. 

Let me highlight three of these: the Corporate Recovery and Tax Incentives for Enterprises or CREATE Act, the Financial Institutions Strategic Transfer or FIST Act, and the proposed Government Financial Institutions Unified Initiatives to Distressed Enterprises for Economic Recovery or GUIDE Bill. 

The CREATE Act is the largest economic stimulus program for businesses in the Philippines’ recent history. It provides an immediate 10 percentage point cut –  from 30 percent to 20 percent - in the corporate income tax rates of micro, small and medium enterprises. 

On the other hand, large firms will have a 5-percentage point cut - from 30 percent to 25 percent. The CREATE law also provides flexibility in granting fiscal and non-fiscal incentives that are performance-based, time-bound, targeted, and transparent. 

The FIST Act, on the other hand, will reinforce banks’ capital and liquidity position in the long-term by allowing financial institutions to dispose their non-performing assets, increase their risk-bearing capacity, and boost their capability to provide financial services to productive sectors of the economy. 

Meanwhile, the proposed GUIDE Bill aims to strengthen the capacity of government financial institutions to assist micro, small, and medium enterprises cope with the effects of COVID-19.

Rest assured that the BSP will continue to work closely with the whole of government until such time that sustainable economic recovery is assured. 

On its part, the BSP has implemented extraordinary measures in response to the pandemic, including a mix of decisive monetary policy adjustments, liquidity-enhancing measures, and regulatory relief packages. 

These extraordinary measures are temporary and time bound. They were done mainly to shore up market confidence in the face of this unprecedented crisis. 

Thus far, the BSP has infused Php2.2 trillion or US$44 billion—equivalent to about 12.5 percent of GDP—in liquidity to the financial system.

While we remain ready to deploy additional monetary policy measures as needed, we believe that fiscal policy will remain crucial in restoring confidence and reviving domestic demand. 

The National Government’s targeted fiscal intervention, including the accelerated vaccine rollout, is expected to support a stronger recovery. 

To date, the government has already secured a total of 195 million vaccine doses to inoculate a hundred percent of our adult population.

Looking ahead, we remain confident that the Philippine economy will be back on its high-growth trajectory. We forecast that the economy will grow by 7.0-9.0 percent in 2022 and 6.0-7.0 percent in 2023 and 2024 on the basis of the accelerated vaccine rollout, continued implementation of its bold infrastructure program, the effective implementation of recent reforms, and the enactment of proposed structural reforms. 

The BSP is committed in sustaining necessary policy measures in support of the whole-of-government approach in addressing the pandemic, to the extent that they are consistent with its price and financial stability objectives.  

On the unwinding of these measures, we will be consistent with our data-dependent approach. 

Only when we see sustainable economic recovery will we implement a gradual stimulus exit strategy. This will include a gradual phasing out of direct budgetary financing to the national government, upon close coordination with fiscal authorities.

Given these developments, we look forward to seeing you taking part in rebuilding a post-COVID Philippine economy that is stronger, more resilient, technologically advanced, and inclusive than ever. Thank you.​

Title: Message of BSP Governor Benjamin E. Diokno for the launching of the Philippine Sustainable Finance Roadmap and the Sustainable Finance Guiding Principles
Occasion: Launching of the Philippine Sustainable Finance Roadmap and the Sustainable Finance Guiding Principles
Speaker: BSP Governor Benjamin E. Diokno
Transcription:
Her Majesty’s Ambassador to the Republic of the Philippines LO-BOFIS, Department of Finance Secretary Carlos G. Dominguez III, Ernst & Young Director Russell Marsh, our colleagues from the Green Force, guests, partners, and fellow sustainability champions, good afternoon!

Today marks a significant milestone in our sustainability journey as we launch “The Philippine Sustainable Finance Roadmap” and “The Sustainable Finance Guiding Principles”. 

The BSP is honored to be part of this milestone brought to life by the Green Force members with the support of the United Kingdom Government.

The BSP and the banking industry consider the Roadmap and the Guiding Principles as key enablers in unlocking financing to sustainability projects and initiatives for three reasons. 

First, this will facilitate implementation of the Sustainable Finance Framework, which  was issued in 2020 to mainstream sustainability principles in the banking sector in line with our national aspirations for sustainable development. 

While multiple efforts are underway to rethink and reset banking strategies to meet the expectations under the Framework, there is an undeniable need for a clear and strategic direction from the government side. 

The Sustainable Finance Roadmap will provide the necessary guideposts that will complement the objectives of the Sustainable Finance Framework. 

More importantly, it will harmonize future policy initiatives, regulatory interventions, and business strategies towards a genuinely sustainable and low-carbon transition. 

Second, this initiative will promote participation and strengthen the confidence of market players. 

The BSP recognizes the considerable progress in the adoption of green or sustainable finance among banks, as seen in the increase in green, social and sustainability bonds issuances by major banks. 

However, we can do more in for green or sustainability loans.  

This type of financial product not only provides an opportunity for smaller banks to participate in sustainable financing, but also promotes inclusivity as it caters to a wide variety of borrowers including the unserved sector. 

Like the Roadmap, the Guiding Principles serve as a platform for the common understanding of varied stakeholders in identifying economic activities that are considered ‘sustainable.’ 

This will open up various opportunities and accelerate the mobilization and reallocation of capital towards green and sustainable activities. 

Third, this will steer the banks’ climate and environmental and social risk management. 

The Roadmap and the Guiding Principles serve as the green light for stakeholders to pursue priority areas which will contribute to low carbon transition. 

This will enable financial service providers, businesses, and investors to make parallel actions and optimal shifts in their capital allocations, thereby minimizing transition risks. 

At the same time, this will promote adequate and meaningful disclosures among market players, thereby supporting the stakeholders’ decision-making processes.

Ladies and gentlemen, while we celebrate these two key accomplishments of the Green Force, this is only the beginning.

We are set to release the second issuance on the Sustainable Finance Framework, which aims to provide granular expectations in managing environmental and social risks in relation to credit and operational risk areas. 

Likewise, we are completing our various initiatives under the Sustainable Central Banking Program, which aims to embed sustainability principles in the BSP’s operations and functions.

We are only a few weeks away from the 26th Conference of the Parties or COP26, which is a much anticipated event for climate action around the globe. 

This is where the Philippines will prove its commitment to reduce carbon emissions and fight climate change. 

On this note, I would like to enjoin everyone – the policymakers, regulators, banking industry, business sectors, development agencies, and partners--to continue our collaboration and turn our ambitions into realizations for the future generation. Thank you and Mabuhay! ​

Title: Message of BSP Governor Benjamin E. Diokno for the AMLC 20th Anniversary
Occasion: Anti-Money Laundering Council 20th Anniversary
Speaker: BSP Governor Benjamin E. Diokno
Transcription:
​

Anti-Money Laundering Council (AMLC) Members, Insurance Commissioner, Atty. Dennis B. Funa; 

Securities and Exchange Commission Chairperson, Atty. Emilio B. Aquino, AMLC Secretariat Executive Director, Atty. Mel Georgie B. Racela,

Our colleagues and guests from government and law enforcement agencies and from the private sector,

Ladies and gentlemen of the AMLC Secretariat, good morning and happy 20th anniversary to the Anti-Money Laundering Council! 

I am pleased to say that despite the challenges posed by this unprecedented pandemic, the AMLC marched on, carrying out improvements and initiatives against money laundering and terrorism financing.

First. Using its database and other sources of information, the AMLC has released the following risk assessments, strategic studies, and typologies in 2021 for the guidance of government and law enforcement agencies; and covered persons:


1. Terrorism and Terrorism Financing Risk Assessment, which is an update of the Second National Risk Assessment, 


particularly on the understanding and assessment of terrorism and terrorism financing risks in the country;


2. Foreign Terrorist Fighters Study using Suspicious Transaction Reports


3. Money Service Business [MSB]: 2021 Money Laundering and Terrorism Financing Sector Risk Assessment, 


which indicates how certain services and products of MSBs are exploited by criminals to facilitate and expand illegal activities;


4. Real Estate Sector: A Money Laundering/Terrorism Financing/Proliferation Financing Assessment, which examines the potential criminal threat environment, and vulnerabilities associated with the real estate sector;


5. An Assessment of the Philippines’ Exposure to External and Internal Threats Based on Suspicious Transaction Reports for 2018 to 2020, which looks into the country’s risk and exposure to money laundering, terrorism financing, and different predicate offenses 


by gathering information on the generation, movement, and behavior of illicit funds and by evaluating the threats originating within and outside the country’s jurisdiction;


6. An Analysis of Suspicious Transaction Reports with Possible Links to Tax Crimes, which is a study on the potential exposure of the Philippines to tax crimes 

prior to the inclusion of tax evasion as a predicate offense to money laundering by focusing on selected suspicious transaction reports (STRs)


7. Suspicious Transaction Report Quality Review: 2017 to 2020 Data Discovery that covers 2.4 million STRs, which the AMLC received from 2017 to 2020 from covered persons which aims to provide a trend analysis for the covered periods; assess the technical compliance and investigative value of the STRs; and identify the reporting gaps and challenges of covered persons to provide guidance on how to improve the quality of STRs.


Most of these are available in the AMLC’s website for the guidance of our stakeholders.

Second. The AMLC continues to strengthen its ties with other local agencies and other jurisdictions for further effective and efficient coordination and collaboration. 

To date, the AMLC has signed memoranda of understanding (MOU) with 51 jurisdictions; and memoranda of agreements (MOAs) with 39 law enforcement and government agencies, the most recent of which are with the Philippine National Police (PNP) and Philippine Health Insurance Corporation this year.

Notably, the MOA with PNP created a “fusion center” to foster cooperation and coordination to effectively prevent, control, detect, investigate, and prosecute terrorism financing and money laundering as well as its predicate crimes. 

This fusion center is the core of information and intelligence-exchange between the PNP and the AMLC. It will ultimately optimize resources, simplify processes, and build the anti-money laundering and counter-terrorism financing (AML/CTF) capacity of both agencies.

We also adopt a whole-of-government approach with the implementation of the National Anti-Money Laundering and Countering the Financing of Terrorism Strategy for 2018 to 2022 (NACS). The NACS continues to progress through its National AML/CFT Coordinating Committee and its subcommittees. 

Moreover, the AMLC has signed 18 Information-Sharing Protocol Agreements with eight (8) banks, nine (9) MSBs, and one (1) industry association. 

The Information-Sharing Protocol enables collaboration between the AMLC and private sector in the areas of information-exchange and capacity-building. 

Third. From January 1 to August 31, 2021, the AMLC has filed a total of 85 cases, civil and criminal, involving over PhP1.31 billion and other assets.

Fourth. The AMLC amended the AML/CTF regulations this year to strengthen the Philippines’ AML/CTF supervisory framework. These amendments include the 2021 AMLC Registration and Reporting Guidelines; 2021 Anti-Money Laundering/Counter-Terrorism Financing Guidelines for Designated Non-Financial Businesses and Professions; 2021 Sanctions Guidelines: Targeted Financial Sanctions Related to Terrorism, 

Terrorism Financing, and Proliferation Financing [of Weapons of Mass Destruction]; Guidance for De-Listing and Unfreezing Procedures; among many others. 

Lastly, bound to strengthening its AML/CTF system, the Philippines has issued and has been implementing AML/CTF laws and regulations, which has led to upgrades in Recommendations 4, 6, 7, 20, 22, 23, 24 to largely compliant; and Recommendation 29 to compliant under the Financial Action Task Force 40 Recommendations. 

Thus, with a more robust framework in place, improvements in AML/CTF operations are expected, demonstrating the Philippines’ progress toward a more effective AML/CTF regime.

The Philippine National AML/CFT Strategy (NACS) has also integrated the International Co-Operation Review Group (ICRG) Action Plan to ensure a whole-of-nation approach. 

Moreover, through the issuance and extensive dissemination of a Guidance for De-Listing and Unfreezing Procedures, the Philippines has accomplished one of the 18 ICRG Action Plan items - that is, the ICRG Immediate Outcome 11 action plan item to “issue a step-by-step guidance for the de-listing, unfreezing procedures and publish it widely.”

By now, we understand that the country’s exit from the list of Jurisdictions under Increased Monitoring or the grey list requires commitment and cooperation among the public and private sectors in addressing all 18 ICRG action plan items. 

The country must demonstrate that its AML/CTF system is delivering expected results, and failure to do so will have repercussions on the economy. 

But beyond mere compliance, we must also grasp that this is about fundamentally strengthening our AML/CTF system that would prove beneficial to the country even beyond our lifetime.

Let me take this opportunity to thank the AMLC Secretariat and the rest of the AMLC Council for our enduring commitment and cooperation. 

There are many more challenges to overcome as we preserve the integrity of the Philippine financial system. We look at our future without fear but with fervor as I have absolute confidence in the indelible resolve of our nation.

Thank you and happy anniversary once again!​

Title: Kindling to Recovery: Vaccination, Innovation, and Communication
Occasion: Security Bank 2021 Economic Forum
Speaker: BSP Governor Benjamin E. Diokno
Transcription:
​

Security Bank President and Chief Executive Officer Sanjiv Vohra, Dr. Michael Taylor of Moody’s Investors Service, Security Bank’s officers, staffs, clients and partners, good day to all of you. 

Thank you for inviting me to be part of today’s activity. 

Many people say that Filipinos are like bamboo. “we bend, but we do not break.” 

These words also apply to our approach to life, business, and relationships. Like the bamboo, Filipinos are resilient. And this has been the case during this pandemic. 

The unintended consequences of the efforts to preserve lives at all cost has resulted in a recession. 

A recession that we, along with many other economies, are trying to recover from.

The good news is, after five consecutive quarters of economic contractions, the Philippine economy posted an expansion in the second quarter of 2021 as real GDP increased by 11.8 percent, from a 17.0 percent decline in Q2 2020. 

The expansion was mainly contributed by manufacturing, construction and wholesale and retail trade in terms of production, and by household consumption, public construction and investment in durable equipment in terms of expenditure. 

Almost all sectors and expenditure segments of the economy bounced back during the quarter. This bodes well for the country as we learn how to live with the virus by managing risks through the safe reopening of the economy and calibrated reimposition of granular quarantine restrictions only where it is necessary. 

In July 2021, the country’s unemployment rate declined to 6.9 percent, the lowest rate since the start of the pandemic. 

In August, unemployment rose to 8.1 percent as labor force participation rate picked up. At the same time, underemployment rate declined sharply. 

Clearly, we are not out of the woods yet. 

The country’s year-on-year headline inflation increased to 4.9 percent in August 2021 from 4.0 percent in July, bringing the year-to-date average inflation to 4.4 percent, above the Government’s inflation target of 3.0 percent ± 1.0 percentage point for 2021. 

Inflation increased due mainly to higher price increases of key food items, particularly vegetables and fish owing adverse weather conditions, and meat, but partly due to base effects. Non-food inflation also went up due to increased electricity rates and prices of liquefied petroleum gas (LPG). 

Yet, the latest inflation outturn is consistent with the BSP’s assessment that inflation could settle close to the high end of the target range in the near term before decelerating back to within the target by end of the year.

In any case, the risks to the inflation outlook remain broadly balanced over the policy horizon.

Meanwhile, inflation expectations remain firmly aligned with the baseline projection path for 2022-2023. 

Results of the BSP’s survey of private sector economists for September 2021 showed an elevated mean inflation forecast of 4.3 percent for 2021, which would fall within the target range at 3.2 percent for both 2022 and 2023. 

This is similar to most of the multilaterals and market analysts. They expect that risks to the inflation outlook this year will remain tilted to the upside due to supply disruptions and rising global oil prices.

Liquidity in the financial system remains ample, expanding by 5.9 percent year-on-year in July 2021. 

This was slower than the 6.5-percent (revised) growth recorded in June.

However, credit activity remains weak due to risk aversion amid growth uncertainty. Bank credit continues to fall as measures to address the still elevated number of COVID-19 cases constrain domestic economic activity and continue to dampen market sentiment. 

The outstanding loans of universal and commercial banks (U/KBs), net of reverse repurchase (RRP) placements with the BSP, declined by 0.7 percent year-on-year in July. 

This is less than the 2.0 percent fall in June, and on a month-on-month seasonally adjusted basis, bank lending rose by 0.5 percent.

As of end-July 2021, gross NPL ratio of the Philippine banking system (PBS) stood at 4.5 percent, higher compared to 2.7 percent a year ago. 

The uptick in NPL ratio, however, was accompanied by loan-loss provisioning with an NPL coverage ratio of 82.4 percent. 

Despite the recent increase in NPLs, the Philippine banking system remains well-capitalized. 

As of the first quarter of 2021, its capital adequacy ratio (CAR) is at 16.9 percent, well above the 10 percent minimum threshold set by the BSP. 

The BSP will continue to closely monitor the impact on the banking system of emerging COVID-19 variants and the re-imposition of stricter quarantine measures. 

Meanwhile, the country’s external sector remains manageable. The sustained rebound’ in key economies has spurred external demand. The country’s exports of goods increased by 21.3 percent in the first half of 2021. 

Similarly, imports of goods grew by 31.6 percent on stronger domestic demand for raw materials. Cash remittances from overseas Filipinos (OFs) are also strengthening, with 5.8 percent growth in January to July 2021, from a slight contraction in 2020. 

Meanwhile, BPO services in the first half of 2021 remained strong despite the disruption to business activities around the world. 

Net foreign direct investments for the first semester of 2021 increased due to positive foreign investor sentiment on the country’s macroeconomic fundamentals and strong growth prospects. 

The country’s outstanding external debt also remains prudent. External dept to GDP ratio slightly eased to 26.5 percent in end-June 2021. 

Notably, a large portion of the country’s external debt has medium-and-long term maturity profile and carry fixed interest rates. 

These support a manageable debt repayment schedule and make foreign borrowings less susceptible to volatilities in global interest rates and foreign exchange fluctuations.

The gross international reserves (GIR), which stood at US$108.0 billion as of August 2021, continue to provide more than adequate external liquidity buffer. 

The GIR level is equivalent to 11 months’ worth of imports of goods and payments of services and primary income. 

It is also about 7.6 times the country’s short-term external debt based on original maturity and 5.3 times based on residual maturity. 

The GIR is supported by improving inflows of cash remittances from overseas workers and business process outsourcing.  

That said, our economic recovery remains uneven.

These uneven impacts of the pandemic result in not only the k-recession we have experienced but also what is looking to be a k-recovery that we face. 

Technology-driven businesses will recover quickly. On the other hand, small firms and households employed in sectors that have high human or tactile interaction could be left behind in the recovery. 

In addition, overleveraged and cash-flow dependent small businesses will be hit hard and might fold up. 

Innovation is a common denominator for those which thrived during pandemic and those likely to thrive post-pandemic. 

As such, the pace of recovery will not be the same for everyone. Our path to recovery rests on our ability to live with the virus and rebuild our macrofinancial resilience. These rest on our vaccination, innovation, and communication.

The vaccine is crucial to our quick recovery. Our vaccination rate has been gaining momentum as more vaccines arrive and the capacity to administer injections improve.

Innovation is our primary weapon in overcoming the negative effects of this pandemic. We need to strengthen our long-term macroeconomic and financial resilience. 

Policy interventions must consider consumer preferences and habits that resulted both from health protocols and concern for personal safety. 

Effective communication by policymakers is crucial. Frequent and open discussions are important in identifying the problems, in clarifying expectations, minimizing avoidable friction costs, and in strengthening partnerships.

Moving forward, the BSP’s actions and policy thrusts will continue to be anchored on its core mandates of promoting price and financial stability. Towards this end, the BSP will continue to pursue appropriate policy actions.

On monetary policy: the BSP will remain vigilant over the current inflation dynamics to ensure that the monetary policy stance continues to support economic recovery to the extent that the inflation outlook would allow. It will carefully scan the operating environment with a forward-looking perspective to move in a pre-emptive fashion to address any risks to our price stability mandate.

On the financial sector: the BSP will intensify its monitoring and surveillance over its supervised institutions to ensure that they remain resilient to emerging risks and continue to be sound, stable, and inclusive, particularly through the pursuit of enhanced digitization.

Finally, on the external sector: the BSP will support policies that will strengthen the economy’s resilience to external shocks, including that of maintaining a market-determined exchange rate, keeping a comfortable level of reserves, and  keeping the country’s external debt manageable.

Considering the recent economic developments and significant improvement in our vaccination program, we are optimistic that there is sufficient support for the country’s recovery this year and in the near term. 

The latest projection indicates that the average inflation is likely to exceed the upper end of the target range in 2021 at 4.4 percent, but it will ease towards the midpoint of the target range in 2022 of 2 to 4 percent and 2023.

The risks to the inflation outlook have tilted towards the upside for the remaining months of 2021 but remains broadly balanced for 2022 and 2023. 

Meanwhile, the current account surplus is expected to be narrower, mainly due to an accelerated rebound in demand for capital goods, raw materials and intermediate goods. 

Overseas Filipino cash remittances are seen to pick up at a faster pace as host economies recover. Inflows of foreign direct investments (FDIs) are expected to rise amid improvements in the domestic and global investment climate.

In closing, let me leave you with these key points:

• The country’s macroeconomic fundamentals remain sound. 

o The latest GDP growth suggests that the economy has started its gradual recovery. 

o The currently high inflation is due to transitory factors. 

o Banks remain sound and while NPL has increased, banks remain highly capitalized.

o External position is strong with more than adequate external liquidity buffer and improving OF remittances. 

• Economic activity has improved. But it remains tentative. It needs strong fiscal support and quicker vaccine rollout. 

• BSP’s monetary policy stance will continue to provide liquidity in financial system and supportive of the economy 

• Nevertheless, BSP’s actions and policy thrusts continue to be anchored on its core mandates of promoting price and financial stability

Thank you for your attention and good day, once again​.

Title: QR Ph P2M: Bringing Digital Payments Closer to the Filipino People
Occasion: QR PH P2M Launch
Speaker: BSP Governor Benjamin E. Diokno
Transcription:
​

Good afternoon to our colleagues from the government, to our partner institutions, ladies and gentlemen.

We are very pleased that you are with us today, albeit virtually, to witness the virtual full launch of the QR Ph P2M: Bringing Digital Payments Closer to the Filipino People. 

With today’s event, are well on our way to becoming a cash-lite society. This milestone is testament to our commitment to overcome the challenges of broadening digital transformation in the country in our pursuit of the delivery of universal access to safe, affordable and convenient digital payment services for all Filipinos.

The simplicity of QR code-enabled payments gives it the potential to reach even small players because it requires less expensive infrastructure for onboarding - only a smartphone and the internet are needed. 

The use of QR code payments were bolstered with the development of the National QR Code Standard, dubbed as “QR Ph” in accordance with BSP Circular No. 1055. QR Ph aims to transform the fragmented QR-driven payment services into interoperable payment solutions. 

It was in November 2019 when we launched the QR Ph for person-to-person payments or “QR Ph P2P” which primarily catered to remittances and payments within the informal sector. 

From only 6 pilot participants during the launch, we now have 23 participants by the end of August 2021. 

From the second quarter last year, transactions have likewise surged. The volume expanded by almost thirteen times its Q2 2020 level and the value surged by more than forty-five times its Q2 2020 level, exhibiting an average quarterly growth rate of 110% and 229% for volume and value, respectively, over the period.

To complement the P2P component of the QR Ph, the QR Ph for person-to-merchant or “QR Ph P2M” was developed and its pilot run started in April this year. 

QR Ph P2M enables merchants such as department stores, pharmacies, supermarkets, hardware stores, and restaurants to accept e-payments with ease even in the safety of their customers’ homes. QR Ph P2M may also make bills payments faster and more convenient.

For this full launch, customers who have accounts with – 

1) AllBank, 

2) AUB, 

3) Cebuana Lhuillier Rural Bank, 

4) Chinabank, 

5) Landbank, 

6) RCBC, 

7) StarPay, 

8) Union Bank, and 

9) USSC Money Services, Inc. 

— can now make QR Ph payments in over 30,000 locations of more than 20,000 participating merchants who have accounts with – 

1) AllBank, 

2) AUB, 

3) BDO, 

4) Cebuana Lhuillier Rural Bank, 

5) Metrobank, 

6) PayMaya, 

7) RCBC, 

8) StarPay, 

9) Union Bank, and 

10) USSC Money Services, Inc. (A final list of participating institutions and the final number of merchants/locations will be provided.)

We anticipate that more payment service providers and merchants will be onboarded to the QR Ph P2M platform after today’s event.

Indeed, the use of QR codes for payments has been gaining traction as an alternative to the traditional debit and credit card payments, given the ease, convenience and speed of merely scanning the code compared to having to bring a card, tapping, dipping or swiping it, and signing a charge slip in many cases. 

QR Ph empowers consumers by giving them the freedom to choose their digital payment service through the interoperability feature of QR Ph-payments, and this is aligned with the United Nation’s principles on the responsible use of digital payments.

So, what are the features of QR Ph and why do we advocate its adoption?

• First is that QR Ph is cost-effective. With the QR technology, all you need is a smartphone. Small entrepreneurs need not invest in costly electronic data capture equipment like point of sale (POS) terminals. 

• Merchants only need to print the QR Code that their payment service providers will generate for them, display those codes, and obtain payments by simply asking their customers to scan the codes.

• Second is that QR Ph minimizes encoding errors. By simply scanning the merchants’ QR code, both merchants and customers can be assured that the payment is sent to the correct account number of the merchant. 

• Third is the convenience of QR Ph. Compared to other modes of payment, QR code is extremely quick and easy. Customers need not bring their physical wallets to pay or to manually input the merchant’s account information since such is already embedded in the merchant’s QR code. 

• Fourth is that QR Ph is secure. QR codes are one of the safest payment methods. Customers do not have to store sensitive payment information and data transferred via QR codes is encrypted, thus making payments secure.

• Fifth is the contactless feature of QR Ph payments. With the ongoing pandemic, customers now prefer using digital payments like QR Ph because they can pay for purchases without having to touch shared surfaces like payment terminals, pens, or change. This helps the customers feel safer knowing the only thing they will touch is their own device.

• Last, but not the least, is that QR Ph allows you to pay the exact amount. With QR Ph, customers can pay the exact amount for the purchase of goods and services. Merchants looking for “change” or barya will be a thing of the past.

• With this, we will be able to move towards our envisioned coinless state as we transition towards a cash-lite economy.

Needless to say, QR Ph P2M is a key digital payment stream developed to further advance digital payments adoption.

We just recently announced the results of the e-payment measurement for the full year 2020, reporting that we even slightly surpassed the initial “20% by 2020” target of the BSP when we launched the National Retail Payment System (NRPS) in 2015. 

In the 2020 report and in the previous diagnostics, P2M has consistently been among the key drivers for growing digital payments usage in the country. 

This trend is expected given that merchant payments comprise over 70% of the total monthly retail payments in the country. As such, we are prioritizing merchant payments given its huge potential to further advance digital payments adoption in the country.

Since the P2M use-case covers a big consumer base – both individuals and businesses – it stands to provide a far-reaching impact to society in terms of the benefits that may be realized when merchant payments are digitalized. 

Imagine onboarding the micro and small enterprises that comprise over 98% of registered businesses in the country to offer QR Ph P2M to their consumers. 

We will not only drive digital payments usage, but we will also empower micro and small businesses to realize greater opportunities for growth which, in turn, could positively impact our country’s overall economic growth. 

Ten (10) years ago, it may have seemed daunting to even set a target of transforming 50% of retail payments into digital form by 2023.

This is due, in large part, to the study that showed that, in 2013, out of the 2.5 billion payments made by Filipinos in a month, only 1% are done electronically. 

We also did not have any laws or holistic regulatory frameworks in place governing the provision of digital payment services. 

Looking back, it really seemed impossible to achieve this target.

However, given the landmark regulatory reforms implemented these past several years, significant developments were realized in our bid to modernize the country’s payments landscape.

As a result, we have seen the accelerated rate of increase in the progression of digital payments adoption from 2013 to 2020. 

From 2018 to 2020, we witnessed a continuous rise in the share of digital payments in the country, with the volume growing significantly from 10% in 2018 to 20.1% in 2020, up by more than 10 percentage points compared to the more than 9 percentage point increase in the previous 5-year period from 2013 to 2018.

Considering the developments and the strengthening partnership between the public and private sectors in reforming our national payment system, the BSP is optimistic that it will realize its objective under the Digital Payments Transformation Roadmap of transforming at least 50 percent of total payments into digital form by the year 2023.

The BSP will continue to play its catalytic role by issuing supportive regulations that aim to strike the right balance between fostering innovation while ensuring the overall safety, efficiency and reliability of the national payment system. 

Aligned with this payment system oversight approach, the BSP recently issued policies that promote good governance and sound risk management standards for the critical participants in the national payment system. 

These regulations set the BSP’s expectations on the payment system participants’ adherence to the Principles for Financial Market Infrastructures to help them become more resilient to financial crises, and likewise prescribed the quality of stewardship among operators of payment systems.

Moreover, we continue to develop appropriate cyber security and anti-money laundering policies to protect the financial consumers. 

We have also launched digital literacy programs to educate consumers on the responsible use of digital payments, thereby reducing their vulnerabilities to scams and frauds, and fortifying the confidence in digital payments. 

But the BSP cannot create a well-functioning digital payments ecosystem alone, everyone has a role to play.

We enjoin you to be a part of this big change. Let us work together to build an inclusive and vibrant digital payments ecosystem as we forge pathways towards our vision of a cash-lite society.

So next time you need to pay for something, just SCAN QR Ph. Let’s go digitALL!

Thank you and have a great day!

Title: Responding to Today's Crisis and Building Foundations for a Better Tomorrow
Occasion: Standard Chartered Bank’s Sovereign Investor Forum
Speaker: BSP Governor Benjamin E. Diokno
Transcription:
Finance Secretary Carlos Dominguez III, officers and staff of Standard Chartered Bank, and all the participants of this virtual investor forum, warm greetings to all of you. 

I’m here today to present updates on the Philippine economy under the purview of the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP), to help guide you in your assessment of the country’s economic outlook. 

I’ll begin by saying that while the road to full recovery remains bumpy for the Philippines and many other economies at present, the medium- and long-term prospects for the Philippines are promising. 

This opinion is shared by relevant third-party observers, including credit rating agencies. 

As Secretary Dominguez had also shown earlier, throughout the pandemic—amid a wave of rating downgrades worldwide—the Philippines has maintained its investment grade credit ratings. 

Beyond the short-term challenges of the pandemic, debt watchers say that sound fundamentals and policies will help the Philippines return to a sustainable growth path once the dust settles. 

Let me share some of the latest economic indicators and macroeconomic projections for the short term.

Gross domestic product (GDP) grew by a robust 11.8 percent in the second quarter, thus ending the pandemic-driven recession. 

Growth was broad-based, fueled by manufacturing, construction, and wholesale and retail trade on the supply side, as well as household consumption, public construction, and private-sector investments on the demand side. 

Unemployment rate had improved to 6.9 percent in July.  However, with re-imposition of stricter quarantine classification on affected areas due to the threats from the more transmissible Delta variant, unemployment rate rose to 8.1 percent in August.

But with calibrated approach to the lockdowns, more economic activities were allowed which helped bring down unemployment from the pandemic’s historic high of 17.6 percent in April 2020. 

Foreign direct investments (FDIs) jumped by 40.7 percent in the first semester, signaling return of investor confidence.

Meanwhile approved investment applications from foreign investors rose by over 45 percent in the second quarter, with bulk of the investments going into industries with high potential for job creation such as Information and Communication, construction and manufacturing.  

Manufacturing activity is improving, as shown by the recovery of Purchasing Manager’s Index in September after a temporary setback in August due to stricter quarantine measures to curb the delta variant. 

Factory output sustains an upward trend with a triple-digit growth in volume and value of production indices, as well as, sustained average capacity utilization rate. 

Merchandise trade has recovered. For the first seven months, exports and imports sustained double-digit growth.  

Remittances, which have a been a steady source of foreign exchange throughout the pandemic, grew by 5.8 percent in the first seven months.  

Gross international reserves are hefty and provide adequate liquidity buffer.

Meanwhile, the Philippines’ exposure to foreign currency debt remains manageable, at only 26.5 percent of GDP as of end-June 2021, and low compared to neighbors.  

Inflation averaged 4.5 percent in the first nine months of the year. This was slightly above the target range of 2.0 to 4.0 percent on account of supply-side pressures, but nevertheless remains manageable. 

The BSP expects inflation to settle at the upper end of the target range of 2-4 percent in 2021 at 4.4 percent due to the impact of recent transitory supply-side pressures.

However, inflation is seen to ease towards around the midpoint of the target at 3.3 percent for 2022 and 3.2 percent for 2023.  

We see the risks to the inflation outlook remaining broadly balanced over the policy horizon.  

The banking system remains sound. 

Banks remain adequately capitalized as the average capitalization of banks exceed minimum regulatory requirement while the pandemic-driven increase in non-performing loans is manageable. 

In view of the resurgence of covid cases in the third quarter and the imposition of calibrated mobility curbs, the government had to trim its growth projection for 2021 from 6.0 to 7.0 percent to 4.0 to 5.0 percent. 

For 2022, the government retained its 7.0-9.0 percent growth projection. 

In any case, the Philippine Government has taken a whole of government approach in tackling the pandemic-induced challenges. 

There have been massive responses from both the fiscal and monetary sides.

On the part of the BSP, we have done quite a lot to help safeguard livelihoods, maintain order in the financial markets and put the economy back to a robust growth path. 

Besides slashing the reserve requirement and the key policy rate, which now stands at a historic low of 2.0 percent. We have extended liquidity support to the National Government, purchased government securities in the secondary market, among others.

So far, the BSP has infused a total of ₱2.3 trillion (or US$ 44 billion) in liquidity to the financial system, equivalent to 12.7 percent of GDP.    

As the favorable inflation outlook allows, the BSP will continue to support the economy until there is clear evidence of robust and sustainable progress to economic recovery. 

The decision on the timing and circumstances under which BSP will dial back its pandemic-induced support measures depend primarily on the evolution of various domestic factors, as well as global developments and spill overs.

BSP’s policies are data-dependent to avoid the premature withdrawal of policy stimulus, while also safeguarding against emerging risks to our price and financial stability objectives.

When domestic developments warrant a withdrawal of policy support as economic recovery gains traction, the BSP will ensure a smooth transition in winding down its time and state-bound measures.

At the same time, the BSP will continue to coordinate closely with fiscal authorities to ensure enough policy support remains for the economic recovery to be sustained.

Here are some of the latest near-term macroeconomic assumptions which reflect our confidence on the economic recovery: 

For next year and in 2023, growth is expected to accelerate to a range of 7.0 to 9.0 percent and 6.0 to 7.0 percent, respectively. 

Inflation will provide an enabling environment for higher consumption and investments, as this is seen within the 2.0- to 4.0-percent target range next year and in 2023. 

FDIs are expected to reach US$7.0 billion for the full year this year, and US$ 7.5 billion by next year.  This will be aided in part by government efforts toward easing doing business, supported by a liberalized FX environment put in place by the BSP. 

Trade is expected to pick up further amid recovery in global demand and improving business sentiment here and abroad. Exports are expected to grow by 14.0 percent this year and 6.0 percent next year; and imports by 20.0 percent and 10.0 percent over the same period.  

The country’s external accounts will remain robust, with the GIR staying well above USD 100 billion. This will continue to be supported by steady inflows of remittances and business process outsourcing (BPO) receipts.    

Speaking of the country’s strong external payments position, this will continue providing support to the peso. I would like to point out that the peso’s recent depreciation is manageable and in line with the behavior of regional and emerging economies currencies.

While short-run fluctuations in the peso are affected by market sentiment, its medium- to long-term movements are largely supported by economic fundamentals as indicated by the relative stability in the movement of the real effective exchange rate of the peso. 

As a matter of policy, the BSP does not target any particular level of the exchange rate and in fact, maintains a market-determined exchange rate.

Nevertheless, the BSP retains some scope to intervene in foreign exchange (FX) markets in response to excessive FX volatility in order to ensure orderly market conditions, avoid excessive volatility in the exchange rate, and therefore minimize any undue impact on inflation and inflation expectations. 

When warranted, the BSP can provide dollar liquidity to ensure that legitimate demands for foreign currency are satisfied.

The banking sector is expected to remain resilient to the pandemic. 

We expect bad debts to stay below 10 percent—far from the levels seen following the Asian financial crisis. 

The Financial Institutions Strategic Transfer (FIST) law enacted earlier this year—which allows banks to unload bad assets to FIST corporations—serves as a pre-emptive measure against any material rise in non-performing assets. 

Let’s move on to my next point on the Philippines’ medium and long-term prospects.

The Philippines does not simply aim to recover from the crisis. 

There is a whole-of-government effort toward a post-COVID Philippine economy that is better than ever. This means an economy that is stronger, more technologically advanced, more inclusive, and sustainable. 

I will briefly tackle each of the four aspects and how the BSP is contributing to their attainment. 

First, a stronger economy. Government has implemented various measures geared toward investment and job creation, including policies on ease of doing business, tax reforms, and critical infrastructure projects. It is also investing heavily on human capital development. 

The government also continues to pursue critical legislative measures such as further liberalization of the economy as earlier mentioned by Finance Secretary Dominguez.

The BSP has a range of initiatives complementing these efforts.  

For instance, to name just a few.

Several waves of foreign exchange liberalization help enhance the ease in doing business. 

Properly calibrated limits on bank loans support infrastructure development. 

Opening of the banking sector to more foreign players help boost economic activities and bring in innovative financial technology. 

Prudent management of external accounts and structural current account inflows have led to accumulation of FX reserves and boosted the economy’s resilience to external shocks. 

On top of these, consistent with our financial stability mandate, we have a regulatory framework that allows innovation while emphasizing risk management. This has led to a banking system that can withstand headwinds and support the economy during good and bad times. 

And, consistent with our price stability mandate, prudent monetary policy has put in place a manageable inflation environment that protects the purchasing power of households and supports productive activities.

Second, a more technologically advanced economy. Technology aids exponential growth in output. In the area of finance, it makes transactions easier and faster, which in turn, speeds up income generation.  

Amid this backdrop, the BSP is at the forefront of efforts to achieve a more technologically advanced economy. 

Last year, we launched the BSP launched the “Digital Payments Transformation Roadmap,” wherein we aim to transform the Philippines into a cash-lite society by 2023 through digitalization of financial services. 

Through active involvement of industry players, infrastructure is now in place to accommodate the growing electronic financial transactions in the country. 

In addition, the BSP is also actively promoting digital banking. 

Following our issuance of the regulatory framework for digital banks in December last year, we now have six purely digital banks in the country. 

We expect the digital banks to help fuel recovery and long-term growth for the Philippines, alongside conventional banks. 

Third, a more inclusive economy. Another goal under our Digital Payments Transformation Roadmap is for at least 70 percent of Filipino adults to have bank accounts by 2023. We expect to achieve this mainly through financial technology (FinTech).  

FinTech makes affordable financial products and services accessible to more people, including low-income earners and those residing in remote places, which in turn, enhances financial inclusion. 

On top of this, the BSP has a long list of regulations and initiatives meant to ease access of low-income earners, as well as micro, small, and medium enterprises (MSMEs) to formal credit and other financial services. 

Among which are rationalized “know your customer” rules, rules on basic deposit accounts that require no maintaining balance, and regulations that encourage risk-based rather than collateral-based lending, among others.

Also, the BSP fully supports the rollout of the National ID system, which will allow many marginalized Filipinos to have proper identification that will give them access to a wide range of financial services.

Lastly, a more sustainable economy. The threats posed by climate change require massive and urgent response, and the BSP recognizes the financial sector’s potential to push the sustainability agenda forward. 

As such, in April last year we issued the “Sustainable Finance Framework,” which sets out broad expectations for banks to integrate sustainability principles in their operations. Soon, we will be issuing more regulations that champion sustainability. 

Given the threats of climate change to socioeconomic development and to life itself, the only path to a prosperous future is the sustainable one. As such, the BSP is one with the entire world in helping support efforts in squarely addressing the climate crisis. 

Allow me to highlight three take-aways. 

First, the Philippine economy’s recovery process is underway, as evidenced by various indicators. 

Second, the Philippines does not simply aim to recover. We are actively striving to achieve a post-COVID economy that is stronger, more technologically advanced, more sustainable, and more inclusive than ever before. 

And third, as long as manageable inflation outlook allows, the BSP will continue to support the economy until sustained recovery is evident.

In closing, I would like to highlight that while the Philippines has its hand full in addressing the short-term challenges of the pandemic, we are also building the foundations for a post-COVID Philippine economy that is better than ever. 

With the whole-of-government effort, I am confident we will get there—and the Philippines will remain a sound value proposition for investors.

Thank you very much for listening, and I look forward to a productive engagement with all of you in the Q and A.​

Title: Building on Strong Macroeconomic Foundations Toward a Stronger, Digitalized, and Inclusive Economy
Occasion: The Asset 16th Philippine Summit
Speaker: BSP Governor Benjamin E. Diokno
Transcription:
​

To the officers and staff of The Asset, our stakeholders in the banking and finance industry, and everyone joining us in this virtual gathering, good afternoon.

Thank you for inviting me to the 16th Philippine Summit. This is a timely occasion for the industry to share insights and best practices, as we pave the way for recovery and growth. 

My speech this afternoon is divided into three parts.

First, I will briefly discuss the latest developments on the Philippine economy. 

Second, I will tackle the BSP’s response to the crisis brought about by COVID-19. 

And last, I will share insights on the BSP’s way forward.  

A year-and-a-half since the pandemic, we are getting back on our feet. 

We have learned to live with the virus better with the government shifting to a risk-based approach to mobility restrictions. 

This strategic shift has resulted in better economic and health outcomes. 

In the second quarter of this year, the Philippines’  Gross domestic product (GDP) grew by a robust 11.8 percent.  

This strong recovery reflects  more than just base effects but the impact of the  fiscal and monetary policy support during the pandemic and the calibrated imposition of mobility restrictions, which enabled many businesses, including public transportation, to continue operations. 

Manufacturing is on the rise, with the purchasing managers index on expansion mode for 6 out of 9 months this year. 

It suffered a temporary setback again in August similar to April and May owing to the imposition of stricter lockdown to curb the spread of the virus but recovered strongly in the month of September. 

Unemployment rate improved to 6.9 percent in July from the pandemic’s historic high of 17.6 percent in April 2020.  

However, with the re-imposition of stricter quarantine classification on affected areas due to the threats from the more transmissible Delta variant, unemployment rate rose to 8.1 percent in August. 

What our GDP and employment numbers show is that once the number of covid cases taper off, and restrictions are eased, the economy has the dynamism and flexibility to bounce back quickly and restore incomes and jobs. 

A stable inflation environment is also necessary to support our nascent economic recovery. 

While supply-side pressures pushed the average inflation rate this year to levels slightly above target, latest estimates show it will ease and settle at around the mid-point of the official target range of 2.0 to 4.0 percent next year and in 2023. 

The country’s external accounts remain sound. 

Gross international reserves are hefty and provide adequate buffers against external headwinds.

Remittances remain resilient throughout the pandemic and continue to be a steady source of foreign exchange. 

With the improvement in global trade, merchandise imports and exports increased substantially in the first seven months of the year. 

Foreign direct investments (FDIs) have similarly rebounded reflecting confidence on the Philippines’ recovery and growth prospects. 

The Philippines’ strong external payments position, driven in part by steady inflows of remittances, recovery of exports and investments, as well as the progress of our economic recovery will provide ample support to the peso moving forward. 

May I note that the peso’s depreciation lately—which has happened amid the anticipated policy normalization by the US Fed—remains manageable and is broadly in line with the behavior of other emerging market currencies. 

The banking sector remains sound and continues to support the financing requirements of the recovering economy. 

Capitalization of banks remain well above regulatory requirements. 

While non-performing loans may have risen during the pandemic, they remain manageable. 

Lending has improved, expanding by 1.3 percent in Aug from a year ago. 

This was the first expansion following the declines posted since December last year amid improvements in sentiment brought about by the continued rollout of COVID-19 vaccines and the gradual easing of quarantine restrictions. 

Along with these indicators, the country has kept its investment grade credit ratings intact throughout the pandemic. 

This is a testament to the confidence of debt watchers on the Philippine economy’s medium- and long-term growth prospects. 

Moving on to the BSP’s crisis response. 

The BSP has implemented a long list of crisis-response measures, amid a whole-of-government effort to address the challenges brought by the pandemic and to accelerate economic recovery. 

First are measures to boost market confidence on the availability of credit. The BSP lowered the reserve requirement and slashed the key policy rate by a total of 200 basis points last year to a record low of 2.00 percent. 

Second are extraordinary measures meant to ensure sufficient liquidity at a critical time. 

These include extension of provisional advances to the National Government, purchases of government securities in the secondary market, and advance remittance of dividends. 

And third, time-bound regulatory relief measures meant to help banks and their customers cope with the crisis. 

These include counting of loans to micro, small, and medium enterprises (MSMEs) as compliance to the reserve requirement, staggered booking of loan losses, and increase in the single borrower’s limit, among others.

The BSP has done quite a lot to respond to the crisis. Nevertheless, we will continue to support the economy until there is clear evidence of robust and sustainable progress toward full economic recovery. 

In total, BSP’s policy and liquidity-easing measures has injected into the financial system about ₱2.3 trillion liquidity in total, equivalent to 12.7 percent of the country’s full year nominal GDP for 2020 as of 26 August 2021 

The decision on the timing and circumstances under which BSP will scale back its pandemic-induced support measures would depend primarily on the evolution of various domestic factors, as well as global developments and spill overs.

BSP’s policies are data-dependent to avoid the premature withdrawal of policy stimulus, while also safeguarding against emerging risks to our price and financial stability objectives.

When domestic developments warrant a withdrawal of policy support, the BSP will ensure a smooth transition in winding down its time and state bound measures.

At all times, the BSP will coordinate closely with fiscal authorities to ensure adequate policy support remains for the economic recovery to be sustained.

The BSP is one with the government in the pursuit of a post-COVID Philippine economy that is better than ever. 

Let me cite two of  our initiatives toward this end. 

One is the Digital Payments Transformation Roadmap for 2020-2023. We aim to transform the country into a cash-lite society, where at least 70 percent of Filipino adults have transaction accounts—to be achieved largely through digital services—and where at least half of financial transactions are done electronically. 

Data show that we are on track with these twin goals. 

Second is our sustainability agenda. As you know, climate change poses drastic socioeconomic problems if left unaddressed. It is incumbent upon everyone to act with a sense of urgency. 

On the part of the BSP, we have issued the Sustainable Finance Framework, which calls on on banks to institutionalize sustainability principles in their operations. 

We will be issuing more enabling environmental, social, and governance (ESG)-related guidelines moving forward. 

Moving forward, the BSP’s actions and policy thrusts will continue to be anchored on its core mandates of promoting price and financial stability. Toward this end, the BSP will continue to pursue appropriate policy actions responsive to the needs of the time.

On monetary policy: the BSP will remain vigilant over the current inflation dynamics to ensure that the monetary policy stance continues to support economic recovery to the extent that the inflation outlook would allow. It will carefully scan the operating environment with a forward-looking perspective to move in a pre-emptive fashion to address any risks to our price stability mandate.

On the financial sector: the BSP will intensify its monitoring and surveillance over its supervised institutions to ensure that they remain responsive to emerging risks and to promote the continued soundness, stability, resilience and inclusivity of the banking system, particularly through the pursuit of enhanced digitization.

Third, on the external sector: the BSP will remain supportive of policies that will help strengthen the economy’s resilience to external shocks, including that of maintaining a market-determined exchange rate, keeping a comfortable level of reserves, and keeping the country’s external debt manageable.

In closing, I would like to highlight three take-away messages. 

First, the Philippines’ economic fundamentals remain sound; inflation is manageable, external payments is robust; and the banking system remains resilient and stable.

Second, as indicators show, the Philippines has begun the recovery process. The central bank will keep its policy settings and regulatory relief measures supportive of the economy as needed. The withdrawal of policy measures will only be done once 

full recovery is underway.

And third, the monetary authorities will continue to provide an enabling environment for the attainment of the Philippines’ long-term economic goals, such as through price and financial stability, and promotion of financial digitalization and sustainable finance. 

While the Philippine economy draws on solid fundamentals to boost the recovery, we encourage concerned stakeholders to take the opportunities from this pandemic challenge to help ensure the benefits from digitalization and financial sustainability reverberate in the economy and our people’s lives sooner than later. 

Thank you very much for your attention.

I wish you the best for this virtual Philippine Summit.​

Title: Thrift Banks: Moving Forward to the Next Economy
Occasion: Chamber of Thrift Banks 2021 Virtual Convention
Speaker: BSP Governor Benjamin E. Diokno
Transcription:
​

Officers of the Chamber of Thrift Banks led by the Convention Chairman Lorenzo T. Ocampo and President Cecilio “Paul” D. San Pedro, our partners from the thrift banking industry, guests, ladies and gentlemen, good morning!

I am honored to be your keynote speaker in this year’s virtual convention of the Chamber of Thrift Banks. 

I am grateful for this opportunity to engage with every one of you, our stakeholders, and discuss our shared goal of moving forward to the next economy.

I will start my presentation today by providing an overview of our current economic landscape and the performance of the thrift banking industry. 

Next, I will cover the BSP’s temporary relief and structural measures that will help propel the industry forward, including our sustainable finance initiatives and financial inclusion efforts. 

Regarding the updates on the economy -

The country's gross domestic product in the second quarter of 2021 reached 11.8 percent and is seen to average between 4 and 5 percent this year.  GDP growth is projected to further improve to a range of 7 to 9 percent in 2022.  

Our macroeconomic fundamentals remain sound and are expected to register strong recovery. We anticipate interest rates to remain low and the peso to be stable. 

Inflation is expected to remain manageable. Headline inflation slowed to to 4.8 percent year-on-year in September 2021 from 4.9 percent in the previous month. 

The year-to-date average inflation rate of 4.4 percent was above the target range of 2 to 4 percent. The latest inflation outturn is consistent with the BSP’s assessment that it could settle close to high end of the target range in the near term before decelerating back to within the target by year-end. 

Overseas Filipino remittances are expected to rebound this year.

In the first half of 2021, the cumulative remittances rose to US$16.6 billion, up from the US$15.6 billion recorded in the comparable period in 2020, or by 6.7 percent.

The country’s Gross International Reserves of US$108.1 billion as of end-August 2021 is hefty. It represents 12.3 months’ worth of imports of goods and payments of services and primary income. 

It was also 7.8 times the country’s short-term external debt based on original maturity and 5.4 times based on residual maturity. 

Thrift banks are strategically positioned to be a catalyst for financial inclusion with an extensive network of 2,744 banking offices as of end-August 2021 that are spread in different regions throughout the country. 

Amid the pandemic, the thrift banking industry remained sound and stable as shown by sustained growth in assets and deposits, strong capital position, adequate liquidity buffers, and profitable operations.

Total assets of the industry registered at PHP1.2 trillion as of end-July 2021, posting a 6.8 percent year-on-year growth rate. Meanwhile, deposit liabilities in the same period grew by 7.9 percent, highly indicative of the public’s continued trust and confidence in the industry.
