The risk-based capital adequacy ratio of the industry stood at 18.8 percent as of end-June 2021. This is above the minimum thresholds set by the BSP and the Bank for International Settlements. 

The minimum liquidity ratio of the industry was 36.5 percent as of end-June 2021, surpassing the 16 percent minimum. 

Net income registered at PHP6.6 billion in the six-month period ending June 2021, higher by 15.3 percent compared to last year’s level.

We are optimistic that the thrift banking industry is well-equipped to withstand the risks posed by the COVID-19 crisis.  

Recovery in the country’s macroeconomy and the industry’s financial performance will serve as a strong foundation for thrift banks in charting their course under the new economy.

Let me now focus on the key enablers which will help support the thrift banking industry as it navigates the post-COVID economy.

First, the BSP’s time-bound regulatory relief measures remain in place until end of this year.  This includes the easing of prudential requirements which will help thrift banks support financing requirements of micro, small and medium enterprise clients.

The BSP allowed the recognition of peso-denominated loans to MSMEs as alternative compliance with reserve requirements against deposit liabilities and deposit substitutes. 

In addition, the BSP reduced the credit risk weights of loans granted to MSMEs that are current in status to 50 percent until end-December 2021.  

The BSP deferred the implementation of the amendments to the risk-based capital adequacy framework for stand-alone thrift banks, rural banks and cooperative banks to 1 January 2023, instead of 1 January 2022.

Moreover, the BSP reduced the minimum liquidity ratio of stand-alone thrift banks, rural banks and cooperative banks from 20 percent to 16 percent until the end of December 2021.

Overall, these measures aim to provide thrift banks with sustained capacity to expand lending activities and support the recovery of local communities.

Second, thrift banks can take advantage of the fiscal incentives under the FIST Act to manage the level of non-performing assets, increase liquidity and support financing requirements of productive enterprises and households.

The BSP recognizes the vital role of thrift banks in promoting the development of MSMEs.  

The third enabler relates to initiatives aimed at enhancing the country’s credit infrastructure and improving access of the MSME sector to formal financial channels. 

The BSP is working on a Credit Risk Database project in partnership with the Japan International Cooperation Agency. The project will improve access to credit by small and medium enterprises by promoting collateral-free and risk-based lending through the use of statistical scoring models that will facilitate risk profiling and assessment of the paying capacity of these enterprises. 

In order to improve banks’ risk assessment and accelerate turnaround time in the processing of loan applications, the BSP is also working closely with key government agencies and the private sector, including the banking industry, in the adoption of a Standardized Business Loan Application Form.  

This project aims to make the loan application process simple, more streamlined and borrower-friendly, particularly for small enterprises. 

Fourth, the COVID-19 pandemic provides a window of opportunity to bolster the integration of green or sustainable finance in the country’s recovery response. 

Toward this end, the BSP is working on policy reforms that will promote sustainable finance and mitigate climate-related risk. The BSP has issued enabling regulations that will promote green finance through the Sustainable Finance Framework for banks. 

The regulations require banks to integrate sustainability principles into their strategic objectives, corporate governance, risk management systems, and in their operations. In addition, the BSP has strengthened engagement with various stakeholders domestically and internationally in line with its intensified campaign to adopt the sustainability principles.

Based on the results of the latest Banking System Outlook Survey, more than half of thrift bank respondents view sustainable finance as highly important. Although the willingness to finance sustainable project is high, thrift banks, in particular, indicated that the lack of demand for these projects and the lack of expertise or skill as the major barriers in pursuing sustainable financing. 

As such, the BSP is providing support in this area by developing the capacity of banks with the help of developmental institutions and training partners. 

Fifth, the BSP recognizes the potential of digital technology to further advance the financial inclusion agenda. As such, the BSP is committed to develop a digital finance ecosystem that supports the evolving needs of the public, particularly the low-income and unserved and underserved segments.  

One reform area where financial institutions, including thrift banks, can leverage on is participation in the National Retail Payment System. 

As of end-July 2021, there were only 17 thrift banks offering PESONet and 11 offering InstaPay electronic fund transfer services.

And so we encourage thrift banks to leverage on these technologies since this will further expand your customer reach and maintain competitiveness. 

Lastly, the BSP is pursuing key policy issuances and initiatives to strengthen the digital infrastructure, promote safe and efficient digital payment streams, safeguard electronic customer data, and build digital mindset and skillsets inline with the BSP’s digital transformation roadmap.

Related to this, the BSP has issued the Open Finance Framework which espouses consent-driven data portability, interoperability, and collaborative partnerships among incumbent financial institutions and third-party providers. 

Through “permission-based” access to customer financial information, financial institutions and third parties will gain access to financial information necessary to develop innovative products and services that are suited to the changing consumer needs.

The forthcoming BSP policy issuances on outsourcing and regulatory sandbox or the “test and learn” framework are expected to further facilitate digitalization among smaller institutions such as thrift banks 

The BSP is also considering developing a course on digital transformation to assist thrift banks in preparing for a digital-ready culture and environment. 

The BSP also continues to support the implementation of the Philippine Identification System, or PhilSys, which will provide every Filipino with a unique, verifiable and biometric-based digital identity. This will not only address the persistent onboarding issues due to lack of acceptable IDs, but also boost account ownership by enabling remote and more seamless onboarding. 

The BSP is working on complementary initiatives that will facilitate digital onboarding of clients through the operationalization of the PhilSys electronic Know Your Customer, or e-KYC, and authentication facility. 

The ongoing digital transformation of the Philippine economy is improving the way Filipinos make payments.  For Filipino consumers, this is the first step towards accessing a wider menu of digital financial services.

Given the rapid technological advancements, digital transformation of thrift banks’ systems, processes and services is now crucial. 

Thrift banks will have to evolve and consider new business strategies to keep up with the fast-changing times. 

In closing, allow me to share a quote from the best-selling American author, coach, and speaker John C. Maxwell.  He once said that “While a good leader sustains momentum, a great leader creates it.” 

As industry leaders, you have the means and ability to further elevate the strong performance of the thrift banking industry in the post-Covid-19 economy by leveraging on key enablers such as risk management, digital transformation and sustainability practices. 

On behalf of the BSP, I wish to thank the Chamber of Thrift Banks for its continued support for BSP’s efforts and for our continued collaboration to bring financial services to the Filipino people.

Congratulations and more power to the Chamber of Thrift Banks! Thank you and Mabuhay! ​

Title: Closing Remarks of BSP Governor Benjamin E. Diokno for the Turn-over Ceremony of Donation of the Anti-Money Laundering Council and Its Secretariat
Occasion: Turn-over Ceremony of Donation of the Anti-Money Laundering Council and Its Secretariat
Speaker: BSP Governor Benjamin E. Diokno
Transcription:
​

Commissioner of the Insurance Commission, Atty. Dennis B. Funa.

Chairman of the Securities and Exchange Commission, Atty. Emilio B. Aquino.

Executive Director of the Anti-Money Laundering Council (AMLC) Secretariat, Atty. Mel Georgie B. Racela.

Administrator of the Hospicio De San Jose, Sister Maria Socorro G. Evidente, DC.

Rector of the National Shrine of Our Mother of Perpetual Help, Father Victorino A. Cueto, CSsR.

On behalf of the AMLC and its Secretariat, I would like to thank the Hospicio de San Jose and the National Shrine of Our Mother of Perpetual Help—also known as Baclaran Church—for its efforts and initiatives, especially during this unprecedented time. 

We hope that our donation today can help further your endeavors to help those who are most in need.

As you may know, the AMLC is mandated to protect the country from terrorism financing, money laundering, and related crimes. While law enforcement and government agencies, such as the AMLC, are there to promote peace and order, civic and charitable organizations are just as crucial. 

Through various programs, these groups not only provide refuge to the impoverished, the downtrodden, and the marginalized but also open doors to opportunities and maybe even a new lease on life. 

They say crime is a reflection of a society. If so, then perhaps, wellbeing among its people can protect a society from the ills of lawlessness. And this is where we come together, despite the differences in our mandates and responsibilities.

We are grateful for such humanitarian organizations. May the Hospicio de San Jose and the National Shrine of Our Mother of Perpetual Help continue to bless our country with their altruism and may many others follow their lead. 

Thank you.

Title: The Philippines’ Response and Economic Recovery Amid the Prolonged Pandemic
Occasion: Meeting with Credit Rating Agencies
Speaker: BSP Governor Benjamin E. Diokno
Transcription:
​

The Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas welcomes this opportunity to update you on BSP's policy measures amid the pandemic as well as latest developments on the monetary, external and banking sectors.

As with the rest of the world, the Philippines continues to face challenges brought on by the pandemic.

Let me first discuss the BSP's policy interventions to address the pandemic-induced challenges. 

When the health crisis started early last year, the BSP acted swiftly to ensure ample liquidity in the financial system, support orderly functioning of the financial market, and shore up market confidence. 

We implemented a mix of decisive monetary policy adjustments, extraordinary liquidity enhancing measures, and regulatory relief and forbearance measures. 

In particular, to maintain stability of the financial system and ensure public access to financial services, we implemented a long list of measures to ease the impact of the crisis on the balance sheet of banks, so they can help their crisis-hit customers as well. 

We have discussed most of these measures with you last Spring and in subsequent reviews.

As an update, BSP's policy and liquidity-easing measures has injected into the financial system about ₱2.3 trillion liquidity in total, equivalent to 12.7 percent of the country's full year nominal GDP for 2020 as of 26 August 2021.

As the Philippine economy recovers, the decision on the timing and circumstances under which BSP will dial back its pandemic-induced support measures would depend primarily on evolution of various domestic factors, as well as global developments and spill overs.

When domestic developments warrant a withdrawal of policy support, the BSP will ensure a smooth transition in winding down its time and state-bound measures.

At all times, the BSP will coordinate closely with fiscal authorities to ensure adequate policy support remains for the economic recovery to be sustained.

Moving on to the latest developments on the monetary front

Headline inflation in September slightly eased to 4.8 percent from 4.9 percent in August. The slower inflation was mainly due to lower annual rate of increase in transport index. Year-to-date inflation has averaged 4.5 percent.  

The BSP expects inflation to settle at the upper end of the target range of 2-4 percent in 2021 at 4.4 percent. Inflation is seen to ease towards 3.3 percent for 2022 and 3.2 percent for 2023. 

We see the risks to the inflation outlook remaining broadly balanced over the policy horizon. The increase in inflation this year is not unique to the Philippines. Our neighbors are also experiencing the same.

Given a manageable inflation path, the BSP has kept the key policy interest rate at 2.0 percent in its recent policy review last month. 

The Monetary Board has decided that the revailing monetary policy settings remain appropriate given the manageable inflation environment and the nascent economic recovery. 

Together with appropriate fiscal and health interventions, keeping a steady hand on the BSP's policy levers will allow the momentum of economic recovery to gain more traction by helping boost domestic demand and market confidence.

On the banking system

Philippine banks have shown resilience to the COVID-19 crisis, benefiting from risk-management and other regulatory reforms of the past two decades. 

Banks continue to have ample buffers against shocks. 

The capital adequacy ratio (CAR) remains well above regulatory and international standards.

Exposure to soured debts remains manageable. Average non-performing loans (NPL) ratio of the banking system stood at 4.5 percent as of August this year, much lower than the double-digit figures in the aftermath of the Asian financial crisis. 

The BSP estimates that NPL ratios of the banking sector will settle between 5.0 percent to 6.0 percent by end-December 2021. 

Going forward, we expect NPLs to remain manageable. The FIST Act, which facilitates the sale/transfer by banks and other financial institutions of their non-performing assets is projected to reduce average NPL ratio of the banking system. 

Liquidity in the financial system remains ample, expanding by 6.9 percent year-on-year in August 2021—faster than the 5.9 percent growth recorded in July.

The BSP ensures that domestic liquidity remains adequate in support of economic activity.

The outstanding loans of universal and commercial banks (U/KBs) increased by 1.3 percent year-on-year in August. This is the first reported expansion in outstanding loans of U/KBs after eight consecutive months of contractions.

This improvement in may be attributed to the accelerated vaccine rollout and the gradual easing of quarantine restrictions.

The BSP's consumer expectations survey andbusiness expectations survey shows broad improvements in outlook for the coming months.

Meanwhile, the external sector remains strong. The Philippines' foreign debt remains manageable.

As of end-2020, the total external debt-to-GDP ratio of the Philippines was 27.2 percent much lower than Malaysia's 69.1 percent, Indonesia's 39.4 percent and Thailand's 37.8 percent. 

As of end-June 2021, our external debt had declined to 26.5 percent of GDP.

Gross international reserves continue to be hefty at US$108 billion, as of end-August, equivalent to 10.8 months' worth of import cover.

At US$108 billion, GIR exceeds total external debt worth Php101.7 billion.

We expect the overall BOP position to post moderate surpluses in the next two years, supported by resilient structural flows.

Overseas Filipino remittances in 2020 reached almost US$30 billion, slightly less compared to 2019, defying forecasts that it will fall by double-digit rates. 

From January to July this year, cash remittances increased year-on-year by 5.8 percent to US$17.8 billion. 

The increase in remittance inflows is expected to continue as COVID-19 vaccine rollout accelerates in the Philippines and in OFW host economies as travel restrictions ease further and countries safely open to foreign workers. 

Similarly, BPO receipts reached US$10.8 billion as of the first half 2021, 7.1 percent higher than the Php10.1 billion level a year ago.

Meanwhile, net foreign direct investments rebounded by 43.1 percent to US$5.6 billion in the first seven months of 2021.

On the exchange rate, the peso's performance is broadly in line with the behavior of other regional currencies.  

The peso has depreciated by 5.02 percent (as of 7 October 2021 close) against the US dollar since the start of the year.

Our hefty gross international reserves, the steady inflows from remittances, BPOs, and recovery of exports and FDIs—all these will support the peso.

The BSP remains committed to a flexible exchange rate regime. It will intervene only to smoothen the volatility in the exchange rate.

Moreover, the BSP will also continue to rely on measures such as maintaining a healthy level of foreign reserves as buffers and reviewing and calibrating existing macro-prudential measures to maintain the stability of the peso.

We cannot overemphasize enough that the Philippines came into the pandemic with ample policy space. This has enabled the government to address the challenges from the pandemic head on.   

Moving forward, the BSP will continue to pursue appropriate policy actions responsive to the needs of the time.

On monetary policy: the BSP will remain vigilant over the current inflation dynamics to ensure that the monetary policy stance continues to support economic recovery to the extent that the inflation outlook would allow. 

It will carefully scan the operating environment with a forward-looking perspective to move in a pre-emptive fashion to address any risks to our price stability mandate.

On the financial sector: the BSP will intensify its monitoring and surveillance over its supervised institutions to ensure that they remain responsive to emerging risks and to promote the continued soundness, stability, resilience, and inclusivity of the banking system.

Third, on the external sector: the BSP will remain supportive of policies that will help strengthen the economy's resilience to external shocks, including that of maintaining a market-determined exchange rate, keeping a comfortable level of reserves, and keeping the country's external debt manageable.

Thank you and I look forward to your questions.​

Title: Achieving Financial Inclusion for the Filipino People
Occasion: Financial Executives of the Philippines 53rd Annual Conference
Speaker: BSP Governor Benjamin E. Diokno
Transcription:
​

Good morning!

Thank you for inviting me as a speaker to this 53rd Annual Conference of the Financial Executives Institute of the Philippines. 

With all the disruptions in the current environment, the challenge is for us to transform these developments into something that is beneficial for the country. 

That is precisely what the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas has been doing—leveraging on technological progress to hasten economic growth and financial inclusion.

Even before the coronavirus pandemic, we have embraced financial technology to bring more Filipinos inside the financial loop and help improve their lives. 

These developments have enabled the Filipino people to continuously transact business within the safety of their homes during this time of the pandemic. 

Though the pandemic hit us hard, the Philippine economy is expected to recover in 2021 and 2022. 

In fact, the economy has started to rebound: The economy grew by 11.8-percent in the second quarter.  

Based on the latest government projections, the economy will grow anywhere between four and five percent this year and expand to a range of seven to nine percent next year. 

The economic recovery will be supported by manageable inflation, stable banking sector, and robust external payments sector. 

Estimates show that inflation is expected to slightly exceed the two- to four-percent target range this year due to supply factors, though this is expected to ease by next year. This manageable inflation will continue to provide an enabling environment for investments that will result in more jobs and higher income.

Philippine banks are sound and well-capitalized. As such, banks will remain capable of supporting economic growth.

The country’s external liquidity buffers continue to be more than adequate. Our gross international reserves of 108 billion US dollars, the steady inflows from remittances and business process outsourcing, and the recovery of exports and foreign direct investments will support the peso.

However, the BSP does not only intend to simply to be back where the economy was before the pandemic. We aspire for a stronger, more resilient, more technologically advanced, and more inclusive post-COVID-19 economy.

We are working towards this goal in three ways.

The first is through the pursuit of relevant reforms that will support economic recovery and growth and build its resilience. 

These reforms include the passage of the performance-based fiscal incentives under the Corporate and Recovery and Tax Incentives for Enterprises, or the CREATE Act, which will attract foreign direct investments in the long run, and the Financial Institutions Strategic Act, or FIST, which will keep the financial sector stable amid the pandemic. 

The second way is by contributing to infrastructure development through the adoption of regulatory measures that will make it easier for infrastructure companies to finance projects, such as increasing single borrower’s limit and deepening the capital market.

Third is through the inclusion agenda. The BSP has put in place regulations and programs so that micro enterprises can have easier access to credit and other financial services, and thus boost digital financial inclusion in the country. We also continue to work on our financial literacy programs to   improve the knowledge of Filipinos on savings and investment.

Indeed, the pandemic has highlighted the importance of inclusive digital finance. Early groundwork on digitalization has enabled many Filipinos to shift easily and rapidly to digital platforms. The foundations of the digital finance ecosystem—the Basic Deposit Account, the network of low-cost touchpoints, and the National Retail Payment System—earned remarkable gains during the pandemic.

The number of basic deposit accounts opened in 133 banks has reached 6.6 million accounts amounting to 4.71 billion pesos in 2020.

With 61 electronic money issuers in the country, around 34.7 million active e-money accounts were recorded last year. 

We have also noted a continued expansion of low-cost touchpoints enabling access to financial services.  Last year, there were 58,000 cash agents and over 84,000 e-money agents nationwide. This translates to 91 percent of local government units with access to agent banking services that enable financial institutions to serve a wider client base, particularly in low-income and rural areas, at greater efficiency but less cost. 

Physical and mobility restrictions heightened the use of electronic fund transfer schemes. The volume of PESONet transactions totaled 31.6 million for the first half of 2021, representing a 164-percent growth. Similarly, the volume of InstaPay transactions for the same period increased to 200.7 million, posting a 223-percent growth. We now have a total of 87 participants for PESONet and 55 participants for InstaPay, and these figures are growing. 

Serving as the cornerstone of the BSP’s digitalization agenda, the Digital Payments Transformation Roadmap outlines priority policy initiatives and strategies to advance an efficient, inclusive, and secure digital finance ecosystem.  It also seeks to drive innovation in the delivery and development of financial services catering to various client needs and capabilities. 

By 2023, the roadmap hopes to achieve the following—First is the conversion of 50 percent of the total volume of retail payments into digital form. Second is the expansion of account ownership to 70 percent of Filipino adults. 

To build use cases for account ownership and digital payment rails, the BSP has collaborated with different government agencies such as the Department of Labor and Employment, Department of Social Welfare and Development, and Department of Transportation.

Furthermore, the BSP launched the national Quick Response standard or QR Ph to promote interoperability and reduce costs of digitalization for small businesses.

The BSP is also expanding engagements with other target segments to promote inclusive digital finance. 

We are engaging the National Council on Disability Affairs for greater financial inclusion of the persons with disability sector.   Our initiatives include information sessions on the benefits of financial inclusion, and issuance of regulation on upholding non-discriminatory policies, providing mobility ramps in bank premises, and Braille on automated teller machines. 

We have also invited the Department of Interior and Local Government to be the 21st member of the inter-agency Financial Inclusion Steering Committee in July 2021, given its unique position to promote financial inclusion among the local government units.

To sustain the efficiency of delivery of financial services, the BSP has advocated initiatives to strengthen the country’s digital finance infrastructure.  

The BSP supports the rollout of the national ID System or PhilSys, which targets 50-70 million Filipino registrants by year-end. The PhilSys provides a unique and verifiable digital identity that can be used as an official document for availing financial services, such as opening an account and receiving government assistance.  

A co-location arrangement between the Philippine Statistics Authority and the LandBank of the Philippines has allowed PhilSys registrants to open a bank account onsite. This arrangement has resulted in the onboarding of over 5.3 million unbanked Filipinos to date. 

The BSP is involved in efforts to mainstream PhilSys adoption through policy development and issuance of relevant industry regulations such as acceptance of PhilSys ID as an official and sufficient proof of identity.

The BSP, as the Chair of the Financial Inclusion Steering Committee, endorsed Executive Order No. 127, which promotes the use of satellite broadband technology. This technology will be able to address digital connectivity gaps in rural and remote communities, as well as reduce the cost of delivering digital financial services nationwide. 

While digitalization is safe, convenient, and effective, the BSP is aware that it comes with risk. 

Accordingly, the BSP issued the governance policy for operators of payment system, as part of the phased-in implementation of the National Payment Systems Act. 

The governance policy provides for the regulatory expectations and governance standards that operators of payment systems must follow, considering their critical roles in ensuring the smooth circulation of funds in the economy in a safe and efficient manner. 

In addition, the BSP also requires designated payment systems to adopt international standards to further protect public interest and promote confidence in the use of payment systems. 

This is embodied in a circular on the Principles for Financial Market Infrastructures developed by the Bank for International Settlements and the International Organization of Securities Commissions.

For your information, the country’s first designated payment system is the Peso Real-Time Gross Settlement System operated by the BSP. This was approved by the Monetary Board in July 2021. 

The proposed Financial Consumer Protection Act is also necessary as it has far-reaching benefits to consumers especially amid the rise in digital transactions. 

This will allow regulators to further ensure that appropriate mechanisms are in place to safeguard the interest of financial consumers. 

The BSP has upgraded the country’s 17-year-old real-time gross settlement system with a next-generation system—the PhilPaSSplus, which went live last July 26. With the upgraded system, PhilPaSSplus is able to settle larger numbers and complex financial. This will help the financial services industry keep pace with the rapidly progressing digital transformation of both the local and global economies.

PhilPaSS Plus shall significantly enhance risk reduction, security levels, business continuity provisions, liquidity management, and the generation of data and information. 

Among the many features of PhilPaSS Plus is the adoption of the ISO 20022 international message standards, which shall advance interoperability of payment systems across the Philippines and with those in other jurisdictions.

All these disruptions lead us to a new frontier. It brings a lot of opportunities, only if we are willing to embrace them as chances for growth and development. 

Technological breakthroughs are here to improve lives, make things easier for everyone, and help us survive the global health crisis.  

And the BSP shall continue to use all these to bring every Filipino inside the financial loop, as we make our way towards a sustainable and digitally inclusive post-COVID-19 economy. 

Thank you and good day to everyone!​

Title: Open Finance Towards a Collaborative and Inclusive Digital Finance
Occasion: European-Philippine Business Summit
Speaker: BSP Governor Benjamin E. Diokno
Transcription:
​

Good afternoon to all the participants of the 2021 European-Philippine Business Summit. 

I’m glad to be here to talk about the opportunities and potential of Open Finance. 

As you know the BSP has always allowed innovations to flourish, while safeguarding effective risk management.

But before I dive into the BSP’s Open Finance Framework, let me take you quickly to the BSP Digital Payments Transformation Roadmap.

The BSP developed the Digital Payments Transformation Roadmap 2020-2023 to harmonize efforts towards building an inclusive and robust digital payment ecosystem in the country

The Roadmap is anchored on three pillars and is envisioned to transform the Philippines from a cash-heavy into a cash-lite economy. 

First, the Digital Payment Streams embody the BSP’s key initiatives of creating compelling, large scale digital payments use cases, in collaboration with strategic partners in the government and the private sector.

Second, the Digital Finance Infrastructure seeks to enhance key infrastructures that support the expansion of an inclusive digital payments’ ecosystem.

Third, the Digital Governance and Standards aims to provide overarching principles on the digital governance expectations and ethical use of data. 

Let me walk you through the milestones and the BSP’s initiatives under each pillar.

The BSP has been collaborating with the payment services industry led by the Philippine Payments Management, Inc. and other government agencies in order to develop more digital payment streams that cater to the needs of the local economy.

The QR Ph P2M, which expands the use case of QR Ph to cover person-to-merchant payments or P2M, will be rolled out by Q4 2021. This will facilitate efficient digital payments to the small unbanked vendors such as sari-sari store owners and tricycle drivers.

Aside from this, we are pushing for several other payment streams such as the Multiple Batch Settlement for PESONet that is set to be operationalized by Q4 2021. 

The Bills Payment Facility, which is set to be rolled out by early next year, will enable a customer to settle recurring payments even if the customer's Payment Service Provider is different from the biller's Payment Service Provider.

The Request to Pay Facility, which is projected to be launched by Q2 2022, allows payees to initiate collections by simply sending a “request to pay” to the payor. 

The Direct Debit, set to be implemented next year, will enable billers to pull funds from the account of the payors for authorized recurring payments.

Meanwhile, the BSP and the Department of Labor and Employment have been working for the digitalization of wage payments through remittance to transaction accounts.

Likewise, the BSP also supports the Department of Transportation’s Project on Automated Fare Collection System, which is set to be implemented towards the end of 2022.

Indeed, there is a big opportunity in digital payments. In fact, as of August 31, 2021, payment providers have increased with 87 BSP-Supervised Financial Institutions participating in PESONet and 55 in InstaPay. 

The participating institutions include thrift and rural banks, as well as non-bank e-money issuers, indicating a diverse reach of these services.

From Q1 2021 to Q2 2021, the combined PESONet and InstaPay transactions increased by 17% in volume and 14% in value. 

During that period, the volume grew from 107 Million to 125 Million while the value increased from Php1.5 trillion to Php1,7 trillion.

Since the start of the pandemic in 2020, the average quarterly growth rate for volume and value is 28% and 19%, respectively.

More evidence shows our progress in widening the adoption of digital payments.

In its first ever diagnostic for the Philippines in 2013, The Better Than Cash Alliance revealed that out of the 25 million monthly retail payments in the country, only 1% is electronic. 

Fast forward, the early estimates from the first half of 2020 suggest that digital payments rose to 17% or 782 million of all monthly payments, propelled by payments made to merchants and person-to-person payments. 

During the same period, the average monthly value of digital payments rose to 25% or 29 billion USD.

The second pillar of the BSP’s Digital Payments Transformation Roadmap pursues key initiatives to develop digital finance infrastructure.

To this end, the BSP upgraded the country’s 17-year-old PhilPaSS, the country's Real-time Gross Settlement, with a next generation system called PhilPaSSplus. 

Launched in July 2021, the PhilPaSSplus settles larger value, diverse, and complex financial transactions at a faster speed and with comprehensive functionalities. 

The BSP continues to support the implementation of the Philippine Identification System or PhilSys. The PhilSys ID is seen to address the challenge of proper identification with the added benefit of reducing customer onboarding costs. 

According to the Philippine Statistics Authority, about 26.3 million Filipinos have already completed Step 2 registration (which involves the capture of biometric information, as well as facial photographs) for the Philippine Identification System (PhilSys) as of August 18, 2021. 

Out of these registrants, 4.47 million have already been onboarded for bank accounts with the Land Bank of the Philippines. The accounts have no initial deposit requirement and comes with a Landbank Agent Banking Cards free of charge. 

In addition, Information and Communications Technology policy reforms aim to address digital connectivity gaps to promote fast and reliable internet connectivity. 

In combination with the roll-out of the PhilSys ID and e-KYC facility, greater internet access will allow more unbanked rural clients and low-income sectors to use digital financial services and benefit from digital innovations.

As you know, the goal of our rapid digitalization efforts is financial inclusion. And we are working to address this gap in financial services.

Through BSP’s efforts, there are now 133 banks offering basic deposit accounts to around 6.6 million depositors as of fourth quarter of 2020. At the same time, the number of e-money accounts has reached 34.7 million offered by 61 e-money issuers nationwide.

We also have over 58,000 cash agents and over 84,000 e-money agents in the country. These agents have enabled financial institutions to efficiently serve wider client base, particularly in low-income and rural areas. 

As of the fourth quarter of 2020, 91% of local government units already have access to an agent.

In addition, our efforts to develop the Digital Finance Infrastructure are gradually unlocking financial technology innovations offering alternative source of financing to MSMEs.

For instance, instead of depending on collateral, P2P lending provides non-collateralized loans to small businesses at competitive rates using credit scoring models and big data analytics to assess the credit worthiness of MSME borrowers.

Equity crowdfunding supports business startups by raising capital using online platforms. In 2019, the Philippine Securities and Exchange Commission issued the regulations on crowdfunding that will help support MSMEs while providing alternative investment opportunity for the investing public.

E-commerce finance offers working capital loans to small businesses selling goods on e-commerce platforms, while invoice financing allows them to monetize outstanding receivables in a quicker, easier, and more flexible manner than selling their receivables to a third party.

Indeed, fintech has the potential to help MSMEs grow and become competitive.

The final pillar of the BSP’s Digital Payments Transformation Roadmap commits BSP to providing an enabling regulatory environment that fosters digital innovation and adoption while ensuring effective risk management. 

The Digital Banking Framework, which was issued through Circular No. 1105 dated December 2, 2020, will support the expansion of the use of digital financial and payment services. 

A digital bank offers financial products and services that are processed end-to-end through a digital platform and/or electronic channels with no physical branches. To date, the Monetary Board has approved the application of 6 digital banks.

To further strengthen BSP-supervised financial institutions’ cybersecurity capabilities, the BSP shall be issuing amendments to the electronic banking guidelines to upgrade the baseline security controls for electronic payment and financial service providers.

On August 26, 2021, the Monetary Board has approved the local adoption of the Principles for Market Infrastructure among BSP designated payment systems essential in fortifying their resilience against financial crises and participant defaults.

The latest set of foreign exchange reforms that were issued through Circular No. 1124 dated August 10, 2021 allow authorized agent banks and foreign exchange corporations to sell foreign currencies, without prior BSP approval, if the foreign currencies will be used for digital payments for e-commerce transactions.

The BSP has also issued the policy on the governance arrangements and standards to be adhered to by all Operators of Payment Systems.

At this juncture, let me dive deeper into the Open Finance Framework.

Under Circular No. 1122 dated 17 June 2021, the BSP Open Finance Framework aims to facilitate the move of the local digital payments landscape towards an open finance ecosystem.

An open finance ecosystem fosters data sharing scheme that espouses consent-driven data portability, interoperability, and collaborative partnerships among incumbent financial institutions and new third-party players who adhere to the same standards of data security and privacy.

With access to consumer data, banks and third-party providers could tailor a broader array of financial products such as, banking products and services, investments, pensions, and insurance. 

The Framework sees customers as owners of their transaction data, which can be shared if they wish to do so. 

With more data shared in the ecosystem, financial institutions and third-party players are incentivized to adopt a customer-centric product development cycle.

For example, your main banking app can insert a feature that lets you add accounts from your other banks to help you monitor all your accounts at once. Your investing app can also let you add your bank account to let you see how much you can invest this month.

This is the promise of open finance.

To kickstart the Open Finance initiative, the BSP has identified key components requiring the BSP’s immediate attention.

The first component is Consultations and Capacity Building where BSP shall carry out activities in partnership with development agencies and other stakeholders to enhance its capability to foster an enabling policy and regulatory environment for open finance.

The second component is the Establishment of Governance Standards with BSP as lead in the conduct of consultation meetings and workshops to set up the Open Finance Oversight Committee.

The third component is Approval and Monitoring of Open Finance Pilot Implementations where BSP will permit regulated entities and service providers to participate in pilot activities under the Test-and-Learn environment.

In establishing the open finance ecosystem, a single body to oversee these efforts is necessary. As such, the Open Finance Oversight Committee is being constituted to perform this function. 

The Committee shall formulate open finance standards and procedures. Likewise, it shall promote non-discriminatory membership by ensuring that key areas of interest of the financial industry are adequately represented and that all participants and applicants are treated fairly and consistently. 

The BSP recognizes the need to institutionalize a “test and learn” approach and is working on establishing guidelines on regulatory sandbox aimed at setting a formal structure for piloting new financial technology solutions. 

In addition to BSP Supervised Financial Institutions, the “Test-and-Learn” or Regulatory Sandbox Framework will apply to third-party service providers and new financial technology new players offering products/services within the BSP’s regulatory purview.

The “test and learn” approach aims to discover “good” innovations without the weight of regulatory compliance costs.

We are doing a Pilot of this sandbox which is proposed to last 12 months commencing from the launch of retail Open Finance products among participating BSFIs. 

As of September 2021, fifteen BSP-Supervised Financial Institutions have signified their intent to participate in the pilot for account opening, statement sharing or account aggregation, and direct debit payments or fund transfers use cases. 

The BSP welcomes more participants in the Open Finance pilot and endeavors to approve additional Open Finance use cases.

As you can see, there are many opportunities ahead in the area of digital payments and finance. And we encourage everyone to participate and innovate in this flourishing space. 

The BSP is open to collaboration to encourage industry players to participate and develop innovative solutions, while recognizing the varying level of technical readiness of the different institutions.

This collaboration between the BSP and the industry will sustain the momentum in building a broader ecosystem benefitting not only the financial service providers, but, more importantly, the MSMEs, the underbanked, and the unserved segments. 

Thank you again for letting me be part of this Summit. Good afternoon.​​​

Title: Keynote Speech Governor Benjamin E. Diokno during the Regional Macroeconomic Conference Series
Occasion: Regional Macroeconomic Conference Series
Speaker: BSP Governor Benjamin E. Diokno
Transcription:
​

To our guests and partners from the banking and business communities in the Central Visayas region, our colleagues in government, ladies and gentlemen, maayong buntag kaninyong tanan.  

On behalf of the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas, I welcome all of you to the first Regional Macroeconomic Conference Series or RMCS. Allow me to thank and congratulate my colleagues in the BSP for initiating this program. This is one of our many continuing efforts to bring the BSP closer to the Filipino people. 

Much as we would like to conduct this program as a face-to-face live event, the COVID-19 pandemic has changed the way we do things.  Nevertheless, I am sure that this virtual conference would be engaging and productive.  

Today’s regional conference is the first of a series that will be replicated nationwide. We are happy that we are doing it first in Central Visayas because it is home to Cebu, the center of economic activities in the Visayas and Mindanao areas. Cebu is also the second largest urban economic center in the country, making it an appropriate venue for this maiden event. 

As you know, BSP is more than just the printer of banknotes and minter of coins. We make decisions that impact on a wide range of sectors of the economy. In doing all of these, we know that it is crucial for you—our stakeholders—to understand what we do, how or when we do it and, most importantly, why we do it. We recognize the importance of accurate information in your business plans and decisions. And this is what we will impart to you this morning. 

At the same time, the BSP will benefit a lot from your input to aid our policy recommendations.  

You are the people on the ground, the ones with first-hand experience of what is going on, and our primary source for the most reliable information on local concerns. 

This synergy is the essence of our Regional Macroeconomic Conference Series.  Numbers can only provide so much.  You provide the context behind the figures.  Your stories complete the whole picture. 

For this event, we will cover topics most relevant to you. Two topics stood out as your top concerns—one on recent economic developments with focus on regional perspective, the other on our micro, small and medium enterprises or MSMEs. Both will be discussed in the context of the current health crisis. 

Today, our speakers will tackle the state of the economy and what we are doing to navigate the challenges of the pandemic. We will zero in on MSMEs and our policy responses to keep as many businesses afloat during these uncertain times.

Considering that MSMEs are the backbone of the economy, measures to help them recover would significantly redound to the resurgence of the entire country. 

On that note, allow me to say a few words on our country’s economy. We are now seeing green shoots of recovery.  We posted a growth of 11.8 percent in the second quarter of 2021, a reversal of the 17.0 percent contraction in the second quarter last year.  Unemployment has declined. Both consumer and business sentiments have also improved. We have received credit rating affirmations and even an upgrade, which are votes of confidence in our ability to stage a strong recovery from the health crisis. 

Our trade performance continue to improve. Foreign direct investment inflows are on the rise. Remittances remain resilient, while our international reserves continue to expand. 

Although there is clearly room for optimism, economic recovery will depend largely on the speed of the vaccination rollout, the expansion of the capacity of our healthcare system, and the citizens’ commitment to observe the health protocol. These will allow us to safely re-open the economy and resume more economic activities. 

The challenges of the pandemic may stay with us for a while, but we are hopeful that we will get back to where we were before the pandemic by the second half of next year. Now, more than ever, each one of us need to walk together and watch each other’s back so that no one gets left behind in this continuing journey. As Henry Ford said, “Coming together is a beginning; keeping together is progress; working together is success.”

I trust that this session will enrich all of us and equip us with the right information and mindset that we can share with our colleagues or family members later. 

I hope that in our next RMCS event in Central Visayas, we can all meet in person, but until then, please stay safe and healthy. Maayong buntag ug daghang salamat!​

Title: The Rise of Challenger Banks
Occasion: MAP Webinar Series
Speaker: BSP Governor Benjamin E. Diokno
Transcription:
A pleasant day to everyone! Thank you for inviting me to speak at this webinar entitled “The Rise of Challenger Banks”. 

Indeed, this event by the Management Association of the Philippines is an excellent opportunity to collaborate and see the digital revolution from different perspectives.

But first, allow me to share with you the country’s digital payments landscape based on the 2019 update and 2020 preview on Philippine digital payments conducted by the Better Than Cash Alliance or “BTCA” in partnership with the BSP. 

In terms of the total volume of payments in the country, 17 percent were made digitally in the first half of 2020, as compared with 10 percent in 2018. Consumer payments make up 78 percent of the 4.6 billion monthly payments, followed by corporate payments at 21 percent. 

Consistent with the previous diagnostics, the government continues to lead the way in digitization with some 87 percent or P319 billion equivalent of payments by the government (G2X) already in digital form, up from 64 percent in 2018.  

The same is followed by payments made by people (P2X) and businesses (B2X) at 35 percent and 15 percent, respectively.

Noteworthy is the rise in volume of digital merchant payments by 66 percent since 2018. 

Essentially, this increase pushed the strong upward trend in the overall volume of merchant payments driven by electronic fund transfers and the heightened usage of prepaid cards.

As you know, the BSP launched in 2020 the Digital Payments Transformation Roadmap, a blueprint for the development of an efficient, inclusive, safe and secure digital payments ecosystem that supports the diverse needs and capabilities of individuals and firms alike. 

In this journey, two strategic outcomes are emphasized. First is the goal to convert at least 50 percent of the total volume of retail payments into digital form, and second is to make available varied innovative and responsive digital financial products and services. 

The roadmap also aims to onboard at least 70 percent of Filipino adults to the financial system through the ownership and use of a transaction account. 

Over time, the increased usage of transaction accounts will enable Filipinos to build financial profiles that further unlock access to more complex financial services. 

According to World Bank article entitled “Digital Financial Services” published in April 2020, access to affordable financial services is critical for poverty reduction and economic growth. 

Countries with deeper, more developed financial systems enjoy higher economic growth and larger reductions in poverty and income inequality. Fintech-enabled Digital Financial Services (DFS), has the potential to lower costs, increase speed, security and transparency and allow for more tailored financial services that serve the poor at scale. 

DFS would also allow governments to provide welfare grants and other forms of financial assistance to vulnerable people in a fast and secure way. 

With the issuance of Digital Banking Framework, the Philippines is a step closer to reaching its strategic outcomes. On our end, the BSP has long recognized the role of digital platforms in finding greater efficiency in the delivery of financial products and services. 

We also see the recent issuance of the digital banking framework as an integral building block in promoting an enabling regulatory environment that fosters responsible innovation, promotes cyber resilience and contributes towards advancing the digitalization of the financial sector. 

As such, we established a specific classification for digital banks. Due to their digital-centric business model, the operation of these banks should be underpinned by sound digital governance, robust, secure and resilient technology infrastructure, and effective data management strategy and practices. 

This digital banking framework is particularly relevant as billions of people affected by the COVID-19 pandemic are driving a “historic and dramatic shift in consumer behavior”. That’s according to the latest research from PricewaterhouseCoopers or PwC. 

The consulting and accounting firm's June 2021 Global Consumer Insights Pulse Survey reported a strong shift to online shopping as people were first confined by lockdowns, and continued to work-from-home. 

Another significant finding from the report is that consumers do not think they’ll go back to their old ways of shopping once the pandemic is over. This may change the business models of companies. 

This remarkable result us supported by a the study conducted by Visa in the Philippines which also showed that around 70 percent of Filipinos who used digital payment channels during the lockdown will likely continue to do so.

To date, the Monetary Board (MB) has already approved the applications of six (6) banks. 

The Monetary Board approval refers to the first of the three-stage licensing framework of the BSP on the establishment of banks. 

• On March 25, 2021, the MB approved the first application which is from the Overseas Filipino Bank (OFBank) seeking to convert its banking license from a thrift bank to a digital bank.  

• On June 3, 2021, the MB approvedthe applications of (1) Tonik Digital Bank, Inc., for conversion of its rural banking license to a digital bank license, and (2) UNObank, Inc. for the establishment of a new digital bank. 

• On July 15, 2021, MB approved the application of Union Digital Bank, a wholly-owned subsidiary of UnionBank of the Philippines.

• On August 12, 2021, MB also approved the application of GoTyme Bank, a partnership between JG Summit Holdings and a South African banking group.

• And lastly, on September 16, 2021, MB also approved the application of Maya Bank, Inc., an affiliate of PLDT’s Voyager Innovations, Inc.

Based on their profiles, these digibanks intend to serve the OFWs, underserved, unbanked and the mass market, but are open to venture into investments, insurance, and payment services, to broaden their reach.

On August 19, 2021, the BSP issued Memorandum No. M-2021-046  announced the closure of the application window for new digital banks, including converting banks after August 31, 2021. This is to closely monitor the digital banks’ performance and contribution to the country’s financial inclusion goals, impact on the banking system, and level of competition.

Following such announcement until August 31, the BSP received nine applications from new players and existing banks.  These are on top of the two digital bank applications which were under evaluation prior to the announcement. 

 These nine applications are processed on a first-come, first-served basis. 

The application documents are also assessed by the BSP for completeness and sufficiency against the documentary requirements and applicant bank’s compliance with the licensing criteria for the establishment of digital banks. 

Currently, with the recent approval of Maya Bank, only one digibank license remains to be contested by nine aspirants. 

In any case, this new category is not without its unique challenges. Data privacy concerns, money laundering, and electronic frauds are among the issues that can undermine the confidence in this policy initiative. 

We therefore expect that the key stakeholders particularly the financial institutions, to adopt adequate measures and controls to manage such risks.  

Foremost of which is the conduct of an effective information campaign to ensure that customers are aware of the risks and how they can perform their transactions securely.  

I want to emphasize that consumers must be made aware of consumer protection mechanisms. 

On the other end of spectrum, other government agencies are also expected to collaborate and address the digital divide. It entails ensuring access to IT infrastructure by people from all walks of life to achieve inclusivity. 

Given all these developments, what does it mean for MAP? As the COVID-19 wreaked havoc and put every facet of life on a virtual standstill, MAP’s theme for the 2021 “The Great Reset: Leading for the Common Good” sets the tone on how we should act and face the reality head on. 

Along with this great reset is the rise of challenger banks that can change the game on how the brick-and-mortar banks deliver their products and services. 

Intuitively, these digital banks can be viewed by traditional banks as formidable contenders which can reduce their market share. 

But there are strong arguments for allowing the establishment of digital banks.

First, it can usher prosperity and alleviate poverty. Second, it can advance financial inclusion as the new entrants can provide affordable financial services to the mass market. 

Lastly, it can nudge the incumbent bank’s digital transformation moves as a way of staying relevant and competitive. In all of these, it’s the customers and the business community who will reap the benefits.

More than the challenger banks, we believe that the journey of our BSP-supervised financial institutions towards digital transformation is another equally important aspect that the MAP members can draw inspirations from. 

In particular, the BSP publication entitled “BSP Unbound: Central Banking and the COVID-19 Pandemic in the Philippines” released in 2020, showed that investing in the right technology and tools, involving all departments in developing the strategy, and investing in staff training are the critical factors towards the success of digital transformation. 

In the same publication, we noted how the pandemic made our supervised electronic money issuers and virtual asset service providers realize the importance of introducing new products suitable to the new normal, strengthening business continuity framework and pursuing digitalization initiatives. 

Clearly, such way of thinking is also the gist of a Harvard Business Review article in 2020 that highlighted the importance of pivoting to business models conducive to short-term survival along with long-term resilience and growth. 

It emphasized the need for disintermediation by going directly to the buyer’s buyer, supported by changes in marketing, logistics and information technology, particularly e-commerce platforms. 

In closing, let me stress that digital banking forms part of a bigger picture. 

For easier visualization, we can say that achieving inclusive digital finance is similar to establishing a sustainable community. Just like a community with its key establishments, inclusive digital finance is attained when its key pillars are deeply founded and strongly visible. 

On the part of the Bangko Sentral, we are committed to establish the policy and regulatory environment that will enable innovations to flourish while ensuring that the controls and safeguards are in place. 

We also firmly recognize that innovations should not be stifled. They should be allowed to develop in an environment where the associated risks are understood and addressed and where there is a judicious and proportionate application of sound principles.  

Achieving all of these is not just the sole responsibility of BSP. We must espouse a “whole-of-government” approach, taking into consideration the multiplicity of players and multi-layered relationships among fintech innovators, and financial sector players in ensuring policy consistency and preventing regulatory arbitrage. 

Continuing engagement with industry players like MAP has been crucial in fostering a shared understanding of risks, a collective action towards financial inclusion goals and a consensus in market conduct expectations. The key has been to maintain an active multi-stakeholder collaboration.

Now, how does digital banking form part of this picture? Indeed, just like an automobile bringing its passengers to their desired destinations, digital banking framework, along with the other mobilizers such as Open Finance and Philsys ID, contributes to transporting the country to deeper financial inclusion and to move us closer to a well-managed financial system in the Philippines. 

We are living in exciting times and we all have a role to play. Let this initiative be just one of many more opportunities for us to work together to truly provide better ways of serving our constituents. 

With our vast network, we hope that this presentation be the starting point of another meaningful initiative.

Thank you and a pleasant day to all of you.

Title: Welcome Message of BSP Governor Benjamin E. Diokno for the NCDA Webinar Empowering Persons with Disabiliites Through Digital Financial Inclusion
Occasion: NCDA Webinar on Empowering Persons with Disabilities Through Digital Financial Inclusion
Speaker: BSP Governor Benjamin E. Diokno
Transcription:
​

Good morning to all the participants in today’s NCDA webinar. I am happy to be here with you again.

Alam natin na hindi sapat ang paglago lamang ng ekonomiya. Dapat maramdaman ng lahat ng Pilipino ang mga benepisyo nito. 

All Filipinos should be able to make better lives for themselves as the economy improves. This requires that we continuously work toward the NCDA’s vision of “full participation and equality of rights and opportunities for persons with disabilities.”

This is why financial inclusion is among the top advocacies of the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas. We believe that everyone should have effective and easy access to a wide range of financial services. 

Over the past few years, the BSP has been laying the foundations of an inclusive digital financial ecosystem. 

As financial transactions are increasingly conducted through digital channels, more and more consumers gain convenient access to legitimate financial services, making them less vulnerable to onerous practices, such as the nefarious 5 - 6 scheme.

The theme of this webinar is both noble and timely. We consider the empowerment of our countrymen across all sectors as a vital outcome of digital financial inclusion. This inclusion will also help us recover from the adverse economic impact of the pandemic and make us better prepared for a post COVID-19 economy.

An exciting development is the emergence of sacheted financial services. Such novel and groundbreaking services include micro-savings, micro-insurance and investments, micro-credit and remittances, which are designed to be affordable and accessible to all, with far-reaching benefits. 

In order to access these services, one needs a transaction account in the form of a bank or e-money account. Such a transaction account is the gateway to financial inclusion. That is why one of our main strategies is to make it easy to own a Basic Deposit Account or BDA, which is especially designed to meet the needs of the unbanked.

With a minimal deposit of just one hundred pesos and simplified identification requirements, anyone can open an account through their nearest bank, cash agent, or even via mobile app. Presently, 133 banks in the country offer BDAs.

As part of our commitment to protect the interests and welfare of the persons with disabilities sector, the BSP has issued Memorandum No. M-2021-040 to all banks and BSP-Supervised Financial Institutions or BSFIs to implement non-discrimination policies.

We have likewise introduced enhanced features in our banknotes to help the visually-impaired in identifying denominations.

To further boost these initiatives, the BSP supports the implementation of the Philippine National ID System or PhilSys. 

Makakatulong ang PhilSys na pabilisin ang pagbukas ng account, pagtanggap ng ayuda mula sa pamahalaan, at iba pang mga proseso. 

The BSP also supports the passage of the Financial Consumer Protection Bill, which aims to strengthen protections available to financial consumers. The initiative has far-reaching benefits, especially amid the rise in digital transactions. 

We also applaud the issuance of Executive Order 127, signed by President Rodrigo Roa Duterte last February. EO 127 seeks to liberalize access to satellite Internet technology, enabling our kababayans in rural areas to connect and benefit from the digital economy.

The BSP invites you to be active and dynamic participants in the shaping of a stronger and more vibrant post-COVID-19 economy by using and promoting legitimate digital financial services. Digital financial inclusion means that no one is left behind. 

Kapag kabalikat namin kayo, mas madali nating maibabangon ang ating ekonomiya tungo sa pag-unlad para sa bawat Pilipino.

Maraming salamat po!

Title: Opening Message of BSP Governor Benjamin E. Diokno during the Retail Dollar Bonds (RDB) Launch
Occasion: Launching of the Retail Dollar Bonds
Speaker: BSP Governor Benjamin E. Diokno
Transcription:
​

Good afternoon, everyone. The Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas is proud to support the Bureau of the Treasury’s first-ever offering of Retail Dollar Bonds.

Retail Dollar Bonds provide a special opportunity for small and mid sized investors to earn and, at the same time, help fund the government’s recovery and resilience programs. This initiative of the Bureau of the Treasury is also aligned with our aim of bringing the BSP closer to the Filipino people. 

Consistent with this measure, the Monetary Board approved-in-principle the country’s proposed onshore dollar bond issuance last June 2021.

The issuance of the Retail Dollar Bonds will help promote activity in the country’s bond and capital markets. By providing this alternative and affordable investment vehicle, the Retail Dollar Bonds encourage individual investors to mobilize their domestic savings for potential yields. 

It will also enable them to diversify their investment portfolios for better liquidity management.

The availability of the Retail Dollar Bonds will help encourage foreign exchange inflows from investors. It could be particularly attractive to our overseas Filipinos who have funds to invest. This bodes well for them and their families. 

As you may know, personal remittances from Overseas Filipinos increased by 7.3 percent to US$2.936 billion in June 2021.

Rest assured that there will be no impact on the US Dollar-Philippine Peso exchange rate if an investor withdraws from his foreign currency deposit account.

The proceeds of the Retail Dollar Bonds will help the national government fund its financing needs to aid economic recovery. 

These funds will serve as additional source for a stimulative fiscal policy which, together with the current accommodative monetary policy, will remain crucial in restoring confidence and reviving domestic demand. 

Taken together, these initiatives will help the national government fight the adverse effects of the pandemic through targeted fiscal interventions, which are aimed at boosting market confidence and safely reopening more sectors of the economy.

I am proud to say that the BSP has played its part in preparing for the launch of the Retail Dollar Bonds.

First, opening a bank account is now easier, more accessible, and affordable. The BSP supported the use of the electronic Know-Your-Customer verification process. Customer onboarding has become more seamless through online customer registration and technology-aided face-to-face verification. Partner banks have also agreed to waive the minimum initial deposit and the daily maintaining balance for those who want to purchase Retail Dollar Bonds. 

Second, the BSP has enabled a regulatory environment supportive of digital transformation. As such, individual investors can buy Retail Dollar Bonds through e banking apps and which they can transfer to their bank accounts seamlessly through PESONet or InstaPay. 

At this point, I would like to recognize the crucial support of our banks, which have been very active in introducing financial innovations. Thank you for your partnership in championing our policies and regulations.

Third, the peso is relatively stable. This is attributed to the adoption of the inflation targeting framework for monetary policy, as well as years of foreign exchange regulatory reforms. The fluctuations in the exchange rate have also had a declining impact on inflation outturns. Thus, we do not expect this activity to contribute to any significant upside risks to the inflation outlook.

Finally, the BSP has ensured that the country’s foreign exchange regulatory framework remains appropriate for the needs of a dynamic economy. 

Over the past years, the BSP has undertaken a series of liberalization reforms to ease foreign exchange rules and facilitate transactions of banks, SMEs, overseas Filipinos, and the public in general. 

As a result of these reforms, interested investors could now easily buy dollars from their banks to be used for purchasing retail dollar bonds.

Let me end by saying that there is no better time to invest than now. The economy is on its way to recovery. Together with a manageable inflation outlook, we are on track to achieve positive economic growth this year.

For the BSP’s part, we remain keen on sustaining monetary policy support for as long as necessary to support the momentum towards economic recovery. 

While the past year has not been easy, I know most of us are eager to play a part in our country’s recovery. I encourage every Filipino here and abroad to support the retail dollar bonds and contribute towards a healthier and future-ready Philippines. Thank you very much.​

Title: The Philippine’s Path to Economic Recovery Amid the Pandemic
Occasion: Joint General Membership Meeting of ACI and MART
Speaker: BSP Governor Benjamin E. Diokno
Transcription:
​

To the officers and staff of the Financial Markets Association; Fund Managers Association of the Philippines; Investment House Association of the Philippines; Money Market Association of the Philippines; National Association of Securities Broker Salesmen, Incorporated; Trust Officers Association of the Philippines; and partners and stakeholders in the banking and finance industry; ladies and gentlemen, good afternoon. 

Thank you for this opportunity to share the good news as our country continues on its path towards economic recovery. 

It has been a year-and-a-half since the onslaught of the pandemic. Uncertainties remain. But the country’s sound economic fundamentals give us reason to be optimistic during these times.  

Let me give you an overview of the state of the economy right now, how we at the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas have responded towards recovery, and how we defy the odds as we push forward.  

Overall, we have started this year in a position of strength.

We saw signs of recovery when our country’s gross domestic product or GDP recorded a double-digit growth in the second quarter of 2021. You see there in red five quarters of pandemic-induced recession before we hit the 11.8-percent growth. 

This second quarter of 2021 saw most industries and services, including public transportation, continuing its operation amid the reimposition of the Modified Enhanced Community Quarantine in the National Capital Region.

As I mentioned in the previous slide, the 11.8-percent growth is a strong rebound as it marked an end to 15 months of economic slump. 

Our labor force continues to recover as we build on this growth in the second quarter. Unemployment rate fell to its lowest since the start of the pandemic—down to 6.9 percent in July 2021.

We also see favorable trends in our manufacturing indicators particularly in the Purchasing Managers Index, the volume and value of production indices, as well as the average capacity utilization rate. 

In terms of confidence in the market, we have observed improvement in both the overall consumer and business sentiment.

However, the less optimistic outlook in the second quarter of this year was attributed to the surge in covid cases, the reimposition of the lockdown, and higher prices due to supply constraints.   

Another source of optimism is the credit rating upgrades and affirmations, which are votes of confidence in the government’s ability to stage a strong recovery from the health crisis. 

For August, inflation rate rose to 4.9 percent.  This is at the high end of BSP’s monthly forecast range of 4.1 to 4.9 percent, and above the target band of 2 percent to 4 percent, which is consistent with the BSP’s assessment that inflation could settle above the high end of the target range in the near term before decelerating back to within the target by year end.  

Moving forward, we will continue to monitor price developments to help ensure that we achieve our primary mandate of price stability.

Moving on to the external sector….

The export and import of goods both increased by more than 10 percent in the first quarter of 2021. These amounted to US$12.9 billion and US$ 24 billion, respectively, reflecting an US$ 11.1 billion trade deficit as imports outpace exports. 

This development reflects the sustained recovery momentum of the trade sector in the wake of the government’s containment measures at the onset of the pandemic. 

We also see a 37.8-percent increase in the foreign direct investment inflows for the period January-June 2021 as compared to the same period last year. However, there is a decline in net inflow in May, which reflected the renewed investor concerns on the rising cases of the new COVID-19 variants. 

The seven-percent increase in June in cash remittances from overseas Filipinos hit its highest level in six months, climbing to nearly US$15 billion the year-to-date remittance level. We can expect the uptrend in remittance inflows as travel restrictions ease further and global economies now reopen. 

Meanwhile, our country’s gross international reserves reached US$ 108.05 billion by end-Aug 2021. This reflects a more-than-adequate level of external liquidity buffer equivalent to 12.3 months’ worth of imports of goods and payments of services and primary income.

Our outstanding external debt narrowed to US$ 97 billion in March 2021.  Related to this, our external debt-to-GDP ratio of 26.7 percent in the first quarter of the year shows our strong position to service foreign borrowings in the medium to long-term. It ensures that our debt payments remain manageable and sustainable. 

Liquidity and credit conditions also remain supportive of growth. Domestic liquidity or M3 remains ample. M3 expanded by 5.9 percent year-on-year to about P 14.4 trillion in July 2021.

Meanwhile, bank lending activity shows some signs of improvement. The year-on-year rate of decline in outstanding loans is slower at 0.7 percent relative to the previous month, while the month-on-month change is positive. 

Total outstanding loans for production activities expanded by 0.8 percent in July following a contraction of 0.6 percent in the previous month. 

This is the first time that outstanding production loans has increased since the reported growth rate of 0.5 percent in November 2020.

Philippine banks remain well-capitalized. The capital adequacy ratio of the banking system in the first quarter of the year is at 16.9 percent, well above the 10-percent minimum threshold set by the BSP. 

On the whole, banks have continued to rein in the non-performing loan ratio within manageable levels, reflecting gains from prudent reforms and improvements in banks’ credit risk management systems. 

More than maintaining these indicators, the Bangko Sentral is committed to sustaining a sound financial system conducive to a strong and inclusive economic recovery. 

We keep up with the whole-of-government tempo with these three major interventions:

First, the BSP put in place measures to boost market confidence on cost and availability of credit resources, such as cuts in the policy rate and the reserve requirement. The BSP reduced its policy rate by a total of 200 basis points to help bring down the cost of borrowing and shore up market confidence. Meanwhile, the lower reserve requirement—or the proportion of deposits banks must keep as reserves in the BSP—increased the volume of loanable funds. 

The BSP also allowed banks to count newly granted loans to micro, small and medium enterprises, and large enterprises as alternative compliance to reserve requirement.

Second, the BSP adopted extraordinary liquidity measures. These include purchases of government securities in the secondary market, remittance of P35 billion in advance dividends, and provisional advances to the national government.

In sum, the BSP has infused about P 2.23 trillion in liquidity, equivalent to 12.5 percent of the country’s GDP for 2020.

Third, the BSP implemented regulatory and operational relief measures to maintain stability of the financial system and ensure public access to financial services were implemented. 

The BSP issued time-bound and targeted regulatory and operational relief measures to encourage BSP-supervised financial institutions to continue their support to the economy, with particular emphasis on the MSME sector.

Indeed, we have done much in implementing extraordinary measures. Yet our action will remain anchored to our mandate of promoting price and financial stability, working on appropriate policy responses as necessary.

On monetary policy: we will remain vigilant over the current inflation dynamics to ensure that the monetary policy stance continues to support economic recovery. 

We will carefully scan the operating environment with a forward-looking perspective to move in a pre-emptive fashion to address any risk to our price stability mandate.

On the financial sector: we will intensify its monitoring and surveillance over BSP’s supervised institutions to ensure responsiveness to emerging risks. 

At the same time, we will intensify the pursuit of financial digitalization to enhance the soundness, stability, resilience, and inclusivity of the banking system.

Third, on the external sector: we will remain supportive of policies that will help strengthen the economy’s resilience to external shocks, including that of maintaining a market-determined exchange rate, and keeping a comfortable level of reserves and manageable external debt.

On top of these initiatives, we will also promote financial digitalization and a sustainable finance. The desired outcome is a “post-COVID-19 economy” that is stronger, more technologically advanced, and more inclusive than ever before. 

Towards this end, the BSP launched the Digital Payments Transformation Roadmap for 2020-2023 last year. With this roadmap, we aim to transform the country into a cash-light society through digitalization of payments and increasing the number of Filipinos with access to financial services. 

The use of digital payments also helps reduce the need for mobility and prevent health risks from face-to-face and over-the-counter financial transactions. 

The recent figures confirms that the value of transactions done through InstaPay expanded by more than 180 percent, and through PesoNet, by more than 80 percent in the first seven months of 2021.

While we move towards a post-COVID-19 Economy, we will continue to complement the national government’s broad-based pandemic-relief initiatives and provide the needed liquidity to support economic activity and maintain the favorable market sentiment. 

There is no doubt that we have already made solid economic strides amid these trying times. 

We reaffirm that the monetary policy stance will remain accommodative until economic recovery is fully underway.

Thank you. ​

Title: Moving from Crisis, to Recovery, and further to the 'New Economy'
