Occasion: Official Monetary and Financial Institutions Forum
Speaker: BSP Governor Benjamin E. Diokno
Transcription:
Officers and staff of the Official Monetary and Financial Institutions Forum (OMFIF), fellow central bankers and regulators, other public and private-sector guests, ladies and gentlemen, a pleasant day to all of you.  

I thank OMFIF for inviting me again to speak before your stakeholders.  

My task here is to update everyone on economic developments in the Philippines—a year-and-a-half into the global COVID-19 crisis. 

My presentation will be divided into three parts: (i) where the Philippine economy is; (ii) where we envision the Philippine economy will be; and (iii) how we intend to reach our desired destination. 

The Philippine economy has started to recover, growing by 11.8 percent in the second quarter of 2021, thus  ending the pandemic-induced recession.

The second quarter growth was not solely due to base effects. 

Growth was broad-based,  driven by manufacturing, construction and wholesale and retail trade on the production side and by household consumption, public construction and investment in durable equipment on the expenditure side. 

Unemployment rate improved to 6.9 percent in July this year, the lowest since the pandemic’s historic high of 17.6 percent in April 2020. 

Manufacturing activity was on expansion mode, with the purchasing manager’s index (PMI) at 50.8 in June and 50.4 in July this year.

But it suffered a temporary setback in August owing to the imposition of stricter lockdown to curb the spread of the Delta variant.

By the way, the decline in PMI  is Asia wide. 

Meanwhile, inflation rose to 4.9 percent year-on-year in August.

The year-to-date average inflation rate of 4.4 percent in the first eight months is above the upper bound of the Government’s annual inflation target of 3.0 percent ± 1.0 percentage point. 

The increase in headline inflation was driven mainly by higher price increases of key food items, particularly vegetables and fish due to supply disruptions from damages caused by monsoon rains in parts of the country. 

Meanwhile, increased electricity rates due to higher generation and transmission charges along with increased prices of liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) contributed to the rise in year-on-year non-food inflation.

The latest CPI outturn is consistent with the BSP’s assessment that inflation could settle close to the high end of the target range in the near term before decelerating back to within the target by year end. 

In 2022-2023, inflation is expected to decline towards the midpoint of the target, supported by the continued and timely implementation of non-monetary measures and reforms to address directly supply-side pressures on key food items. 

Our inflation projections are in line with expectations of relevant observers. 

Given manageable inflation, and in support of economic recovery, BSP kept policy rates steady during the policy meeting last August 12. 

Latest figures on actual and pledged investments are encouraging. 

Foreign direct investments (FDIs) jumped 40.7 percent from January to June. 

Foreign investment applications approved in Q2 2021 grew by 45.5 percent, reaching PHP22.5 billion (USD445.5 million). The top foreign nationals investing in the country came from United Kingdom, South Korea, USA, Netherlands and China.

Trade has recovered from last year’s contraction…  

Imports grew by 24.0 percent in July. With bulk of the country’s imports being raw materials and intermediate goods, imports recovery is a welcome signal of rising investments in anticipation of higher demand. 

Similarly, exports jumped by 12.7 percent in the same period.  

Overseas Filipino remittances in 2020 reached almost USD30 billion, slightly less compared to 2019, defying forecasts that it will fall by double-digit rates. 

During the first six months of this year,   remittances grew by 6.4 percent. 

The uptrend in remittance inflows is expected to continue as COVID-19 vaccination levels increase domestically and in OFW host economies, travel restrictions ease further and countries safely open to foreign workers. 

External accounts remain robust. Gross international reserves (GIR) are equivalent to more than one year of imports—versus the received doctrine that three months of import cover is already sufficient.  

The banking system remains stable and resilient, thanks to regulatory reforms over the past two decades. 

Loan quality remains manageable, with the non-performing loans ratio of universal and commercial banks was at 4.0 percent as of end-June this year. 

This is far from the double-digit figures seen in the aftermath of the Asian financial crisis.   

Banks have ample buffers, with the capital adequacy ratio of 17.4 percent. 

This is well above the international standard of 8 percent and the central bank’s regulatory requirement of 10 percent.   

All these indicators show that the Philippines is well into the recovery process, aided by COVID-response measures from the fiscal and the monetary side. 

The  Central Bank implemented extraordinary measures to ensure ample liquidity in the financial system, support orderly functioning of the financial market, and shore up market confidence. These measures include a mix of decisive monetary policy adjustments, liquidity enhancing measures and regulatory relief and forbearance measures. 

The BSP has so far infused PHP2.2 trillion or US$44 billion—equivalent to about 12.5 percent of GDP—in liquidity to the financial system. 

To maintain stability of the financial system and ensure public access to financial services,  we implemented a long list of measures to ease the impact of the crisis on the balance sheet of banks, so they can help their crisis-hit customers as well.  

With the Philippines’ economic recovery underway, we remain optimistic that the country’s medium – to   long-term growth prospects remain robust.  

Nevertheless, we recognize that the road to full recovery is not a walk in the park. 

With the spread of the more contagious Delta variant in many Asian countries in recent months, the Philippines’  COVID cases have also spiked. 

We are  proactively containing the spread of the Delta and other variants through a  risk-based approach in quarantine restrictions allowing important businesses/sectors to operate, including public transportation, but restricting non-essential activities.  We are also using this period to vaccinate as many as we can.  

The lockdown is expected  to dampen the Philippine economy’s  nascent  recovery —but only temporarily. 

There is basis for cautious optimism.  

Nationwide vaccinations have accelerated. The Philippines is now inoculating more than 400,000 individuals per day. 

At this rate, the country may achieve “population protection” by the fourth quarter of this year.  

Moving on to my second point on where we envision the Philippine economy to be… 

Before the pandemic, the Philippines was poised to transition  from “low middle income” to “upper middle income” status in 2020. 

We also had achieved great progress in poverty reduction.

Poverty rate fell from 23.5 percent in 2015 to 16.7 percent in 2018—and was poised to drop further to 14 percent by 2022.  

Unemployment rate was down to a record low of 4.5 percent in October 2019. 

The economy posted 21 years of uninterrupted growth up to 2019, expanding even at the height of the Global Financial Crisis. 

These achievements were made possible in part by price and financial stability, aided by the BSP’s sound monetary policy and financial sector regulation.   

With the Philippine economy starting to recover, the National Government’s fiscal and public health measures remain crucial in sustaining the momentum.  

The road to economic recovery requires purposeful and coordinated efforts  - a whole of government approach. 

The BSP—complementing the stimulus from the fiscal side—will continue supporting the economy, until the recovery fully gets underway. 

Looking ahead, we do not aim to simply regain the economic losses from the pandemic. We aspire for a “Post-COVID-19 Philippine Economy” that is stronger and more resilient, more technologically advanced, and more inclusive than ever before.  

The BSP supports the realization of the "Post-COVID-19 Economy”  through commitment to its price and financial stability mandates, and push for innovation in the financial sector.  

The Philippines also aims to be a technologically advanced economy that has high regard for the environment.

On sustainability, the Philippines last April submitted its commitment with the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change to reduce its projected carbon emission by 75 percent by 2030. 

By then, we want sustainability deeply engrained in the consciousness of Filipinos and factored in by businesses in their operations

On my third point – on how we are moving towards our desired destination 

The Philippines is pursuing its goals in many ways, but three are top of mind.  

First is by further liberalizing the economy and making it even more investor friendly. The Philippines is a signatory to the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership (RCEP)—a mega free-trade deal signed by select Asia-Pacific economies in November last year.  

RCEP signatories account for nearly a third of global output. Once it takes effect, RCEP will open the gates of member economies to much more trade and investments.  

RCEP is important for the Philippines, more so because it will drive growth of our micro, small, and medium enterprises (MSMEs), which account for two-thirds of employment in the country. Businesses operating in RCEP economies will be able to source raw materials within the bloc at cheaper cost, and export finished goods to other RCEP members under preferential arrangements.  

Also, RCEP will help the Philippines attract export-oriented firms that want to take advantage of free trade with our neighbors. 

There is much economic energy waiting to be unleashed in the coming period. Our recovery will also get a boost with the implementation of the CREATE law or the Corporate Recovery and Tax Incentives for Enterprises. This is the largest economic stimulus program for businesses in our recent history.

This law provides an immediate 10 percentage point cut in the corporate income tax rates of our micro, small and medium enterprises, from 30 percent to 20 percent of profits. The rest of the corporations enjoy a 5-percentage point reduction, from 30 percent to 25 percent. 

CREATE grants tax relief annually to the corporate sector to sustain employment or use for reinvestments. Publicly listed companies, acknowledged that CREATE helped them maintain or increase their profitability and their ability to cope with the pandemic. 

In addition, the CREATE law provides flexibility in granting fiscal and non-fiscal incentives. This introduces an enhanced incentives package that is performance-based, time-bound, targeted, and transparent. 

Through CREATE, we see an opportunity to draw in high-value  investments  by incentivizing industries that will introduce new technologies and innovations and create more jobs. 

Moreover, the President has certified as urgent three bills seeking to further open the Philippines to foreign investors; these bills are in the advanced stages of the legislative process.

These include a bill that seeks to lower the capitalization requirement for foreign retailers;  a bill that will redefine “public services” to essentially lift foreign ownership restrictions in sectors like telecommunication and transportation; and a bill that seeks to allow foreigners to operate small and medium enterprises in the country provided they either bring in advanced technology or employ a minimum number of Filipinos. 

On the part of the BSP, we support investment promotion through a regulatory environment that is welcoming to foreign investors and technological innovation. 

In 2014, we further liberalized foreign banks entry into the Philippines. As a result, to date, there are 29 foreign banks in the country, of which, 24 are operating as foreign bank branches and 5 as foreign bank subsidiaries. 

Since the issuance of the regulatory guidelines for the operation of digital bank guidelines in December 2020, the BSP has so far approved license applications of 5 purely digital banks . 

Last year, we launched the Digital Payments Transformation Roadmap. Under this, we target half of financial transactions to be done electronically and 70 percent of Filipino adults to have financial accounts by 2023.  

The roadmap entails leadership from the BSP and collaboration among industry players in putting up safe and efficient systems that allow electronic fund transfers.

Financial technology accelerates payments processes and makes affordable financial products and services accessible, thus providing income-growth opportunities to more people.  

The second way the Philippines is pursuing its long-term goals is through infrastructure development. 

Over 5,000 infrastructure projects are listed in the country’s Public Investment Program for 2017-2022, with a combined cost of Php 6.7 trillion (about USD 130 billion).  

With the government’s aim to usher the country’s “Golden Age of Infrastructure,” public infrastructure spending has risen over the years, from 3.9 percent of GDP in 2016 to a projected 5.1 percent this year.  

Infrastructure flagship projects include railway systems, airports, roads, water systems, and information and communication technology development.  

The BSP is contributing to infrastructure development through regulatory measures such as by increasing the Single Borrower’s Limit as well as deepening of the capital market that make it easier for infrastructure companies to finance projects. 

Finally, another way the Philippines is pursuing its long-term objectives is through policies geared toward inclusivity. 

Besides infrastructure development, the other objective of the Philippine government  is to invest in human capital development. 

Government spending for social services takes the lion share of the budget.

For this year, it accounts for 37 percent of the national budget with  PHP1.668 trillion (US$33 billion) allocation.  

This budget is used to fund recently enacted laws on universal access to tertiary education and healthcare. 

Investments in education and health help  the Philippines—whose population has a median age of 25 years old—harness its demographic advantage. 

Having a young population in an aging world is an asset provided we are able to mold them into competent and agile work force. 

The BSP actively contributes to the inclusion agenda…  

Regulations and advocacy programs meant to ease access of micro enterprises to credit and other financial services are in place and are constantly revisited for enhancement.  

The BSP likewise implements financial literacy programs that improve knowledge of Filipinos on savings and investments.  

In closing, I would like to highlight three take-away messages. 

First, the Philippines’  economic fundamentals remain sound;  inflation is manageable, external payments is robust; and the banking system remains resilient and stable.

Second, as indicators show, the Philippines has begun the recovery process. The central bank will keep its policy settings and regulatory relief measures supportive of the economy as needed. The withdrawal of  policy measures will only be done once full recovery is underway. 

And third, the monetary authorities will continue to provide an enabling environment for the attainment of the Philippines’ long-term economic goals, such as through price and financial stability, and promotion of financial digitalization and sustainable finance. 

Thank you very much for your attention. I look forward to the Q&A.​

Title: Amplifying Momentum Towards a Strong PH Economic Recovery
Occasion: DBCC Briefing to Senate Committee on Finance
Speaker: BSP Governor Benjamin E. Diokno
Transcription:
​

Senate President Vicente Sotto III, Committee Chair Juan Edgardo Angara, members of the Senate Committee on Finance, members of the economic team, colleagues, ladies and gentlemen, good morning. 

The Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas, as a resource institution of the Development Budget Coordination Committee, will present the macroeconomic assumptions underlying the fiscal year 2022 proposed National Government budget along with the key developments and prospects supporting our assessment on monetary, external and banking sectors.

More than a year since the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic, the Philippine economy is gradually recovering. The unprecedented crisis called for an unprecedented response and the whole-of-government acted promptly and decisively. The government’s mass vaccination program is picking up its pace and scope and is expected to accelerate further. 

The Bayanihan 1 and 2 as well as the provisions under the 2021 National Budget were designed to support the safe re-opening of the economy. 

Moreover, the government passed into law reforms that could foster a strong and faster economic rebound while limiting the scarring effects of the pandemic on the economy. This includes the passage of the Financial Institutions Strategic Transfer or FIST Act (RA 11523) and the Corporate Recovery and Tax Incentives for Enterprises or CREATE Act (RA 11534). 

Meanwhile, the proposed Government Financial Institutions Unified Initiatives to Distressed Enterprises for Economic Recovery or GUIDE Bill aims to strengthen the capacity of government financial institutions such as the Philippine Guarantee Corporation, Land Bank of the Philippines, and the Development Bank of the Philippines, to assist micro, small, and medium enterprises (MSMEs) cope with the effects of COVID-19.

Given that the nature of the current crisis is primarily an issue of public health, the government’s public health measures, fiscal stimulus, and structural reforms have stood as the country’s major response against the pandemic.

Complementing the government’s responses, the BSP has implemented temporary and time-bound monetary policy measures to ensure ample liquidity in the financial system, restore financial market functioning, and shore up market confidence. These measures include a mix of decisive monetary policy adjustments and extraordinary liquidity measures along with regulatory relief and forbearance measures. 

On its recent policy meeting, the Monetary Board decided to keep its monetary policy settings unchanged. The Monetary Board remains keen on sustaining monetary policy support for as long as necessary in order for the momentum of economic recovery to gain more traction as well as to help boost domestic demand and market confidence, especially as risk aversion continues to temper credit activity.

As of 2 September 2021, the BSP’s measures have injected into the financial system about ₱2.3 trillion in liquidity, equivalent to 12.7 percent of the country’s full year nominal GDP for 2020.

Given the whole-of-government response and bolstered by years of resolute reforms, the resulting 2020 key economic indicators show that the domestic economy had remained resilient against the adverse effects of the global pandemic.

The country’s macroeconomic fundamentals remain generally intact as evidenced by the quarter-on-quarter improvements in gross domestic product outturn towards the year-end; within-target inflation; ample financial system liquidity; and robust external payments position.  

At the same time, the banking system continues to be stable and resilient while the public sector debt remains manageable.

In the next slides, I will go through the recent trends and developments for 2021 in the real, monetary, financial, and external sectors of the economy.

The Philippine economy begins its positive growth. After five consecutive quarters of economic contractions, the economy posted a positive growth in the second quarter of 2021, with real GDP expanding by 11.8 percent from a 17.0 percent contraction in Q2 2020.  

In terms of production, the expansion was mainly contributed by manufacturing (Q2 2021: +22.3%, Q1 2021: +0.5% ), construction (+25.7%, -22.6%) and wholesale and retail trade (+5.4%, -3.4%).  By expenditure, growth was driven by household consumption (+7.2%, -4.7%), public construction (+49.7%, +25.3%),  and investment in durable equipment (+89.2%, -10.3%). 

Almost all sectors and expenditure segments of the economy bounced back during the quarter. 

This seems to indicate that the country is learning how to live with the virus by managing risks through the safe re-opening of the economy and calibrated re-imposition of granular quarantine restrictions only where it is necessary. 

Headline inflation rose to 4.9 percent in August 2021 from 4.0 percent in July, bringing the year-to-date average inflation to 4.4 percent.

The increase in headline inflation was driven mainly by higher price increases of key food items, particularly vegetables and fish, reflecting impact of strong monsoon rains.   

Meanwhile, increased electricity rates due to higher generation and transmission charges along with increased prices of LPG contributed to the rise in non-food inflation. 

Core inflation, which excludes selected volatile food and energy items to depict underlying demand-side price pressures, also increased to 3.3 percent in August from 2.9 percent in July.

Average inflation is projected to settle slightly above the upper end of the government target band in 2021. Nevertheless, with the continued and timely implementation of direct supply measures and programs to mitigate supply-side pressures on meat and other food prices, inflation is projected to ease towards the midpoint of the target range in 2022 and 2023. Latest assessment likewise indicates that the risks to the inflation outlook remain broadly balanced over the policy horizon. 

Moving on….

Domestic liquidity in the financial system remains ample. 

M3 expanded by 5.9 percent year-on-year in July 2021, slower than the 6.5-percent growth recorded in June. 

Meanwhile, bank lending activity shows some indications of improvement.

Preliminary data show that outstanding loans of universal and commercial banks (U/KBs), net of reverse repurchase (RRP) placements with the BSP, decreased by 0.7 percent year-on-year in July, slower compared to the 2.0-percent contraction in June. 

On a month-on-month seasonally-adjusted basis, outstanding universal and commercial bank loans, net of RRPs, went up by 0.5 percent. However, credit activity has remained weak due to risk aversion and weak economic sentiment.  

Bank credit continues to decline as the necessary measures to address the still elevated number of COVID-19 cases constrained domestic economic activity and dampened market sentiment.

On the whole, Philippine banks have continued to rein in the NPL ratio within manageable level, reflecting gains from prudent reforms and improvements in banks’ credit risk management systems.

Gross non-performing loans ratio increased to 4.5 percent while the NPL coverage ratio of the banking system declined to 82.4 percent in June. 

Moving forward, the BSP anticipates that the non-performing loans of the banking system will remain within manageable levels. The existing regulatory relief measures serve as an interim measure pending the full operationalization of the FIST Act in 2021.  

The FIST Act will reinforce banks’ capital and liquidity position in the long-term by allowing financial institutions to dispose their non-performing assets, increase their risk-bearing capacity, and enhance their capability to provide financial services to productive sectors of the economy.

Moreover, Philippine banks remain well-capitalized. As of the first quarter of 2021, the capital adequacy ratio (CAR) of the banking system is at 16.9 percent, well above the 10 percent minimum threshold set by the BSP.

The BSP stands committed and ready with its enhanced onsite and off-site surveillance tools and prudential policy toolkit to promote the financial sector reform agenda for sustaining the sound and stable financial system conducive to a strong, dynamic and inclusive economic growth recovery of the country.

On the external sector, the gross international reserves (GIR), which stood at US$107.2 billion as of July 2021, continue to provide more than adequate external liquidity buffer. The GIR level is equivalent to 12.2 months’ worth of imports of goods and payments of services and primary income. It is also about 7.7 times the country’s short-term external debt based on original maturity and 5.2 times based on residual maturity.

The GIR is supported by improving inflows of cash remittance from overseas workers. 

On the foreign exchange market, the recent peso depreciation is partly influenced by broad US dollar strength driven by risk-off sentiment over the spread of the Delta COVID-19 variant and to markets’ perceived shift to a hawkish tone by the US Federal Reserve. 

In addition, the observed pick-up in corporate dollar demand as the economy gradually re-opens and the Fitch Ratings’ outlook downgrade 

for the country’s sovereign credit rating added pressure on the peso.

However, the more than adequate gross international reserves is expected to temper the peso depreciation. In addition, we expect the peso to be supported by structural FX flows through recovery in exports, overseas Filipino remittances, and business process outsourcing receipts. FX inflows related to foreign direct investments are also expected to help shore up the currency. 

Mr. Chair and the members of the Senate Committee on Finance, let me now present the macroeconomic assumptions underlying the FY 2022 National Government budget:

As mentioned, inflation is projected to settle close to the high end of the inflation target for 2021 and decelerate near the midpoint of the target band for 2022.

On global crude oil prospects, elevated global oil prices could persist in the near term given improvements in world oil demand.  

Nevertheless, international oil prices could moderate as the Organization of Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) and its allies, alongside US oil producers expand their oil production. We expect the peso exchange rate to be within the Php48-53/US$1 range. 

While we expect some depreciation pressures on the peso from the eventual US Federal rate adjustment, structural FX flows and hefty GIR could provide support on the peso.

Moreover, the 364-day T-bill rates and 180-day LIBOR could remain relatively low in the near term, followed by a gradual rise over the forecast horizon as the global economy recovers. 

On external trade, sustained recovery momentum in the country’s trading partners notably US, Japan, and China, could underpin the pick up in goods exports. At the same time, goods imports could recover as restrictions subside amid widespread vaccinations, and as domestic demand recover from a contraction in 2020.

While we see some signs of economic improvements, we should also recognize some risks ahead. 

The global economic recovery is expected to be uneven, especially between advanced economies and emerging market economies. The path to recovery would depend on the reach of mass vaccination and effectiveness of policy support. In addition, potential further rise in international commodity prices due to improving global demand amid lingering supply-chain bottlenecks could pose upside pressures to inflation. 

On the domestic front, the threat of further increases in COVID-19 infections remains, 

especially with the emergence of more contagious and more resistant virus variants, such as the delta COVID-19 variant. 

Clearly, economic recovery is highly contingent on the speed of the vaccination rollout, the existing capacity of the country’s healthcare system, and the citizens’ willingness to observe the appropriate health protocol.

Moving forward, the BSP’s actions and policy thrusts will continue to be anchored on its core mandates of promoting price and financial stability. Toward this end, the BSP will continue to pursue appropriate policy actions responsive to the needs of the time.

On monetary policy: the BSP will remain vigilant over the current inflation dynamics to ensure that the monetary policy stance continues to support economic recovery to the extent that the inflation outlook would allow. 

On the financial sector: the BSP will intensify its monitoring and surveillance over its supervised institutions to ensure that they remain responsive to emerging risks and to promote the continued soundness, stability, resilience and inclusivity of the banking system, particularly through the pursuit of enhanced digitization.

Third, on the external sector: the BSP will remain supportive of policies that will help strengthen the economy’s resilience to external shocks, including that of maintaining a market-determined exchange rate, keeping a comfortable level of reserves, and keeping the country’s external debt manageable.

Furthermore, the BSP has long recognized the role of digital platforms in achieving greater efficiency and financial inclusion. The acceleration of digital transformation will help bolster the path towards a more technologically advanced and more inclusive Philippine economy in the post-pandemic era.  

Last year, the BSP launched the Digital Payments Transformation Roadmap for 2020 - 2023. With this roadmap, we aim to transform the country into a cash-light society through digitalization of payments and increasing the number of Filipinos with access to financial services. At the same time, we intend to make available more innovative and responsive digital financial products and services. Recent data suggest increased utilization of electronic platforms.  

In the first seven months of 2021, the value of transactions done through InstaPay expanded by more than 180 percent and through PesoNet by more than 80 percent. In terms of volume, the transactions via InstaPay and PesoNet nearly doubled relative to the previous year. The diligent use of digital payments could also help reduce the need for mobility and prevent health risks from face-to-face and over-the-counter (OTC) financial transactions.

Last June, the BSP issued the Open Finance Framework, a key enabler for digital transformation and financial inclusion, by promoting consent-driven data portability, interoperability, and collaborative partnerships between financial institutions and fintech players. 

Given all our efforts toward digitalization, we envision a Philippines where everyone is empowered with financial accounts and will be able to make use of a wide range of financial transactions digitally. 

Mr. Chair and members of the Committee, allow me to end with the key messages of this presentation. 

This presentation provides evidence that the country’s economic fundamentals have remained generally firm amid the adverse impact of the Covid-19 pandemic. 

There is optimism over the macroeconomic prospects given acceleration in COVID inoculation in the country, continued policy support, and improved global economic outlook.

At the same time, the effective management of risks through safe re-opening of businesses, expansion of country’s health system, and targeted implementation of quarantine restrictions as necessary could help the economy pave the path towards a safe and strong recovery.

We must keep this momentum going and stay on guard against emerging risks.

Coursing the road to recovery requires consistent, purposeful and coordinated efforts. 

The National Government’s fiscal and public health measures remain crucial in sustaining the recovery. Its commitment to pursue the infrastructure program and key structural reforms will also help address the long-term scarring effects of the pandemic. 

The BSP remains one with the National Government in supporting the Philippine economy towards economic recovery. The BSP re-affirms its commitment to sustaining monetary policy support until the recovery fully gets underway.  

We will remain watchful of domestic and global developments and stand ready to adjust our policy settings as needed to ensure price and financial stability conducive to a sustainable economic recovery.

Together, let us continue to fuel the country’s momentum towards a safer, stronger, and more inclusive Philippine economy.

That ends my presentation. Thank you for your attention.​

Title: Paving the Way to Recovery and New Post-COVID-19 Economy
Occasion: Virtual Philippine Economic Briefing in Japan (2021)
Speaker: BSP Governor Benjamin E. Diokno
Transcription:
​

Ambassador Jose C. Laurel, fellow officials and colleagues from the economic cluster of the Philippine government, officers and staff of SMBC Group, guests, ladies and gentlemen, good afternoon. 

I thank our Japanese audience for being here and for the interest on the Philippine economy.   

The covid-19 pandemic has brought unprecedented challenges across the world. The Philippines was not spared, as the economy contracted last year after 21 consecutive years of growth.

But a year and a half since the onset of the health crisis, we have learned to better deal with its challenges.  

To expound on this, I will cover three things in my speech:

• First, macroeconomic, monetary, and external accounts updates.

• Second, banking sector developments. 

• And third, our vision of a Post-COVID 19 Economy. 


On macroeconomic, monetary, and external accounts updates…

The Philippine economy is recovering. It rebounded strongly in the second quarter, with a growth of 11.8 percent, thus ending the pandemic-driven recession.

Inflation averaged 4.4 percent for the first seven months of this year. 

The Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP) expects inflation to average slightly above the upper end of the 2.0- to 4.0-percent target band this year due to supply issues, such as rising global oil prices and constraints in meat importation.

Then, we see inflation easing toward the midpoint of the target range by next year and 2023 amid government measures to improve supply of meat and other food items. 

Our inflation projections are in line with expectations of relevant observers. 

Given manageable inflation, and in support of economic recovery, BSP kept policy rates steady during the policy meeting last August 12. We will again review the policy settings on September 23. 

The policy rate stands at a record low of 2.0 percent after BSP did a series of policy rate cuts last year.  

We also cut the reserve requirement and did other actions to ensure ample liquidity in the financial system, which in turn buoyed market confidence during a critical time.  

These include purchases of government securities in the secondary market, as well as advance remittance of dividends and extension of short-term financing to the National Government.

In total, the BSP has so far infused PHP2.2 trillion (or US$44 billion) to the financial system, equivalent to 12.5 percent of the country’s GDP. 

Recovery is at its nascent phase. We are mindful that unwinding policy support prematurely will be costly. 

As such, as the inflation outlook allows, BSP commits to keeping monetary policy accommodative until we see hard evidence of full recovery. 

The country’s external accounts remain robust. 

Gross international reserves (GIR) are hefty at US$107.2 billion as of end-July this year. 

This is 7.7 times the country’s short-term external debt and provides 12.2 months’ worth of import cover, which is above the internationally accepted threshold of 3 months. 

GIR is supported in part by overseas workers’ remittances, which have been resilient throughout the pandemic.  

Overseas Filipino remittances in 2020 reached USD30 billion, the same as in 2019, defying forecasts that it will fall by double-digit rates.

Remittances grew by 6.4 percent in the first semester and are expected to grow by 4.0 percent for the full year 2021. 

Japan is a steady source of remittances, accounting for over 5.0 percent of total last year. 

Receipts from business process outsourcing (BPO) industry is another steady source of foreign exchange. In 2020, BPO receipts remained resilient, declining only by 1.3 percent and it is projected to increase by 5.0 percent this year. 

Foreign direct investments (FDIs) have risen, reflecting improving investor confidence. 

Japan has been a vital source of FDIs, more so during this pandemic. 

Bucking trends, Japan’s FDIs to the Philippines more than doubled last year to nearly US$700 million. 

Moving forward, we expect FDIs to rise further given latest developments, such as enactment of the Corporate Recovery and Tax Incentives for Enterprises (CREATE) law. 

As the Finance Secretary will expound later, this law improves the competitiveness of the country’s corporate tax and fiscal incentives regime. 

Driven by the sources of FX, plus the rise in imports mostly of capital goods amid the recovery process, the overall balance of payments (BOP) posted a small deficit in the first semester. 

We expect BOP to end this year with a surplus of US$7.1 billion, equivalent to 1.8 percent of GDP.  

Healthy external accounts will continue to support the exchange rate. 

The peso, together with other emerging market currencies, depreciated lately due to strengthening of the US dollar amid anticipation of policy normalization by the US Fed. 

But the peso volatility has been manageable. Moving forward, the peso will be supported by our hefty GIR, exports revenues, remittances, FDIs, and BPO receipts. 

The country’s external accounts are also supported by enabling policies. 

BSP further liberalized FX rules last month. We now allow electronic submission of documents, use of e-signatures, and funding of peso deposit accounts of non-residents with peso receipts from loans and investments. 

We also lifted the prior approval requirement for derivatives transactions of non-bank government entities. 

Constant enhancement of FX rules supports overall efforts toward capital market development. 

BSP’s bilateral arrangements also promotes strong external payments position of the Philippines. 

The BSP has signed a Bilateral Swap Arrangement and a Cross Border Liquidity Arrangement with the Bank of Japan. 

The BSP is keen on pursuing other areas of cooperation with Japan such as the  establishment of a Philippine Peso-Japanese Yen Direct Settlement Framework. 

Moving on to banking sector developments… 

Philippine banks have shown resilience to the COVID-19 crisis, benefiting from risk-management and other regulatory reforms of the past two decades.  

Banks have ample buffers against shocks. Capital adequacy ratio (CAR) is at 17.4 percent, well above the 8.0 percent prescribed by the Bank for International Settlements (BIS) and the BSP’s 10.0 percent minimum requirement. 

Exposure to bad debts remains manageable. Average non-performing loans (NPL) ratio stood at 4.0 percent as of end-June this year, much  lower than the double-digit figures in the aftermath of the Asian financial crisis.  

Banking sector stability throughout the pandemic was also aided in part by BSP’s regulatory relief measures for banks and their customers. 

The time-bound relief measures will be in place until such time that the new Financial Institutions Strategic Transfer (FIST) Act, signed earlier this year, becomes fully operational. 

Under this new law,  financial institutions may dispose their non-performing assets through FIST corporations, thereby maintaining soundness of their asset quality.  

BSP’s support measures, together with government’s pandemic response, have supported confidence and optimism in the banking industry. 

The latest Banking Sector Outlook Survey showed that banks are optimistic for the next two years, expecting double-digit increase in assets, net income, investments, deposits, and loans. 

Now let me talk about our vision of a “Post-COVID-19 Economy.” 

The Philippines aims not only to regain what was lost from the COVID crisis. We want the economy to be stronger, more technologically advanced, more sustainable, and more inclusive than ever before. 

BSP is actively contributing to this vision. 

One way we are doing so is through financial digitalization. 

BSP has launched the Digital Payments Transformation Roadmap, under which we aim to achieve two major objectives by 2023: 

• At least half of financial transactions in the country are done digitally; and 

• At least 70 percent of Filipino adults have financial accounts.  

But with the pandemic as the catalyst, we expect to achieve both goals sooner than planned.   

Financial digitalization accelerates income growth and makes affordable financial products and services accessible to more people. 

To achieve the twin goals of financial digitalization, BSP has several initiatives. 

We have issued the “Open Finance Framework,” which allows consent-driven use of customers’ information for the creation of innovative financial products and services catering to their needs. 

We have also released regulatory guidelines for digital banks, thus providing an enabling environment for growth of digital banking. 

So far, BSP has approved license applications of five purely digital banks. 

We are confident of hitting our goals under the Digital Payments Transformation Roadmap.  

The volume of electronic payments has grown by leaps and bounds. Also, since the onset of the pandemic had limited mobility, over 4 million electronic financial accounts have been created. 

One positive, unintended consequence of the lockdown, and the associated mobility restrictions caused by the pandemic is that people have embraced the convenience of digital payments. 

As we build our digital finance ecosystem, the Philippines hopes to attract foreign investments, which may bring advanced technologies and technical expertise. 

Foreign investors are welcome to do business in the Philippines, to take advantage of untapped potentials in the financial services space and, in doing so, be our partners in achieving our economic growth and financial inclusion objectives. 

Another way BSP is pursuing the post-COVID-19 economy is through work on sustainable finance…

As the world endeavors to end the pandemic and move on to the “new normal,”  mankind is obligated to ensure this does not mean reverting to ways that harm the environment. 

BSP is supporting legislation that will count loans to green projects as part of banks’ compliance with the mandatory lending for agriculture. 

We have also issued the Sustainable Finance Framework, under which banks are encouraged to design instruments that will help mobilize funds for green or sustainable projects. 

Moving forward, we will issue more regulations and use moral suasion to push sustainable finance. 

We believe in the capacity of capital markets to fund projects geared toward reducing carbon emissions, such as in the agriculture, wastes, industry, transport, and energy sectors.

Foreign banks can underwrite green, social, and sustainability bonds, or develop innovative sustainable finance instruments. They can also pool funds to finance projects, such as in renewable energy, low carbon transport, sustainable water management, and sustainable waste management. 

Speaking of ESG-related bonds, BSP, in collaboration with other government agencies, is pursuing initiatives, as shown in this slide,  that will help deepen the domestic capital market and broaden investor access to securities markets. 

The  much-improved supply of COVID-19 vaccines from multiple sources and quickened vaccination rollout are key to sustained economic recovery.  

Highest number of jabs of 710,482 in a day was recorded last August 5. In the month of August, average daily jabs reached 426,653. 

These performances suggest that the administrative machinery needed for a massive vaccination drive exists. More than 100 million doses of vaccines are expected to arrive on or before the end of the year.  

At this rate, the Philippines’ goal to reach “population protection”  by the end of the year appears doable. 

In closing, I would like to highlight three take-aways:

• First, the Philippines’ economic fundamentals remain sound 

• Second,  BSP will keep its policy settings and regulatory relief measures supportive of the economy as needed; withdrawal of  policy measures will only be done once full recovery is underway. 

• Third,  the accelerated vaccination program, implementation of  economic recovery measures  and pursuit of further reforms will help address the potential  long-term scarring effects of the pandemic and smoothen the path to full recovery. 

Over the years, Japan has been a partner of the Philippines, serving as a major source of official development assistance, investments, and trade. 

As we work our way through the pandemic to a “post-COVID Economy” that is safer, stronger, more technologically advanced, and more inclusive, we will be pleased to continue having Japan—and Japanese investors like all of you—as our valuable partner. 

Thank you for your attention. ​

Title: The Philippines: Recovery and Beyond
Occasion: Nomura Fireside Chat Session
Speaker: BSP Governor Benjamin E. Diokno
Transcription:
​

A pleasant day to everyone. I thank Nomura for inviting me to update its investor clients and guests on the Philippine economy.  

Let me start by providing a glimpse of where the economy is right now, as the world continues to cope with the COVID-19 crisis.   

The Philippine economy is slowly recovering. 

In the second quarter of this year, the Philippines grew by 11.8 percent, finally ending the pandemic-induced recession. 

This was not solely due to base effects. 

Growth was broad-based, driven by household consumption, investments, consumption, and public construction. Manufacturing has been improving.  The purchasing manager’s index (PMI) was in an expansion mode from June to July. 

The PMI, however, declined in August  in view of the recent lockdown imposed to slow down the spread of the covid 19 delta variant.   

By the way, the fall in the PMI waws Asia-wide.  

Unemployment rate, which peaked 17.6 percent in April last year, dropped to 7.7 percent in June this year.  

On the monetary front, inflation has been slowing down, settling at 4.0 percent in July to bring the average for the first seven months of this year to 4.4 percent. 

Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas expects inflation to average slightly above the upper end of the 2.0- to 4.0-percent target band this year due to supply issues, such as rising global oil prices and constraints in meat importation.

Then, we see inflation easing toward the midpoint of the target range by next year and 2023 amid government measures to improve supply of meat and other food items. 

Our inflation projections are in line with expectations of relevant observers. 

Given manageable inflation, and in support of economic recovery, BSP kept policy rates steady during the policy meeting last August 12. 

External accounts remain strong with the Philippines’ usual sources of foreign exchange remaining resilient amid the pandemic.   

Overseas Filpino remittances in 2020 reached USD30 billion, the same as in 2019, defying forecasts that it will fall by double-digit rates.  

In the first half of this year, it grew by 6.4 percent to USD15 billion. 

In 2020, business process outsourcing (BPO) receipts declined by only 1.3 percent to USD22.4 billion. 

In the first quarter of this year, BPO revenues grew 3.0 percent to USD5.5 billion.  

Philippine exports and imports have rebounded alongside the recovery of its trading partners.  

In the first half of the year, imports rose by 29.8 percent, largely due to higher demand for imported raw materials and intermediate goods. 

Exports jumped by 20.9 percent in the same period amid recovery in global demand. 

Actual investments are also rising, which bodes well for job creation.  

For the first five months of the year, foreign direct investments (FDIs) jumped by almost 38 percent.   

The overall balance of payments (BOP) posted a small deficit in the first semester, driven mostly by the rise in imports mostly of capital goods amid the recovery process.  

Nonetheless, we expect BOP to end this year with a surplus of USD7.1 billion, equivalent to 1.8 percent of GDP. 

External liquidity buffers continue to be more than adequate.

The gross international reserves (GIR) remains hefty amounting to about USD107 billion as of end-July this year, providing more than one year worth of import cover.  

At US$107 billion, the GIR exceeds the Philippines total external debt which stood at USD97 billion dollars as of end March 2021.

The peso is relatively stable. It has depreciated by 3.5 percent against the US dollar since the start of the year. But such depreciation is broadly in line with the behavior of other emerging market currencies. 

Our hefty gross international reserves, the steady inflows from remittances, BPOs, and recovery of exports and FDIs will support the peso. 

The market determined exchange rate policy has been our first line of defense against external shocks.   

International debt market continues to warmly receive Philippine government bonds.  

Credit default swap (CDS) spread for the Philippines’ 5-year bonds remain lower than our rating peers. 

Moving on the banking sector - the banking system is stable and resilient, with manageable asset quality and ample capitalization. It benefitted from regulatory reforms of the past two decades. 

Non-performing loans (NPL) ratio of universal and commercial banks, rose to 4.0 percent as of end-June this year, up from the pre-pandemic level of 1.6 percent.

Yet, the latest NPL number is still far from the levels seen right after the Asian financial crisis. 

Capital adequacy ratio (CAR) of UKBs stood at 16.8 percent on solo basis and 17.4 percent on consolidated basis as of end-March this year. 

These numbers are better than the 15.3 and 15.8 percent, respectively, recorded in the same period last year, and much higher that the 10 percent threshold set by BSP and 8 percent level prescribed by the Bank for International Settlements. 

All these developments suggest that the Philippine economic recovery is underway. Yet, we recognize that the road to full recovery is a bumpy one. 

Last month, the government imposed another strict lockdown in Metro Manila and other areas to contain the spread of the more contagious COVID Delta variant.   

Consequently, the government had to bring down its economic growth projection for this year to a range of 4 to 5 percent, from 6 to 7 percent previously.  

But for the succeeding years, robust growth projections were retained at 7 to 9 percent for 2022, and 6.0 to 7.0 percent for 2023 and 2024.  

This means that while challenges remain significant over the near term, our medium- to long-term growth prospects remain bright owing to its sound economic fundamentals and the government’s steadfast commitment to structural reforms. 

The much-improved supply of COVID-19 vaccines from multiple sources and quickened vaccination rollout are key to accelerate economic recovery. 

Highest number of jabs of 710,482 in a day was recorded last August 5. In the month of August, average daily jabs reached 426,653.    

These performances suggest that the administrative machinery needed for a massive vaccination drive exists. More than 100 million doses of vaccines are expected to arrive on or before the end of the year.  

At this rate, the Philippines’ goal to reach “population protection”  by the end of the year appears doable. . 

The accelerated inoculation drive will help boost business sentiments as well as consumer sentiments and sustain the momentum for investments, job recovery, and overall economic growth. 

Now allow me to share other official macroeconomic assumptions for the Philippines.  

Inflation will remain manageable, thus provide an enabling environment for investments and consumption. 

Latest estimates from the central bank show that full-year average for this year will settle at 4.1 percent. This is slightly above the 2.0 to 4.0 percent target range, driven by supply-side factors including rising global oil prices. 

For next year and in 2023, inflation is seen to ease to 3.1 percent.    

Exports will rise by 8.0 percent this year and 6.0 percent next year.  

Imports will grow by 12.0 percent this year and 10.0 percent next year.  

Remittances will grow by 4.0 percent this year and next.  

GIR will rise further to USD115 billion by the end of this year and USD117 billion next year.

The banking sector will remain stable, thus able to support economic recovery and growth through financial intermediation.  

The new Financial Strategic Transfer (FIST) will provide additional support for banks in managing soured debts. 

Based on our baseline projections for the short term, the average NPL ratio of UKBs will stay within single digit levels. 

Moving on, I would like to touch on COVID response measures, which have helped fuel the economic recovery process.  

In the Philippines, there is a whole-of-government approach to winning the COVID-19 battle. On the economic front, significant support has come from both the fiscal and the monetary sides.  

On the fiscal side, the National Government adjusted its budget deficit program to accommodate the huge cost of response measures. 

From the pre-pandemic level of 3.0 percent of GDP, the budget deficit rose to 7.6 percent last year and is programmed to reach 9.3 percent this year.

The national government’s outstanding debt stood at 60.4 percent of GDP as of end-June this year, which remains manageable. 

As shown in this graph, general government debt, as percent of GDP, is several percentage points lower than national government debt. 

As of  end-September 2020  shows general government debt stood at 45.1 percent of GDP.   

Throughout the COVID-19 crisis, fiscal authorities have endeavored to strike an appropriate balance between recovery needs and fiscal prudence, with the priority given to health, social, and infrastructure spending.

On the monetary side, the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP) has done quite a lot. We cut the policy rate to its historic low of 2.0 percent, following a series of rate cuts last year.  

The reserve requirement is now down to 12 percent following the 200-bp cut last year.   

We continue to buy government securities in the secondary market to ensure ample liquidity in the system. However, the volume of our purchases, has declined from last year’s, given much improved liquidity conditions.  

The BSP has also extended bridge financing to the National Government to boost its resources for COVID response. After previous ones were settled, the latest outstanding amount stands at PHP540 billion (about USD10.8 billion).  

This lifeline support is short-term—as allowed under the BSP’s charter during times of crisis. This will not cause permanent increase in the monetary base and will not be a regular source of funding for the government.  

In total, the BSP has infused over PHP2.2 trillion (or USD44 billion) in liquidity to support the economy, equivalent to 12 percent of GDP. 

The liquidity enhancement measures have helped buoy market confidence. 

Meantime, besides the liquidity enhancing measures, the central bank has also implemented a wide range of time-bound regulatory relief measures. These are meant to help banks cushion the impact of the pandemic so they can service their crisis-hit customers as well.  

For instance, we have counted loans to micro, small, and medium enterprises (MSMEs) as part of compliance to the reserve requirement. 

We have assigned zero risk weight to loans extended to MSMEs that carry guarantee from select state-owned institutions and reduced to 50 percent the risk weight of other MSME loans.  

We have also allowed temporary exclusion from “past-due” and “non-performing classification” of loans granted to crisis-hit customers and that have been covered by grace periods or restructuring.  

Subject to BSP approval, we have allowed banks to stagger the booking of allowance for credit losses for a maximum period of five years. 

Moving forward, the BSP’s actions and policy thrusts will continue to be anchored on its core mandates of promoting price and financial stability.  

Toward this end, the BSP will continue to pursue appropriate policy actions responsive to the needs of the time.  

On monetary policy: the BSP will remain vigilant over the current inflation dynamics to ensure that the monetary policy stance continues to support economic recovery to the extent that the inflation outlook would allow. 

It will carefully scan the operating environment with a forward-looking perspective to move in a pre-emptive fashion to address any risks to our price stability mandate. 

On the financial sector: the BSP will intensify its monitoring and surveillance over its supervised institutions to ensure that they remain responsive to emerging risks and to promote the continued soundness, stability, resilience and inclusivity of the banking system.

Third, on the external sector: the BSP will remain supportive of policies that will help strengthen the economy’s resilience to external shocks, including that of maintaining a market-determined exchange rate, keeping a comfortable level of reserves, and keeping the country’s external debt manageable. 

Furthermore, the BSP has long recognized the role of digital platforms in achieving greater efficiency and financial inclusion. 

The acceleration of digital transformation will help bolster the path towards a more technologically advanced and more inclusive Philippine economy in the post-pandemic era. 

Last year, the BSP launched the Digital Payments Transformation Roadmap for 2020 - 2023. With this roadmap, we aim to transform the country into a cash-light society through digitalization of payments and increasing the number of Filipinos with access to financial services. At the same time, we intend to make available more innovative and responsive digital financial products and services. 

Specifically, under our Digital Payments Transformation Roadmap to 2023, we want at least half of financial transactions done digitally and at least 70 percent of Filipino adults with financial accounts.   

But with the pandemic as the catalyst, we expect to achieve both goals sooner than planned.  

Recent data suggest increased utilization of electronic platforms. In the first seven months of 2021, the value of transactions done through InstaPay expanded by more than 180 percent and through PesoNet by more than 80 percent. In terms of volume, the transactions via InstaPay and PesoNet nearly doubled relative to the previous year.

One positive, unintended consequence of the lockdown, and the associated mobility restrictions caused by the pandemic is that people have embraced the convenience of digital payments.

The BSP is also promoting digital banking. We have issued the Open Finance Framework, which allows consent-driven use of customer information for the creation of various financial products and services that cater to their needs.  

We also released the regulatory guidelines for the operation of digital banks last December. Since then, the BSP has approved license applications of 5 purely digital banks.  

Given all our efforts toward digitalization, we envision a Philippines where everyone is empowered with financial accounts and will be able to make use of a wide range of financial transactions digitally.

I would like to highlight three take-aways from this presentation 

First, the Philippines’ economic fundamentals remain sound; inflation is manageable, our external payments is robust and the banking system remains resilient and stable 

Second, accelerated vaccination,  effective risk management, implementation of economic support  measures, and further structural  reforms  will help underpin economic recovery  and bolster medium-term growth prospects 

Third,  the BSP will keep its policy settings and regulatory relief measures supportive of the economy as needed

In closing, let me share this quote that describes the current state of mind of the Philippines’ economic leadership: 

“The average is only consumed with today, but the champion is obsessed with tomorrow before it arrives…”  

Indeed, the Economic team is bent not only on regaining over the short term what was lost from the crisis.

We are keen on building a post-COVID-19 economy that is safer,  stronger, more technologically advanced, and more inclusive. 

We will be pleased to continue having investors like all of you—as our valuable partner, as we forge a better future for the Filipino people. 

Thank you. ​

Title: Keynote Address of BSP Governor Benjamin E. Diokno during the Makati Business Club's Webinar Series on Good Governance
Occasion: Makati Business Club's Manila Webinar Series on Good Governance
Speaker: BSP Governor Benjamin E. Diokno
Transcription:
​

On behalf of the Anti-Money Laundering Council (AMLC) and its Secretariat, it is my pleasure to join today’s virtual forum, “Out of the Grey List: Meeting Global Standards Against Financial Crime and Corruption Prevention,” hosted by the Makati Business Club, Center for International Private Enterprise, and K2 Integrity.

As you may all know, the AMLC is the Philippines’ Financial Intelligence Unit, mandated to implement the Anti-Money Laundering Act of 2001, as amended; the Terrorism Financing Prevention and Suppression Act of 2012; and the Anti-Terrorism Act of 2020. 

The AMLC is tasked to protect and preserve the integrity and confidentiality of bank accounts and to ensure that the Philippines will not be used as a site for the money laundering of proceeds of any unlawful activity and for terrorism financing.

Money laundering, in particular, is defined as a crime, where the proceeds of an unlawful activity are transacted, thereby making the proceeds appear to have originated from legitimate sources.: 

It only occurs after a predicate crime has been committed. And among these predicate crimes are those related to corruption, specifically:​

• Violations against the Anti-Graft and Corrupt Practices Act;

• Plunder;

• Bribery and corruption of public officers; and

• Malversation of public funds and property.

Although the AMLC may already scrutinize suspicious activities prior to the determination of a predicate crime, investigations on predicate crimes are primarily handled by law enforcement agencies. 

And in the case of those related to corruption, the Office of the Ombudsman also steps in as required by their mandate. 

Investigations on money laundering, on the other hand, are primarily handled by the AMLC as the country’s Financial Intelligence Unit.

Unlike most Financial Intelligence Units of other countries, the Philippines’ AMLC is a hybrid one. Not only does the AMLC receive and analyze covered and suspicious transaction reports, it also investigates money laundering and terrorism financing and causes the filing of forfeiture proceedings and money laundering and terrorism financing cases.

As the threat of money laundering and terrorism financing are evolving, there is a need to adequately manage and monitor the level and direction of these risks in coordination with various stakeholders and to further strengthen this hybrid-type of organizational structure. 

As such, the AMLC then underwent a two-phase reorganization in 2017 and 2018. This expands the financial intelligence analysis functions to address specific areas as mirrored in the Financial Action Task Force (FATF) recommendations, such as the Compliance and Supervision Group and other specialized units. One of the AMLC’s investigation units is, in fact, dedicated to anti-corruption.

As a result of this renewed structure, the AMLC now works as a fully functional Financial Intelligence Unit; a reliable partner in law enforcement, prosecution, and asset forfeiture; and an efficient supervisor.

Now, let me share some highlights of the AMLC’s efforts and initiatives this year in undertaking its anti-money laundering and counter-terrorism financing (AML/CTF) operations. 

The AMLC requires and receives covered and suspicious transaction reports (STRs) from covered persons. The AMLC also collects, evaluates, and analyzes financial information, regarding potential money laundering and terrorism financing; and disseminates financial intelligence reports to law enforcement agencies, foreign financial intelligence units, and other AMLC units to support and assist investigations. 

Using its database and other sources of information, the AMLC has released the following risk assessments, strategic studies, and typologies in 2021 for the guidance of government and law enforcement agencies; and covered persons:

1. Terrorism and Terrorism Financing Risk Assessment, which is an update of the Second National Risk Assessment, particularly on the understanding and assessment of terrorism and terrorism financing risks in the country; 

2. Foreign Terrorist Fighters Study using Suspicious Transaction Reports; 

3. Money Service Business [MSB]: 2021 Money Laundering and Terrorism Financing Sector Risk Assessment, which indicates how certain services and products of MSBs are exploited by criminals to facilitate and expand illegal activities; 

4. Real Estate Sector: A Money Laundering/Terrorism Financing/Proliferation Financing Assessment, which examines the potential criminal threat environment and vulnerabilities associated with the real estate sector; 

5. An Assessment of the Philippines’ Exposure to External and Internal Threats Based on Suspicious Transaction Reports for 2018 to 2020, which looks into the country’s risk and exposure to money laundering, terrorism financing, and different predicate offenses. 

6. An Analysis of Suspicious Transaction Reports with Possible Links to Tax Crimes, which is a study on the potential exposure of the Philippines to tax crimes prior to the inclusion of tax evasion as a predicate offense to money laundering by focusing on selected suspicious transaction reports (STRs); and 

7. Suspicious Transaction Report Quality Review: 2017 to 2020 Data Discovery that covers 2.4 million STRs, which the AMLC received from 2017 to 2020 from covered persons and that aims to provide a trend analysis for the covered periods; assess the technical compliance and investigative value of the STRs; and identify the reporting gaps and challenges of covered persons to provide guidance on how to improve the quality of STRs. 

Most of these are available in the AMLC’s website for the guidance of our stakeholders. 

From January 1 to June 30, 2021, the AMLC has filed 63 cases, varying from money laundering and terrorism financing cases; civil forfeiture cases; and even administrative cases.

Through these cases, the AMLC has deprived money launderers and other criminals of over PhP3.3 billion and various assets, including 121 hectares of real properties that were subject of freeze orders related to terrorism and terrorism financing and a five (5)-hectare land from two (2) United Nations Security Council Resolution-designated individuals frozen in 2019. 

In a Council-issued Resolution in March 2021, real property owned by a certain alleged associate of a designated-terrorist group was also subject of a freeze order. 

Further, this year, there has been a money laundering case conviction predicated on the violation of the E-Commerce Act in relation to cybercrime.

As an efficient supervisor, the AMLC adopts necessary policies, procedures, and guidance, using its assessment of money laundering and terrorism financing trends and standards. 

The AMLC ensures compliance of covered persons with AML/CTF laws and their corresponding rules and regulations by conducting regular and targeted onsite examinations and offsite supervision of covered persons.

So far in 2021, the AMLC has issued several AML/CTF regulations to strengthen the Philippines’ AML/CTF supervisory framework. Among these are: 

1. 2021 AMLC Registration and Reporting Guidelines;

2. Amendments to Certain Provisions of the 2018 Implementing Rules and Regulations of Republic Act No. 9160, as amended;

3. 2021 Anti-Money Laundering/Counter-Terrorism Financing Guidelines for Designated Non-Financial Businesses and Professions;

4. Amendments to Certain Provisions of AMLC Regulatory Issuance No. 4, Series of 2020;

5. 2021 Sanctions Guidelines: Targeted Financial Sanctions Related to Terrorism, Terrorism Financing, and Proliferation Financing [of Weapons of Mass Destruction];

6. Guidance for De-Listing and Unfreezing Procedures;

7. Notice of AMLC No. TF-42, Series of 2021, directing the issuance of sanctions freeze order to take effect immediately against the National Democratic Front, also known as the National Democratic Front of the Philippines, pursuant to its designation as terrorist by the Anti-Terrorism Council (ATC) Resolution No. 21 (2021);

8. Notice of AMLC Resolution No. TF-41, Series of 2021, directing the issuance of sanctions freeze order to take effect immediately against members of the Abu Sayyaf Group and other terrorist groups, pursuant to their designation as terrorist by ATC Resolution No. 20 (2021); 

9. AMLC Resolution TF No. 35, Series of 2021 on Anti-Terrorism Council Resolution No. 10, Series of 2020 on the Designation by Adoption of the Consolidated Lists under UNSC Resolutions 1267 (1999), 1989 (2011), 2253 (2015) and their Successor Resolution;

10. AMLC Resolution No. TF-39, Series of 2021 on sanctions freeze order against property or funds that are owned or controlled, directly or indirectly, including property or funds derived or generated therefrom, by the subject of domestic designations by the ATC under Resolution Nos. 16, Series of 2021; and

11. AMLC Resolution No. TF-40, Series of 2021 on sanctions freeze order against property or funds that are owned or controlled, directly or indirectly, including property or funds derived or generated therefrom, by the subject of domestic designations by the ATC under Resolution Nos. 17, Series of 2021.

The AMLC’s core functions are supported by the AMLC’s overarching support services, that, among others, ensure the country’s compliance with international AML/CTF standards. 

In 2018, the Philippines underwent its Third Mutual Evaluation, where the country was assessed on its levels of technical compliance with international AML/CTF standards; and effectiveness compliance of its existing AML/CTF mechanisms. It will be recalled that the country’s First and Second MEs only involved technical compliance.

With the passage of the Anti-Terrorism Act of 2020; the passage of Republic Act No. 11521, which further amends the Anti-Money Laundering Act of 2001; and the issuance of necessary implementing rules and regulations last year, the Philippines was able to address its technical deficiencies. 

Adopting compliant laws and regulations, however, is not sufficient.

The effectiveness assessment focuses on the extent to which the AML/CTF legal and institutional framework is producing the expected results over a sustained period. 

Thus, the country has been identified as a “jurisdiction under increased monitoring” or, in other words, placed in the “grey list” generally because the Philippines would need time to implement its new AML/CTF laws, regulations, and other relevant issuances to demonstrate their effectiveness.

Grey-listed jurisdictions, such as the Philippines, must swiftly resolve all identified deficiencies within a timeframe and must report its progress to the FATF frequently, thus, the term “increased monitoring.”

Particularly, the Philippines must address 18 International Co-operation Review Group (ICRG) action plan items within the timelines provided by the FATF. 

It must be emphasized that all AML/CTF players, such as law enforcement and government agencies; and covered persons, are required to demonstrate effectiveness to address these 18 action plan items, whichever applicable. 

A significant challenge then is ensuring accountability among government agencies on the action plan items that they need to deliver. 

We are grateful that we already have the National AML/CFT Coordinating Committee or the NACC in place as early as 2018 when it was created pursuant to Executive Order No. 68.

Said NACC is chaired by the Executive Secretary and is vice-chaired by yours truly, the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas Governor and AMLC Chairman. The Executive Secretary can solicit the commitment of government agencies concerned, which is currently being done as we speak.

Thus, the AMLC and the rest of the Philippines is continuously working toward the country’s removal from the FATF ICRG grey list. 

Despite the constant adversity brought about by the COVID-19 pandemic and other obstacles, we ultimately pursue a more robust regime not only against financial crime but against other lawlessness related to it. 

Thank you very much for your attention, and I wish all of you a productive and empowering exchange ahead.

Title: BSP Governor Benjamin E. Diokno Speech for the Financial Literacy Summit
Speaker: BSP Governor Benjamin E. Diokno
Transcription:
​

Good morning to all participants and guests of the Financial Literacy Summit 2021. Congratulations to the officers of The Global Filipino Investors (TGFI) for successfully organizing this event online.

Indeed, the pandemic has given all of us a “wake-up call" and has prompted us to prioritize the essential. This Includes our financial lives.  

However, financial literacy remains a challenge in the Philippines. Based on our 2019 Financial Inclusion Survey (FIS), only half (55%) of Filipino adults know the effect of inflation on their purchasing power; and a third (33%) could not figure out the impact of compounding interest rates on the value of their bank deposits, or its implications on their borrowings. 

Without knowledge of the time value of money and other financial literacy concepts, Filipinos would be unable to make informed decisions when comparing financial products and selecting financial institutions that would best fit their needs. 

Low financial literacy could lead to neglect of one’s financial health, cause financial distress and impact negatively the life of one’s family. On the other hand, financially-literate persons have the farsightedness and capability to prepare financially for the future. 

Planning ahead; saving for emergencies and specific goals; managing debt prudently; and investing in productive endeavors – these are all crucial in securing one’s financial future.

Financially-literate persons tend to be more resilient and less vulnerable to financial distress when confronted with external shocks, like this COVID-19 crisis. 

Hence, the BSP intensified our financial education (fin-ed) programs, in partnership with like-minded institutions from the public and private sectors. We have institutionalized fin-ed partnerships covering a wide array of targeted audiences. 

These include civil servants; the armed forces; the police; and firefighters. We are also working with partners to implement financial education programs for overseas Filipino workers; and underbanked sectors like micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs); fisherfolk and farmers; and beneficiaries of government cash transfer programs. 

One of the biggest gains In our program Is our partnership with the Department of Education. Last June 3, 2021, the DepEd has Issued a Financial Education Policy that mandates the intensified integration of financial literacy lessons in the K to 12 curriculum, spanning various subjects across all grade levels. 

It also covers the capacity building of teachers, ensuring that they themselves subscribe to prudent personal financial management to be more effective in teaching financial literacy. 

The Policy represents our hope that financial literacy becomes a core competency of every learner who goes through the basic education system; and eventually becomes a part of the next generation of political and business leaders. 

The BSP is also currently working with the Commission on Higher Education to embed personal finance classes in tertiary education. 

These initiatives, when taken together, are estimated to potentially reach millions of Filipinos in the country and abroad. Designed as sustainable, scalable, and measurable programs, these fin-ed initiatives intended to generate the multiplier effect to reach more people. 

The BSP’s ultimate aim is to level-up the financial literacy of our kababayans, so they can enjoy healthy financial lives, and benefit fully from an increasingly inclusive and digital financial system.

We may not see the transformational effects of our fin-ed programs overnight, but we are confident that the right seeds of financial literacy and awareness of its importance have been planted. 

I urge the Filipino public to stock up on financial knowledge and implement the financial skills that you will learn from this Summit. While we are in our most productive working years, let us take financial literacy to heart, in order to avoid the pitfalls of a burdensome retirement. 

Despite this time of economic, emotional, or psychosocial loss, let view this as an opportunity to adequately prepare for a better future. 

Together with fin-ed advocates and partners like TGFI, we can nurture these seeds and raise generations of financially-literate Filipinos confident to use a wide range of financial services; and capable of making prudent financial plans, building reserves, accumulating assets, managing debt, and exercising their rights and responsibilities as financial consumers. 

Mula po sa Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas, we wish everyone a very productive learning session. Maraming salamat, at magandang umaga muli sa ating lahat.

Title: BSP Governor Benjamin E. Diokno's Message for the Virtual Event on the BSP's Donation of 13 units of Multi-Currency Bill Counters wih Printers to the Bureau of Customs
Occasion: Virtual Event on the BSP's Donation of 13 units of Multi-Currency Bill Counters wih Printers to the Bureau of Customs
Speaker: BSP Governor Benjamin E. Diokno
Transcription:
​

Bureau of Customs Commissioner Retired General Rey Leonardo B. Guerrero, Anti-Money Laundering Council Executive Director Atty. Mel Georgie B. Racela, my colleagues from the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas and Anti-Money Laundering Council, and friends from the Bureau of Customs, ladies and gentlemen, good morning.

Today’s signing of the Memorandum of Agreement and Deed of Donation for the 13 units of multi-currency bill counters with printers from the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas marks another milestone in our joint efforts to ensure the effective implementation of the rules on  cross-border transfer of currencies. 

In 2005, the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas, Anti-Money Laundering Council and Bureau of Customs entered into an inter-agency Memorandum of Agreement Manila International Airport Authority, Philippine National Police, Bureau of Immigration, Air Transportation Office (now, Civil Aviation Authority of the Philippines), and Philippine Ports Authority. 

Its purpose was to protect and safeguard the integrity of the monetary system and to ensure that the country will not serve as a money laundering site for unlawful activities.
