Success on the public health front combined with carefully targeted fiscal support will help boost consumer and business sentiment and lead the economy to its sustainable growth path. 

Building confidence in the fundamental strength of the Philippine economy in an environment of uncertainty and volatility requires skillful handling of our policy levers. 

Moving forward, we anticipate the communication challenges related to the scaling back of the accommodative monetary policies, when necessary, as economic recovery gets underway. Monetary policy needs to be flexible to shifts in economic and market conditions.

As the BSP closely monitors any emerging risks to financial stability, various macroprudential measures and monitoring tools remain in place. We also look at external risk factors, including global economic growth and shifts in monetary policy in major economies, as we assess how they can impact domestic financial and growth conditions. 

More importantly, an integral part of the BSP’s policy agenda is making sure that the Philippines is able to get back on a balanced and sustainable growth path as soon as possible. 

In this regard, the BSP is working closely with the national government to advance the structural reform agenda, including transforming the financial landscape so that it is future-ready through digitalization and environmentally sustainable practices. 

Digital payments transformation has been helping us cope with the mobility restrictions put in place. It is a good thing that the country had been gradually embracing financial technology even before the pandemic hit. The rapid acceleration of digital transformation was in fact catalyzed by the COVID-19 pandemic.

In 2020, the volume of PESONet transfers surged to 15.3 million, up by 376 percent year-on-year. The value of PESONet transactions rose by 188 percent, year-on-year, to reach nearly 951.6 billion pesos—equivalent to about 5.3 percent of the country's GDP. 

In the same period, the number of payments made through InstaPay reached 86.7 million, up by 459 percent year-on-year. Said transactions were valued at 463.4 billion pesos, which was a 340-percent increase year-on-year. 

This amount of InstaPay transactions is equivalent to about 2.6 percent of GDP. 

The BSP took this opportunity to advance initiatives that would push digitalization in the financial industry even further. To this end, launched the Digital Payments Transformation Roadmap last year. 

The roadmap identifies two critical strategic objectives. The first objective, also my personal goal as BSP Governor—is that at least 50 percent of the country's total financial transactions be done digitally, and at least 70 percent of Filipino adults must have financial accounts.

The second objective involves the availability of more innovative digital financial products and services. These products and services, designed to be responsive to consumers' needs, will be enabled by a digital PhilSys ID and supported by a next-generation payment and settlement system that facilitates the real-time processing of financial transactions.

All these measures are integral parts of the strategy to become the central bank that understands the needs of the Filipino people and help them achieve their aspirations in life. 

While the ongoing crisis has subjected us to extraordinary challenges, it has also given us the opportunity to accelerate our efforts in bringing the BSP closer to the Filipino people. 

Through digitalization, we help create opportunities for them to improve their lives and participate in the formal sectors of the macroeconomy and the financial system. 

This way, we also promote financial inclusion, as digital payments help consumers confidently engage in economic activities with ease and security. 

In fact, in a report titled “Global Microscope 2020: The role of financial inclusion in the Covid-19 response” by the research arm of The Economist Group, the BSP was recognized for its initiatives to mitigate the adverse economic impact of the current global health emergency. 

In closing, I would like to highlight three strengths that we are pitting against the trio of shocks we are facing:

• First, we continue to maintain strong macroeconomic fundamentals. Together with carefully thought-out public health responses and an efficient rolling out of the vaccination program, these will carry the Philippine economy toward sustainable recovery. Monetary policy will remain accommodative until domestic demand and overall macroeconomic activity recovers, keeping in mind our price and financial stability objectives.

• Second, targeted fiscal support remains central to the COVID-19 response during the pandemic, and these are meant to minimize any permanent scars on the Philippine economy.

• And third, we reiterate our continued support for structural reforms that are aimed at raising the country’s competitiveness and helping transform the financial landscape so that it is future-ready through digitalization and green finance.

In this time of the pandemic, we realize more than ever before that the production of objective and comprehensive research and the promotion of the research culture in the BSP is important. 

Central banks have long benefitted from academic contributions to monetary policymaking and many other aspects of central bank practice. Academics and independent researchers, and the institutions that they come from, provide guidance in theoretical foundations as well as in the actual conduct of policy.

It is, therefore, a privilege and an inspiration for me to be among the distinguished researchers today who have conducted top-caliber and rigorous research on the impact of the pandemic amid these difficult times. 

A total of ten research papers would be presented over the next two days of our Research Fair. Just to mention a few, the paper titled ‘Stay at Home! Macroeconomic Effects of Pandemic-Induced Job Separation Shocks’ to be presented by Dr. Batu examines the importance of monetary policy in limiting the economic damage caused by labor market uncertainties related to the COVID-19 pandemic; their empirical evidence finds that there is indeed a link between uncertainty in the job separation rate and macroeconomic variables. 

Meanwhile, based on the empirical evaluation utilizing a Disaster Index rooted on four health and economic indicators by Drs. Mariano and Ozmucur in the paper ‘Fighting COVID-19: Patterns in International Data’, Singapore is among the best performers in the sample. 

Our very own Dr. Basilio of BRAc will be sharing with us the empirical results from an application of the S-I-R Pandemic Model in the case of the Philippines, where he is able to estimate the macroeconomic impact of this pandemic under various scenarios. 

I am just as eager to listen to the presentations from our institutional and junior researchers during the Research Café tomorrow, which we are conducting in collaboration with the SEACEN Centre. 

Our promising authors will be discussing equally relevant central banking issues such as the analysis of the Fintech model for PESONet, the impact of the digital payments system to financial inclusion indicators, and an empirical analysis of the evolution of market interest rates during the pandemic, to name some of them.

I am looking forward to the research paper presentations for this year’s Fair. In the words of Leonardo da Vinci: “Learning never exhausts the mind.” 

When you look at history, innovation comes from creating environments where ideas can connect, where there is an exchange of ideas.  It is, in fact, the father of Economics John Maynard Keynes who said: “Ideas shape the course of history.”

Thank you everyone and good morning.​

Title: Message of BSP Governor Benjamin E. Diokno for the 2021 Youth Summit
Occasion: 2021 BSP Youth Summit
Speaker: BSP Governor Benjamin E. Diokno
Transcription:
​

Sa libu-libong kabataang Pilipino na kasama natin ngayon sa BSP Youth Summit, magandang hapon sa inyong lahat!

Nagtuturo ako dati sa mga kagaya n'yong college students kaya masaya ako na kasama ko kayo ngayon. 

At dahil namimiss ko na rin ang pagiging professor, hayaan n'yong magkwento muna ako ng konting history ng ating financial system.

Hindi pa ipinapanganak ang karamihan sa inyo nang magsimula ang electronic banking sa Pilipinas noong 1980s. 

During that time, when we said e-banking, limitado ito sa mga automated teller machines, o ATM—na uso pa rin naman hanggang ngayon at nakikita sa mga shopping malls, convenience stores, bank branches, at kung saan-saan pa.  

Noong 2000s ay naging laganap ang paggamit ng Internet, na naging game-changer sa larangan ng financial technology. 

Ito ang naging daan upang mas nagging maayos ang serbisyo ng mga bangko at iba pang financial service providers. 

Sa tulong ng Internet banking facilities, nagkaroon ng 24/7 access ang mga kliyente ng bangko sa kanilang mga accounts. 

Maaari na silang mag-fund transfer, magbayad ng bills, mag-apply ng loan, at magsagawa ng iba pang banking at payment transactions gamit lamang ang kanilang personal computers, at ngayon, pati mobile phones.

Isang trivia para sa inyo—alam n'yo bang sa Pilipinas nag-umpisa ang paggamit ng mobile money services?

Ang konseptong ito ay unang ipinakilala ng isang telecommunications company noong 2001. 

Ito ay para sa mga Pilipinong malalayo na hindi naaabot ng serbisyo ng mga bangko. Gamit ang SMS technology, ang isang tao ay maaaring mag-fund transfer, magbayad ng bills, at bumili ng kanyang mga kailangan.

Noon pa man, interesado na ang Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas sa mga ganitong klase ng teknolohiya. 

Bilang texting capital of the world, nakita at ginamit natin ang mobile technology upang maabot ang mga kababayan nating nasa malayo at isali sila sa mga tinatawag nating “financially included.” 

Noong 2015, ipinakilala ng BSP ang National Retail Payment System Framework na siyang nagbigay-daan sa interoperable fund transfers sa pagitan ng iba't ibang bangko. 

Ito ang dahilan kung bakit nagkaroon tayo ng mga automated clearing houses—ang PESONet at ang InstaPay. 

Ang PESONet ay ginagamit sa pagta-transfer ng malalaking halaga ng pera habang ang InstaPay naman ay ginagamit sa real-time fund transfer ng mas mababang halaga ng pera. 

Sa panahon ng pandemya, malaki ang naitulong ng PESONet at InstaPay, lalo na’t kailangan nating manatili sa loob ng bahay upang maiwasan ang panganib ng COVID-19. 

Unti-unting natutuklasan ng mga Pilipino na posible palang gumawa ng mga financial transactions kahit hindi gumagamit ng aktwal o pisikal na pera. 

Safe na, convenient pa!

Dahil sa digital at online banking, nagawa nating i-monitor ang ating mga bank accounts at mag-transact sa kabila ng mga community quarantines at lockdowns. 

Sa pamamagitan ng electronic money, nakakapag-"add to cart" tayo. Nakaka-order tayo online ng pagkain, gamot, damit, at kung anu-ano pa, at nai-dedeliver pa right to our doorsteps. 

Gamit ang mga digital payment channels, naipamahagi rin ng pamahalaan ang ayuda nito sa ating mga kababayan.

Marahil ay marami sa inyo ang nakagawa na ng mga digital transaction at naranasan na rin ninyo kung gaano ito ka-convenient at ka-efficient. Sa ngayon, patuloy pa rin ang paggamit ng digital payments sa ating bansa. Nagiging bahagi na ito ng tinatawag nating “New Economy.”

May ilang mga layunin ang BSP sa ilalim ng “New Economy.” Kabilang dito ang mga sumusunod. Una, by 2023, at least 50 percent ng kabuuang financial transactions sa bansa ay digital na at, pangalawa, 70 percent ng Filipino adults ay magkaroon na ng financial accounts. 

Sinisiguro din ng BSP na ang payment systems ng bansa ay safe, efficient, reliable, at secure sa pamamagitan ng pag-issue ng mga polisiya at pagsuporta sa mga kinakailangan pang mga batas. 

Kasama rin dito ang aming ginagawa pagdating sa mga kailangan ng mga consumers sa larangan ng payment systems tulad ng Interoperable Bills Pay at Request to Pay facilities, at ang QR Ph.  

May ilan na siguro sa inyo ang nakasubok bumili ng mga bagay sa convenience store, botika, o shopping mall gamit ang QR code. 

Patuloy din tayong nakikipagtulungan sa Philippine Payments Management, Inc., upang mas maging reasonable ang mga fee sa paggamit ng mga digital payment systems at mas magkaroon ng mga innovative payments-related products and services.

Pagdating naman sa digital infrastructure, sinusuportahan ng BSP ang Philippine Statistics Authority sa pag-iimprenta ng ating National ID na tinatawag na Philippine Identification System o PhilSys. 

Umaasa tayo na sa tulong ng PhilSys, magiging mas madali ang pagbukas ng bank accounts at mababawasan ng requirements ang pag-apply sa trabaho. 

Mahalaga rin para sa amin sa BSP ang financial education kaya naman nariyan ang PisoLit, ang ating Facebook page na gagabay sa ating personal finances. 

Ipinapakilala rin namin ngayon ang kaibigan ni PisoLit na si Ekolit na syang tutulong sa inyong mas maintindihan ang mga kumplikadong economic concepts.

Sina PisoLit at Ekolit ay nariyan upang tulungan tayong mas maintidihan ang epekto ng bawat economic at financial decision natin. Sana ay matulungan nila tayo sa pag-unlad ng ating mga pamilya, at maging ng ating bansa. 

I-follow nyo na lang ang kanilang mga social media account, pati na rin ng BSP.

Ang kinabukasan natin ay nasa inyong mga kamay. Let us maximize all the possibilities and opportunities of digitalization. 

Nakita natin kung gaano kabilis magbago ang teknolohiya. Kailangan nating makisabay o mas mauna pa para hindi tayo mahuli sa takbo ng mundo.  May kasabihan nga: “daig ng maagap ang masipag.” Kaya natin maging pareho.

Sa loob ng ilang taon, kayo na ang mamamahala sa ating ekonomiya at sa ating bansa. Mag-aral kayong mabuti. Magmasid, mag-eksperimento, at matutong hamunin ang mga nakagisnan kung kinakailangan. 

At sa pakikibahagi at paglahok ninyo sa Youth Summit na ito, punong-puno ng pag-asa ang aking puso at diwa. 

Maraming salamat sa organizers, sa mga teams na nag-submit ng proposal, at sa inyong lahat na narito ngayon.

The challenge is on: ibangon natin ang ekonomiya, i-digital mo na! ​

Title: BSP’s Monetary Policies amid the Pandemic and Vision Beyond COVID-19: Journey through Digitalization and Financial Inclusion
Occasion: Joint Foreign Chambers Economic Briefing
Speaker: BSP Governor Benjamin E. Diokno
Transcription:
​

To the esteemed members of the diplomatic corps, and Board Directors and members of the organizing group, as well as to my other colleagues in government, and to all guests, a pleasant day.

Thank you for this opportunity to speak in this economic briefing for the foreign chambers of the Philippines.

As delivered to Joint European Foreign Chambers of Commerce

1. Advantage Austria

2. Australian - New Zealand Chamber of Commerce

3. British Chamber of Commerce of the Philippines

4. Dutch Chamber of Commerce in the Philippines

5. European Chamber of Commerce of the Philippines 

6. French Chamber of Commerce and Industry in the Philippines

7. German-Philippine Chamber of Commerce and Industry

8. Nordic Chamber of Commerce of the Philippines

9. Philippines-Swiss Business Council (PSBC)

10. Polish Investment and Trade Agency (PITA)

11. Spanish Chamber of Commerce in the Philippines (La Camara)

  

After the World Health Organization (WHO) declared COVID-19 as a pandemic about 1 year and 4 months ago, we can now say that the worst is behind us. 

The development and global distribution of vaccines within such a relatively short period since the start of the pandemic has proven once again the great crisis-coping ability of mankind. 

But with the uneven vaccine rollout globally, risks persist. 

After an estimated contraction of –3.3 percent in 2020, the IMF expects the global economy to grow at 6 percent in 2021 and then moderate to 4.4 percent in 2022.

The growth forecast for the global economy by other institutions are also shown in this slide.  

In the case of the Philippines, we have started to see green shoots as early as the third quarter of last year.  

Foreign direct investments (FDIs) surged by 45.1% percent for the first three months of the year. 

Further, investment pledges with the Board of Investments increased  by 65.6% percent in Q1 2021 and with the Philippine Economic Zone Authority (PEZA) by 53.9% percent in Q1 2021 from a year ago.  

As you know, investment approvals are a good leading indicator for actual investments, two or more years down the road.  

The passage of CREATE is expected to help attract more investments, both foreign and local, moving forward. 

Further, investment pledges with the Board of Investments increased  by 65.6% percent in Q1 2021 and with the Philippine Economic Zone Authority (PEZA) by 53.9% percent in Q1 2021 from a year ago.  

As you know, investment approvals are a good leading indicator for actual investments, two or more years down the road.  

The passage of CREATE is expected to help attract more investments, both foreign and local, moving forward. 

Further, investment pledges with the Board of Investments increased  by 65.6% percent in Q1 2021 and with the Philippine Economic Zone Authority (PEZA) by 53.9% percent in Q1 2021 from a year ago.  

As you know, investment approvals are a good leading indicator for actual investments, two or more years down the road.  

The passage of CREATE is expected to help attract more investments, both foreign and local, moving forward. 

Trade has picked up. In the first four months of this year, exports and imports expanded by 19 percent  and  21.9  percent,  respectively, from the same period last year.  

Meanwhile business confidence weakened for Q2 and Q3 2021, primarily due to concerns on the surge of COVID-19 cases in March and April this year. 

Country’s consumer sentiment, on the other hand, continued to improve citing expectations of more jobs and permanent employment, additional/higher income as government continues to ease mobility restrictions amidst accelerated vaccine rollout and the sustained implementation of measures to address the challenges from the pandemic.  

Remittances jumped by 4.8 percent  for the first four months of the year from a year ago.  

This highlights the sustained resilience of overseas Filipino remittances. Last year, they declined by a mere 0.8 percent versus the double-digit decline projected by private sector analysts.

The contraction in our gross domestic product (GDP) is on a decline, and according to the National Economic and Development Authority (NEDA), we an look forward to a positive GDP growth in the second quarter of this year despite the stricter quarantine restrictions due to the recent virus surge. 



Crisis Response from the BSP

Going into the crisis, the Philippines had ample fiscal and monetary buffers to deal with shocks—and these have been used extensively and wisely to aptly respond to the crisis. 

On the monetary front, manageable inflation allowed the BSP to cut the overnight borrowing rate by 200 basis points from 4.0 percent to a record low of 2.0 percent. 

The BSP also cut the reserve requirement further to 12 percent from 14 percent, thus freeing up more funds for lending to businesses and households. 

On top of these conventional monetary actions, the BSP implemented unprecedented measures to squarely respond to the crisis. 

We granted provisional advances worth Php540 billion (US$ 11.2 billion) to the National Government to augment its resources for COVID response. 

The BSP’s charter allows us to extend lifeline support to the government in times of crisis, with proper safeguards. 

This facility, which allows short-term financing, does not serve as a long-term source of funds for the government because they are temporary, time-bound, and capped. 

The BSP has also purchased government securities in the secondary market to lift market confidence. However, this activity has been scaled down, as the economy recovers.

In sum, the BSP has so far injected Php2.2 trillion (US$45 billion) into the financial system, equivalent to about 12 percent of GDP (as of June 10, 2021). 

Domestic liquidity has remained ample through the liquidity-easing measures of the BSP. 

Preliminary data show that domestic liquidity expanded by 4.7 percent year-on-year to about ₱14.3 trillion in May 2021. 

Bank lending growth, however,  remains tepid.  Preliminary data show that outstanding loans of universal and commercial banks fell by 4.0 percent in May following a 5.0-percent decline in April. 

The BSP also implemented various time-bound regulatory relief measures so banks and their customers can manage the impact of the crisis on their balance sheets and finances, and so there is more room for lending.  

Among these are grace periods for loan payments, capping of interest rates on credit card usage, staggered booking of loan losses, counting of loans to micro, small, and medium enterprises (MSMEs) as compliance to the reserve requirement, increase in the single borrower’s limit, and higher limit on real-estate loans. 

Meantime, on top of the time-bound regulations to help manage the impact of the pandemic, the BSP also continues the task of enhancing the regulatory environment for financial sector and overall economic development. 

One of our most recent initiatives is the enhancement of the Know Your Employees (KYE) guidelines to enhance operational risk management of banks.  

Another is the set of amendments to regulations on securities custodianship and securities registry operations, consistent with the aim of strengthening investor protection and developing the domestic capital market.  

We also recently launched the Rural Banking Strengthening Program (RBSP), under which an Interagency Working Group (IAWG) chaired by the BSP was created to help fulfill the objective of rural banking development. 

An initial package of proposed policies, programs and reforms for the rural banking industry will be submitted to the BSP’s Monetary Board by the end of 2021 


Exit Strategy

Meantime, given the enormous stimulus from the BSP, the question on unwinding always surfaces. 

We recognize that economic recovery is still in its nascent phase. As such, we will keep our monetary policy supportive of growth and allow previous monetary easing to work its way to the economy.

The BSP will withdraw monetary support only when there are indisputable signs of solid economic recovery amid a manageable inflation environment, as well as a sustained downtrend in community transmission of the virus. 

When it comes to exit strategy, the BSP recognizes the necessity of carefully balancing the need to ensure sustainability of recovery and the need to guard against risks to the BSP’s price and financial stability objectives. 

 


Build Back Better

For the Philippines, the theme that has resonated amid the pandemic is “Building Back Better.” 

This means we do not merely aim to recover from the crisis; instead, we want to have a “New Economy” that is stronger, more technologically advanced, and more inclusive than before the COVID crisis.

When talking about building back better, two things come to fore: digitalization and sustainability.


Digitalization

Last October, the BSP launched the “Digital Payments Transformation Roadmap.” 

With it, we aim to transform from a cash-heavy into a cash-light society where at least half of financial transactions are done digitally and where the presence of digital financial services increases the number of Filipinos with financial accounts to at least 70 percent of the adult population by 2023. 

The rationale of financial digitalization is simple: it makes financial transactions easier and faster, thereby accelerating income growth. It also makes financial products and services accessible to a greater number of people, thereby enhancing financial inclusion. 

Financial transactions done via the digital platforms InstaPay and PesoNet jumped 155.4 percent and 22.0 percent year-on-year, respectively, in May 2021 vs. May 2020. 

Also, more than 8 million electronic money accounts were created since last year.  

We expect further growth in electronic money accounts, especially with the BSP’s recent approval of three license applications of three digital banks, namely Overseas Filipino Bank, Tonik Bank, and UNO Bank. 

The recently issued Open Finance Framework will also help accelerate digitalization and inclusion. 

Under this framework, consent-driven data portability, interoperability, and collaborative partnerships between financial institutions and fintech players are promoted. Consumers will have the power to grant access to their financial data that will shape a customer-centric product development objective. 

The framework covers different financial institutions and a broader array of financial products such as, but not limited to, banking products and services, investments, pensions, and insurance. 

We have also launched programs that will allow more extensive use of QR codes for payments. Soon we will see QR codes being used for various retail payments. 

Given all our efforts toward digitalization, we envision a Philippines where everyone is empowered with financial accounts and will be able to make us of a wide range of financial transactions through digital means. 


Sustainability

The Philippines recently submitted its “Nationally Determined Contributions” to the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change. Under its commitment, the Philippines aims to reduce its projected carbon emissions by 75 percent by 2030.

The BSP is one with the entire Philippine nation in stepping up efforts toward sustainable economic development. Our work on sustainability falls on various areas:

First, capacity building. 

The BSP has joined global and regional networks that aim to promote sustainable finance for capacity-building purposes. 

Such networks include Sustainable Banking Network (SBN) and the Network for Greening the Financial System (NGFS), Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), Executives' Meeting of East Asia and Pacific Central Banks (EMEAP), and the Alliance for Financial Inclusion – Inclusive Green Finance (AFI-IGF).]

Second, enabling regulations. 

In April last year, the BSP issued the Sustainable Finance Framework (Circular No. 1085), which forms the first phase of our enabling regulations on sustainability. 

The framework sets out broad supervisory expectations on the integration of sustainability principles in the corporate and risk governance systems, as well as in the business strategies and operations of banks. 

The second phase of regulations – for which a draft is already out for industry comments – will focus on more specific expectations on the integration of climate change and environmental and social risks to the enterprise-wide risk management frameworks of banks. 

The third phase will include potential incentives to banks to accelerate the process of adopting sustainable principles. 

The BSP has also strengthened governance on treasury activities and streamlined processes to allow for more bond issuances of BSP-supervised financial institutions and contribute to the growth of capital markets.

More than USD 1.0 billion and PHP 85.4 billion worth of green, social, and sustainability bonds have been issued by “first mover” banks since 2017. 

Third, collaboration with other government entities. 

The BSP collaborated with key government agencies through the Green Force. 

The group aims to institutionalize and facilitate the implementation of a roadmap for sustainable finance. 

It also aims to facilitate investments in public infrastructure and mobilize funds to finance SDG-related projects such as clean energy.  

The inter-agency group is currently reviewing the draft principles-based taxonomy and finalizing the sustainable finance roadmap for the Philippines. 

Fourth, internal program. 

The BSP launched its internal Sustainable Central Banking Program, which fosters environmentally responsible and sustainable policies and work practices within the BSP. Among which, we have started prohibiting single-use plastics within our premises. 

This should help instill environmentally sound habits among our employees—ahead of the anticipated nationwide ban on single-use plastics that comes along our commitment on carbon emission reduction.  

 

Other initiatives. 

Meantime, the BSP invested $350 million in the Green Bond Fund launched by the Bank for International Settlements (BIS) as part of sustainable investing on reserve management. 

Also, our financial digitalization agenda—besides the obvious goals of enhancing financial inclusion and faster economic growth—will help significantly reduce the country’s carbon footprints.  

Various reports have said that amid the pandemic, air, and water quality in various parts of the world has considerably improved. 

However, as economies start to recover whether the environmental improvements are sustainable remains questionable.  

The lesson from COVID-19 is loud and clear: The world needs urgent and drastic actions toward sustainability. The quest for economic progress should go hand in hand with the goal of environment protection.    

Central banks are able to help achieve the desired change through regulations that encourage the financial sector to adopt sustainable practices.  

The BSP is up to this task. And we enjoin our regulated entities and the entire public to join us in this pressing and worthy cause.  

Moving on to the outlook on the Philippine economy. 

For 2021,  

● The Development Budget Coordination Committee expects the economy to grow by 6.0 to 7.0 percent this year. 

● Inflation to settle at the high end of the target range of 2-4 percent;

The risks to the inflation outlook remain broadly balanced around the baseline projection path. 

The uptick in international commodity prices amid supply-chain bottlenecks and the recovery in global demand could lend upside pressures on inflation. 

However, downside risks to the inflation outlook continue to emanate from the emergence of new coronavirus variants, which could delay the easing of lockdown measures and temper prospects for domestic growth.

● Goods exports and imports to rebound to a growth of 10.0 and 12.0 percent, respectively;  

● Remittances to grow by 4.0 percent.

● Net inflow of foreign direct investments to rise to USD 7.5 billion from last year’s USD 6.5 billion; 

● External accounts to remain healthy, with hefty gross international reserves and surpluses in the current account and the balance of payments (BOP); and

● The peso to continue reflecting emerging demand and supply conditions in the foreign exchange (FX) market as well as external developments, including increasing availability of anti-COVID vaccines, recovery of remittances, foreign investment inflows, and exports rebound as world economic conditions improve.  

The expected growth drivers on both the demand and supply sides are shown on this slide.

The banking sector have also kept the impact of the crisis manageable.  

Among other indicators, capital adequacy ratio (CAR) remains well above the regulatory requirement, non-performing loans ratio remains manageable and far from levels seen in the aftermath of the Asian financial crisis. 

The implementation of the FIST Act is projected to reduce average NPL ratio of the banking system by 0.6 to 5.8 percentage points for the years 2021 to 2025. 

Liquidity coverage ratios also are above regulatory requirements. 

We expect the banking sector to continue supporting the Philippine economy, through financial intermediation, toward recovery and further to the New Economy. 

In closing, I would like to highlight three take-away messages:

• First, the Philippine economy is on the mend and is expected to revert to robust pre-pandemic growth levels by the middle of next year.

• Second, the BSP will continue to support the economy. The BSP recognizes that the timing for the unwinding of our response measures is crucial. We will carry out disengagement strategies in a way that avoids risks associated with early or late implementation; and

• Finally, before the pandemic, the Philippines was on its way to become an upper middle-income economy. But we do not simply aim to recover. In the post-pandemic era, we want to be stronger, more technologically advanced, and more inclusive than ever before. 

Strong economic Indicators are showing we are headed there. 

As such, we hope to have you as our partners as we build back better and endeavor to reach new heights in the post-pandemic era. Thank you.

Title: Building Back a Better Economy: Prospects and Challenges for the Philippines in the Post-Pandemic Era
Occasion: The Manila Times 2021 Mid-Year Economic Report
Speaker: BSP Governor Benjamin E. Diokno
Transcription:
​

Good morning, everyone. It is a pleasure to join you in this business forum.

As you know, the COVID-19 pandemic adversely affected businesses and households. Quarantine restrictions inhibited spending, resulting in billions of lost income. 

Since the onset of the pandemic, the government has implemented various measures to mitigate the spread of the virus and restore lost economic output. 

Although risks remain amid the discovery of new COVID variants, recent macroeconomic developments have shown encouraging signs that the economic recovery is underway. 

As I will discuss in the succeeding slides, the BSP affirms its support to the economy for as long as necessary to ensure its strong and sustainable recovery. 

These are the topics that I will cover in my presentation:

First, I will start with a discussion on the state of the Philippine economy, 

Next, I will discuss the BSP’s current monetary policy stance and the key considerations that fed into our most recent policy meeting.

I will also share with you some sectoral updates and the BSP’s policy measures to support these sectors. 

Finally, I will end with some key takeaways and the BSP’s way forward.  

The economy continues to recover gradually. For the first quarter of 2021, real GDP contracted at a relatively subdued rate of 4.2 percent. 

While the first quarter growth rate was lower than expected, green shoots of recovery can already be observed in some sectors such as in manufacturing. 

The continued safe reopening of the economy and the calibrated reimposition of lockdown restrictions, where necessary, contributed to this gradual improvement.

Moving on to high frequency indicators monitored by the BSP, the Purchasing Managers Index (PMI) and mobility indicators suggest that economic activity is gradually recovering. On a month-on-month basis, mobility indicators and the composite PMI significantly improved in April and May 2021, showing signs of partial restoration of economic activity in the manufacturing and services sectors.

The increasing mobility is a welcome development to our consumption-driven economy. However, there are still risks to our growth outlook as the presence of the delta coronavirus variant might give rise to renewed restrictions, similar to what is happening in select cities in Asia, Europe, and Oceania. 

Moving on to high frequency indicators monitored by the BSP, the Purchasing Managers Index (PMI) and mobility indicators suggest that economic activity is gradually recovering. On a month-on-month basis, mobility indicators and the composite PMI significantly improved in April and May 2021, showing signs of partial restoration of economic activity in the manufacturing and services sectors.

The increasing mobility is a welcome development to our consumption-driven economy. However, there are still risks to our growth outlook as the presence of the delta coronavirus variant might give rise to renewed restrictions, similar to what is happening in select cities in Asia, Europe, and Oceania. 

The unemployment rate declined to 7.7 percent in May from 8.7 percent in April. Total employment increased to 44.7 million from 43.3 million in April as mobility improved due to the re-imposition of less stringent lockdown measures in mid-May. 

All major economic sectors posted net job gains on a month-on-month basis as easing lockdown measures enabled businesses to resume operations and increase production capacities. The overall labor market condition improved as the government applied more strategic risk-based restrictions. 

Furthermore, the labor force participation rate (LFPR) improved to 64.6 percent in May 2021 from 63.2 percent in April. 

The unemployment rates for the first five months of the year are within the government’s target range of 7.0-9.0 percent for 2021. 

We expect the labor market to moderately improve in the succeeding months as high frequency indicators point to better economic prospects in June and July.

The overall business confidence index or the CI decreased to 1.4 percent in the second quarter of  2021 and 31.4 percent for third quarter of the year but remained positive and optimistic. 

The upsurge of COVID-19 cases, reimposition of stricter lockdown measures, and elevated inflation rate due to supply constraints led to the dampening of the overall business confidence index.

On the other hand, consumer sentiment continued to improve in the second quarter of 2021 as the overall confidence index increased to -30.9 percent from -34.7 percent in the first quarter. 

Moreover, consumer expectations for the third quarter is positive at 1.3 percent. 

Consumers’ optimism significantly improved on the back of increasing availability of jobs, reopening of businesses, and rising access to COVID-19 vaccines.

Looking now at price levels, the year-on-year headline inflation declined to 4.1 percent in June 2021 from 4.5 percent in May. 

Inflation decelerated as food inflation continued to slowdown amid the government’s efforts of addressing supply-side issues.

Inflation expectations remain well-anchored to target. Results of the BSP’s survey of private sector economists conducted in June showed steady mean inflation forecast for 2021 at 4.1 percent. 

Meanwhile, the mean inflation forecasts for 2022 and 2023 are at 3.2 percent and 3.1 percent, respectively. Analysts expect inflation to gradually move towards the government’s target range in 2021, with risks to the inflation outlook generally tilted to the upside on expectations that the continued global vaccine rollout will help further reopen economies. 

Needless to say, inflation expectations remain firmly anchored to the government’s target of 2-4 percent for 2022 and 2023.

Meanwhile, credit activity remains weak, as measures to address the still elevated number of COVID-19 cases constrained domestic economic activity and continued to dampen market sentiment.

Banks remain risk-averse as gross non-performing loans increased to 4.5 percent in May, up from 4.4 percent in April. 

Lockdown restrictions inhibited the ability of households and firms to meet their financial obligations and as a result, the NPL coverage ratio of the banking system declined to 80 percent in May from 81.5 percent in April. 

Despite the recent increase in NPLs, Philippine banks remain well-capitalized. As of the first quarter of 2021, the capital adequacy ratio (CAR) of the banking system is at 16.9 percent, well above the 10 percent minimum threshold set by the BSP.

The country’s external sector indicators show promising signs of recovery. The sustained rebound in key economies has spurred external demand. The country’s exports of goods increased by 11.1 percent in the first quarter of 2021. Similarly, imports of goods grew by 10 percent on stronger domestic demand for raw materials. 

Net foreign direct investments for the first four months of the year increased due to positive foreign investor sentiment on the country’s macroeconomic fundamentals and strong growth prospects. 

The gross international reserves or the GIR, which stood at US$106 billion as of June 2021, continue to provide adequate external liquidity buffer. 

At this level, the GIR represents a more than adequate external liquidity buffer equivalent to 12.1 months’ worth of imports of goods and payments of services and primary income. 

The GIR is supported by the resilient inflows of cash remittance from overseas workers. Remittances amounted to US$2.4 billion in May, 13.1 percent higher than the previous year’s US$2.1 billion. 

Let us now go to the BSP’s current monetary policy stance.

Given a manageable inflation path, the BSP kept the key policy interest rate at 2.0 percent in its recent policy review on June 24, 2021. Economic activity has improved in recent weeks, but the overall momentum of the economic recovery remains tentative, as the threat of COVID-19 infections continues. 

Nevertheless, the sustained implementation of targeted fiscal initiatives, as well as the acceleration of the government's vaccination program, should help boost market confidence and recovery of the economy in the coming months.

The BSP believes that sustained monetary policy support for domestic demand should help the economic recovery gain more traction. 

Looking ahead, the BSP is committed to support the economy for as long as necessary to ensure its strong and sustainable recovery. 

The BSP will also remain vigilant against any emerging risks to the outlook for inflation and growth and will adjust its policy settings as needed to safeguard its price and financial stability objectives.

Furthermore, the BSP has implemented extraordinary measures to ensure ample liquidity in the financial system, restore financial market functioning, and shore up market confidence. These measures include a mix of decisive monetary policy adjustments and regulatory relief and forbearance measures. 

We note, however, that the BSP did not use unconventional monetary policies, including quantitative easing. Our liquidity-enhancing measures in response to the COVID-19 pandemic have remained largely in line with the definition of conventional monetary policy.

The BSP’s provisional advances to the national government is a temporary “bridge financing” mechanism to support its broad-based pandemic-response programs. 

This financing is capped, timebound, and authorized under the BSP Charter In total, the BSP’s policy and liquidity-easing measures has injected Php2.2 trillion or 12.3% of GDP. 

At this point, let me share with you sectoral updates and the BSP’s policy measures to support these sectors. 

Focusing now on the country’s micro-, small-, and medium enterprises (or MSMEs).

Most firms lacked the funds necessary to maintain their businesses after the lockdown This is especially true for smaller firms. 

Due to the vital role of MSMEs in the Philippine economy, the BSP has deployed a wide range of policies and regulatory and relief measures to support them. This includes the innovative measure to allow loans to MSMEs as alternative compliance with BSP’s reserve requirement.

This is available to banks or non-banks with quasi-bank functions from April 24, 2020 to December 29, 2022.

As of the week of June 17, 2021, the banking system allocated an average of P183.9 billion loans for MSMEs as alternative compliance with the reserve requirements. 

This level is significantly higher than from the P8.7 billion average MSME loans that were reported for the week ending April 30, 2020. 

The latest level is equivalent to 12.6 percent of the total required reserves, up from 0.6 percent on April 30, 2020. 

The Monetary Board also temporarily reduced the risk weights of loans granted to MSMEs. 

Additionally, the implementation of the revised risk-based capital framework for banks was deferred from end-2021 to end-2022

The period of relief on the reporting of past due and non-performing loans of borrowers affected by the COVID-19 was also extended to December 31, 2021 from the original timeline of March 8, 2021.

These policy issuances reinforce BSP’s earlier pronouncements that relax the Know-Your-Customer requirements for retail clients to facilitate their access to formal financing channels. 

The MSMEs are also supported in the following ways:

(i) Promotion of innovative financing mechanisms. Under this approach, the BSP supports the development of supply chain financing or the SCF, which allows businesses to turn receivables and inventory flows as well as supply chain relationships to working capital. 

This enables MSMEs with no credit history to secure favorable terms of bank financing based on the creditworthiness of their large corporate buyers;

(ii) Improvement of digital and financial infrastructure by addressing the risks and cost issues that have made lending to MSME and agriculture a high-risk and low-margin proposition. 

The BSP is also working to develop a credit risk database for the Philippines and actively promotes the credit surety fund or the CSF. This is a credit enhancement scheme, which aims to give MSMEs access to non-collateral bank financing by way of surety cover issued jointly and severally by the parties of the CSF; and

(iii) Bridging the information and data gap for more evidence-based policymaking and address information asymmetry in the market. The BSP is facilitating strategic partnerships to facilitate information sharing.

Now let me share with you the way forward for the BSP.

The country’s recovery prospects hinges largely on the credible management of the health crisis. Recent vaccination data show that vaccine inoculation is ramping up.

From about 1.5 vaccinated persons per one hundred population in April, there are now around 8.8 vaccinated persons per hundred population as of July 12. The rising number of vaccinated Filipinos is a precursor for the economy to further recover from the pandemic. 

To address the risk of economic scarring, the government has designed a recovery package supporting the safe reopening of the economy: The Bayanihan 2, the 2020 budget, the 2021 and 2022 budget, as well as several legislative measures in the pipeline: 

a) The Financial Institutions Strategic Transfer Act (FIST), was passed in January 2021 aimed at encouraging the private sector, government financial institutions, and government-owned or controlled corporations to incorporate and invest in FIST Corporations and help in the rehabilitation of distressed businesses, thereby contributing to economic growth. 

b) The recently passed Corporate Recovery and Tax Incentives for Enterprises Act (CREATE) will alower corporate income tax. The tax savings may be used by MSMEs to fund their operations and retain employees. 

c) Meanwhile, the proposed Government Financial Institutions Unified Initiatives to Distressed Enterprises for Economic Recovery Act (GUIDE) expands the loan assistance program, rediscounting and other credit accommodation facilities of government financial institutions to help MSMEs cope with the effects of COVID-19.

​

The global recovery is increasing, which should have positive implications for the country’s economic rebound. In their latest global outlook report, the World Bank raised its full-year economic growth projection for 2021 relative to initial forecasts in January 2021. 

The upward revision reflects the stronger-than-projected economic recovery across regions due mainly to expectations of wider vaccine availability, as well as the impact of additional fiscal response in the US.

In advanced economies, the projected recovery is due to widespread vaccination, reopening of more economies, and sustained monetary policy accommodation. 

Meanwhile, the growth outlook in emerging market and developing economies is projected to recover at a faster rate as higher commodity prices and improving external demand underpin the recovery of lost economic output. 

However, significant downside risks remain as new COVID variants, uneven vaccine access, and partial withdrawal of fiscal support moderate aggregate consumption and investment in emerging market and developing economies. 

In any case, we are optimistic that there is sufficient support for the country’s recovery this year and in the near-term. The easing restrictions alongside improvements in the health sector, revitalization of key industries to be supported by structural reforms, and an improving global economy should help GDP to recover in 2021 and accelerate in 2022. 

Consistent with expectations of a stronger global economic rebound this year, the growth forecast for goods exports is raised to 8.0 percent for 2021. Meanwhile, goods imports is seen to grow by 12.0 percent.

Overseas Filipino cash remittances are seen to remain resilient, supported by the reopening of destination countries in 2021 and 2022.

Moreover, the positive outlook for remittances should help to support the buildup in the country’s GIR. 

In fact—according to Moody's Investors Service—the Philippines' fiscal metrics are stronger than its peers, despite the effects of the pandemic. 

In a fresh report released on Monday, Moody’s  said, "The Philippines has sustained its position compared with rating peers because of the strengthening of its fiscal metrics ahead of the pandemic shock."

Nonetheless, the country’s road to recovery will not be easy. We will continue to monitor recent developments, here and abroad, and assess their impact on the inflation outlook, financial stability and growth. 

The BSP remains committed to staying the course amid the COVID-19 pandemic by: 

• maintaining price stability; 

• ensuring financial sector soundness and stability; 

• strengthening resilience against external shocks; and 

• Supporting the National Government’s whole-of-government approach in addressing the current crisis and ensuring stronger recovery post-COVID.


Moreover, the BSP expects inflation to settle within the government’s target for 2021-2023. The BSP’s latest baseline inflation forecasts are 4.0 percent for 2021 and 3.0 percent for 2022 and 2023. 

The inflation path is seen to remain near the high end of the target range for the rest of the third quarter of 2021. 

However, we expect inflation to decelerate close to the midpoint of the target range by the fourth quarter of this year due to the government’s supply-side interventions in addressing shortages of select food items.

The risks to the inflation outlook appear to be broadly balanced for 2021 to 2023. 

The uptick in global commodity prices due to strong global demand amid supply chain bottlenecks, the impact of easing of quarantine measures, and stronger global growth could pose upside risks to inflation. 

In contrast, downside risks emanate from the spread of new COVID-19 variants which might delay the easing of containment measures and dampen domestic economic growth.

To summarize allow me to share with you some of the key points that I wish to highlight:

High frequency indicators suggest that the economy is gradually recovering from the adverse effects of the pandemic. But it would appear that the recovery is slower than previously anticipated. As such, the BSP will maintain its accommodative stance, for as long as necessary, to support and sustain the economy’s recovery.

Inflation expectations remain anchored within the policy horizon. The BSP is mindful that headline inflation is currently above the government’s target range due to transitory factors. 

We reiterate that increases in prices owing to supply shocks are best dealt with supply-side interventions. 

The government’s recovery package, accelerated vaccine rollout, and rising foreign demand are necessary to further support domestic economic activities. 

Additional fiscal spending is critical in sustaining the recovery, as well as preventing the long-term scarring effects of the pandemic.

However, COVID-19 variants pose emerging downside risks to the growth outlook. 

Let me end this speech with the words of the late U.S. President John F. Kennedy. 

“We are not here to curse the darkness, but to light the candle than can guide us through the darkness to a safe and sane future.”

This is precisely what we hope to achieve, as we navigate the dark that is the COVID-19 pandemic. 

While recovery will not be easy, I hope that the country’s whole-of-nation approach will provide enough light to lead us to a brighter future at the end of this dark tunnel. 

Thank you.

Title: One with the Nation: Forging Public-Private Partnerships toward Digital Financial Inclusion in the Philippines
Occasion: GCash Event
Speaker: BSP Governor Benjamin E. Diokno
Transcription:
​

A good day to the organizers and participants.  Our thanks to GCash for inviting us to this important event.  

Today’s webinar with the theme: “One with the Nation: Forging Public-Private Partnerships toward Digital Financial Inclusion in the Philippines” comes at an extraordinary but opportune time. 

The COVID-19 pandemic has led to unprecedented, adverse effects expected to persist for years to come.  It has disrupted our economy and daily life.  However, it has also opened a path of opportunities for broader inclusive development.

One of these opportunities is accelerated digitalization of the financial services and their clients.  

Digitalization in the financial system can create a catalytic, transformative impact by making essential financial services less costly and more affordable for most people.  

The BSP has therefore made digitalization and digital financial inclusion a major and urgent priority, especially in light of the ongoing pandemic. 

From a macro perspective, digital financial inclusion creates a wider and diversified client base for financial services who not only can benefit from, but also contribute to, the system’s strength and dynamism.  

More people having access to welfare- and productivity-enhancing financial services can likewise boost livelihood opportunities and economic dynamism in communities across the country. 

To an individual, the benefits of digital financial inclusion are manifold. These would include: access to a wider range of financial services tailored to the customer’s needs; lowered transaction costs; better protection against fraud. 

All these represent greater empowerment for the financial consumers, especially the marginalized ones.

Now we ask: can we as a country achieve digital financial inclusion? My short answer is yes.   

The 2019 Financial Inclusion Survey showed that even prior to the pandemic, account ownership, and with it - the use of digital financial services – has increased. Account ownership among Filipino adults rose from 23% in 2017 to 29% in 2019, translating to an additional 5 million Filipinos being financially included in the span of two years. 

 More important, we saw an impressive increase in account ownership among the poorest or the socio-economic class “E” segment. 

From just 14% in 2017, it doubled to 27% in 2019 – a good indicator of this group’s readiness for digital finance. 

The uptake in e-money account ownership also grew from 1% in 2017 to 8% in 2019. The percentage of account holders who use their accounts for payment transactions also doubled – from just 18% to 39% in the same 2-year period.  

Indeed, we saw a rapid shift by customers, businesses and the government to digital payments. Cash withdrawals and check transactions significantly fell. While electronic fund transfers went up based on comparative date for 76 days before and during the enhanced community quarantine period.  

E-money also experienced a 61.6% growth in the number of active e-wallets at 14.2 million as of third quarter 2020, versus the 8.8 million level posted in 2019.  We expect this growth to persist as more Filipinos transact online.

These developments have been made possible by the foundations we have put in place for an inclusive digital finance ecosystem, which is characterized by three things:

First is the democratization of account ownership through the no-frill, low-cost basic deposit account and e-money accounts. The BDA was introduced in 2018 to address the needs of the unbanked for an account with zero required maintaining balance, simple documentary requirements, and minimum opening deposit. 

As of fourth quarter 2020, 133 banks are offering BDA to 6.6 million depositors, up from 4 million depositors as of end-2019.  

There is also of course our pioneering e-money regulation, BSP Circular Number 649 issued in 2009, which led to the creation of non-bank e-money issuers such as G-Cash providing innovative mobile wallet services for the mass market. 

The second element is the expansion of access points, particularly for cashing in and out.  These access points serve as a bridge that facilitate the transition of certain segments of consumers from cash transactions, to agent-assisted digital transactions, then to mobile financial transactions. 

This has been made possible through BSP’s agent regulations allowing banks and other financial service providers to tap retail outlets such as pharmacies, grocery stores, even pawnshops from which clients cash-in or cash-out from their BDA or E-money wallets.

There are now more than 17,000 cash agents, more than 54,000 e-money agents, resulting in 91% of local government units being serve by at least one agent.   

The third key element of our inclusive digital finance ecosystem are the digital payment rails of Instapay and PESONet, which enable electronic fund transfers from one account to any account.  

As of end-April 2021, there are 82 participating financial service providers for PESONet and 52 for InstaPay.  Building on these payment rails are the innovative payment solutions that we are now pursuing with industry, including the QR-code. QR code facilitates secure and cost-efficient solution for merchant digital payment acceptance as well as person-to-person or P2P real-time payments.

What do all these mean for an individual - your constituents?

 

The inclusive digital finance ecosystem has made opening of a transaction account – which is a basic step to financial inclusion – not only accessible and affordable but also compelling and practical, even for low-income individuals.  

Let’s imagine Aling Nena, a market vendor who previously does not have an account because aside from not having enough money to meet the maintaining balance, she did not really see the need to open an account because there is not enough money to save anyway. 

Why else would she need an account? Add to that the inconvenience of going to a bank branch during her store hours. 

But now because of e-money and BDA, agents and Instapay, Aling Nena finds that she can easily open an account even with just Php 100, in a convenience store just beside the wet market. In fact, she can open it by just downloading an app on her secondhand smartphone.  

She has also changed her mind about the necessity of owning an account. She now knows that having an account is useful and practical because with it, she can instantly pay her utility bills with a few clicks on her phone, and no longer having to waste time queuing up under the sun. 

She can even now invest in a money market fund for as little as Php 50 through her mobile account.  

And when she had to send money to her family in the province for emergency, she was able to do so instantly, anytime, anywhere.  More important, as a market vendor, she now accepts digital payment from many of her ‘suki’ who prefer cashless transactions for health and security considerations.  In fact, her sales have been going up! 

But that’s not the end of it.  Aling Nena realized that with her digital payment transactions, she has been able to build a rich digital profile that a formal lender used to assess her credit worthiness. That’s why she was able to get micro-credit line at much better terms than what the 5-6 lenders offer. A mobile phone and an account have brought Aling Nena new opportunities and opened doors. 

We want to empower more Aling Nenas in the country.  In fact, we have set as a target in our Digital Payments Transformation Roadmap. Our target is that by 2023, at least 70% of Filipino adults should have an account. 

This is an ambitious target but we are confident of hitting it. The remaining roadblocks are being addressed, not only by the BSP but also by financial inclusion advocates in government and the private sector. 

For instance, the the 20-member interagency Financial Inclusion Steering Committee chaired by the BSP helped successfully push for the issuance of Executive Order No. 127 which was signed by President Duterte in March 2021. 

The executive order is a policy reform that aims to address internet connectivity challenges in many unserved rural areas by liberalizing the satellite broadband market.   

With improved internet access, financial service providers can deploy and connect automated teller machines, agents, and other access points to serve more Filipinos, especially those in rural communities.  

Another critical digital gamechanger for financial inclusion is the Philippine Identification System or PhilSys.  As a foundational ID system, PhilSys will not only address the long-standing documentary barriers faced by many unbanked but also enable seamless and cost-efficient digital onboarding.  

With the PhilSys online authentication and eKYC features, identity proofing will be done digitally without needing to manually verify, and photocopy identification documents. 

This will enable financial service providers to tap the low-income mass market as a viable and strategic segment.  

To encourage more people to open transaction accounts, it is not enough that we make it easy and affordable. Equally important is demonstrating account ownership as a basic necessity. 

This means we need to integrate the use of transaction account in their financial lives – whether for receiving emergency cash assistance from government or friends, or getting paid by their employers or customers. 

Thus, the BSP continues to build use cases that show the use of an account and shift the preference of the public from cash-based to account-based payment transactions.  

Toward this end, the BSP is collaborating with the Department of Social Welfare and Development (DSWD), Department of Labor and Employment (DOLE), and Department of Transportation (DOTr) to promote account-based transactions and digital payments in cash assistance distribution, wage payments, and public transport.

These initiatives are supported by our financial and digital literacy campaigns. 

These campaigns are undertaken with various partners, including the Department of Education and the DSWD.  

During the pandemic, we conducted the #SafeAtHome Sa E-payments campaign to increase public awareness on digital payments.  We shared ways to practice cyber-hygiene and vigilance against online frauds and scams.    

We are also enhancing our Consumer Assistance Mechanism to improve customer trust and confidence in using financial services. In July last year, we launched the BSP Online Buddy or BOB.  

Powered by artificial intelligence and natural language processing, BOB provides an expedient channel for the public to raise queries and complaints.

The future is digital. And it is here.  We need to make sure that our constituents are not left behind.  Let us prepare them for the new economy and equip them with access to transformative digital financial services. 

 How can we do this? Let me share three concrete ways that we in the public sector can take.  

 The first is to adopt digital payments in our social welfare programs and public services. In promoting use of accounts in distributing cash assistance, we provide the necessary nudge for our constituents to start using and benefitting from formal financial services.  

We can organize community events for account onboarding and digital payments of strategic target groups such as the wet market vendors, sari-sari stores, tricycle operators and drivers associations.  When these essential community service providers start to accept QR-code payments, digital payments will be widely embraced even among our low-income constituents. 

Second, is to seek partnerships with and support from government agencies, civil society and private sector, including financial service and technology providers. We will need the combined expertise, resources and networks of vital stakeholders to effectively implement our digital financial inclusion programs. This is the same mindset that we bring in our own big digital push at the BSP.

Finally, we can and should support digital and financial literacy effort for our constituencies. They need to gain the knowledge and skills to effectively use digital financial services. 

These include knowing the available products in the market that are appropriate for their needs, as well as understanding and exercising their rights as financial consumers.  The BSP stands ready to support your financial literacy programs. 

In closing, let me once again thank G-Cash for organizing this event and giving the BSP the opportunity to share our thinking on digital financial inclusion.  

May we all take to heart our role in making access to welfare-enhancing financial services a reality for all Filipinos.  Let us all work together toward a more inclusive, resilient and prosperous Philippines.  

Thank you very much.​

Title: Keynote Speech of BSP Gov. Benjamin E. Diokno for the Signing of the Multilateral MOA on the Implementation of a Centralized System for Accreditation/Selection of External Auditors in the Financial Sector
Occasion: Signing of the Multilateral MOA on the Implementation of a Centralized System for Accreditation/Selection of External Auditors in the Financial Sector
Speaker: BSP Governor Benjamin E. Diokno
Transcription:
​

Good morning.  It is my pleasure to welcome our Financial Sector Forum (FSF) Principals, Emilio Aquino, Chairman of the Securities and Exchange Commission; Dennis Funa, Commissioner of the Insurance Commission; and Roberto Tan, President of the Philippine Deposit Insurance Corporation. Our partners from the Professional Regulatory Board of Accountancy headed by Chairman Noel Quinañola, to witness another milestone for the accountancy profession and the Financial Sector Forum. 

It was in 2009, when the FSF member-agencies and the Board of Accountancy (BOA) forged a partnership on the accreditation or selection process for external auditors.  

The FSF member-agencies and the BOA hurdled significant roadblocks to come up with a unified stance that only those external auditors who meet the qualification criteria set and adhere to by recognized standards in auditing will be allowed to express an opinion on the financial statements of financial institutions.  

This is recognition of the critical role of external auditors in promoting the fairness and integrity of financial statements and in strengthening market discipline in the financial industry.  

Since then, the FSF and the BOA continued working together to capacitate the external auditing profession and in promoting awareness of relevant developments in the regulatory sphere.   

As the business and the regulatory environments evolved, new challenges and opportunities emerged that required us to revisit the arrangements we have put in place more than 10 years ago.  

This led to the adoption of a centralized or a “one stop shop” accreditation framework which further streamlined the accreditation and selection process and promoted ease of doing business.  

Under the new framework, external auditors only need to file their applications with the Securities and Exchange Commission, while the FSF member-agencies leverage on the information sharing platform between and among agencies to complete the accreditation process. 

As such, let me take this opportunity to thank Chairman Emilio Aquino and the Securities and Exchange Commission for accepting the role as the central agency for this process.  

In line with this development, we would like to reaffirm our commitment by signing a new Memorandum of Agreement on the Implementation of a Centralized System for Accreditation/Selection of External Auditors in the Financial Sector.  

The MOA provides the respective roles and responsibilities of the member-agencies under the one-stop shop framework as well as the arrangements on the conduct of the Nationwide Regulator’s Forum to apprise external auditors of the latest regulatory issuances and internationally recognized standards relevant to the accounting and auditing profession.

All said, let me conclude by sharing a quote from the American anthropologist, Margaret Mead.  She said that “Never doubt that a small group of thoughtful, committed people can change the world.  Indeed, it is the only thing that ever has.”  

Congratulations to the FSF member-agencies and the Board of Accountancy for taking this step to implement this change for the benefit of the Filipino people.

Thank you and good morning!​

Title: The Management of Reputational Risks in Banks
Occasion: Bank Marketing Association of the Philippines General Membership Meeting
Speaker: BSP Governor Benjamin E. Diokno
Transcription:
​

Bank Marketing Association of the Philippines President Miguel Angelo Villa-Real, BMAP directors and officers, distinguished members and everyone joining this webinar, a pleasant morning.   

I would like to thank BMAP for inviting me as your guest speaker for this month’s general membership meeting. This is an opportune time to share about the BSP’s expectations on the reputational risk management framework for banks.  

As you know, continued trust and confidence in the banking system is crucial to securing economic recovery and growth. The COVID-19 crisis has also accelerated digital transformation within a financial landscape. 

As such, it is imperative for banks to adopt a holistic risk management approach to address emerging threats, especially risks that may affect their reputation and impair the sustainability of their operations. 

Allow me to first begin with the macroeconomic backdrop, followed by a snapshot of the condition and performance of the Philippine banking sector. 

Second, I will discuss the evolving governance landscape and the BSP’s reform agenda. 

Third, I will share the highlights of the recently issued guidelines on reputational risk management as embodied under BSP Circular No. 1114. 

I will then tackle some of the strategies for managing reputational risk in the digital age. 

Let me conclude this presentation with some key takeaways.

A financial system that is sound and resilient reinforces a country’s strong macroeconomic fundamentals. 

In the Philippines, the domestic economy contracted by 4.2 percent in the first quarter of 2021—a sustained improvement from the 8.3 percent decline recorded in the last quarter of 2020. For the full year 2020, gross domestic product fell to its sharpest decline at negative 9.6 percent since 1946. 

As the Philippine economy further reopens and vaccination coverage improves, we project growth to range between 6.0 percent to 7.0 percent this year. 

The latest inflation forecasts indicate that average inflation is likely to settle at 3.9 percent in 2021, which is within the 2 to 4 percent target band.

Gross international reserves posted a 14.7 percent increase to $107.0 billion as of end-May 2021, indicating adequate external liquidity buffer equivalent to 12.2 months’ worth of imports of goods and payments of services and primary income. 

Cash remittances from overseas Filipino workers amounted to US$7.6 billion. This rose by 2.6 percent in the first quarter of 2021 compared to US$7.4 billion during the same period a year ago as host economies began to ease pandemic-related restrictions. 

Meanwhile, the peso averaged P48.28/US$1 in Q1 2021 depreciating slightly by 0.03 percent from the Q4 2020 average amid the surge in COVID-19 infections in the country. 

Amid this backdrop, the National Government and the BSP have been working closely with the industry and other key stakeholders in instituting stimulus measures to help address the unprecedented challenges caused by the pandemic. 

We expect improvement in the country’s macroeconomic fundamentals in 2021 with the country’s accelerating rollout of the COVID-19 vaccination, the easing of quarantine restrictions and reopening of the economy. 

Meanwhile, the Philippine banking sector remains stable and resilient. Banks have strong capital position with ratios registering well above the BSP thresholds and that of international standards. As of end-March 2021, capital adequacy ratios of banks stood at 16.8 percent and 17.4 percent on solo and consolidated bases, respectively. 

The industry’s solo liquidity coverage ratio was at 194.3 percent as of end-March 2021 which was above the regulatory minimum of 100 percent. This indicates banks’ ability to fund its requirements during short-term liquidity shocks. Minimum liquidity ratios of stand-alone thrift, rural and cooperative banks stood at 33.8 percent, 58.9 percent and 38.7 percent, almost three times the minimum requirement of 16 percent. 

Trust and confidence in the banking system remain high as shown by the sustained year-on-year growth in its assets and deposits of 3.9 percent and 6.0 percent as of end-April 2021, respectively.

In line with the slowdown of our economy last year, the gross total loan portfolio (TLP) of banks decreased year-on-year by 2.5 percent to P10.6 trillion as of end-April 2021, slower than the 7.3 percent growth rate posted in April 2020.  

In terms of asset quality, the Philippine banking system’s gross non-performing loans ratio rose to 4.4 percent as of end-April 2021 compared to the 2.3 percent posted a year ago. 

Nonetheless, this was matched by higher loan loss provisions resulting in a non-performing loan coverage ratio of 81.5 percent. The passage of the Financial Institutions Strategic Transfer Act is expected to help keep the non-performing loans ratio of banks in check.  

We believe that the banking system’s capital and liquidity buffers complemented by sound corporate and risk governance and the BSP’s prudent financial supervision, would enable the industry to withstand the challenges that will come our way as the country pushes towards a solid recovery.

The sustained strength and resilience of the Philippine banking system is largely due to the progressive implementation of financial sector reform agenda, particularly on the areas of corporate and risk governance. The BSP implemented this reform agenda in three phases.  

First, we defined the fit and proper requirements and laid down our expectations from the board of directors and senior management in setting the tone of good governance from the top and ensuring that this is consistently adopted across the organization. 

Second, we established standards for checks and balances, which include the internal audit and compliance functions.   

Third, specific guidelines on the management of key risk areas such as credit, market, liquidity, operational, information technology, as well as environmental and social risks were issued by the BSP, all geared towards fostering strong risk governance in supervised financial institutions.  

The BSP recognizes that building and sustaining a good reputation is a critical element in promoting a bank’s safety and soundness. Hence, we released Circular No. 1114 to articulate the principles and practices underpinning sound reputational risk management.

What exactly is reputational risk? It refers to the risk to earnings, capital, and liquidity arising from the negative perception on the bank by various stakeholders such as the customers, shareholders, investors, market analysts, or media, that can adversely affect the ability of the bank to maintain existing business relationships, establish new businesses or partnerships, or continuously access varied sources of funding. 

Simply put, reputation is the collective perception of a bank’s relevant stakeholders whose expectations, if not satisfactorily met, may result in severe adverse impact on the banks’ business and bottom line. 

As Warren Buffet said, “It takes 20 years to build a reputation and five minutes to ruin it. If you think about that, you’ll do things differently.” 

Considering the implications of a reputational risk crisis, as well as the immense effort and resources to rebuild stakeholder trust, it is crucial for banks take a proactive stance in managing the risks to reputation. This is aligned with the extraordinary diligence required of the banking system. 

The reputation of an organization may be affected by stakeholder perceptions on the bank’s corporate and risk governance, the integrity of its officers and personnel, staff competence, organizational culture, business practices, product or service quality, employee and customer relations, financial soundness or business viability, and legal or regulatory compliance.  

The BSP guidelines highlight how reputational risk is closely linked to other risk exposures such as credit, market, liquidity, and operational risks, such that reputational risk can be triggered by a risk or a host of other risks. In the same way, reputation events can have spillover effects to other risk categories.  

Reputational risk may also arise from environmental, social and governance issues, especially now when banks are being called to respond to the challenge of meaningfully embedding sustainability in their strategies and business models. 

While it remains to be seen whether green banks will outperform non-green banks in terms of financial and operational performance, there is no doubt that climate change concerns are a relevant concern of key stakeholders. And beyond business, this is something that we must address for future generations.  

Banks belonging to a conglomerate must also be vigilant of external reputation events affecting the parent bank, subsidiaries, affiliates, and other related companies. 

Similarly, business relationships with key clients and counterparties which are engaged in unethical or unlawful acts, as well as with major service providers that have substandard service quality or lax controls may give rise to contagion effects on reputation. Other external events, such as unfounded rumors and accusations may likewise have a damaging impact on the financial institution’s reputation and the level of public confidence. 

Due to interdependencies with other risk types, financial institutions should take a holistic approach in managing reputational risk, one that leverages on existing corporate and risk governance frameworks. Circular No. 1114 sets out the supervisory expectations for BSP supervised financial institutions on the identification, assessment, and management of reputational risks. 

Reputational risk management should be integrated not only in the bank’s enterprise-wide risk management system, but also in the organization’s crisis management discipline.

In any case, banks are afforded the flexibility to design their reputational risk management function depending on how reputational risk exposures are being managed within the organization. In fact, we are aware that existing reputational risk management tools may already be in place. As such, the Circular allows for the continued use of such measures. 

Banks may also consider adopting the tools suggested in the guidance to identify possible reputation events and to assess their potential impact to the organization. The framework that will be adopted by banks should be commensurate to their size, nature and complexity of operations, overall risk profile, and systemic importance with due regard to the principle of proportionality.
