Everyone in the organization has a role to play in the management of reputational risk. Each employee, through the individual’s conduct, can influence the perception of stakeholders on the institution. Governance and management of reputational risk, therefore, requires having a well-established decision process, setting clear accountability and building engagement across the various organizational functions. 

Nevertheless, the board of directors is ultimately responsible for ensuring that an effective and efficient reputational risk management framework is in place and implemented by senior management. Business units and process owners should ensure that all significant risks to the organization’s reputation are identified and adequately managed and reported to senior management on a timely basis. 

The self-assessment functions must oversee reputational risk management efforts across the institution, ensure right conduct of business in accordance with relevant laws, rules, regulations, and maintain effective of control structure in the organization.  

Having a fully integrated risk management approach that is mandated by the board and adopted consistently across the organization is key to maintaining and strengthening the institution’s reputation.

Meanwhile, supervised financial institutions are expected to promptly notify the BSP of any reputation event, including issues raised in different social media platforms, which, if not timely and effectively addressed may lead to a full-blown crisis. These reputation events must be reported within five (5) calendar days from determination. 

In the case of operational risk events, major cyber-related incidents and/or disruption of financial services and operations, or liquidity shortfall, supervised financial institutions shall comply with the reporting requirements prescribed under existing regulations.

Meanwhile, the BSP fully embraces the ongoing digital transformation of the Philippine economy, especially in light of the ongoing COVID-19 pandemic. Amid the digital disruption, there has never been a greater need for banks to equip themselves with the right strategies to managing their reputation.

First, banks must be digital ready. Banks must be ready to jump on the digital bandwagon to remain competitive. Digitally-focused banks are in a better position to enhance organizational resilience, increase operational efficiency and meet customer expectations. 

This leads me to the next strategy, address clients’ needs and feedback. Banks looking to maintain and enhance their reputation should focus on meeting their clients’ needs as well as promptly addressing their concerns. 

Mishandled complaints have the potential to reach the media which can magnify reputational damage. In this regard, banks must adopt a sound consumer redress mechanism.  

Third, intensify cybersecurity measures and digital literacy. Cybersecurity soundness is imperative in maintaining the reputation of banks. Successful cyberattacks can lead to compromised IT systems, data breaches and financial losses which would undermine customer trust. The BSP, for its part, has continuously been advocating digital and financial literacy efforts towards this end. 

Lastly, strengthen crisis management. Mitigating the impact of reputational risk requires rapid and calculated response measures in the immediate aftermath of a crisis. Banks should have a well-documented plan in place for how it will deal with a crisis, considering the underlying cause of the incident, the extent of reputational damage, and the bank’s direction and business objectives. 

Ladies and gentlemen, as I close, allow me to leave you with some key takeaways.

First, banking is a business built on trust. A holistic reputational risk management approach is, therefore, central to a bank’s success and survival. 

Second, reputation is everyone’s business. Building and maintaining stakeholder trust is a shared effort and responsibility.

Lastly, as banks undergo their digital transformation process, customer expectations should be prioritized, and cyber security risks should be guarded. Indeed, banks will have to be more engaged, vigilant, and prepared to protect one of their most valuable assets – a good reputation. 

A good day to you all. Thank you and stay safe!

Title: Opening Remarks  of Governor Benjamin E. Diokno for the Satellite Broadband and Financial Inclusion Webinar
Occasion: Satellite Broadband and Financial Inclusion Webinar
Speaker: BSP Governor Benjamin E. Diokno
Transcription:
Good morning ladies and gentlemen. 

As you know, the BSP is committed to advancing financial inclusion in the country. 

What started as an advocacy program has evolved into an institutionalized policy and strategic objective of the BSP in support of its vision of improving the quality of life of all Filipinos. 

Financial inclusion, at its core, is about ensuring every Filipino has access to financial services as tools that can help them better manage their finances, transact safely and conveniently, seize income opportunities, and protect their family and businesses against financial losses.

In pursuit of this, we launched the 3-year Digital Payments Transformation Roadmap (DPTR) in 2020 as a tangible demonstration of our commitment to promote financial inclusion and digital payments. 

Under the Roadmap, we aim to strengthen customer preference for digital payments with at least 50% of the total volume of retail payments transacted digitally and at least 70% of adult Filipinos owning a formal account. We also want to see the provision of more innovative digital financial services that are truly responsive to the needs of consumers.

We are optimistic that we will achieve these bold targets with the concerted efforts and collaboration of the BSP, the industry, and the government.  

As an example, the progress in the ongoing PhilSys registration has resulted in the onboarding of almost 3.8 million unbanked Philsys registrants as part of the Philippine Statistics Authority’s partnership with the Land Bank of the Philippines.

Under BSP’s directive and guidance, the payment services industry led by the Philippine Payments Management, Inc. (PPMI) held a pilot launch of the QR Ph for Person-to-Merchant (P2M) payments last April 30 2021. 

With QR Ph P2M, consumers need not memorize details of their bank accounts as the relevant information will now be securely stored in the QR code, thus facilitating easy and convenient retail digital payment transactions.

The coronavirus pandemic has quickened our digitalization agenda. It highlighted the significance of cashless and digital transactions—not just for convenience, but as a necessity. 

In fact last year, at the height of the lockdown, the Department of Social Welfare and Development implemented account-based distribution of the 2nd tranche of the social amelioration program with participating financial service providers. 

This has resulted in a speedy and efficient distribution of aid to our most affected pandemic-hit countrymen. 

We have also seen the quantum jump in the use of digital payments as indicated by the exponential rise in InstaPay and Pesonet transactions. 

Yet, as digitalization gains momentum, the pandemic also highlighted digital connectivity as a basic need for a truly inclusive new economy. Internet access, or the lack of it, has been a constant challenge, especially in the countryside.  

Thus, the BSP could not overemphasize the significance of the recently issued Executive Order No. 127 by President Rodrigo Roa Duterte to our digital financial inclusion agenda. 

The policy now allows non-enfranchised but duly registered internet service providers (ISP) and value added service providers (VASP) to directly access satellite systems to build and operate broadband facilities to offer internet services. 

By promoting greater competition and investment in the country’s satellite broadband services market, this new policy can bridge the massive internet infrastructure gaps in rural and remote communities within a short period of time. 

The BSP, and the Financial Inclusion Steering Committee which I chair, are honored to have played a role in the passage of this new policy.

The BSP has benefitted greatly from the paper of The Asia Foundation and the Better Broadband Alliance on the country’s ICT policy landscape and emerging technologies, including satellite broadband. 

I also wish to acknowledge Monetary Board Member (MBM) Bruce Tolentino for his proactive stance in taking up this initiative to support the furtherance of the BSP’s financial inclusion initiative. 

We have seen the potential of satellite broadband in the experience of Bank Rakyat Indonesia (BRI), whom we invited to grace this webinar. 

And finally, we thank the Department of Information and Communications Technology under the leadership of Secretary Gregorio Honasan III, and the National Telecommunications Commission (NTC) under the leadership of Commissioner Gamaliel Cordoba for supporting this game-changing reform initiative.

We envisioned this webinar as a venue for our financial service providers to recognize and seize the opportunities that the new policy brings for their digital financial inclusion strategy.  

Lastly, it is our hope that the participants here become active advocates for policy reforms and programs toward reliable and affordable internet access for all. 

Before I end, allow me to thank all the resource persons who have accepted our invitation to share their knowledge and experiences. 

Let me also thank The Asia Foundation for co-organizing this webinar with the BSP and for its valuable work in promoting our shared goal of improving the lives of Filipinos.

I wish you all a wonderful and meaningful discussion ahead. Thank you and a pleasant morning to everyone.​

Title: BSP Governor Benjamin E. Diokno's Message of Support for the RBAP and RCBC MOU Signing
Occasion: RBAP and RCBC MOU Signing
Speaker: BSP Governor Benjamin E. Diokno
Transcription:
The BSP welcomes the collaboration of RCBC and RBAP using the BANKONNECT, an innovative product that will help boost current efforts towards digitalization of financial services and further increase financial inclusion. 

As you all know, the BSP is proactively working on these two objectives prominently indicated in our Digital Payments Transformation Roadmap (DPTR) for 2020-2023. 

Using the Roadmap, we would like to achieve strengthened customer preference for digital payments, which we intend to pursue by increasing the volume of digital payments to 50%, and for 70% of the adult population to own a transaction account in order to see financial inclusion for a great majority of the population. 

We also advocate to see more innovative and responsive digital financial services, which will be achieved by fostering the innovation-driven use of consumer data for product development. 

The BANKONNECT, a “banking-as-a-service” (BaaS) digital platform, suitably responds to our DPTR objectives, and is truly a welcome concerted effort from RCBC and the rural banking industry. 

It is also a testament to RCBC’s continuous support of the BSP's efforts to modernize the digital retail payments landscape since the launch of the National Retail Payment System several years back. 

This laudable effort towards digital transformation has also been recognized internationally in 2020 as RCBC was named as the Philippines’ “Most Innovative Internet Banking Service Provider” by the London-based, The Global Economics Limited, and the country’s “Best Digital Bank” by the Hong Kong-based institutional investment magazine Alpha Southeast Asia. 

The BSP recognizes that innovation is truly imperative for today’s banking. There are growing operational cost pressures coming from running a day-to-day business, intense competition within the industry, and fast-changing customer preferences and expectations.

The BANKONNECT, a “banking-as-a-service” (BaaS) digital platform, suitably responds to our DPTR objectives, and is truly a welcome concerted effort from RCBC and the rural banking industry. 

It is also a testament to RCBC’s continuous support of the BSP's efforts to modernize the digital retail payments landscape since the launch of the National Retail Payment System several years back. 

This laudable effort towards digital transformation has also been recognized internationally in 2020 as RCBC was named as the Philippines’ “Most Innovative Internet Banking Service Provider” by the London-based, The Global Economics Limited, and the country’s “Best Digital Bank” by the Hong Kong-based institutional investment magazine Alpha Southeast Asia. 

The BSP recognizes that innovation is truly imperative for today’s banking. There are growing operational cost pressures coming from running a day-to-day business, intense competition within the industry, and fast-changing customer preferences and expectations. 

As you know, the Covid-19 pandemic has also accelerated the public’s preference for contactless digital transactions, with consumers now less likely to go out of their way to brave traffic and health safety risks to do payments and banking transactions in person. 

These circumstances thus present an opportunity for consumers to more likely embrace digital payments services. A trend that is expected to last even after the pandemic.

This significant development offers tremendous opportunities to transform banking better, particularly in terms of offering products and services that are customized to the specific needs and personalized banking solutions responsive to each customer’s preferences.

Open banking is ushering in an era of productive collaboration between banks, non-banks, fintechs and consumers, as compared to the outdated model of competition among banks serving a market where products and services are definitive rather than responsive. 

The rapid rise of technology and the internet expanded the reach of the market for financial services, which rightly, now includes all income classes of the society.

It has also altered the tastes and preferences of consumers, thus raising the bar of expectations and demand for more innovative and responsive financial services. 

This bodes well for smaller financial institutions like rural banks which can now take advantage of BaaS to increase their customer base, offer innovative products and services, as well as increase their revenues and profit. 

Open banking can enable ‘last mile’ providers like rural banks to realize their full potential as agents of financial inclusion. 

We are excited to see rural banks catering to the unique customer banking needs of a rural customer thru BANKONNECT. We will be more than happy to see rural banks provide customized financial products and services that are tailor-made to the business banking needs of micro, small and medium enterprises, particularly those engaged in agriculture and agri-value chains. 

We will be very supportive to see rural banks provide customer-centric banking services that will offer conveniences and safety in payments, remittances, and bills payments, among others.

As Open Banking continues to develop, flourish and deliver results, it is useful to keep financial inclusion in mind. 

The BSP certainly welcomes collaborations in the financial services industry that will enable banks to work together in delivering innovative and responsive products and services for the unserved and underserved.  

Congratulations to RBAP and RCBC, and we look forward to the successful implementation of the BANKONNECT.​

Title: Message of BSP Governor Benjamin E. Diokno for the "Saya ng Buhay, Level App" Campaign
Occasion: konek2CARD FB Live Event
Speaker: BSP Governor Benjamin E. Diokno
Transcription:
​

A good day to the members of CARD Mutually Reinforcing Institutions led by Founding Chairman, Dr. Jaime Alip, and to the officers, personnel, and clients of CARD Bank, Incorporated led by President and Chief Executive Officer, Ms. Marivic Austria.

We extend our congratulations for reaching one million registered konek2CARD users.  CARD Bank has been a longtime partner and champion of financial inclusion, and we are glad to mark this achievement with you today. 

The growth of digital financial services in general highlights the necessity and advantages of digitalization.  For one, going digital enabled Filipinos to transact at the safety and convenience of their homes during this pandemic.

We were fortunate to witness the beginnings of konek2CARD, along with digital cash machines and cash agent operations – all of which were on introductory rollout only a few years ago. 

The significant gains in a short period reveal the vast opportunities available to financial service providers when they maximize enabling policies and adopt an innovative, financial inclusion-oriented mindset.

We thus set our goals higher and build on the momentum of the current digital wave.  By adopting digital financial inclusion as a priority, we now focus on empowering Filipinos to ensure they thrive in the New Economy.

Guided by the Digital Payments Transformation Roadmap 2020-2023, we are advancing digitalization initiatives that will have practical benefits and transformative impact through and beyond the pandemic. 

Let me share some of them. 

With key government and industry partners, we recently launched the QR Ph Payment-to-Merchant pilot to boost digital payments and digitalization of our small businesses.  We envision its usage to extend all the way to the low-income segment.

Sa pagpapalawig ng paggamit ng QR Ph, maari tayong magbayad sa tindahan, palengke, pati ng pamasahe gamit ang ating cellphone.  Hindi na kailangan ng barya sa umaga, sakto pa ang bayad.

With the Philippine Identification System or PhilSys, every Filipino will have a reliable proof of identity.  The PhilSys effectively dispenses with documentary requirements and makes the onboarding process faster and less costly.

Sa pamamagitan ng PhilSys, maaring mag-avail ng bank account at ibang financial services gamit ang ating PhilID.  Hindi na kailangan ng ibang ID. Mapapadali rin ang pagtanggap ng ayuda mula sa gobyerno.   

We recognize the need for reliable mobile and internet connection to bring financial services within easy reach of Filipinos, especially those in the last mile. 

Thus, we are pushing to mainstream technologies like satellite internet and open doors to more players in our broadband market. 

These reforms efforts specifically aim to make digital financial services affordable and accessible to the public.

Layunin nating magkaroon ng maasahan at murang mobile and internet connection para maraming pang Pilipino, saan man sa bansa, ang mahikayat na gumamit ng digital financial services.

While the COVID-19 pandemic has disrupted the way we live, work, and play, it also created exceptional opportunities to boost digital financial inclusion in the country. 

The phenomenal growth of the konek2CARD clientele amid the pandemic sends an unmistakeable message to the industry at large; And that is: financial inclusion makes good business sense. 

It also shows how digitalization can improve the lives of the common man. Think of a housewife who can now get micro-insurance with just a few clicks on the phone; or a farmer who can now check his account while working in the field.[*]

Indeed, by embracing our financial inclusion mission, we can improve lives and create shared prosperity in ordinary and extraordinary times.

And so, to the officers and personnel of CARD Bank, keep up the outstanding work. Thank you and good day.


[*] Examples based on an actual interview of CARD Bank clients conducted in August 2019, in Barangay Manggahan, Dolores, Quezon Province.​

Title: Opening Remarks of BSP Governor Benjamin E. Diokno during The BSP Corporate Financial Trends  Survey (CFTS) 2021 CFTS Information Session
Occasion: BSP Corporate Financial Trends  Survey (CFTS) 2021 CFTS Information Session
Speaker: BSP Governor Benjamin E. Diokno
Transcription:
​

Our partner respondents from the private sector, guests, colleagues, ladies and gentlemen, good morning!

It gives me great pleasure to welcome all of you in this important event – The BSP Corporate Financial Trends Survey (CFTS) Information Session.

I say important because this endeavor aims to address one of the most pressing issues that policymakers are facing today, the need for timely, reliable, granular and accurate financial data on the country’s corporate sector.

As most of you here would agree, a necessary condition for any sound decision is getting the right information. 

Our ability to formulate the appropriate policy largely depends on our capacity to correctly identify causal relationship between two or more variables. 

This, in turn, depends on our ability to access and generate relevant, timely and accurate statistics.

In this regard, the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP) conducts the CFTS to gather financial data from the domestic economy’s important driver of growth – the corporate sector. 

Our goal is to improve our understanding of the recent financial trends and conditions of various industries. 

In particular, the CFTS aims to gather more granular data on corporates’ sources of funds, spending activities, and profitability. 

This survey helps address some of the data gaps the BSP encounters due to long lags in financial reporting of private firms. 

The availability of more granular data enhances our capacity to undertake the macrofinancial surveillance necessary in pursuing policies that foster monetary and financial stability. 

The BSP recognizes that monetary policy causes changes in the macroeconomic and financial market conditions, which in turn, affect corporates’ borrowing behavior, investments and production activities.

Thus, having information on the corporate production and leverage allows us to effectively assess the transmission mechanism of monetary policy and its impact on the real economy.

Moreover, developments in the corporate sector could have important implications on the overall stability of the financial system. 

Literature and experience have shown that balance sheet weaknesses and excessive leverage in the corporate sector could exacerbate the costs of economic and financial crises. 

For instance, in the aftermath of the Global Financial Crisis (GFC), corporate balance sheet weaknesses and high levels of debt contributed to a more sluggish and protracted recovery of the global economy. 

Clearly, the stability of the corporate sector is vital to the stability of the whole economy. The sector accounts for a large share of employment and output. 

As such, the monitoring and understanding of the financial conditions of corporations are vital in the early detection of weaknesses in the sector and in the prevention of these weaknesses to develop into a full-blown crisis. 

The information we gather from the survey would allow us to identify potential vulnerabilities of the corporate sector. 

In turn, these could lead to the formulation of policies that would help safeguard macroeconomic and financial stability.

This is particularly important as the domestic economy, including the corporate sector, continues to grapple with the challenges of the Covid-19 pandemic. 

Our preliminary assessment indicates that the disruptions in business operations due to the COVID-19 pandemic and the lockdown measures implemented by the National Government (NG) resulted to a sharp fall in corporate income. 

In turn, this weakened markedly the ability of firms to service their debt. 

Based on available 2020 annual reports of PSE-listed firms, the exposure of corporates to the pandemic resulted in some sectors showing vulnerabilities in their operating performance, liquidity and leverage. 

In terms of profitability, most firms from industrial, holdings, services and financial sectors reported declines in revenues.

The 2020 GDP growth numbers show that many sectors, such as, accommodation and food service, transportation and storage, mining and quarrying, real estate, construction, manufacturing, education, and professional and business services have contracted.

Lower corporate incomes could potentially expose firms to balance sheet weaknesses and vulnerabilities such as increased leverage and reduced ability to service debts. 

It is therefore imperative that regulators closely monitor the borrowing behavior of corporates and their capability to service their existing loans during the pandemic.  

This is to allow us to accurately assess the magnitude and extent of the pandemic’s impact on the country’s corporate sector, and in turn, measure the corporate sector’s spillovers and spillbacks to the financial system and the economy.

Moving forward, the conduct of the Corporate Financial Trends Survey will serve as an important tool to accurately assess the state of the country’s corporate sector. 

The survey would allow the BSP to conduct a more intensified surveillance to enhance its monitoring of corporate financial conditions in a more comprehensive and timely manner. 

Moreover, results of the survey will enhance the BSP’s assessment of various corporate exposures and vulnerabilities and their sensitivity to shocks such as supply-side disruptions, and changes in financial market conditions.

Indeed, the CFTS is a step further to developing a corporate sector database necessary for formulating appropriate policies that help promote a stronger and more stable macroeconomy and financial system. 

In closing, I thank all our participants for attending this information session and for your invaluable support to this important undertaking. 

Welcome once again and good morning. ​​​

Title: Policymaking in the Time of COVID-19: Insights from BSP’s Experience
Occasion: UBS OneASEAN Conference
Speaker: BSP Governor Benjamin E. Diokno
Transcription:
​

To the officers and staff of UBS, and to all the participants of this virtual conference, a pleasant afternoon. 

As the Philippines continues the battle against COVID-19 at the tail-end of this crisis, the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP) remains one with the government and the entire Filipino people in pushing the economy toward full recovery.

My presentation will be divided into three parts: 

• First – the BSP’s policy interventions amid the pandemic;

• Second –  policy challenges faced by the BSP and our responses; and 

• Third – outlook for the Philippine economy

On policy interventions…

Ample monetary and fiscal space enabled the Philippines to aggressively respond to the crisis. 

On the fiscal side, the government debt-to-GDP ratio was only 39.6 percent back in 2019. The bulk or 68 percent of government debt was denominated in local currency. Moreover, with fiscal prudence and tax reforms, revenue effort and tax effort rose to 16.1 and 14.5 percent, respectively, the highest level since 1998. 

Amid this backdrop, the government had resources to implement Bayanihan I and II, the laws on wide-ranging COVID-response measures, including relief for the most vulnerable. 

On the monetary front, the BSP had ample policy space, which was in part a result of a tightening cycle in 2018 -- when it raised the policy rate by a total of 175 basis points to 4.75 percent -- to rein in inflation pressures and anchor the public’s inflation expectations. 

The monetary space allowed the BSP to implement a series of unprecedented easing and liquidity-enhancing measures to mitigate the economic impact of the pandemic. 

The BSP’s COVID interventions fall under three categories:

First were measures to boost market confidence on availability of credit resources. 

The BSP reduced the policy rate by a total of 200 basis points (bps) to help bring down the cost of borrowing, shore up market confidence, and address liquidity concerns in the financial system. 

The BSP also cut the reserve requirement to increase the volume of loanable funds.

The BSP reduced the policy rate by a total of 200 basis points (bps) to help bring down the cost of borrowing, shore up market confidence, and address liquidity concerns in the financial system.
