I encourage the industry to actively provide inputs to the sequencing of priority areas in the plan. A vibrant capital market can serve as an alternative source of financing for the industry and powerfully complements bank lending.

In Closing

As I close, let me reiterate the truths I have shared so far…  First, economic conditions are favourable and allow for robust lending and leasing operations…  Second, we have in place, a sound and evolving legal and regulatory framework to ensure prudent and responsible financing practices…  Third, we urge players in the industry to recognise and serve markets - especially the MSME sector… seize opportunities not just for profit but to actively participate in financial inclusion efforts… leverage on digital technology… and engage in continuous training and development…  Fourth, industry players would benefit from collaboration and cooperation… Fifth and finally, continuous dialogue and a healthy partnership between regulators and the regulated would result in greater industry support, rationalised regulations and national development. We encourage you to help us in this regard.

Rounding these points up, I will end with sage advice … (again from Shakespeare)… The world’s pre-eminent dramatist and poet said, “Our doubts are traitors, and make us lose the good we oft might win, by fearing to attempt.”

Given the crucial role we play in economic development and even in financial inclusion… Let us not fear to attempt.  It is our pleasure in the BSP to stand with you, friends and colleagues of PFAI,  to endeavour to believe in the great strides we can make together for the betterment of the  business environment … for the credit, financing and leasing industries… for MSMEs… for our nation.

Thank you for your kind attention.  Congratulations to your new officers.  Mabuhay ang ating mahal na bansang Pilipinas.

Title: Imagining New Possibilities: Embracing Challenges and Recognizing Opportunities in Microfinance
Occasion: Microfinance Council of the Philippines, Inc. (MCPI) Annual Conference
Speaker: BSP Gov. Nestor A. Espenilla, Jr.
Transcription:
Thank you for the opportunity to close this important conference. I am particularly heartened by your theme, “Embracing new milestones and challenges in Philippine Microfinance.”

This choice of theme represents a positive mindset for growth…A resolve to keep moving forward. This outlook is fully encouraged by the Bangko Sentral. 

The reality is that the operating landscape is rapidly evolving.  We at the BSP foresee significant change in the way financial services – even micro-finance services – will be delivered.  Thus, its players – the regulators and supervisors included – must adapt…not just for success… but even for survival for some.

Industry watchers say that the area of financial services is ripe for disruption.  What an ominous forecast!  Disruption is synonymous to disturbance…an unwelcome and often sudden interruption of a normal and comfortable way of doing things….

What are industry watchers saying? Basically, there is awareness that with rapid digital innovation, new business models and market players have, and will continue to emerge.  The nature of competition is being changed and there is a need to keep up. 

Harking back to your theme… you have declared through this conference that challenges in Philippine microfinance are welcome!  They are to be embraced!  Good!  This is the name of the game.  What will make us rise to meet the challenges? 

Motivation for Taking Microfinance to the Next Level

Several years back, Muhammad Yunus was consumed by a revolutionary idea that challenged mainstream thinking.  He believed that the poorest can be enabled to use credit productively and… (an even more surprising proposition to the majority:)… that they would be able to repay it! 

Luckily, Mr. Yunus’ idea transcended from theory to reality.  At the heart of his bold idea, was a passion that I believe, needs constant rekindling. To push microfinance ever forward, we need to honestly examine our dreams for the poor in this country.

Our dreams have to be audacious and ambitious enough to compel us to overcome inertia… rethink our approaches… and aggressively seek opportunities.  Are we bold enough to imagine new and greater possibilities for the poor we serve?…Or are we perfectly content with business as usual? 

Income inequality remains a challenge.  Poverty incidence stands at 21.6%.   21.9 million Filipinos survive on a monthly income below P1,813.  This poverty is more pronounced in the rural areas. Farmers, fisherfolk and workers in the informal sector registered high poverty incidence rates of 34.3%,  34% and  25%, respectively - all higher than the national average.

As BSP Governor (I assumed the post early this month), and even when I was Deputy Governor of the Supervision and Examination Sector (a post I held since 2005), people would often ask me how the BSP addresses poverty.

This very noble task is not directly in our mandate. This is surprising to many. This is not what Central Banks do…  Rather, what the BSP does is to foster an economic and financial environment to promote the alleviation of poverty.  Our charter allows us to craft monetary policies and conduct sound banking supervision so that our supervised entities exercise discipline, and so businesses are empowered to make informed decisions and plan.  When businesses are able to do this, they are able to expand.  Employment increases.

Jeffrey Sachs, a celebrated economist said that the problem of inequality stems from a failure of moral insight and moral imagination. In the BSP, we are aware of the limits of our Charter… this is why we constantly apply creativity and conviction in creating a regulatory framework that encourages an ecosystem where the poor are granted increased access to and usage of financial services. Not having the express mandate to address poverty did not stop us in the BSP from adopting financial inclusion as a flagship advocacy.  It is for us a compelling purpose.

How much more for you…for this audience?  I believe that the capacity to imagine new possibilities for the poor runs very deep in the DNA of the microfinance industry.  With bold thinking, a solid plan, and execution discipline, you, our industry players, can take microfinance to the next level.

How Microfinance Can Be Taken to the Next Level

To take microfinance to the next level, there are several opportunities that the industry should not overlook.  I will mention three (3) circumstances in the operating environment, which I hope you will recognize and seize as opportunities: First, the democratization of technology; Second, the BSP’s digital finance policy package; and Third, the intensified focus by the national government on rural development.
 
(1)  Democratization of Technology

Digital technology enables efficiencies and scale in financial service delivery.  This is a well-recognized fact. But far from being alienating, technology is fast becoming democratized. Mobile devices are cheaper.  There are digital platforms and cloud computing services.  Social media is familiar to and used by an increasing number of people. 

Technology, once available only to the wealthy, is now within reach. The sooner we realize this, the sooner we can adopt digital technology as a strategy enabler. Our inability or refusal to use technology can undermine our efforts to deepen the impact of microfinance and drive financial inclusion. 

(2) BSP’s Digital Finance Policy Package

The BSP recognizes the power of digital technology and has adopted a policy package geared to expand the digital finance ecosystem.

First in BSP’s policy package is the National Retail Payment System (NRPS). The NRPS is a regulatory framework promoting the efficiency and safety of retail payments in the country, as characterized by the increased usage of digital payments. The NRPS is a platform to serve the needs of millions of Filipinos who remain outside the formal financial system. Central to this initiative are payment schemes that will facilitate seamless, convenient, affordable and secure fund transfers between bank and e-money accounts. 

We have identified two priority payment schemes under the NRPS: the “PESO Net” for batch fund transfers, and “InstaPay” for 24/7, real-time low-value transfers. PESO Net and InstaPay are expected to catalyse the delivery of digital finance products to serve the diverse needs of the users.
 
The second piece in our digital finance policy package is the use of cash agents.  Under Circular 940, retail outlets like convenience stores, pharmacies and pawnshops can now become a bank’s cash agents.  Cash agents are low-cost, low-key touchpoints through which bank clients can open an account, make real-time deposits and withdrawals, receive loan proceeds and pay loan amortization and bills.  This facilitates development of an expansive network of access points that will allow users, particularly the low-income segment, to move from cash to digital and vice versa.

Another key policy initiative to promote inclusive digital finance is on the risk-based KYC.  Lack of a valid ID and similar issues faced by the low-income segment should not be barriers to opening a financial account.  That is why under Circular 950, we facilitate adoption of streamlined and risk-based KYC procedures. For instance, covered institutions are now allowed to offer a restricted account to micro-entrepreneurs even without valid IDs.

This notwithstanding, the BSP has been working closely with the national government for the adoption of a government-run biometric-based ID system.  This initiative is envisioned to facilitate the provision of more efficient, transparent and equitable government services, as well as financial services.  A universal digital ID system will bring millions of unbanked and previously disenfranchised Filipinos to participate in the digital finance ecosystem.

With BSP’s digital finance policy package, banks and other financial service providers now have a better platform to expand their reach and deliver better and cheaper products to their clients through digital solutions.

(3) Government Focus On Rural Development
 
Another opportunity in the operating landscape is government’s intensified focus on rural and MSME development. This matters as investments in crucial infrastructure like roads and irrigation systems support agriculture and local businesses.  Investments in these sectors improve the productivity and risk profile of your target market - rural workers and microentrepreneurs.
 
In parallel, the financial infrastructure is also being strengthened with the planned adoption of an enhanced credit guarantee system for agriculture and MSMEs.  These market-enabling interventions will make rural financing a fertile ground for service providers looking to expand their client base.

How These Opportunities Apply

I believe there are three crucial things institutions need to develop in taking advantage of these opportunities in the operating environment. 
 
First, your organizations must use digital innovations strategically. I refer not just to your IT infrastructure but also to your organizational strategy, culture and human resource skills.   Yes, this will necessarily involve financial and investment commitment.  But the gains will be worth it and there are cost-effective approaches that can be explored, such as outsourcing and cloud-based services.  Strategic industry partnerships, and market utility arrangements can also be considered to drive down the cost of IT requirements.
 
I can understand how some institutions might resist digital solutions, thinking that it will mean abandoning a high-touch client engagement approach. This is not necessarily the case.  In fact, digital solutions can complement and enhance this high-touch approach. To make the change, strong leadership support, a compelling vision, and strategy for the digital transformation journey are needed.
 
Second, good governance is needed. The viability and sustainability of your institutions will be determined ultimately by the quality of your corporate governance, which the Microfinance NGO Act aims to promote.  This is important not just as a matter of regulatory compliance but because good governance is a strategic asset that will drive value to your businesses and your clients.

Finally, your organizations need to develop customer-centricity.  This is what will ultimately set you apart from competition. We serve clients best when we give them products that fully meet their needs, improve their financial resilience, and reduce their vulnerability.

To do this, we must first understand them, their motivations, their values, and other factors that drive their behavior. Without this understanding and relationship, we will be ineffective in persuading them to avail of financial products like savings and microinsurance to make them more financially resilient.  We must educate our clients to avail of more than just credit.  As Jeff Bezos of Amazon puts it, “even when they don’t know it, customers want something better.”   For the Microfinance Industry, ultimate satisfaction comes from being able to give customers something better so that they would have better lives.

Launching of 15th Citi Microentrepreneurship Award

That Microfinance betters lives is not just rhetoric.  Some of the real results and stories will be featured tonight as we launch the 15th Citi Microentrepreneurship Award or the CMA. 

CMA honors microentrepreneurs who have demonstrated the power of microfinance through their improved quality of life and contribution to the community.  In 2002, Citi Foundation, MCPI and the Bangko Sentral conceptualized the CMA as a vehicle to inspire microentrepreneurs in the country and promote microfinance as a poverty reduction tool.

Aside from cash incentives, winners are also given entrepreneurship training, life and health insurance, and technological support.

Later, you will be hearing from Honie Navor who was last year’s National Winner, and the youngest ever at that.  Honie started her business as a tombstone maker with P1,000.  She was just 18 years old.  In less than 10 years, she was able to grow it into a full-blown distribution business of tiles, granites and other stones.  She is proof that with determination, smarts and access to finance, one can work his or her way towards a better life. 

The story of Honie and the countless others like her is an inspiration to other Filipino microentrepreneurs striving to give their families a decent life and a brighter future. For the microfinance community, their stories are reminders of the value and nobility of our work.  You are, after all, in the business of nation building and I am proud to be with you here today, imagining new possibilities.
 
Maraming salamat at mabuhay ang microfinance!

Title: Of Becoming Advocates - Partnering for a Stronger Legal Environment for Banking and Finance
Place: Big Function Room, Manila Golf Club
Occasion: Luncheon Fellowship Reception of the Philippine Bar Association, Inc.
Speaker: BSP Governor Nestor A. Espenilla, Jr.
Transcription:
Philippine Bar Association (PBA) President Fina Cuesta-Tantuico, officers, trustees and members of the PBA, my BSP colleagues (led by our General Counsel Elmore Capule),  esteemed guests, ladies and gentlemen, good afternoon!

Once upon a time, I was a first-year law student.  Sitting in U.P. Diliman’s famed Malcolm Hall, I was both thrilled and terrified… Professors used the Socratic Method and wielded it over our young idealistic heads like Damocles’ sword…  Remember that Fina? (Fina was my batchmate).

For all the horrors inflicted on law students, the Socratic Method, was, and still is, widely regarded as a valuable tool to train one to – “think like a lawyer”.

But how do lawyers think?  As my father and my eldest daughter, Jackie, are both lawyers, and as the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas has one hundred sixty (160) lawyers in its employ (with a significant number of our Departments and Offices headed by lawyers) – I have made observations through the years. 

A lawyer’s thought process is predominated by rules, precedent and authority. I have noticed too that lawyers engage in continuous internal questioning.  Lawyers debate with themselves (and others) until a contradiction or flaw in reasoning is exposed (and they are quite triumphant when it is!). Parang may built-in Socratic method. The flaw, once identified, is addressed. Tama ba? 

This is a good thing.  It is good because engaging in internal (and actual) continuing dialogue is not about “just being argumentative.” Rather, this type of discourse allows one to closely examine if a belief or a proposed solution can withstand scrutiny given different assumptions and premises, alternative situations, and changing times. 

Laying the Foundation

Economists are the same way, always considering “one hand” and “the other.” It is said that U.S. President Truman once demanded that he be given a “one-handed economist,” implying that one could not be found… Economists and Central Bankers, like lawyers, play-out different scenarios before making decisions… carefully and sometimes aggressively.

This similar way of thinking, and the complementary roles that we play in society, make us – the BSP and the legal community – ideal partners to help move our country forward.

The Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas was established as an independent central monetary authority in 1993 by Republic Act No. 7653. This independence or autonomy does not mean isolation.  Our constitutional mandate is to craft “policy direction in the areas of money, banking, and credit” ….as well as to supervise “the operations of banks and exercise regulatory powers over other institutions performing similar functions” … Our policies and programs affect the national economy and Filipino lives.  Thus, we believe that to perform our mandate better, there must be clear understanding and support for our functions.  For this, we count on your partnership.   

I will present an overview of BSP’s policy directions and reform agenda specifically with respect to the legal framework in the following format: (1) statement of relevant facts, (2) issues; and (3) the decision.  Facts, issues, decision. Familiar format di ba? Don’t worry, this is a digested version.  And there will be no graded recitation.

Relevant facts.  My predecessor, former Governor Amando Tetangco, Jr. and the highly competent Team BSP kept the house in order. I am happy to report that the Philippines continues to be one of the fastest growing economies in the region, with growth anchored on sound macroeconomic policies.
 
The banking system is fundamentally sound and stable. It is well-positioned to further support the growing needs of the domestic economy. Key performance indicators show stronger bank balance sheets with a steady growth in assets, loans, deposits and capital. Banks continue in profitability with an improved ability to absorb shocks and contain imbalances at the firm and industry levels. 

What are issues? The questions of special relevance to this forum are: whether or not the current legal framework is attuned to the changing economic and financial environment… whether or not it is poised to protect our earlier gains… and whether or not it can promote sustainable economic growth.

In legal cases, issues are always framed this way: “whether or not”… answerable by “yes” or “no.”… But because I have evolved to be an economist, my answer is not “yes,” neither is it “no”. My answer is, “we have been working and will continue to work with, and work on the legal framework.” Fervently, with you: our legal practitioners, Congress, the academe, and other stakeholders as our partners.

Legislative Framework and the Changing Environment

Oliver Wendell Holmes, Jr. said, "The life of the law has not been logic; it has been experience." The law must necessarily evolve according to "the felt necessities of the times, prevalent moral and political theories (and) intuitions of public policy”.

And how fast the world is evolving!  From the time I first joined the Central Bank, almost thirty-six (36) years ago, to this present day, the economic landscape has changed so much and at such a fast pace!

Markets are now more closely interconnected. There are implications on how financial stability must be secured.  The operating environment has shifted. Technological developments and digitization has redefined how markets operate. There are cyber-security risks to consider.  There is social media to monitor. Even preferences are changing.  We have a new breed of financial consumers who are young, upwardly mobile, and technology-savvy.  It is a more impatient and demanding consumer base. To service this base, there is enhanced competition.  There is globalization, regional integration. Information in itself is a prized, valued, and fiercely protected commodity. In considering legislative initiatives, we must have these new trends in mind.

In the BSP, we are conscious of this and are working to provide an enabling regulatory environment for fin-tech while balancing the need to maintain prudent credit underwriting and technology risk management and to uphold information security standards. 

The BSP supports a Senate Bill on Cybercrime Prevention which redefines offenses of aiding, abetting and attempting to commit cybercrime; imposing a higher penalty for violations committed using information and communications technology; and the addition of a provision that prosecution under the law shall be without prejudice to liability under the Revised Penal Code or other special laws.

The BSP also endorses enactment of a Payment Systems Act for a safer, more efficient and reliable operation of payment systems to control systemic risk.  Some key proposals include granting the BSP formal authority over payment systems with authority to coordinate with other government agencies and overseers of payment systems of other countries to facilitate safe, efficient and reliable cross-border payment transactions.

To address the global community’s call for a more transparent financial system while protecting the rights of bank depositors from unwarranted intrusion, and to enable more effective investigation of questionable actions and the prosecution of money launderers, the BSP endorses amendment of the law on Secrecy of Bank Deposits and the Foreign Currency Deposit Act. 

Recent events have also highlighted the urgency to amend the Anti-Money Laundering Act (AMLA): to strengthen the BSP’s authority to look into deposits when checking AMLA compliance; to allow disclosure to BSP of Covered Transaction and Suspicious Transaction Report information; to designate BSP as supervising authority of foreign exchange dealers, money changers, and remittance and transfer companies for AMLA purposes; to increase the amount of administrative penalties for AMLA violations and to spread a wider and more effective net to include casinos and other non-banks among AMLA covered entities.  (Daming information nito… siguro puede pang MCLE compliance.)

Legislative Initiative:  to Protect Earlier Gains

Kidding aside, ladies and gentlemen, despite challenges in the external environment, the Philippine economy continues to expand. Our growth in the first quarter of 2017 was characterized by manageable inflation and more than adequate gross international reserves. Overseas Filipino remittances, revenue from the business process outsourcing sector and tourism income contribute to higher consumption spending. 

Solid macroeconomic fundamentals are buffers against potential external shocks and the BSP continues to strengthen its framework for financial risk surveillance.  We do this with tools within the limits of our present charter, Republic Act No. 7653.  These tools are twenty-four (24) years old!

To strengthen these tools, supplement mechanisms for the protection of depositor savings, ensure the smooth flow of financial system transactions, as well as enhance its corporate viability, the amendment of the BSP Charter is on the very top of our legislative agenda.
  
Republic Act No. 7653 was passed more than 2 decades ago. As I have mentioned, the economic and financial landscape here and overseas has changed significantly in scale, scope, reach, and complexity. There is thus urgency in having the proposed amendments passed to enable BSP to formulate and implement even better and more timely policies and programs to achieve price stability.  Amendments will allow BSP to act even more swiftly to ensure that supervised institutions are doing business in a safe and sound manner with a healthy discipline for risk-taking activities. 

Salient in our proposed charter amendments are: the formal recognition of financial stability as a BSP mandate; oversight of the payment and settlement systems; authority to require data and information from non-banks and enhanced supervisory and regulatory powers, among others.
  
We believe that a stronger BSP will translate to a more stable and resilient macroeconomy and a robust Philippine financial system that is attractive to investments and businesses to generate employment and promote inclusive growth.  We believe this is how the legislative framework can improve to protect earlier and future gains.

Legislative Reforms to Promote Sustained and Inclusive Growth

At the heart of my governorship is the desire to bring BSP closer to the public it serves.  In the BSP, we firmly believe that for economic growth and progress to be more meaningful, its benefits, the products that allow people to save, borrow, invest and insure risks must be made available to them.

In the BSP, we have reformed the regulatory framework for allowing this to happen… to increase financial access and usage points for our countrymen, beyond brick and mortar bank buildings. We collaborate and cooperate with stakeholders from the private and public sectors to build a more inclusive financial system, focusing on increasing financial literacy and education and consumer protection.  What was once only a flagship advocacy has now become a compelling purpose with departments within the BSP created for this very end:  the Inclusive Finance Advocacy Office, the Financial Consumer Protection Department and the Economic and Financial Learning Center.

We have worked with Congress to push bills to promote inclusive financial growth. We were heartened with the passing of Republic Act No. 10744, granting juridical personality to existing and future Credit Surety Fund Cooperatives, so that the credit-worthiness of micro, small and medium enterprises would be increased and so that they would be able to obtain loans from banks.

We recently launched the Personal Equity and Retirement Account System under Republic Act No. 9505. The PERA promotes capital market development and long-term savings mobilization, allowing persons with a capacity to contract (and with Tax Identification Numbers) to voluntarily open personal accounts with banks and invest in certain products to save more for their retirement.

But there is still much to be done with respect to financial inclusion.  The BSP is pushing for the Bill on the Enactment of Islamic Banking in the Philippines.  We aim to develop a suitable and clear legal and regulatory framework to promote a truly responsive Islamic banking system that positively complements the existing conventional banking system. 

The Decision: Becoming Advocates

What now?  How can we be partners in working for a more enabling and responsive legal environment that will foster a safer, more efficient, reliable and inclusive financial system?

I began with a narrative of my first-year law experience.  Some of you may wonder why I did not continue with law school… Even then I was already a young economist of the Central Bank.  I recognized a trade-off.  I was a working student and law school was taking a toll on the pursuit of my chosen career.  I had to choose where I wanted to excel.  And I made my strategic decision… Recognizing trade-offs, deciding and acting on costs and benefits, we do this every day, perhaps every hour. 

I would like to close with the message that yes, there is a trade-off in working towards a more responsive legal framework.  But we must focus on the gains… gains for not just one sector or group… but gains for the nation as a whole.  There is a cost to financial exclusion and a very clear and meaningful benefit to financial inclusion.

I urge you… as fellow professionals who engage in meaningful internal discourses… as fellow Filipinos who know the value of the one hand and the other… to partner with us as advocates of financial inclusion, as advocates for a more responsive legal framework for economic and financial stability. 

A way this is done is through discourse (Socratic or otherwise) and collaboration with peers and colleagues, with regulatory and supervisory authorities, with stakeholders, with government… even with your students.  You are all in a position to influence the narrative of how our laws evolve – as predicted by Justice Holmes, and as desired by posterity. 

The BSP relies on your support.  We hope you will come to this decision.  Maraming salamat sa inyong lahat.  Mabuhay ang Philippine Bar Association. Mabuhay ang mahal nating Pilipinas.

Title: Bangko Sentral Mandates and How They Help Maintain a Stable Business Environment
Occasion: Wallace Business Forum Roundtable
Speaker: BSP Governor Nestor A. Espenilla, Jr.
Transcription:
Chairman and President, Mr. Peter Wallace, Excellencies, distinguished guests, ladies and gentlemen, thank you for having me in your company this morning.

I assumed office as Governor of the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas twenty-three (23) days ago, on July 3…  Thus, some, or most of you, might be wondering what kind of changes will be instituted, and how new policies under my governorship (if any), might affect the Philippine business environment…  These are valid musings. 

Ladies and gentlemen, I reiterate my intention that the next six years of my being at BSP’s helm will be characterized by continuity – more specifically, “continuity plus plus” – a line, that to my surprise, gained some popularity upon my appointment.

I may interest you to know that the phrase, “if it ain’t broke, don’t fix it” as initially documented, is attributed to Burt Lance,  Director of the Office of Management and Budget under U.S. President Jimmy Carter? … I find it interesting that this was first used in a public service context.

My predecessor (former BSP Governor Amando M. Tetangco, Jr.) left a strong and resilient Philippine economy, a stable banking system, and a safe and reliable payments system (among other accomplishments) as legacies… Continuity is not just desirable, it is necessary.

Macroeconomic Policies

Our economy continues to expand.  The Philippines is in a position of strength notwithstanding external challenges. We have had manageable inflation and high growth.  The 2017 inflation outturn still well-within the National Government target range of 2-4 pct… Our updated forecast over the policy horizon is that inflation would still be within the target range of 2-4 pct and probably staying close to the mid-point.

The numbers look good.  This notwithstanding, BSP will continue to monitor shifts in market sentiment along with trends in commodity prices and other inflation drivers.  As always, BSP will be continually refreshing its liquidity forecasting and inflation models so they are in tune with evolving impulses.  But no significant deviation from previous monetary policy approach is anticipated.   We can continue to rely on the BSP’s flexible inflation targeting mechanism periodic review of monetary policy, and transparent communication of policy decisions.

I realize that this - inflation targeting - may sound esoteric.  But, really, the goals are down-to-earth.… This particular BSP focus has very practical significance – to those in this ballroom! Maintaining price stability by keeping inflation low and stable reduces uncertainty and allows businessmen and investors (like yourselves) to better plan and make informed consumption, investment, saving, and production decisions… Thus, at its very heart, the BSP’s primary mandate is central to fostering a stable business environment…  We are fully dedicated to this responsibility and we hope you would regard us as strong partners in this respect.

Strong and Stable Banking System

Team BSP under Governor Tetangco also did very well in working for the fulfillment of the BSP’s second mandate.  Through the BSP’s pursuit of progressive and prudent banking reforms, our banking system currently enjoys double-digit growth in resources, expansion in lending, adequate capitalization at levels above both the national requirement of 10 pct and the Basel Committee norm of 8 pct.  Philippine banks continue to have improved asset quality and profitable operations.  Significantly bringing this about was the alignment of our regulatory frameworks with international standards (such as Basel Core Principles for Effective Banking Supervision) while remaining sensitive to domestic conditions.

Notably, BSP adopted a corporate governance framework emphasizing the responsibilities and qualifications of the bank’s board of directors and senior management. 

The BSP is currently phasing-in the issuance of enhanced guidelines which will further integrate risk management and responsible conduct to the overall governance framework. We also enhanced local standards on risk-based capital and risk-management practices of banks to allow them to withstand internal and external shocks. 

A strong and stable banking system translates to development for the rest of the nation, as banks support the financing needs of our continuously growing economy and allocate resources efficiently.  Again, a practical goal.

BSP and Bankers of the Wallace Business Forum

While bankers would deem the BSP, as first and foremost, their supervisor/regulator – I ask (of the bankers inside and outside of this room) that another dimension be added to this perspective: that the BSP be viewed as a partner (Yes, even of its supervised entities!).

This proposition is not too alien… with respect the regulations and reforms I mentioned, there has always been close consultation with the banks. When this reforms were instituted there was a phasing-in with BSP allowing parallel run periods for banks to gain familiarity BSP’s new conduct of supervision.  Banks were also given time to build up capital as required under the new Basel standards. The result of this partnership is that banks are better-run and adequately capitalized.

I believe that when rules and regulations are merely imposed from the top-down, results can be unsustainable.  For sustainability, the interests of the supervisor/regulator and the regulated must converge. This convergence in essence, births a strong partnership. 

We would agree that common ground is found in our shared desire to maintain an environment that encourages and is conducive to progressive business and healthy competition. 

BSP Initiatives: Stronger Business Environment

For the last twenty-four (24) years since its establishment in 1993, the BSP has worked towards this end. Let me cite six (6) recent and concrete examples of our initiatives to accomplish this purpose (These examples are in no particular order):

First, the BSP was instrumental to the approval of Republic Act No. 10641 further liberalizing the entry of foreign banks into the Philippines.  With this law, foreign banks may establish or acquire up to 100 percent of the voting stock of an existing domestic bank or to put up a branch.  To accept this as a gain may seem counter-intuitive to local bankers as it has the effect of fostering strong competition. 

The benefit desired is for the long-run as it paves the way for foreign banks to serve as vehicles for foreign direct investments into the Philippines.  Also the increase in competition pressures allows a leveling-up of services and less complacency. Sophisticated players that can offer financial technology solutions have already entered the market, ushering in a notable, gradual unbundling of the traditional value chain.  The competition will make everyone work harder and seek new markets that hitherto not been well-served.

The same benefits can be said to stem from the BSP’s implementation of the ASEAN Banking Integration Framework (ABIF).

Second, since 2007, the BSP has been introducing waves of FX regulatory reforms to address the dynamic needs of the Philippine economy that have evolved with the interconnection of global markets. 

Regulations were amended to raise the FX threshold residents can purchase from the banking system.  This allows the sale of FX for settlement of resident-to-resident transactions, relieving the private sector from securing prior BSP approval and registration requirements. Moreover, to ensure greater transparency in the FX market, BSP continues to develop regulations to cover non-bank entities including money service businesses. These efforts to liberalize the FX market are forward-looking and geared towards regional integration.  Our next moves will be increasingly more ambitious.  We are liberalizing further registration and approval rules for foreign borrowings and investments to eliminate red tape and capture more information. 

Third, the BSP established the Interest Rate Corridor System (IRC).  The objective is to make market interest rates move closer to the BSP policy rate.  In the long run, this supports Philippine capital markets by encouraging money market transactions and better liquidity management.  These lie as the key foundation of a well-function domestic debt market. You may agree with me that active money market transactions promote real price discovery and transparency.  Thus, the IRC will lead to the generation of more reasonable interest rate benchmarks that enable effective and efficient pricing of financial products in the local market.

Fourth, to ensure an efficient payment and settlement system, the BSP adopted the National Retail Payments System (NRPS), a flagship program for digital finance.  The NRPS bridges the country’s transition from a cash-heavy economy, where 99 percent of transactions are done in cash, to a cash-lite economy, where at least 20 percent of retail transactions by volume will go electronic. 

BSP is mindful that innovations, particularly financial technology, reduces costs and accelerates the on-boarding of currently excluded markets into the formal financial system.   I think this trend of modernization that supports e-commerce is also of particular interest to business people such as yourselves. 

But let me also quickly point out, that even as we embrace technology, we are also very cognizant of new risks and have introduced enhanced rules to control cyber-crime and other technology risks.
 
Fifth, BSP took a primary role in amending the Anti-money Laundering Act.  AMLA rules have expanded to cover non-bank financial institutions such as pawnshops and money service businesses.  Recently, President Duterte signed a law amending the AMLA to cover casinos.

(While the list can still go on), I will cite as my final and Sixth example, the BSP’s initiatives in helping develop a deeper, more efficient and integrated domestic financial and capital market.  The BSP, Bureau of the Treasury, Securities and Exchange Commission and the Department of Finance are jointly proposing an operational roadmap for local currency debt market development.  Three areas are prioritized:  (1) the creation of reliable financial benchmarks and valuation of financial instruments; (2) deepening the local bond market by adopting reforms in the primary dealer system, increasing supply of short-term debt securities, and developing an effective regulatory framework for the derivatives and repo markets; and (3) the establishment of an integrated financial market infrastructure to promote price discovery, transparency and orderly trading, clearing, and settlement of the full range of financial transactions.

More inclusive financial system

As I close, allow me to speak about the need to work towards greater financial inclusion.  I saved this for last not because of its insignificance.  Quite the opposite.  It is most important and is the “plus plus” in “continuity plus plus.”

I speak of Financial Inclusion often and with passion. With conviction, I have said that for progress to be meaningful, it must be inclusive; that Filipinos from the grassroots, at the peripheries, must be given usage and access to financial services that will allow them to save, invest and borrow for productive uses.  Our countrymen must be provided with financial literacy and education so that they may make informed financial decisions to better their lives and that of their families. 

It sounds like a matter of corporate social responsibility… It sounds like a charitable endeavor.  But, friends, esteemed pillars of the business community, may I stress that the drive for financial inclusion is not just this. 

As business people, it is understandable that the primordial concern is the bottom line.  But let me put forward – or reintroduce - a revolutionary thought.  (This is not original).     Perhaps you are familiar with C.K. Prahalad’s theory on “the bottom of the pyramid”? 

The idea is that those in the lowest socio-economic group is actually a large and profitable consumer base!  This is a demographic to be empowered:  First, as a financially literate populace;  Next, as active and thoughtful consumers!  This is an exciting prospect that we hope you, our partners in business and industry would support the BSP in achieving.

On the BSP’s part, we spearhead the implementation of the National Strategy for Financial Inclusion to make the financial system accessible and responsive to the needs of the entire population, to support a broad based and inclusive growth.   There is still much to be done.

We count on you, our partners in the Wallace Business Forum to help usher in the ideal of financial inclusion and to work with us more closely, collaborating towards maintaining a more stable, conducive and stronger business environment.

Thank you for your kind attention.

Title: Building on Built Foundations:  Continuity and Change
Place: Manila Golf and Country Club, Makati City
Occasion: Fellows Meeting of the Foundation of Economic Freedom
Speaker: BSP Governor Nestor A. Espenilla, Jr.
Transcription:
Former Central Bank Governor and Ambassador Jose Cuisia… Monetary Board Member and Foundation for Economic Freedom (FEF) Trustee Philip Medalla… SEC Commissioner Ephyro Amatong… FEF Chair Bobby Ocampo… FEF Vice-Chair Romy Bernardo… FEF President Toti Chikiamco… members of the Board of Trustees of the FEF… Executive Director Peter Perfecto of the Makati Business Club… friends from the US Embassy led by Mr. David Schnier… esteemed guests, ladies and gentlemen, good evening!

I thank the FEF for the invitation to speak at this Fellows meeting.  And what a group of distinguished Fellows it is! Giants of Philippine business, banking and financial industries, the academe and government… The energy in this room is palpable and I am happy to be among like-minded Filipinos with a heart for economic liberty and good governance.

Tonight, I am among former bosses, colleagues, and friends who know me better as “DG Nesting” – Deputy Governor of the BSP’s Supervision and Examination Sector (an integral part of my identity since 2005). 

Twenty-three (23) days ago, on July 3, 2017, things changed (quite dramatically for me), and I now have the privilege to represent the remarkable institution that is the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas, as its Governor and as Chairperson of the Monetary Board…I am both deeply humbled and proud to do so.

In FEF President Chikiamco’s letter invitation – which I received sometime in May, soon after I was announced, – the request was specifically for me to speak about my “plans for continuity and change in the BSP as incoming BSP Governor.”  

That there is room – No, that there is necessity – for both continuity and change is a simple but very powerful idea.  Often, we think of the two concepts as mutually exclusive/ as an either/or… as two ideals on polar ends of a dichotomy… But this is not necessarily true.  For even as I stand here and look around this room, I see where both continuity (stability) and change (dynamism) combine and reconcile for the good of our nation. 

All of us here, have in one way or another, been entrusted with building on the foundations built by those who came before us.  We do not start from scratch.  There is no tabula rasa in the task of achieving national development.  The challenge is to find balance between steadfastness and progress given the demands and specificities of the times… 

Somehow (despite the initial excitement), when I first learned of my appointment as BSP Governor, I was able to articulate this need for equilibrium in the phrase, “continuity plus plus.” It is a phrase that has gained some popularity (especially with media) in predicting how my term will be.  In the phrase, there is recognition that change is a given, but a stable and familiar anchor is essential to move new initiatives forward effectively. 

Stability Amidst Change

Greek Philosoper, Heraclitus said, "change is the only constant in life." This may very well describe our economic journey. 

We are fortunate that despite challenging times brought about by the US Fed rate hike, Brexit, geopolitical events in the Middle East and North Asia, and lingering global market uncertainties, the domestic economy continues to be in a relative position of strength. The Philippines is still one of the region’s fastest growing economies, with growth solidly anchored on sound macroeconomic policies.

Domestic inflation remains to be manageable because it is low and stable.  It is within Government’s target and is aligned with market expectation.

Domestic liquidity is adequate to support further economic expansion.  Money supply grew by 11.3 percent to P9.6 trillion as of end-May 2017.  Accordingly, total credits to the private sector grew by 18.3 percent, driven by a sustained increase in bank lending which expanded by 17.8 percent year-on-year.  And credit growth is not necessarily associated with weakening asset quality, precisely because of lessons learned.

The country’s external position is strong. Gross international reserves (GIR) at US$81.3 billion can cover 8.6 months’ worth of imports as of end-June 2017. This is equivalent to 5.4 times the country’s short-term external debt based on original maturity, and 4.0 times based on residual maturity. For the first quarter of 2017, the country’s outstanding external debt declined by 1.3 percent quarter-on-quarter (QoQ) to US$73.8 billion. The maturity profile of these debts is mostly in the medium to long-term. Sufficient buffers and longer maturity of debts ease foreign exchange requirements for debt servicing.

The banking system likewise continues to be a source of strength and is well-positioned to further support domestic economic needs.

Banks have stronger balance sheets with steady growth in assets, loans, deposits and capital.  Asset quality significantly improved as the non-performing loan (NPL) ratio stood at 2.0 percent as of end-May 2017.  Compare this with its peak of 16.9 percent in 2001!  Banks are liquid with an assets-to-deposits ratio of 49.6 percent during the same period. Banks are likewise well-capitalized with the capital adequacy ratio (CAR) at 15.3 percent as of end-March 2017. 

Overall, banks are sound and profitable. These numbers demonstrate how banks successfully adjusted to the challenging external environment and the evolving landscape.

Continuity and “the Plus-Plus”

I am blessed that Team BSP under Governor Say Tetangco left a legacy of excellence. What a solid and formidable foundation to continue building on!

In Homer’s Odyssey, when the king of Ithaca fought in the Trojan War, he entrusted his son and household to a reliable aide named, Mentor.  In time, the word “mentor” has become synonymous with the “advisor, friend, teacher and counselor.” 

History is replete with examples of meaningful mentor-mentee relationships.  There is Socrates and Plato, Haydn and Beethoven, Emerson and Thoreau and even Buffet and Gates! … How fortunate I am that in my thirty-six (36) years of being a Central Banker, I can add the mentorship provided me by Governor  Tetangco and the illustrious Governors before him starting from Governor Laya.   

It is because of the example and mentorship that I can dare, with Team BSP, to insightfully identify components of the “plus plus” and work purposely and decisively on them.

Under my watch, the BSP will continue to focus on financial sector policy reforms.  The interest rate corridor (IRC) system was implemented last year. With this, we have started to move forward, to make the conduct of monetary policy more efficient and market-oriented.  Our agenda is to further refine the IRC and to progressively dial down onerous reserve requirements whenever the timing is right. 

BSP is also highly supportive of capital market reforms.  The aim is to provide a viable alternative source of financing for long-term investments, including the development of the necessary financial market infrastructures (FMI). Last year, we started the groundwork for enabling prudent project financing under Circular No. 914.  It revisits the concept of SBL to create space for self-sustaining big ticket projects.

The BSP is likewise actively collaborating with the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) and the Bureau of the Treasury (BTr) and the DOF to further accelerate the development of the domestic debt market. Market participants will soon be engaged to discuss an operational roadmap. In the works is a sequenced approach to implement key reforms to develop the local currency debt market.  We believe this is a crucial component to sustain the economy’s growth momentum.

Further liberalization of existing rules on foreign exchange transactions is necessary to achieve a more risk-focused, transparent and market-determined policy framework.  Notwithstanding waves of liberalization, we recognize that the foreign exchange market framework remains restrictive, difficult, opaque, and shallow.

It is a throwback to a time when foreign exchange was scarce, our reserves so meagre, and market confidence was low.  Today, it is an impediment to growth and adds to the cost of doing business. 

We will continue to reshape the financial system so that it is fully responsive to the needs of the domestic economy. The enabling regulatory environment for fin-tech and digital finance needs to be developed without sacrificing prudent credit underwriting, market integrity, consumer protection,  and information security standards.  The digitalization of finance is essential to achieve significant inroad against financial exclusion and payments inefficiency.

Parallel to this is the commitment to advance our financial inclusion agenda, with the goal of furthering financial education and consumer protection.   The day will soon come where financial consumers and investors will have an increased ability to make informed business decisions with options from a longer, fresher and more innovative menu of available financial products and services.

Legal Framework Initiatives

At noon today, I spoke to the Philippine Bar Association.  I shared with them the necessity to evaluate our current legal framework for economics, banking and finance.  It is important to consider if the current legal framework is attuned to the changing economic and financial environment… if it is poised to protect our earlier gains… and if it is sufficient to promote sustainable economic growth.  A lively discussion followed after the challenge was posed.

I had the opportunity to share with them BSP’s initiatives in working closely with both Houses of Congress for the enactment of laws to create an even stronger and more enabling legal environment compatible with aspiration of high growth and more equitable economy.

I shared with them the move to amend the BSP Charter (which is twenty-four (24) years old), the Anti-Money Laundering Act (AMLA) (which was recently amended when President Duterte signed a law to include casinos in the list of covered persons), and the Deposit Secrecy Law to allow transparency and enable swifter and more efficient investigation of questionable actions and the prosecution of money launderers while protecting the rights of bank depositors from unwarranted intrusion.

I also spoke about the enactment of a Payments System Act to formalize BSP’s oversight of the national payment system. This will build trust and confidence that are necessary to grow our payments system. I disclosed that the promulgation of an Islamic Banking Law to revitalize Islamic banking in the Philippines by allowing greater participation in the market is also a priority.  I shared that BSP also intends to provide a harmonized legal framework for pooled vehicles of investments through a Collective Investment Schemes Law.  I spoke as well of our strong support for the establishment of a National ID System that will promote financial integrity, inclusion, and transparency.

Closing Remarks

Ladies and gentlemen, there is much to be done and it is through our collaboration and partnership that we will be able to sustain our growth momentum.

All of us here are involved in an ever continuing endeavour.  In our various fields, torches are passed from one leader to another, with mentors imparting wisdom and guidance, not to foster stagnation but to champion improvement and development …  In the BSP, while there was a changing of the guard, the mandates remain the same. We shall persist in the pursuit of these mandates, with greater vigour and more imagination.

In doing so, we are, as always, grateful for your invaluable partnership and support. Maraming salamat po sa Foundation for Economic Freedom for bravely espousing progressive economic policies that make for a better, more prosperous, and fairer society.  Mabuhay po tayong lahat!

Title: BSP and BAIPHIL Moving Mountains: New Heights in Banking Excellence
Place: Rizal Ballroom C of the Makati Shangri-La Hotel
Occasion: the Induction Ceremony and General Membership Meeting of the Bankers Institute of the Philippines (BAIPHIL)
Speaker: BSP Governor Nestor A. Espenilla, Jr.
Transcription:
Distinguished Monetary Board Colleagues, Juan de Zuniga and Tony Abacan, BAIPHIL President Irene Arroyo, immediate past President, Liza Ortiz, other BAIPHIL past presidents, BAIPHIL directors, officers and members, BAP President Nestor V. Tan, bank CEOs, my PDIC colleagues, esteemed guests, friends, fellow BSPers past and present, ladies and gentlemen, good afternoon!

It is an honor and pleasure to carry on the tradition of inducting the new board members and officers of BAIPHIL.  As new BSP Governor…   [I assumed the post eleven (11) days ago]… it is auspicious that I now address the new leadership of BAIPHIL …On behalf of my colleagues in BSP and the Monetary Board, let me extend our congratulations. 

As new leaders, it is natural for us to aspire greater achievements for the teams we lead.  This is why I find your theme: “Scaling New Heights in Banking Excellence” very engaging.  The theme is both timely and relevant as we come into our fresh roles and as the financial system evolves.

The theme mentions heights. To add imagery to this message, let me take Mt. Everest as a starting point. Everest, known as the roof of the world stands twenty-nine thousand and thirty-five (29,035) feet above sea level. This is the ultimate goal of hard-core mountain climbers, the highest of heights. 

On 29 May 1953, a New Zealander, Sir Edmund Hillary and a Sherpa, Tenzing Norgay, successfully climbed Mt. Everest in the face of great risk.

As documented, they were the very first mountain climbers to reach the summit. Now, sixty-four (64) years later, the peak of Everest is decidedly less lonely and more than 3,500 climbers have already reached the top or “summitted”.

A myriad of things have changed since then. But from the time it was first done to the present day, scaling Everest or any mountain, consistently demands: First:  intense training and preparation;  Second:   sensitivity to the environment and possible changes to climate;  Third:   possession of well-maintained equipment;  Fourth:  a team of highly trusted and reliable individuals; Fifth:  leadership of competent guides; and Finally: tenacity and courage to keep going amidst challenges.

Training and Preparation

In mountain climbing, each team member has to be skilled, fit, and prepared physically and mentally. This takes years of conditioning if one is to take on the tasks involved.

As the banking industry’s premier training arm, BAIPHIL plays an important role in providing required skill sets and competencies for modern banking. BSP commends BAIPHIL for continually being proactive in responding to the training gaps and emerging requirements of the banking industry in line with on-going developments in the regulatory and operating environment.

With its expertise, synergy and collaborative partnership with the BSP, BAIPHIL is in the best position to design a comprehensive training program to foster and strengthen expertise, excellence and integrity among banking professionals. 

Environmental Sensitivity

The conditions for climbing higher look good!  The Philippine economy remains in a position of strength. It continues to expand, despite challenges in the external environment. This expansion is increasingly broad-based with notable rebound in agriculture and exports sectors.

The sustained strength of the economy in the first quarter of 2017 was underpinned by manageable inflation,  more than adequate gross international reserves and a steady stream of inflows from overseas Filipino remittances, revenue from the business process outsourcing sector  and tourism income, all contributing to higher consumption spending.

Moreover, the Philippine banking system continues to be a stable anchor for the economy with key performance indicators showing double-digit growth in resources, expansion in lending, adequate capitalization, improved asset quality, and profitable operations.

These gains driven by our common vision will fuel us to pursue greater heights.

Well-Maintained Equipment and Gear

As Central Monetary Authority, the BSP has a well-articulated policy framework and an enhanced policy tool kit.  Like good and ready mountain climbers, our gear is ready and we have improved surveillance methods.
Assessing the mountain, we are thoughtful about weather shifts. For instance, the increasingly clear signal for policy normalization in advanced western economies points to a rise in global interest rates, just a question of timing and pace. 

Mindful of these, BSP continually strengthens its framework for financial risk surveillance, sharpening assessment of market conditions. We consider the interconnectedness of economic agents, credit concentration and liquidity, and the evaluation and pricing of risks. 

Our approach is pre-emptive to mitigate any undue risk build-up in the financial system, but we have also built up solid macroeconomic fundamentals that serve as buffers to weather potential external shocks. These safeguards notwithstanding, BSP continues to refine existing early warning systems, distress indices  and stress tests. BSP is constantly developing financial and economic models that improve our understanding of how relevant variables move.

Trusted and Dedicated Team

To be successful in mountain climbing  (like facing the challenges of the banking industry) one cannot go up alone. It is not a solitary undertaking. Climbers must learn the basics from other climbers, as well as help each other up from time to time.

In our industry, this means we must develop close collaborations and relationships and encourage communication.

I am fortunate that I have inherited a very capable and competent team BSP  where each public servant contributes to the fulfilment of our mandates. We can also depend on the collaboration and synergies among valued stakeholders like BAIPHIL.  Indeed we cannot do it alone.

Competent Leadership

Ladies and gentlemen, possessing close familiarity with “the mountain and mountains” of banking, we could consider the Bangko Sentral and BAIPHIL as the industry’s ‘sherpas’. 

We provide guidance and direction to others in the industry as we walk the same path.  We guide towards the shared vision of upholding a stable and inclusive banking system. Under my stewardship, this will be pursued with fervour.  
As our fellow Sherpa, the BSP counts on BAIPHIL to take on even greater significance in this age of global convergence.

Together, we have to prepare the banking community by anticipating harder but more fulfilling climbs ahead. Through continuous training and education, the banking profession will be better equipped and prepared to keep pace with the ever evolving financial services industry.

Tenacity and Courage

In the book, “The Last Step:  The American Ascent of K2” / it is said that, “the courage of mountain climbers is not blind, inexplicable, meaningless; it is courage with ability, brains, and tenacity of purpose.”

In this industry, this is the same brand of courage we must have to achieve our goal of banking and financial stability.

Our courage is not based on a false sense of security. But we are motivated to always raise the bar of professional excellence and business integrity for banks. We have the determination and passion to excel in our current craft, of pursuing excellence and constantly improving our work  so that we could deliver the best financial services to the Filipino consumer and our country.

Moving Mountains

That I used Mt. Everest in an analogy to illustrate our present and on-going journey together is perhaps ambitious enough…  And while I have built parallelisms between the two endeavours,   I dare say that in our industry the mountains are not static.
Banking is not unmoving like the formidable Everest. There is no final peak to overcome. 

The Bangko Sentral celebrated its twenty-fourth (24) anniversary last week. I have been a Central Banker for the last thirty-six (36) years. BAIPHIL marked its seventy-sixth (76th) year this June. As veterans in this field, we know that in banking and in central banking, the process of scaling new heights is an active and continuing endeavour. 

Friends: banking products, financial services and needs, technology and consumer preferences are always levelling up. We have to keep pace. We do this with training and education. We do this with updated and relevant regulations. 

We do this with partnership as we are confronted with an evolving market landscape of international standards and prudential regulations. Our shared strategy necessitates taking a more holistic view of these developments. 
 
We do this too by strengthening corporate governance standards and risk management practices.  We at the BSP have raised the bar of prudential standards  to promote resilience in the banking system and market discipline for risk-taking activities.

Because of growing regional financial integration and the entry of foreign banks, competition pressures have increased. New sophisticated players such as financial technology solution providers have entered the market.  This is a good thing as these bring about a notable and gradual unbundling of the traditional value chain in the Philippines and intimately links banks closer to customers.

While FinTech provides interconnectivity, convenience, and efficiency in delivery of financial products and services, we must also be vigilant as it also ushers in cyber-security concerns. In this regard, the BSP has been laying the groundwork on promoting cyber-security and related regulation on technology. 

But there is still much to be done.  Ladies and gentlemen, we know from science that the mountains are moving due to continental drift and that we, BSP and BAIPHIL,  must therefore continue to move with the mountains even as we scale the one in front of us. 

In Closing: Inclusion as We Climb

I’d like to think also that there are several summits in banking and central banking… That as one reaches a vantage point, more and more of the surrounds are taken into perspective…  As one climbs, one’s view becomes wider.

I have heard from mountain climbers that when you reach the top, it is actually quite a humbling experience. I certainly felt that way when I climbed Mt. Fuji as a millennial graduate student in Japan in 1988.  At higher heights, one sees the bigger picture more clearly and wishes for others to experience the same.  

The same holds true as we experience more economic gains and successes. We want more and more people  – our countrymen  – to be included in the experience.  Our goal is for more of our countrymen to save and borrow for productive uses, avail of investment and insurance products, and send and receive payments securely and efficiently. We firmly believe that this financial empowerment is the only way for economic growth to be truly meaningful.

We trust in BAIPHIL to help us move this vision forward.  BAIPHIL can in turn count on the full support of the BSP for its future endeavours.

Mabuhay ang BAIPHIL at BSP!

Maraming salamat po!

Title: Turning Vision Into Partnership
Occasion: Awards Ceremony and Appreciation Lunch
Speaker: BSP Governor Nestor A. Espenilla, Jr.
Transcription:
PDIC President Roberto Tan, National Statistician Lisa Bersales, Members of the Monetary Board, sector heads, fellow BSPers, former Central Bank Governor Jaime C. Laya, guests, a pleasant good morning to all of you. Magandang umaga especially to our stakeholders and awardees.

Every year for the last fourteen (14) years we at the BSP have held this annual ceremony traditionally right around this time: our Anniversary month… There is significance in this chosen timing.  The message we wish to convey is that, not only do we value you: our stakeholders...  More so, we recognize that the BSP would not have achieved all it has if it were not for your partnership.  This is why we celebrate with you during our milestone month of July. 

The theme of our 24th Anniversary here at the BSP is “together moving forward: a new season of excellence.”  There is a journey implied, and a needed collaboration and cooperation expressed.  This theme includes, not just the members of the BSP family progressing onward in unity, but this includes you too, our esteemed stakeholders, whom we honor today. 

I have been with the BSP – then, the Central Bank of the Philippines – since 1981… And as a young Central Banker one of my tasks was to draft technical speeches…  So even thirty-six (36) years after, I still have a passion for words. 

Let me focus on this event’s keyword.  Stakeholder.  It sounds quite ominous.  Its origin is consistent with this sense of foreboding.  The word “stakeholder” first appeared in the Oxford English Dictionary in 1708.  It referred to one holding a wager, a bet. 

Thankfully, for us now, the word has evolved into a dynamic -- even an exciting and active concept, where speculation has no role.  As presently understood, stakeholders are partners and can be involved in the successes of an enterprise, from whose accomplishments they too can greatly benefit.

The importance of collaboration and partnerships was stressed by Governor Amando M. Tetangco, Jr. in his two (2) terms at the BSP’s helm…  Gov. Say repeatedly said that in the BSP, our work could not be accomplished by the BSP working alone, but only through continued discussion and cooperation with others, like government agencies, institutions, other regulatory bodies, private organizations and entities.  This is a belief we strongly hold and will continue to hold here in the BSP.

This morning we have one-hundred and forty six (146) outstanding partners that we acknowledge. You are government agencies and departments… private businesses… leaders in your respective industries.  You, our honorees and stakeholders are here today because you helped the BSP in its programs.  But did you know that beyond the altruism you displayed, where you extended assistance willingly and often without expectation of anything in return from the BSP, there was in your actions, a reward that will ultimately redound to the fulfillment of a shared vision and dream? 

In the BSP, all employees know our vision by heart.  Memorize nila ito.  Our vision is to be a world-class monetary authority and a catalyst for a globally competitive economy and financial system that delivers a high quality of life for all Filipinos.  A high quality of life for all Filipinos.  This includes each person here in this Assembly Hall.  And with your contribution, with the assistance you gave us, this is precisely what you are helping us achieve.  So, for this, we thank you.  Please give yourselves a warm round of applause.

This is not rhetoric.  For example, the outstanding survey respondents and information partners here who assisted the BSP, helped us in formulating data-driven monetary policy.  The responses you gave and the information you provided underpinned enabling decisions that allowed the Philippine economy grow by 6.4 percent in the first quarter of 2017.  You helped so that the Philippines continues to be one of the fastest growing economies in Asia. Stakeholder participation is essential so that even amidst confounding global developments such as the Brexit and the United States’ seeming turn to protectionist policy, we can stand resilient and stay calm, with inflation at 3.1 percent in the first half of 2017, well within the government’s inflation target range for the year.

Our external payments position remains manageable. Robust remittances from overseas Filipinos and ample receipts from the business process outsourcing sector continue to fuel economic growth. The country’s external debt remains at sustainable levels, with the ratio to GDP improving in Q1 2017 to 24.1 percent from 26.5 percent in the same quarter last year. In addition, the country’s Gross International Reserves remain more than adequate at US$81.4 billion as of end-June 2017, equivalent to nearly 9.0 months’ worth of imports of goods and payment for services and income.  These are achievements that were brought about by sound policy-making built on our collective dedication and willingness to cooperate for the sake of something larger than ourselves.

In this assembly hall are exemplary partners who have enabled us to carry out programs that reinforce the BSP’s three pillars of central banking. You have contributed to BSP’s initiatives and programs in financial inclusion and education… consumer protection… payments and settlements... overseas Filipino remittances… coin recirculation… the clean note policy… and demonetization of our new design series currency. 

The banking system today is very robust and is poised for broader reach and better service.

The number of operating banks as of March 2017 is 599 (head offices) with an overall branch network of 10,679 units.  Assets of the banking sector also grew by nearly 12.42% percent year-on-year as of December 2016 boosted by an increase in deposits, profits, and fresh equity.  No less important, assets grew without compromising their quality. The Philippine banking system’s capital adequacy ratio as of Q3 2016 has reached 15.59 percent, almost double the global-minimum.

Prudent policy-making has led to a sturdy financial system and a stable economy. The critical contribution of our partners as exemplified through your compliance with the BSP’s various surveys, provision of information, and participation in our diverse programs, advocacies and initiatives, assisted the BSP in fulfilling its mandates.

To reinforce the importance of data gathering and increasing our interface with the public, we are pleased to announce the formal launching of the user-friendly BSP e-Survey Portal.  This online facility will make it easy and convenient for respondents to participate in the surveys of the BSP. 

The Coordinated Direct Investment Survey went online last June. The Coordinated Portfolio Investment Survey (CPIS) and monthly Cross Border Transactions Survey questionnaires shall be included in the e-Survey by the end of this month.  The launch of the BSP e-Survey Portal aims to improve efficiency in generating the Cross Border Transactions Survey results which are used as inputs for the Balance of Payments and International Investment Position Statistics. These indicators help the BSP craft and assess our policy settings.

So as you can see, there are more exciting times ahead, more collaboration planned, and better avenues to make them more successful and productive.  We look forward to continuing the journey with you.  Congratulations to all our stakeholders.  Mabuhay kayo.  Mabuhay ang BSP.  Mabuhay ang ating bansang Pilipinas!

Title: The Philippines and Japan: Enhancing Strategic Partnership
Place: Mayuree 2 Ballroom, Dusit Hotel, Makati City
Occasion: Cocktail Reception hosted by the Philippines-Japan Society, Inc. (PJS) and the Philippines-Japan Economic Cooperation Committee, Inc. (PHILJEC)
Speaker: BSP Governor Nestor A. Espenilla, Jr.
Transcription:
Ambassador Kazuhide Ishikawa, Prime Minister Cesar Virata, distinguished members of the Philippines-Japan Society, Inc. (PJS) led by President, Mr. Francis C. Laurel, and the Philippines-Japan Economic Cooperation Committee, Inc. (PHILJEC) led by Chairman, Mr. Aniceto G. Saludo, Jr., Secretary General JJ Soriano, my BSP colleague Deputy Governor Cyd Amador, esteemed guests, ladies and gentlemen: Good evening (Konbanwa)!

What a pleasure and honor it is for me to be here tonight… As recently appointed Governor of the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas, opportunities to speak before groups and organizations that enhance economic cooperation and greater financial stability in the region, is always a welcome engagement…  This goes without saying… 

But my delight in being able to address this group tonight also has a personal angle, close to my heart.  Thirty-one  (31) years ago, in 1986, I was a Monbusho scholar… a scholarship I received from the Japanese Government.  Through this generous grant, I earned  my masters in Policy Science from the Saitama University’s National Graduate Institute for Policy Studies (GRIPS) which is now in Tokyo.

What a different world it was in 1986!  Since then, there have been many rapid developments in technology and we continue to be in a period of an evolving geopolitical and economic climate.  Yet, despite all these vast changes,  the Philippines-Japan Society has been unwavering in its commitment to foster closer ties between our nations – even as early as 1972, when it was formally established! I likewise commend the Philippines-Japan Economic Cooperation Committee for its steadfast initiatives to promote closer economic ties between the Philippines and Japan.

Living and being educated in Japan truly made a positive impact on me.  Such that when I addressed the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas for the first time as Governor last week on July 3, my message began by acknowledging the importance of the principle of “kaizen,” stressing the need for “continuous improvement,” and recognizing it as an evolutionary process.

But aside from kaizen, there is much to be learned from Japanese culture… An important observation I made while living in Japan is that while the west cultivates a sense of self that is independent and unique… in Japan, there is an emphasis on  cultivating a sense of self vis-à-vis others and society. 

I believe this emphasis on harmony and collaboration accounts for our countries’ long-standing relationship.  Cooperation between our nations has paved the way for the advancement of our economic and trade relations.

Japan is one of our main trading partners and is the second largest source of imports at 12.4 percent or US$3.59 billion of the total import bill for the period January to April 2017. Japan also ranks first in terms of export with receipts valued at US$3.09 billion, for a total trade value of US$6.68 billion for the same period.

Recently, several agreements to further enhance economic and security cooperation have been signed by our nations.  Among the agreements reached were: the creation of business opportunities through Official Development Assistance (ODA) and private sector investments to spur infrastructure projects, including the promotion of agricultural businesses, as well as building capacity for maritime security.

We can thus look forward to further strengthening of the bilateral relations between our countries, particularly in light of ongoing initiatives to pursue massive infrastructure projects.  It is worth noting that under its Partnership for Quality Infrastructure program, the Japanese government announced in 2015 its plan to actively support the construction of modern infrastructure in the neighboring Asian nations.  As a result of this plan, the Philippines and Japan committed to cooperate on the roadmap for better transport infrastructure in the Metropolitan Manila area by 2030, taking advantage of the Japanese technology and the ODA.

As BSP Governor, I would like to take this opportunity to give information on the favourable prospects for growth and investments in the Philippines for Japanese investors and firms. 

Ladies and gentlemen, the Philippines’ macroeconomic fundamentals remain solid and intact.  They provide a stable anchor for sustained expansion, amid lingering volatilities and uncertainties coming mainly from the external environment. 

Recent economic data shows that in the first quarter of 2017, real GDP grew by 6.4 percent. Economic expansion remains broad-based with notable rebound in both the agriculture and exports sectors. The Philippines is still one of the best performing economies in the region.

In fact, the overall confidence index of businesses for the second quarter of 2017 has improved, reflecting optimism in the economic prospects of the country. This is also evident in the sustained inflows of foreign direct investment which registered at USD 1.6 billion net inflows in the first quarter of 2017.

I have said that I am blessed to continue building on the legacy of my predecessor, Governor Amando M. Tetango, Jr. as the sustained strength of the Philippine economy was underpinned by manageable inflation, adequate gross international reserves, and a steady stream of inflows from overseas Filipinos (OFs) remittances, revenue from the BPO sector and tourism income. These contribute to higher consumption spending.  These are fundamentals that we will build on and continue during my term as BSP Governor.

Under my term, the BSP will ensure that an enabling monetary and financial environment is maintained to achieve the country’s growth objectives, while safeguarding price and financial stability. That is the macroeconomic picture. 

In the banking system, full liberalization of foreign banks’ entry in the Philippines under Republic Act (R.A.) No. 10641, has allowed increasing presence of foreign banks in the country.
