In the area of banking supervision, our focus will be on reducing the stock of non-performing loans with the help of congress in extending the SPV Law; enhancing the prudential regulatory environment of the banking system to align it with international standards and best practices; strengthening corporate governance standards and market discipline mechanisms;  developing the domestic capital market further; enhancing the payments system; and improving the BSP’s supervision technology and capacity . 

In the pipeline are the issuances of the guidelines on the implementation of Basel II Accord, and the new financial reporting package in line with the adoption of international accounting standards. While there will be initial friction costs related to the transition, these will strengthen the banking system for the long haul . 

To speed up  the development and deepening of the domestic capital market, the BSP will continue to work with other government agencies and the private sector for the completion of critical market infrastructure to further enhance system integrity and overall market confidence

And in response to the need to further enhance financial information critical to investor decisions, BSP will also continue to work on the establishment of rating agencies, highlighting their role particularly in the conduct of banks’ risk management  in addition, we continue to work with Congress on the creation of a centralized credit information bureau system to help private enterprises get better access to credit, reduce borrowing costs, and minimize the risk exposures of financial intermediaries. 

Similarly, we will continue to work with market players to widen the investor base for domestic financial instruments. 

All these reforms require the support and cooperation of the banking sector the BSP therefore takes heart in having in the banking community a responsive partner and support force in shaping the future of our financial system .

A special advocacy for the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas is our National Coin Recirculation Program.  In this regard, we are particularly pleased that tonight, the entire banking sector  is expressing its support for this crucial advocacy that stands to benefit  consumers, retailers, banks, and  the BSP  

In particular, we are happy that the Bankers Association of the Philippines, the Chamber of Thrift Banks, the Rural Bankers Association of the Philippines, the Bank Marketing Association of the Philippines, and the Philippine Retailers Association have declared their full commitment to support our Coin Recirculation Program under a Memorandum of Agreement for this purpose . 

We are also pleased that Archbishop Gaudencio Rosales of the hugely successful Pondong Pinoy, our inspiration for our coin program, is here with us to sign a Memorandum of Agreement for the servicing of its coin deposits. Under the adopt-a-parish program of the Bankers Association of the Philippines, there are initially three participating banks: Bank of Philippine Islands, Metrobank, and Equitable-PCIBank  

Ladies and gentlemen, this is definitely a fine way to start the new year: committing to work together for the greater good. 

Indeed, the translation of the final outcome of our reform programs should be sustainable growth and development to the man on the streets, it is jobs and income to the nation, peace and prosperity  these are goals we should all work for  the cooperation of everyone is of utmost importance. 

With your continuing support, we are confident of achieving greater gains in reforming and energizing the economic and financial system, as well as in keeping the transmission mechanism of monetary policy in high gear .

Finally, on behalf of the Monetary Board and our co-workers at the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas, I wish all of you a fruitful, meaningful and a hugely successful new year!  

Marami pong salamat  thank you all.

Title: Turning Challenges into Opportunities
Place: Oasis Country Resort, Sevilla, San Fernando City, La Union
Occasion: 50th Anniversary Celebratory Luncheon of Rang-ay Rural Bank, Inc.
Speaker: Governor Amando M. Tetangco, Jr.
Transcription:
Governor Victor Ortega and Mayor Mary Jane Ortega, officers and staff of Rang-ay Bank led by Chairperson Eufrosina Nisce and Rang-ay President Ives Nisce, co-workers in the banking sector and colleagues from the government sector, distinguished guests, ladies and gentlemen:  

Naimbag nga malem ‘yo amin (Good afternoon)!

I am indeed honored to be among the witnesses of this momentous occasion.  Thank you for this privilege of being with you in celebrating your 50th anniversary.

Today, we all are witnesses to the realization of your founders’ vision 50 years ago. And it is certainly one exhilarating experience.  This feat has significant impact to the banking industry and most especially to the community that Rang-ay has been serving for half a century.  Thus, I also take this opportunity, to express Bangko Sentral’s appreciation to the entire family of Rang-ay, particularly for being consistently in congruence with all our policy and regulatory reform initiatives all these years.

Rang-ay at 50

 Rang-ay Bank has undoubtedly lived up to its name. It has been bringing progress or should I say “karangyaan” to the community it serves from the first moment it opened its doors as a pioneer private bank in San Fernando, La Union on January 16, 1956. 

Today, you understandably have the right to be proud of your accomplishments. The last time we looked, you are still this region’s number one bank and among the top 25 rural banks nationwide in terms of both physical and financial resources. 

Your strong presence in Region 1 as well as in the nearby Cordillera Region is made possible by your network of ten branches (including that of a former affiliate - RB of Burgos).  

You continue to enjoy the trust and confidence of over 15,000 depositors[1] whose savings are now close to half a billion.

Likewise, you have a relatively strong capitalization of 120 million.  Rang-ay’s risk-based capital adequacy ratio (CAR) of 18.5 percent is also well above industry and regulatory standards. 

Your total loan portfolio is nearly half a billion which accounts to 65.5 percent of your total assets. Your lending activities have surely provided farmers and  other entrepreneurial rural folks with wider latitude in accessing credit which translated to better lives for the rural community. 

With your wide array of deposit products and credit lending programs, you managed to sustain bottom line figures at very good levels. 

Rang-ay’s performance definitely did not go unnoticed as evidenced by the various accolades from financial and non-financial organizations[2], the Bangko Sentral included.

As such, one can say that rang-ay is poised to further improve its level of efficiency to ensure continuous market leadership during these challenging but equally rewarding times.

Industry outlook 

Let me therefore take the next few minutes to outline the banking industry prospects in 2006 to help you firm up your strategic plans for this year and beyond. 

We are optimistic that the rural banking industry will sustain its positive performance this year and remain in the forefront of reforms as catalysts of a broad-based development in the countryside.  

For our part at the regulatory front, the BSP remains committed to the continuous implementation of our reform program to sustain financial stability and growth.  Specifically, our objective is to have a more stable, more efficient and a more depositor and friendly banking system.  

We are still advocating clean up of banks’ balance sheets through the expedient and innovative disposition of non-performing assets. This is central to restoring the credit supply to the productive sectors of the economy. 

Our goal is to bring the banking industry’s NPA/NPL ratio to single-digit level. As of end-June 2005, the rural banking industry’s NPA/NPL ratios stood at 11.9 and 14.7 percent, respectively. This is still double the pre-crisis period since the sale of NPAs under the SPV Law only created a small dent on the inventory of acquired assets arising from soured loans. 

We, thus, welcome the approval by the House of Representatives of the extension of the SPV Law[3] by another two years. We are hopeful that the senate will approve the counterpart bill soonest so that banks can immediately resume the wholesale clean up of bad assets. We expect that this extension will result in the unloading of at least another 100 billion in bad assets so that NPL ratio will more or less be lowered to about 7 percent.  

We are also studying if Joint Venture Agreements (JVA) can give greater flexibility to banks to dispose of their bad assets apart from availment of incentives under the SPV Law. The unloading of foreclosed real estate properties through joint venture agreements[4] (JVAs) that will develop and enhance the marketability of banks’ acquired assets, particularly undeveloped properties, will not only clean up banks’  balance sheets but also potentially boost the housing market and even tourism.         

Beyond asset clean up, the BSP is following through with its regulatory reforms aimed at further strengthening corporate governance, risk management and capital adequacy in our banks through a more effective and efficient enforcement. 

Last year, we began the changeover to International Accounting Standards/Financial Reporting Standards. This would further strengthen the current transparency and disclosure requirements in financial reporting.  The pivotal role of external auditors during this transition period is also being given higher importance. 

Recently, we have issued new regulations on internal audit designed to adopt a code of ethics and establish mechanisms for the reporting of financial improprieties, malpractices and acts of misconduct (corporate whistle-blowing).  

We are also sustaining our lobbying efforts in congress for the passage of the amendment to the BSP Charter and the enactment of the Credit Information System Act.  The first will make the BSP a more effective monetary authority and banking regulator while the other will pave the way for the establishment of a truly comprehensive credit information system that is expected to lower the cost of borrowing, provide greater access to credit in general and reduce the dependency on collateral based lending. 

Beyond regulatory initiatives, the BSP is also equally committed in its advocacy to promote a sustainable microfinance program as a tool to alleviate poverty.  

The present poverty situation in the Philippines has given rural financing a new dimension, concretizing the significant role of rural banks in countryside development[5]. Toward this end, we have recently allowed the selective[6] lifting of moratorium on bank branching to facilitate the expansion of financial services in underserved areas. Under Circular No. 505, we foresee, among others; the growth of bank microfinancing to benefit rural folks with greater access to formal banking services that in turn, mobilizes savings and investments. 

Moreover, we foresee an accelerated consolidation process in the banking industry in the next 3 years.  This will be brought about by (1) a stronger regulatory framework that will hasten the exit of weak banks, hopefully on a voluntary and market-based basis; (2) the increasingly stronger competition by new foreign investors coming in, in existing banks; and (3) the rigorous technical demands posed by modern banking and finance standards.   

All these changes will dramatically transform the competitive environment. Down the road, we see a banking landscape characterized by a handful of main banks complemented by an abundance of smaller banks that serve various well defined market niches. 

Final note

In closing, let me call on this generation of  the family behind rang-ay bank to transform these reform initiatives into opportunities and further stretch your vision over the next years to come.  

With your wealth of experience, rang-ay can lead in turning the heavy flywheel of remaining reforms for the rural banking industry.  

I trust that rang-ay will harness its core expertise, geographic advantage and strong ties with the community in promoting a safe, sound and responsive banking system. 

Let us all work together in keeping the wheels of change turning. 

Agyamannak (thank you) and happy anniversary!


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

 [1] To date, the Rang-ay Bank has 1 head office, 9 bank branches and 1 affiliate bank (Rural Bank of Burgos, which will be consolidated with Rang-ay, Inc. following the grant of the certificate of authority to operate by the BSP)

  [2] Rang-ay received 1 award from the BSP, 7 awards from other banks, 1 award from Rural Credit and Guarantee Corporation and 3 awards from a private non-government organization (NGO).

 [3] Target is first quarter of 2006.

  [4] A proposal is currently under study for approval of the Monetary Board. Upon approval, this will initially allow U/KBs to dispose their Real and Other Properties Owned or Acquired (ROPOA)s to various JVAs with real estate developers. At present, ROPOA still accounts to 46.0 percent of the banking system’s overall level of NPAs

  [5] At present, there are 4 microfinance-oriented rural banks and 158 rural banks engaged in some level of microfinance with a total loan portfolio of P2.3 billion catering to a total of 441,963 borrowers.

 [6] Prohibition on bank branching remains in the cities of Makati, Mandaluyong, Manila, Parañaque, Pasay, Pasig and Quezon including the Municipality of San Juan

Title: Philippine Economy: Recent Economic Developments, Outlook and Policy Directions for 2006; Making the Best of Times
Occasion: Meeting of the Rotary Club of Manila
Speaker: Governor Amando M. Tetangco, Jr.
Transcription:
A.  Prologue

Distinguished officers and members of the Rotary Club of Manila, friends, ladies and gentlemen, good afternoon.

Thank you for inviting me to your first Membership Meeting for 2006.  This is also my first speech after the crossover to 2006.  As in all maiden things of importance, you can expect me to assess the year past and to figure out the economic outlook in 2006.
 
Central banking is much more than a strong peso and fast accumulating dollar reserves.   I will therefore share with you my thoughts on what the economic prospects imply for the monetary and financial policies of the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas.

B.  Recent economic developments

My first take of the year 2005 is that we were more resilient than what the numbers would credit us. In terms of growth, we chalked up an economic performance that is quite remarkable, not for the growth rate itself because by comparison that is not exactly spectacular, but for the odds that we beat. The challenges were indeed formidable: high oil prices; increasing global interest rates; political developments and negative credit outlook ratings.

What do we have to show? Real gross domestic product (GDP) expanded by 4.6 percent in the first three quarters of 2005 and by all indications, this is expected to further inch closer to 5.0 percent rather than 4.0 percent for the whole of 2005.

What should also be recognized is that the expansion in economic activity was sustained without fuelling further inflationary pressure.   Inflation has continued to ease, helped mainly by softening prices of food and oil as well as the strong peso on the supply side.   Headline inflation has fallen to about 7.0 percent in the last half of 2005 while core inflation has steadily slowed down.  Core inflation is of key importance to monetary policy.  As this is headline inflation net of volatile food- and energy-related items, it suggests to us the magnitude of demand-related pressures that must be dealt with.  I will discuss later the monetary response under this very interesting combination of events.

My second take of 2005 is that the seeds of fiscal sustainability, sown during the year, should allow us to reap some dividends starting 2006.  We saw the implementation of two crucial tax measures: Sin taxes and the VAT.   We also saw the intensification of tax administration efforts.  While the VAT is yet to show its full impact, the government’s fiscal consolidation efforts have already shown good results.   In the first eleven months of 2005, the National Government (NG) deficit declined to P122.8 billion, certainly lower compared to the programmed budget gap for the period and the year-ago level.   The NG therefore has good reasons to envision a balanced budget by 2008.   This should lead us to that inflection point at which we should be seeing more fiscal surpluses and our debt level becoming more sustainable.

My third take of 2005 is that while the domestic economy shaped up in a number of areas, the country’s external position also went through a critical phase of consolidation.   Estimates for the first eleven months of 2005 show a balance of payments (BOP) surplus of US$2.2 billion, a reversal from the previous year’s deficit. Despite the weak merchandise trade, the BOP surplus was achieved due mainly to two factors: heavy remittances from overseas Filipino workers (OFW) and foreign investments, both portfolio and direct investments.

These foreign exchange inflows helped raise the country’s gross international reserves (GIR) to US$18.1 billion as of end-November 2005. Our international reserves remained comfortable, providing ample cover for 4 months of imports of goods and payment of services and income.

Such strong inflows and the confidence generated by increasing international reserves and tax reforms helped support the peso, making it the top performing currency in the Asian region.  At the end of 2005, the peso was stronger by 6.17 percent relative to end-2004.  Given our import dependence especially for petroleum, the strong peso contributed to moderating domestic inflation.

Another development in 2005 was the reduction of external debt to US$55.5 billion as of end-September 2005.  More importantly, medium- and long-term debt liabilities (almost 90 percent) comprise the bulk of the country’s external debt. Key debt service ratios have also continued to improve, indicating better manageability and sustainability of external debt.

My fourth take of 2005 is that the banking system continued to show improving soundness and resiliency. There has been an improvement in loan quality as commercial banks’ non-performing loans (NPL) ratio as of end-October 2005 remained at a single-digit mark. The capital adequacy ratio of commercial banks at 17.46 percent in June 2005 was well above the international benchmark of 8.0 percent.

The challenge in the financial system in 2005 was that lending activity remained sluggish.   As of end-October 2005, commercial banks’ loans outstanding were only 1.3 percent higher than the year-ago level.   This is traceable, in part, to the banks’ cautious lending stance alongside weak corporate credit demand.

Finally, 2005 was a difficult year because of the challenging combination of monetary and price conditions.  First, there was ample liquidity which pushed interest rates lower and fanned inflationary pressures. Second, price pressures also came from the supply side particularly high oil prices and weak harvest in the beginning of 2005.  Third, lower domestic interest rates contributed partly to exchange rate volatility which rendered price stabilization more complicated.

Against this backdrop, the BSP carefully calibrated monetary policy to be able to navigate between price stability and economic growth. Our main focus has been on responding to potential breaches of the inflation target, keeping the public’s inflation expectation anchored and managing the rapid growth in domestic liquidity.  We raised our policy interest rates by a total of 75 basis points and increased reserve requirements by 200 basis points last year.  The fruit of this calibrated approach is the easing inflation starting in the second half of 2005.

C. Economic outlook

Looking ahead, let me give you my own idea of what to expect in 2006 by reiterating that old saying that most of the footprints on the sands of time were made by work shoes.  In fact, Winston Churchill went as far as to say that most of the significant contributions that have been made to society have been made by people who were tired.

Last year, we worked together to achieve positive things for this country.   In a larger sense, we were all tired from the many challenges of 2005. You, the Rotarians, also made your mark, in your own fields, taking great strides for our country and people.   We should be able to build upon our labor and do better.  We should also be able to sustain the policy reforms we put in place last year and before, in order to put more solid form and substance to our efforts this year. 

What do we see this year?

Output growth is expected to continue at a reasonable pace and will be driven by services and industry, along with agriculture that stands to benefit from more favorable weather conditions.   Nevertheless, the rise in oil prices over the past year is likely to exert some impact on domestic demand, particularly on consumption spending.   Therefore, the emerging scenario by the Development Budget Coordination Committee (DBCC) for GDP growth suggests a real increase of 5.7 percent for 2006.

Inflation is expected to be higher in 2006 but the recent strengthening of the peso and the easing of world oil prices from their peak in 2005 will help counterbalance the effects of the VAT.  Nevertheless, the risks to inflation continue to be mainly on the upside.   This is because oil prices are still likely to remain high relative to their historical trend given limited production capacity.  Thus, inflation is expected to be in the range of 7.5-8.2 percent in 2006.  But what is significant is the expected slowdown in inflation in the second half of 2006 as the impact of vat diminishes since its implementation took place in the last quarter of 2005.

Meanwhile, the improving fiscal performance, ample liquidity, moderate credit growth, and prospects for better sovereign credit rating are expected to cushion the impact of inflationary pressures on market interest rates.  Thus, it is likely that interest rates will remain stable at current levels during the year.

On the external front, dollar inflows are expected to continue mainly from OFW remittances and investments and these give us reason to expect a strong external position this year.   With healthy inflows, the exchange rate would likely remain stable at current levels.

D. Challenges and strategies

In the period ahead, the task for economic managers is to focus on macroeconomic stabilization in the short term while also preserving the momentum for economic reforms to ensure sustained growth in the long term.   The BSP’s contribution to these efforts will be drawn from its twin responsibilities of conducting sound monetary policy and banking supervision.   The bsp will continue to address the risks to price stability and sustain the pace of reforms in the financial sector.

Monetary policymaking at the bsp will therefore be pitched against the following risks: volatility in world oil prices; build-up of excessive liquidity owing to dollar inflows; possible exchange rate reaction to narrowing interest rate differentials; and adverse shifts in the public’s inflation expectations. The public can expect that the bsp will be thorough in ensuring that these risks will not be allowed to materialize.  The bsp will deny any breeding ground for any incipient inflationary pressures especially those coming from the demand side.

In the conduct of effective financial supervision, the BSP will continue the reform process.  We are cognizant of the fact that the build-up of non-performing loans in the past has dampened bank lending activity, despite ample liquidity in the system.  For the monetary transmission mechanism to work efficiently, the bsp will continue to help facilitate disposal of banks’ non-performing assets.

Other initiatives in financial supervision will be focused on: (1) improving the BSP’s supervision technology and capacity; (2) enhancing the prudential regulatory environment of the banking system to align it with international standards and best practices; (3) strengthening corporate governance standards and market discipline mechanisms; (4) developing further the domestic capital market; and (5) enhancing the payments system.

More specifically, in the pipeline are the issuances of (1) the guidelines on the implementation of Basel II Accord, and (2) the new financial reporting package in line with the adoption of International Accounting Standards. These initiatives will further strengthen the banking system by aligning local banking practices with internationally accepted standards.

To further develop the domestic capital market, the bsp will continue to actively work with other government agencies and the private sector for the completion of critical market infrastructure to enhance system integrity and overall market confidence.

We recognize the value of enhancing financial information to guide investor decisions.  We are closely working with congress in the creation of a centralized credit information bureau system to help private enterprises get better access to credit, reduce their borrowing costs, and also to minimize the risk exposures of financial intermediaries.

We are also working to widen the investor base for our financial markets through a number of new investment products which would better reflect market prices.   These products will help encourage more institutional investors like insurance companies, mutual funds, and pension funds to participate in the capital market.  Our future reform initiatives will eventually lead to the introduction of exchange-based products that can further stimulate market activity and deepen liquidity.

The economic indicators on the past year’s performance give us reason to be optimistic about the year ahead.   Our capacity for hard work makes us doubly optimistic.   But nothing comes without a price.  The year ahead will most certainly be challenging.   We should make the best of times regardless of circumstances. As Thomas Jefferson once quipped, ”It is wonderful how much can be done if we are always doing.” We proved it last year. We should prove it this year and beyond.

Thank you and good day

Title: Welcome remarks
Occasion: Welcome Cocktails for delegates to the 2005 World Congress of Financial Executives
Speaker: Governor Amando M. Tetangco, Jr.
Transcription:
Finex president and former Monetary Board Member Melito Salazar, Jr.; Chairperson of the International Association of Financial Executives Institute Dr. Conchita Manabat; Chairman of the World Congress Committee Edgardo Limon; other distinguished Congress organizers, delegates to the 2005 World Congress of Financial Executives; my friend Governor Pridi Devakula of the Bank of Thailand, special guests, colleagues from the Bangko Sentral, ladies and gentlemen.

On behalf of Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas, I welcome all of you to our Head Office complex.   However, as you may have noticed, we are not in an office setting.   This is deliberate.

It is said that finance is both art and science.

In this regard, we thought it best to hold our welcome cocktails here at the Metropolitan Museum.  This museum is special to us since it houses choice pieces from the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas art collection….from paintings to pre-hispanic gold artifacts, some of which were crafted by our forefathers 2,000 years ago. 

In other words, quite a number of what you will see here are priceless art pieces that have thrived...and survived… shifting financial landscapes through the centuries.  

This should serve, therefore, as an inspiring start to your World Congress which has adopted for its theme “Global markets: thriving in the shifting financial landscape.”

I must say you have chosen a most timely conference theme, because we truly are seeing dramatic shifts in economies and financial markets all over the world. 
    
The drivers of change are many and varied.  As markets become more connected in tandem with great strides in technology, there are, at the same time, structural changes taking place in varying degrees…driven mainly by the deregulation of industries and by liberalization policies.

This rise in globalization brings not only greater opportunities but also new challenges in the form of new types of risks.

Similarly, we cannot overemphasize that the shifts we are seeing in the international financial landscape are also shaped in part by recent macroeconomic headwinds.  For one, the rapid increase in oil prices has contributed to rising inflation in many countries.  In response, monetary policy has also shifted to tightening cycle leading to the current rise in world interest rates.  For another, rising interest rates pose additional challenge as they could have a negative impact on the real sector and in turn, also on the financial system.

In response to the challenges posed by this shifting financial landscape, central banks have mandated regulated institutions to continue enhancing risk management and adherence to good corporate governance.  This should provide financial institutions incremental flexibility to hedge their operations from sudden market reversals.   

Ladies and gentlemen,   we all know we need to plan for,  and adopt to,  shifting financial landscapes.  We can do it individually, but if we work closely together, we should be able to thrive on…. not merely survive…. the changing financial landscape.

As Governor Pridi will tell you, ASEAN and other central banks have been working together in formulating solutions to common concerns.  These initiatives have given rise, for instance, to the Chiang Mai Initiative.   We can discuss this later, as you tour the museum.

For now, allow me to wish you all a fruitful and successful conference.

Thank you and mabuhay!

Title: Closing keynote address
Occasion: 30th Annual Conference, Federation of ASEAN Economic Associat
Speaker: Governor  Amando M. Tetangco, Jr.
Transcription:
Introduction

Distinguished officers and members of the affiliate economic organizations comprising the Federation of ASEAN Economic Associations, ladies and gentlemen, good afternoon.

It is a pleasure and privilege to deliver this keynote address at the closing of the 30th Annual Conference of the Federation of ASEAN Economic Associations (FAEA)·  the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas takes pride in having participated in this conference.  FAEA has a very distinguished track record as a vehicle of regional understanding and mutual support.  Through its thirty years of existence, the FAEA has provided an effective forum for cooperation among the member economic societies in the ASEAN region.  In the process, it has significantly advanced the discussion of economic issues and challenges that transcend national jurisdictions.  It has provided voice to the depths of these challenges and brought to the fore those approaches that made good economic sense.  By its fruit, the FAEA has attracted and added the Cambodia Economic Association and the Vietnam Economic Association to the original ASEAN economies’ economic associations, namely:

- Indonesian Economists Association,
- Malaysian Economic Association,
- Philippine Economic Society,
- Economic Society of Singapore, and
- Economic Society of Thailand,
 
I must, therefore, congratulate all the member associations of FAEA, and the Philippine Economic Society for successfully organizing and hosting this year’s conference.  There was indeed wisdom in the choice of the theme China and India:  Challenges and Opportunities for the ASEAN.  This has definitely enhanced FAEA’s role as a catalyst for drawing up a more definitive view of future economic powerhouses in the global economy.  One is a dragon that is now very much awake, so very conscious of and recognized for, its pivotal role in both global trade and investment.  The other is an elephant with a long memory, one that is capable of doing enormous tasks including the expansion of its large domestic market.

Implications for the region and for the Philippines

The emergence of China and India as regional, and indeed global, economic players is undoubtedly shaping up as the single most important driver behind the long-term prospects of the Southeast Asian region in particular and the whole Asian region in general. 

It must have been obvious in the last two days of this conference that China and India impact the region in several respects.  The two countries are emerging as the latest success stories in the globalization of Asia, to levels unprecedented among emerging market economies. Many manufacturing and industrial concerns have, for example, relocated to China, while India is becoming a giant in the software industry. These have profound implications on the pattern of trade both within the region and globally.   

I am sure that the regional importance of such developments is what provided stimulus to a spirited discussion in the last two days.  In the case of China, the implications for the region are two-pronged—China represents one of the biggest potential markets for ASEAN products, and it is also the biggest competitor in the market for exports and foreign investment. This stares us in the face and, therefore, our response cannot be protectionist; rather, we must find a suitable way in which we can fit into the emerging trade patterns.  In this regard, it is heartening to note that efforts are underway in the ASEAN economies towards greater integration, both within the ASEAN and with China. ASEAN has recently completed negotiations for its goods liberalization package and the schedule for the ASEAN-China Free Trade Agreement (ACTFA). The ASEAN has also decided to speed up its own economic linkages towards setting up an ASEAN Economic Community (AEC). This will not come tomorrow but the establishment of such a regional community is seen to enhance the competitive edge of the ASEAN in the face of rising challenges from globalization.

India, on the other hand, has demonstrated an extraordinary capacity to undercut the competition in technology industries, both in terms of cost and innovation.  With increasing integration between the south and southeast Asian economies, India’s growth will translate into greater imports from the ASEAN·  given its increasing importance, the ASEAN is expected to pursue much closer economic ties with this other economic powerhouse·  

Let me now turn to the Philippines.  The rapid expansion of the chinese economy continues to have a very positive imprint on Philippine trade.  The importance of China as a market for Philippine exports continues to grow, as it rose from about 2.0 percent of the total in 2000 to more than 10.0 percent for the first seven months of 2005·  In particular, the strong link between Philippine exports and the chinese economy is illustrated by the fact that information technology related products such as semi-conductors, and office machines and automatic data processing machines have dominated our exports to China· in the first eight months of 2005, exports of semi-conductor devices was more than 40.0 percent of total exports to China, while exports of office machines and automatic data processing machines stood at more than 33.0 percent of aggregate exports to China.  We are taking into account the impact of China on our exports in our assessment of the outlook for our balance of trade.  In the case of India, our trade has been relatively small. India and the Philippines are in fact emerging largely as competitors in information technology and in business process outsourcing.  In this area, the thrust should be for the Philippines to achieve and maintain a comparative advantage in terms of skilled human resources.

On top of such structural linkages in trade and industrial markets, one other major factor affecting trade and capital flows both within and outside the region is the recent revaluation of the yuan.   As i recall, the concern a few months back was the risk of a hard landing for the chinese economy due to possible overheating·  that concern has now abated.  While greater flexibility in the yuan decreases the risk of disruption in trade flows, it does pose some new challenges.  China has become one of the world’s largest consumers of oil.  Even as the yuan revaluation can be expected to contribute to the reduction of China’s trade surplus, it would also help in inducing greater oil imports by China, thus increasing the pressure on available oil stocks.  In this sense, therefore, developments in China can impact on our inflation outlook—something that policy makers need to consider in formulating appropriate policy stance.

Our reckoning of regional dynamics will not be complete unless we recognize that the stability of the yuan helped minimize the headwinds of the difficult years of the Asian crisis through the middle of 2000’s.  Today, it seems that a more flexible yuan could contribute to China’s more balanced economic growth.  In the future, it will be interesting to see whether its convertibility could further mitigate global financial imbalance by helping recycle all those dollars more evenly across Asia. 

Opportunities for regional cooperation

But one should not look at China in the region solely as a trade competitor.  China and the ASEAN have been active partners in efforts to promote freer trade.  The framework agreement on comprehensive economic cooperation between the ASEAN and the People’s Republic of China was signed in 2002, with the parties agreeing to negotiate in order to establish an ASEAN-China free Trade Area (ACTFA) within 10 years. 

The ACTFA represents a landmark in pushing for freer trade between China and the ASEAN countries. It goes without saying that free trade will significantly increase trade and investment in the region.  However, it bears emphasizing that the benefits from closer integration can be enhanced if the economic relationship between China and the ASEAN countries can be transformed from competition into complementation.  This is our great challenge—to transform China-ASEAN trade into one of complementation, so that growth in one area, instead of impinging on growth prospects in other economies in the region, can instead act as an engine of growth for the region as a whole.  Currently, ASEAN and China are direct competitors for foreign investment.  In the long term, we hope to see China and the ASEAN as investors in each others’ economies. We also hope to see more cooperative efforts in the region towards ensuring greater financial stability, so that a repetition of the Asian financial crisis can be prevented.

In this respect, we have had important initial initiatives; notably, the regional network of swap arrangements among the ASEAN+3 countries under the Chiang Mai Initiative (CMI).

The development of regional financial arrangements has been a high priority following the crisis period. Crisis-hit countries in East Asia recognized the importance of establishing a regional facility that would provide timely and adequate international liquidity during times of currency attacks. Thus, countries in the region worked together to establish the Chiang Mai Initiative (CMI), formally launched during the meeting of the ASEAN+3 finance ministers in Chiang Mai, Thailand, in may 2000.  The CMI is designed as a regional network of swap arrangements among the ASEAN+3 countries to supplement the existing international facilities to address short-term balance of payments difficulties.

Another important component of regional initiatives is the launching of the Asian bond market initiative. The thrust of this program is to chart the roadmap for developing the domestic capital markets of the ASEAN countries.  Our authorities expect that this initiative would lead to the greater ability of ASEAN to absorb foreign investments and channel domestic investments into new and creative financial instruments that address currency and maturity mismatches attendant to bank financing.  We hope to be absolved of the first original sin.

Conclusion

Let me reiterate therefore that the main challenge for the ASEAN economies is to respond not only to the enhanced competitive pressure emanating from China and India, but more importantly, to identify further channels of cooperation between ASEAN and the other Asian economies.  In the oriental tradition, we must consider each challenge as an opportunity.  With this, Southeast Asia, South Asia and East Asia can emerge as a pan-regional bloc that will enhance the free flow of resources and production within the region.

Finally, and on a lighter note, for those of you who are visiting the Philippines for the first time, I hope you will have a chance to enjoy Manila.  I hope there will be other opportunities in the future for you to come back and stay longer to experience the countryside and to savor our unique Filipino hospitality.  To all, good day and mabuhay!

Title: Welcome Remarks
Occasion: 30th Annual Conference of the Federation of ASEAN Economic Associations
Speaker: Governor Amando M. Tetangco Jr.
Transcription:
Ladies and gentlemen from the Federation of ASEAN Economic Associations (FAEA), the Philippine Economic Society, special guests, dear friends.  On behalf of the Monetary Board, I welcome all of you to the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas.

The whole day today, you have been engrossed on discussions regarding challenges and opportunities for ASEAN.

Tonight, we invited you here to experience Philippine culture, through the art pieces at the Metropolitan Museum…as well as the musical numbers you will hear and witness.     

The setting of our outdoor dinner tonight is the Fort San Antonio Abad, a fortress built in the 16th century during the Spanish colonial period, to guard against pirates and other unwanted  company.
 
In modern times, Fort San Antonio Abad serves as a special venue for receptions for visiting dignitaries.  This tradition continues tonight as we host this reception for you, our special guests. 
   
I will spare you from listening to my thoughts on FAEA’s conference theme this year.  There will be time enough for that tomorrow when I deliver the closing keynote speech at noon.

And so, friends, let us proceed to our agenda tonight: relaxation and camaraderie! We hope you will enjoy the food and the music we have prepared for you.

An observer once said that… and I quote, “The easiest way to start an argument these days is to get two economists together.”

Fellow economists, let us prove this person wrong. Obviously, he is not an economist; otherwise, he would know about the infinite range of variables we can cite as assumptions, whenever we agree to disagree.  
Tonight, as we share food representative of our respective ASEAN countries, swap personal anecdotes, and discuss stories about our economies, I am sure the ties that unite and bind us in ASEAN will be ever stronger.

Again, to all, welcome and mabuhay!

Title: Remarks
Place: Executive Business Center, Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas
Occasion: Signing Ceremony for the new US$500 Million BSP Term Loan Facility
Speaker: Governor Amando M. Tetangco, Jr.
Transcription:
Members of the Monetary Board, distinguished representatives from the participating banks, co-workers at the Bangko Sentral, friends from the media, ladies and gentlemen, good afternoon.

Let me start by welcoming everyone to this signing ceremony. I am glad to see the successful closing of another term loan facility for the BSP. We are delighted to see  once again, the support and commitment of the participating banks. Like previous transactions, we have here a combination of local and foreign banks, and we find a number of creditors under existing term loans. Their commitment to the BSP and the Republic by joining this facility is most appreciated. 

The proceeds of this term loan facility will be used to partially refinance a maturing BSP note,  and to maintain a healthy level of gross international reserves or GIR, which amounted to over USD18 billion in October.  We expect to maintain it above USD17 billion by yearend.  At USD17 billion, the GIR will be 3.4 times of imports of goods and payments of services and income, and 1.5 times the country’s short term debt based on residual maturity.

We have also seen positive developments in other areas.  Our balance of payments (BOP) position for instance, has improved significantly. The overall BOP position for the first nine months of 2005 showed a surplus of USD2.73 billion, compared to USD176 million deficit in the comparable period last year.  This positive development resulted from the steady increase in OFW remittances, which grew by 28.0 percent to USD7.0 billion in the first eight months.  Strong foreign direct and portfolio investment flows and continued growth in exports also contributed to the BOP surplus. Net foreign portfolio investment registered by the BSP from January to November 4  amounted to USD2.1 billion, more than 7 times the USD279 million recorded a year ago. As a result, the peso has strengthened, posting a 3 percent improvement vis-à-vis the USD year to date.

I wish to thank all the participating banks for your continuing confidence, and congratulate the arrangers for bringing this transaction to a successful close.

Thank you and good day.

Title: The BSP’s Barya sa Pagkakawanggawa
Occasion: Flag Raising Ceremony
Speaker: Governor Amando M. Tetangco, Jr.
Transcription:
Thank you….Thank you for that rousing version of the happy birthday song.   It was……..well,  happy!

Ladies and gentlemen of the BSP,  last week, I was at the meeting of the President with the private sector.  Faced with so many pressing issues, she still found the time to tell me….twice that day….that we at the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas are doing a great job for the economy!  

We are doing a great job!?  Do you agree with that assessment?…Let us review our report card.

Well, we continue to post gains in our drive to strengthen the banking sector and deepen the capital market.  At the same time, our monetary policy decisions are producing positive results: inflation is slowing down, we have a balance of payments surplus, record high international reserves and an increasingly strong peso which hit a five-month high last Friday.  We truly are performing quite well…  I want to take this opportunity therefore to thank all of you for a job well done and for the solid support you have given me and your monetary board.  For this, we should give ourselves a well-deserved round of applause.

But fellow workers at the BSP,  while we have accomplished much, there is much more that we can do, particularly for the less fortunate in our country. 

We in government can do this directly and indirectly: by using our resources wisely and avoiding waste, as well as by providing direct support and assistance to those who need help.  I am very pleased to announce therefore that the program we are launching today will achieve both objectives.       

I refer specifically to a component of our coin recirculation program - the Barya Sa Pagkakawanggawa or BSP for short - a coin collection contest for charity organized by the Currency Management Committee in partnership with the BSP Employees’ Association.
   
As you know, providing enough coins to the economy is part of our currency management function.  Thus, the BSP invests regularly in producing coins.  Today, we have roughly 10 billion pieces of coins in circulation or about 100 pieces of coins for every Filipino.  This is double the regional average of 50 coins per person! And yet, the perception of a coin shortage persists.

Clearly, the problem is not supply, but its circulation.  Coins, especially those below one peso, are imprisoned and forgotten inside our drawers, huge piggy banks and other containers.    We must stop this practice and keep our coins circulating so we can produce less coins.  The savings from this will revert to the National Government in the form of dividends that may be used to fund basic services and infrastructure such as schools, hospitals, and health centers. 

Under our barya sa pagkakawangga program, we are encouraging BSP employees to donate barya or coins below one peso – these are 25 sentimo, 10, five and one sentimo.   The money we will raise will be donated to Gawad Kalinga, the successful Philippine model for developing integrated and self-reliant communities.

I am excited about Barya Sa Pagkakawanggawa because it is a vehicle for employees to share their blessings with the poor, as well as to help BSP lower its expenses.
 
Among others, Gawad Kalinga builds permanent homes for the poor.   You have to see a GK site to see how it can transform families into self-reliant units.  I have seen it happen in three separate GK sites.  I hope therefore that our coin collection program will be successful.   GK can build a house for P50,000.  This should be easy to raise.  For instance, we only need a contribution of at least seventeen pesos (P17) each from all 3,000 employees at the main office to build one house;  P34 each for 2 units; and P50 each for three units!  Kaya ba natin ‘to?

Of course, we expect the BSPers at the Security Plant Complex  as well as the Regional Offices and Branches to participate actively in this program. The more houses we can build, the more people we can help.   Remember, the BSP vision aims to deliver a high quality of life for all Filipinos.  

But beyond building homes, the challenge before us is to make Barya Sa Pagkakawanggawa a success as this also serves as our model for the national launching of our Coin Recirculation program within the next two weeks.         

Ladies and gentlemen of the BSP,  we cannot expect others to respect and circulate our coins, if we ourselves from the BSP do not do so.   We have to walk our talk, so to speak.  Today, we make the symbolic first step.  It is my hope that this will be an extremely successfully two-week program.  As the program slogan goes, Barya ay mahalaga, huwag ipitin, paikutin.

Kaya ba natin ‘to?  I believe so.   Marami pong salamat sa inyong lahat.

Title: Accounting Reforms Toward Good Corporate Governance
Place: Balagtas Room, The Peninsula Manila Hotel, Makati City
Occasion: 3rd Asian Accounting Firms (ASNAF) Conference
Speaker: Governor  Amando M. Tetangco, Jr.
Transcription:
Distinguished guests, ladies and gentlemen, good morning.

I am deeply honored to be part of this gathering of accounting experts from the Asia Pacific Region. I understand there are also delegates from Europe, particularly France and Belgium. I wish to join ASNAF Chair Cherry Bernaldo in welcoming all of you to Manila.  This is a rare opportunity to be with the movers in the profession who are at the forefront of the crusade of coping with the accounting evolution happening globally.  To the men and women who continue to heed the call to serve in this noble undertaking, we salute you.

The accounting profession has truly evolved into a vital catalyst of global convergence particularly with the adoption of the International Financial Reporting Standards (IFRS). The twin objectives of the new standards of promoting transparency and comparability in financial reporting transcends all regional boundaries and redounds to a greater cause of enhanced corporate governance and oversight.

The Philippines believes in the cause of adopting  uniform accounting standards across the globe. We have expressed an unyielding commitment to the international community that these standards will be implemented in the country for the year 2005 and the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas is spearheading its adoption in the financial industry.

Let me share with you our valuable experiences in adopting the standards in the financial industry.

Adoption of IFRS in the financial industry– the Philippine experience

It is fitting to say that the new accounting standards are a phenomenon.  The changes infiltrated the backbone of financial reporting, which affected the way transactions are recorded and reported.  The old school’s concept of conservatism and materiality were overshadowed with new thoughts on fair valuation and substance over form.  The new accounting standards modified our paradigm in evaluating the financial position and performance of institutions. 

In addition to the already difficult task of adopting the standards, the BSP also has to contend with the difference in perspective between the principles of IFRS and the regulatory bodies.  A popular example of which is the concept of loan provisioning wherein the IFRS provides losses on financial assets based on an incurred loss concept while the regulators provide losses based on incurred and expected loss concepts.  Another contentious provision of the standards is the fair value option, which has been the subject of criticisms from the regulatory community.

The BSP has taken bold steps on these issues.  At the onset, we emphasized that all financial institutions under BSP supervision should comply with the provisions of the new standards in all respects in preparing their audited financial statements.  However, we remained steadfast in our position that financial institutions should provide for both incurred and expected losses.  In this regard, they have to comply and reflect the BSP recommended valuation reserves in the prudential reports or in the reports submitted to BSP.

On the other hand, considering the amendments of the iasb on the fair value option provisions, we allowed financial institutions to use the said classification, subject to certain regulatory conditions such as:

  • Having an appropriate risk management system prior to initial application of the fair value option for a particular activity or purpose and on an ongoing basis;
     
  • The fair value option may only be used for instruments for which fair values can be reliably estimated; and 
  • Financial institutions should provide BSP with supplemental information as may be necessary, to enable BSP to assess the impact of the financial institution’s utilization of the fair value option.

The adoption of the standards does not only call for alignment of existing regulations with the provisions but also necessitates the establishment of the infrastructure for prudential financial reporting.  In this respect, we have revised the manual of accounts and developed a new reportorial requirement for banks. The advantage of going through this exercise is that we, as regulators, were given an opportunity to design the reportorial structure to create a common platform serving all our information requirements. The amount of information that we will be able to generate from the new reporting structure will enhance our off-site supervision capabilities.

The Philippine transition to IFRS is a consultative process involving the regulators, industry players and external auditors. The different perspectives shared in this endeavor helped us in understanding the principles behind the standards and the impact of adoption on our interrelated functions. 

Disclosures and good governance

One of the key features of the standards is the overwhelming amount of disclosure requirements. This has made financial reporting a complex process.  However, looking at the upside of it, these disclosure requirements will empower the stakeholders in making relevant decisions.

The BSP believes that this uncovering of more information, will help us realize our vision of full transparency, which is one of the pillars of good corporate governance.  Disclosures along with the other reforms that we have implemented such as requiring the board of directors to create corporate governance and audit committees, imposing more stringent fit and proper standards for the qualification and disqualification of bank directors, and requiring at least two independent directors in the board, among others, are keys in strengthening the confidence of the public in the financial industry. We believe that gaining the public’s trust is the cornerstone of development.

Trust is what binds the components of an economy together. It creates a level playing field for all market players, which fosters an environment conducive to investments. Trust bestowed upon a system goes beyond the basic economic infrastructure. It gives an unwavering assurance that through progress or crisis, the public would remain committed to pull the strings for development. 

Challenges

The adoption of the standards only provides the gateway to achieving good governance. Several other hurdles will bask along the way as we strive to reach this goal.  Each discipline in the accounting profession would have its share of issues to resolve and responsibilities to carry out that would be vital for corporate oversight. 

 Auditors would play a more expansive role in this undertaking.  They would give us an independent view on how the risk exposures and other activities of the business ultimately affect the financial statements.  They would keep watch over compliance with the standards and maintaining fairness and accuracy in the reports.  Accountants in the academe are handed with the noble task of passing on the learning from one generation to the next to keep the same passion seamlessly running through time.  Corporate accountants would document the evidence of evolution in accounting through their books and financial reports.  The regulators on the other hand, would anchor the industry on prudent grounds amidst the changing standards and practices.   

An even greater challenge is to channel this harmonious interplay of responsibilities to a regional effort of establishing a common set of regulations similar to the Sarbanes-Oxley Act in the United States or the EC 8th Directive in Europe.  This vision may already be in the drawing boards in some of the countries represented here or better yet this may stir a united stance to echo a regional commitment on corporate governance. 

Conclusion

We are in the middle of a monumental evolution of accounting standards and other best practices.

Let us not focus on the difficulties and complexities of change, rather let us take this opportunity to correct the mistakes done in the past, strengthen our fortress for growth and seize the chance for global convergence.

I would like to congratulate the organizers of this event for this worthwhile endeavor.  Thank you and I wish you all a successful conference.

Title: Banking for Sustainable Development Through a Socially-Responsible Financial Sector
Occasion: Technical Experts Conference, ADFIAP-EU Proj. on Environmental Governance Standards for DFIs in Asia
Speaker: Deputy Governor Diwa C. Guinigundo
Transcription:
It is my honor to speak again before a distinguished group of delegates and technical experts on a topic that is fast changing the landscape of the global financial system. And I am particularly elated at the fact that this is being held in Manila. This is an exciting time for us in the Philippines. This shows we have passions other than politics and democracy. We can also be exhilaratingly exuberant about development finance and the environment. Let me therefore extend my warm congratulations to the organizers of this event and their foreign partners and sponsors for convening this forum that seeks to recognize an important aspect of environmental reality: a new orientation towards more environmentally-sound policies and practices in development finance . To me, it is high time for development finance institutions (DFIs) in Asia to strengthen their important role as stakeholders in the pursuit of sustainable development by advancing awareness and adopting environmental management standards in their lending operations.  

Initiatives to promote sustainable development 

Let us refresh our memories. As early as 1992, through the United Nations Environment Program Finance Initiative (UNEP FI), the financial sector has taken to task the protection of the environment as a fundamental aspect of sound business management. The UNEP FI formalized the financial institutions’ commitment to sound environmental and sustainability management principles. This initiative emphasized collective responsibility between governments, businesses and individuals in using market mechanisms toward common environmental goals .

On a broader scale, the adoption of the Equator Principles (EPs) by 10 of the world’s largest banks from 7 countries[1] in June 2003 changed the nature of project finance. The Equator Principles challenged UNEP FI's leadership in the area of finance and sustainability by setting specific environmental credit procedures and standards for financial institutions in determining, assessing and managing environmental and social risks in project finance. Adherence to these principles  entails the adoption or refinement of environmental strategies in such areas as internal controls, financial and credit risks, public relations, and marketing. Borrowers seeking financing from the so-called “equator banks” should factor these guidelines into the design and execution of their projects. On the part of “equator banks”, adopting the principles is mainly about managing social, environmental and reputational risks. These banks acknowledge that good business entails striking a balance between environmental protection and social responsibility. After two years since its adoption, the Equator Principles have become the new market standard by which financial institutions evaluate loan proposals. Today, 34 global financial institutions have adopted the Equator Principles.  

In the Philippines, the local financial sector has joined the growing community of international financial institutions engaged in promoting the integration of environmental concerns in their lending operations. To date, seven domestic banks are already signatories to the UNEP FI statements[2], closely following Japanese and Australian banks in the number of bank signatories in the Asia-Pacific. But this is not a cause for jubilation. On a regional level, only 12 percent of signatories to the UNEP FI statements come from this region compared to 72 percent among our European counterparts. Thus, the challenge for us in Asia is to further align our regional banks’ environmental governance standards with international best practices.  

Going further, the Bankers Association of the Philippines, Chamber of Thrift Banks and the Rural Bankers Association of the Philippines signed a joint statement on the environment and sustainable development in June 2001—a testimony to the importance given by Philippine banks to environmental risk management. The initiative rests on the following core principles: (1) good ecology is sound economics; (2) to be pro-environment is to be pro-development; and (3) environment and sustainable development are hallmarks of responsible individual, corporate, as well as global citizenship. We know that such a decision is an individual bank’s business decision, but let me ask this important question anyway: What about the rest of the Philippine banks? This is a big challenge to their vision and mission.  

On the part of the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP), its role as a supervisor and regulator of banks and non-bank financial institutions is to ensure that these financial institutions comply with good corporate governance and internationally-accepted best practices in their operations . Among others, the BSP is now considering the possible recognition of the banks’ determined efforts to be strong on the environment as a manifestation of their adherence to good corporate governance and operations. Moreover, our monetary operations sub-sector is now reviewing our guidelines on rediscounting to see the possibility of assigning a higher weight on projects that are strong on the environment . On the other hand, compliance to best practices can be properly evaluated if there is an efficient monitoring system. Towards this end, the BSP is supporting the enactment of a law that will establish a strong credit information bureau that will anchor a comprehensive credit information system that could include, among others, information on borrowers’ compliance with environmental standards. this is a major step towards achieving an efficient monitoring system to determine compliance of financial institutions with the principles of sustainable development.

Environmental governance standards and practices

Over the last decade, the volume of lending by multilateral development banks (MDBs) to domestic financial institutions (FIs) in developing and transition economies has grown considerably. MDBs maintain that the delegated nature of FI lending gives the domestic financial institution almost complete responsibility over investments in subprojects. Such decisions extend to identifying, assessing, and mitigating the likely environmental and social impacts of subprojects. By providing credit, capital and financial services often unavailable from mainstream financial institutions, DFIs can align business values, goals, strategies and decision-making structures with sustainable development.

DFIs can do well to promote “ecology-friendly goals” from its clients by requiring an environmental and social management system. in this way, you can incorporate the screening of environmental and social aspects in your lending operations. A full environmental impact assessment should be done to examine a project’s potentially negative and positive environmental consequences and compare them with those of feasible alternatives.

Your responsibility, however, does not end with pre-screening loan proposals.

Monitoring is another key element of good environmental governance. It is necessary to ensure the continuance of sound environmental practices during the course of the project cycle. It is equally important to develop and improve environmental accounting by requiring your clients to comply with the sustainability reporting of the project. This entails having them declare the wastes generated by the project, its environmental impact, and the measures undertaken to mitigate these effects.

Still, beyond pre-screening and monitoring is technical assistance and follow up support: providing the training and know-how to maintain the environmental soundness of the projects you finance. This may mean training your own experts in the field of ecology to be able to provide effective follow up support.

Commitment to the UNEP FI statements will keep you focused towards achieving your “green goals” in your internal operations. Commitment entails action, not just “lip service”. Compliance with local and international environmental regulations, updating your practices to incorporate relevant developments in environmental management, and continuous research and development in the area of good environmental governance will measure your strong commitment to these goals.

By improving environmental governance standards, DFIs are committing to the un millennium development goal of integrating the principles of sustainable development into its programmes and contributing to the reversal of the loss of environmental resources by 2015. 

Issues and challenges

Now that we have the equator principles as the new standard for assessing environmental risks to project financing, implementation is the order of the day. however, banks are faced  with issues  because traditionally, they have never been environmental regulators. neither have they viewed environmental governance as a core banking function until the last decade. up to now, the process is still evolving. banks continue to suffer from limited experience in monitoring environmental and social compliance to EPs. This weakness puts banks/FIs under the glare of non-government organization’s (NGO) scrutiny. A case in point. in July, Banktrack—a network of civil society organisations tracking the operations of the private financial sector and its effect on ecology—has been gathering support from financial institutions to withdraw financing Shell’s Sakhalin II project[3]. Banktrack argues that Sakhalin II violates the equator principles’ natural habitats and indigenous peoples policy—violations which should preclude financing of the project by equator banks. Now that the global financial community has established a framework to address environmental issues, a big responsibility to protect the environment seems to have been shifted squarely to the shoulders of financial institutions. We should expect NGOs and environment activists to be more vigilant in exacting clear implementation from the banks/FIs with regard to the principles they themselves have formulated.  

To address this challenge, banks and FIs may have to step up capacity building measures. These can take the form of consultations with experts and  organizing fora such as this technical experts meeting .We expect such measures will foster the exchange of information on relevant environmental issues, policies and procedures. It is a means to train project finance staff in the environment-friendly standards of project finance.         

Another area of concern is transparency due to the lack of reporting standards with regard to implementing the EPs. Without a standardized method of reporting or any independent auditing or compliance mechanism, it is difficult to assess how one bank’s/FI’s sustainability performance compares with another. Thus, we see a great need to institutionalize reporting standards to come up with a clear evaluation of an institution’s compliance with the equator principles . To enhance transparency, banks/FIs should adopt internationally accepted standards of reporting such as the United Nations’ Global Reporting Initiative (GRI) for reporting on the economic, environmental, and social dimensions of their activities, products, and services.

Conclusion 

Finally, let me pose this question: “Why DFIs in environmental management?” Your role as financiers affords significant opportunities to promote responsible environmental stewardship and socially responsible development. A standard setting has been done with the formulation of the equator principles, but much needs to be done. the preamble of the equator principles: “We will not provide loans directly to projects where the borrower is unable to comply with our environmental and social policies and practices” is a strong statement. But rhetorics do not make a successful endeavor. We have to reinforce our preaching with practice. Here lies the importance of leadership by DFIs. We are fully aware that environmentally and socially sound lending can have huge long-term benefits. society expects DFIs to deliver on the lofty principles advanced by the equator principles and the UNEP FI statements. Protecting the environment must prevail over business opportunities. As development finance institutions, you take on a unique role in financing sustainable development.  The challenge for you is to define with clear social and ecological limits the space for activities you want to be involved in. In achieving a sustainable future, all stakeholders, whether private or public, non-governmental organizations, individuals and communities should work together. The BSP will support your collaborative efforts towards this end.

Thank you and good day.  

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

[1]  The banks that originally adopted the Equator Principles were ABN AMRO Bank, N.V., Barclays PLC, Citigroup, Inc., Crédit Lyonnais, Credit Suisse First Boston, HVB Group, Rabobank Group, The Royal Bank of Scotland, WestLB AG, and Westpac Banking Corporation.  

[2]  These banks include the Bank of the Philippine Islands, Development Bank of the Philippines, Land Bank of the Philippines, Metropolitan Bank and Trust Co., Philippine Bank of Communications, Planters Development Bank and the Rizal Commercial Banking Corporation.

[3] The Sakhalin II gas and oil project is located on Sakhalin Island in Russia’s Far East, and is being developed by a consortium led by Shell. It will consist of three offshore platforms, offshore and onshore pipelines, an onshore processing facility, a liquefied natural gas (LNG) facility and oil and gas export terminal. Environmental activists point out the project’s severe environmental and social impacts, including threatening the critically endangered Western Gray Whale with extinction, undermining the livelihoods of indigenous peoples, damaging habitats of endangered bird and fish species, and polluting important fisheries. Experts have reported that the project design falls way short of industry best practice, and that its risk assessments are inadequate. As a result, the project risks causing a catastrophic oil spill, as well as major routine impacts. Local and international environmental organisations have demanded substantial design changes, and Russian groups have initiated lawsuits against the project. With a capital cost of at least $12 billion, the project is expected to seek project financing later in 2005.

Title: Stimulating the Growth of Microfinance in the Philippines
Occasion: NCR Stakeholders' Forum on Microfinance
Speaker: Governor Amando M. Tetangco, Jr.
Transcription:
Introduction

Good morning. I am happy and honored to be part of this Stakeholders’ Forum which aims to look at the role of microfinance in job generation and entrepreneurial growth, specifically in the National Capital Region (NCR). The NCR continues to have the highest unemployment rate nationwide, resulting in poverty and inequality. It is indeed an opportune time to conduct a forum such as this to address these pressing problems.

Microfinance: Benefits beyond one household

In the face of these problems, one possible intervention is the provision of microfinance services. Although microfinance is not a panacea, it has been proven, here and around the world, to be a powerful intervention in tackling the various facets of poverty.

As most of you already know, the practice and provision of microfinance has been growing in the Philippines. This increase is driven by the numerous empirical evidence and many success stories that demonstrate microfinance as an effective tool for economic development.

Microfinance provides the necessary push for microenterprises to help them grow. This bears significance for the Philippines where micro, small and medium enterprises make up 99.6% of our total industries and employ 70% of our workforce. It becomes even more significant when we learn that around 4.1 million families belonging to the lowest income strata are engaged in microenterprise activities. Without access to financial services, these microenterprises are forced to rely on more expensive sources of credit such as informal money lenders which limits their capacity to grow their businesses. It is clear therefore that by invigorating these microenterprises, microfinance can have a direct contribution and impact for economic development and poverty alleviation. Microfinance can then empower the many Filipinos living in poverty to increase their economic activity and income, build up assets, prepare against emergencies and better invest in education, health, and housing thereby improving the overall quality of their lives. In addition, the benefits go beyond the client’s household. These microbusinesses generate the much needed employment and increase the economic activity in local economies.

Growth of the microfinance industry

Given these benefits of microfinance and its potential for far reaching gains, the question that is asked of us today is how we can further develop and stimulate the growth of microfinance in the country.

Growth in the microfinance industry may be characterized by an increase in the breadth and depth of outreach of existing microfinance institutions, heightened competition among microfinance service providers, diversification of product and service offerings, and the presence of private and commercial funds for microfinance activities.

There is no standard blueprint to show us how to achieve these characteristics and to ensure the growth of the microfinance industry. To a large extent, the growth will be, and should be, market driven. But there are some enabling factors and necessary conditions that must be present to achieve such growth.

Necessary conditions for growth

First and foremost, there must be an enabling policy and regulatory environment that supports and promotes the development of sustainable and viable microfinance institutions that will best serve the microfinance clients. The Philippines is among the few countries in the world with a national strategy for microfinance.

The national strategy envisions a viable and sustainable private microfinancial market with the main objective of providing low income households and microenterprises access to financial services. Anchored on the national strategy, a policy framework was created and several laws and issuances were passed to promote greater involvement of the private sector, the non-participation of government line agencies in credit programs and the adoption of market oriented financial and credit policies. These are the Social Reform and Poverty Alleviation Act, Agriculture and Fisheries Modernization Act, Executive Order 138 which rationalized government directed credit programs, the General Banking Law of 2000 and the Baranggay Micro Business Enterprise Act.

The General Banking Law in particular has paved the way for the flourishing of microfinance within the banking sector. The Bangko Sentral was mandated to recognize microfinance as a legitimate banking activity and we have, since then, taken a pro-active stance in developing a “microfinance-friendly” policy environment, in increasing the capacity of the BSP and the banking sector as well as in engaging in promotion and advocacy efforts.

I am happy to note that these initiatives have played a catalytic role for banks to engage in microfinance. Before the year 2000, there were about 55 banks claiming that they had microfinance operations. Today, we have 187 banks engaged in microfinance covering all the regions of the country. That is well over a 200% increase in just less than five years. With this increase in banks providing microfinance, we will see more of the unbanked yet bankable receive the much needed access to financial services.

The BSP is committed to continue to support this development with the primary objective of creating a policy environment that will allow banks to have a wider scope for their microfinance operations, while protecting their depositors and the financial system. In some cases, it may entail more flexible provisions, while in other cases it may entail more rigorous standards. What is essential is that the policies and regulations seriously consider the needs of banks with microfinance operations in order to increase in outreach and sustainability.

Aside from the laws, issuances and national strategy, the Philippines also boasts of a clear regulatory framework for microfinance institutions. This framework focuses on the key areas of transparency, portfolio quality, efficiency and outreach.
