We are currently finalizing revisions to the BSP manual of examination to incorporate microfinance operations.   We have started to train a core group of bank examiners knowledgeable in microfinance operations.

We are also intensifying our efforts, in partnership with the national credit council, to set up a credible and comprehensive credit information bureau.   We have just completed the first phase of the project which we highly think will greatly benefit microfinance practitioners, in terms of promoting stronger credit discipline and reducing the risk of credit pollution.

Enhancing training and capacity building

Another priority area in the BSP microfinance agenda is our continuing training and capacity building program for bank examiners, officers and employees, as well as the microfinance practitioners, in the banking sector.   This is being implemented through a series of trainings, workshops and study tours . For the benefit of the banking sector, the BSP has begun incorporating microfinance into the basic rural and thrift banking courses .So far, these courses have already been offered to 1,500 participants . In June 2004, we launched a series of seminars designed to educate banks on the importance of internal controls, performance standards and best practices for sound microfinance operations.

To further augment our capacity to effectively supervise microfinance activities within the banking sector, we have created a top-level microfinance committee to oversee BSP’s microfinance initiatives. Likewise, we have set up a microfinance unit within the BSP to implement and coordinate all microfinance activities. We are among the first central banks in the Asia-Pacific region with a permanent office dedicated to microfinance.  

Encouraging promotion and advocacy

Our ongoing initiative on microfinance is also focused on promotion and advocacy. In 2003, we launched a regional advocacy program where we conducted microfinance seminars in strategic regions in the country.   To date, we have been successful in conducting information seminars for a total of 1,350 participants in 9 regions across the country. Our advocacy program is aimed at encouraging potential practitioners from the banking, cooperative and NGO sectors, as well as establishing links with corporations, foundations and international organizations that could lend support to existing microfinance institutions (MFIs) by way of technical assistance and other capacity development needs.

All of these initiatives underscore BSP’s strong commitment to promote the development of microfinance.

Concluding remarks

Let me just point out that although the BSP’s mandate is to focus on the banking sector, our involvement in microfinance extends beyond the banking community. We are also interested in working with other microfinance practitioners and organizations, such as NGOs and credit cooperatives, so that together we can ensure the long-term viability and sustainability of microfinance. Possible areas for collaboration include the transformation of non-bank MFIs into banks, development of a uniform set of standards, and the promotion of best practices for sustainable operations within banks, NGOs and cooperatives.

It is vital that we pool our resources if we are to achieve progress in this crusade against poverty.

On that note, I would like to wish everyone a pleasant day and a meaningful discussion ahead.

Thank you.

(Note: 2nd International Forum on Microfinance, INAFI-Philippines, August 25, 2004, PRRM Building, Quezon City)

Title: Sustaining Macroeconomic Stability Through Fiscal Consolidation
Occasion: 77th General Membership Meeting Semiconductor and Electronics Industries of the Philippines
Speaker: Governor Rafael Buenaventura
Transcription:
Ladies and gentlemen, good afternoon:

1.  Introduction

I have been asked, in my capacity as member of the Government’s Economic Management Team, to speak to you today about the new tax initiatives of the Arroyo administration. I can understand SEIPI’s interest in the Administration’s planned tax initiatives.    Taxes, after all, are a part of business costs. And just as Keynes used to argue, there are only two great certainties in this world:  death and taxes!

Your Government proposes to expand the tax base and increase tax collection. This is the bad news. The good news is that doing so, while admittedly painful in the short term, would arrest the incredibly large decline in the tax effort ratio and the significant climb in public sector debt. Let me cite a few numbers. The budget deficit of the National Government has been on a rising trend in the past decade, from less than 1 percent of GDP in 1995 to 5.2 percent of GDP in 2002. This was driven in recent years by higher-than-programmed expenditures and, more importantly, revenue shortfalls due to below-target tax collections, changes or lack of changes in tax policy, and to some extent, reductions in the tariff duties on imports. [1] the overall result has been a rising level of Government debt, as the Government resorted to borrowing to compensate for the financing gap.  The total stock of debt for the National Government alone has grown from P1.2 trillion or 61 percent of GDP in 1995 to P3.4 trillion or 77 percent in 2003. Such levels of fiscal deficit and public debt are generally considered to be high for an emerging economy like the Philippines. Unless we can tame the fiscal deficit and reduce our public debt, our growth prospects for the medium term are significantly at risk. You would not want to see recession and reduced capacity of your Government to provide the general public with basic public goods and services!

The message is clear. Reducing the fiscal deficit and public debt is the most urgent and critical task facing our country today, and raising fiscal revenues should be the Government’s main strategy for achieving this. It will enable the government to have enough funds for key budget items such as infrastructure, education, health and other basic services. Infrastructure spending, in particular, is important for enhancing our international competitiveness and ability to achieve sustained growth over the medium term. Closing the fiscal gap will also help raise the level of national saving, free up funds for investments, prevent a buildup of inflation expectations, reduce domestic interest rates, and restore investor confidence in the country’s macroeconomic fundamentals.

Let me clarify an important issue of tax administration. While we expand the tax base, we shall not stop intensifying tax administration. We shall address the issue of graft and corruption as much as we shall run after tax cheaters and evaders to plug the reportedly large tax leakage.

And so, with due apologies to my colleagues at the Department of Finance, let me now describe to you, in broad terms, the package of fiscal measures being planned by the government. 

2.  Sustaining  macroeconomic stability

2.1  medium-term objectives

The new tax initiatives are best viewed as part of a broad, comprehensive package of fiscal measures aimed at the following objectives:  (1) achieving a balanced NG budget in six years; (2) reducing the CPSD from more than 6 percent in 2003 to 3 percent of GDP in six years; (3) reducing the public sector debt in line with the NG deficit and CPSD reduction; and (4) meeting these objectives without sacrificing economic growth targets. As I have indicated earlier, such goals require a two-pronged action plan that consists of, firstly, raising revenues through improved tax administration, adjustments in tax policies as well as new revenue measures, and secondly, controlling public spending through austerity measures, civil service reform, and better governance of GOCCs. 

2.2  new tax policy measures 

Let me now run quickly through the new tax policy measures of the Government. The new measures consist of, firstly, legislative reforms designed to increase fiscal revenues and secondly, administrative reforms. The proposed amendments to existing tax laws are along the following lines:

  • A two-step increase in the value-added tax (VAT) rate;
  • Re-imposition of franchise tax on telecommunication  companies;
  • Adoption of a gross income tax system for corporations & business income-earning individuals;
  • Rationalization of the system of fiscal incentives;
  • Indexation of the excise tax on so-called “sin products”;
  • Granting of a general tax amnesty conditional on the submission of statements of assets, liabilities and net worth (SALN);
  • Establishment of a lateral attrition system; and
  • Increase of the excise tax on petroleum products.

These reforms are mainly designed to stem the leakages in the tax system that have weakened fiscal revenue-generation over the years. Fiscal incentives, for example, will be rationalized on the basis of how much they actually contribute to new investments.  Meanwhile, the proposed indexation of excise taxes will address the decline in the real value of excise tax revenues due to inflation. Such measures have long been proposed by fiscal experts and economists, and the economic team believes that they are quite overdue.

Proposed administrative tax reforms include the following:

  • Upward adjustments in the fees and charges of government agencies;
  • Increase in duty on petroleum products from 3 percent to 5 percent, through an executive order; and
  • Other measures to enhance the revenue-generating potential of selected GOCCs, e.g. PEA, PAGCOR, etc.

These measures are expected to bring in some p10 billion in additional fiscal revenues.

2.3  fiscal discipline measures         

The other half of the fiscal deficit problem is government spending. Fiscal authorities intend to bring fiscal expenditures under control through the following: (1) fiscal austerity measures, aimed at reducing non-essential expenditures; (2) civil service reform, aimed primarily at the rationalization of personnel services costs in the budget; and (3) improvement of management and control of the GOCCs and other government corporate entities (OGCEs).    Proposed austerity measures include the abolition of inter-agency bodies not created by law; the giving of compensatory time-off for employees in lieu of overtime pay; the suspension of foreign and local travel; and the imposition of cost-cutting measures on utilities and supplies. Measures on civil service reforms begin with the issuance of executive orders to trim the bureaucracy.    Functions that are either no longer relevant or redundant will be abolished, and employees will be offered a voluntary but time-bound separation scheme. Authorities will also be submitting for Congress’ approval a reengineering bill to reorganize the entire executive branch, including GOCCs, and offer the appropriate incentives to employees. Also in the pipeline are bills to rationalize the government compensation and retirement system.

The final item on the expenditure agenda is improvement of management and control of GOCCs, whose financial operations bear significantly on the public sector bottom line. An executive order is expected to be issued that will (1) improve oversight of GOCCs by their supervising departments or agencies as well as by the Office of the President; (2) establish a binding set of corporate duties and responsibilities for all presidential appointees to boards of GOCCs/ogces; and (3) impose a moratorium on the creation of subsidiary GOCCs pending an assessment of the operations of existing subsidiary GOCCs. 

3.  Concluding remarks 

In closing, I believe that our ability to reverse our poor fiscal position will be a key factor in determining the pace and sustainability of economic growth over the next several years. Our ability to balance the budget and reduce our public borrowing will determine how much funds will be available for public investments, and how much resources will be allocated to key economic needs such as infrastructure, education and training, health services, and so on.

A better fiscal performance will also be a key factor in strengthening investor confidence in the Philippine economy. Concerns about the government’s ability to manage the deficit partly prevents foreign capital flows, since investors think that the government may not have enough funds for the upgrading and maintenance of public infrastructure.  Good public infrastructure, after all, is a key ingredient to a sound business environment.

Reducing the public deficit to me is therefore one of the urgent and critical tasks for the government. Raising revenues through tax initiatives is a crucial part of the strategy to bring the deficit under control. Let us bear in mind, therefore, that the Government’s tax initiatives are part of the Government’s macroeconomic program to secure our economic growth prospects for the medium term. The other pillars of this program is the reform of the power sector, the reform of the financial sector, including the development of the capital market, and buildup in infrastructure and external competitiveness. It is, to be sure, a very difficult program, one that will require the support of every Filipino. And because the fiscal budget affects not only the delivery of government services but also inflation and national income, every Filipino has a stake in ensuring that our fiscal objectives for the medium term are achieved. Always remember, no pain, no gain! We can help in these efforts not only through supporting the government’s tax initiatives but also pushing our authorities and legislators to exercise fiscal responsibility and discipline.


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

[1]  Rosario G. Manasan (2002), "Explaining the Decline in Tax Effort,"  Philippine Institute for Development Studies (PIDS) Policy Note No. 2002-14,  December 2002.

(Note: 77th General Membership Meeting, Semiconductor and Electronics Industries of the Philippines (SEIPI), July 30, 2004, Tagaytay City)

Title: Housing as Catalyst for Economic Recovery
Occasion: 1st National Socialized Housing Expo & LGU-Private Sector Housing Conference
Speaker: Governor Rafael Buenaventura
Transcription:
Introduction

Distinguished officers and members of the Chamber of Real Estate and Builders Associations, Inc., ladies and gentlemen, good afternoon!

It is an honor and a pleasure for me to be invited by your Chamber to its monthly business meeting and on the occasion of the First National Socialized Housing Expo and LGU-Private Sector HousingConference.  CREBA’s work of more than thirty years in improving the standards of the different disciplines in the housing sector; in instilling among its members the social objectives and the public interest behind the business of real estate; in pushing for important pieces of legislation for the benefit of the different stakeholders in the industry; and in creating a foundation to complement the socially oriented housing projects of the government, has firmly established itself as a strong and reliable partner of the government in the implementation of the national shelter program.

Today’s choice of theme is very appropriate.      Housing and the LGU projects that support it at grassroots level will undoubtedly act as a catalyst for economic recovery.    An active housing sector has positive linkages to many other industries in addition to its direct employment generation and unquestionable impact on the quality of life of people by meeting a very basic necessity.    On the other hand, successful LGU projects on housing, the door for which was opened by the local government code of 1991 and the urban development housing act of 1992, have proven the capacity of the local governments to undertake housing developments and take the lead in land use planning in their respective jurisdictions.

Bangko Sentral actions

As Bangko Sentral, our basic contribution is the control of inflation as the foundation for macroeconomic stability. This is the critical pre-condition to a healthy housing market. Average inflation in 2003 has been cut to just 3.1 percent. For 2004, we expect inflation to range between 4–5 percent. As a result of the success in controlling inflation in the last five years, we have seen lending rates reaching their lowest levels in twenty years. Lower interest rates were achieved notwithstanding the impeachment of a president, street protests, military coup, and the overshooting of our budget deficit by a substantial amount, among others.

Although the peso has depreciated during this period amid many uncertainties, its overall volatility has been kept under control. In spite of weak exports and minimal foreign direct investment, we managed to minimize peso volatility to 29 cents or half a percent as of July 2004 and peso has depreciated by only 3.2 percent.

But we realized that achieving price stability, low and stable interest rates and a relatively stable currency are not enough. We are taking other actions to contribute more directly to the national shelter program, support the housing sector, and the economy as a whole.

It is known to all of us that one of the major factors stifling the growth of a more robust industry is the inadequate supply of long-term housing finance. The ability to structure mortgage payments affordably is vital in the decision to invest in housing because of the huge upfront cash outflow it typically requires. The lack of financing effectively restricts demand for housing. This situation can be remedied by a deep and strong capital market, which opens sources of long-term finance.

There are other compelling reasons for Bangko Sentral to have vital interest in the full development of the domestic capital market particularly the undeveloped debt market. The capital market will encourage more domestic savings by broadening the array of investment opportunities to match actual investor preferences. For the same reasons the capital market will help keep domestic savings on shore as well as attract foreign institutional investors. It will promote the resilience of the financial system by having an alternative pillar to cushion against external shocks, contagion and possible reduced access to international capital markets.

Today, about 98 percent of domestic credit is still being channeled through the banking system, while in other countries such dependence had been reduced to less than 60 percent.    This situation makes the banks vulnerable to cyclical downturns and other economic shocks.    We have seen this in 1997 that resulted in an outbreak of bad loans. Banks are still struggling to get rid of this burden that continues to hamper new lending and undermine profitability and solvency.

A stronger capital market ultimately supports a stronger banking system even though it would inevitably change the nature of the banking business. Our banks will have to improve their ability to compete for the public’s savings as well as widen their array of lending products and other services. The competition is healthy and long overdue.

For Bangko Sentral, a strong capital market will enable monetary policy to operate more efficiently by providing us with more market-based tools to fine-tune economic activity and maintain price stability.

Developing the capital market

Developing the domestic capital market needs our collective effort and our clear vision to overcome the short-term challenges and pains that it may entail.

We need a better legal framework to lay down clear and transparent rules that allow widest possible participation by the investing public under proper safeguards. We need to strike a fairer balance between the interest of debtors and creditors to nurture a sustainable market. We need to provide financial regulators with adequate powers and sufficient legal protection to effectively police the system and to protect particularly the small depositors and investors. We need to re-think our taxation framework to remove the distortions that have stunted the development of an efficient and continuous financial market that ideally spans seamlessly the full range of financial products and transactions across the maturity spectrum and into secondary markets. Short-term markets are just as important as long term markets because they provide the liquidity that makes the capital market deep and robust. We need to put in place basic financial infrastructure for the orderly and efficient trading, clearing and settlement of securities transactions as well as proper protection of investors through the use of independent registries and custodians. And most important of all, good corporate governance must be achieved all around.

To be sure, real progress is finally being made as never before although much remains to be done.

The enactment of the Securitization Act of 2004, an initiative that Bangko Sentral keenly supported, is a very promising development that can directly support the housing sector. It will allow banks and other primary credit providers to sell the mortgages for repackaging into securities that can be sold to a much wider investor base. Moreover, the Securitization Law also provides incentives and institutional mechanisms for the secondary trading of such securities.    As experiences in other countries has shown, this will set the stage for increased volume of financing for the housing sector at better terms: lower amortization due to longer repayment period, greater predictability of payment obligations, and lower contractual interest cost.

The implementation of the SPV Act, primarily designed to help banks clean up their non-performing assets so they can start lending again, also creates additional opportunities for the housing sector. Developers should be interested in picking up the idle properties being made available at bargain prices to make them more productive again through re-development into housing projects.  The law is also flexible enough to allow creative structuring of financing arrangements to fit cash flows and to open up the transaction to outside financiers.

The recent removal of DST on secondary trading will also go a long way in deepening the domestic capital market.

Important progress is likewise being made in terms of building market infrastructure.    The fixed income exchange, under the enlightened leadership of the BAP and other stockholders, is set to open very soon. This will create a transparent and efficient trading platform for all kinds of debt securities.  The Bangko Sentral is a strong supporter of this private initiative and we have demonstrated this commitment with appropriate regulatory adjustments. We also stand ready to act as custodian of banks’ proprietary securities holding even as we have already mandated the use of independent custodians and registries for the proper segregation of customer accounts from banks’ own accounts.

Earlier on, we launched the PhilPaSS to facilitate the real time gross settlement initially of large value inter-bank cash payments. When property linked with securities settlement, this will pave the way for an international standard delivery-versus-payment or DVP system which will eliminate settlement risk that add to the costs of doing business. Already, this is being put to good use in inter-bank peso-dollar trading and, more recently, government securities trading.

We have started accrediting credit rating agencies which will play a big role in assisting the public make informed investment decisions. Work is also under way to put in place a basic central credit information bureau by the first half of next year so that good borrowers can be rewarded with easier, faster, and cheaper credit access without being too strictly bound to collateral.  Because reliable financial information is the foundation of transparency, we are working closely with SEC to get external auditors to do a better job of ensuring the fairness of financial statements.

Very recently, the Monetary Board approved new rules paving the way for the formation of unit investment trust funds. These are essentially non-deposit collective investments of retail clients professionally managed by bank trust departments in a transparent manner.  These funds can potentially become major institutional investors in the capital market for such things as mortgage-backed securities and LGU bonds that directly benefit the housing sector.

All of these developments will clearly improve the financial system so that it can better support your undertakings.

But there are still important outstanding tasks. More specifically, we need your help to get Congress to act quickly on our proposed amendments to the Bangko Sentral Charter to strengthen our ability to clean up the banking system and properly enforce prudential standards that are primarily intended to protect small depositors. Because the banking system lies at the heart of our financial system, its fragility will seriously handicap the economy.

We will need special legislation to freely allow fair credit reporting that can support a comprehensive and reliable credit information system.  We also need public support to prioritize the Corporate Recovery Act in the legislative agenda to put in place a proper bankruptcy resolution framework that will open up lending to the extent that enforcement of legitimate creditor claims will become more efficient and predictable. We need the PERA and RICA laws to create more institutional investors to invest in long-term securities.

We need further refinement of the taxation of financial transactions to minimize friction cost. Taking the broadest perspective, the potential lowering of direct government borrowing costs and the revitalization of investment activity as direct consequences of the deepening of the domestic capital market should more than compensate for any perceived short-term revenue loss.  I am very certain that perceptive analysts will look at these initiative very positively in its totality and will reward our efforts with more capital inflows that will trigger a virtuous cycle of growth.

In spite of significant progress, the quality of corporate governance, the foundation of investor confidence, leaves room for improvement. This will require further fine tuning of the securities code to better protect minority interests and to further strengthen sec as securities regulator, among other things.

Conclusion

I have purposely avoided extensively reviewing with you the more specific banking measures that we have been doing to support the housing sector. That list is already quite long.  And you can count on our continuing support in these traditional areas of cooperation but it is extremely important for all of us to think more strategically to address the fundamental issues and not just improve the edges.  This is the only way we can make genuinely meaningful progress.

The banking system will always have an important role to play especially in assessing credit risk.  But building a strong domestic capital market is our best hope of mobilizing stable large scale financing to support a truly dynamic housing sector that can consistently address our massive need for affordable housing for all.

Thank you and good day.

(Note: 1st National Socialized Housing Expo & LGU-Private Sector Housing Conference coinciding with the Monthly Business Meeting of the Chamber of Real Estate and Builders' Association, Inc. (CREBA): Challenges for Central Banks, July 29, 2004, Westin Philippine Plaza)

Title: Fostering Economic Recovery Through Capital Market Development
Occasion: Prosperity Talks entitled "The Outlook for Peso-Dollar Exchange Rate and Dollar Interest Rates"
Speaker: Governor Rafael Buenaventura
Transcription:
Introduction

I am delighted to participate in this gathering of investors and stakeholders in our economy. You represent an important constituency that is actually the real strength of our financial system.  Whether as bank depositors, stockholders, bond investors, or participants in mutual funds and other similar schemes, you provide the savings that allow our economy to build productive assets.  As policymakers, we need to focus on the goal of increasing the base of domestic savers so we can wean ourselves away from foreign debt.

Bangko Sentral’s actions

As Bangko Sentral, our basic contribution is the control of inflation as the foundation for macroeconomic stability. This is the critical pre-condition to many things including a healthy housing market. Average inflation in 2003 has been cut to just 3.1 percent. For 2004, we expect inflation to range between 4-5 percent. As a result of the success in controlling inflation in the last five years, we have seen lending rates reaching their lowest levels in twenty years. Lower interest rates were achieved notwithstanding the impeachment of a president, street protests, military coup, and the overshooting of our budget deficit by a substantial amount, among others.

Although the peso has depreciated during this period amid the many uncertainties, its overall volatility has been kept under control. In spite of weak exports and foreign direct investments, we managed to minimize peso volatility to 29 cents or half a percent as of July 2004 and the peso has depreciated by less than 1 percent year to date.

But we realized that achieving price stability, low and stable interest rates, and a relatively stable currency are not enough. As we scan the multiple issues besetting the economy, it is clear that our underdeveloped domestic capital market represents a critical bottleneck to more rapid growth.  It is unlikely that we can sustain a 6 percent growth rate without overheating unless we can make the proper investments in infrastructure and other productive assets.  These require long term financing whether in debt or equity.

The Bangko Sentral has a vital interest in the full development of the domestic capital market.  It will encourage more domestic savings by broadening the array of investment opportunities to match actual investor preferences.  For the same reasons, the capital market will help keep domestic savings onshore as well as attract foreign institutional investors. It will promote the resilience of the financial system by having an alternative pillar to cushion against external shocks, contagion and possible reduced access to international capital markets.

Today, about 98 percent of domestic credit is still being channeled through the banking system, while in other countries such dependence has been reduced to less than 60 percent.    This situation makes the banking system vulnerable to cyclical downturns and other economic shocks. We have seen this in 1997 when it resulted in an outbreak of bad loans. Banks are still struggling to get rid of this burden that continues to hamper new lending and undermine profitability and solvency.

A stronger capital market ultimately supports a stronger banking system even though it will inevitably change the nature of the banking business. Our banks will have to improve their ability to compete for the public’s savings as well as widen their array of lending products and other services. The competition is healthy and long overdue.

For Bangko Sentral, a strong capital market will enable monetary policy to operate more efficiently by providing us with more market-based tools to fine-tune economic activity and maintain price stability.

Developing the domestic capital market needs our collective effort and our clear vision to overcome the short term challenges and pains that it may entail.

We need a better legal framework to lay down clear and transparent rules that allow widest possible participation by the investing public under proper safeguards. Title: Message
Occasion: Gantimpala Agad Award Ceremony
Speaker: Governor Rafael Buenaventura
Transcription:
sang magandang umaga sa aking mga kapwa kawani sa bangko sentral. Katatapos lamang nating parangalan ang ating walong kawani dahil sa kanilang katangi-tanging ginawa.     Itong mga kawani na ito ang larawan at ehemplo ng katangian ng katapatan, kahusayan at pagmamahal sa bansa.

The Gantimpala Agad Award is given as recognition of our employees who exemplify and give life to the core values of the BSP – “Excellence”, “Integrity” and “Patriotism”.  Those three words are not merely core values in the abstract, rather, they best describe who we are, what we are, and what we aspire to be. These eight (8) awardees are living proof that in the BSP, these three words are not empty slogans, but are real – values deeply ingrained in the basic character of our employees.  These awardees therefore represent each one of you, our employees, who try to live up to these values in your ordinary everyday activity.

The “pamantayan” or standard of values refers to a body of traditionally established principles and rules governing behavior. Here at the BSP, we have a family that can be compared to a laboratory for rearing good citizens and active participants for nation building. The BSP family has a culture that our employees reflect on, understand, realize and assimilate. The values of moral responsibility has been imbibed by BSP personnel, which means to accept what is required of us, honor the role which has been entrusted to us and to perform extraordinarily well and make a difference.

This is the best legacy we can leave behind.

Bangko Sentral will continuously be on top of its outstanding performance if more employees will imbibe the core values of the bank.

Nawa’y lagi kayong maging isang huwaran na magbibigay ng magandang larawan ng Bangko Sentral at ng bansang Pilipinas.

Join us then in paying tribute to all the awardees.  To the awardees, our congratulations!

Let us all give them a round of applause.

(Note: Gantimpala Agad Award Ceremony July 26, 2004, Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas)

Title: Strong Corporate Governance - Banks' Passport to Basel 2
Occasion: General Membership Meeting Banker's Institute of the Philippines
Speaker: Governor Rafael Buenaventura
Transcription:
Ladies and gentlemen, good afternoon.

I am very pleased to be here this afternoon to speak before the officers and members of the Bankers Institute of the Philippines, inc. (BAIPHIL).  In line with your theme, I would like to talk this afternoon on the close relationship between corporate governance and Basel 2 compliance.  By the way, Basel 2 was formally unveiled last June 26 after an extended period of development and consultations.

Basel 2 has potentially major implication for the banking industry and on how banking supervision is done.  Our progress towards meeting its expectations is viewed by the BSP as a journey which the Philippine banking system will soon embark. But before presenting you with our latest itinerary, let me first describe to you, as a background, the initial preparatory journey we had already taken. 

The initial journey

In 1995, the BSP recognized the greater risk exposure in the system brought about by derivatives activities. To mitigate this, the BSP issued Circular No. 102 prescribing the minimum standards for risk management of derivatives.  This was probably the first BSP regulation that specifically focused on banks’ risk taking activities and risk management practices.

In 1997, the thrust of bank supervision started to shift its focus to measurement of banks’ risk-exposures and to how banks manage risks, instead of just mainly performing financial audit and compliance review.

In March 2001, the BSP adopted the original Basel 1 framework through Circular No. 280. This Circular provided the guidelines for the computation of risk-based capital for credit risk. The BSP’s risk-based capital adequacy framework was further enhanced with the issuance of Circular No. 360 in December 2002.  Circular No. 360 incorporated market risk into the risk-based capital framework.

The BSP’s effort to focus on risk management is really ultimately intended to give banks greater flexibility to respond to changing opportunities under a more deregulated environment and at a time of rapid technological advances.

Traditional bank supervision tended to instruct banks to avoid risks that seem too high.    The new approach to supervision favors assessment of the quality of risk-management practices, and generally allows banks to take risks so long as the banks demonstrate the ability to manage and price for those risks.

In carefully loosening the regulatory grip on banks’ risk-taking activities in order to give them more elbow room for success, the BSP must necessarily underscore the responsibility of the banks’ board of directors and senior management to ensure the soundness and stability of their respective banks. The regulators’ role is primarily to evaluate the quality of oversight and management provided by these parties – that is, the quality of corporate governance.

Strengthening banks’ corporate governance has been the theme of a number of BSP regulations. In June 1997, Circular No. 130 requiring the Board of Directors of banks to, among others, adopt and maintain adequate risk management policy was issued.  A few months after, or in October 1997, the BSP also issued Circular No. 145 requiring banks to develop and implement a compliance system and to appoint/designate a compliance officer to oversee its implementation. In September 2001, the BSP issued Circular No. 296 which implemented the fit and proper standards for directors and officers of banks and non-banks. The same circular also prescribed a mandatory orientation program on corporate governance for banks’ board of directors. Moreover, the BSP issued in October 2003 Circular No. 410 which provided the accreditation guidelines for banks’ external auditors.

This year, the BSP has continued to issue a number of guidelines that aimed to further enhance governance practices in banks.  In January, the BSP issued the guidelines for the management of banks’ large exposures (Circular No. 414).  Last March, the BSP has strengthened the DOSRI rules by expanding the definition of related interests (Circular No. 423).    In may, the BSP issued Circular No. 429 which aimed to further strengthen banks’ compliance function.  Finally, just a couple of weeks ago, the BSP issued the guidelines for the development and implementation of banks’ internal credit risk rating systems (Circular No. 439). The guidelines emphasize the oversight function of the board of directors over these systems.

We have already traveled quite a distance. Our productive initial journey us the confidence to embark on an even more challenging journey – Basel 2.    Strong corporate governance will be banks’ passport to be able to join and even enjoy the ride. 

The next journey

So what is Basel 2?

Basel 2 is a set of proposals that aim to revise Basel 1 to make regulatory capital more risk sensitive and reflective of all, or at least most of the risks banks are exposed to.

As such, Basel 2 is structured as a three-pronged approach that transcends regulatory capital requirements. That is, Basel 2 not only presents us a risk-based capital framework, but an entire risk-based supervisory framework. The three pillars of Basel 2 are (1) minimum capital requirements (pillar 1), (2) supervisory review process (pillar 2), and (3) market discipline (pillar 3).

Pillar 1 sets out the detailed guidelines for computing regulatory capital for credit risk, market risk, and operational risk.

Major changes are introduced with respect to credit risk. Basel 2 presents three options: the Standardized Approach, the Foundation Internal Ratings Based Approach, and the advanced Internal Ratings Based (IRB) approach. The standardized approach assigns risk weights applicable to sovereign, bank, corporate, and retail exposures. Depending on the external credit risk ratings. The foundation IRB approach, on the other hand, allows banks to use their internal ratings assessment to determine the appropriate capital charge of their exposures. The advanced IRB approach is very similar to the foundation IRB.  The only difference is that under the advanced IRB, banks are allowed even greater discretion in using their internal ratings model to calculate capital requirements.

Capital treatment for market risk as currently implemented through Circular No. 360, remains generally unchanged except for some minor changes in the standardized computation of specific risk charges. Whereas, specific risk weights in the current market risk framework depend on the type of issuer, Basel 2 requires that these now depend on the external ratings of the issue to be consistent with the credit risk standardized approach.

An explicit change for operational risk is a new element. Basel 2 presents three options: the basic indicator approach, the standardized approach, and the advanced measurement approaches. Under the basic indicator approach, a bank’s operational risk charge is computed as a fraction of its gross income. Under the standardized approach, banks operations are divided into specific business lines. Operational risk charge for each business line is determined as a fraction of gross income attributed to each line. Lastly, operational risk charge under the advanced measurement approaches would depend on statistics-based advanced measurement models developed by banks themselves or by outside vendors.

Pillar 2 of Basel 2, on the other hand, prescribes sound principles that should be followed in the process of supervisory review.  It works on the principle that banks can take on risk, but the board of directors and senior management should be responsible to assess the appropriate capital requirement in relation to its risk exposures, including exposures to risks not captured in pillar 1. Banks therefore will be asked to present to the supervisory body their internal capital allocation process. Again, this is where strong corporate governance comes into play    supervisors are then expected to be able to evaluate the process by which banks came up with their “appropriate” capital measures in order to intervene at an early stage before capital goes below what is prudently acceptable.

Pillar 3 of Basel 2, meanwhile, proposes an extensive list of bank disclosure requirements.  It recognizes that markets contain disciplinary mechanisms that can reinforce the efforts of supervisors by rewarding banks that manage risk effectively and penalizing those whose risk management is inept or imprudent. Pillar 3, therefore, is envisaged to result in well-founded counter-party risk assessments. In addition, pillar 3 is also envisaged to support efforts to foster strong corporate governance within banks.

In summary, Basel 2 is based on the principles that (1) banks should have capital appropriate for their risk-taking activities, (2) banks should be able to properly assess the risk it is taking and supervisors should be able to evaluate the soundness of these assessments, and (3) banks should be disclosing pertinent information necessary to enable market mechanism to complement the supervisory oversight function. 

Checking out where we are going

I am assuming that we have all packed our “bags”.  However, we cannot just go rushing into the unknown. Checking out the local conditions in one’s destination is a must for all travelers.  Thus, the BSP conducted a Quantitative Impact Study (QIS) in late 2002 until early 2003 with six (6) of our largest banks. The QIS was aimed to simulate the likely changes in banks’ capital requirements once Basel 2 is adopted.  Let me highlight to the group the important findings of the study:

(1) The sample banks had an average increase in risk-weighted assets (RWA) of 25%, translating to an average 200 basis points reduction in the capital adequacy ratio (CAR) as currently measured; and

(2) Of the 25% increase in RWA, 8% was contributed by credit risk, while the remaining 17% came from the introduction of operational risk charge.

It is apparent from the results that banks’ capital requirements will surely increase with the adoption of Basel 2 since it already covers more risk types. However, given the latest capital adequacy ratio for the entire banking system of 17.8 percent, there is some buffer available, at least on average.  A more positive way of looking at things is that Basel 2 will present our banks with more opportunity to lower their capital charges, if they have the appropriate risk management systems in place. 

The itinerary

Now for our itinerary: where do we intend to go and when.

The BSP has now lined up certain projects that aim to set standards with regard to (1) the computation of banks’ capital requirements, (2) banks’ risk assessment and management, and (3) banks’ disclosures. These projects involve studying the applicability of certain Basel 2 prescribed risk weights and disclosure requirements to local conditions.  The output of the projects will be a comprehensive set of guidelines for banks. Such guidelines will be released not later than end-2006, for implementation in 2007.

Universal/commercial banks are expected to implement the standardized approaches of Basel 2 by 2007 in line with the recommended international timetable.  As a general rule, however, banks are not expected to be in a position to implement the more advanced IRB approaches until perhaps 2010. This is because it would take a minimum of 5 years of data to estimate default probabilities based on banks’ internal rating systems. As mentioned, the BSP just recently issued Circular No. 439 which adopts the Basel 2 prescribed minimum standards for such systems with respect to credit risk.

However, foreign bank branches whose head offices are using the advanced approaches, will be allowed to use them provided that they can show that their models are suited to domestic conditions.

Thrift banks and rural banks, meanwhile, are expected to stay on the existing capital adequacy framework. However, it is the BSP’s goal to make the existing framework a little bit more risk-sensitive, as well as apply pillar 2 and pillar 3 components as warranted.

Speaking of pillar 2, we will continue therefore to push banks to improve their risk management practices and risk assessment capabilities – and this implies pushing for continued improvement in corporate governance. This, of course, goes hand in hand with improving the supervisory tools and resources needed to evaluate such risk assessments.

With regard to pillar 3, appropriate disclosure requirements prescribed under Basel 2 is targeted by 2007.

The timeframes mentioned are only indicative at this stage. To be sure, we will be closely coordinating with the banking industry on the specific implementation details prior to promulgation of implementing regulations. 

On with the ride

From what I have just described, it is clear that Basel 2 is a journey that demands a lot from both the supervisors and the banks.

For the supervisors, foremost of our concerns are (1) the need to examine our existing charter to see to it that we have the necessary powers to implement the new capital standards, particularly pillar 2, and (2) the need to ensure that our supervisory personnel are up to the challenge being posed by Basel 2.

For banks, I say the primary challenge is not so much to buy the most sophisticated and the latest risk management technology, as to foster a sound risk-control environment founded on strong corporate governance.

The role of training, from basic principles to the most complex risk management processes, will be critical as never before. BAIPHIL must rapidly gear up to meet the challenges.

Ladies and gentlemen,

Our bags are packed, destination surveyed, and itinerary set.    Thus, let me just wish all of us a rewarding journey.    We will be taking off shortly…fasten your seatbelts and enjoy the ride.

Thank you very much.

(Note: General Membership Meeting, Bankers Institute of the Philippines (BAIPHIL), July 21, 2004, Shangri-La Hotel, Makati City)

Title: Closing Remarks
Occasion: Farewell Dinner  SEACEN-BIS Seminar on Structural Changes in the Financial Sector
Speaker: Governor Rafael Buenaventura
Transcription:
Dr. Subarjo Joyosumarto, Executive Director of the SEACEN Centre, our distinguished resource speakers from the Bank for International Settlements (BIS), Mr. Paul Van Den Bergh, Mr. Herbie Poenisch and Mr. Ma Guonan, officials from the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas, participants from SEACEN countries and guests, ladies and gentlemen, good evening.

It is a distinct honor for the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas to host this joint seminar/workshop of the SEACEN Centre and the Bank for International Settlements (BIS).       This tripartite undertaking underscores the importance of linking international and regional organizations to the national authorities in mounting activities aimed at capacity building.

I am truly grateful that a notable team of experts from the BIS generously shared their time and their insights on the current changes taking place in the international financial structures. These changes were ushered significantly by the consolidation process and growing competition in the financial sector, the establishment of asset management companies and the development of markets for credit risk transfers.

No doubt, the three-day seminar/workshop may be quite short to fully cover the vast changes taking place in the financial sector. Nonetheless, I am confident that you now have a broader understanding of the evolving structural changes in the financial sector and the need to put up safety nets in the face of these changes.

I am sure our counterparts in Europe and the US would agree that the structural evolution currently happening here in Asia is no different from what they have gone through in recent years. In Asia, many banks have already passed the middle stage of the evolution spectrum of credit business models and are steadily moving towards the advance stage of credit portfolio management. Many of these banks today have successfully transformed their credit risks into marketable products through the adoption of asset management companies and special purpose vehicles.

It is important that as we keep pace with these structural changes, the banking system remains financially sound and stable. The insights and experiences shared by your fellow participants would certainly provide some guideposts in responding to the challenges in your own countries brought about by the ongoing changes in the financial landscape.

Notwithstanding our country differences, our main task as financial supervisors and regulators remains that of ensuring monetary and financial stability. That is why we need to keep banks financially sound.  We need to ensure that banks are properly managed. That is why we need to develop our capital markets to diversify fund sources of investment and corporate activities. We need to ensure that all infrastructures are put in place so that debt instruments can provide additional vitality to the rest of the financial system. We need to install the right policy mix that would support the changing financial environment while at the same time, provide the needed balance to maintaining stability in the monetary system.

Let me close by reiterating our special thanks to the course organizers—the SEACEN Centre, the BIS and our own BSP staff—and all the resource speakers for mounting this seminar and selflessly sharing their expertise and valuable time. To all the 31 participants, I extend my congratulations for your active participation in this seminar. As we bring this seminar to a close, I hope you have been enriched not only by the new learnings shared but also by the new friendships formed.

I wish you all a pleasant evening and an enjoyable trip to Villa Escudero tomorrow.  I wish you also a pleasant and safe trip home.

(Note: SEACEN-BIS Seminar on Structural Changes in the Financial Sector: Challenges for Central Banks, July 21, 2004, Metropolitan Museum of Manila)

Title: Message
Occasion: Second Annual Meeting of Business Expectations Survey (BES) Respondents
Speaker: Governor Rafael Buenaventura
Transcription:
Members of the Monetary Board, distinguished guests, friends, colleagues, ladies and gentlemen, good morning.

I recall we had our first respondents' meeting at about this time last year. We stressed in our remarks that closer partnership between the BSP and our respondents was critical in ensuring that this undertaking remains an effective tool for ascertaining business trends. This is indispensable in calibrating monetary policy response to various shocks in the system. Today we are so pleased that the response rate has improved significantly and most important, this hall is now more full of friendly faces. This is the first point I wish to stress this morning.

Secondly, let me reiterate that expectations play an important role in the business cycle.  In particular, they make the difference between plans that get shelved and those that eventually get off the ground. Usually, it is only after these plans have been implemented that statistics become available to statistical compilers and policymakers. However, if compilers are able to sit down with business managers to get them to talk about their expectations and plans before they are implemented, then a very useful information for policymakers could become available ahead of the traditional information that we get from the business sector. It is indeed business expectations that provide the driving force to business plans which are translated into macroeconomic reality.

Herein lies the importance of the BSP's Business Expectations Survey. The BES is precisely designed to generate this type of advance business information. For one, the survey is conducted well in advance of the reference period.  For another, the quick feedback is facilitated by the fact that the questions are mostly qualitative in nature, allowing the respondents to answer without referring to actual records. But for the survey to be really useful and effective, we need reliable information from the respondents.  That is why my challenge for all our respondents this morning is to further improve, not only on the timeliness and completeness but also on the accuracy of their responses. We cannot overemphasize that the credibility of the survey relies mainly on the quality of the inputs that we get from the respondents.

Beyond this challenge, let me assure our business partners that the BSP will remain committed to this undertaking of producing the data on business expectations. We shall continue to strengthen partnership between the Bangko Sentral and the business community. Through this data base, we are able to sharpen not only the Bangko Sentral's tools for the conduct of monetary policy but also the business sector's own planning and pricing models.

As an initial step toward this end, let me recall with you that we agreed last year to implement certain measures to further improve and expand the survey and how best to disseminate the survey results to the public. Today, one year after the first annual meeting of BES respondents, significant improvements and refinements in the conduct of the survey have been made particularly in the expansion of the survey to include three regions outside the NCR. Major projects are also in the pipeline in the second half of this year and into 2005. Our overall goal, as we indicated last year, is to design something along the lines of the Bank of Japan's Tankan Survey, which provides Japanese policymakers with timely snapshots of various key aspects of the Japanese economy from the perspectives of both business and the consuming public. Over the medium term -- with your continuing support -- we hope to implement a comprehensive system of leading indicators that would tell us the likely path of business and consumer activities in the Philippines.

Let me close by saying that we are very grateful to the business community for the continuing support extended to the BES. We would like to believe that this year's BES respondent awards should somehow express this message of thanks. Our trophies are not silver cups, for the business community is not our cupbearers, but heavy, crystal vases which convey both our transparent, open and heavily-regarded partnerships as well as the best of our hopes for our economy and people.

Thank you and good day.

(Note: Second Annual Meeting of Business Expectations Survey (BES) Respondents, July 07, 2004, Philippine International Convention Center)

Title: Strengthening the Financial System Through a World-Class Payments and Settlements System
Occasion: Signing of the Memorandum of Agreement on the Participation of the Bureau of Treasury...
Speaker: Governor Rafael Buenaventura
Transcription:
National Treasurer Mina Figueroa, Mart Vice president Narciso Eraña, special guests, fellow workers in government, good afternoon.

Allow me to thank all of you for joining us today in our celebration of the 11th anniversary of the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas.  We are celebrating it in simple, but meaningful ways.

This morning the Monetary Board and all our fellow workers at the BSP renewed our commitment to pursue the mandate entrusted to the BSP:  that is, to serve as guardian of price and banking stability.  To us at BSP, ensuring stable conditions in these two critical fronts go a long way in fostering and sustaining long-term economic growth that uplifts the quality of life of Filipinos.

This afternoon, we mark this special occasion with our partner institutions who continue to work with us, to define and implement measures that further strengthen and enhance the stability and integrity of our banking and financial system.

In particular, we continue to make headway in providing a world-class payments and settlements infrastructure system that is aligned with the standards set by both the Bank for International Settlements and the International Organization of Securities Commissions. This is the subject of the Memorandum of Agreement we are signing this afternoon with the Bureau of Treasury and the Money Market association of the Philippines.

After this, BSP will also sign a Memorandum of Agreement with the Securities and Exchange Commission, Insurance Commission and the Philippine Deposit Insurance Corporation for the Financial Sector Forum. This will result in even better and stronger coordination among regulatory agencies of the financial system as we implement consolidated supervision.

The significance of continuing improvements in both payments infrastructure and regulatory aspect of our financial system cannot be over emphasized.

Specifically, the payments system represents a major component of the infrastructure of any modern economy and systemic failure therein can undermine the effectiveness of monetary policy, the soundness of financial institutions, and the economy in general.

This is the reason why BSP has invested time and resources in setting up a real time gross settlements system which we call the Philippine Payments and Settlements System or PhilPaSS.  Launched in December 2002, PhilPaSS has been expanding in terms of both volume and application. Transactions of PhilPaSS now go up to as high as P200 billion a day based on transactions of 93 participating banks.

With PhilPaSS, systemic risk is minimized as real time high value payments between banks are made using their deposit accounts with the BSP.  This allows BSP to monitor liquidity positions of participating banks throughout the day on a transaction-per-transaction basis, so that settlements are made only when banks have sufficient funds.

In effect, PhilPaSS is a tool for ensuring sound risk management.  This is the reason why the Megalink network has also signed up with PhilPaSS.  here before it took three days to settle interbank ATM transactions of Megalink participating banks, now same day settlements are being done under PhilPaSS.

In addition, PhilPaSS is now an important component for implementing a payment versus payment (PVP) system for U.D. dollar-peso foreign exchange transactions.  PVP results from the linkage of two real time gross settlement systems, in this case BSP’s PhilPaSS for peso transactions and Citigroup’s Philippine Domestic Dollar Transfer System for dollar transactions of commercial banks. Under this, final transfer in one currency takes place only if a final transfer in the other currency occurs.  In local parlance, PVP is a “kaliwaan” system.

This afternoon, the MOA we are signing with the Bureau of Treasury and the Money Market Association is DVP or delivery versus payment, for government securities that are traded in the secondary market.  I understand that the value of the Bureau of Teasury’s transactions for securities traded in the secondary market averages P2 billion a day or roughly P500 billion a year. Under the old system, government securities are moved from the seller to the buyer prior to receipt of payment.

Under DVP, PhilPaSS will link up with the Bureau of Treasury’s state of the art electronic backroom processing and information system called the Registry of Scripless Securities or ROSS. This will allow the Bureau of Treasury to move government securities in ROSS account from the seller to the buyer, only after the equivalent cash payment has been debited in the buyer’s demand deposit account with the BSP.  As such, the Bureau of Treasury and sellers of government securities will no longer be exposed to potential credit and settlement risk.

Down the road, I expect more users to sign up with PhilPaSS.  Among others, I understand the Philippine Stock Exchange has expressed interest in using PhilPaSS. Indeed, the increasing use of our world-class payments and settlements system should serve our financial system in good stead.

Ladies and gentlemen, on behalf of BSP, I thank you once again for joining us this afternoon as we celebrate both our anniversary and our joint efforts to further enhance the stability and integrity of our financial system.

We shall now proceed with the signing of our Memorandum of Agreement. Thank you.

(Note: Signing of the Memorandum of Agreement on the Participation of the Bureau of Treasury & the Money Market Association of the Philippines in the PhilPaSS, July 5, 2004, Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas)

Title: FSF: Strengthening the Philippine Financial System
Occasion: Signing of the Memorandum of Agreement to Establish the Financial Sector Forum
Speaker: Governor Rafael Buenaventura
Transcription:
His excellency Peter Sutherland, Ambassador of Canada, Chairperson Bautista, Commissioner Malinis, President Tan, distinguished guests, fellow Monetary Board members, colleagues at the Bangko Sentral, guests and friends, good afternoon.

It is indeed an honor for the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas to serve as the venue for the signing of the master memorandum of agreement between all four agencies represented in the Financial Sector Forum or the FSF. I believe it is also quite fitting that we are marking this very important milestone in the financial services industry of the Philippines at the same time that the BSP is celebrating its 11th anniversary, since it is likewise a significant step forward for the bank.

As set out in our vision, it is the Bangko Sentral’s paramount concern to strive for excellence. In the realm of banking supervision, we have manifested this commitment in continuous efforts to improve our supervisory process.  This is why alongside our internal initiatives, we likewise forged cooperative arrangements with other agencies that also have responsibility for overseeing other financial institutions.  Thus, alongside the improvement of our practices, we have worked on establishing guidelines for information sharing with the PDIC, and the efficient sharing of supervisory responsibilities - including joint examinations – with the SEC.    Soon, too, we will be signing an agreement with the IC.

The FSF represents a different kind of synergy from our past undertakings, though it does not take away from their importance.  In this present alliance, the BSP, SEC, PDIC and IC all evolved from being solitary oversight agencies to a seamless supervisory system.

The forum reflects the steadfast commitment of the BSP, the sec, the IC and the PDIC to promoting a more stable financial system by addressing issues on a continuing basis.  The concerns of the FSF cover a broad spectrum.  And at this point, I would like to share with you some of our plans.

One of our priorities is developing policies that are in accordance with international standards.  This will most likely involve adoption, application, and enhancement of risk-based frameworks for most of the institutions that we supervise.  While this will certainly strengthen the capabilities of our financial institutions, this will also hopefully help us improve our performance in country assessments.  For this, we will look to the work of the standard-setting bodies such as the bank of international settlements, the international organization of securities commissions, and the international association of insurance supervisors, all of which we are members of, by the way.

We will also devote time to harmonizing policies across agencies. This will not only improve our capability to supervise financial conglomerates but will also make supervision of financial institutions more efficient.  The effort will likewise promote a level playing field for all financial institutions.

I believe the industry players will appreciate my saying that the application of uniform policies across supervised institutions will definitely cover rules on corporate governance, particularly the requirement for independent directors, and the guidelines for the accreditation of external auditors.

The strength of financial markets is likewise dependent on market discipline. Thus, the Forum is committed to promoting the integrity of financial data and disclosures.  We may do this by broadening the scope of disclosure requirements but on our end, we will also be working out ways of reducing the reportorial burden.  In terms of delivery of data, we will make use of technological developments to explore possibilities for database linkages between the four agencies.

The last thrust of the Forum that I will mention for today is certainly not the least important task.  This is consumer empowerment. Since the maturity of our markets is largely dependent on the level of maturity of investors, we will help them acquire knowledge on various aspects of financial markets.  In order to carry this out, we will partner with other government and private institutions.  So for the representatives of industry associations here today, we will be knocking on your doors to enlist your assistance.  Help us to inform our consumers of their rights and responsibilities so that they will no longer experience collective losses.  In the process, they will look toward investing in legitimate institutions only.

I hope I have given more than a snapshot of what we intend to achieve by putting up this formal venue for interagency coordination. Truly, the sheer volume of issues makes our task a tall order. However, we face this with enthusiasm and optimism, confident that our efforts will result to a more robust financial system.

Before I end and we actually proceed to seal the Cooperative Bond, I would like to acknowledge the valuable support of the Canadian International Development Agency through its Policy Training and Technical Assistance Facility for helping us put things in motion.

Thank you and good day.

(Note: Signing of the Memorandum of Agreement to Establish the Financial Sector Forum, July 5, 2004, Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas)

Title: Mind the Gap
Occasion: Opening Remarks Capital Market Development Council (CMDC) Workshop
Speaker: Governor Rafael Buenaventura
Transcription:
Ladies and gentlemen, good afternoon.

All of us gathered here this afternoon are direct stakeholders in our country’s capital market, but the ultimate stakeholder of capital market development is of course our economy.    The economic literature has always emphasized that limited access to capital presents a critical challenge to economic growth and stability. It is therefore imperative to establish a well-functioning domestic capital market to ensure that corporations efficiently mobilize capital for economic growth.

In the normal course of things, an active money market should first be established in order to develop markets in foreign exchange and government securities. A well-developed government debt market consequently facilitates the development of capital markets (that is, market for long-term corporate debt, equity, and asset-backed securities).

In the Philippines, our money market is fairly liquid. Latest figures we have on money market transactions, for instance, show that volume of transactions was about 73% of GDP.    Our government debt market, on the other hand, is significant in size due to regular issuance of debt by the government with sizeable volume and variety of tenor. Last year, outstanding government securities amounted to p1.7 trillion, or about 39% of last year’s GDP.

Despite these, our corporate equity and debt markets have been lagging behind. Last year, value of transactions in the Philippine stock market was only 3.4% of GDP. Worse, corporate bond issuance was only 0.2% of GDP during the same period. It seems that in the Philippines, development of the capital market is not a natural consequence of the development of the government bond market. There seems to be a gap that separates the two. In thinking of ways to develop our capital market, we should therefore be always mindful of this gap and how to bridge it.

From where I stand, the challenge involves increasing market liquidity by widening the base of domestic investors who will buy the securities that local public companies issue. Increasing the number of investors entails fostering the growth of savings. Fostering savings, in turn, require a sustainable macroeconomic environment, i.e. Low inflation environment. I am proud to say that the Bangko Sentral has been successful on this front. Average inflation last year has been cut to just 3.1% and the prospects for contained inflation this year despite recent developments are quite good.

Widening the investor base also involves enhancing the transparency in the market. The availability of reliable and timely information on market players complements regulatory oversight by promoting market discipline. However, before one can enhance transparency, the accounting standards need to be improved. To address this, the BSP and the sec have both committed to implement IAS 39 and IAS 32 by 2005.

Lack of reliable public information on the creditworthiness of corporate entities can also be remedied by the development of the credit ratings industry.  The BSP has already recognized the sole credit rating agency in the country, and is now reviewing the application for recognition of one foreign rating agency.

However, the presence of all these information would be all for naught if the investors are not educated about the methods for assessing the relative merits of the different instruments in the market.  Towards this end, the BSP has formed a consumer education committee to design a comprehensive action program to strengthen financial literacy of consumers, as well as of key influence groups such as the mass media.

Notable progress is being made.  We have already made a major upgrade of our payment system by putting in place the Philippine RTGS or PhilPaSS.  In addition, the BAP’s fixed income exchange is scheduled to open this month. On the regulatory front, we are set to launch later this afternoon, also here in the Executive Business Center, the Financial Sector Forum which will seek to deepen coordination among its four participating agencies, namely: the BSP, the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), the Philippine Deposit Insurance Corporation (PDIC), and the Insurance Commission (IC).  But in all these, we must not forget to continuously improve the corporate governance standards in the Philippines as this serves as the foundation in the further development of our capital market.

Ladies and gentlemen, I thus wish you well in this workshop. May the session this afternoon be a productive exercise in identifying ways to advance capital market development in the Philippines.

Thank you very much.

(Note: Opening Remarks. Capital Market Development Council (CMDC) Workshop, July 5, 2004, Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas)

Title: 11th BSP Anniversary Message
Occasion: BSP's 11th Anniversary Celebration
Speaker: Governor Rafael Buenaventura
Transcription:
Members of the Monetary Board, fellow central bankers here at the BSP head office, the Security Plant Complex and our regional offices and branches. Good morning. And more appropriately happy anniversary!

As late as Friday last week, the BSP Ad Hoc Anniversary Committee still did not know where exactly this flag raising ceremony will finally take place.  While it preferred the podium, the committee nevertheless set up the Assembly Hall as an alternative venue if it rains. Very BSP,I should say. We would go to great extent to ensure that we attain our objective. And we did this past year.

I must say that as a result of our collective efforts, the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas, once again, did very well.

Truly, it has been a most challenging year for any monetary authority. In our case, not only did we have to navigate through an increasingly complex and difficult environment, we had to contend with a lot of noise from various fronts.

Really, we do make a lot of noise in this country. I just wish it is true that noise drives away negativism and brings good luck. This way, the Philippines can be restored to its rightful place as one of the most vibrant and dynamic economies in this part of the world, where the quality of life is good.

Well, this is still possible. If all of us, all sectors of our society, will work together and set aside personal differences for the common good.

This is the reason why I am particularly proud of BSP. United by our vision, we continue to deliver on our mandate: we continue to have low and stable inflation that is well within target; benchmark interest rates that remain at single-digit levels and have therefore lowered the cost of doing business; and improving numbers of our key banking indicators that tell us we are on the right track in terms of making sure we have a sound banking system.

But much remains to be done if we are to catch up with our more developed ASEAN neighbors.  We have a capital market that is in its infancy.  Much needed legislative reforms were slow in coming.  After 10 years of lobbying for the elimination of the Documentary Stamp Tax (to develop the secondary market for long term paper), we finally got it in the last session; the Asset Securitization was just passed and is still awaiting the implementing rules and regulations. The much needed Corporate Recovery Act still needs to be passed. The protection of the investors is as important as the protection of the borrowers. In a developed capital market, there are just as many small investors as there are small borrowers.

Other legislative work still has to be done – the banks have to work harder to do their share of developing the market.

The regulatory environment has to be improved to ensure regulatory compliance and greater transparency from our own perspective. We still need vital amendments to our Charter if we are to be effective regulators, a pre-requisite for a really sound banking system, not to mention the fact that we still need the SSL removed from our Charter.  Fortunately, recent legislation on this issue has been passed, we just have to work on ours.

I think it is fair to say that BSP helped provide the silver lining for our economy.    Independent observers here and abroad have noted it. Some even gave us awards in recognition.

For these, I give credit to our formidable BSP team -- our employees, our officials, our Monetary Board.

Today, BSP enters its 11th year practically alongside the newly-elected president’s induction into office. It gives us reason to be hopeful that, this time, we will make a lot of headway in making life appreciably better for more Filipinos.

I also expect this fresh wind of hope to inspire the corporate planning sessions that we will hold a few days from today. Our environment is constantly evolving and we have to make sure that we are able to correspondingly fine-tune our template for attaining the BSP vision.

I will not bore you with the specifics on our gains in inflation targeting, the pursuit and promotion of good governance and the adoption of world standards and best practices in the banking sector.  You must have read the circulars that were issued and routed to the staff as well as extensive media reports on the same.

I do wonder if you have noticed, and this I would want to point out, that BSP is by design gradually breaking out from its exclusive and reclusive shell. It has gone into areas that have begun to give traditional esoteric central banking work a common or mass appeal. Our groundbreaker was microfinance which we continue to promote aggressively as our response to poverty alleviation. Anti-money laundering and small business-friendly rediscounting provisions have also been doing their share to strengthen BSP linkage with the public-at-large, in general, and with enterprising Pinoys in particular.

Last year, we intensified our campaign for clean money both in form and content. There was a significant increase in the volume of mutilated and unfit notes that were turned in for exchange or retirement. We attribute this in part to the cooperation and support of the banks and the greater public awareness on the merits of keeping our money in circulation clean and in good condition.

The clean note campaign, launched during our 10th anniversary, has been a good complement to our anti-counterfeiting efforts.

This year, we go a step further. In partnership with the Department of Education, we will involve the schools in the campaign to protect the integrity of our currency. In addition, we will develop training and activity modules that will encourage students to develop the habit of regularly saving money.

In this regard, we are re-launching, after more than a decade, a national savings campaign to instill among the children the habit of saving and to impress on them the vital role of savings to our economic development as well as to their future.

Aside from working with schools, BSP will also be setting up an economic and financial literacy center that will cater principally to students. Our goal is to set up similar centers in our regional offices and branches.  The center will provide students the opportunity to learn how seemingly esoteric economic policies and programs affect people’s lives.  This should serve them in good stead when it is their turn to lead the country.

Information campaigns to protect the public from investment scams will also be pursued.  We will also continue working with the financial sector in developing and implementing measures that will further enhance consumer welfare.

These initiatives inject elements ordinary people can relate to.  This could go a long way toward generating wider public support for BSP, especially when we would need it most.

Internally, we have been moving on as well.
