Impact on inflation.  Equally important from the BSP’s perspective, the practical experience of many industrial and developing countries, including the Philippines, suggests that large fiscal deficits also contribute to inflation. This is based on the economic theory that governments running persistent deficits have to, sooner or later, finance those deficits with money creation (or seigniorage), which produces inflation. This theory has been supported by empirical evidence. A recent IMF study involving data on 107 countries (including the Philippines) over the period 1960-2001 uncovered a strong positive correlation between fiscal deficits and inflation among high-inflation and developing country groups, but not among low-inflation and advanced economies. [3]

Let me quickly point out, however, that the ultimate impact of fiscal deficits on inflation depends on a number of factors, such as monetary policy credibility and the presence of institutional safeguards against fiscal dominance. For example, credible inflation-fighting central banks and deep financial markets tend to facilitate the continuous rolling over of sizeable levels of public debt, thus avoiding the need for deficit financing through money creation. [4]

Let me also emphasize that the Philippines has enough institutional safeguards against excessive deficit financing and seigniorage that help ensure the BSP’s independence from fiscal sector constraints. The New Central Bank Act of 1993 (R.A. 7653) sets out clear limits on the size and the repayment period of the BSP’s financial assistance to the National Government.

Impact on interest rates.  Fiscal deficits also affect the economy through interest rates, particularly in cases where large fiscal gaps compel the NG to borrow heavily from the market through the issuance of government securities. Such a situation leads to not only unsustainably high levels of public debt but also high level of interest rates. This, in turn, raises the cost of capital and dampens investments.

In essence, persistently large public sector deficits tend to contribute to a lower level of national saving, which implies less money available for investments at the macro level, and therefore slower economic growth over the long term.

Herein lies the challenge to the next administration: The need to balance the budget and ensure fiscal sustainability over the long term. These two priorities are closely interlinked. Closing the fiscal gap is a key component in the strategy to ensure fiscal sustainability over the long term, because a balanced budget also helps reduce the overall level of public debt. There will be less need for new borrowing and the debt burden will also be lower. It goes without saying that lower public debt means lower interest payments that have to be programmed into the annual budget. We need to attack the heart of the problem.

Impact on market and business confidence. The fiscal situation also has an international dimension: It affects the confidence in the Philippine economy of foreign investors and financial markets. The widening budget deficit was one of the main reasons cited for the threat of a pull-out of investments by a U.S.-based investment fund manager as well as the recent credit rating downgrade of the Philippines by an international rating agency. Lack of confidence in the government’s ability to manage the deficit tends to keep foreign capital from flowing into the Philippines, since investors know that the government will not have enough funds for the upgrading and maintenance of crucial public infrastructure including road network and other forms of public works. Good public infrastructure, after all, is a key ingredient of a sound business environment.

4. What needs to be done:  some ideas

How then do we go about balancing the budget and ensuring long-term fiscal sustainability? Since we know that declining revenues are the main factor behind the widening of the budget deficit, strategies to balance the fiscal deficit must begin with raising fiscal revenues. And since we also know that expenditures have been growing at a relatively high rate annually, it may also be worthwhile for fiscal authorities to look into expenditure reforms.

I have to admit that these two key points are easier said than done.

On revenues. The current fiscal situation will require a very strong effort, I would call it a tenacious political will, to rebuild the government revenue base. This means that the National Government’s present medium-term target of achieving a balanced budget by the year 2009 must be supported by a credible package of revenue measures. Such a package would include measures to strengthen and broaden the tax base, improve tax administration by addressing corruption and inefficiency in all revenue-collecting agencies, and stem the leakages in revenues from, for example, income taxes and the VAT. Another source of revenue leakage that has been pointed out by local and foreign economists is the current system of generous fiscal incentives to selected industries. The present system needs to be revisited in terms of how much they actually contribute to investments and rationalized accordingly. Fiscal authorities will also need to consider raising existing tax rates, or indexing them to inflation to prevent the erosion of their real value by inflation.

Let me add here that efforts in this area have already begun. The recent passage of the bill on the restructuring of the Documentary Stamp Tax (DST) is a welcome move. In addition, the National Government is also pushing for the passage of bills on the indexation of excise tax on sin products and the creation of the more powerful, more independent, and more performance-oriented national revenue authority, which will replace the present BIR.

Expenditures.  Meanwhile, the incoming administration will also have to examine the prevailing patterns of public spending with an eye to reducing wastage and preventing the government from spending beyond its means. This is obviously a tall order for any administration, and will require much careful thought. Some economists have advocated trimming down the bureaucracy as a means of reducing government expenditures. [5]  Significant expenditure savings can only come from a forceful civil service reform program, which would include a significant reduction in the number of government workers, an improvement in the skills mix, an increase in the compensation of supervisory staff, and an examination of the generous but poorly targeted non-wage benefits for government employees that are contained in the budget. The main problem with this, of course, is the political resistance that it is likely to generate. Nevertheless, this aspect of public finance should not be ignored. We also need to improve the quality of government expenditures to ensure that sufficient resources are spent on capital outlays.

Institutional Issues. Political resistance appears to be the main stumbling block to the fiscal reforms that need to be carried out. To this end, the next administration must exert a very strong but careful effort to explain to the Filipino public the necessity of undertaking major fiscal reforms and to outline the actions that are necessary in order to achieve fiscal consolidation and government debt reduction over the medium term. In this regard, fiscal authorities may benefit from the innovations in monetary policy implementation that have gained popularity among central banks in recent years. Economists have recently argued the case for the use of fiscal policy rules and fiscal policy committees, which are taken from the idea of monetary policy rules and the monetary policy committees of central banks. [6] Fiscal rules would help set stringent allowable limits on the deficit and public debt levels that fiscal authorities may generate, while fiscal policy committees, composed of technical experts, would be responsible for delivering fiscal discipline and debt sustainability in the long run, in the same way that central banks are responsible for price stability.

5.  Concluding Remarks

In conclusion, I assure all of you that there is no shortage of ideas on how to solve the fiscal problem, and I have managed to convey in very broad strokes only a few which I think need to be highlighted. No doubt some ideas are easier to implement than others, and indeed some of the measures I mentioned are already in the legislative pipeline.

An important point to remember in discussing the fiscal situation is that fiscal reforms should be accompanied by structural reforms to boost growth prospects. Historical experience suggests that it is difficult to bring down deficits and public debt levels without an accompanying robust economic growth. This means that fiscal consolidation efforts are best undertaken within the larger context of a broad-based agenda of structural economic reforms that will help guarantee the continued growth of the economy over the medium term.

I have a final point to make. The next administration that will be facing this fiscal situation will need to summon not only the political will to push through with a very difficult macroeconomic program, but also the ability to enlist the support of the Filipino public. That process begins with a candid declaration that the fiscal environment needs to be seriously addressed and a strong commitment to the people and to the global community that the government will be placing fiscal issues first on its agenda.

Thank you and good afternoon.


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

[1]  Rosario G. Manasan (2002), "Explaining the Decline in Tax Effort,"  Philippine Institute for Development Studies (PIDS) Policy Note No. 2002-14,  December 2002.

[2] Gabriela Inchauste (2002),  “Philippines: Issues in Fiscal Sustainability,” Unpublished background paper for 2002 IMF Article IV consultation.  International Monetary Fund.

[3]  Luis Catão and Marco Terrones (2003). “Fiscal Deficits and Inflation,” IMF Working Paper No. 06-65. April 2003.

[4]  Ibid.

[5] See Inchauste (2002).

[6]  See for example Charles Wyplosz (2002), "Fiscal Discipline in EMU: Rules or Institutions?" Paper prepared for the April 16, 2002 meeting of the Group of Economic Analysis of the European Commission,  and Wyplosz (2002b), "A better way to balance budgets,” Financial Times, 3 December 2002. Available in pdf format on the author’s website at http://heiwww.unige.ch/~wyplosz/FT_041202.pdf.

Title: Closing Remarks
Occasion: First Quarter Meeting Philippine Statistical Association
Speaker: Governor Rafael Buenaventura
Transcription:
Distinguished guests, officers and members of the Philippine Statistical Association, colleagues at the Bangko Sentral, ladies and gentlemen, good morning.

Inflation is a central concern for policymakers like us. Beyond us, it is an important anchor of economic decisions for businesses, households, workers, and just about anybody. We are well aware that economic decisions that people make are linked to price developments. As a result, consumer price movements have significantly affected the behavior of the various agents in the economy. Empirical evidence and experience of many countries have shown that high and volatile rates of inflation distort the decisions that economic agents make, ultimately leading to slower economic growth. Central banks exist precisely to achieve price stability conducive to a balanced and sustainable economic growth.

Measures and analysis of inflation are thus vital decision tools for both the private sector and the government. We are therefore pleased to note that this morning two excellent papers on the measurement of inflation in the Philippines were presented. I think this is a rich area for research where future work will greatly benefit not only policymakers but also the general public in terms of better understanding the dynamics of the inflation process in our country.

Good measurement of inflation is critical. It will secure the credibility of economic reports as well as the policies crafted on such basis. We cannot overemphasize that under the BSP's inflation targeting framework of monetary policy, the credibility of monetary policy, and our commitment to price stability are the building blocks for a successful management of price movements in the Philippines.

This makes core inflation important in ensuring that monetary policy is more efficient and more accountable. Removing transitory elements of price movement will render monetary policy more focused. A more focused target of monetary policy will clarify to the public the scope of the central bank's accountability.

Finally, let me thank the Philippine Statistical Association for giving the Bangko Sentral the opportunity to participate in and host the first quarter meeting for 2004. I would also like to thank everyone who took time out from their busy schedules to join us this morning and participate in the lively discussions. I look forward to seeing you again in one of your future meetings in the BSP Complex.

Thank you and good day.

(Note: First Quarter Meeting, Philippine Statistical Association (PSA), April 14, 2004, Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas, Manila)

Title: HSBC: Keeping Faith in the Philippines and its Potentials
Occasion: Announcement of HSBC's Expansion Plans in the Philippines
Speaker: Governor Rafael Buenaventura
Transcription:
Secretary Cesar Purisima, Mr. Warner Manning, Mr. David Sutton, special guests, ladies and gentlemen, good morning and welcome to Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas.

We at the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas are very pleased to host this briefing on HSBC’s expansion plans in the Philippines.

The HSBC group is one of the world’s largest banking and financial services organizations with over 9,500 offices in 79 countries and territories in Europe, the Americas, the Middle East, Africa and the Asia-Pacific region.

HSBC has been in the Philippines since 1875. In other words, they have been in our country for 129 years now.  It is therefore safe to say that HSBC knows the Philippines quite well.

Today, the HSBC group has 21 branches and more than one thousand employees in the Philippines. With its expansion, HSBC’s workforce is expected to increase by 50%…..or by 500 people by the end of 2004. And between 2005 and 2006, HSBC plans to employ 2,000 more….. here in the Philippines.

This vote of confidence for our country is important to us. It is a signal…..and a validation to other investors…..that the Philippines is indeed a good and viable option. And so therefore, we thank HSBC for keeping faith in the Philippines and its potential.

Definitely, this decision of HSBC to expand its operations in the Philippines will benefit our economy. It also underscores the integral role of international banks in our local financial services industry.

As we have said before, a foreign institution which embraces the concerns of the community as its own, ceases to be foreign to the community. It becomes part of the community.

In particular, not only does HSBC support our growth aspirations; as a good corporate citizen, it also supports the education of our underprivileged children and the protection of our environment. And so, to us in the Philippines, HSBC is…..truly…..the world’s local bank.

Ladies and gentlemen…..let us therefore give a round of applause to the enduring partnership between HSBC and the Philippines.

Thank you everyone. May I now invite Warner Manning, the chief executive officer of HSBC Philippines, to discuss the bank’s expansion plans in our country.

(Note: Announcement of HSBC's Expansion Plans in the Philippines, April 13, 2004, Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas, Manila)

Title: Remarks
Place: Executive Business Center, BSP Complex, Malate, Manila
Occasion: Graduation Ceremony of Batch 4, Basic Security Training
Speaker: Governor Rafael Buenaventura
Transcription:
Distinguished guests, officers and members of the Philippine Statistical Association, colleagues at the Bangko Sentral, ladies and gentlemen, good morning.

My fellow workers at the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas, ladies and gentlemen:

Good morning to all of you.

First of all, I would like to extend my congratulations to the 38 graduates of the 4th batch of the Basic Security Training (BST).  Such congratulation is indeed in order. The BST, after all, --- and I know all of you will agree with me --- is not just an ordinary course. On paper, the course is designed to “equip security personnel with the basic knowledge of all aspects of bank security and law enforcement functions.”  That is what is stated in the course manual.   But for the participants, that is translated to mean 60 days of intensive, rugged and laborious training that consist of physical and mental courses that are designed initially to test your endurance and then to develop your skills and agility as security personnel of the BSP.

And I understand it is a course that you will never forget, especially the reception and recognition ceremonies of the training.

Definite reasons to be here

I am very happy to be a part of your graduation exercises for several reasons.

First, it allows me to share in, and be a part of, the honor and pride that you all feel now that you have survived “literally” the grueling requirements of the course. Out of the 40 original participants who enlisted for the BST, you are the ones who can proudly say, “I have been weighed, I have been measured, and I have been found deserving!”

Second, it gives me a chance to be with BSP employees in a more personal manner. Due to the many pressing demands of my office and my work, it is not often that I get to have the chance to be up close and personal with the employees so I try to grab the occasion when the window of opportunity presents itself.

A third reason why I am here is to personally thank all the members of the SITD for your tireless efforts to make BSP a more secure and a safer office to work in. Often, I get to see you doing you working --- checking cars and bags, interviewing visitors, doing your security rounds of the bank premises --- some are even in shorts and riding bicycles, which, I understand, is a first in the history of the SITD.

These security policies, though cumbersome to some, are major ingredients that deter would-be troublemakers. With the SITD at the helm, they have to think twice before they attempt anything against the bank or its employees.  After all, they have to contend with the “A-team” of the BSP, which is the SITD!

Kudosto the SITD management

I am happy that the SITD management in coordination with branch operations has risen to the challenge to ensure that the BSP remain a safe workplace and its operations to continue uninterrupted. I also extend my congratulations to them for their tireless efforts in prioritizing and addressing the skills development of the BSP security and improve its standards and operating procedures that can match the ever changing and increasing sophistication of the challenges that may confront the bank.   These challenges are not unique for the bank for we see it happening everywhere.  That is why there is no excuse and no reason for laxity.  After all, the consequences can be catastrophic for the BSP in particular and the country’s economy in general.

The proof of the pudding is in the eating

It is because of these that I am asking all of you to exercise vigilance in your work. Do not fall prey to viewing regular tasks as routine, as some of our colleagues have mistakenly assumed their work to be. Never relax your guard nor compromise the standards that the BST training has taught you.  Now that you have completed your training, the only thing left to do now is to practice what you have learned.  In the process of doing so, always imbibe in your work definition that you are part of the bank’s front-liners, and how the public will first taste and appreciate the BSP credo of patriotism, integrity and excellence.  These core values should serve as foundations in your work. Over the years, it should take root as you gradually become immersed in the core operations of the SITD.  But as the training transformed the tissues in your bodies into muscles, I also hope that as you grow in years in the bank the muscles on your chests will not become fats on your bellies.

Twin tasks of the SITD

In the July-December 2003 Makati Business Club’s survey, the BSP has, for the 14th time been chosen as the best performer besting 34 other government agencies. This recognition is not any ordinary feat, even for the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas.  And I would like to say that it is an achievement that I am very proud of.

A major reason for the good review of the bank is the public. And this is where the SITD can contribute immensely. While I want the SITD to the vanguard of the bank’s welfare, its vigilance in the screening of visitors should be balanced with polite and courteous service, no matter how unique or at times absurd their issue with the BSP may seem to be.

Bear in mind that you will always be the first and last employee of the bank that they will interact with when they visit the BSP.

The BSP challenge

Finally, I would like to extend an equal challenge to my colleagues in the BSP. Let us help these graduates succeed in what they have been trained to do. Ripe with idealism and high in morale, let us not be the cause of their disillusionment and frustration. Rather, let us become their reason for excelling and be their guidepost for success.

Final words

I look forward to speaking before the next batch of recruits of the basic security training.   Security has always been a major concern of mine.  And I am glad that courses like the BST help us prepare for any eventually.  But we are always praying that it never comes!

Again, my congratulations to all of you and I look forward to seeing you in the bank as you perform your duties, this time not as trainees but as bonafide members of the BSP security force.

Thank you.

(Note: Graduation Ceremony of Batch 4, Basic Security Training, Security, Investigation & Transport Department, April 2, 2004, Executive Business Center, BSP Complex, Manila)

Title: PRAISE: Excellence Beyond Expectations
Occasion: Awarding Ceremonies for PRAISE 2002 Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas
Speaker: Governor Rafael Buenaventura
Transcription:
Magandang hapon po sa inyong lahat!

Once again, we have gathered together to salute those among us who exemplify the core value that we all strive for:  Service excellence.

You and I know, achieving excellence is not an easy task. Excellence goes beyond competence, skill and expertise. Excellence demands focus, tenacity of purpose, the passion to do better all the time.

And so, fellow workers at the BSP, once again, let us honor our awardees this afternoon by giving them another well-deserved round of applause. Palakpakan po natin sila.

Fellow workers. The truth is, it would have been extremely difficult for the model departments and the model employees to achieve their level of excellence…if they did not get the support and cooperation of their colleagues and other departments.

For that matter, it would be impossible for BSP to establish…and maintain…a solid reputation for excellence if only a handful of departments were turning in exemplary performance.

Clearly, model employees and departments receive the support and cooperation they needed. Working as a team, we accomplish our goals together. On behalf of the members of the monetary board therefore, I thank all the departments and offices of the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas!

The truth is, we all deserve praise….you and I… all of us who work at the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas. Whether you are a bank examiner, a FOREX trader, a security personnel, a lawyer, a museum guide, a cashier, an economic analyst, a receptionist, a museum guide, a director, a member of the Monetary Board…whatever it is that we do….we helped BSP establish a solid reputation for excellence.

And so, let us all give a round of applause to all BSPers.  Unahin po natin ang lahat ng BSPers who have since retired and moved on – Palakpakan po natin sila.  This time, let us give ourselves a well-deserved round of applause.

Indeed, ours is a champion team.  But you and I know, there are still many areas we have to improve on here at the BSP so that we can rightfully claim a world-class status. Besides, excellence has no finish line.

BSP will continue to need the support and cooperation of everyone to work well individually and collectively. As team members…as members of committees, as members of team BSP.

BSP needs us to do our work well…in a consistently excellent manner….so that together we achieve and sustain our vision of BSP as a world-class monetary authority.

Having said that, we should not miss the opportunity to say thank you to all those who worked long and hard on the selection of our 2002 awardees. Obviously, theirs was a most difficult task.  As in any major undertaking, there were differences in opinion that led to long and serious discussions.

Nevertheless, the professionals that they are, they all came through. So here we are.    Let us therefore give a round of applause to all those who worked for our praise awards!

Ladies and gentlemen, awards program such as praise are important. They are landmarks. They inspire us to raise the bar, each time a milestone is accomplished. It makes us excel beyond expectations.

I hope therefore that all of us will continue to help make praise a successful program within BSP.  Together, let us subject our praise program to constant improvement and fine-tuning so that it can serve as model for other institutions to follow.

Ladies and gentlemen of the BSP…. I am already looking forward to the 2003 PRAISE awards.

Marami pong salamat sa inyong lahat!  

(Note: Awarding Ceremonies for PRAISE 2002, Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas, March 31, 2004, BSP Assembly Hall, Malate, Manila)

Title: Response
Occasion: Gold Quill Awards Ceremonies  International Association of Business Communications
Speaker: Governor Rafael Buenaventura
Transcription:
I would like to thank the Board of Directors, the management and members of the International Association of Business Communications or IABC for this unique award in Excellence in Communication Leadership. As Governor of the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas, I don’t get this kind of citation too often.

I also find much meaning in this award because communications is one aspect of business that is so easy to take for granted, particularly when things are going well for us.

In this day and age, when our country enjoys a very free press; when conjectures, posturing and grandstanding on economic and business matters come to fore from politicians or from men or women on the street, I constantly remind myself that I shouldn’t judge their competence nor the lack of it. Instead, I see it as an opportunity to gauge the public’s ability to properly absorb issues or matters that we in the BSP need to be able to educate the public about. This way, we are able to respond accordingly with either policy moves or appropriate explanations.

My openness, my accessibility for comments, the BSP’s switch to inflation targeting and the Monetary Board’s pro-active approach to communicating our policies, more importantly, the reasons behind them, lead to one ultimate objective: the duty to educate our public of the dynamics of monetary and financial management. This all boils down to eliciting responses that we require in helping build a healthy economic environment. We at the BSP are duty bound to improve the lives of our countrymen by keeping inflation at its lowest, and providing stability to financial markets so that businesses can flourish and grow. This is our mandate, even if in the course of performing our tasks, we would have to deal with speculative activity brought about by non-economic factors.

Modesty aside, the BSP and the National Government have worked hand in hand to keep inflation and interest rates at their currently low levels. No, they don’t just happen. In fact, they require deliberate moves over a two-year horizon to get where they are. Yes, you heard that right: Two years--that’s how far ahead we need to think, and to act.

However, much more needs to be done to bring the message down to Juan Dela Cruz; for him to appreciate that something is being done to address his yearning for a better life ahead. But the BSP can’t do this alone. We need your cooperation in highlighting our achievements because we need to build on them to restore confidence in ourselves, and our investors. Mind you, brooding on items we can’t have as a nation, instead of counting our blessings ain’t gonna help any.

So, I pose this challenge to you: Help us create a more positive business environment through positive and constructive communication. Regardless of politics, this nation must move forward. We have only to gain and grow further from such a move.

Thank you very much again for this prestigious award.

(Note: Gold Quill Awards Ceremonies, International Association of Business Communications, March 30, 2004, Shangri-La Hotel, Makati City)

Title: Closing Remarks
Occasion: Appreciation Lunch Capital Market Development Council
Speaker: Governor Rafael Buenaventura
Transcription:
Our meeting this afternoon is a very important one. We are honoring our Congressional leaders who have skillfully shepherded through Congress very important pieces of legislation that are highly critical to the development of the domestic capital market and the modernization of our financial system.

Rising above the din and noise of the political season, our Congressional leaders have worked hard and showed remarkable vision, tenacity and statesmanship in getting these complex tasks done that have put the country firmly back on track on the path of financial reform. We are keenly looking forward to their continuing efforts to follow through with other important legislative initiatives that Chit Manabat mentioned earlier.

The Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas has a vital interest in seeing to the health not just of the banking system, but also of the broader financial system including the local equity and debt markets. We need all of these components working together efficiently to have a truly robust system that not only effectively responds to the full range of financial services needs but is also resilient to various external shocks that every so often hit any economy.

Our banking system will also operate more smoothly and more safely in the presence of deep capital markets. This is a point that has been emphatically made by Mr.. Alan Greenspan in trying to explain the remarkable resiliency of the U.S. banking and financial system.

The Bangko Sentral is strongly committed to supporting and implementing the reform initiatives of congress. We have been doing our best to faithfully implement the General Banking Act of 2000, the Anti-Money Laundering Act, the SPV Act and other important laws. You can count on us to do our share for the new laws that have been recently enacted.

I am also happy to highlight the excellent working relationships we have established and nurtured with other financial regulators particularly the Securities and Exchange Commission and the Office of the Insurance Commission. We believe that this cooperation is essential if we are to effectively discharge our duties. Many of the reforms have cross-cutting effects that overlap our defined jurisdictions. And many of our regulated entities whether as individual entities or conglomerates, operate in multiple financial markets. We hope to cement these relationships going forward so that we will be better able to respond to the needs of the industry as well as to the expectations of the general public for world class financial services.

I believe we should keep the momentum going on our partnership—Congress, the private sector, and the regulators—in advancing the financial reform agenda that is focused on promoting the long-term interest of our economy. The challenges ahead are still many but I am confident that the spirit of cooperation toward our common purpose will lead us to success.

Lastly, the Bangko Sentral believes in the mission of the capital market development council, and shall remain a strong supporter of and an active participant in the council.

Thank you and “Mabuhay ang Pilipinas”.

(Note: Appreciation Lunch, Capital Market Development Council, March 29, 2004, Inter-Continental Hotel, Makati City)

Title: Banking Reforms and the Development of the Domestic Capital Market
Occasion: General Membership Meeting Trust Officers Association of the Philippines
Speaker: Governor Rafael Buenaventura
Transcription:
Distinguished officers and members of the Trust Officers Association of the Philippines, fellow professionals. Ladies and gentlemen: good evening.

It is an honor and a pleasure for me to speak before you tonight on the occasion of your General Membership meeting. I value this opportunity because TOAP has always stood at the vanguard of developing a robust asset management industry and of providing other trusted agency services to complement the normal menu of banking services. You are therefore a vital partner in your own right in helping us build a deeper, more complete, more versatile, more resilient and more efficient financial system.

The reform agenda

Let me share with you our agenda for promoting comprehensive financial system reform.

As the government agency mandated by law to supervise the banking system, the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas is deeply committed to its reform. But I believe we will be too myopic, and ultimately ineffective, if we ignore the condition of the broader financial system in which it is embedded. It is pointless to build an elegant living room when the house as a whole remains rickety and decrepit.

Bangko Sentral has vital interest in the full development of the domestic capital market particularly the very underdeveloped debt market. First, it will stimulate domestic savings by broadening investment opportunities and by allowing better portfolio diversification. Second, it will improve the intermediation of domestic savings and attract foreign investors. Third, it will promote the resilience of the financial system by having an alternative pillar to cushion against external shocks, contagion and possible reduced access to international capital markets. As Alan Greenspan has pointed out, the presence of a deep domestic capital market is a major reason why the united states is able to quickly contain and recover from banking crises. Fourth, it will enable monetary policy to operate more efficiently by providing us with more market-based tools to fine-tune economic activity and maintain price stability.

A well-functioning domestic capital market will also contribute to a more robust banking system by providing healthy competition that is essential for effective market discipline. At the same time, it will provide banks with business opportunities as investors and asset managers, as issuers, as underwriters and arrangers, as guarantors, as market-makers and as agents, custodians, and registries.

The case for capital market development is very compelling indeed and our inability in the past to make it happen is therefore so frustrating. I think we have largely allowed the myriad problems to immobilize us into inaction.

The time has now come to break free from that inertia.

BSP initiatives

Bangko Sentral is taking action across a broad front based on interlocking and complementary reforms to finally jump-start the domestic capital market. By working in close partnership with other government agencies and the private sector, I am convinced that we will finally succeed.

At Bangko Sentral, our basic contribution is the control of inflation as the foundation for macroeconomic stability which in turn is a critical pre-condition to a healthy capital market. Average inflation in 2003 has been cut to just 3.1 percent and the prospects for maintaining the low inflation environment are quite good. Naturally, lower inflation has led to lower interest rates which has created a conducive environment, and indeed a demand, for a bond market.

But we realize that achieving price stability is not enough.  Thus, we are taking parallel action on other key fronts.

We are championing better corporate governance and financial transparency so that investors will have more confidence in placing their funds and have more reliable financial information to guide their judgments. Our natural starting point has been the banking system where such reform is sorely needed and where we have direct influence. But the impact goes well beyond that as banks themselves enforce better standards of governance in their corporate clients that prepare them for the capital market.

In the same vein, we are demanding higher standards of conduct from external auditors so that reliable financial statements can be properly enforced. We are complementing the governance initiative by developing a program to promote improved financial literacy so that investors can impose proper discipline.

We have also tightened prudential and risk management standards. This will definitely strengthen the banking system but it will also stimulate in the process the potential supply of debt issues in the capital market as banks adjust to the new arrangements. In particular, tougher risk management guidelines have compelled banks to issue tier 2 instruments and consider other long-term debt instruments, including LTNCDs and senior notes.

Moreover, in quick succession we are issuing tougher standards on the management of large exposures, on single borrowers limits, and on DOSRI lending. These will likely spur corporate borrowers to diversify their funding sources beyond the usual friendly banks and in the direction of the capital market.

But not all regulatory initiatives have been towards tightening.  We have also introduced changes to remove obstacles to capital market development and create opportunities for banks with respect to capital market related business. These include selective lowering of reserve requirements for repo transactions that meet certain standards as well as for other financial products. Over the medium-term, we hope to effect a phased generalized lowering of reserve requirements to be more competitive with low reserve requirement regimes found in most other countries. We have likewise supported the creation of new and innovative financial instruments including derivatives products under appropriate regulatory arrangements.

I’d like to make special mention at this point our joint initiative with TOAP to reform the Common Trust Fund (CTF) and replace it with a better product called the Unit Investment Trust Fund (UITF). It will be better in the sense that it will more realistically reflect underlying market values so that investors will be properly guided and trust departments, acting with full independence from their bank proper, will more effectively avoid any residual risks arising from misunderstandings with customers on the nature of their investments. On the other hand, as a true investment product, UITF will not be subject to regulations as if it is a deposit product. Once this pilot initiative is adopted and implemented, we can work together to improve other trust products.

As institutional fund managers, trust departments of banks have a very important role to play in developing the domestic capital market. We will be needing your experienced and steady hand in promoting order and depth in the market. You will also provide the vital link that will allow retail investors, ordinary citizens, to reap the full benefits of access to the capital market.

You will also note that we have been enforcing more stringently mark-to-market regulations and looking at their further strengthening.  Our aim is not just to improve financial transparency but also to promote more active secondary market trading.

Other related initiatives include the nurturing of domestic credit rating agencies. Already we have recognized one, Philratings, and we will likely recognize a second one in the near future. We attach high priority to the objective credit opinion that independent credit rating agencies can provide.

Similarly, we have engaged a comprehensive legal study of how we can put together a comprehensive domestic credit bureau service at the earliest possible time. This will have many positive benefits including lowering borrowing costs and promoting better credit discipline.

I am also happy to inform you that we are intensifying our coordination efforts with other financial regulators like the SEC and the Insurance Commission so that we can achieve a more level regulatory playing field. I know that this is important to you as you compete with similar products marketed by other players like mutual funds and insurance companies.

However, it is not enough to develop a more conducive regulatory environment. A more direct contribution is to help develop appropriate market infrastructure.  In this regard, we are strongly supporting private sector initiative, led by the BAP, to establish the fixed income exchange and its related infrastructure to ensure efficient and safe clearing and settlement of securities transactions. This will be linked with the PhilPaSS so that delivery-versus-payment can be achieved and thus minimize settlement risk. We are reasonably confident this can be finally launched by the second half of this year. Closely related to this initiative, is the establishment of effective independent custody systems to ensure proper investor protection and to promote their confidence.  The relevant policy on this is now being finalized following close consultations with the banking community.

Finally, our reform initiatives are benefiting from the support of Congress which has decisively acted on certain vital pieces of legislation including the elimination of DST on secondary trading, the SPV Law and the Asset Securitization Law. All of these measures will help spur the domestic capital market. The BSP has worked hard with other interested partners to get these laws enacted and we will continue to do so for other pending legislation that support capital market development.

Concluding remarks

I have mentioned the numerous projects that are all currently underway to finally achieve critical mass for the domestic capital market and achieve lasting bank reform.  There are others that are in the pipeline that seek to reinforce the themes that I have raised tonight.

What is more important is to convey to you our sense of determination and urgency in getting the job done. I know that many of these changes will profoundly affect the way you have been used to doing business all these years. But I am confident that you will be fully supportive because these reforms will ultimately create better opportunities for all. Also rest assured that we will work patiently with you to effect smooth and orderly change to the greatest extent possible.

Thank you and more power to TOAP.

(Note: General Membership Meeting, Trust Officers Association of the Philippines, March 22, 2004, InterContinental Hotel, Makati City)

Title: The State of the Thrift Banking Industry and its Future
Occasion: National Convention Chamber of Thrift Banks
Speaker: Governor Rafael Buenaventura
Transcription:
Mr. Tomas V. Clemente, Jr., President of the Chamber of Thrift Banks (CTB), CTB Board of Directors, members of the Chamber, distinguished guests, ladies and gentlemen: good morning.

It is always an honor and a pleasure to address the Chamber. We, at the Bangko Sentral, always welcome the opportunity to dialogue with the banking community.

To start with, let me begin with a brief assessment of the current economic environment and later, examine the present state of the thrift banking industry.

The Economy

Against a backdrop of benign inflation, our economy continued to post favorable performance in 2003.

Average inflation for the year settled at 3.1 percent, lower than the government target of 4.5-5.5 percent.

For 2004, we expect inflation to track broadly the 4.0-5.0 percent target.

The benchmark 91-day T-bill rate averaged 6.0 percent in 2003. GDP expanded by 4.5 percent, certainly well within the full-year target of 4.2-5.2 percent.

The level of foreign reserves remained comfortable. Gross international reserves rose to US$16.9 billion in the fourth quarter of 2003 from the previous quarter’s US$16.2 billion. This was equivalent to 5 months’ imports of goods and services.

For 2004, we will continue to keep inflation under control. We strongly believe that low and stable inflation anchors overall financial stability, a sustained low interest rate environment, and a reasonable exchange rate.

While we firmly believe that the economy will continue to perform well this year, we need to stay alert and vigilant to manage possible destabilizing financial market disturbances in the run-up to the national elections. Orderly and non-controversial elections will clearly benefit the economy and sustain its recovery.

The Thrift Banking Industry

Moving on now to developments in the thrift banking industry. Looking at the overall picture, the industry remains fundamentally sound.

Despite the decrease in number of thrift banks to 92 banks in December 2003 from 94 in December 2002, the industry’s total resources grew by 8.2 percent to P274.2 billion from P253.4 billion a year ago. Moreover, deposit levels posted double-digit growth of 14.0 percent, indicating strong confidence in the industry.

But the industry has absolutely no room for complacency. Profitability remains weak as the industry’s return on assets and return on equity ratios faltered anew to negative 0.1 percent and 0.3 percent from positive ratios of 0.3 percent and 1.5 percent, over the same period last year.

The industry’s underlying weakness is its relatively poor asset quality. At end-December 2003, non-performing loans (NPLs) remained high at roughly P 19.2 billion, increasing the industry’s NPL ratio to 12.1 percent as against 11.6 percent at end-December 2002. ROPOA amounted to P29.1 billion or approximately 7.4 percent higher than the P27.1 billion ROPOA at end-December 2002.  Likewise, non-performing assets (NPAs) reached P 45.7 billion, higher by 2.6 percent from year ago’s P44.5 billion.

I strongly urge you to act decisively to reduce the stock of NPAs. High NPAs remain a major threat to the soundness and stability of the banking industry.

The SPV Law, which became fully effective last 9 April 2003, is intended to help banks dispose of their NPAs. I encourage the takeout of the bad accounts through the availment of the SPV to clean up your balance sheets.

The BSP has stretched the limits of acceptable accounting rules to allow banks to defer recognition of losses from NPA sales. More recently, we lengthened the deferral period from 7 to 10 years and backloaded the distribution. We are now even allowing existing provisions on NPAs that are sold to be applied to other accounts. We have also relaxed restrictions of dividends. We only require that availment of these concessions to be properly disclosed to uphold financial transparency. With these changes, banks will be able to greatly cushion the impact of NPA clean-up on their capital position. I don’t think that banks have any more good reasons to avoid doing the right thing. Banks that still fail to address their NPA problem decisively will inevitably regret their lack of resolve.

So far, we have issued 19 certificates of eligibility to 6 banks involving a total amount of P713 million worth of NPAs transferred under the SPV Law.

We are also currently processing applications from 9 banks with NPAs aggregating around P6.4 billion.

Sustaining Banking Reforms

As the ultimate preserver of financial stability, our basic agenda is to ensure the basic safety and soundness of the banking system as a whole and promote greater efficiency of the financial system.

Towards this end, we are sustaining the implementation of banking reforms. We are counting on the industry to continue supporting us in this endeavor.

The BSP reform agenda is generally geared towards the strengthening of the financial sector with emphasis on improving risk management practices and promoting good governance. A key objective for the thrift banking industry is the upgrading of credit underwriting standards to the level of best international practice. Credit risk management remains the foremost operational challenge. The asset and loan quality problems of today eloquently attest to this. Thus the need for diversification of risk to the various activities available in the market.

A vital piece of our banking reform agenda is the development of a comprehensive strategy to raise the standards of corporate governance in the financial system. Good corporate governance is the most fundamental of banking and financial institution reforms.

Our agenda on corporate governance is essentially designed to further strengthen financial institutions through improved standards on transparency, accountability and fairness. We have started to initiate measures intended to enhance the practice of effective corporate directorship through a mandatory orientation program for bank directors, emphasize the critical role of independent external auditors in promoting transparency, and strengthen compliance systems of banks.

Very recently, the monetary board approved strengthened rules limiting DOSRI on connected lending as a means of further strengthening culture of good corporate governance, reducing risk concentrations, and promoting capital market development. Under the new rules, DOSRI limits will now cover bank lending to all their related corporations whether upwards, sidewards or downwards.

Similarly, single borrower’s limits (SBL) have been strengthened to also achieve more comprehensive coverage on a consolidated basis of bank exposure to related parties.

We will stay committed to the implementation of banking reforms so that we can further improve the quality of our banking system.

As key industry players that serve an important niche of our economy: consumers and small business, thrift banks play a significant role in the successful implementation of banking reforms. I strongly encourage you to assist us in building strong and viable banks.

Future of the thrift banking industry

With the continuing reforms, we see a leaner but more stable and viable thrift banking industry. We also see a better managed industry with much improved risk control. We expect a marked improvement to take place in the industry’s bottomline figures in due course.

Let me also note for you an important initiative that we would like to see completed this year. I am referring to a central credit information bureau. In coordination with the National Credit Council (NCC), the BSP has commissioned a legal study to guide us in implementing the initiative on the basis of available laws. This project is vital because it will enable us to move away from collateral based lending, improve credit access of responsible borrowers, lower cost of borrowing, and promote better credit discipline. I am certain, the thrift banking industry will be a major beneficiary.

Concluding remarks

In closing, I would like to commend CTB’s efforts for leading the industry in adopting a proactive approach to address the challenges ahead. This will certainly help in fast-tracking reforms in the banking system. So let us work together towards a stronger and more effective banking system and strive to establish our presence in the service of the people.

Thank you and a pleasant day to all.

(Note: National Convention, Chamber of Thrift Banks, March 11, 2004, Dusit Hotel, Makati City)

Title: Message
Occasion: Formal Opening of Branch at Fort Bonifacio HSBC Savings Bank
Speaker: Governor Rafael Buenaventura
Transcription:
Ladies and gentlemen, good afternoon.

Congratulations to the officers and staff of HSBC Savings Bank on the inauguration of its branch here in Fort Bonifacio, one of the country’s rising business centers. This, indeed, marks a high point primarily because it signifies the bank’s confidence in our country’s future. Through this new branch, HSBC Savings Bank will be able to reach out to a wider client base and provide high quality banking services.

HSBC Savings Bank continues to be a model of a progressive and financially sound thrift bank.  I am confident the bank can maintain its exemplary status.

Bangko Sentral reform initiatives

The steady implementation of reforms remains the key to the sustained viability of the banking system.

By now, I am sure you are well aware of key BSP reforms that seek to promote greater safety, efficiency and competitiveness of the banking system.

In particular, thrift banks need to embrace reforms that would improve overall efficiency, strengthen risk management, build up capital base, and enhance corporate governance standards.

With substantial reforms in place, we can build a stronger banking system.

As a key industry player, the thrift banking industry can take the lead in stimulating economic development by effectively responding to the needs of important niche markets.  In particular, the industry can maximize opportunities now unfolding in the area of SME lending.

The government has strongly demonstrated its advocacy for the development of small and medium scale enterprises as a way of generating employment and fostering economic growth.    In support of this agenda, the Bangko Sentral has established regulatory initiatives to improve access to credit of SMEs.

In compliance with the Magna Carta for SMEs (R.A. No. 6977), all lending institutions are required to set aside a portion of their total loan portfolio and make it available for SMEs – at least 6 percent for small enterprises and at least 2 percent for medium enterprises.

To date, the ratio of compliance of thrift banks with the credit allocation requirements is quite high at around 22 percent for small enterprises and 11 percent for medium enterprises.

To further boost SME lending, the BSP is set to undertake additional regulatory initiatives.  We strongly rely on thrift banks, in their capacity as specialist players, to assist us in this endeavor.

HSBC Savings Bank, with its large network, first-rate service, and extensive banking savvy, is certainly more than capable in breaking new ground in SME lending, as well as in other important niches, such as consumer loans and housing loans.

Finally, I would like to call on the bank to remain supportive of our continuing financial reforms. As a strong financial institution, you are in an excellent position to be the leader in this regard.

Thank you.

(Note: Formal Opening of Branch at Fort Bonifacio, HSBC Savings Bank, March 04, 2004, Fort Bonifacio, Makati City)

Title: Promoting Microfinance: The Role of the Central Bank
Occasion: Alliance of Philippine Partners in Enterprise Development (APPEND)
Speaker: Governor Rafael Buenaventura
Transcription:
Good morning. In behalf of the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas, I am very honored to address the delegates to the 2004 Global Conference of the Opportunity International Network. From our perspective, this conference presents us with a dynamic forum for sharing ideas and experiences, developing strategies, and forging plans of action for the future. I thank Opportunity International for this chance to speak to you about Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas’ response to the global campaign against poverty. 

The road to microfinance

As a central bank, our primary mandate is to secure overall price stability, through the pursuit of sound and responsible monetary policies, in order to achieve a balanced and sustainable growth of our economy.  This is a classic role for a central bank where it enjoys competitive advantage vis-à-vis other governmental agencies. In this role, we are in a unique position to help the poor in a very fundamental way by preserving purchasing power and supporting the steady generation of jobs. Nowadays, we try to achieve this objective through an explicit targeting of a suitably low inflation number, currently between 4-5 percent.

At the same time, the Bangko Sentral is also entrusted with the responsibility of supervising the banking system to keep it safe and strong, as well as dynamically responsive to the needs of our economy.  In this sense, we are similar to about half of the central banks of the world with such a dual responsibility.

So far so good. This will be the familiar and comforting conclusion if I am addressing today the banking and financial community, our traditional constituency.

The question is, why did we get involved in microfinance at all?

For the Bangko Sentral, certain key elements fell into place.

As a major economic institution in a developing economy, we have always strongly felt a responsibility to try to do something more direct and immediate than our traditional tools allow us to alleviate the poverty surrounding us, a poverty that injects a basic element of instability into everything.

However, the reality is good intentions do not always translate to good interventions.    Fortunately for us, microfinance technology, as originally pioneered by NGOs, offered interesting possibilities for reaching out to the poor through appropriately designed credit and savings products. This is an area that we understand and one where we have influence. Microfinance is inherently attractive to us because its successful practice is basically founded on sound credit principles rather than credit subsidy.  As such, it is market-oriented and therefore a viable proposition for the banks that we are responsible for.  At the same time, we believe that for microfinance to have broader impact on poverty, it must enter the mainstream through the banking system that has the ability to self-finance through deposit mobilization.

The third element, the crucial element that allowed us to act with legal basis to fully support microfinance, may be found in three criticial provisions that were included when the General Banking Law (GBL) was amended in year 2000. Essentially, the novel provisions gave the Bangko Sentral sufficient flexibility in formulating banking regulations that take into consideration the peculiarities of microfinance lending: cash flow-based, typically unsecured and short-term, high frequency collections, and often featuring group guarantee and other non-traditional forms of security.

BSP implementation strategy

Since the year 2000 when we first identified microfinance as our institution’s flagship program for poverty alleviation, the BSP has made substantial progress in promoting microfinance in the banking sector.

At the outset, we have defined our policy agenda which is to encourage the establishment of new microfinance-oriented thrift and rural banks and the setting up of microfinance operations in existing banks. We believe that through this approach, a larger number of entrepreneurial poor or e-poor will be reached by the banking system. This would complement other microfinance delivery channels like credit cooperatives and NGO that have their own strengths and weaknesses.

In support of this agenda, we have focused our efforts towards creating an enabling policy and regulatory environment for sustainable microfinance, enhancing training and capacity building, and actively taking part in promotion and advocacy.

The primary concern is to establish a supportive and appropriate policy environment and institutional framework that would encourage the creation of sustainable and viable microfinance institutions.

Initially, we issued Circular 272 in January 2001 to implement the provisions of sections 40, 43 and 44 of the GBL 2000 and set out the regulatory guidelines for engaging in microfinance.

We recognize that microfinance is serious business. Without proper safeguards, it can cause banks plenty of trouble. From the start, we encourage banks to adhere to best practices and high performance standards.  This is why we have implemented additional requirements for licensing of microfinance-oriented banks, aside from the standard requirements set for the establishment of regular banks through the issuance of Circular 273. As a basic requirement, we require the organizers to have not just sufficient banking experience but also a good track record in microfinancing. As a minimum operational requirement, banks should have a loan tracking system in place that can adequately monitor and manage a microfinance portfolio.

The same Circular also provided for the partial lifting of the moratorium on the opening of new thrift and rural banks and branches to allow the entry of microfinance-oriented banks.

As a further incentive, the BSP issued in April 2001 the guidelines governing the rediscounting facility for microfinance loans of rural and cooperative banks (Circular 282). A year later, we expanded the coverage of the rediscounting facility to include thrift banks (Circular 324).

We have issued several other regulations to provide further incentive to banks to engage in microfinance in a sustainable and prudent manner.  These are:

Circular 340, Circular 365, and Circular 369 further liberalized the rules and regulations for the establishment of bank branches provided these are microfinance-oriented

Circular 409 prescribes guidelines for the measurement of portfolio-at-risk and the respective provisioning requirements to ensure sound and prudential microfinance operations of banks.

The BSP is undertaking continuous review of its existing policies and regulatory guidelines to make them even more attuned to the growing needs of the microfinance sector.    But moving beyond regulatory initiatives, we are strengthening our ability to supervise the activity of microfinance-oriented banks. This is essential to maintain the credibility of the whole set-up.    In this regard, we have developed special examination manuals and have started to train a core group of bank examiners well-versed in microfinance operations.

We are currently working, in partnership with the National Credit Council (NCC), on establishing a central credit information bureau.  This project, although beneficial to the banking system as a whole, will particularly benefit microfinance operations by reducing the risk of credit pollution, promoting greater borrower discipline, and lowering credit risk especially on unsecured lending.

We are also stepping up our training and capacity building program to enhance expertise of our general examiners, officers and employees, as well as the microfinance practitioners in the banking sector. This is being implemented through a series of training programs, workshops and study tours. For the benefit of the banking sector, the BSP has begun incorporating microfinance into the basic rural and thrift banking courses.

We have likewise launched a regional advocacy program in 2003 in keeping with our promotion and advocacy agenda.  Our goal is to conduct microfinance seminars in strategic regions in the country where we hope to entice potential practitioners. So far, we have conducted regional information seminars in 8 regions across the country. Another focus of advocacy is by way of establishing working ties with other institutions for a broader microfinance network.    Towards this end, we have conducted briefings for major corporations, foundations and international organizations.

This broad set of initiatives in the banking sector validates our strong commitment to microfinance.  It is our initial contribution to the microfinance cause. But we intend to do more.

Right now, we have a total of 122 banks engaged in microfinance activity. These banks, which consist of 2 microfinance-oriented thrift banks, 3 microfinance-oriented rural banks and 117 rural and cooperative rural banks with some level of microfinance operations, were able to give out microfinance loans amounting to P2.5 billion to 432,475 borrowers. Over time, we hope to increase these figures and be able to serve a greater number of the e-poor.

Conclusion

As the Philippines’ central monetary authority, we have a social responsibility to fully serve the needs of a developing economy.  This need becomes even more urgent in light of the country’s poverty incidence where nearly 40 percent of almost 80 million Filipinos live below the poverty line.[1]  in this role, we share opportunity international’s mission to empower the poor.

Let me assure everyone of the BSP’s continuing support for the promotion of sustainable microfinance.

Thank you.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

[1] Poverty Incidence, National Statistics Office, 2002.

Title: E-Banking Climate in the Philippines
Occasion: Launching of HSBC's Guide to Cash and Treasury Management in Asia Pacific (2004 edition)
Speaker: Governor Rafael Buenaventura
Transcription:
Mr. Warner manning, Mr. Lawrence Webb, fellow panel discussants, distinguished guests, ladies and gentlemen, good afternoon.

I am deeply honored and pleased to be a guest speaker and a panelist on a subject matter that is both timely and dynamic. If we simply observe the current lifestyle of the young professionals and students today (cellphones, internet cafes, money cards), and the Philippine population seems to keep getting younger, we can safely say that we are racing past the computer age and straight into the information technology age.

E-banking in the Philippines

In the Philippines, it was in the 1980s, with the introduction of automated teller machines (ATMs), when e-banking made an auspicious debut and in a way revolutionized how we viewed the conventional, brick-and-mortar bank structure. Today, ATMs are widespread, totaling 4,395 units as of June 30, 2003. Of the total, 28 percent are located off-site from bank premises. It’s safe to say that ATMs now form a major part of our normal banking routine especially in more urbanized areas and are integral to banks’ customer delivery channels.

Banks keep expanding the reach of the ATM network in an effort to enhance customer convenience and at the same time lower transaction cost for both customer and bank. I am especially pleased to note that our overseas workers are able to use banks’ ATM networks to be able to transfer funds to their beneficiaries back home on near real-time basis. To be sure, the system can still be improved but the concept is already proven.

Other e-banking innovations have also come in like phone banking, internet banking, and mobile banking. Their common denominator is that they further enhance customer convenience by making banking transactions feasible on a 24 by 7 basis from the workplace, from the home, and indeed from wherever the customer can use a mobile phone.

However, pure e-banking has not yet fully replaced the bricks-and-mortar structure although pure internet-only banks do exist. Indeed, we have already licensed one pioneer internet-only bank in the Philippines. What we are seeing today are more like bricks-and-clicks, the incorporation of e-banking into the more traditional banking structure.

Security is still a major concern although the technology to protect transactions is already pretty good and keeps getting better. For the Bangko Sentral, this is a major reason for regulating e-banking activity both from the perspective of prudential regulation as well as consumer protection. Let me be clear, however, that Bangko Sentral welcomes the full development of e-banking.

As of June 30, 2003, 36 banks have been authorized to engage in e-banking activities ranging from phone banking, internet banking, and mobile banking.< /p>

Regulatory approach

The enactment in year 2000 of the Electronic Commerce act, as well as the revised general banking law that gave Bangko Sentral authority to regulate electronic banking, has laid down the basic legal and regulatory framework governing e-banking. The Bangko Sentral has since issued various implementing circulars.

Our regulatory approach is primarily aimed at mitigating and ensuring proper control of operational risks that are inherent to the technology. In allowing banks to do e-banking, there are two basic things we evaluate: First, the underlying soundness of the banking institution itself; Second, the soundness of risk management control surrounding the e-banking activity.

We believe it is necessary to look at the underlying soundness of the banking institution because this is a basic source of resiliency in case of accidents. This also serves to screen out weak players that may just increase the possibility of systemic risk.

As far as the e-banking activity itself, we are placing primary responsibility on the board of directors and bank management to make sure that all foreseeable risks, from hacker attacks to internal fraud to system failures, to failures of service providers and outside contractors, are all properly subjected to controls, periodic review and appropriate contingency planning. Banks are also required to educate its customers on the proper use of e-banking products.

We believe it is appropriate to emphasize proper risk management from the outset because the dangers are real if vigilance is inadequate. There are enough bad experiences that we are aware of even in developed countries where e-banking has been more advanced. We also don’t want banks to rush headlong, unprepared, into e-banking driven due to competitive pressure.

Emerging trends

Now allow me to scan recent developments and trends in local e-banking. Many of these initiatives in fact arise from innovations pioneered offshore.

First, major players are rolling out increasingly sophisticated e-banking products that allow corporate and high net worth customers to more actively manage their whole gamut of banking transactions.

Second, the linkage of ATM platforms and e-banking is lowering the barrier to entry of smaller banks.

Third, the mobile phone in conjunction with e-banking is emerging as a potential major payment instrument to rival more established credit and debit cards. This is especially interesting considering the widespread local acceptance of mobile phones.

Fourth, the convenience and cost of cross-border remittances is likely to improve dramatically in the future through the creative combination of low-cost e-mail messaging with e-banking and ATM platforms. Yahoo and HSBC already have pioneered a service in this area.

Fifth, government agencies have started to recognize the value of e-banking in improving the efficiency of revenue collection and other transactions with the public. Thru the internet, the Bureau of Internal Revenue (BIR) embarked on electronic tax filing and payment project that involves the electronic processing and transmission of tax return information and taxes due. The Bureau of Customs has also been a proactive innovator in this area as it moves to fully convert to electronic collection of duties at all ports of entry. The SEC has likewise embarked on an electronic corporate registration process linked to a local bank electronic platform. Other government agencies are likewise moving in this direction to collect fees.

Sixth, we note an innovative local project to allow small and medium enterprises (SMEs) to potentially benefit from e-banking by creating electronic documents to speed-up the factoring of SME receivables thus increasing access to credit and lowering financing costs.

I’m sure there are many more but I’ve just noted those that are especially interesting.

For our part, in addition to our regulatory role, we are directly supporting the healthy growth of e-banking in the Philippines through the provision of a major payment infrastructure through the creation of PhilPaSS. This is our local version of a Real Time Gross Settlement System (RTGS) for large value interbank payments. It is vital for reducing settlement risk that can have potential systemic risk for the financial system. Already, PhilPaSS has linked with the ROSS system to achieve greater safety in settlement of government securities. ATM switches are also linking up with PhilPaSS to allow settlement of net claims of banks against each other. Likewise, it has become the basis for payment versus payment (PVP) settlement of foreign exchange transactions.

Conclusion

At this point, let me conclude by saying that e-banking is providing a major driving force for change in the local banking industry.  It challenges our banking institutions to rethink the old ways of doing business. Equally, it challenges us, as regulator, to adopt new approaches in order to keep pace with market developments without being an obstacle to progress.

Before I get carried away any further, let me again thank HSBC for the invitation. Accept my heartfelt congratulation for the successful launching of your guide to treasury and cash management in Asia-Pacific 2004 and the introduction of HSBCNet.

Thank you and good afternoon.

(Note: Launching of HSBC's Guide to Cash and Treasury Management in Asia Pacific (2004 edition), February 17, 2004, Makati Shangri-la Hotel, Makati City)

Title: Remarks
Occasion: Press Conference on the 4th Qtr 2003 BSP Inflation Report
Speaker: Governor Rafael Buenaventura
Transcription:
Good morning, everyone.

Transparency is a hallmark of good monetary policy, and for this reason the BSP continually strives to bring across its policy message to the public and present its view of the future inflation environment. This is the main reason why we publish a quarterly inflation report, and we would like to thank everyone here for joining us at this morning’s presentation.

Among other things, the presentation by MD Guinigundo will show that the BSP’s expected path for inflation continues to be favorable. Inflation should see a moderate increase in 2004-2005 as GDP growth strengthens, aggregate demand conditions improve, and cost-side adjustments exert their influence on consumer prices. Average headline inflation is expected to remain broadly in line with the Government’s target of 4-5 percent for both 2004 and 2005. In the meantime, the stance of monetary policy will continue to emphasize prudence in responding to the changes in the outlook for inflation and output growth, keeping always in mind the potential risks to the future path of inflation.

Let me end by saying that the BSP remains strongly committed to good monetary policymaking. This includes ensuring our accountability, which we try to do by formally submitting ourselves to public judgment on the basis of the Government’s inflation targets. It also implies making sure that the stance of monetary policy is properly communicated by means of a comprehensive, well-organized and lucidly written document such as the inflation report. We therefore welcome your feedback on the contents of the report and hope that you will continue to support the BSP’s efforts in communicating its monetary policy strategy to the public.

Thank you and good morning.

(Note: Press Conference on the 4th Qtr 2003 BSP Inflation Report, January 30, 2004, Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas)

Title: Remarks
Occasion: Launching of the Second Citibank Microentrepreneur of the Year Award
Speaker: Governor Rafael Buenaventura
Transcription:
Good morning, ladies and gentlemen! Welcome to the Executive Business Center of the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas.

I am pleased and honored to join you this morning in launching the second Citibank microentrepreneur of the year award.

Today we officially begin the search for remarkable individuals who, with the support of microfinance institutions, were able to liberate themselves from the clutches of poverty and became successful in their own right.

At the outset, I would like to commend Citibank and the Microfinance Council of the Philippines for their strong advocacy for microfinance. This award that you are collaborating on is certain to stimulate the progress of microfinance in the country. By recognizing successful micro-entrepreneurs, you are encouraging the growth of microenterprises which, if properly motivated and managed, can serve as the driving force to invigorate local economies. This will definitely help boost our efforts to fight poverty in the country.

With the success of the first Microentrepreneur of the Year Award, we now face the challenge of making this year’s search even better in terms of putting together the selection criteria and refining the guidelines to benefit a larger segment of the microfinance industry.

I call on all microfinance practitioners here – representatives from the banking sector, cooperatives, non-government organizations – to help us in drawing up a list of possible awardees for this year’s search. I urge you to submit the names of your microfinance clients whom you believe embody the core values espoused by microfinance, namely, ingenuity, patience, hard work, honesty, responsibility, among others. With a broader selection base, we can give due credit to deserving microentrepreneurs.

I am positive that there are many more unsung heroes out there who reinforce our belief that microfinance can indeed be a powerful tool in improving one’s quality of life.

Their success as microentrepreneurs is also your success. As microfinance service providers, you are in a key position to help bring about change in the lives of your clients. With your continued support, the entrepreneurial poor can have access to capital which they can use to help put up a small business and increase their income. This way, the poor can truly rise above their difficulties and lead better, more productive lives.

At Bangko Sentral, microfinance is, and will continue to be, our humble share in the nationwide campaign against poverty.

Where are we now in our microfinance agenda? As far as the banking sector is concerned, we have made substantial progress in pushing for microfinance initiatives.

For the record, close to half a million borrowers have been granted loans by the banking sector. As of 30 October 2003, we have a total of 122 banks engaged in microfinance activity. So far, these banks which consist of 2 microfinance-oriented thrift banks, 3 microfinance-oriented rural banks and 117 rural and cooperative rural banks with some level of microfinance operations were able to give out microfinance loans amounting to P2.5 billion to 432,475 borrowers.

While these numbers are encouraging, we, at Bangko Sentral, are bent on surpassing them as we go along in our initiatives to encourage the establishment of more microfinance-oriented banks and the setting up of microfinance operations of existing banks.

We have gone full force in pursuing our three-part microfinance program that is essentially geared towards: (1) creating an enabling policy and regulatory environment for sustainable microfinance, (2) enhancing training and capacity building within BSP and the banking sector; and (3) actively taking part in promotion and advocacy.

We are currently working on establishing a credible and comprehensive credit bureau model in the country. A credit bureau will ensure the presence of a more transparent information system and lead to an improved credit process. It will also serve to prevent high incidences of credit pollution where one client borrows from multiple institutions.

The BSP has also launched a regional advocacy program in 2003 in keeping with our promotion and advocacy agenda.
