Further, we are now putting in motion a procedure that will allow BSP to continuously gauge the performance of accredited external auditors. Once an external auditor obtains accreditation, the next level is evaluation and monitoring of performance. This means accreditation will be a continuing process.

Compliance officers

Consistent with the principle of accountability, a BSP circular prescribes a compliance system.

The objective is to ensure a bank’s identification of relevant laws and regulations, analysis of risks of non-compliance, and prioritization of compliance risks. The compliance program must be in writing, approved by the Board of Directors, and subsequently submitted to the BSP. The frequency of periodic compliance testing shall be commensurate with the identified risk levels.

One of the basic elements of the compliance program is a constructive working relationship with regulatory agencies. The appointment of an institution’s compliance officer requires prior approval by the BSP Monetary Board. The officers and staff of the compliance program are trained on the regulatory requirements through regular meetings, distribution of manuals, and dissemination of regulatory issuances.

BSP handbook on corporate governance

The BSP recently released a handbook on corporate governance. It is a compilation of various BSP initiatives which will guide banks in developing their own corporate governance standards and practices.

Ladies and gentlemen, the Board of Directors faces the responsibility of hiring the best management available. Corollarily, it also bears the responsibility of changing failing management in a timely fashion when necessary.

The management team‘s credibility and integrity are major considerations for investors. Management need to do what they say they are going to do. Like it or not, investors have long memories and will hold management to what they have said. As investors and stakeholders analyze an institution and its financials, they are also assessing management’s culpability to hide things. That is why for members of the investment community, access to management is key. Portfolio managers want to meet key people running the business and shaping the strategy for tomorrow. At all times, it is necessary that dealings be fair and truthful.

The conceptual framework for transparency is effective communication. In a period of market turmoil and heightened investor skepticism, when there is a flood of news concerning the legitimacy of financial statements, the organization needs effective communication to target and focus on the statement to and from all their stakeholders. It is imperative that commentaries be placed in context, and issues addressed right away.

Thus, another challenge for the board is to keep abreast of current developments, to know when to change and to be sufficiently independent to make the change.

At the point when high-stakes decision are made, the Board needs to engage in a delicate balancing act of nurturing confidence, addressing dissent, and generating commitment within the organization. Therefore, fair and equal opportunity to voice opinions during the decision process are important. Timely decisions are needed, as indecision could lead to costly delays.

Expectations

Although BSP issuances cover banks and financial institutions, we hope that good corporate governance practices will be cascaded to their corporate clients as well. For in managing credit risks, banks should be looking into the corporate governance of its clients.

Conclusion

In closing, let me reiterate the BSP’s view that improved corporate governance is the most fundamental of banking and financial institution reforms. Corporate governance systems need to be consistent with a free and open market that submits to the rigors of market competition and discipline as well as public scrutiny.

I think I am getting carried away here. Let me now move to my final message.

As communicators, you, the members of IABC can help transform your respective institutions into fair, accountable and transparent institutions  Help all your stakeholders participate and be involved so that in the end, with good governance as part of our corporate culture, we will all benefit from having a better country.

I am also happy to learn that corporate representation here today is quite broad-based, coming as you do from small to medium to large operations and from different industries at that. Indeed, advocates of good corporate governance is a growing breed in our country. This should be good for all of us.

A proponent of corporate governance once said: "Boards of Directors are like subatomic particles--they behave differently when they are observed.

It is in this light that IABC members should look at their role in ensuring good governance in our country.

Thank you and good day everyone.

(Note: International CEO Forum on Ethical Business Practice, International Association of Business Communicators (IABC), September 6, 2002, Tower Club, Philamlife Tower, Makati City)

Title: Building Local Economies Through Rural Banks
Occasion: 45th Charter Anniversary Symposium, Rural Bankers Association of the Philippines
Speaker: Governor Rafael Buenaventura
Transcription:
Mr. Jerry Coloma, the officers and members of the Rural Bankers Association of the Philippines, my colleagues in the banking sector, guests, ladies and gentlemen.  Magandang hapon po.

It is always a pleasure to renew ties with the members of RBAP. As your anniversary theme this year very clearly states, rural banks help build local economies. Indeed, the rural banking system has been Government’s partner in accelerating countryside development for 50 years now.

Prior to 1952, there were only the defunct Agricultural Bank of the Philippines Islands, the limited agricultural lending programs of Government, and the ever-present next-door usurers to whom farmers can ran to for loans.

Today, 50 years hence, the rural banking system has a network of 1,919 head offices and branches spread out all over the country. Combined, they provide farmers and other entrepreneurial rural folks that much wider latitude in accessing credit.

The synergy between rural banks and rural communities may be gleaned from the continuing growth of the agricultural sector, which today accounts for half of the country’s gross domestic product. In other words, roughly one-half of the country’s economic output comes from the countryside in terms of agricultural products.

Employment generation in rural communities also represents a significant share of the country’s total labor force. Imagine what could happen then if the financial services of rural banks dries up: food supplies will be scarce and unemployment will soar.

The parallel growth of rural economies and rural banks is a classic example of a win-win situation. To illustrate: deposit accounts in rural banks have maintained a steady uptrend and have reached over P49 billion as of March 2002.  At the same time, total loan portfolio of the rural banking system reached p44 billion and investments, P3.5 billion.

I do believe that the liberation of rural folks from the limited credit funnel of 50 years ago is due to a large extent to the advent of rural banks and government’s enabling policies and programs.

Of course, the creation of a viable and sustainable credit system for small farmers, fishermen and rural businessmen did not come without pain; there were, and are, pitfalls and mistakes. The implementation of supervised credit and commodity specific programs come to mind.

However, I would like to believe that now we know enough to work for the further strengthening of the rural banking system.

Now, more than ever, good and responsive services of rural banks are needed at the countryside. With millions of our countrymen living below the poverty level, most of them in rural communities, the challenge for rural banks is to find better and faster ways of helping rural folks build strong local economies.

Let us identify some of the challenges facing the rural banks today.

The rural banking system's existence in the last 50 years is proof of its resiliency and fundamental soundness. However, it must be able to compete in an increasingly liberalized market-driven financial environment. One option is through mergers and consolidation.

I am happy to note that this option is gaining ground as a means to consolidate, rebuild and reinforce financial capability and strength. Presently under evaluation of the Bangko Sentral are 8 applications for mergers and consolidation involving 19 rural banks and 1 thrift bank. Earlier, BSP approved six applications for merger/consolidation involving 13 rural banks; these are now awaiting approval of the Securities and Exchange Commission.

Please note that even as mergers and consolidations take place among rural banks, new players are coming into the rural banking system. For instance, BSP has received 22 applications for conversion into rural banks, 13 of which have been granted. Another 4 will start operations upon completion of their papers with SEC.

Rural banks also need to conform and adapt to the reforms BSP is implementing to integrate the Philippine banking system for global competition.

Among others, we have adopted the capital adequacy ratio framework using the criteria of the bank for international settlements. As of December last year, 556 have complied with our capital adequacy ratio; I would be happier though with a 100 percent compliance.

BSP is also instituting reforms for good governance. Banks owe it to depositors and investors to run their operations in a prudent and sound manner. Banks or other institutions for that matter cannot afford to have a cavalier attitude toward good governance and expect to last. The multi-billion-dollar corporate scandals that have rocked some of the biggest American companies are rooted in bad governance.

Good governance builds trust and confidence; without it, no financial system can survive for long. In other words, good corporate governance is a must. This is the reason why BSP has issued the following circulars:

1.   Circular No. 283 issued in May last year which states and delineates the powers, duties and responsibilities of the Board of Directors.

2.   Circular no. 296 issued in September last year which contains the powers, qualifications and disqualifications of the Board of Directors. Please note three important provisions of this Circular:

A)   first, that the Board should have at least two independent directors.

B)   second, the fit-and-proper test which prospective directors and officers must pass in addition to those prescribed under the General Banking Law of 2000. Banks need directors with integrity/ probity, competence, education, diligence and experience/ training.

C)   third, that directors of banks must attend the special seminar on corporate governance. We want the highest body in the bank to plant the seeds of good governance and nurture it in their banks.

3.   Another is Circular 325 issued March this year, extending to December 2002 the deadline within which directors must attend a good governance seminar.  In response to queries of further extension, I regret that the MB is not inclined at this point to grant another extension.  We have accredited several corporate governance providers precisely to facilitate your compliance.

4.   Then we have Circular No. 341 which was issued early this month.  It provides guidelines on unsafe/ unsound banking practices to ensure clear understanding of good governance measures.

For the further guidance of banks, BSP has prepared a handbook on corporate governance. It is now available for sale at the BSP corporate affairs office.

We are also undertaking some organizational changes at BSP to complement reforms on your end. Among others, BSP has reorganized its Supervision and Examination Sector following its adoption of the consolidated approach to bank supervision. Institutional responsibilities have been redistributed to four supervising departments in our Supervision and Examination Sector. Each department will have charge over all the operational aspects and financial activities of the banks -- the life cycle of the bank in fact --under its supervision. For instance, a microfinance thrift bank will fall under the supervision of the Rural Cooperative and Microfinance Banks Supervision Department and not under the Mid-Sized Banks and Non-Bank Supervision Department.

There is one other matter which I hope rural banks can help address. This is the matter of educating the rural folks in handling and investing their money wisely. You are closer to them and they talk to you. Help guide them so they can avoid financial scams that have victimized many urban investors.

Ladies and gentlemen, the present poverty situation in the country has given rural financing a new dimension. With 50 years experience behind it, the rural banking system is equipped with the experience and the reach to support the successful implementation of microfinance, BSP’s flagship program in support of national poverty alleviation objectives.

The rural banks know the countryside best: the people, their economic potential, and financial requirements. You are the most strategically situated to engage in microfinance. The entrepreneurial poor or what we call e-poor is a segment in your niche market that remains largely unserved. Fortunately, a number of institutions have taken up the challenge and we expect more to do so. The Banco ng Masa set up by Mr. Enrique Zobel in Batangas is the latest micro-finance oriented unit BSP has approved.

Of course, we at BSP are aware of the many things RBAP has done to promote and support microfinance. For this I commend you; but I know you can do more.

On our part, we at the BSP are ready to provide support to rural banks in facing up to the many challenges before it. We are committed help you, so that we can count on you to be around for another 50 and more years in building strong local economies.

Together, we can realize the vision of our pioneer rural bankers: to make more rural folks productive and the countryside truly progressive.

Maraming salamat po at maligayang anibersaryo.

 

(Note: 45th Charter Anniversary Symposium, Rural Bankers Association of the Philippines, August 29, 2002, Century Park Hotel, Manila)

Title: Bankers and Chambers: Creating Good Synergy for the Country
Occasion: Joint Meeting of the Chambers of Commerce & Industry hosted by Las Pinas Chamber of Commerce & Ind.
Speaker: Governor Rafael Buenaventura
Transcription:
Mr. Jesus Tibayan, Mr. Sergio Ortiz-Luis, Atty. Mike Varela, Mr. Jesus Tanchanco, the officers and members of Las Pinas Chamber of Commerce and Industry, other Chapter members, guests, friends. Good afternoon.

First, allow me to congratulate the Las Pinas Chamber of Commerce and Industry for hosting this joint meeting of various Chambers of Commerce and Industry under the theme “Bankers as chambers business partners.” To me, this meeting is most timely and is, in fact, necessary.

Let me tell you why: there is no way that banking can be divorced from commerce and industry; they will always be partners, whether they like it or not.

In the Philippines, equity levels still remain on the low side. As such, the banking sector accounts for as much as 90% of the funding requirements of Philippine business.

In contrast, developed economies normally have banks and the capital market sharing the funding requirements of business 50-50. Therefore, until such time as the domestic capital market realizes its full potential, the fate of banking and commerce & industry will remain closely intertwined in our country.

And so, today, I take this opportunity to address this forum so I can personally update you on how your banker-partners are doing, the challenges they are facing, what you can do to help them, and how you can maximize the benefits from such a partnership.

As of the first quarter this year, the banking system had about 7,600 head offices, branches or agencies, 57% of which are those of commercial banks, 25% rural banks and the balance thrift banks. In other words, we have banks all over the country to serve the needs of business and consumers.

The Philippine banking system is fundamentally sound and more than adequately capitalized, following the adoption of risk-based capital adequacy framework last year. The ratio of its net worth to risk assets averaged 16% in 2001, above the BSP-required level of 10% and double the international standard of 8% set by the Bank of International Settlements, the bank of the world’s central banks.

It can be said therefore that, today, Philippine banks, in general, are better prepared to handle potential reversals.

As of March 2002, the banking system had total assets of P3.3 trillion, investments worth P750 billion and a consolidated loan portfolio of P1.7 trillion. Of the loans, roughly P614 billion or 34% went to the sectors you represent: commerce and industry.

Now, you have an idea as to the degree of interest our banks have in ensuring that Philippine business make good. In addition, banks are mindful of the fact that much of the money they are lending to business come from savings or deposits entrusted to them by the public. As of March, total deposits in the banking system was P2.2 trillion while capital accounts stood at P450 billion.

All told, the banking system made a consolidated net income of about P6 billion in the first quarter this year.

Now, about the challenges facing the banking sector. Banks burdened with non-performing loans prefer the safety of investing in government securities to lending money to business. Generally speaking that is. To companies with good credit rating, access to bank financing, at competitive rates, will not be a problem.

It is in the best interest of companies therefore to make sure that they achieve, and maintain, favorable credit standing. In fact, now is a particularly good time for companies to cash in on one’s good payment track record because the Philippines has one of the lowest lending rates in the Asian region today.

BSP estimates indicate that the Philippines’ real lending rate (i.e., lending rate adjusted for inflation) of 4.95 percent in July was the third lowest in a sample of 10 Asian countries. South Korea and Japan had the lowest rates of 4.1 percent and 3.0 percent, respectively. On the other hand, the highest rates of 8.2% and 7.8 were registered by Hong Kong and Taiwan.

Interest rates are at record low levels in the Philippines because the Monetary Board of the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas has progressively and substantially lowered key policy rates. This should lower the cost of capital for businesses gearing up for higher demand in the Christmas holidays.

Government, which is a net borrower, is also benefiting from the low-interest rates regime. In the first six months this year, government has accumulated savings of about P16 billion from lower interest rates.

For private companies, one option would be to take the opportunity to borrow at low rates and use its proceeds to retire higher and more expensive loans. This is a strategy we have been implementing at BSP.

On the other hand, cash-rich companies who have no need, nor desire, to borrow money from banks may opt instead to buy non-performing assets from banks. The price of such assets are quite competitive and represents good investment opportunities. At the same time, your purchase of such NPAs will help shore up banks’ balance sheets.

BSP is actively supporting the passage of the bill and the implementation of necessary banking reforms in accordance with its mandate to safeguard the stability of the banking sector.

The passage of the Special Purpose Asset Vehicle (SPAVE) Bill should facilitate such sale, as the proposed incentives should mitigate bank losses on such assets. We are optimistic the bill will be passed before the end of the year as the Lower House has already approved its version on third and final reading, while Senate is working on its counterpart version. The passage of other important economic legislations including the Securitization Law and the Corporate Recovery Act should further enhance the investment climate in the Philippines.

In the meantime, some of you may be interested in acquiring properties BSP will be selling at the E-Home Expo which will be held next month at the SM Megamall. Up for sale are more than 400 properties with an estimated value of at least P2.7 billion.

Ladies and gentlemen, various survey results are showing consistent results. Business expects the economy to sustain its growth momentum through the second half of this year.

Higher employment is foreseen as more companies expand to meet projected demand growth. The time to act is now.  Consult your bank. Your banker. Your partner.

Finally, always remember that while companies are dependent on banks for funds, banks are trustees of people’s money. Therefore, it is in the mutual interest of the banking and the business sectors to sustain public trust and confidence to ensure stability and long-term growth. It is imperative therefore that these two sectors adhere to the basic principles of good governance, at all times.

The Philippine economy today has good fundamentals conducive to business with record low interest rates and low inflation. However, we should be vigilant that corporate misdeeds of the type and magnitude we read and hear about from overseas are not duplicated here. Erosion of public confidence is the one thing we should guard against.

It is my hope therefore that bankers and businessmen, in words and in deeds, commit to the path of good governance. It is our responsibility as individuals and citizens of this country.

Thank you.

(Note: Joint Meeting of the Chambers of Commerce & Industry hosted by Las Pinas Chamber of Commerce and Industry, August 27, 2002, Dusit Hotel Nikko, Makati City)

Title: Championing Corporate Governance in Banking
Place: Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas Business Center
Occasion: Special One-Day Seminar on Corporate Governance for Bank Chairmen and CEOs
Speaker: Governor Rafael Buenaventura
Transcription:
As we deal with the daunting challenge of rebuilding from the Asian financial crisis and, more recently, as the world economy reels from the moral crisis in corporate America, there is sweeping recognition around the globe of the critical importance of good corporate governance.

Promoting good corporate governance calls for a governance structure and practice that ensures that there is fairness, accountability and transparency in the way a bank operates. Hopefully, our one-day seminar today has helped in clarifying these core principles.

The banking system at present

Up to this point, the Philippine financial system manifests overall stability, but there are vulnerabilities that must be decisively addressed.

A key vulnerability is the problem of non-performing assets, which is limiting the scope for more active lending and balance sheet expansion. It is likewise necessitating higher provisioning that imposes a major drag on profitability.

To immediately address the deterioration in asset quality now ticking away in bank books, the Government and the BSP are supporting legislation in the form of the SPAV bill allowing the establishment of private Asset Management Companies (AMCs) with incentives. The special purpose corporations contemplated under the bill will allow outside investors to buy out the NPAs of banks and other financial institutions in essentially market-driven transactions. The availability of incentives is meant to reduce the losses banks are expected to absorb during such clean-up.

The lower house has already approved on third and final reading their version of the SPAV bill.   We are ready to work with the senate on their counterpart version so that we can have a law before the end of the third quarter of this year.

Asset clean-up is a very important first step but right behind it are the challenges of replenishing bank capital and of achieving fundamental operational restructuring to achieve better efficiency, competitiveness, and risk management in the much tougher banking environment ahead.  All three issues are closely inter-linked with the quality of corporate governance.

The severe build-up in non-performing assets today reflects a past failure of corporate governance. Boards of Directors have not exercised sufficient vigilance in ensuring adequate credit management practice: from loan underwriting standards, to administration, grading and provisioning, and timely remedial management.

On the other hand, the fragility of capital adequacy stems from a lack of foresight and political will in mobilizing capital commensurate to the businesses that have been pursued and risks taken on. It is reflective of a short-term perspective that unduly focuses on returns and pays insufficient attention to risks.

We should be no less concerned that the operating efficiency of Philippine banks leaves much room for improvement. It is very revealing that our commercial banking system’s cost-to- income ratio, at around 77 percent, stands out as among the highest compared to our peer countries. This is a sad reflection of complacent governance.

Now, if the banking system is to continue to serve as a locomotive of economic growth, banking reforms must be sustained. Thus, the Bangko Sentral is taking an activist stance in pursuing a multi-pronged banking reform agenda: (1) strengthening the supervisory framework; (2) restructuring the local banking system for greater safety, efficiency, and competitiveness; and (3) promoting good corporate governance. The legal basis for many of these reforms is now in place through the General Banking Law of 2000. Moreover, we have already issued the critical mass of its implementing rules and regulations, but the real challenge lies in the effective implementation.

The central focus of an improved supervisory framework is the full shift to consolidated, risk-based supervision. This involves the alignment of banking regulations with international standards; reorganization of the BSP’s Supervision and Examination Sector; the updating of processes and procedures; the large scale deployment of information and communication technology to achieve the highest synergy in off-site analysis and on-site examination; and the wholesale skills upgrading of our SES staff. Truly I can assure you we have set in motion a far reaching reform of how we conduct business. This will be given even greater impetus once congress acts on the proposed amendments to the BSP Charter.

On the restructuring of the local banking system, our primary agenda is still to promote fewer but stronger main banking organizations in the context of the larger picture where the banking system shares a healthy and balanced partnership with a more developed domestic capital market. We will achieve this by raising the bar on capital adequacy based on BASLE Committee recommended standards; by actively encouraging mergers and acquisitions; by strengthening the rules disciplining connected party transactions; and by allowing the entry of strong foreign players to the extent allowed by law.

Conclusion

There is much work ahead of us. The Board’s challenge is to stay adequately informed of current performance, to be concerned with the future and the risks being taken, to know when to change and to be sufficiently independent to make the change.

But more than committed and competent leadership, our banks equally need leadership integrity and the desire to serve the general good, not just the narrow objective of profit. This can best be shown as we lead our respective organizations to adhere to high standards of ethical business practice and overall compliance with the letter and spirit of laws, rules and regulations.

Good governance in the banking system cannot be effected by the BSP alone. It must voluntarily spring from every bank as they define their role as benevolent contributors to the public good. While the BSP endeavors to create the appropriate regulatory and supervisory environment, the fulcrum of viability for our banking system rests in the quality of bank’s own corporate governance. It is the sound decisions at the individual bank level that remains indispensable to the creation of a strong and effective banking system. Ultimately, in the quality of banks’ corporate governance lies the prospects for growth, profitability and financial stability.

Finally, let me just recognize the outstanding work of Dr. Jess Estanislao who together with his team enthusiastically led today’s seminar. He has been instrumental in sensitizing all of us to the virtues of corporate governance reform. In recognition of his achievements, he recently received the laureate award from the prestigious International Corporate Governance Network (ICGN) based in London.

Thank you and a pleasant evening to all.

(Note: Closing Remarks, Special One-Day Seminar on Corporate Governance for Bank Chairmen and CEOs, August 07, 2002, BSP Executive Business Center)

Title: A Salute to Prime Assets of the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas
Occasion: BSP Luncheon Program for 1999 to June 2002 Retirees
Speaker: Governor Rafael Buenaventura
Transcription:
Magandang tanghali po…..at maligayang pagbabalik sa ating mga retirees.

Let me confess that for this lunch, I was expecting really mature-looking individuals. Instead, I am looking at fresh-looking happy faces.

I must say you give retirement a good name. I bet, most of you can outlast the members of the Monetary Board at the dance floor. Let me see…Governor Gabby Singson has even beaten me in a round of golf. Of course, when I was still a private banker and Gabby was still Governor of BSP, he always won against me…but kidding aside.

Truly we are honored that you have accepted our invitation today. It is always a happy and special occasion when we meet those who have come before us. It is you who have laid a solid foundation for the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas that we know today. Through your own respective works, you have helped make BSP what it is today: an independent central monetary authority known for its competence and integrity.

Competence and integrity. An institution earns these attributes because of the overall quality of its people. And collectively, you have made this possible.

I know for a fact that Governor Gabby Singson here, the first BSP Governor, won a back-to-back citation from Asia Money as Central Bank Governor of the year in 1996 and 1997. And he topped this further in 1998 when he was chosen to receive the prestigious Management Man of the Year award.

On the other hand, Deputy Governor Ed Zialcita here is acknowledged as the mentor of the current crop of economists in BSP, schooled in the no-frills, no-fuss writing style that has promoted easier and better understanding of economic trends and BSP policies.

Based on the computation of our human resources management department, the collective experience of the retired central bankers with us today is equivalent to 2,578 years. Imagine, 2,578 years of central banking expertise.

I must say, your legacy has served BSP in good stead. Last week, the Makati Business Club announced that once again, BSP earned the highest approval rating among government agencies. This is two semesters in a row, back-to-back so to speak. And early this year, the Financial Times of London publication - The Banker - also cited yours truly as Central Bank Governor for Asia. I believe they take a closer look at BSP because you have paved the way in proving to local and overseas entities that indeed, BSP has world-class talents.

But more than awards and citations, BSP continues to deliver, where it counts the most: we have a stable banking sector, interest rates are at record lows, the peso is stable, our international reserves are at record high levels, while inflation rates are at record lows. For your information, BSP shifted this year to inflation targeting as our new monetary policy framework, to focus on our principal mandate of maintaining price stability. By and large, I think we have done fairly well.

The low inflation rates indicate that our monetary policy response has been effective and that our inflation targeting formula is working. This is important to us because this will be a principal yardstick against which our performance will be measured. And in keeping with the good governance mantra of transparency and accountability, we have been very transparent in our assessments of the path that inflation could take.

I am also pleased to report to you that BSP has managed its resources quite well, even now when it has started paying taxes. From an initial capitalization of P10 billion, BSP has remitted to the National Government a total of P73 billion in taxes and dividends in its first nine years of operation. BSP has therefore emerged as one of the biggest sources of government revenues.

We are also providing a better working environment for BSPers, starting here at our 30-year old manila complex. We have started rehabilitation and modernization works at the 5th floor with the completion of an Executive Business Center, which by the way, has hosted international conferences. For instance, the first ever meeting in Asia of the BIS or the Bank for International Settlements was held at our Executive Business Center last June. By the way, we are inviting all of you to come and visit our Executive Business Center this afternoon, after our lunch.

Currently onstream are similar works at the second floor cafeteria and the third floor executive dining lounge. We have also drawn up a three-year master plan for the upgrade of the Security Plant Complex to a world-class facility. In other words, we are not engaged in mere facelifts; we are also building for the long-term.

And equally important, BSP continues to invest in its people…to provide for the general well-being of the staff…to nurture their professional growth and their total development as team players. And of course, we continue to work for the exemption of our rank-and-file from salary standardization as part of the amendments to the new central bank act. You know of course that we are lobbying for these amendments to strengthen BSP and vest it with broader supervisory powers over banks and quasi-banks.

I am telling you all these because I know that BSP is an institution that you care for, and because we know that you actively promote and support BSP. In this regard, you are BSP’s prime assets…this is the reason why the plaque of recognition that you received today carries with it our heartfelt thank you. To those who want to do more, be mentors for BSP. You have the institutional memory and the expertise. We can invite you as resource persons in some of our future training modules.

Gusto ko pong ulit-ulitin: you are always welcome here at BSP. This is your second home…and retirees have a special room here at the 11th floor. Keep in touch and stay organized. There is much that we can still do together.

Finally, I want to pick up on the President’s State of the Nation Address yesterday. She said all of us must help build a strong republic. And for this, each of us must give the finest stone within our ability to shape…a stone by which we will be remembered.

Already, you have contributed stones that have built a strong foundation for BSP. It is therefore most inspiring to see that having left BSP, most of you continue to work on new stones for our country. I understand that the association of BSP retirees continue to work together in support of social projects. Lita Arenas here is still active in BSP’s Leveriza projects; Greg Suarez is in Microfinance; while Atty. Fe Barin, the brave lady that she is, is making sure that electric companies do not exploit consumers like us, in her capacity as chairman of the powerful Energy Regulatory Commission.

What can I say. You are not only world-class central bankers, you are also good citizens of our country.

Again, thank you for honoring us with your presence. May god’s blessings be with us always. Maraming salamat sa inyong lahat.

(Note: BSP Luncheon Program for 1999 to June 2002 Retirees, July 23, 2002, Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas)

Title: Message
Occasion: Inauguration and blessing of BSP Lucena Branch
Speaker: Governor Rafael Buenaventura
Transcription:
Quezon Province Governor Wilfrido L. Enverga, Congresswoman Lynette A. Punzalan, Lucena City Mayor & Mrs. Ramon Talaga, Rev. Msgr. Oscar Leaño, fellow workers in government and in the Bangko Sentral, honored guests, ladies and gentlemen, good morning.

Amidst the many uncertainties brought about by the Asian financial crisis, the economic slowdown in the U.S. and an impending global recession, the Philippine banking system has continued to be at the center of the flow of funds that connects savings, investments and expenditures which are requisites to national progress. Given this, the Bangko Sentral has intensified its program of institutional and structural reforms within the supervisory framework defined by the General Banking Law of 2000 and the Central Bank Act of 1993.

The BSP initiatives have been aimed at further promoting the development of a sound, effective and modern banking system, at the same time upgrading our compliance with international banking standards. These include the adoption of risk-based capital adequacy norms, measures to address dollar speculation and exchange rate volatility, consolidated supervision of financial conglomerates and the issuance of guidelines for banks offering e-banking services. The BSP has also issued rules and regulations designed to combat money laundering.

Anti-money Laundering, Micro-finance, the Special Purpose Asset Vehicle Bills have become the latest advocacies of the BSP in pursuit of our mission of providing pro-active leadership in bringing about a strong financial system that is supportive of the requirements of economic growth.

Parallel to the efforts of maintaining the soundness of the banking system, the Bangko Sentral has been the guardian of price stability.

Ø       The average inflation of 6.1 percent last year was at the lower end of the 6.0-7.0 percent target range. For the six months of 2002, average inflation was 3.6 percent, lower than the government’s target of 4.5-5.5 percent for the whole year.

Ø       Interest rates are at the record low levels. As of June, BSP’s policy rates stood at 7.0 percent for the overnight borrowing rate and 9.25 percent for the overnight lending rate, the lowest in ten years. Bank lending rates have also declined substantially.

Ø">       The peso, which faced depreciation pressures in 2001, has strengthened since the beginning of 2002. The gross international reserves have continued to climb. As of end June 2002, the GIR stood at almost U.S. $17 billion, which can adequately cover 5.6 months worth of imports of goods and services.

These figures also show that our inflation targeting formula as a monetary policy framework is working. The BSP has been very transparent by regularly conveying to the public our monetary policy actions and reasons for these actions.

In line with the bank’s decentralization policy, we are implementing an aggressive but realistic branch development program to further improving the delivery of basic central banking services to the countryside. By establishing our presence in the different parts of the country, we hope to accelerate banking and business activities, thus opening up new opportunities nationwide.

Since October 1977 when the CB Regional Clearing Unit opened in Lucena City, the Bank has established a significant presence in Quezon province. More services were made available with the commencement of the regional cash operations in May 1985.

With the completion of the Lucena branch building, we hope to substantially upgrade the quality of our services to this community:

Ø       First, we expect to be able to efficiently service the currency requirements of some 200 branches of commercial, thrift and rural banks in the cities of Lucena, San Pablo and Batangas and in the provinces of Quezon, Laguna, Batangas and Marinduque by making available crisp currency notes and new coins.

Ø       Second, payments of rediscounted loans and other obligations with the BSP are now accepted and processed by our Lucena branch. Bank branches need not go to BSP Manila to remit payments to settle their obligations with the BSP.

Ø       Third, updated information and statistical data on BSP operations will soon be available on-line through our Lucena branch.

In closing, we extend our thanks and appreciation to all government officials, as well as private individuals who contributed their valuable time and efforts in the realization of this building construction project.

Finally, we sincerely hope that in improving the delivery of BSP services to the local banking and business communities, we will be contributing a significant share in hastening the economic development of Lucena city and the entire southern Tagalog region.

Thank you and good day.

(Note: Inauguration and blessing of the BSP Lucena Branch, July 18, 2002, Lucena City)

Title: Team Philippines: Sustaining Growth for the Long-Term
Occasion: Foreign Correspondents Association of the Philippines (FOCAP)
Speaker: Governor Rafael Buenaventura
Transcription:
Good morning friends, ladies and gentlemen of the Foreign Correspondents Association of the Philippines.

Thank you for inviting me once again to your forum. For your information, I just marked my third year anniversary as BSP Governor last July 6. In other words, I am half way through my term. Therefore, today is a good opportunity to review what has come to pass and what we can look forward to in terms of economic and monetary policies.

When I met FOCAP members in March last year, I was content to report the respectable performance pulled off by the economy in 2000, despite adverse global developments and concerns in the domestic front. Today, nearly 16 months later, my satisfaction level has gone notches higher as I anticipate the surge of an economy that continues to sustain the momentum of recovery.

Let me just to take you back a little and cite random notes to illustrate that the Philippine economy is on the mend. Let me start with the year-end 2001 figures.

Last year, GDP growth was 3.4%, surpassing Government’s own 3.3% growth target. This was achieved in the face of external shocks and domestic anxiety spawned by the political transition and the peace-and-order situation. In fact, the Philippines was cited as having one of the highest economic growth rates in the region.

Along with economic growth, the number of employed persons increased by 6.1% from the previous year. At the same time, inflation rate stayed at single-digit levels or an average of 6.1%, aided by prudent monetary policy and favorable supply factors.

And our peso, which exhibited sharp swings at some points, increasingly stabilized toward the end of the year. By year’s end, our international reserves was at a comfortable level of $15 billion.

Meanwhile, our banking system remained broadly stable and sound, amid heightened tensions in financial markets in the aftermath of the September 11 attack on the world trade.

Strict adherence to fiscal discipline measures considerably raised the level of confidence in government’s ability to manage its resources. By December 2001, the budgetary deficit came in just a shade higher than the programmed P145 billion deficit. We missed it by just P2 billion.

The economic horizon was definitely brighter at the close of 2001.

Fast forward to July 2002. Now, where do we stand and where are we going?

The Philippine economic team, which includes BSP, is confident that the economy is on a sustainable growth track. The following bear us out:

First, the continued growth of the economy during the first quarter of the year: GDP growth at 3.8% and GNP up by 4.9%.

Second, record low inflation numbers. Last month, the rate of price increases slowed down further to 3.0%, after remaining steady at 3.6% in the previous three months. These figures are well below the full-year target of 4.5% to 5.5%.  This is of particular importance to us at Bangko Sentral because our principal mandate is to ensure price stability, through the adoption and implementation of sound and responsive monetary policies.

Third, the financial market remains liquid, as benign inflation and lower foreign interest rates have enabled BSP’s monetary board to relax our monetary stance through reductions in policy rates. Overnight borrowing and lending rates are now at 7.0% and 9.25%, respectively. Overall, policy rates have declined by 800 basis points since we started easing up in December 2000. The impact of this stance was reflected mainly on the decline of market interest rates to historic low levels. The rate of the bellwether 91-day Treasury bill as of last auction was 4.8%.

Fourth, the peso has not been showing any of the volatility that it had displayed last year. Although not impervious to concerns on political and fiscal issues, it has nevertheless remained relatively stable with fundamental support coming from healthy international reserves level.

I also wish to point out that international reserves reached over $17 billion in March this year, our highest on record.

Investor confidence has been building up, as reflected in the strong recovery in portfolio and direct investments. Investors had responded positively to bond issues of Government in the international markets, partly underpinning the $1.511 billion net inflow in portfolio investments. On the other hand, net inflows in direct investments in the first three months more than doubled to $1.224 billion.

And then, the balance of payments or BOP for the first three months of the year yielded a surplus of $2.157 billion, a turnaround from the $512 million deficit in the same period last year.

By the end of the first semester this year, our dollar holdings was $16.9 billion, ahead of the 2002 projection of $14.8 billion.

Truly, signs of increasing business activity are evident. Exports have rebounded. Imports have risen, a sizeable portion of which was accounted for by capital goods, raw materials and intermediate goods for production. There is an upturn in other leading indicators like electric consumption as well as in car and appliance sales.

Interestingly, the export sector is marked not so much by our products going to traditional markets like U.S. and Japan, but by its incursion to non-traditional markets -- China, Malaysia, Taiwan, Korea and Hong Kong. Philippine exports to these countries have risen sharply, suggesting the growing trade relations of the Philippines with Asia's growth tigers.

That the Philippine economy has recovered a lot of ground is clear. I can also say that the macroeconomic environment today is much kinder to a renewal of confidence and expansion of productive undertakings. Thus, while some sectors point to the adverse economic impact of recent political developments, I personally believe that this is temporary in nature as we do have solid and good economic fundamentals.

In fact, even as concerns are raised over the budget deficit and non-performing loans, independent analysts - including ratings agencies and IMF - acknowledge that the Philippines has performed better than its neighbors.

Consumer confidence is also on the rise, as indicated by the latest perceptions survey conducted by New York-based Roper ASW Asia Pacific for Business World last June.

At the same time, business remains optimistic about the short-term economic prospects of the economy, according to the latest Executive Outlook Survey of the Makati Business Club. While the survey reveal some underlying concerns on investment levels, three of the five top positive developments that respondents observed in the January-June 2002 period were economic in nature: stable currency, lower interest rates, and lower inflation rate. The other two were the neutralization of the Abu Sayyaf and the conduct of the Balikatan Exercises.

I also consider it as a vote of confidence from the Makati Business Club that the five government agencies leading the country’s economic team landed in the top six slots in the survey: Bangko Sentral, Department of Finance, Department of Budget and Management, National Economic and Development Authority and the Department of Trade slid to no. Please note that the agencies were mentioned in the order of their ranking.

This much I can say: the economic team is single-minded in achieving sustainable economic growth for the country.

Finally, may I just outline, very briefly, BSP’s policy thrusts along this line:

1.  Maintaining price stability. Thus far, we have been doing very well, but the ultimate goal is for price stability to be a norm rather than the exception.

2.  Continue adhering to a flexible exchange rate policy.

3.  Promoting bank lending activity while addressing the high NPL levels.

4.  Strengthening the banking system further.

5.  Enhancing efforts to combat money laundering.

6.  Modernizing the payment structure.

7.  Managing the country's external debt effectively through longer maturities and cost reduction.

Suffice it to say that we at the BSP will continue to work on reforms that are needed to enhance our operations. We may not always succeed, but rest assured that it will not be for lack of trying.

I will end this opening statement now, so you can ask me the questions you have wanted to ask me, since I came inside this room I am also looking forward to listening to your comments on issues of concern to you, for these help us focus on matters which we may have overlooked.

And so, again, thank you FOCAP for this opportunity.

Marami pong salamat.

Title: BSP at 9: High Scores for Price and Banking Stability
Occasion: 9th Anniversary Celebration of Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas
Speaker: Governor Rafael Buenaventura
Transcription:
Magandang umaga po sa inyong lahat.

Espesyal po ang araw na ito para sa ating lahat: buong araw, ipagdiriwang natin ang ika-siyam na anibersaryo ng ating mahal na Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas.

Bilang pinuno ng Bangko Sentral, bilang Governor, I must say we have a good reason to celebrate. We have been united and focused on a common goal…and so, together, we have made the BSP a true guardian of price and banking stability.

Today, our inflation rates are at their lowest levels in 15-years, while interest rates are at record low levels. Our peso remains stable, while international reserves are at all-time high levels.

At the same time, Philippine banks are better prepared to handle potential reversals, following the adoption of the risk-based capital adequacy framework in July last year. The ratio of their net worth to risk assets averaged 16% in 2001, above the BSP-required level of 10% and double the International Basle standard of 8%. The reforms we adopted to enhance good governance also served to strengthen the banking sector.

Indeed, we can rightfully take pride in these.

Price increases have slowed down during BSP’s 9th year and has been steady at 3.6% in the last three months up to may, well below the government target of 5-6 percent for the year. The average last year was also within target.

These figures not only indicate how we fared in maintaining price stability, but also how our inflation targeting formula is working. This is significant as we have shifted to inflation targeting as our new monetary policy framework. This will be a principal yardstick against which our performance will be measured and as called for, we have been very transparent in our assessments of the path that inflation could take.

By and large, i think we have done fairly well vis-à-vis the targets, as well as in giving the public a more predictable reading of monetary policy, which is important to policymakers and businessmen for mid-and long-term planning.

Our monetary policy had been generally accommodative. We continued to cut policy rates to encourage bank lending to productive economic activities. The reductions, however, were carefully calibrated in terms of timing and amount to maintain price stability. The impact of this approach was reflected mainly in the decline of market interest rates to historic lows.

BSP likewise took the high road as it defined and assumed the lead in the pursuit of critical measures that will boost economic growth and the strengthening of our financial system. Anti-money laundering, microfinance and corporate governance have become our new advocacies, sending signals that we are ready and determined to blaze new trails to attain our objective of providing an environment conducive to a balanced and sustainable growth of the economy.

I must say that BSP’s accomplishments have not gone unnoticed. However, so that we cannot be accused of bias, let me cite what others have been saying about BSP.

Let us start with President Gloria Macapagal-Arroyo. In her many public statements, the President said the prudent monetary measures undertaken by BSP help boost the general confidence of both local and foreign investors in the country’s economy.

And as you may remember, the members of the Makati Business Club again voted BSP as the top performer among all government agencies early this year.

Last week, Fitch ratings of London noted the following in its country report on the Philippines: “Despite a severe external shock that saw current external receipts drop by 16% in 2001, the current account remained in surplus to the tune of $4.5 billion and the economy recorded real GDP growth of 3.2% in 2001, among the highest in the region. This outcome owed much to a flexible exchange rate and sound macro-economic policy management that has seen inflation and interest rates touch record lows in recent months.”

While we are far from perfect, clearly, BSP has gained a reputation for excellence, here and abroad.

This positive image of BSP, has served us in good stead. Just the other day, BSP’s five-year term loan facility attracted such an overwhelming response that it was oversubscribed: the initial size of $500 million increased to $675 million, making it the largest Asian sovereign loan in 2001, as well as the largest U.S. dollar-denominated loan in Asia, outside of Japan.

To top it all, we got very good rates too. This will considerably lower our cost of holding international reserves.

As you are aware, the savings we generate here at BSP benefits the country as a whole. In its first nine years of operation, BSP has remitted to the National Government a total of P73 billion in taxes and dividends. BSP has therefore emerged as one of the biggest sources of government revenues, in spite of having an initial capitalization of only P10 billion.

The challenge before us, therefore, is to sustain our momentum so that we can continue to pursue our mandate, in the service of our country.

This is the reason why BSP continues to invest in its people…to provide for the general well-being of the staff…to nurture their professional growth and their total development as team players.

Thus, last year, BSP management further improved its employee benefits package through the following:

  • The adoption of a new salary scale with an increase in the monthly basic salary for SG 19 and below positions, and a corrected scale for the exempt class.

  • An increase in the (1) medical insurance subsidy, (2) financial assistance to the family of an employee who dies while in the service of the bank, and (3) inner ceilings of certain benefits in the hospitalization and medical benefits plan;

  • Back pay of the cost-of-living-allowance or cola and amelioration allowance for non-exempt employees;

  • An increase in the economic assistance given middle of the year and in November, and grant of an additional economic assistance in December;

  • An increase in the bank share in the provident fund for personnel recruited after Oct. 31, 1989 to replace benefits that they do not enjoy because of the restrictions of the salary standardization law; and

  • An increase in the proportion of an employee’s accumulated vacation leave and sick leave credits that he can monetize.

On top of these material benefits, there were further improvements in personnel policies, systems and procedures, organizational groups, and the workplace. All these should prepare us well for the many challenges that still lie ahead.

As of latest count -- and we are still counting -- there are 4,641 regular officials and employees at BSP… people of of varied persuasion, inclination, values, experiences, capabilities and skills. Forming and maintaining out of this diversity, cohesive teams that will focus on ways to further improve our performance and the way we do things is a challenge we must work on collectively and persistently.

To this end, training programs were intensified and aligned with BSP objectives. Deputy Governor Suratos reports that last year, various training programs drew more than 7,000 participants. I am particularly happy that there are more people taking up computer training programs, a must for us at BSP. Skills aside, we also have values formation program which, I am pleased to note, has attracted the participation of 40% of our people.

We have also been reviewing the BSP organization to align it with the changing environment. This has resulted in organizational changes in the SITD, Dept. of General Services and OMD/OAG-SPC; OSI; DLC; Provident Fund Office; and ISTD.

We have also created new departments, namely, Investor Relations Office, Corporate Planning Office, Systems and Methods Office, and the Anti-Money Laundering Secretariat to take care of unique concerns that have emerged in recent years and which require focused attention.

We have also gone beyond the intangibles to measure up to international standards. For instance, we have drawn up a master plan for the upgrade of the Security Plant Complex to a world-class facility.

We have also started upgrading basic service facilities at main office. After 30 years, the BSP complex deserves a facelift.

So far, we have completed the Executive Business Center; the upgrading and modernization of our dining areas is next in line. By September this year, I will be joining you for lunch in our upgraded dining areas at the second and third floor. Magkakaroon din po tayo ng bridgeway café o kapihan sa the third floor.

We are also improving our regional offices. For instance, we will be inaugurating our new building in Lucena city this month, while three other branches in Mindanao are under construction.

Given all these developments, one thing is sure: we can look forward to more work and, hopefully, more rewards. Mag-uumpisa na po yan mamaya, sa afternoon raffle ng cash prizes.

On a personal note…July 6 will be my third year anniversary as BSP Governor.

This is just my half-way mark…and already I have the honor of being chosen as the first recipient of the Asian Central Banker of the Year award by a publication of the Financial Times of London. Two local media groups have also given me awards of distinction as Governor of the BSP. I have also been named as a distinguished Son of San Fernando, La Union, my hometown.

I am telling you all these, because I want to share these awards with you. These awards rightfully belong to all of us here at BSP...to my colleagues at the Monetary Board, and to my co-workers at the Top Management Sector, the Resource Management Sector, the Banking Services Sector and the Supervision and Examination Sector. There is no way I would have earned these citations without you and without your support.

On my part, I commit to do my best at all times for and in behalf of BSP and its people. I commit to pursue necessary reforms and the passage of legislations that will help BSP accomplish its mission and vision. This includes asking our legislators to grant immunity to our people from being sued in the pursuit of their work. As government employees, it takes a lot of integrity and courage to stand up to people of influence with huge resources. Having to face suits from the performance of one’s duty unduly exposes them to more risks and harassment.

Our vision statement refers to BSP as having the values of integrity, excellence and patriotism.  These are the very same values that I see here at BSP every day. And it is patriotism that gives us the will and the courage to adhere to our pledge to do good for our country, at all times.

And it is also patriotism that leads the people of BSP to share their blessings with the less fortunate in their midst.

And so, I thank and congratulate all of you for a job well done. Let us pledge to again work together as a team to accomplish our mission and vision.

It is a privilege working with all of you at Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas.

Maraming pong salamat at maligayang anibersaryo!

(Note: 9th Anniversary Celebration of Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas, July 03, 2002, Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas, Manila)

Title: Remarks
Place: Yuchengco Tower, RCBC Tower, Makati City
Occasion: US$675,000,000 Term Loan Facility Signing Ceremony
Speaker: Governor Rafael Buenaventura
Transcription:
Fellow bankers, friends from the media, ladies and gentlemen.

On behalf of the Bangko Sentral, I would like to thank the twenty-two (22) participating banks for making this refinancing exercise of the bank an astounding success. This new loan facility will allow the BSP to reduce its cost of holding reserves and improve the maturity profile of its foreign currency obligations.

Let me congratulate the co-ordinating arrangers for successfully pulling the transaction together despite the volatile market conditions. They have raised 175 million dollars more than the targeted 500 million dollars and solicited a broad participation for the facility. I am pleased to see the continued support from the existing creditors, and very delighted to find the new names in the syndicate.

I believe that the success of this transaction is evidence to the continuing investor confidence in the Philippines. I hope that this loan facility can serve as a benchmark transaction for subsequent corporate deals.

Thank you and good afternoon. 

(Note: US$675,000,000 Term Loan Facility Signing Ceremony, July 01, 2002, Yuchengco Tower, RCBC Plaza, Makati City)

Title: Stronger RP-U.S. Links Against Money Laundering
Occasion: Signing Ceremony of the Memorandum of Understanding
Speaker: Governor Rafael Buenaventura
Transcription:
Ambassador Francis Ricciardone, USAID Director Patricia Buckles, our guests from the U.S. Government, friends from media, my co-workers in government.  Good morning.

On behalf of BSP and the Anti-Money Laundering Council, I thank all of you for joining us this morning. In particular, I thank the United States Government for its all-out support for our training programs through USAID and AGILE, the U.S. State Department’s Anti-Terrorism Training Program and the U.S. Financial Crimes Enforcement Network.

Already, 32 participants from our multi-agency network group on anti-money laundering activities have been trained at the Federal Bureau of Investigation Academy on the financial underpinnings of terrorism while 15 participated in a seminar of the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network on international money laundering and financial intelligence units.

Indeed, we need all the support we can get. . . And that coming from USAID is deeply appreciated.

Among others, our Memorandum of Understanding with USAID this morning further expands and strengthens our areas of cooperation in banking supervision, a vital frontline activity in ferreting and stamping out illegally-acquired funds. We are also looking forward to receiving more support from the U.S. Government in terms of training, support for software and hardware acquisition and more important, database sharing.

We do need to strengthen international cooperation to detect, and prevent, the misuse of our financial system by criminal and terrorist elements who undermine world peace and economic and political stability.

Michel Camdessus, former International Monetary Fund Managing Director, has estimated that the volume of worldwide money laundering is between 2 and 5 percent of the world’s gross domestic product – some $600 billion or P30 trillion, even at the low end of the range. This is the extent of financial power at the disposal of criminals and terrorists.

And so, we thank the U.S. Government for supporting the Philippines in its campaign to weaken criminals and terrorists in our midst by cutting off their access to their lifeblood: illegally-acquired funds

Maraming salamat sa inyong lahat.

 

(Note: Signing Ceremony, Memorandum of Understanding (on anti-money laundering cooperation between the United States Agency for International Development (USAID) and the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas, May 22, 2002, Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas, Manila)

Title: Strengthening Links with AMLC Partners
Occasion: Roundtable Discussions on Anti-Money Laundering
Speaker: Governor Rafael Buenaventura
Transcription:
Good afternoon everyone.

Today we take an important step towards integrating what we have learned in the first few months of operation of the Anti-Money Laundering Council, as well as from the training workshops and seminars you have attended. 

That we are gathered at a time when AMLC has just won a crucial procedural victory at the Court of Appeals, makes this meeting doubly significant.  As you are aware, the Court of Appeals granted our request for an extension of a freeze order on eight bank accounts suspected to contain proceeds of illegal activities. 

By doing so, it upheld our position that only the Court of Appeals and the Supreme Court have jurisdiction over money laundering cases. In this case, AMLC is ably supported by the Office of the Solicitor General.

The fight is on. . . And we have won the first round. But we are realistic and we know that more difficult and complex cases lie ahead.

I am therefore glad to note that the other key agencies AMLC will depend on for support are represented here: the Department of Justice, National Bureau of Investigation, the Philippine National Police, the Bureau of Immigration and Deportation, and the Philippine Center on Transnational Crime. Of course the core agencies composing AMLC are also here: Securities and Exchange Commission, Insurance Commission and the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas.

For your information, AMLC will be meeting soon with Justice Secretary Hernando Perez and NBI Director Reynaldo Wycoco to define the terms of cooperation and support for AMLC; the rules of the game, so to speak, to strengthen institutional links and broaden areas of cooperation.

On behalf of AMLC, I also acknowledge the support we have been receiving from multilateral and bilateral institutions In particular, we thank the U.S. Government for providing unstinting support for our training programs through USAID and AGILE, the U.S. State Department’s Anti-Terrorism Training Program and the U.S. Financial Crimes Enforcement Network.

I understand that 32 participants from our different agencies here were trained at the Federal Bureau of Investigation Academy on the financial underpinnings of terrorism while 15 participated in a seminar of the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network on international money laundering and financial intelligence units. We now have the beginnings of a core multi-agency group.

Indeed, AMLC will need unrelenting support from all of you, as well as the respective agencies you represent. It will take team effort to track down the activities of money launderers and terrorists so that we can put them behind bars.

We have to mount a coordinated and comprehensive effort to detect, and prevent, the misuse of our financial system by criminal elements. By cutting off their access to illegally acquired funds, we weaken the criminals and terrorists in our midst. . . and we make our world safer for our people.

Michel Camdessus, former International Monetary Fund Managing Director, has estimated that the volume of worldwide money laundering is between 2 and 5 percent of the world’s gross domestic product – some $600 billion or P30 trillion, even at the low end of the range. This is the extent of financial power at the disposal of criminals and terrorists.

And so, today, let us pledge to work together to ensure an intensified and sustained fight against money laundering. Let the Philippines be one of the strongest links in the coordinated international efforts to curb crimes and terrorism. Marami pong salamat sa inyong lahat.

 

(Note: Roundtable discussions on Anti-Money Laundering, Accelerating Growth Investment and Liberalization Equity (AGILE), May 14, 2002, Manila Hotel)

Title: Closing Remarks
Occasion: Second Bilateral Meeting between the BSP and Bank of Thailand
Speaker: Governor Rafael Buenaventura
Transcription:
We are deeply grateful for this opportunity to share information as well as best practice experiences on inflation targeting, risk-based supervision and securitization of non-performing assets of financial institutions with our distinguished guests from the Bank of Thailand. The rest of today and tomorrow will provide us more opportunities on an even wider range of issues, although the interaction would be on a more informal basis.

We have always emphasized the value of fostering greater cooperation between the bank of Thailand and the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas. Our two countries share mutual interests that arise beyond geographic proximity. As we have experienced both during the Asian economic crisis and the global economic slowdown in 2001, financial market globalization is often characterized by the pervasiveness of a “neighborhood effect” on emerging economies, including Thailand and the Philippines. Our two economies, therefore, share many similar challenges, and there is much to be gained from our mutually coordinated, common response to such trials.

Cooperation between the Philippines and Thailand has taken many forms, including through information sharing in terms of both data as well as best practice experiences. For many years, these have taken place in a major way through such regional organizations as the Association of Southeast Asian nations (ASEAN), the Executives’ Meeting of East Asia and the Pacific (EMEAP), and the south East Asian Sentral Banks (SEACEN) Research and Training Centre, among others. Our bilateral meetings, of which this is the second of what we hope would be a continuing series, both deepen and expand the scope of cooperation between our two institutions.

Our two peoples have become known worldwide for their warm hospitality. The bank of Thailand has had occasion to prove this during our visit to Bangkok in December last year. Kindly allow us, therefore, to reciprocate your hospitality, and it is my hope that the rest of your stay in the Philippines will be pleasant and memorable.

Thank you.

 

(Note: Second Bilateral Meeting Between the Bank of Thailand and the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas, May 3-5, 2002, Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas, Manila)

Title: Opening Remarks
Occasion: Second Bilateral Meeting between the BSP and Bank of Thailand
Speaker: Governor Rafael Buenaventura
Transcription:
Honorable Governor Pridiyathorn Devakula, distinguished officials of the Bank of Thailand and the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas.

Good morning.

It is with great honor that we welcome you, Governor Pridiyathorn Devakula, and your distinguished colleagues from the Bank of Thailand to the second bilateral meeting between our two institutions. Our second meeting both expands our areas of discussion and follows on the success of our first bilateral meeting that benefited immensely from the Bank of Thailand’s initiative and graceful hospitality.

Our agenda for this morning takes off from the discussions in our first bilateral meeting, which centered on issues brought on by recent macroeconomic developments such as the impact of the 2001 global economic slowdown; consolidated supervision and implementation of the new Basel capital accord; exchange rate policy management; and risk management in monetary policy implementation. In this second bilateral talks, we consider further some of the responses that both our central banks have undertaken in the aftermath of the Asian financial crisis, in order to pursue both macroeconomic and financial stability. This meeting provides us a unique opportunity to share our experiences, challenges faced, and responses to issues in the course of our adoption of inflation targeting as the framework for monetary policy, as well as on risk-based supervision, and securitization of non-performing assets of financial institutions.

The rapid technological advances and structural change in financial systems have greatly reduced the importance of monetary aggregates as an anchor of monetary policy, while the Asian financial crisis and developments in Latin American economies have pointed out the vulnerability of managed exchange rate systems to speculative attack. Thus, inflation targeting holds out the greatest promise in terms of how monetary authorities can best achieve the goal of price stability. However, inflation targeting offers special challenges to small, open economies such as Thailand and the Philippines, and I am sure that our collective sharing of experiences in this area will contribute much to our mutual success.

Stability of the financial sector in today’s globalized environment represents the second pillar of sustainable economic growth.  An important step in this effort is the adoption of a more forward-looking and risk-based bank supervision framework, which will involve the reorientation of the bank examination process towards quality of decision-making processes rather than just compliance with rules and regulations. Another dimension of this effort is the implementation of consolidated supervision of financial conglomerates. This will lead to a more comprehensive assessment of the risks involved in banks’ activities. Going forward, one key element to sustained viability of the financial system over the medium- and long-term would involve decisive action to reduce the overhang of non-performing assets to more manageable levels. This could be achieved through securitization of non-performing assets and their transfer to asset management corporations, which is an important component of our strategy for non-performing assets.

I am positive that we will proceed from this meeting not only with greater awareness of the issues on our agenda; more so, I am confident that our discussion will identify new areas for future collaborative undertakings and developing closer ties between our two institutions and our countries.

We look forward to a fruitful discussion ahead of us.

(Note: Second Bilateral Meeting Between the Bank of Thailand and the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas, May 3-5, 2002, Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas, Manila)

Title: Speech
Occasion: Financing Forum for Exporters
Speaker: Governor Rafael Buenaventura
Transcription:
Distinguished members of TIDCORP, honored guests, ladies and gentlemen, good afternoon.

As most of you are aware of by now, the Philippines has an economic plan focused on fiscal discipline, good governance, market-oriented reform, and poverty-reduction. As the Governor of the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas, I would like to reiterate my continued support for this plan and its implementation. I also reiterate my confidence that the Philippine economic team is in place to ensure that the objectives included in the plan will continue to be achieved and more importantly, create an enabling environment that everyone in the business community particularly, the exporters will benefit from.

Among the initiatives that we, at the Bangko Sentral, have been taking to support the Government's economic plan include three important areas: first, is price stability; second, is introducing banking sector reforms; and third, is introducing institutional reforms to pave the way for good governance practices. All these are aimed toward creating a level playing field for all the key players in Philippine business.

Price stability

To my mind, one of the most crucial steps being taken by the Arroyo administration is the emphasis on instilling fiscal discipline throughout the public sector. The ability to meet revenue and expenditure targets, and thus reduce the budget deficit are significant steps toward stabilizing the cost of funds.

While the Government is focused on instilling fiscal discipline, my team at the Bangko Sentral is working to ensure that price stability becomes the norm rather than the exception.

As you all know, the Bangko Sentral has shifted monetary policy to inflation-targeting since January of this year. This practice, which is employed by many other countries, has price stability as a primary focus. With this policy, the Bangko Sentral and the National Government are both committed to reach an explicit nominal inflation target directly, without compromising the broad economic targets.

The Bangko Sentral is also highly focused on maintaining calm in the currency markets. Our goal in this regard is to achieve overall price stability, root out speculative activity and to continue to support the Government in meeting its fiscal targets.

The maintenance of a market-determined exchange rate policy has to be supported by a strict and effective foreign exchange monitoring system and a strong commitment to apply penalties to institutions or individuals who violate foreign exchange regulations. You know as well as I do that a relatively stable exchange rate is important for keeping inflation under control and is good for business planning.

So far this year, the peso has been trading at a much lower 100-day volatility of only 4.4% as of mid-April this year, from 19.6% during the same period last year.

The Bangko Sentral is also ensuring that the financial system is sufficiently liquid. The issue of addressing rising NPL’s ranks high in our list of priorities and is being dealt with a mix of short and long-term measures. Among the short-term measures are the monitoring of capital adequacy ratios on account of their cushioning effect, and the aggressive reduction in policy rates to encourage banks to reduce their lending rates accordingly.

Long-term measures being taken to reduce NPL’s include supporting the passage of the bill creating special purpose asset vehicles. The lower House version of this bill has been approved on 3rd reading and now awaits the senate version before the Bi-cameral Committee meets to ratify a unified version, hopefully before Congress goes into recess in June.

Other institutional measures we have taken are the preservation of an appropriate interest- rate differential to encourage investors to maintain their peso denominated assets.

And finally, our efforts to support price stability include work we are carrying out to develop secondary markets for fixed income and derivative products.

Instituting banking reforms

The Bangko Sentral is also committed to increasing foreign participation in the Philippine banking sector. We are introducing reforms that are preparing domestic banks to effectively compete in a globally integrated banking environment.
