The reforms fall within the framework of first, improving the banking sector’s structure through such steps as imposing capital requirements in accordance with international standards, and by promoting greater competition which will certainly encourage banking sector consolidation and provide opportunities for greater foreign participation in the sector.

Second, we are enhancing the Bangko Sentral’s supervisory and regulatory powers in line with international standards by introducing risk-based capital requirements, tighter loan classification and provisioning rules, and consolidated reporting. We will also be imposing stiffer penalties for any violations of Philippine banking regulations.

Third, we are heightening bank transparency and disclosure. As you have read in the papers, we are reviewing the audit process for banks to improve and strengthen their financial reporting system; we will also require strict adherence to the “know your customer rule”. We will require the quarterly publication of statements of condition, key financial indicators, non-performing loans, and related-party lending.

Fourth, we are improving risk management practices; by instituting early warning systems for bank failures, assist banks to better match their foreign currency assets and liabilities, and carry out reviews to identify regulatory loopholes in the transactions of bank-affiliated forex corporations.

And finally, we are stimulating the consumer-oriented credit environment through the licensing of micro-financing activities and by providing a credit facility through our re-discounting window. The rediscounting facility with a budget of PHP20 billion mainly supports export activities. At present, less than half of this budget has been utilized. Thus, we still have a significant amount that can be utilized.

We will also relax certain collateralization requirements and partially lift the general moratorium on the licensing of new thrift and rural banks to allow the establishment of institutions who are committed to micro-enterprise financing.

Institutional reforms and good governance

These reforms, if they are to have the desired impact, must be complemented by both good governance practices and strong political will. For this reason, we are seeking amendments to the BSP Charter that will institutionalize many of these reforms and reinforce the position of the Bangko Sentral as a governing and independent body for monetary policy and banking regulation and supervision.

In considering amendments to the Central Bank Charter, we are looking to add criteria to close or place banks or other financial institutions under receivership in line with international standards. We also want to strengthen criminal and administrative penalties for any violation of banking laws, and to introduce measures that will increase the central bank's operational efficiency.

Finally, the passage of an Anti-Money Laundering Bill and its implementing rules and regulations stress the Bangko Sentral’s commitment to promoting and enforcing international standards of banking regulation and supervision. Because of this, we have zero tolerance for illegal practices such as money laundering.

These are not empty words. My team and my colleagues in government are steadfast in instituting the reforms that will strengthen our banking sector and promote good governance. You have seen in the last several months our determination to work with the government to achieve its growth targets.

Having said that, a conducive environment has unfolded where, despite challenging external conditions, a stable economy has emerged underpinned by stable prices, stable currency, and low policy rates. Much of our work is in the area of further enhancements for sustaining growth and development.

The rest is for the private sector to follow suit on our initiatives. I trust that you all will.

Thank you very much and have a good day.

(Note: Financing Forum for Exporters, Trade and Investment Development Corporation of the Philippines (TIDCORP), April 26, 2002, Westin Philippine Plaza, Pasay City)

Title: Opening Remarks
Occasion: 2002 Corporate Planning Conference
Speaker: Governor Rafael Buenaventura
Transcription:
Over the past two months, we have worked hard in redefining the vision and mission of the BSP in the light of the changing global environment. We defined our vision of the BSP as a world-class monetary authority, and a catalyst for a globally competitive economy and financial system that delivers a high quality of life for all Filipinos. Our mission is to promote balanced and sustainable growth of the economy by maintaining stable prices and a sound financial system.

To concretize these goals, we conducted strategic planning exercises at the sectoral level, formulating the mission statements, key result areas and action plans for the various departments and offices of each sector. Our task in the next 1½ days is to go through these sectoral strategies and plans and determine how they can best fit together into coherent and consistent initiatives for the bank as a whole that would help us achieve our objectives.

During the past year, we committed ourselves to building a more effective central banking organization. We worked on instituting best practices in bank supervision, creating a better work environment in the bank, enhancing the bank’s corporate image, and strengthening corporate governance within the BSP organization itself. Looking back on the results of our efforts in these areas, I believe that they were by and large successful, and that we all deserve commendation for our hard work.

As we go through the various action plans, let us keep in mind that the Bangko Sentral has played a major role in putting the Philippine economy on the path to durable growth and long-term prosperity. Our strategies and plans, therefore, have an impact on the country’s macroeconomic performance, and on the quality of life of all Filipinos.

As with last year, I am confident that we will have the same kind of open, positive and constructive discussion of relevant issues. Our goal today is to strengthen the bank’s ability to cope with the changing times, improve our decision-making processes, and define more clearly the roadmap to achieving our corporate vision of making the BSP a world-class monetary authority. Given the more intensive pre-planning exercises that everyone went through, I expect that our inputs in the discussions will have greater strategic value. I think this is also an excellent time to conduct our strategic planning. Global economic activity is now on the mend, and the favorable economic environment will allow us to implement initiatives that will further strengthen the BSP as a central banking institution.

I will leave you now to reflect on these words: “Our goals can only be reached through a vehicle of a plan, in which we must fervently believe, and upon which we must vigorously act. There is no other route to success.” With that in mind, let us use this strategic planning exercise as a basis for vigorous action that will transform the BSP into a world-class institution.

Thank you and good day.

(Note: 2002 Corporate Planning Conference, Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas, April 12-13, 2002, Philippine International Convention Center)

Title: Message
Place: Baluarte de San Diego Garden, Intramuros, Manila
Occasion: Formal Turnover of the Allied Warehouse to the Department of Finance
Speaker: Governor Rafael Buenaventura
Transcription:
Today, the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas formally turns over a prime property, more popularly called the Allied Warehouse, to the Department of Finance and the Department of Tourism for the latter’s project, which is to set up a light and sound museum of Philippine history.

We are proud to support the Government’s tourism program and the Department of Tourism’s promotion of the country’s rich cultural heritage. The light and sound museum of Philippine history is clearly one such project.

We at the BSP are elated and excited at the prospect of passing on possession and ownership of the Allied Warehouse to a department at whose helm is a proven achiever, for we know that this property will be put to excellent use.

The BSP, within its powers, will continue to assist the DOT in achieving its responsibility to encourage, promote and develop tourism as a major socio-economic activity for the generation of foreign currency and employment.

(Note: Formal Turnover of the Allied Warehouse to the Department of Finance and Department of Tourism, April 03, 2002, Baluarte de San Diego Garden, Intramuros, Manila)

Title: Remarks
Occasion: Citibank Launching of the Microenterprenuer of the Year
Speaker: Governor Rafael Buenaventura
Transcription:
I am happy and honored to be able to participate in these ceremonies to launch Citibank’s search for the Microenterpreneur of the Year. Truth to tell, I originally had another important appointment this morning but, as luck would have it (for Citibank), the appointment was put off for another day and so I am free to come here today.

I am happy to be here for two reasons. It always feels good to be back in the company of former colleagues in Citibank, especially the Chairman and CEO, my good friend Victor Menezes, who I remember trained in Citibank Manila before embarking on an eminently successful banking career. The second reason is I strongly believe in microfinance as the major factor that will get our countrymen out of the clutches of poverty.

At the outset, I would like to congratulate Citibank, therefore, for this initiative and I refer particularly to my good friend Cathy Weir, the Country Corporate Officer, who now has the added distinction of presiding over the celebration of Citibank’s centennial in the Philippines.

To properly appreciate the significance of microfinance and this award that we are launching this morning, consider these statistics. In a population of 74 million Filipinos, 37% live below the poverty line. This poverty incidence translates to 5.2 million number of poor households or approximately 29 million people. That is the extent of the poverty problem in the Philippines. It is true that some 4 million poor families are engaged in some form of entrepreneurial activity. However, only 961,000 families can avail of credit because of the exploitative interest rates charged by so-called five-six operators and the inability of borrowers to produce collateral that is normally required by banks.

If this search for Microenterpreneur of the Year succeeds in making the poor realize that there is a credit mechanism called microfinance, which dispenses small loans without collateral, and at affordable interest rates, it will have made a meaningful contribution to poverty alleviation in our country.

We bankers sometimes overstate the importance of economic statistics like GNP growth and increase in per capita income. Quite obviously, these growth indicators do not filter down to the masses of our people and this gives rise to the refrain that the rich become richer and the poor remain poor. The plight of the poor must be addressed with specific solutions and the one solution that we in the Bangko Sentral can see that will make a difference is microfinance. Microfinance, which means loans of as little as P2,000.00 and no more than P150,000.00, is the means by which the entrepreneurial poor can improve their quality of life and join the mainstream of society.

No less than President Arroyo identified microfinance in her State of the Nation Address last year as the cornerstone of her fight against poverty. Given the fact that there are only 400,000 microfinance borrowers today, her goal is to raise this figure to 1 million by 2004, or something like 300,000 new borrowers a year. This is a specific goal that is at once a challenge to all of us.

Microfinance services are currently being provided by the formal and informal sectors. Tied to the People’s Credit and Finance Corporation, the quasi-government Apex Microfinance Institution, are 180 active conduits composed of 62 cooperatives, 28 NGO’s, 24 cooperative banks, 64 rural banks, and 3 thrift banks all over the country. While it seems that we have this large number of microfinance providers, there is still much to be done. It is estimated that the current providers are reaching only 10% of the intended market.

At the Bangko Sentral, we are doing our part in encouraging the spread of the microfinance gospel, so to speak, and encouraging the poor to avail of their services. We have been aggressive in creating enabling policy and the regulatory environment for the establishment of sustainable microfinance institutions. We are conducting training and information dissemination on microfinance technologies and best practices to the end that these institutions remain viable and effective service providers.

I am pleased to see that we are not alone in this effort. This project of Citibank of recognizing successful microenterpreneurs will provide additional impetus to the effort. Properly motivated and managed, microenterprises can serve as the driving force to invigorate local economies. The success of these businesses, no matter how small, has a multiplier effect on the lives of the individual entrepreneurs, their families and their community. And they showcase not just their businesses but also their discipline in meeting their obligations, and their social responsibility.

And yet this is not all that this project is bound to achieve. It will showcase as well the very microfinance institutions that provided the services for the successful enterprises. The fact will emerge that these institutions have stayed in the business because of good governance, meaning the priority they give to viability and sustainability in their operations, their effective and innovative delivery methods, and the breadth and depth of their reach. The beneficial effects of this award will go far and wide in creating role models for microfinance institutions and client entrepreneurs among the very poor.

Citibank hopefully will be only the trailblazer in instituting this award, and that other banks will follow and move in the same direction. As the President has repeatedly stated, poverty is the enemy that is the root cause of problems that are getting in the way of our progress as a nation. Let us all work for the success of microfinance which is one effective way to solve it.

The Microenterpreneur Award is a good beginning.

(Note: Citibank Launching of the Microenterpreneur of the Year, March 26, 2002, Shangri-La Hotel, Makati City)

Title: Remarks
Occasion: Annual Membership Meeting, Bankers Association of the Philippines
Speaker: Governor Rafael Buenaventura
Transcription:
I would like to begin by greeting all of you on this annual membership meeting of the Bankers Association of the Philippines.

I would like to take this opportunity to discuss a major issue which is both current and relevant, not to say urgent, in our efforts to overcome obstacles in the way of faster economic growth. This is the implementation of the Anti-Money Laundering Act of 2001, now referred to as AMLA. We signed the Implementing Rules and Regulations (or IRR) last March 13. The signatories were the representatives of the BSP, the Securities and Exchange Commission, and the Insurance Commission, who constitute the Anti-Money Laundering Council, and the members of the Bicameral Congressional Oversight Committee who are mandated by the law to approve the IRR.

Let me discuss the salient features of the IRR.

The Law, if you remember, was greeted with doubts and criticism when it was passed last year, on the heels of threats of countermeasures from the Financial Action Task Force. Among other things, critics said it did not have enough teeth and may not meet the standards of the FATF. Much was said about the requirement for a court order, to enable the Council to inquire into bank deposits, as well as the very short list of covered crimes. The FATF itself observed that the threshold amount of P4 million was too high for the Law to be able to cover all attempts, to use the proceeds of unlawful activity.

I am happy to inform you that the IRR, apart from being merely a guide in the implementation of the Law, has addressed these issues to our satisfaction. It explains in detail, for a better understanding of the magnitude and intent of the Law, what the provisions mean and how to carry them out.

On the issue of predicate offenses, the Law mentions only 14 covered crimes which, in the view of some people, were too few considering the numerous ways and means by which criminal elements can unload dirty money. The IRR has broken down the 14 covered crimes under the Law, and came up with 114 specific offenses.

The enumeration is not exclusive. Some violations of the E-Commerce Act and the Securities Regulation Code may not have been listed in the IRR, but the Council is clear that all such violations are predicate offenses. In fact, similar offenses punishable under the penal laws of other countries, are also predicate offenses in our jurisdiction.

Regarding the question of the threshold amount, while the IRR upholds the mandatory filing of covered transaction reports, in excess of P4 million, the IRR requires supervising authorities to report all, and I repeat all, suspicious transactions, regardless of the amount involved, to the Council. A transaction is suspicious when, in the words of the IRR, “There is reasonable belief that a money laundering activity . . . is about to be, is being, or has been committed.”

The rule is money laundering is money laundering, regardless of the amount involved. In other words, the P4 million threshold amount is for mandatory reporting only. In fact, the Bangko Sentral has issued a reminder to the traveling public, to declare in writing, foreign currency in excess of US$10,000 that they are bringing in or out of the country, together with information as to the source and the reason for transporting the money. This is part of our effort to close all possible loopholes that may be exploited to move dirty money.

Another contentious issue, which we hope the IRR has put to rest, is the anxiety over the need for a court order, to inquire into bank accounts of suspected money launderers. This is perceived to be one red tape, that may give a chance to the perpetrators to withdraw their money before the Council can put its hands on it.

The fact is that under the rules – and the Law itself – the Council can freeze an account without a court order, and when it does, the account is effectively immobilized for 15 days. The bank is prohibited from touching the frozen account, without prior clearance from the Council. Under the Law, no court can issue a temporary restraining order, or writ of injunction, against the freeze order, except the Court of Appeals and the Supreme Court.

The intervention of the court comes only when, first, there is a need to extend the 15-day limitation of the freeze order and, second, when the Council needs an authority to examine the deposit prior to or during the institution of criminal proceedings, involving the offense for which the deposit is related. Again, the freeze order is valid regardless of the amount of money found in the deposit account. All that the Council needs to be able to issue a freeze order, is a determination of a probable cause, that the account is in any way, related to any unlawful activity or a money laundering offense.

The IRR is very particular about customer identification and record keeping on the part of the banks and other covered institutions. The IRR goes to the extent of requiring that “No new account shall be opened and created without face to face contact.” Numbered accounts are allowed but the banks must keep the true identity of the account holders. Records must be kept for five years from the dates of the transactions.

Another issue addressed by the IRR is the effectivity of the Anti-Money Laundering Law. This is important because some critics contend that with the constitutional prohibition on the retroactive application of criminal statutes, deposit accounts opened before October 17, 2001, which is the date when the Law came into effect, can become the “sanctuary” for laundered money. The IRR says this will not happen. It says the Law will apply to all transactions on or after October 17, 2001, even if they relate to or involve deposit and investment accounts opened before that date.

The Council and the Bicameral Congressional Oversight Committee spent many days and long hours discussing and reviewing the Implementing Rules, and we are confident that we have crafted a document and a process that works.

We have since submitted the IRR to the FATF and we hope that its meeting in Australia in June this year will begin the process of removing the Philippines from the list of countries described as non-cooperative in the global campaign against money laundering. While the FATF considered our Anti-Money Laundering Law signed last year as insufficient, it acknowledged that we had made significant progress and effectively withheld the imposition of countermeasures that could have wreaked havoc on the economy. The determination of our compliance with the FATF standards of cooperation will take sometime, because they will need to find out first, if our Law and the Implementing Rules work.

This brings me to make this new appeal for the cooperation of all covered institutions, especially the banks. We all know now our role in the Law and in the Implementing Rules and Regulations. It is in our interest as a nation participating in a global campaign to make this effort work. Let me close these remarks with a word of gratitude and confident in the thought that the Bangko Sentral can count always on the understanding and cooperation of the Bankers Association of the Philippines. I have, as you all know, a close affinity with the BAP and will continue to rely on this personally in the pursuit of our common goals.

(Note: Annual Membership Meeting, Bankers Association of the Philippines, March 25, 2002, Shangri-La Hotel, Makati City)

Title: Keynote Address
Occasion: Annual Meeting, Philippine Economic Society
Speaker: Governor Rafael Buenaventura
Transcription:
Introduction

Good morning ladies and gentlemen. Allow me to welcome you all to the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas and to thank you for inviting me to keynote this timely event.

The discussions that will take place here today on the sustainability of the economic gains we have achieved so far is of particular relevance when taken in the context of Filipino culture.  We are a nation that likes celebrating our successes. I guess this is why we have fiestas, although not as much now in Metro Manila as in the provinces. It is a good custom because it is our way of thanking the Lord and our patron saints for giving us good weather and the right elements for either a good harvest or for whatever positive results we seek from our efforts and hard work. It is not only good, it is also a lot of fun.

But somewhere along the way, we yield to our huge hangovers and forget where all the merriment came from. We begin to relax and go back to a very laid back attitude until we reach a stage of inertia. We forget that we have to regain the energy and momentum to get back to work and continue to nurture the seedlings that have nicely grown from our earlier efforts until they eventually die on us and we are left with having to start again from scratch.

I am talking about a very common trait among us Filipinos. We refer to it as “ningas cogon”.

As economists, you are all aware that the Philippines lagged its Asian neighbors in growth and development. While I laud the fact that our historical growth had been steady and sustained on account of strong consumer spending, we just never seem to grow at rates that befit our potential as a nation. Our nation has a wealth of resources, the most important being our human capital resource, which is now being recognized as one of, if not, the best in many skill-based sectors globally. We have a wealth of amazing natural wonders that are far more beautiful than many of the tourist attractions I have seen in the foreign countries I have visited. Yet, somehow, and I am troubled by this, we can’t seem to overcome our inertia.

We need to overcome this cultural peculiarity because other than that, we have all that it takes to become a tiger economy.

And I have no better desire than for our nation to become a regional growth driver.

Recent performance

Last year, the Philippine economy displayed newfound strengths, enabling it to overcome the political shocks caused by the domestic transition in political leadership, the global correction in the high tech sector, and the 911 incident in the United States.

Our DGP grew at a modest pace of 3.4 percent in 2001, outperforming all the projections of independent analysts. We all know the reasons behind such growth by now.

We all had a plan for growth and we pursued it. We persisted and with much perseverance and professionalism, we prevailed.

The plan carved out by the Government is one that aims for higher growth over the medium term, one that aims for sustainable development, one that seeks excellence.

With ningas cogon in mind, we ourselves doubt if we can attain such growth objectives.

So far this year, our targets appear to be highly attainable. In fact, based on trends we are seeing, the numbers continue to surprise us on the upside. The economic team is therefore looking to review the targets.

Prudent fiscal and monetary management will still be our main guiding principles. Fiscal discipline from last year produced amazing results in bringing down our cost of borrowing and perceived risks. Hence, the team effort put forth by the economic managers in order to achieve such results deserve praise and encouragement.

At the BSP I also laud the efforts of the Monetary Board and the rest of the institution for an effective monetary program that, in working with Government, has aided in bringing inflation down to levels we have not seen in a very long time, and has restored stability in our local currency. I am also happy to note that our international reserves are at levels beyond international benchmarks.

Indeed our fundamentals are nearly back in shape. But so much work remains to be done if we are to achieve faster growth.

Targets for 2002 and beyond

Allow me to focus, however, on one task we need to do as a people. This is the inertia that has long gripped this nation. We need to get out of a box that has held our minds and psyche hostage. It is that box that prevents us from seeking our true potential as a nation.

This box, I believe, is borne out of emulating a known Filipino legend we all know as Juan Tamad. Elementary teachers talk about him in schools. He comes across as a comic relief. Local movies even glorify him because he is quite entertaining. Unknowingly however, Juan Tamad has become deeply engrained in our minds as a local legend. But a very dangerous one, because the values he stands for keep us boxed up into mediocrity.

Until now, many Filipinos like focusing on what it is that they cannot do, instead of exploring the many options available to achieve their goals. A favorite past time is self flagellation. Mistakes are glorified. Problems dominate conversations with little or no attention spent in coming up with real solutions. There is perception that problems will find their own solutions.

This reminds me of the picture of Juan Tamad lying under a tree waiting for the fruit to fall into his mouth instead of getting up, picking the fruit and putting it into his mouth. Little does he know that a passerby could come by to grab the fruit, and he would live to wonder where he might have gone wrong.

Similarly, many times as a nation, we miss opportunities because of inertia. Subconsciously, we allow more aggressive competitors to grab them. Hence, we have lagged behind the tiger economies of Asia in the last two decades.

Fellow economists, we have been given another opportunity to pursue our goals with more vigor and valor. Let us rid our minds of the legendary Juan Tamad. In the context of nation building, he is not in the least funny. He has nothing good to teach us. He is lazy, idle, unproductive, and he has no future ahead of him.

Pursuing the plan

For nearly a year now, the Government has been communicating its plan for sustainable growth and development. Materials are available for anyone who cares to know about this plan. NEDA has a book on it. We launched it in briefings and have gone around the world and the country talking about it. We also have websites that contain this plan.

I strongly believe, however, that plans need to be pursued. You see, Juan will die a very sad death from starvation, because he doesn’t dare lift a finger to reach for his goal. Along the way, he might even be cursing the Government for not doing anything about his problem. But shame on Juan for being such a loser. As far as I am concerned, he is an alien and one that should be removed from Filipino consciousness. He does not deserve the kind of attention he has been getting.

And so, I challenge you all to get up and pursue your goals. You cannot forever wait for government to give you everything. You are this country’s most valuable resource. Put yourselves to good use and become millionaires over time. Millions don’t just come from game shows. They also come from hard work.

Persistence pays

Be persistent. Don’t let anything get in your way of achieving your goals. I recall not so long ago when we had to deal with heavy speculative attack on the peso. But our goal of keeping prices stable amid a mandate of maintaining a market driven foreign exchange system proved quite a challenge. Persistence paid. We looked for ways to solve the problem. When hiking reserve requirements proved insufficient, we resorted to harsher measures such as identifying and imposing penalties on speculators. Such moves, gained for us the respect of the financial community and up until now, without having to put good money after bad, our currency remains stable.

Perseverance

Perseverance will likewise help you endure challenges. The change in political leadership last year brought with it pressures for me to step down from my current position. But I kept myself focused on my mandate and worked even harder with my constituents. What you see now are the fruits of our hard labor, but fruits that we still need to guard until they are ripe for the picking.

Professionalism

Finally, the most enduring characteristic that we need to exercise in achieving our plans and our objectives is professionalism. This encompasses many other values we need to keep in mind. First is self appreciation for the innate skills we are gifted with. Enough of self flagellation and negativism. Let us get into the habit of counting our blessings. Second is honing such skills so we can achieve efficiency and expertise in the fields we choose to enter. Excellence is the key to becoming a tiger but excellence can only be achieved through dedication, constant practice, and exposure. Third is the ability to draw respect from your constituents. But drawing respect means giving it first and complementing that with hard work.

Conclusion

If you came here this morning to listen to me give you an earload of monetary policy, you must be disappointed. As a senior member of the economic team, I feel it is my duty to set the tone of the discussions that are yet to unfold today.

Plans and goals are very important. But we sorely lack in implementation because first, we have to work toward adopting the right attitude. I hope I have given you enough this morning to guide you toward this direction. We need advocates of good values and work ethics because as far as I’m concerned, they are the key elements for sustainability.

Join me in waking up a new and exciting character for the Filipino, one that is currently sleeping soundly in our subconscious. So that perhaps, one day, our children and theirs will begin learning about the life and times of Pedro Talipag, whose last name aptly stands for talino at sipag.

Thank you very much and have a pleasant day ahead of you.

(Note: "Regaining Economic Momentum: Macro and Micro Approaches", Annual Meeting, Philippine Economic Society, March 14, 2002, Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas, Manila)

Title: Remarks
Occasion: Annual Reception for the Banking Community
Speaker: Governor Rafael Buenaventura
Transcription:
Good evening ladies and gentlemen…

Tonight, I will refrain from talking about monetary policies and banking fundamentals. You read and hear about that every single day in the papers or on radio and television.

Instead, I would like to share with you a few thoughts about my term to date as the BSP Governor, simply because it has lent much color to my life as a person and to the Bangko Sentral as an institution.

When I was offered the job as Governor of the BSP, I had reservations because I had no experience working in Government. It was a scary thought crossing the line from the private sector to the public sector. I kept thinking then that the risk was high because I was happy enough being in my comfort zone heading up one of the biggest local banks.

But my desire to serve the country prevailed. And the rest is history. Now, you’re stuck with me until 2004.

When the impeachment trial for former President Estrada happened, my job became much harder and heavier. The stability of the whole monetary system was put to extreme test. We, at the Monetary Board, became very concerned about the economic well being of the country.

But all those things came to pass swiftly. Thanks to People Power 2, a new administration was installed and the BSP survived the pressures of that historic event.

Yet, new pressures arose. Some quarters wanted me to step down, while a few analysts and speculators started hitting on the peso.

With the monetary system still on shaky ground, I listened to rational and reasonable advise from people who understood the demands of my job and my primary goal of keeping things in the monetary system in order. My resignation would have meant giving in to mob rule. It would have put the economy at risk. Moreover, it would have compromised the integrity of the Bangko Sentral, which is an institution that is, and should remain independent, and free of any political bias.

Those pressures have likewise disappeared and the peso is now as steady as one can hope for given an equally challenging global environment.

In retrospect, I could not have thought of a more colorful term for a BSP Governor. The events that took place in 2001 was a blessing in disguise because it became a defining moment for the role of the BSP Governor and the institution as a whole.

It gave all of us a unique opportunity to assert our independence, our ability to transcend politics and to rise above challenges that, at that time, seemed to many to be as disastrous as the argentine crisis.

We also feel fortunate that the new administration has recognized that independence and has since worked closely with us in achieving a common goal of promoting macroeconomic stability, long-term growth and development, and winning the war against poverty.

And so, my dear friends in the banking community, we approach 2002 with increased confidence that, with your continued support, cooperation and increased understanding, we can achieve greater goals for the Philippine economy.

I strongly believe that the Philippine banking system has come of age. It is ready to take bigger steps toward increasing its global competitiveness.  It can deepen its market reach toward small-scale borrowers with a view to mobilizing resources in areas where growth opportunities are abundant, but are currently restricted by the lack of financial liquidity.

The BSP, together with the executive and legislative branches of Government, will be steering you toward that direction with the aid of increased efficiency and supervisory powers, incentives, and legislative support.

We realize that we need to make these new directions appetizing enough for you to chase and to pour resources into them.

We are also committed to increased transparency. We realize that a successful economic program requires communicating our agenda to all our stakeholders.

In fact, for the first time in Philippine history, the BSP and the National Government has included in its agenda holding regular economic briefings for both the local and international business community and the media. Just like stockholders meetings, these briefings make us account for our performance against program targets and rate ourselves accordingly. We provide analyses and allow ourselves to be grilled by the audience. As such, we develop a two-way communication process, because we know that feedback is just as important in the proper execution or implementation of our policies.

To prove how strong an advocate I am of open communication within its legal confines, I am, perhaps, the only Central Bank Governor who can be reached wherever I am in the world, that is through texting.  It is a proven theory, as far as I am concerned that, suspicions and speculations are bred by secrecy or by providing cryptic information.

We will also focus on good corporate governance as one of the measures in improving asset quality in the banking system. We continue to seek amendments to the BSP Charter, which will enhance our supervisory powers, and raise our standards for credit risk assessment.

This will be complemented by our commitment to shepherd congress into passing the bill creating special purpose asset vehicles so that we can authorize the entry of financing firms that help in liquefying our non-performing assets.

While 2001 was a blessing in disguise, let us all hope that we have seen the end of it because, for health reasons, I can only take it and all of its pressures once in my lifetime.

Meanwhile, let us welcome 2002 with open arms, and with an air of renewed optimism knowing that we, as a nation have been able to withstand crisis with flying colors. We now look forward to the chance to prove ourselves worthy of higher recognition by the international community, because I know by heart that the Filipino mind, talent, and spirit are among the finest in the world.

Thank you very much and I wish you all the best for 2002.

Have a pleasant evening.

(Note: Annual Reception for the Banking Community, Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas, January 11, 2002, Fort San Antonio, BSP Complex, Manila)

Title: Looking Beyond R.A. 9160
Occasion: Seminar on Anti-Money Laundering Law
Speaker: Governor Rafael Buenaventura
Transcription:
I am happy to have this opportunity to keynote this seminar on anti-money laundering here at the Development Bank of the Philippines. The DBP has the unique distinction of being the bank that is probably the closest to our people in the countryside. I hope that through you and your extensive network of branches and offices, our people would develop a clear understanding of what money laundering is and what we are trying to achieve for their benefit by enacting a law to fight it. The successful implementation of the law needs the full support of all sectors of society.

Republic Act 9160, otherwise known as the Anti-Money Laundering Act of 2001, was passed by Congress and signed into law on September 29, 2001, amidst anxiety over the prospect that if it was not passed the Philippines would be subjected to sanctions by the rich countries organized under the banner of the Financial Action Task Force or FATF. The sanctions would have wrought havoc on our economy that was already suffering from the effects of a global economic slowdown triggered by the September 11 terrorist attacks in the united states.

Much has been said about the sanctions, ranging from our foreign currency transactions, like OFW remittances, being subjected to unnecessary scrutiny, to the issuance of adverse advisories by global financial centers which could have brought the flow of foreign investments into the country to a complete halt. We are off the hook at the moment but not completely. We are going to remain in the list of non-cooperative countries until we have proven to the satisfaction of the international community that R.A. 9160 works and can in fact discourage money launderers from using the Philippines as a haven where they can convert money derived from illegal activities like kidnapping, drug trafficking and smuggling into what would look like legitimate income.

This is why, soon after the enactment of the Law, I went to Hong Kong and Tokyo and Finance Secretary Camacho went to the United States to begin the campaign to persuade foreign audiences that we have a good, clear and enforceable law, and one that meets international standards. There will be continuing dialogue with foreign officials and organizations and I am confident that these would lead to the recognition and acceptance of this Law by the international community as an effective instrument in the global campaign against money laundering.

There are five provisions of R.A. 9160 that directly address concerns that the FATF expressed when we were advised about our inclusion in the list of non-cooperative countries last year.

The first is criminalization, meaning that money laundering is now a crime in the Philippines.

The second is the establishment of a system of covered transaction reporting. The Law identifies the forms of business institutions or “covered institutions” which are required to submit reports about suspicious or “covered transactions” to authorized persons.

The third is the creation of an Anti-Money Laundering Council that will administer the implementation of the Law.

The fourth is the amendment of Bank Secrecy Laws which have been blamed for making our country a potential haven for money laundering. The Law assures, however, that while the objective of the law is to ensure that the country is not used for money laundering, the policy continues to be to protect and preserve the integrity and confidentiality of bank accounts.

The fifth is the institution of procedures and arrangements that facilitate cooperation between the Philippines and foreign governments in the investigation, tracking and prosecution of money launderers.

A key provision of the Law is the creation of the Anti-Money Laundering Council which has the responsibility to implement the Law. The AMLAC, as we call it, is composed of the Governor of the Bangko Sentral as Chairman, and the Chairman of the Securities and Exchange Commission and the Insurance Commissioner as members. The composition of the AMLAC is reassuring. It is tantamount to a vote of confidence on the reputation of the constituent agencies for neutrality, independence, trustworthiness and good performance. The most essential attribute of an anti-money laundering program is its integrity and I am confident that the BSP, the SEC and the Insurance Commission will be able to deliver on that.

We have, in the meantime, completed the implementing rules and regulations and submitted them to an oversight committee composed of representatives of both houses of Congress created by the Law. The Committee is mandated to act on the draft of the implementing rules within a few days from its promulgation after which the Anti-Money Laundering Council can begin to work in earnest. This can be as early as a few days from now.

Our fervent hope is that we will have the support and cooperation of all sectors to make R.A. 9160 work to the end that we can effectively block all avenues for money laundering attempts in our country.

Apart from the need to respond to possible international countermeasures against the Philippines in September, it is in our national interest to join the community of nations in the fight against money laundering. Money laundering can undermine the integrity of financial markets, can adversely affect currencies and interest rates in view of distortions that can be caused by volatile funds, and can thereby threaten monetary stability.

Above all, money laundering poses a threat to national security as it contributes to the expansion and empowerment of criminal organizations, which can ultimately undermine political and economic stability. The September 11 terror attacks in America demonstrate how proceeds of money laundering can destabilize even the most powerful nation on earth.

Even as we speak, our Congress is looking beyond the limits of the Anti-Money Laundering Law. We are aware that similar bills have been filed in both houses of Congress following the lead and format of R.A. 9160 in order to address the growing menace of terrorism in the country. We wanted to include terrorism in addition to the 14 “covered crimes” or predicate crimes in the Anti-Money Laundering Bill but we could not do so because terrorism is not yet a crime in the Philippines. And so, in the same manner that R.A. 9160 criminalized money laundering, the effort in Congress now is to declare terrorism a crime in the statute books as well.

The Anti-Terrorism Bills would have their own anti-terrorism action council that can similarly be authorized to inquire into money deposited in banks by persons engaged in terrorism or associated with terrorist activities. The objective is to prevent or at least make it harder for terrorists to carry out their evil plans and cut off their access to financial resources.

An anti-terrorism law would be a timely and fitting partner of R.A. 9160 in thwarting threats to destabilize the country and bringing about peace and tranquility to our people.

Again, I reiterate my admiration for this seminar initiated by the Development Bank of the Philippines to enable its staff to learn more about the ramifications of the new Anti-Money Laundering Law. Let us all stand united and committed in this crusade together.

(Note: Seminar on "Anti-Money Laundering Law (R.A. 9160): Its Whats, Whys and Wherefores", Development Bank of the Philippines, December 10, 2001, DBP Building, Makati City)

Title: Working Towards a Revitalized Banking Industry
Occasion: 60th Anniversary Celebration, Bankers Institute of the Philippines, Inc. (BAIPHIL)
Speaker: Governor Rafael Buenaventura
Transcription:
Distinguished Board of Directors, officers and members of the Bankers Institute of the Philippines (BAIPHIL), ladies and gentlemen: good evening.

Being a part of the BAIPHIL family, I am truly honored and pleased to attend this momentous event. As sustaining life member, a title which was conferred to me while I was still with PCIBank, I have known of BAIPHIL’s generosity and selfless efforts to uplift the banking sector’s image. I would like to commend BAIPHIL for this and for all the other meaningful endeavors it has embarked on for the past 60 years.

Through the years, BAIPHIL has been a key force in the banking community with its wide-ranging activities that promote productivity enhancement through research, information exchange and education. In this capacity, it has remained supportive of Bangko Sentral’s call for upholding, at all times, a highly professionalized approach in the conduct of banking -- one that is anchored on excellence and safe and sound banking practices. Indeed, this makes BAIPHIL a vital partner of the Bangko Sentral in its goal of revitalizing the industry and sustaining overall soundness and stability.

This occasion is a perfect opportunity to reaffirm that partnership as we gather to assess the current situation of the banking system and find workable solutions to the challenges that confront it.

The banking system at present

The Philippine banking system today remains fundamentally sound, but there is urgent need to sustain reforms if it is to fully regain its vitality and vigor.

We all realize that the current economic environment, burdened by a global economic slowdown, is a particularly tough environment for banking. However, it would be immensely counterproductive to simply hunker down, hoping to ride out the business cycle, and avoiding real reforms that improve operating efficiency, strengthen risk management, build up the capital base, and above all, improve corporate governance. Now is the time to act decisively while we still have sufficient maneuvering room.

As of September 2001, the banking system continued to be very liquid and well capitalized. Deposits grew further by 9.2 percent. The net worth-to-risk assets ratio stood at 16.4 percent (as of end-August 2001), which is way above the indicative minimum of 10 percent. The overall asset base still managed to expand by a respectable 6.8 percent.

However, appetite for new lending has remained rather muted; loan growth has stayed essentially flat. To an important extent, weak economic conditions have dampened loan demand but a rising level of non-performing assets is also clearly a factor. Deteriorating asset quality has in turn adversely affected bank profitability.

This state of affairs cannot be sustained in the long run as, eventually, it will erode the solvency position of the banking system.

A comprehensive response

What should be done to address the problem?

First of all, there is need to stimulate economic recovery. Toward this objective, the Bangko Sentral has significantly reduced policy interest rates by 675 basis points since December 2000. This was made possible by lower inflationary pressures. We are looking forward to reducing interest rates further under the right conditions that will not compromise basic monetary stability essential to sustaining confidence.

However, easing monetary policy alone cannot be expected to do all the work. This will only create an unsustainable macroeconomic imbalance. Other elements will also need to be put in place. I am glad to note that the Government is responding comprehensively to address all relevant issues including security, trade and investment, agricultural productivity, and fiscal concerns.

Second, there is need to focus on the asset quality problem. In the last couple of years, the Bangko Sentral has been strongly encouraging banks to build up loan loss reserves in response to growing pressures on loan portfolio. This has resulted in a buildup of loss provisions to the equivalent of 43.4 percent of non-performing loans and 27.4 percent of total non-performing assets from 34.6 percent and 26.5 percent, respectively, in June 1997. This effort has strongly contributed to protecting financial system soundness and maintaining overall public confidence.

However, the accumulated stock of non-performing assets, totaling P486.2 billion as of end-September 2001, needs to be trimmed substantially from bank balance sheets so that banks can operate more normally, be less distracted, and focus again on providing fresh credits to the economy.

In this regard, the Bangko Sentral fully supports the creation of Asset Management Companies (AMCs) as vehicles for reducing the non-performing assets in bank portfolios. However, this will have to be primarily funded by the private sector and be market-driven. Neither the Bangko Sentral nor the government have plans to set up a publicly funded AMC to absorb the non-performing assets of banks. This is not a realistic option from a budgetary standpoint.

In my view, the role of the Bangko Sentral should be primarily supportive and enabling in nature. This is best achieved by formulating banking regulations that are flexible and conducive to the operation of private AMCs. The Government can also provide further incentive to private AMCs by reducing or even eliminating transactions related taxes and fees on the transfer of non-performing assets. Doing so is likely to encourage more voluntary transactions and more effective asset cleanup.

Recently, we have also initiated a review of our loss provisioning framework. This primarily aims to rationalize the requirements to achieve a better matching between minimum required provisions and underlying asset quality. As a result, we are lowering the general loan loss provision on normal, non-problematic loans from 2 percent to 1 percent to be calculated on the latest loan balance. However, we are imposing a 5 percent minimum provision on restructured loans even if these are in current status. Furthermore, we are simplifying the provisioning requirement on substandard loans to 25 percent if unsecured, and 10 percent, if secured.

With respect to ROPOA or acquired assets, we are now requiring mandatory re-appraisal of such assets every other year to effect a closer alignment between book value and economic value. This will lead to a more transparent presentation of financial statements.

This brings me to the third crucial ingredient. There is need to rapidly implement banking reforms to prevent the recurrence of future crises. The key reforms involve the promotion of better corporate governance and greater commitment to risk management.

Towards enhanced corporate governance

At this point, let me highlight the initiatives undertaken by the Bangko Sentral specifically aimed at promoting better corporate governance; encouraging greater transparency and disclosure; pursuing anti-money laundering campaign; and upholding risk management practices.

Working on the premise that a bank’s good corporate governance is the primary responsibility of the Board of Directors, we have clearly defined an expanded set of duties and responsibilities of the bank Board of Directors in line with international best practice (Circular No. 283 dated 17 May 2001).

Said duties and responsibilities accentuate the need to select highly qualified and competent directors who can collectively act as a board to guide corporate strategy, shape policy, and oversee management.

Meanwhile, the implementing circular (Circular No. 296 dated 17 September 2001) on the fit and proper rule based on Section 16 of the General Banking Law of 2000 prescribes more demanding qualification requirements for directors and officers, and expands the grounds for their disqualification. An innovative feature of this Circular is a mandatory Director Education Program.

In line with improving the quality of bank disclosures, we require banks to disclose relevant and timely information in their quarterly published statements, audited financial statements, and annual reports.

Meanwhile, relevant information on the Philippine banking system, including published statements on individual banks, are now made available to the public through the BSP website.

For the record, we are reviewing our disclosure rules to further boost transparency in line with latest international practices.

The fight against money laundering

Last 29 September 2001 the Anti-Money Laundering Act or Republic Act (RA) 9160 was enacted. The Anti-money Laundering Council has now been established to spearhead implementation.

In the months prior to this development, the BSP has been actively crusading against money laundering activities. >We rapidly set up a regulatory framework to thwart money laundering activities that may be conducted through banks and other financial institutions. In line with this, we issued pertinent regulations establishing criteria for customer identification, record-keeping, and reporting of suspicious transactions. Likewise, we have required banks to develop anti-money laundering programs.

Building on these early initiatives, I am confident we will be able to immediately implement fully the Anti-Money Laundering Law.

Strengthening risk management

In line with the focus on risk management, we have formally shifted to a risk-based capital adequacy framework with the issuance of BSP Circular No. 280 on March 29, 2001. The new framework took effect on July 1, 2001.

Given this new framework, banks are now required to have a minimum regulatory capital equivalent to at least 10 percent of their total assets weighted according to relative credit risk.

The next step is to incorporate market risk, particularly exposures to currency risk, interest rate risk and equity risk, into this framework. Draft guidelines are now being exposed to the industry for comment.

We are also working closely with the industry to develop the standards and benchmarks to help guide banks’ compliance with international risk management practices.

In cooperation with the BAP, a market risk reference manual has been developed. This will be the basis for banks to develop their own operating procedures and for the BSP to update regulations in this area. A similar project to strengthen credit risk management is under consideration.

In terms of our supervisory approach, we are emphasizing a risk-based approach that focuses on the ability of banks to detect, evaluate, and respond appropriately to their risk exposures. We want to make sure that banking institutions understand and control the types and levels of risks they assume.

We are also upgrading our off-site surveillance systems to improve our ability to detect problems early and allow more proactive intervention.

We are looking forward to the early enactment of amendments to the BSP charter to institutionalize supervisory reforms and to strengthen problem bank resolution arrangements.

Concluding remarks

This broad range of initiatives will go a long way towards reinvigorating the banking system and ensuring its long-term efficiency and viability.

To support reforms in the banking system, I strongly believe in the parallel development of the domestic capital market. This is long overdue. A more developed capital market will reduce funding demands on the banking system and facilitate better diversification of risks.

I would also like to highlight our strong support for microfinance. Through microfinance, our banks can make a more direct contribution to the fight against poverty and reach out to our countrymen who have long had minimal access to the banking system. At the same time, this is not necessarily inconsistent with sound and prudent banking principles since microfinance, when it is properly executed, is really dependent on sound credit principles for its success.

There is so much to be done. True, the challenges are formidable. But the opportunities are more exciting.

BAIPHIL, with its decades of experience, especially in training and professional education, has a very important role to play in keeping all of us abreast with all the developments taking place. More than ever, the demand for high-quality training will continue to rise. I am confident BAIPHIL will be more than ready and willing to respond to the challenge.

I wish you success in all your future endeavors.

Thank you and happy anniversary!

(Note: 60th Anniversary Celebration, Bankers Institute of the Philippines, Inc. (BAIPHIL), December 4, 2001, Manila Polo Club)

Title: Remarks
Occasion: Welcome Dinner, 11th Meeting of the EMEAP Working Group on Banking Supervision
Speaker: Governor Rafael Buenaventura
Transcription:
Mr. David Carse, Deputy Chief Executive of the Hong Kong Monetary Authority and Chairman of the Executives’ Meeting of the East Asia Pacific Central Banks, distinguished delegates, EMEAP secretariat, guests, friends and colleagues, ladies and gentlemen, good evening.

It is my distinct honor to welcome you to the 11th meeting of the EMEAP working group on banking supervision.

Inspite of the current international situation after the tragedy in the United States and amidst the challenges that surround the banking industry today, we can always find opportunities to convene in important meetings like this.

The EMEAP meetings have nurtured the regional network of information exchange and mutual trust among member central banks and supervisory authorities.

Despite the recent proliferation of international meetings and institutions, EMEAP has succeeded in maintaining its uniqueness as a meeting for central banks in the region. The ongoing work of EMEAP and the organized working groups seek to draw upon this unique position to further strengthen policy analysis and advice within the region, while continuing to develop and encourage co-operation with respect to operational and institutional central banking issues.

This meeting is a step toward strengthening the cooperative relationships among member central banks in the areas of banking and supervision via discussions of current developments in member economies’ banking sector and latest developments on the new capital accord, exchange of ideas, information and experiences and development of consensus on issues that affect each member-countries bringing them in line with international standards.

On behalf of the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas, I would like to welcome you to the 11th meeting of the EMEAP working group on banking supervision. I trust that this meeting will be a very fruitful one.

Thank you and good evening.

(Note: Welcome Dinner, 11th Meeting of the EMEAP Working Group on Banking Supervision, November 8, 2001, Shangri-la, Makati City)

Title: Remarks
Occasion: Business Meeting, Subdivision and Housing Developers Association, Inc.
Speaker: Governor Rafael Buenaventura
Transcription:
Introduction

I would like to begin by thanking the Subdivision and Housing Developers Association (SHDA) for inviting me to speak today at its business meeting  My remarks today will focus on the enduring dynamic partnership of government and the private sector, and the ways in which policymakers, and the BSP in particular, are helping provide an enabling economic environment to spur economic activity.

The government-private sector partnership

Building the path to sustained non-inflationary growth remains a shared challenge for both the government and the business sector. Amidst the challenges of the global economic environment, the crucial role of the private sector has become even greater in providing the sustaining momentum for economic growth. The housing and real estate sector, in particular, plays a major role in economic pump-priming efforts because of its impact on ancillary industries such as construction and the building materials sector. More importantly the housing sector serves not only as a valuable instrument to spur economic growth but also as a vital component of the National Government’s social policy towards the eradication of poverty. We therefore look to the efforts of private developers, such as the members of SHDA, both in providing the catalyst for more vigorous economic activity and in producing affordable housing for the masses.

The role of government

At the same time, the government is also doing its own part in fostering the development of the housing and real estate sector. For the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP), this involves providing a supportive economic environment through sound and coherent macroeconomic policies. It also means implementing policy measures that would assist in the development of the real estate industry, particularly the housing sector. I would like to discuss these briefly.

Our efforts to ensure a supportive macroeconomic environment have centered on our principal mandate of preserving price stability, while also supporting the economy’s output growth objective. Ensuring a reasonably low level of inflation helps reduce the uncertainty in economic decision-making, so that individuals and businesses have a reliable basis for long-range decisions and plans.

Thus, the monetary policy stance of the Bangko Sentral has remained focused on this objective.  Subdued inflation, spare capacity, and broad currency stability have enabled us to pursue an accommodative monetary policy–one that is supportive of an interest rate environment consistent with the BSP’s price stability objective for most of 2001. In the past 10 months or so, the BSP has reduced its policy interest rates by a total of 425 basis points. This reduction has contributed to the general decline in domestic interest rates over the same period. The average 91-day T-bill rate, for example, averaged at 9.9 percent during the last auction on 22 October 2001, a significant drop from about 15.8 percent in November 2000. Similarly, bank lending rates have also declined noticeably to a range of 13.2–14.8 percent in the last week of October 2001 from a high of 18.9–20.8 percent in November 2000.

Fostering a supportive macro environment also involves ensuring a sound banking system, one that can serve as a reliable channel for the transmission of monetary policy and an effective intermediary of funds between both savers and investors. To this end, the BSP has continuously implemented various reforms in the banking sector. This is borne out of the belief that better financial intermediation will give freer rein to vigorous business activity. We are also aware that stronger business confidence is part of the key to increased domestic demand, and the best way for the Government to boost private sector confidence is to reaffirm its proven commitment to policy reforms.

Measures implemented in the banking sector during the period 2000-2001 have been aimed at achieving the following:

  • Setting the framework for financial reforms through the passage of the General Banking Law of 2000. Among others, the GBL 2000 provides the legal basis for the shift to risk-based capital, for improving corporate governance standards in banks, for implementing consolidated supervision, for further promoting competition in the banking system.

  • Implementing risk-based capital adequacy framework with the promulgation of Circular 280 effective July 1, 2001.

  • Strengthening disclosure standards and aligning them with international norms to enhance the bank’s transparency and accountability.

  • Improving risk management practices of banks through such initiatives as joint development with the industry of a market risk reference manual. As a template for best practice exchange rate and interest rate risk management a similar project is planned to improve credit risk management. These initiatives are being reinforced by BSP’s accelerated shift to risk-based supervision.

  • Promoting and improving corporate governance in banks.  Circular 283 was issued outlining the duties and responsibilities of directors. Additionally, Circular 296 prescribes more stringent qualification standards for bank directors and senior officers. It also emphasizes director education.

  • Creating a stronger and more competitive banking system through mergers and consolidations and further liberalization of foreign bank entry.

  • Passing into law the Anti-Money Laundering Act of 2001.

Improving economic activity

The various policy initiatives of the BSP have continued to pay off in terms of a stable economic picture. During the first ten months of 2001, inflation was within the Philippine government’s target of 6-7 percent for the entire year. This is a result partly of the continued prudence of monetary policy and stable food prices. Latest readings on inflation also bolster our confidence that the inflation target of 6.0-7.0 percent for 2001 will be achieved.

Equally important, the country posted one of the strongest economic growth rates in the Asian region in 2001, with a GDP growth rate of 3.3 percent in the first half. This was due to the better-than-expected GDP growth performance in the second quarter, driven largely by consumer spending. For the year, there are also indications that the agriculture sector will achieve about 3 percent growth and that the services sector will maintain its steady growth performance. I believe that these factors point to the underlying strength of the Philippine economy, and should contribute to an encouraging growth performance in 2001.

At the same time, the housing sector continues to show its resilience in these difficult times, registering a 1.9 percent growth in Goss Value Added (GVA) partly as a result of government’s efforts in implementing shelter programs for the poor. In the months ahead, the combination of subdued inflation and improving credit conditions should provide a boost not only to the overall economy but also real estate and construction activity. These conditions will allow domestic demand to take over the reins of growth while external demand remains weak due to the global economic slowdown.

Meanwhile, the banking system continues to be sound and generally stable amid the challenging environment. This is reflected in the 11.3 percent year-on-year growth in its total resources as of July 2001. Asset quality remained manageable despite a recent uptrend in non-performing loans. As of July 2001, the NPL ratio of commercial banks reached 17.72 percent. The capital buffer of the banking system likewise remained adequate as the capital adequacy ratio reached 16.1 percent as of end-July 2001. This is well above the 10 percent minimum required by the Bangko Sentral.

BSP initiatives related to the housing sector

Apart from pursuing sound economic policies, recent BSP initiatives on the housing sector involve measures intended to support socialized and low-cost housing. These measures included the following:

BSP Circular No. 190 dated 16 February 1999 included bank lending to socialized and low-cost housing projects as a form of alternative compliance under the Agri-Agra law (P.D. No. 717). BSP Circular No. 211 (dated 29 September 1999), allowed qualified commercial, thrift and rural banks to rediscount with the BSP, the credits extended to socialized and low-cost housing. We also issued a circular-letter (dated 23 November 1999) which exempted loans to socialized and low-cost housing developers under the Government’s national shelter program from the 20 percent aggregate limit on real estate loans of banks and from the reduction in the loan value of real estate collateral (from 70 percent to 60 percent of appraised value).

More recently, loans for housing purposes were given a preferential risk weighting of 50% instead of the usual 100% for other loans in the computation of bank capital adequacy under Circular 280. Circular 304 was also issued allowing banks to issue 5-year Long-Term Negotiable Certificates of Deposits (LTNCDs). This opens up a potentially lower cost and longer-term funding source for banks that can encourage greater bank participation in housing finance.

Authorities are also aware that funding remains a major problem for the housing sector in the Philippines, and there are wider government efforts to promote the long-term viability of the country’s housing program. One solution to the funding problem is to develop a secondary market for mortgage debt. The BSP is currently part of an inter-agency effort to establish a secondary housing mortgage market in the next few years. This effort is part of the arroyo administration’s commitments to the Filipino public as outlined in the recent State-of-the-Nation Address (SONA).

Related to this, authorities are also exploring the possibility of establishing of a market for mortgage- or asset-backed securities. Right now, the BSP is holding discussions with the private sector on how best to go about with asset securitization and mitigate the associated risks to the financial system and the general public. We are also carefully reviewing the existing regulations concerning securitization. On the whole, the BSP believes that starting right and taking small steps at a time is the best way to ensure the sustainability of an asset-backed securities market. Over the long-term, these efforts will help address the problem of sustainable financing for the housing sector.

Concluding remarks

I would like to bring to a close my remarks today by stressing that the BSP’s role in ensuring broad-based, sustainable growth consists of providing a supportive economic environment for businesses to thrive. We do this through our unwavering commitment to sound macroeconomic policy and financial sector stability.

At the same time, ensuring sustainable growth in the current global economic milieu requires the active participation of the private sector in sustaining domestic demand. This includes the real estate sector’s role in providing the impetus for key sectors such as housing. To this end, I would like to see that the partnership between industry groups like SHDA and the government prospers and even exceeds our collective expectations. I would like to thank again the leadership and members of the SHDA for this opportunity to interact with you and discuss your concerns. My sincere hope is that you will continue to help the National Government in pushing forward our common agenda for a sustainable economic future.

Thank you very much.

(Note: Business Meeting, Subdivision and Housing Developers Association, Inc., November 7, 2001, Shangri-La, Makati City)

Title: The Role of Communications in Times of Economic Uncertainty
Occasion: General Membership Meeting and Formal Launching of Gold Quill Philippines Awards
Speaker: Governor Rafael Buenaventura
Transcription:
Thank you. It is a pleasure to be here this evening to talk about the role communications plays in times of economic uncertainty.

The American commentator Dale Carnegie once said “There are four ways, and only four ways, in which we have contact with the world.  We are evaluated and classified by these four contacts: What we do, how we look, what we say, and how we say it.”  From my perspective this is the essence of communication, be it individual, a company, or in our case, that of a nation.

You might find it interesting, given that central bankers have in the past sometimes been perceived to be secretive in their communication efforts, that a central banker is here to deliver a talk on communications. In reality though, banking is not solely about numbers, and I am well aware of the role that communications plays in the management of an economy.  In many ways it is the critical role as it is key to one of the most important elements of economic management – the promotion of confidence on the part of consumers and investors alike.

Tonight I would like to share some thoughts on the role communications is playing in our current efforts to strengthen the Philippine economy.  I will also outline some of the steps we have taken to ensure we are communicating effectively to our key stakeholders.  I will then spend some time talking about the implications of the September 11 terrorist attacks for our economic communications initiatives.

First of all, why do I consider the role of communications to be important?  As the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP) works with the administration of President Arroyo to maintain macroeconomic stability and to produce sustainable growth, we are also working to enhance confidence in our actions on the part of both domestic and international audiences.

We recognize that we must proactively and aggressively promote our vision for the Philippines if our key stakeholders are to fully understand and support the government’s economic reform agenda.  Such support is fundamental to restoring investor confidence in the Philippines and returning the Philippines to strong and sustainable levels of economic growth.

In the context of my talk tonight, when I refer to key stakeholders I mean the domestic and international financial community.  From the perspective of my job, few relationships are as critical to countries throughout the world as their interaction with the financial community.  Whether these interactions be with investors, portfolio managers, rating agencies, or multilateral organizations ~ each has an immediate bearing on the ability of a country's ability to achieve its objectives.

It is very important that the Philippines works hard to ensure that the international economic community understands the progress we are making and the opportunities that this represents.  We cannot hope that the market will find us.  Rather, we must go out and engage in constructive dialogue about our strengths and enlist support for our economic development objectives. It is vital that we let people know there is cause for renewed optimism in the Philippines.

Given that communications has such an important role to play, what steps have we taken to strengthen our communications capability?  I can point to a number of actions taken this year that clearly demonstrate our commitment to communicate with our key stakeholders.

First of all, a major step towards greater transparency was taken with the establishment of our Investor Relations Office (I.R.O.) to help coordinate and drive the BSP’s and the Government’s economic communications efforts.

An important role for the Investor Relations Office, which is headed by Executive Director Corazon Guidote, is to ensure that different members of the country’s economic management team are communicating with the investment community in a coordinated manner.  President Arroyo has assembled a strong economic team and the I.R.O. has helped ensure that this team is able to communicate proactively, accurately, and consistently.

We have also stepped up our efforts to communicate directly with the domestic and international business communities.  At the start of September, the I.R.O. was responsible for the successful organization of our first mid-year economic briefing.  The objective of this session was to share details of the Philippine economic plan.  This plan has been designed to support our country’s economic development objectives, and one of the main themes underpinning its framework is a recognition that a stable macroeconomic environment is a pre-requisite to stimulating investment and sustaining growth.  The economic briefing was very well received by the business community, and going forward it will be conducted every six months.

We are also making use of other forms of direct communication, including a newly launched investor relations website (www.iro.bsp.gov.ph), and a monthly newsletter entitled “Profile of the Philippine Economy”.  This newsletter provides the latest economic news, highlights key events during the month, and provides news from industry sectors such as Information and Communications Technology (I.C.T.), agriculture, and energy.  It is e-mailed to stakeholders in the Philippines and around the world. In creating these communications tools, we recognize that we must be proactive in communicating our plan, our achievements, and our challenges.  If we do not take this initiative, we become tied to the interpretations of the media and others and we know from experience that is not always accurate analysis.

International roadshows represent another element of our communications strategy.  We are taking our message to business and government centers in Europe, North America, and Asia.   Our goal here is to ensure that the opinion leaders in those locations understand that the Philippines has a vision, a plan to realize that vision, and a team to manage its implementation.  We are also able to provide real time responses to questions our audiences have about our economic performance and the environment for growth that has been created here.
