When the September 11 attacks took place, Finance Secretary Jose Isidro Camacho, Trade and Industry Secretary Manuel Roxas and I were in Tokyo talking to Japanese investors and bankers about growth prospects in the Philippines.  While clearly this proved a difficult time to engage in such an exercise, we were successful in communicating the Government’s medium–term plan for growth and in so doing we were able to lift Japanese private and public sector confidence in the Philippines' economic outlook.

In today's global marketplace, unexpected news can have an unpredictable, immediate and profound impact on the international financial community's perceptions of a country.  As we have just seen, an event of the gravity and magnitude of September 11 can quickly erode confidence in the international financial markets.  In dealing with fast moving events such as this, the challenge for all governments is to show that we are moving forward and that we are not held hostage to international terrorism.

As we work to strengthen relationships with our key stakeholders, we must continue to carefully monitor the external environment for emerging issues that could impact perceptions of our economy, proactively provide relevant information to address those issues, and ensure that our team of economic managers keep communicating on these and other matters in a consistent and timely manner. I am pleased to say that we are successfully meeting this challenge and we are already seeing the results of our commitment to renewed transparency.

After the terrorist attacks, amid concerns of international credit agencies of how the anticipated global economic slowdown would impact the Philippines, we were quick to organize a series of conference calls to those who were in positions that could influence our sovereign ratings.  Our goal was to explain our current position and why we felt that the Philippine government had the policies in place to successfully weather this storm that was affecting all nations.

Finance Secretary Camacho and I conducted calls with major ratings agencies, including Fitch, I.B.C.A., and Standard and Poors.  During these calls we informed the agencies of the steps being taken to ride out the slow down, and noted the distinctions between our nation and that of many other emerging market economies  Among other things, we pointed out that the Philippines has a strong domestic economy, and that our external debts are very manageable.  What we sought to do through clear and targeted communications was to highlight that the position of different nations vary and blanket assessments of emerging markets is not possible.

We also emphasized that our agricultural and services sectors continue to drive growth and consumer confidence, and on the back of the strong performances from both these sectors, our GDP growth has been steady at over 3% throughout 2001.

Soon after those calls, Fitch published an updated report in which it affirmed that the “stable outlook” it assigned to the Philippines was appropriate despite the deterioration of external conditions.  In that report Fitch said it based its assessment on three factors: (1) that we have a flexible exchange rate regime combined with a comfortable international liquidity position; (2) we have modest public external financing needs in 2002; and (3) there is diminished political risk underlined by a strong popular mandate for a government that has committed itself to fiscal discipline and reform.  The report also noted that “The Arroyo administration has projected the image of a government committed to fiscal discipline and reform and the fiscal accounts for 2001 have remained broadly on track.”

This is an excellent example of how, even despite the great uncertainty created by the September 11 attacks, we have been able to credibly communicate that there is a clear agenda for reform and that we are making ground in its implementation.  We believe that our commitment is being translated into financial community confidence.

As we all know, communications must be based on reality, so let me now take a moment to highlight the reality that has formed the basis of our communications efforts.

On September 29, President Arroyo signed into law an Anti-Money Laundering Bill ratified by both Chambers of Commerce.  The Bill has far-reaching implications for our ability to combat terrorism and also to facilitate our fight against corruption and our program to alleviate poverty. Soon after the Bill was passed, I flew to Hong Kong and to Tokyo to meet with officials of the Financial Action Task Force (F.A.T.F.).  In those meetings, I communicated that this new bill was part of our broad-based commitment to the global anti-terrorism campaign.  The F.A.T.F. officials agreed that the Bill signaled to the world the strong commitment of our nation to this important fight, and that we were now able to join the community of nations promoting international-standard banking practices.

In terms of monetary policy, the BSP continues to work diligently to strengthen the monetary system, and I am pleased to say we are having some success.  The average inflation rate for the first eight months of the year now stands at 6.6%, well within our target of 6-7% for 2001.  The continued softening of food prices and relative calm in the foreign exchange market are expected to provide a stabilizing influence on the general price level in the coming months.

At the same time, the peso has stabilized, trading around the 51 to the U.S. dollar mark since August.  We have effectively stamped out speculative activity and the current reserve position combined with the weaker outlook of the U.S. dollar should continue to be supportive of current levels.

Fiscal discipline and deficit reduction are also key elements of the plan, and during the course of the year we have been able to report important gains on this front.  A combination of revenue enhancement measures and disciplined expenditure management program has positioned the Government to meet its full-year deficit management goal of P145 billion for 2001.

We are also seeing better than expected investment numbers with the Board of Investments already registering P82.7 billion in investment projects, significantly above its target of P50 billion for the year.

These are just a few examples of the positive progress that we have been able to communicate in a targeted and co-coordinated manner.  We are helped by a good story that is creating a perception around the world that the Philippines is committed to economic reform in a systematic and disciplined manner.

This is also helping to differentiate us from other emerging markets and it is helping to create an understanding that our prospects are much better than they have been in many years.

To conclude, let me reiterate my belief that the perceptions held by domestic and international audiences of the state of our economy are too important to be left unmanaged.  Given this importance, we recognize that communications is a crucial part of the job of everyone charged with management of the economy.

I hope that tonight, I have been able to assure you that the government and the BSP have clear economic communications objectives, and that we are actively using a range of communications tools to ensure that those objectives are supporting achievement of our larger overall economic goals.

In assessing our performance on the communications front, I believe that we are making good progress and that we are headed in the right direction.  The September 11 attacks have cast uncertainty and anxiety over the world economy.  However we do have a plan to overcome our challenges and this plan is proving effective.

We are making use of all of the communications tools at our disposal – including roadshows, conference calls, and the media. As some of you know, I am even using my mobile phone to send text messages to members of the press and others who have questions about the state of our economy.

Through our commitment to communicating our vision and our achievements we are helping ensure that perceptions keep up with reality.  Yes the global climate is an uncertain one, however by continuing to take the measures I have outlined this evening, I am certain we will be successful in restoring investor confidence in the Philippines.

Those of you in marketing know that in down markets you promote to pick up market share. I would like to believe that we too are picking up market share as we communicate the positive story of the Philippine economy.  I hope we can enlist all of you in that process.

Thank you very much.

Title: Effects of the Anti-Money Laundering Law on the Banking And Financial System
Occasion: Public Forum on the "Anti-Money Laundering Law (R.A. 9160) Its Whys, Wherefores and Hows"
Speaker: Governor Rafael Buenaventura
Transcription:
Atty. Eliseo P. Ocampo, the officers of the Institute of Continuing Legal Studies and Education, ladies and gentlemen:

I find it most welcome to speak in this forum, for which I am thankful to the Institute, as it provides my first opportunity to express in public my thanks to all those – the bankers, the business leaders, the civil societies, the academe, the professional organizations, and to our concerned citizenry – who helped the Government pass the Anti-Money Laundering Law.

Of course, it was also a masterful accomplishment on the part of our lawmakers, both from the majority and minority parties, who linked together in partnership, to enact a law essential to both our domestic and international interests  They also deserve our wholehearted congratulations.

While the law was passed within a limited time, the debates thereon were most intensive and I, together with Secretary Lito Camacho who, by the way, also worked very hard, were personal witnesses to those historic events. Deliberations extended until early morning hours, with the energy and spirit of all the participants unwaning. Discussions of the law proceeded vigorously almost line by line, characterized by the constant balancing between the interest of the individual and of the state, and between the need to protect the innocent, and to impose the deserved punishment on the guilty. In the end, I am proud to say that this law was passed to serve the ends of justice, in full consideration of the Bill of Rights, and in faithful adherence to our constitutional processes. This is a victory for our democratic system, and the Filipino people deserve credit for this achievement.

But an equally, if not more difficult task, lies ahead. We now have to implement the law. And this should be done in earnest commitment. As you know, the Governor of the Bangko Sentral was designated as the Chairman of the Anti-Money Laundering Council or the AMLAC. The members would be the SEC Chairperson and the Insurance Commissioner. How that came about is another story by itself. What I may just state, with modesty, since my own position is involved, is that said composition of the AMLAC is tantamount to a vote of confidence on the neutrality, independence, trustworthiness and good performance of these constituent agencies. The most essential element of an Anti-Money Laundering program is its integrity. As I understand it, congress believed that the Bangko Sentral, the SEC and the Insurance Commission can deliver that attribute of integrity. We therefore feel honored by that recognition. For that, I think we also deserve some congratulations.

We have now begun our efforts to elevate our status as a cooperative country in the fight against money laundering. Last week, I was in Hong Kong and Tokyo and apprised several government representatives there of the features of the law. Secretary Camacho went to the United States to do the same. What we are telling them is that Republic Act 9160 is a good, clear and enforceable law, and one that is aligned with international standards. There will still be continuing dialogues with foreign officials and organizations and we are confident that these would lead to the recognition and acceptance of our legislation by the international community as an effective instrument in the global campaign against money laundering.

Much have already been written about the deleterious effects of money laundering on any country’s economic system. Money laundering can undermine the integrity of financial markets, can adversely affect currencies and interest rates in view of distortions that can be caused by highly volatile funds, and can thereby threaten monetary stability.

In the immediate term, however, the Philippines has been listed as a non-cooperative country resulting in these downsides.

- there have been inconvenience and opportunity losses caused to inward remittances payable to the beneficiaries of our OFWs

- similar difficulties are being experienced in other money transfers

- financial intermediation with foreign institutions entails higher costs and detailed scrutiny; and

- interest by foreign investors in the Philippines is dampened.

The international countermeasures against the Philippines could have been heightened were it not for the timely passage of the law. However, let us remind ourselves that the Philippines remains in the non-cooperative category. And as I mentioned, there is still the challenge of convincing the international community that our law is a good law and meets all established standards in the fight against money laundering. Hopefully, the Philippines will eventually be freed from the adverse measures which have impacted on our economy. Our economy can now be rebuilt without the burdensome effects of the international countermeasures.

We are thus moving quickly to put the law in operation. It will become effective on October 17 and we have thirty days from that day to come out with the implementing rules or the IRR’s. Thereafter, the IRR’s will be approved by the Congressional Oversight Committee. However, there are provisions in the law which do not need an IRR – like the prohibition on fictitious accounts and the numbered accounts for peso and foreign currency checking accounts. These accounts can be attractive conduits for money laundering and we want to immediately immobilize such instruments. This would explain why the Bangko Sentral already issued a Circular to make sure that this prohibition is observed when the law becomes effective.

However, may I quickly add, consistent with my previous statements, that the Anti-Money Laundering Law should not cause any fear or apprehension on the part of the ordinary depositor and legitimate businessmen. Based on statistics, the number of deposit accounts above the threshold amount of four million pesos might not even reach three percent of the total number of depositors in the Philippines. More importantly, to provide comfort and assurance, the law starts with the declaration affirming “the policy of the state to protect and preserve the integrity and confidentiality of bank accounts”. Our bank deposit secrecy laws continue to exist and inquiries or disclosure can be done only under the same instances provided for under Republic Act 1405 and under the Anti-Money Laundering Law, as an additional exception, only where these are used for suspicious or questionable transactions. So only the criminals or those who allow criminals to use their deposit accounts should worry about this law.

This means, however, that banks and all reporting institutions should adopt vigorous programs for the detection of questionable transactions since any failure to report is subject to criminal sanctions. They would have to strengthen their know-your-client policies, oversee its diligent implementation, and upgrade the expertise of their front-line officers.

There should now be more effective risk management for banks to ensure, for their own protection, that they abide with regulations and best practices against money laundering. Indeed it would be better if banks would establish a compliance culture across their organization. It should be everybody’s responsibility, from the top to the lower levels, to see to it that the bank is not exposed to laundering or fraudulent risks that may threaten the bank.

Apart from the benefit of compliance, these measures are beneficial to the banks themselves. As we know, banks are normally targeted for money laundering activities because of their capability to handle huge cashless transactions, and to transmit funds efficiently, and because of their natural trustworthiness in keeping confidential their accounts.

However, as we also very well know, being identified with money launderers can weaken the reputation and standing of any banking institution. This was summed up in the statement of the Bankers Association of the Philippines during the hearings in the House of Representatives which in effect said that our banks would rather deal with clean money, rather than dirty money, for the latter can only prejudice, and never contribute, to the stability of the Philippine banking system.

Compliance with the Anti-Money Laundering Law means good governance, for the most important component of such compliance is the commitment by top management and its Board of Directors to contribute to the cleansing of the system. It is really a policy choice between good corporate citizenship and reputational risks, between compliance and sanctions, between stability and uncertainty. And really, there is only one good answer – it should be in favor of the bank’s good name, good customer relationships, good accounts, and good profits.

Industry-wide, it should also be good competition – for the Anti-Money Laundering Law now establishes a level paying field in the marketing for business transactions. No bank can now transact a questionable transaction under the assurance of secrecy because the law exempts no banking institution from the reporting requirement. All banks are now governed by the same playing rules – know your customer, keep full identification, preserve all records, and report suspicious transactions. And under our watch in the AMLAC, we will see to it that we will have an even, diligent, and firm but fair, implementation of these requirements.

In conclusion, Republic Act 9160 has laid down the foundation for a workable and strong anti-money laundering program. It provides justification for the country to be liberated from the pain and difficulties of sanctions addressed to non-cooperative countries. It can serve to deter crimes and the use of the Philippines as a site to launder dirty money. It can lead to good governance within banks and financial institutions, to their adoption of effective risk management systems, and to healthy competition among themselves.

But the challenge goes on. In much the same way that money launderers would continue to explore new techniques to commit and cover their crimes, governments should ever be vigilant, dynamic and resourceful to thwart and overcome them. The campaign against money laundering should be sustained and evolutionary. We have seen from recent tragic events how laundered money could be used, for example, to commit acts of terrorism. In the congressional deliberations on Republic Act 9160, there were serious proposals to include terrorism among the predicate offenses. However, this was not possible since terrorism does not exist yet as a crime in our statute books. The best that can be done was to include individual offenses which are terrorism-related, like robbery, piracy, hijacking and kidnapping. Hopefully, congress would later on criminalize terrorism and include it as a predicate offense of money laundering.

The fight against money laundering is not the responsibility of the Government alone but is the concern of all sectors. We should not tolerate the spoils of crimes to flow in the midst of society, to undermine our economy, threaten our financial system, corrupt our people and our morals.

As we therefore go on with the implementation of the law, and to seek improvements as may be called for along the way, I know that we will continue to have your unwavering support, and that all of us will stand united and committed in this crusade together.

Title: Keynote Address
Occasion: 5th BSP-DECS NCR Oratorical Contest, 12th National Statistics Month
Speaker: Governor Rafael Buenaventura
Transcription:
Members of the Monetary Board, Undersecretary Jaime D. Jacob, officers of the Bangko Sentral and the Department of Education, Culture and Sports, our contestants and their teachers, parents, and fellow students, distinguished guests, fellow workers in government, ladies and gentlemen, good afternoon:

Let me first welcome everyone here to the 5th Oratorical Contest sponsored by the BSP and the DECS National Capital Region (NCR) in celebration of National Statistics Month. This contest first began in 1996 as the contribution of Bangko Sentral and the DECS-NCR to the activities during National Statistics Month. Our contest themes have touched on a varied range of subjects over the years. In the first year, for example, our contestants spoke about the role of statistics in promoting excellence in education. They also talked about the role of statistics in society in the time of the Philippine centennial in 1998. More recently, we focused on highlighting the important role of women in our society through the use of statistics, with an eye to improving policies on gender-related issues towards the ultimate goal of sustainable and balanced economic development. This was the contest theme for the first national level competition held at the BSP last year. The choice of these particular themes has given us the privilege of watching and hearing our young people put forth their stimulating ideas on various issues relating to the role of statistics in our society. It has also contributed to the nationwide awareness and appreciation, particularly among young students, of the importance and value of statistics.

Let me also welcome our 14 contestants representing the 14 city school divisions of Metro Manila. I am glad to see that this contest has become a popular venue for talented young orators from our secondary schools, so much so that we expanded it to the national level for the first time last year, and every 5 years thereafter.

Talent in our youth is a blessing and a joy to behold, and should be encouraged always. This is one of the reasons why the BSP, together with DECS-NCR, will be publishing in book form a compendium of the speeches of contestants in our oratorical contest. Our aim is to come out with a volume that captures not only the “spirit” and attitudes of today’s Filipino youth, but also preserves, for future generations, their thought-provoking ideas and opinion on the subject of statistics.

This contest also marks the formal closing of this year’s celebration of national statistics month (NSM). The NSM has increasingly become a showcase of unity and cooperation among the various members of the Philippine Statistical System (PSS) and an important forum for tackling the different issues and developments affecting the statistical system. It has also helped us gain the cooperation and support of the Filipino public in upgrading the quality and standard of statistics in the country. Today’s display of vibrant young talent will serve as both a highlight and a fitting conclusion to the various activities held by the members of the PSS for the whole month of October. I understand that we will be holding the closing ceremony for National Statistics Month later this afternoon, also here at the BSP. I hope that our guests here at this contest will be able to join us later for the closing.

Our contest theme this year is “The role of statistics in a knowledge- based economy”, and the subject is a timely one. Our young people today are growing up in a world much different from the generation we, their parents and teachers, were born in. It is a world where the competitiveness and prosperity of nations depend increasingly on the application of knowledge and the skillful application of information. It is a knowledge-based economy that places greater value not on the things that one owns, but on the things that one can do. Information has become the single currency of our knowledge-based future, and we create it by diligently collecting and organizing for analysis all kinds of useful data about ourselves, our society, and our global community.

Why do we need so much information? Well, for policymakers, for example, economic and financial assessment and decision-making are both information-intensive activities. Our economic policies and plans stand and fall on the basis of statistical quality and reliability of information that support them. It is important, therefore, that our system of accumulated information be accurate, timely, well-organized and comprehensive, enabling us to make well-informed decisions and formulate better economic policies. Equally important, as economists have told us, information and knowledge are a key source of economic progress and therefore a critical ingredient for economic development. These are invaluable resources in the face of changing circumstances such as the current global downturn we are experiencing at the moment.

Our system of statistical information is thus the backbone of our knowledge network, and venues such as this one will go a long way toward instilling in our young people the primary value of statistics in our knowledge-based economy. It is thus our responsibility to teach our young to recognize the immense value of having the right information at their fingertips.

But we must not forget also that, as Albert Einstein once said, “Imagination is more important than knowledge. ” The things you know are not quite as important as how these are applied to improve current conditions. To this end, we must also teach our young students the various ways of harnessing knowledge and information to produce the greatest benefit to our country. I think of the amount of creative talent on display today through our young contestants, who have benefited from the guidance and counsel of their teachers and parents and—I am sure—the support of their fellow students. I think I speak for both the BSP and the DECS-NCR when I say that we are more than happy to provide a venue for young students to express themselves, and learn about the various aspects of the use of statistics in our knowledge-based society. We hope to have many more opportunities such as this one in the future.

Maraming salamat po.

(Note: 5th BSP-DECS NCR Oratorical Contest, 12th National Statistics Month, 26 October 2001, Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas)

Title: Republic Act 9160 in Perspective
Occasion: Roundtable on Anti-Money Laundering Law (AGILE)
Speaker: Governor Rafael Buenaventura
Transcription:
Mr. Pulley, Mr. Hecker, Miss Buckles, Mr. Ryan, fellow anti-money laundering advocates, ladies and gentlemen:

I am most happy to welcome you to this forum, which is unlike any other that I have addressed in the last few weeks.  I come, if you will permit me, with a big sigh of relief that finally we have a Philippine Anti-Money Laundering Law, Republic Act 9160.

I am sure that even our foreign guests know the effort that went into the passage of this law.  Considering the proximity of the September 30, 2001 deadline imposed by the Financial Action Task Force, both Houses of Congress went into marathon hearings in their few remaining session days in September, following a two-week recess, to reconcile more than a dozen bills that had been filed separately.  Finally, on Friday, September 28, their Bicameral Committee met here in this building and, together with members of our Inter-Agency Task Force, we worked until early morning of the following day, Saturday, to come up with the bill that President Gloria Macapagal Arroyo signed into law on the same day to beat the FATF deadline by one day.

I hasten to add that while it was important to meet the September 30 deadline to avoid the sanctions threatened by the FATF, the proponents of this law worked for its enactment mainly because it was in the interest of our country to do so.  We live in a global community and the Philippines must be perceived as cooperative in the global campaign against money laundering.  We are only too aware of the corrosive effects of money laundering on financial systems.  We cannot permit our financial institutions to be used to launder proceeds from criminal activities.

We appreciate the interest of our foreign guests in seeking an update on the passage of this anti-money laundering legislation.  What I will try to do is to give you an overview of this new law especially as it addresses the concerns of the FATF and how it works in the context of our desire to protect the integrity of our financial system.

I am happy to note that the department of the treasury of the United States has issued a statement welcoming the passage of the new law.  The FATF in Paris is also reported in the papers to have announced the suspension of countermeasures until presumably they are able to review the law during their meeting in February next year. It was the U.S. Treasury Department that issued an advisory in July last year telling banks in the U.S. that, in view of the supposed lack of counter-money laundering controls in the Philippines, to give, and I quote, “enhanced scrutiny”, unquote to all transactions involving persons and institutions in our country. Accordingly, the FATF tagged us as one of 15 non-cooperative countries in the fight against money laundering.

The FATF raised principally five issues in the case of the Philippines. One, money laundering was not a crime. Two, banking laws were excessively secretive. Three, there was no suspicious transactions reporting program. Four, there was no implementing agency. And five, there was no formal arrangement that allowed cooperation with other countries to prevent money laundering.

All these concerns are covered in Republic Act 9160 and it is our hope that this law and our compliance with the deadline will lead to the removal of the Philippines from the FATF blacklist.

The law declares as a statement of policy the preservation of the integrity and confidentiality of bank accounts and the determination to ensure that the Philippines shall not be used as a money-laundering site for the proceeds of any unlawful activity. The law also commits the country to extend cooperation in transnational investigations and prosecution of persons involved in money laundering anywhere in the world.

The law covers 14 unlawful activities, or predicate crimes as the lawyers call them, and these include kidnapping for ransom, drug trafficking, graft and corruption, smuggling, hijacking and even local gambling games like jueteng and masiao. The institutions covered where money laundering can conceivably occur include not only banks and other institutions regulated by the Bangko Sentral but also insurance companies and investment houses. This is why the implementing agency, the Anti-Money Laundering Council, will be composed of the Governor of the Bangko Sentral as Chairman, the Commissioner of the Insurance Commission and the Chairman of the Securities and Exchange Commission. The Council has the power to freeze accounts, to institute forfeiture proceedings, to file criminal complaints and to cooperate with other countries in going after money launderers.

The benchmark figure for suspicious transactions is P4 million or its equivalent in foreign currencies.

The way the law describes the process, action begins when a covered institution like a bank reports a covered transaction to the Anti-Money Laundering Council. A covered transaction can be a deposit or withdrawal that, in the view of an authorized officer in the bank, may be related to an unlawful activity. When the council determines that a probable cause exists, it orders the bank to freeze the account. The depositor is given time to question the freeze order. If the explanation is satisfactory, the freeze order is dissolved. Otherwise, this is a signal for the Council to file a complaint with the Department of Justice or the Ombudsman. Money laundering cases are tried either at the Regional Trial Court or the Sandiganbayan.

Under the law, a court order is required when the Council wants to scrutinize the account or to extend the freeze period. Critics claim that the resort to a court order can be an obstacle to the speedy response to a money laundering case. What the critics overlook is that even if the case is delayed as a result, the depositor cannot move his money because the account is frozen. Note also that no court can issue a temporary restraining order in a money laundering case except the court of appeals and the Supreme Court. The Bank Secrecy Law is effectively amended because the new law permits the courts to order the examination of an account on the say so of the Anti-Money Laundering Council.

Moreover, as previously mentioned, banks are now permitted to report suspicious deposit transactions, whether in pesos or foreign currency, without violating the bank deposit secrecy laws. This is a major improvement in having access to questionable deposit movements.

Having said that, the confidentiality of deposits continues to be protected under the new law. Following our example, officers of the bank and everybody involved in reporting the questioned transaction are strictly prohibited from disclosing this information to any person. Violators, including the media if the information is published, can be held criminally liable.

Another provision that enhances the confidentiality of deposits is that which allows numbered accounts for both peso and dollar non-checking depositors provided that the banks keep a record of the true identity of the depositors. This protects peso accounts particularly because, heretofore, only dollar accounts are allowed to use numbers. The law, meanwhile, prohibits the use of anonymous accounts or accounts under fictitious names, a prohibition that, heretofore, exists only in administrative circulars of the BSP.

The penalties for violation of the law are stiff. There are fines and prison terms for money launderers and even those who merely facilitate the offense. A person or an institution which fails to report a suspicious transaction can also be penalized. There is a penalty as well for malicious reporting, meaning a person who knowingly reports false information. This provision is there to prevent abuse or harassment.

I have tried to highlight the salient provisions of the law to give our guests an indication of the extent of our commitment to stop money laundering from taking root in our country. This early there are critics who say that this law will not pass the standards of the FATF. One newspaper said the other day we Filipinos seem to be “gluttons for punishment.” To them we say, like in most anything new we have to start somewhere and we honestly feel that R.A. 9160 is a good beginning. The Anti-Money Laundering Council is mandated to submit the implementing rules and regulations to a Congressional Oversight Committee in 30 days from the effectivity of the law. We will do that.

We have now established the legal foundation for criminalizing money laundering. The next thing to do is to make it work. I will be happy to answer your questions.

 

(Note: Roundtable on Anti-Money Laundering Law, Accelerating Growth Investment and Liberalization with Equity (AGILE), 5 October 2001, Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas)

Title: Microfinance: An Opportunity for the Banking System
Occasion: BMAP Executive Forum on Microfinance, Bank Marketing Association of the Philippines
Speaker: Governor Rafael Buenaventura
Transcription:
It is a great pleasure for me to deliver the keynote address at this executive forum on microfinance. I sincerely appreciate the initiative of the BMAP and the various banking industry associations in putting together this forum.

Background and Context

President Gloria Macapagal-Arroyo, in her State of the Nation Address last July 23, 2001, reiterated her “Vision of winning the war against poverty within the decade.” With poverty incidence at 40 percent of the population, poverty is clearly one of the most vexing challenges that gnaws at the very foundation of Philippine society, threatening its stability.

We cannot be indifferent. Fortunately, through microfinance, we, the banking community, have an opportunity to make a direct, immediate, and meaningful contribution to the war on poverty without necessarily compromising on our prudential responsibilities. As President Arroyo declared, “… we will make microfinance a cornerstone in our fight against poverty.”

For the banking community, microfinance is not necessarily a new undertaking but the fresh challenge is to broaden and deepen our commitment.  Today, many of our rural banks and thrift banks are already involved in microfinance in one form or another.

And as early as 1994, while I was its President, the BAP formally launched its initiative called Banking with the Informal Sector as part of the broader social pact on credit. That initiative, acknowledges the limitations of commercial banks in reaching the informal sector and seeks to create mechanisms that bridge banks, NGOs and cooperatives in credit delivery. It focused on credit in the form of direct loans to NGOs through the BAP credit guaranty corporation, on training geared to combining effective credit delivery with sound credit principles, and on practical research.

In the last couple of years, microfinance has made much progress towards the mainstream. Thanks largely to the continuing efforts of the pioneer NGOs. Their methods and practices have been refined further to move the delivery of credit to the poor farther away from the pitiless free-for-all dominated by loan sharks and usurers and towards a paradigm of sustainable free enterprise with a social conscience.

The banking community, with its greater access to resources and its broader network, is in a position to magnify the impact of microfinance. Banks can better serve the poor by combining the effective credit delivery systems of microfinance pioneers with their existing fund and risk management skills.

We don’t need to re-invent the wheel, but we need to learn from the experience of microfinance institutions by offering the poor financial products suited to their needs. Average loan size is small, around P2,000 to P5,000, just enough to provide working capital. Loan terms are short and payment terms depend on cash flow ranging from daily, weekly, or semi-monthly. Interest rates are high enough to cover higher transaction costs, overhead, provisions, as well as profit. Physical collateral is substituted with social collateral that relies on borrower’s reputation. Loan disbursement is quick, and documentary requirements are kept simple.

Using this formula, microfinance institutions have been able to lend successfully to the poor, earning reasonable returns and keeping non-performing loans extremely low. Certainly, much lower than current NPL averages across the whole banking industry. No less important, they are able to mobilize significant amounts of savings from the same base, laying the basis for self-sufficiency.

Bangko Sentral Initiatives

The Bangko Sentral is keen to promote microfinance. To back up our words, we have undertaken major regulatory initiatives.

On 30 January 2001, we issued Circular No. 272, setting the guidelines on microfinancing loans and implementing the provisions found in Sections 40, 43 and 44 of the General Banking Law of 2000. In issuing the Circular, we recognized the peculiar characteristics of microfinancing, particularly its focus on cash flow-based lending that is not normally covered by traditional collateral.

Circular 272 defines microfinancing loans as small loans granted to the basic sectors, on the basis of borrower’s cash flow and other loans granted to the poor and low-income households for their microenterprises and small businesses. These loans are typically unsecured but may also be secured in some cases. The maximum principal amount of microfinance loans shall not exceed P150,000 which is equivalent to the maximum capitalization of a microenterprise as defined in law.

The schedule of loan amortization shall take into consideration the projected cash flow of the borrowers. Microfinance loans may be amortized daily, weekly, semi-bimonthly or on a monthly basis depending on the cash flow condition of the borrowers. Interest on microfinancing loans shall be reasonable but shall not be lower than the prevailing market rates to enable the lending institution to recover its financial and operational costs. As an incentive, microfinance loans shall be considered compliance with SME mandatory credit requirements.

To ensure the safety of lending financial institutions, we have outlined several conditions for compliance. These include, among others, the setting up by lending banks of : (1) well-defined standards, credit policies and procedures for microfinance loans; (2) a loan portfolio and other risk asset review system; and (3) specific measures to ensure collections.

Another regulatory initiative was the issuance of Circular No. 273 on 27 February 2001. This exempts, on a very selective basis, microfinance-oriented banks from the current General Moratorium on the Establishment of New Banks. In order to ensure that new applicants are legitimate and capable microfinance banks, we have set the following criteria in addition to the standard bank licensing requirements:

  • The microfinance-oriented bank to be established shall either be a thrift bank or a rural bank.

  • The capital of the microfinance-oriented bank to be established should be generated from private resources and multilateral entities, not from Government, to promote appropriate conditions for sound internal governance.

  • In the case of a rural bank, the minimum paid-in capital shall be P5 million or the applicable existing capitalization requirement for a new rural bank, whichever is higher. The capitalization requirement under existing regulations shall apply to thrift banks.

  • At least 50 percent of the bank’s gross loan portfolio at all times shall consist of microfinance loans as defined under existing BSP regulations.

  • The organizers must have the capacity to engage in microfinancing, as evidenced by experience and track record.

  • The proposed bank must have as a minimum, an adequate information system that allows daily monitoring of loans releases, collection and arrearages, and any restructuring or refinancing.

To date we have already approved two new microfinance banks that applied for a thrift banking license: Opportunity Microfinance Bank, organized by NGOs, with head office in Antipolo, Rizal, and with an initial paid-up capital of P58.1 million. Another is Micro Enterprise Bank, organized by Planters Development Bank, the International Finance Corporation, and European NGOs. It will be based in Davao City and its initial paid-up capital is P60 million.

To promote the adoption of appropriate microfinance technologies by our existing rural banks, we have also issued Circular 282 dated April 19, 2001, establishing a special rediscounting facility for the purpose of providing liquidity assistance to rural banks that embrace legitimate microfinance programs.

Next Steps

Where do we go from here? We would like to expand the modalities for more flexible bank participation in microfinance. We would also like to accelerate the propagation of proven microfinance technologies as broadly as possible to bring, as a long-term goal, microfinance to every province in our country.

In terms of new modalities, we are considering new guidelines that will allow existing banks, in addition to the option of setting up a thrift bank or rural bank microfinance- oriented subsidiary, to set up new branches or convert existing branches into dedicated microfinance units.

We are also taking steps towards organizing a microfinance foundation. We envision this foundation as a vehicle for mobilizing and administering possible international and local donor funds as well as our own Bangko Sentral funds to be earmarked primarily for microfinance training and research. As a logical starting point, the Foundation can provide financial support to established and credible microfinance training organizations that are engaged in programs to train trainors as well as microfinance replicators. This aims to address the more critical constraint to microfinance propagation, access to technology and know-how, rather than availability of loanable funds.

Concluding Remarks

Let me close my remarks today re-affirming the strong commitment of the Bangko Sentral to the promotion of microfinance as a way for our banking system to provide a more meaningful contribution to poverty alleviation and economic development. However, microfinance must never backslide into the discredited approaches of directed credit and interest subsidy. Rather, it must continue to build its success by providing financial services that the poor want and are willing to pay for at market terms, by maintaining high standards of credit discipline, and by continually educating the public on responsible borrowing.

Thank you and good day.

 

(Note:

BMAP Executive Forum on Micro Finance, Bank Marketing Association of the Philippines, 10 September 2001, RCBC Tower, Makati City)

Title: The Philippine Economy: Monetary, External and
Occasion: Mid-Year Economic Briefing
Speaker: Governor Rafael Buenaventura
Transcription:
Ladies and gentlemen, it is with great pleasure that I address this investor briefing on the prospects and potentials of the Philippine economy. I am pleased to have the opportunity to be able to talk on the recent developments in the monetary, external and banking fronts, as well as the policy directions of the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP).

Monetary Developments and Policy Stance

The BSP’s monetary policy stance continues to be geared toward achieving price stability consistent with sustainable and balanced economic growth.

Inflation during the first seven months of 2001 is within the Government’s target of 6-7 percent for the whole year. The continued prudence of monetary policy and ample food supply have helped keep prices stable.

Benign inflation, the presence of spare capacity, and broad exchange rate stability justified monetary easing during the first half of the year. The reduction in the BSP’s policy rates have contributed to the general decline in domestic interest rates in recent months. The benchmark 91-day T-bill rate averaged 9.5 in August 2001, a significant drop from the levels posted in November-December 2000. Bank lending rates have also declined appreciably in August 2001 relative to their levels in December 2000.

Of late, the BSP has adopted a more cautious stance in further reducing its policy interest rates because of some upside risks to inflation arising from the pass-through effects of the peso depreciation. Since 18 May 2001, the BSP has maintained its policy rates, with the overnight borrowing (RRP) and lending (RP) rates remaining at 9.0 percent and 11.25 percent, respectively. In July and August this year, the BSP also increased the liquidity reserves for commercial banks and non-banks with quasi-banking functions in order to further moderate liquidity and ease pressure on the peso. Looking ahead, the better-than-expected economic performance in the first half of the year should provide the BSP with greater flexibility in conducting monetary policy. This would of course be dependent primarily on the outlook for inflation in 2002.

External Sector Developments

External Payments

The external sector was the main driver of the Philippine economy in 2000. The current account yielded a surplus of over US$9.0 billion owing to the robust growth of exports. However, for 2001, exports are expected to be generally flat at best owing to the projected decline in the sales of major exports, particularly electronics, which account for nearly 60 percent of the country’s total exports. Imports, on the other hand, are projected to increase by 3 percent this year as domestic producers replenish inventories after three successive years of low imports.

For the first six months of 2001, exports of goods declined by 9.3 percent following the slowdown in the U.S. and Japanese economies, as well as the downturn in the electronics technology cycle. The performance of the domestic export industry mirrors that of most of the countries in the region, with Indonesia, Malaysia and Thailand likewise experiencing decelerating export growth.[1]

Meanwhile, imports have started to pick up, with monthly import levels since April until June this year recording year-on-year increases. Specifically, raw materials and intermediate goods imports have been on the rise, indicating that production activity has started to firm up.

Gross International Reserves

Our gross international reserves remained at a comfortable level of $14.3 billion as of end-July 2001, equivalent to 4.3 months worth of imports of goods and payments of services. This level of reserves could cover more than twice the amount of the country’s short-term foreign liabilities based on original maturity and 131 percent of short-term obligations based on residual maturity.

External Debt

Meanwhile, the country’s stock of external debt amounted to US$49.95 billion as of end-March 2001, lower by 4.1 percent from the level recorded at the end of December 2000. More importantly, medium and long-term liabilities comprise the bulk of the country’s external debt, accounting for close to 90 percent of the total.

Exchange Rate Developments

After reaching a low average of P55.013/US$1 on 19 January 2001, the peso showed signs of strengthening following the resolution of the political crisis toward the end of January. However, starting mid-March until the first week of August, the peso was again under pressure due to bearish market sentiment brought about by external and domestic factors, including the volatility in most regional currencies; concerns over the weak U.S. and Japanese economies; and the Abu Sayyaf problem in the south.

To address the foreign exchange situation, the BSP put in place several measures to minimize speculation in the market including: (1) keeping BSP policy rates unchanged since May 2001 despite the recent cuts in the target Federal Funds rate of the U.S.; (2)tightening of monitoring of banks’ foreign exchange transactions; (3) expanding the Coverage of the Currency Risk Protection Program (CRPP); and (4) reducing the ceiling on undocumented over-the-counter foreign exchange sales. It may also be noted that, in the process of easing inflationary pressures by raising banks’ liquidity reserve requirement, the BSP was able to further reduce excess liquidity which otherwise could have been used for dollar speculation. As a result, the pressure on the peso has eased.

The peso’s movement during the year reflects the trends observed for most Asian currencies like the new Taiwan dollar, the Japanese yen, the Thai baht, the South Korean won, and the Singapore dollar.

Banking Sector Developments and Reform Process

The banking system continues to hold its ground amidst a challenging environment.

Developments

The resilience of the banking sector is demonstrated by several key indicators. Its resources grew by 11.5 percent year-on-year as of end-June 2001, underpinned by increased deposit mobilization and build-up in capital.

Asset quality has remained satisfactory despite a recent uptrend in non-performing loans (NPL) due to the residual effects of the weak peso and the high interest rates for the most part of 2000. Recent data for commercial banks show that their NPL ratio reached 16.96 percent as of end-June 2001. In comparison with its Asian counterparts, the country’s NPL ratio was lower than that of Indonesia but higher than those of Thailand and Malaysia. [2] While the ratios have fallen faster in some of the other affected Asian economies, these declines resulted mainly from the turnover of their NPLs to public restructuring agencies. By contrast, no public funds have been used in the Philippines to purchase non-performing assets or recapitalize financial institutions. It should also be mentioned that loan loss provisioning of Philippine commercial banks is equivalent to 45 percent of total NPLs.

Moreover, the capital buffer of commercial banks has remained adequate as their capital adequacy ratio (CAR) as of June 2001 at 16.38 percent was well above the statutory floor of 10.0 percent and the BIS standard of 8 percent.

Meanwhile, outstanding domestic loans of commercial banks have been expanding for the past 17 months since February 2000.

Overall the banking system remains an effective intermediary of funds between savers and investors and a reliable channel for the transmission of monetary policy.

Banking Sector Reforms

The development of a stable, sound and globally competitive banking system remains the main focus of banking sector reform. Toward this end, major banking reforms have been implemented to: (1) improve the risk management practices of banks by shifting to a risk-based capital adequacy framework; (2) strengthen the prudential supervisory and regulatory framework in accordance with international standards; (3) promote bank governance by improving transparency and disclosure; and (4) create a stronger and more competitive banking system through mergers and consolidations and further liberalization of foreign bank entry.

The passage of the General Banking Law (GBL) in may 2000 provided the overarching framework for financial regulation. The GBL 2000 is expected to further strengthen the banking sector by, among other things, putting in place internationally accepted standards relating to risk-based capital adequacy, improving transparency, and enhancing competition. The BSP has crafted a number of rules and regulations to implement the GBL 2000, including those pertaining to foreign stockholdings, outsourcing of banking functions, adoption of risk-based capital adequacy standards aligned with international norms, and guidelines on microfinance.

Anti-Money Laundering Initiatives

In response to the global fight against money laundering, the BSP since July 2000 has passed a series of measures to help prevent the incidence of money laundering, such as requiring financial institutions under BSP supervision to:(1) report suspicious transactions; (2) stop issuing managers’, cashiers’ or certified checks or other instruments payable to cash, bearer or numbered account in amounts exceeding P10,000; (3) phase out anonymous or fictitious accounts; and (4) certify that they have monitored compliance with anti-money laundering regulations. In addition, a special committee was formed to evaluate, investigate and maintain a database on suspicious transactions of banks.

While the foregoing initiatives of the BSP are recognized as steps in the right direction, these are not considered sufficient to institute an effective anti-money laundering system and remove the Philippines from the list of non-cooperative countries in the global crusade against money laundering. Thus, the BSP—together with the other concerned agencies—is pushing for the passage in Congress of a comprehensive law on anti-money laundering. The consolidated bill is already being deliberated upon in both houses of congress. The bill will include, among others, provisions that will criminalize money laundering and define the unlawful activities constituting money laundering. It will also include a proposal for the creation of a multi-sectoral body that will have the authority to investigate money laundering cases while at the same time ensuring depositors’ confidence in the banking system.

Future Policy Thrusts

Monetary Policy

In terms of monetary policy directions, the Bangko Sentral’s main thrust for the rest of 2001 is to maintain low inflation while providing sufficient liquidity to meet the country’s growth requirements. Our commitment to price stability will be enhanced further by the adoption of inflation targeting as the new framework of monetary policy in January 2002. The said framework involves the pre-announcement by the Government of the inflation target that the BSP is committed to attain within a given time horizon. If the target is not met, the BSP will be required to provide explanations and spell out the measures it will undertake in order to get back on track. This new framework is expected to improve further the transparency and consistency of monetary policy and the accountability of the Bangko Sentral in attaining the price stability objective. By stabilizing prices, inflation targeting will encourage longer term savings and investment.

Exchange Rate Policy

The BSP is committed to a market-oriented foreign exchange rate policy. Exchange rate determination will be left to market forces, with some scope for occasional actions to maintain orderly adjustment in the foreign exchange market. In this regard, we will continue to monitor closely developments in the foreign exchange market with a view to determining the appropriate policy responses.

Banking Sector Policy

The future thrusts of banking sector policy will be the continued formulation of implementing rules and regulations of the GBL 2000, amendments of the BSP Charter, continued improvement in the BSP’s supervisory framework over banks, and support for the restructuring of the banking system.

The formulation of the implementing rules and regulations of the GBL 2000 will be continued particularly those pertaining to, among others, the observance of fit and proper rule on the management of banks and more comprehensive coverage of the single borrower’s limit.

Meanwhile, the proposed amendments to the BSP Charter will include reinforcing the authority and capability of the BSP to regulate and supervise the banking system and implement monetary policy more effectively. Major reforms being proposed in this regard involve: (1) granting authority to the BSP to conduct more frequent banking examinations; (2) implementing prompt corrective action in the case of problem/distressed banks; and (3) imposing stronger criminal and administrative penalties for violation of banking laws and regulations.

Aside from the changes in the country’s banking laws, an ongoing initiative by the Bangko Sentral is the improvement of its supervisory framework in line with the evolving structure of the financial system. Important steps in this direction include the adoption of a more forward-looking and risk-based bank supervision approach; and the implementation of consolidated supervision over financial conglomerates to facilitate a more comprehensive assessment of the risks involved in the banks’ activities.

Moreover, policy efforts will be geared toward supporting the ongoing restructuring of the local banking system, mainly through mergers and acquisitions and the entry of foreign investors, to help banks mobilize sufficient capitalization and strengthen risk management. Meanwhile, the rehabilitation of financially-stricken but viable banks will continue to be undertaken. The BSP is also supportive of the creation of private sector-led Asset Management Companies (AMCs). Already, a number of banks have shown interest in setting up such AMCs. In this regard, the role of Government would be in creating an environment that facilitates effective resolution of impaired assets by the banks themselves, including bringing the prudential and regulatory environment in line with best international practice in order to encourage, among other things, private capital injections.

In closing, let me assure you that the Bangko Sentral will remain committed to its strategic role of promoting the sustained growth of the economy by keeping prices low, interest rates at reasonable levels, the peso broadly stable and the banking system safe and sound.

Thank you.


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

[1]For Indonesia, exports contracted by 1.4 percent in January to March 2001 relative to the 27.7 percent growth in 2000 while for Thailand, exports declined by 1.4 percent in January to March 2001 from 19.7 percent growth in 2000. Meanwhile, Malaysia’s export growth decelerated to 8.4 percent in January to May 2001 from 16.1 percent in the comparable period in 2000.

[2] NPL ratio for Indonesia at 18.5% is as of April 2001; Thailand, at 13.0% as of June 2001(commercial banks only); and Malaysia, at 9.9 % as of May 2001 (commercial banks only);

Title: Anti-Money Laundering Law: A Work in Progress
Occasion: Symposium on Anti-Money Laundering, Financial Executives Institute of the Philippines
Speaker: Governor Rafael Buenaventura
Transcription:
I would like to thank the Financial Executives Institute of the Philippines for this opportunity to keynote this symposium on money laundering. I know your organization to be always an active participant in efforts to develop consensus on issues that affect the efficient conduct of business.

Money laundering is a global phenomenon and its detection and control has become a priority by most governments around the world. The Philippines should do no less.

As you are undoubtedly aware, your symposium is also timely because of the proximity of the September 30, 2001 deadline given by the financial action task force for the Philippines to pass an anti-money laundering bill. The very tight deadline, as it appears now, heightens the need to thresh out all issues that can delay the passage of the bill. This forum can make an important contribution to this effort.

To put the subject matter of your symposium in perspective, let me point out that the problem we face today started in June last year when the Paris-based Financial Action Task Force identified the Philippines as one of the 15 countries that were deemed to be non-cooperative in the global fight against money laundering. In June this year, or exactly one year later, the FATF updated the list and, meanwhile, recommended the application of sanctions on the Philippines, Russia and Nauru unless these countries passed needed legislation to address identified money laundering concerns. This is a very serious development because the sanctions can include a whole gamut of countermeasures that would not only make doing business with the rest of the world difficult, costly and time consuming but also give the Philippines a doubtful reputation as being a potential haven for money laundering.

The adoption of these countermeasures may prove costly to the Philippines. We run the risk of having foreign currency transactions including those of overseas Filipino workers, subjected to unnecessary scrutiny. Banks abroad would want to make sure that money used in Philippine related transactions are not proceeds from illegal activity like drug trafficking, kidnapping, corruption and other crimes. We also run the risk of other sanctions being imposed involving stricter surveillance, processing and verification requirements. Another possible consequence of non-compliance is the issuance of adverse advisories by global financial centers like the United States. If these advisories are issued to warn international banks about the Philippines, they create a bias and encourage the international banks to take extra caution when handling Philippine-based transactions. The bottomline is the whole economy could suffer.

Be that as it may and while the threat of sanctions coming from the 29 countries that make up the FATF is real, we in the Bangko Sentral support the anti-money laundering legislation mainly because it is in the country’s interest to do so. It is good for business. It is good for the economy. Money laundering has a corrosive effect on financial systems. When financial institutions are used to launder proceeds from criminal activities, the integrity of the whole financial system in a country could be seriously undermined. Besides, unchecked money laundering activities expose society to the harmful influence of organized crime and could lead to a loss of trust and confidence on the part of domestic and foreign investors. Thus, the absence of a law that addresses the issue could contribute to the proliferation of corrupt officials, abet and accord semblance of legitimacy to criminal syndicates, raise transaction costs in our international financial dealings and open the Philippines to criticism as a non-cooperative country in the global fight against money laundering.

The shocking revelations about financial transactions that kept our eyes glued to the television screen during the impeachment trial might not have happened had there been an anti-money laundering law at the time because the banks, under pain of severe penalties, would have reported the transactions from the start or, more likely, would have refused to process the transactions. With the kind of checks provided in the Anti-Money Laundering Law in place, money coming from the proceeds of illegal activities would note be so easy to move and clear through the banks, and then used again to fund more illegal activities.

This is why, on the part of the Bangko Sentral, we have been issuing since July last year a series of measures that have brought the country‘s regulatory framework closer to international standards, short of having an Anti-Money Laundering Law. These measures included new regulations, enforcement actions, and joint cooperative efforts with the private sector.

In particular, the Bangko Sentral has required banks, including offshore banking units, and non-bank financial institutions to, among others:

Report suspicious transactions,

Phase out anonymous or fictitious accounts and record the true identity of bank clients, and

Stop issuing cashier’s and manager’s checks payable to cash or a numbered account.

The BSP has also required foreign exchange corporations that are subsidiaries of banks, quasi-banks and non-bank financial intermediaries to report details of all their foreign exchange transactions.

On the part of the private sector, the Bankers Association of the Philippines has adopted an agreement on best practices against money laundering which will enable them to detect suspicious transactions on the basis of a know-your-customer culture. The BAP has also been conducting seminars to make the public aware of the campaign against money laundering.

The fact that the Philippines is still in the FATF list of non-cooperative countries indicates that our efforts to strengthen the BSP regulatory framework are not enough. A lot more work needs to be done. Our strict Bank Secrecy Laws and the absence of legislation criminalizing money-laundering activities are seen by the international community as making the country a potential haven for money laundering. This has to be addressed in the proposed anti-money laundering law. We must strike a balance between being able to penetrate the veil of bank secrecy to ferret out dirty money, on the one hand, and protecting the confidentiality of legitimate deposits, on the other. This is a contentious issue.

We have in the last few months participated in the drafting of an Administration Bill together with the Department of Justice, the Department of Finance and the Department of Foreign Affairs. I assume that the features of the Bill will be explained in the course of the Symposium. Basically, the Bill declares the crusade against money laundering as a policy of the state and then proceeds to flesh out the policy to plug every conceivable loophole.

Our draft bill is separate from some 10 similar bills filed in the house of representatives and 5 bills filed in the senate. If we determine success by numbers alone, the number of bills filed in both houses of congress is an indication of the widespread interest in the passage of an anti-money laundering law. But I have also talked to a number of Congressmen and Senators and they are one in the desire to see the passage of law to punish money laundering. They differ only in the means and manner of carrying it out. Hearings have started with a view to bringing about an agreement on the controversial provisions and coming up with a consolidated bill that will become the Anti-Money Laundering Act of 2001. Whether the September 30 deadline can be met is a bone of contention at the moment. There may be a need soon to ask the FATF for an extension of the deadline.

I would like to repeat that we are not rushing the approval of the Bill because the FATF says so but because it is good for us and we want to spare the country from the economic difficulties that the richest countries of the world, which are all members of the FATF can cause through sanctions that they could impose, as I have explained.

In closing, let me again assure everyone of the Bangko Sentral’s commitment to take strong action against money laundering activities in the Philippines. We have already undertaken swift and wide-ranging actions, within the bounds of our authority, to address the deficiencies in our anti-money laundering regulations. But we need to establish the legal foundation for criminalizing economic crimes if we are to prevent financial abuse. Indeed, this is a work in progress and requires not only action from the regulators but also contribution from the legislature and cooperation from the general public. I hope that the private sector will support our initiatives and will do its own share in safeguarding the integrity of our financial system.

Finally, I would like to thank FINEX, the organizers of this symposium for giving me the opportunity to share with you our efforts to combat money laundering.

Thank you.

Title: Rural Banks: Pillars in the Development of Local Economies
Occasion: 44th Charter Anniversary Symposium, Rural Bankers Association of the Philippines
Speaker: Governor Rafael Buenaventura
Transcription:
Introduction

It is a great pleasure for me to once again

address the rural banking community, this time on the occasion of your 44th Charter Anniversary.

I am also glad to note today’s large attendance. This only shows your sustained enthusiasm and commitment to continuously improve and meet the challenges. This is indeed most encouraging.


The Economic Situation

Our general economic situation today is difficult but not hopeless. Indeed the Philippine economy is still expected to grow by around 4 percent this year and by around 5 percent next year at a time when many of our neighboring economies are entering into a period recession. We can largely thank the agriculture and service sectors for this resilience. And the rural banking system should continue to draw strength from this.

We have also managed to contain inflation despite significant shocks such as higher oil prices and temporary currency volatility. Inflation is expected to be maintained at around 6-7 percent this year and should be lower next year, to around 5-6 percent. This is really a key battle that the Bangko Sentral has fought and this should translate to a moderate level of interest rates that will support economic growth and the viability of the banking industry as a whole.

Public confidence has also received a boost from our successful efforts to stabilize the peso in the face of speculative pressure. The Bangko Sentral remains firmly committed to a level of exchange rate that is competitive but not punitive. As part of confidence building, we have maintained our international reserves at more than $14 billion.

Where are the key challenges? Clearly, there is a strong need to improve our public finances by reducing the fiscal deficit. I am glad to note the solid efforts of the present administration to improve revenue collections and to contain expenditures. It is in our common interest for this effort to succeed. Otherwise, there will be severe economic financial instability ahead.

Another key challenge is to improve investor confidence. This is critical to a sustainable balance of payments and is a necessary foundation for economic growth and job creation. Again, a broad range of reforms are being pursued by government to nurture this. In the banking sector, the Bangko Sentral is not letting up in the implementation of reforms to assure public confidence in our banking system.

Our government has also identified poverty alleviation as a high priority goal. To the extent that we are unable to make significant progress here quickly, this is major factor that would undermine basic stability of our economy and our society. For the banking sector, especially our rural banking system, we can make a specific and high impact contribution through the promotion of microfinance. I will elaborate later on regarding the Bangko Sentral’s plans and initiatives in this area.

The Industry Situation

Let me now share with you our latest assessment of the rural banking industry.

I am happy to report to you that the industry-wide picture has continued to improve in key areas.

As of the first quarter of this year, industry profitability has rebounded by 22.8 percent with estimated net income after tax reaching P279 million.

Asset quality is also improving. Our estimates show that industry NPL ratio further eased to 17.3 percent as of end-March 2001 compared with 19.7 percent a year ago. Significantly, loan loss provisioning has also improved to more than 30 percent from less than 24 percent a year ago. I would encourage the industry to remain highly focused on this critical area, both to further lower the NPL ratio and to dispose of non-performing assets (defined as non-performing loans and acquired assets) which remain quite high at close to 20 percent of total assets.

The deposit base has also continued to expand as reflected in a 12.0 percent growth rate. This has contributed to a viable liquidity position.

Combined capital accounts have also risen by 11.6 percent and industry capitalization ratio has been maintained at a very respectable 16.5 percent versus the prescribed minimum of 10 percent.

These improvements in the basic financial fundamentals have been achieved in the context of steady industry growth. Total assets of the rural banking industry have now increased to P66.7 billion as of end-March 2001, up by 8.6 percent from last year. Although the number of rural banks have been further trimmed down to 787 head offices compared with 805 last year, the total branch network has actually increased to 1,121 offices.

These developments are consistent with the Bangko Sentral’s objective of realizing a rural banking industry founded on stability, quality, and impact and not necessarily on sheer massive numbers.

At the end of the day, maintenance of sound financial fundamentals is the one credible assurance that the rural banking industry will be around to sustain its contributions to the economy and the communities that it is committed to serve.

Continuing Reforms

There is strong need to push ahead with deep reform in the banking system so that we will continue to earn and deserve public trust and confidence. The critical importance of mobilizing domestic savings is more than ever being clearly highlighted as we contend with the fickle flows of international capital in the context of globalization. As yet, the rural banking system has vast untapped potential for mobilizing the savings of our local communities and turn this around into productive investments that could first and foremost benefit those same communities.

Our approach to reform is really focused on the very basic elements. First, our banks must have enough capital to match its risks. There must be sufficient buffer to keep a bank’s door open and depositors protected in the event of normal adversity and reversals. Second, our banks must have sound governance. It is vitally important that our banks are fair to all its stakeholders and not just its controlling shareholders; that it is financially accountable and soundly managed; and, that it is transparent.

Many of our policy initiatives are reducible to these elements and we are counting on your support to ensure substantial compliance. In particular, I would like to draw your attention to Circular 280 calling for a minimum capitalization equivalent to 10 percent of risk weighted assets. On the other hand, Circular 283 defines the duties and responsibilities of the banks Board of Directors. t is our experience that many banks fail due to the failure of the Board of Directors to exercise proper governance.

There is also a forthcoming circular on the fit and proper standards for bank directors and officers which include a mandatory director training requirement, guidelines for the implementation of the two independent director requirement, and grounds for qualification and disqualification of directors and officers. We are also currently reviewing the rules on disclosure of information so that the public can make better informed judgments to reward or punish a bank as its performance warrants.

I hope you all realize that the ground rules on banking are shifting radically to better protect the public in light of recent experience But rest assured that these would be essentially fair rules that appropriately reward those that render faithful and competent banking service.

Microfinance Initiatives

I had mentioned earlier and in previous public statements the Bangko Sentral’s strong desire to promote microfinance.

Why are we buying into microfinance? Microfinance, using proven technologies and approaches, promises to effectively deliver credit and other banking services to lower income groups especially the enterprising poor who have long suffered from limited access. As such, it can be a powerful instrument for alleviating poverty and broadening economic empowerment particularly beyond metro manila.

For the banks that go into microfinance, it can be a very profitable undertaking that can also improve the overall viability of the rural banking system.

As a regulator, we are also attracted to the whole idea of inculcating greater credit discipline in the lending process that microfinance very firmly advocates. Indeed, discipline and value formation are the underlying keys to the success of microfinance.

All of these features combine to make microfinance an everybody-wins proposition.

What are the specific steps that Bangko Sentral is taking to promote microfinance? First, we have modified our regulations, consistent with the new general banking law, to accommodate cash flow-based lending rather than lending focused on collaterals.

We have also opened a special rediscount window to provide liquidity for microfinance loans meeting our criteria.

Additionally, we have lifted the moratorium on the establishment of new banks to allow the entry of new microfinance-oriented thrift banks and rural banks. Already, two such thrift banks have been approved by the Monetary Board.

We are also currently working on new guidelines relaxing the moratorium on branching of rural banks provided that new branches shall be microfinance-oriented based on our criteria.

Finally, we are planning to establish a foundation dedicated to the promotion of microfinance in the Philippines primarily through training assistance. We realize that a major obstacle to the propagation of microfinance is not so much the lack of loanable funds. Rather, it is the lack of training and know-how.
