To address this gap, the Bangko Sentral, through the proposed foundation, can be a catalyst for mobilizing donor and other funds to leverage its own resources for the purpose of supporting the large-scale training of qualified rural banks and thrift banks that are prepared to adopt appropriate microfinance technology.

Concluding Remarks

Let me end my remarks today by encouraging the rural banking industry to persevere with its efforts to renew itself and rebuild its foundation on the basis of financial strength, professional management, and sound governance.

As stronger financial institutions, you will be in an excellent position to make a real difference in reducing poverty and reinvigorating our economy.

Thank you and good day.

Title: Towards Innovation in the Rural Banking Industry
Occasion: Rural Bankers Association of the Philippines
Speaker: Governor Rafael Buenaventura
Transcription:
Good morning, ladies and gentlemen!

On behalf of the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas, congratulations on your 43rd Charter anniversary!

It is always a pleasure for me to address the rural bankers association of the Philippines.  After all, you represent the overwhelming numerical majority of our banking industry constituency.

This morning, I would like to take the opportunity to review the current situation of our rural banking industry and the directions it must take to be able to meet the challenges and thrive in the new millennium.

Recent developments in the rural banking industry

First of all, I am happy to report that the rural banking industry continues to recover and rebound from the severe crisis that had affected the banking sector as a whole not only here in the Philippines but in the Asian region as well.   This is in no small measure due to your own commendable efforts to deal with the problems decisively.

As of end-March 2000, the total resources of the rural banking industry expanded by more than 3.4 percent on an annual basis. This was fuelled by a 4.2 percent increase in deposits and a further increase in capitalization that boosted the net worth to risk assets ratio from 17.1 percent to 18.1 percent.

Significantly, a slight decline in the level of past due loans has been accompanied by increased provisioning against loan losses now equivalent to 28.3 percent of past due accounts.    Last year, this was only at 15 percent. However, the average past due ratio had not improved at 19.7 percent due mainly to lack of loan growth.

Profitability has also strongly rebounded.   Net income as of the first quarter was up by nearly 27 percent from last year.

These very basic performance figures clearly point to a fundamentaly viable core rural banking system.  It is therefore rather unfortunate that the attention of the public tends to get diverted to the relatively limited instances when some rural banks have had to be closed.   Bank closures are of course always traumatic especially for the affected communities in spite of the deposit insurance safety net.  They are equally agonizing to the Bangko Sentral as well.  But taking a more constructive view, they at least finally resolve what have become untenable situations and allow the opportunity to learn from the lessons, move forward and build anew.

The tasks ahead

We need to work closely together to make the rural banking system even worthier of the public’s confidence and more efficient and effective in delivering banking services to our rural communities.  There are number of initiatives that need to be pursued.

First of all, the basic banking reforms advocated in the recently enacted General Banking Law have to be decisively implemented and adhered to.  Among others, these include the setting up of enough capital commensurate to the risks being taken in line with best international practice.  Under the forthcoming new arrangements, which have actually started to be implemented, compliance with the risk-based minimum capital adequacy ratio reinforced by more disciplined and fair asset valuations will be critical.

No less important is the necessity of having more responsible bank governance starting with qualified, fully enabled and vigilant boards of directors.  The General Banking Law has several important provisions that support this including the requirement of having at least two independent directors, the adoption of the fit and proper rule that will allow the board to disqualify bank directors and officers when warranted, and stricter provisions against self-dealing.

A key General Banking Law reform that should also be fully supported is the call for more disclosure to the public to promote transparency.  Already, the Bangko Sentral has taken important steps to implement this through new regulations.  But it would be more ideal if all banks go beyond minimum compliance and truly welcome the opportunity to keep its stakeholders well-informed.  This is a sure way to gain the public trust.

I cannot overemphasize enough the first and foremost need to mind the safety and soundness of our banks.  Without this, our banking system would indeed be built upon shaky foundations.

But the challenges of the time also call upon all of us to continue innovating as well.  I strongly believe that it will be a fatal error to assume that rural banking is essentially a low technology business.  It is easy enough to slide into that assumption considering the setting.    Perhaps that’s the reason why the rural banking system has yet to fully meet its potential and promise.

But I am also encouraged to note that there is an emerging generation of new rural bankers, thoroughly modern, energetic, and above all open to examining new credit and management paradigms. They are being supported by enlightened donors and researchers who are bringing to bear their considerable resources, field experience and intellectual capital to deal with long-standing problems that have perpetuated poverty in the countryside.

I am informed that some of your very worthy cooperative projects include the development of a computer-based management information system that will be widely available to our rural banks by early next year.  Through enhanced use of appropriate information technology, our banks should be better able to handle the intensive information requirements of micro-lending from origination to collection.

Hopefully, banks will also be able to meet our information requirements to ensure more effective and proactive supervision as well as better policy analysis.

In this regard, we have announced new reporting arrangements under BSP Circular 249.    We realize that the transition to the new reporting arrangements geared towards paperless reporting may not be that easy given the limitations in a significant number of our rural banks.    Nevertheless, we need to take right away the first steps if ever we are to complete a potentially long journey.   Depending on our assessment of compliance, we would be willing to consider some flexibility in the implementation timetable if warranted.  Rest assured that we will be coordinating closely with the association on this matter as well as in other regulations that concern the industry.

I am also aware of your efforts to adopt new credit delivery technologies that will give traditionally non-bankable clients greater access to credit without necessarily sacrificing credit quality while encouraging them to save as well.

By moving in these directions, I have no doubt in my mind that the rural banking system will continue to find an important and strategic niche in our financial system.  The policy of the Bangko Sentral is to promote a strong and capable banking system and not necessarily to create large banks and eliminate small players.

Let me also assure you that we too as a regulator are changing our ways to ensure that we keep pace with market-driven innovations.  We would like to be perceived as a regulator that adds value by promoting public confidence without necessarily stifling progress.

 Concluding note

In closing, I would like to emphasize that the Bangko Sentral intends to continue with banking reform efforts with its priorities embodied in the new General Banking Law and the proposed amendments to the New Central Bank Act.   Overall, these legislative changes aim to further strengthen our banking system, raise prudential standards to international norms, foster greater competition and enhance the supervisory capability and independence of the Bangko Sentral.

Some have voiced concern that the beneficial provision of the General Banking Law may not accrue to the rural banking industry due to conflict with provisions of the Rural Banks Act.    I don’t believe there are a lot of confilicts in the first place, nevertheless, I wish to inform you that we are now working on the implementing regulations that will rationalize potentially conflicting provisions of different operative laws.  In this regard, we will be generally adopting a liberal interpretation in favor of rural banks in resolving such conflicts.

Echoing the president, I am strongly urging the leaders and members of the association “to continue working together with the government and maintain our sights on the endless possibilities for the nation’s growth.”

I now wish all of you a fruitful and mutually rewarding symposium.

Thank you very much and a pleasant day to all.

  (Note: 43rd Charter Anniversary, Rural Bankers Association of the Philippines, August 29, 2000, Century Park Sheraton Hotel, Manila )

Title: Speech
Occasion: Luncheon Meeting with the Singaporean Financial Community
Speaker: Governor Rafael Buenaventura
Transcription:
Secretary Camacho, Secretary Perez, distinguished members of the Singaporean Financial Community, honored guests, ladies and gentlemen, good afternoon.

As you have heard from Secretary Camacho, the Philippines has an economic plan focused on fiscal discipline, good governance, market-oriented reform, and poverty-reduction.  As the Governor of the Central Bank, I would like to reiterate my support for this plan and its implementation and also my confidence that there is a team and a strategy in place to ensure that the objectives included in the economic plan will be achieved.

Allow me, therefore, to spell out the initiatives that we, at the Central Bank, have been taking to support the Government's economic plan.  Our efforts have been directed in three important areas: first, achieving price stability; second, introducing banking sector reforms; and third, introducing institutional reforms to pave the way for the good governance practices that will assist in making the Philippine economic plan a reality.

Price Stability

To my mind, one of the most crucial steps being taken by the Arroyo Administration is the emphasis on instilling fiscal discipline throughout the public sector.  The ability to meet revenue and expenditure targets, and thus reduce the budget deficit, are significant challenges that must be accomplished.  While also addressing rampant speculative activity in some quarters of the financial markets.

While the Government is focused on instilling fiscal discipline, my team in the Central Bank has also been concentrating on restoring calm to the currency markets. I am pleased to say that we have seen some initial success in this very important area. Our goal in this regard is to achieve overall price stability and to continue to support the Government in meeting its fiscal targets.

As many of you are aware, our currency, the peso, like many other currencies around the world, has been the object of some speculative pressure.  In addressing this pressure, we have taken a two-fold approach to our currency challenges by reducing liquidity levels in the market through hikes in liquidity reserve requirements, and by being diligent and relentless in warding off speculators. We have done this by exposing banks and by imposing fines when they are found to have violated foreign exchange regulations. Our efforts have resulted in a strengthening of the peso from a low of PhP 53.57 to the U.S. dollar three weeks ago to its current level of close to PhP 51. A relatively stable exchange rate is important for keeping inflation under control and is good for business planning.

Our next step is to ensure that price stability becomes the norm rather than the exception. To achieve this, the Central Bank will be implementing a number of institutional measures.  Those measures include:

A shift in monetary policy to inflation-targeting by January of next year.  This practice, which is employed by many other countries, has price stability as a primary focus.  It achieves that stability by committing to reach an explicit nominal inflation target directly without compromising the broad economic targets of the government.  This differs from the present practice of using a monetary aggregate targeting framework, which uses money supply as an intermediate target.

Other institutional measures that we are taking include the preservation of an appropriate interest-rate differential to encourage investors to maintain their peso denominated assets.

They also include the maintenance of a market-determined exchange rate policy. This policy, however, must be supported by a strict and effective foreign exchange monitoring system and a strong commitment to apply penalties to institutions or individuals who violate foreign exchange regulations.

And finally, our efforts to support price stability include work we are carrying out to develop secondary markets for fixed income and derivative products.

Instituting Banking Reforms

The Central Bank is also committed to increasing foreign participation in the Philippine banking sector.  As such, we will soon introduce reforms to prepare domestic banks to effectively compete in a globally integrated banking environment.  The reforms will fall within the framework of first, improving the banking sector’s structure; secondly, enhancing the Central Bank’s supervisory and regulatory powers in line with international standards; thirdly, heightening bank transparency and disclosure; fourthly, improving risk management; and finally, stimulating the consumer-oriented credit environment.

Our work to strengthen the banking sector through such steps as imposing capital requirements in accordance with international standards and by promoting greater competition will certainly encourage banking sector consolidation and provide opportunities for greater foreign participation in the sector.

In enhancing our supervisory powers, the Central Bank has introduced risk-based capital requirements, tighter loan classification and provisioning rules, and consolidated reporting.  We will also be imposing stiffer penalties for any violations of the Philippines banking regulations.

In heightening bank transparency and disclosure, the Central Bank will monitor the banks’ selection of external auditors and require strict adherence to the “Know your customer rule”.  We will also require the quarterly publication of statements of condition, key financial indicators, non-performing loans, and related-party lending.

In improving risk management, the Central Bank will institute an early warning system for bank failures, assist banks to better match their foreign currency assets and liabilities, and carry out reviews to identify regulatory loopholes in the transactions of bank-affiliated FOREX corporations.

In an effort to stimulate bank lending, the Central Bank will encourage the financing of micro-enterprises by providing incentives such as liquidity assistance through re-discounting.  We will also relax certain collateralization requirements and partially lift the general moratorium on the licensing of new thrift and rural banks to allow the establishment of institutions who are committed to micro-enterprise financing.

Institutional Reforms and Good Governance

These reforms, if they are to have the desired impact, must be complemented by both good governance practices and strong political will. For this reason, we are seeking amendments to the Central Bank Charter that will institutionalize many of these reforms and reinforce the position of the central bank as a governing and independent body for monetary policy and supervision.

In considering amendments to the Central Bank Charter, we are looking to add criteria to close or placing banks or other financial institutions under receivership in line with international standards. We also want to strengthen criminal and administrative penalties for any violation of banking laws, and to introduce measures that will increase the Central Bank's operational efficiency.

Finally, I am very optimistic that we will soon see the passage of an Anti-money Laundering Bill in both the Philippine Congress and Senate.  This is something that the Central Bank has been working on over the past several months.  I would like to assure you that this bill is being taken very seriously and has gained popular support not just in the legislative arena, but also amongst the general public.  Let me make it perfectly clear, the Central Bank is committed to promoting and enforcing international standards of banking regulation and supervision.  Because of this, we have zero tolerance for illegal practices such as money laundering.

These are not empty words.  My Central Bank team and my colleagues in government will be steadfast in instituting the reforms that will strengthen our banking sector and promote good governance.  My former associates and colleagues in the Philippine banking sector can certainly attest to my determination to work with the Government to achieve its growth targets.  And while I am holding the reins at the Central Bank, good governance policies and practices will be non-negotiable.

Before I close and take your questions, I would just like to reiterate that we recognize that restoring the Philippine economy to health is a significant challenge.  But, I am very optimistic that this challenge will be met because we are approaching this task with a clear plan, a team of experienced professionals who are managing this process and a commitment throughout President Arroyo's administration to ensure that the Philippine's path to prosperity is based on a strong foundation of economic reform.

Thank you very much and good day.

 

(Note: Luncheon meeting with the Singaporean Financial Community, 24 August 2001, Shargri-La Hotel, Singapore)

Title: The BSP: Ensuring the Proper Environment for Sustainable Growth
Occasion: 5th Membership Meeting, Rotary Club of Manila
Speaker: Governor Rafael Buenaventura
Transcription:
Mr. Edgardo E. Tumangan, officers and members of the Rotary Club of Manila, friends, ladies and gentlemen, good afternoon:

I.  Introduction

It is a pleasure to join you again at this membership meeting of the Rotary Club of Manila. Occasions such as this one bring to mind the importance of a dynamic government-private sector partnership in confronting the challenges we face today.

I believe that, now more than ever, the role of the private sector—in particular, the business sector as represented by groups such as the Rotary Club—is crucial and indispensable in the effort to sustain the economy’s growth momentum.  Given this, the continuing challenge for government, and the BSP in particular, is in providing a sound macroeconomic environment to support economic activity.  The BSP is specifically tasked to provide direction in the areas of monetary policy and banking.  Allow me to discuss some of these issues with you today.

II.  Recent Policy Initiatives

The BSP’s efforts to ensure a supportive environment are centered on its primary mandate of maintaining stable prices, while broadly supporting the economy’s output growth objective.  We did this in the early part of the 2001 by reducing policy interest rates consistent with an accommodative stance of monetary policy.  BSP policy rates were reduced from the beginning of the year by a total of 450 basis points to provide room for market interest rates to go down and thereby encourage economic activity to strengthen.  This was in addition to the earlier reduction of 150 basis points in BSP policy rates in December 2000.

In recent months, however, the movements in international oil prices and the peso-dollar rate have posed upside risks to the inflation outlook.  These factors have prompted us to reassess our monetary policy stance and focus on addressing potential inflationary pressures.

The stability of the foreign exchange market is of particular concern because sharp and sustained movements in the peso-dollar rate have a pass-through impact on consumer prices by raising the cost of imported inputs for production.  To address potential inflationary pressures, the BSP recently increased its liquidity reserve requirement by 2 percentage points.  This was aimed at moderating liquidity growth and, at the same time, helping temper speculative activity in the foreign exchange market.  There are indications that part of the foreign exchange market activities in recent months have been funded by the excess peso liquidity in the system.  Tempering liquidity growth will reduce the potential for speculation in the foreign exchange market.  It will also bring overall monetary growth in line with the downwardly revised growth targets for 2001 based on the weaker-than-expected upturn in economic activity.

We have implemented other policy measures to further ease pressures on the peso.  The BSP expanded the Currency Risk Protection Program (CRPP) by providing a hedging mechanism to a greater number of users, specifically market players wanting to frontload their future foreign currency requirements and borrowers wanting to cover unmatured foreign currency obligations.  We tightened monitoring of foreign exchange transactions of banks and reduced the ceilings on undocumented over-the-counter foreign exchange sales.  We also did away with the 3-tier pricing mechanism for the placement of overnight funds by banks with the BSP.

Some help came from the private sector as well. Notably, member banks of the Bankers’ Association of the Philippines (BAP) agreed to voluntarily reduce their overbought foreign exchange positions so as to help improve foreign exchange supply. With the measures that we have implemented, the exchange rate has stabilized, closing at P53.15 yesterday.

Promoting a stronger domestic banking system remains another key priority for the Bangko Sentral.  We believe that a healthy banking and financial system will be better equipped to provide for the financial intermediation needs of our domestic industries. To this end, the BSP implemented a host of policy changes involving the banking system.

For example, we issued various regulations to implement the General Banking Law of 2000, the basic legal fabric governing the entire banking system.  Various circulars were issued by the BSP in 2001 on the following:

  • Definition and classification of banks and the prerequisites for the grant of universal banking authorities;

  • Guidelines on microfinance loans to small and medium enterprises;

  • Guidelines for the new risk-based capital adequacy requirement, which took effect on 1 July 2001.

Meanwhile, the BSP continues to be at the forefront in pushing for the legislation against money laundering to protect the integrity of our financial institutions.  Thus, the BSP intends to push for the passage in congress of a comprehensive Anti-money Laundering Law, as a key legislative priority.  We take heart that the president in her State of the Nation Address has certified as urgent this law, which incorporates all the basic elements of an anti-money laundering system covering the proceeds of crimes including plunder, graft and corruption, illegal drugs, smuggling, kidnapping, as well as financial and tax fraud.

The reforms introduced in the General Banking Law of 2000 will be complemented by the proposed amendments to the BSP Charter. These amendments aim to enhance the BSP’s supervisory powers, improve prudential standards, and promote greater banking competition. Key reforms include the grant of authority to the BSP to conduct more frequent banking examinations, restoration of the BSP’s tax-exempt status with respect to open market operations, and the enhancement of the scope and strength of administrative sanctions. These proposed changes will lead to what we call a “safer financial architecture” inasmuch as they help fortify our banking system against various potential shocks.

III.  Key Economic Results

The measures I have outlined to you have contributed over the last few months to a more favorable economic environment and a more sustainable path to long-term growth.

For example, inflation has been kept in check in the past few months.  Actual inflation continues to be on track relative to its projected path for 2001, averaging at 6.8 percent in the first seven months.  Latest readings on the inflation environment are consistent with our expectations that the inflation target of 6.0-7.0 percent for the year will be met—although perhaps the actual value will be closer to the higher end of the range.

At the same time, our financial system continues to be for the most part stable and sound. Total assets continue to expand, with the capital-to-risk assets ratio at 16.95 percent as of April 2001 compared to 16.21 percent in December 2000. Asset quality has remained relatively manageable, with the non-performing loan ratio for commercial banks settling at 16.81 percent as of May 2001.

Meanwhile, our accommodative monetary stance earlier in the year has led to a general downtrend in market interest rates.  The 91-day treasury bill rate, for example, fell from a high of 16.72 percent in November 2000, when political tensions were running high, to 9.22 percent at the latest auction on 30 July 2001. Similarly, banks’ lending rates declined to a range of 12.62-14.25 percent for the period 26 July – 1 Aug 2001 compared to 18.3-20.2 percent in the first week of December. As a result, domestic credit continued to expand, rising by 10.08 percent in May with higher loans extended to both the public and private sectors.

The resulting expansion in credit has provided the basis for moderate economic growth in the face of domestic concerns and weak external demand.  Real GNP grew by 3.6 percent in the first quarter of 2001, underpinned by personal consumption and government spending on the demand side, and by the agriculture and services sectors on the supply side.  The resiliency of these productive sectors will provide a steadying influence for economic growth in the face of the ongoing global economic slowdown.

IV.  Concluding Remarks

Despite our progress in pushing the economy further along the path to long-term sustainable growth, much still needs to be done. Uncertainties stemming mainly from external developments are present. The particular concern is how to deal with the ongoing slowdown in global economic growth. The lingering weakness of the major economies such as the U.S. and Japan have affected the exports of their trading partners. As a result, countries like the Philippines have to rely on themselves to provide the impetus for economic growth. We can do this with higher consumption spending, and the key to doing this is by keeping up consumer confidence. This is why I spoke of the role of the private sector at the beginning of my talk.

At the same time, the Government, for its part, recognizes that sustained economic expansion requires the implementation of a credible and consistent policy framework, as a complement to structural reforms aimed a fostering a vibrant economy.  The key challenge is to accelerate the pace of the reforms in the infrastructure, financial, and agriculture sectors to boost domestic and external confidence and to enable a recovery in investments on a durable basis.

We have weathered many difficult challenges in the past, and I have no doubt that we can get through the present problems posed by the weak global economy.  What is different today is that there is a greater collective awareness of the need for genuine economic reforms and a greater commitment to address our problems accordingly.  This is our key to creating the sustaining momentum for economic growth in the years ahead.  Let us strive to preserve this commitment.

Thank you and good afternoon.

 

(Note: Fifth Membership Meeting, Rotary Club of Manila, 09 August 3000, Manila Hotel)

Title: Remarks
Occasion: Briefing on Anti-Money Laundering, Federation of Filipino-Chinese Chambers of Commerce and Industry
Speaker: Governor Rafael Buenaventura
Transcription:
Good afternoon, ladies and gentlemen. I am pleased that you can join us today. You and your businesses are important contributors to the Philippine economy and today, I want to review important initiatives that the government is taking to ensure that there is a regulatory environment to enable you and others in the private sector to carry out your business activities with certainty and transparency.  The Anti-money Laundering Bill, which we will review in a moment, is key to the creation of a stable and predictable environment for the private sector.

Central to this stability, and our economic recovery, is a strong banking system, which requires a regulatory framework in line with international banking standards. Toward that end, the Central Bank is continuing to encourage bank consolidation in accordance with prudent banking standards.  And those banking standards include addressing the global issue of money laundering.

As you know, our country has recently been placed on a list of Non-cooperative Countries and Territories, or NCCT, by the Financial Action Task Force, an agency created a decade ago by the G7 economic powers to co-ordinate international efforts to fight trading in questionable cash.

To give you some background, the financial action task force originated from the G7 summit in Paris in 1989 and has the support of 29 countries, including the global financial centers of the U.S., the UK, Switzerland, Hong Kong and Singapore. The task force also has the support of two other international organizations, the European Commission and the Gulf Cooperation.

Inclusion on the NCCT list is not something anyone should be proud of and it is something that is totally inconsistent with the government’s effort to promote investor confidence and enhance the environment for investment.

We have been working with the international financial community including the U.S. Treasury on this issue for the past year. As the lead agency in developing the Anti-money Laundering Bill, let me say that I believe that this bill will support the maintenance and growth of foreign investment in the Philippines while protecting the rights of businesses and individuals to confidentiality.

Without the bill, we run the risk of increasing the exposure of most, if not all, of our foreign exchange transactions to unnecessary scrutiny. We also run the risk that additional sanctions, together with stricter surveillance, processing and verification requirements, will be imposed – a potential disincentive for investment in, and business with, Philippine companies. That would be a very real consequence should the Financial Action Task Force continue to include the Philippines on the NCCT list.

There are also two other consequences to noncompliance that will jeopardize our efforts for economic recovery and your normal conduct of business. The first is adverse advisories. These, if issued about the Philippines to warn international banks and other financial institutions, will create a bias, encouraging international banks to take caution when handling any Philippine-based transaction. This will mean that your normal business transactions may be considered or treated as possibly suspicious, in many cases discouraging foreign parties from investing or doing business with Philippine companies.

The second consequence is an increased risk of a breach in the confidentiality of deposit accounts since a NCCT inclusion means that foreign banks can require absolute and general waivers on account ownership confidentiality before accepting transactions for processing. This requirement also adds to the cost of business because the additional documentation and verification associated with general waivers translates into more work and therefore more time spent in processing transactions.

It is with these business consequences in mind, along with the spirit of international cooperation and a commitment to see the Philippines benefit from full participation in the global economy, that we are promoting the Anti-money Laundering Bill.

Through the Anti-money Laundering Bill, the government is doing its part to create a stable and predictable environment in which you can continue to conduct your business. We are making this necessary reform to increase the confidence in our banking system. This is consistent with our commitment to economic recovery, which we believe can only take place if it is underpinned by good governance and effective institutional reform.

I can also assure you that implementation of the Anti-money Laundering Bill will be carried out in a fair and transparent manner. We are a business-oriented government and we want to see you succeed and continue to contribute to the Philippine economy. I can also assure you that any questions that you have about the bill will be answered.

Allow me to now turn the presentation to Atty. De Zuniga who will provide you with further details and the structural framework of the bill. He will be followed by a representative from the Bankers Association of the Philippines who will provide you with a private sector perspective on this bill. That perspective has proved to be a valuable guideline as this bill has been developed and reviewed.

Thank you.

(Note: Briefing on Anti-Money Laundering, Federation of Filipino-Chinese Chambers of Commerce & Industry, Inc., Chinese Filipino Business Club, Inc. and Filipino-Chinese General Chambers of Commerce, August 6, 2001, MB Auditorium, BSP Complex)

Title: BSP Supports Global Campaign Against Money Laundering
Occasion: oint Luncheon Meeting, Rotary Club Makati an Rotary Club Makati West
Speaker: Governor Rafael Buenaventura
Transcription:
It is with great pleasure that I join this gathering of professionals and executives of the country’s top corporations and other distinguished members of the Rotary Club of Makati and Rotary Club of Makati West.  The topic I chose for this afternoon is among the most important issues facing law enforcers and regulatory authorities.  Today, money laundering is already considered a global phenomenon and its detection and control has become one of the priorities of authorities.  The use of the world’s banking systems to hide and disguise funds from illegal activities can erode the integrity of financial institutions.  It exposes society to the harmful influence of organized crime.  As such money laundering can result in the loss of trust and confidence of domestic and foreign investors in the financial system. 

Inclusion of the Philippines in FATF list

In June 2000, our country, together with 14 other nations,[1] was identified by the Financial Action Task Force (FATF) as being non-cooperative in the international fight against money laundering.  The FATF is a 29-member international group created at the 1989 G-7 Economic Summit and tasked to coordinate the drive against money laundering.  Our inclusion in their list was on account of what were perceived to be serious deficiencies in the country’s efforts to counter money laundering.  The Philippine’s strict bank secrecy laws and the absence of legislation criminalizing money laundering activities are seen as making the country a potential haven for money laundering.

Last 22 June 2001, the FATF decided to remove the Bahamas, Cayman Islands, Liechtenstein and Panama from the list but retained the Philippines in the updated list of non-cooperative countries.  The FATF has recommended the application of additional countermeasures with respect to the Philippines, Nauru and Russia by 30 September 2001 unless these countries pass the needed legislation to address identified money laundering concerns.   These countermeasures include the possibility of enhanced surveillance and reporting of financial transactions by financial institutions whenever they transact with Philippine-based banks, businesses, and individuals.[2]

The adoption of these countermeasures may prove costly to the Philippines as it may hamper trade and investment transactions of domestic corporations.  These countermeasures will generate greater scrutiny and as a result, information on transactions will unnecessarily be revealed.   Aside from the possibility of higher transaction costs in our international dealings, the countermeasures may also give the Philippines a stigma that it is a non-cooperative country in the global fight against money laundering.  Consequently, this may adversely affect our efforts to attract more foreign investments.

Measures implemented

The tough stance being taken by the international community towards countries with shortcomings in their efforts to curb anti-money laundering prompted the BSP, since July 2000, to immediately take strong actions.  Last year, we issued a number of circulars that would bring the country’s regulatory framework on anti-money laundering closer to international standards.  These measures, among others, included:

1)     Instructing foreign exchange corporations that are affiliates or subsidiaries of banks to report details of all foreign exchange transactions;

2)     Requiring banks and non-banks to establish the true identity of their clients;

3)    Requiring banks and non-banks to report suspicious transactions;

4)    Prohibiting banks from issuing cashier’s, manager’s or certified checks payable to cash or a numbered account; and

5)    Requiring foreign exchange corporations that are subsidiaries or affiliates of banks, quasi-banks and non-bank financial intermediaries to demand documents from resident buyers of foreign exchange in amounts of $10,000 or more.

On the part of the private sector, the Bankers Association of the Philippines adopted an agreement on best practices against money laundering and has helped organize seminars.    Through these information dissemination activities, the public is made aware of the campaign against money laundering while at the same time is able to give feedback. 

Future legislation

We continue to actively support initiatives—including legislation—aimed at penalizing money laundering activities.  In fact, during the meeting of FATF Asia/Pacific Review Group last 21 May 2001, the Philippine delegation reiterated its commitment to prioritize the passage of anti-money laundering laws and regulations to meet international standards and to eradicate the recycling of crime proceeds into the economic mainstream.    In line with this, several measures have been taken.

A draft bill has been prepared by the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas, the Department of Foreign Affairs and the Department of Justice declaring the crusade against money laundering as a policy of the state.  Specifically, the bill defines suspicious transactions as those involving, among others:

i.      cash payments in excess of P500,000 or equivalent foreign exchange with a customer whose true identity has not been established and where the size of the transaction is not commensurate with the business or status of client;

ii.     Unusual purchase of currency without any credible purpose, underlying trade obligation, contract or economic justification; and

iii.     Unusual sale of currencies whose source in not satisfactorily established.

The bill also:

  • Provides penalties for the crime[3];
  • Requires the submission of reports on suspicious transactions;
  • Grants immunity to reporting institutions and officers;
  • Allows access to deposit accounts subject to certain conditions; and
  • Creates a Financial Intelligence Unit (FIU) to be named national anti-money laundering board.

Legislators for their part are also pursuing various initiatives to legally define and criminalize money laundering and to relax the Secrecy Law on Bank Deposits.  There are now several bills filed in both the Senate and the House of Representatives that explicitly define money laundering and establish penalties for such activities.[4]  These bills also contain provisions that define suspicious bank deposit accounts and allow certain government agencies access to information of these suspicious bank accounts.    These agencies include the BSP, the Philippine Deposit Insurance Commission, the Office of the Ombudsman, the Department of Justice or a proposed task force.    The BSP is pushing for the granting of the authority to the BSP to examine bank deposits involving at least P50 million as one of the amendments to the New Central Bank Act. 

International cooperation

The Philippines has established communication lines with the FATF of the Asia Pacific Group for updates on the country’s compliance with the key set of standards to deter money laundering drawn up by the FATF.

To facilitate the adoption of measures and accelerate regional cooperation to combat anti-money laundering, the Asian Development Bank has approved a Technical Assistance Program worth US$650,000 for nine countries, which includes the Philippines.  The implementation period for the program is from May 2001 to August 2002. 

Conclusion

In closing, let me again assure everyone of the Bangko Sentral’s commitment to take strong action against money laundering activities in the Philippines.  We have already undertaken swift and wide-ranging actions, within the bounds of our authority, to address the deficiencies in our anti-money laundering regulations.  But we need to establish the legal foundation for criminalizing economic crimes if we are to prevent financial abuse.  Indeed, this is a work in progress and requires not only action from the regulators but also contribution from the legislature and cooperation from the general public.  I hope that the private sector will support our initiatives and will do its own share in safeguarding the integrity of our financial system.

Finally, I would like to thank the organizers of this meeting for giving me the opportunity to share with you our efforts to combat money laundering.

Thank you.


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

[1] Among the other countries identified as non-cooperative were Bahamas, Cayman Islands, Cook Islands, Israel, Lebanon, Liechtenstein, Marshall Islands, Nauru, Nieu, Panama and Russia.

[2] Recommendation 21 of the FATF states that “[f]inancial institutions should give special  attention to business relations and transactions with persons, including companies and financial institutions, from countries which do not or insufficiently apply these [FATF] Recommendations [on the creation of an effective anti-money laundering framework]. Whenever these transactions have no apparent economic or visible lawful purpose, their background and purpose should, as far as possible, be examined, the findings established in writing, and be available to help supervisors, auditors and law enforcement agencies.” 

[3] Imprisonment from 10 to 20 years and  a fine of not less than P1.0 million nor more than twice the value of the monetary instrument involved; turnover of money laundering proceeds in favor of government; and denial of  plea bargain

[4] The anti-money laundering bills include:  Senator Robert Z. Barbers’ Governing Law on Racketeer-Influenced Activities (GLORIA) Act of 2001; Senator Panfilo Lacson’s  Anti-Money Laundering Act of 2001; Senator  Loren Legarda-Leviste’s  Money Laundering  Control Act of 2001; and Representative Herminio G. Teves’ House Bill No. 282 amending the Secrecy Law on Bank Deposits.

Title: Remarks on Signing of Syndicated Notes Facility Agreement
Occasion: Signing Ceremony, P5 Billion ROP Syndicated 3-and 5-Year Fixed Rate Notes Facility
Speaker: Governor Rafael Buenaventura
Transcription:
I am pleased to witness the successful completion of this undertaking by the National Government today.

For the record, the Monetary Board has approved in principle the issuance of these new class of notes.  In approving this issue, the Board took note of the significant benefits that could accrue to the economy, particularly in terms of helping stabilize the exchange rate market by providing an alternative outlet for investors.  Other important benefits to the economy include the estimated significant savings for the National Government and the expected easing of the pressure on domestic interest rates.

It is for these reasons that the participation of the lenders in this exercise is much appreciated.  The strong investor demand indicated by the 2.5 times over-subscription from the original offer of P5.0 billion sends an important signal that investor confidence in the Philippine peso and in the basic soundness and resiliency of the Philippine economy remains.

Indeed, this positive investor response is an encouragement for us in government to sustain our efforts towards establishing further structural reforms in key areas of the economy.

On the part of the Bangko Sentral, we remain committed to maintaining price and foreign exchange stability conducive to a balanced and sustainable economic growth.    Our recent efforts towards this end include the expansion of the coverage and maturity structure of our Currency Risk Protection Program to provide a hedging mechanism to a greater number of foreign exchange users.    At the same time, we have given notice to those who insist on testing the limits of existing prudential regulations on foreign exchange transactions that the full force of the law will be strictly enforced, with monetary and non-monetary sanctions meted to violators.  We, therefore, encourage all concerned to make the most of the opportunities and alternative mechanisms being provided by government to help promote greater stability in the markets.

In closing, I would like to extend my congratulations to the Department of Finance for successfully steering this project into completion with, of course, the expert assistance from its official arranger, the Hong Kong and Shanghai Banking Corporation, and the crucial participation of the various lending investors.

Thank you and good day.

(Note: Signing Ceremony, P5 Billion ROP Syndicated 3-and 5-Year Fixed Rate Notes Facility, July 25, 2001, Executive Lounge, Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas)

Title: Moving Towards Bank Excellent and Financial Stability in the 21st Century
Occasion: Turnover Ceremonies & 1st General Membership Meeting, Bank Administration Institute
Speaker: Governor Rafael Buenaventura
Transcription:
The newly elected officers and directors of the Bank Administration Institute, Philippine Chapter (BAIPHIL), members of the Institute, distinguished guests, friends in the banking industry, ladies and gentlemen, good afternoon.

It is my pleasure to attend this gathering of distinguished members of the domestic banking community.  Throughout the years, the BAIPHIL has proven to be an important partner in providing training and research to the banking community.  In particular, the Institute has made significant contributions in upgrading the knowledge and skills of the industry as the banking sector has evolved from relatively insular leanings to a more mature and global-oriented system.

A sea of change

The Philippine banking system has undergone a series of reform episodes in the past.  These reform measures were aimed at enhancing the market-orientation of the sector and upgrading the supervisory and regulatory framework governing banks.  The banking system is now reaping some of the “reform dividends” as it was able to withstand and recover quickly from the adverse effects of the 1997 financial crisis.

            Today, the banking system continues to be sound, showing its fundamental strength in many respects.  Assets continue to grow to almost P3.0 trillion as of end-March 2000.  The capital adequacy ratio of commercial banks, which at 17.24 percent as of March 2000, remains well above international standards.  Asset quality has been manageable, with the non-performing loan ratio at 14.41 percent as of May 2000, without the use of public money to bail out distressed financial institutions.  Moreover, banks have also increased their loan loss provisioning in compliance with the higher provisioning requirements. The current favorable state of the banking system is an indication that, indeed, the banking system has avoided the worst effects of the Asian crisis.

            The past decade also saw the rapid transformation of financial markets and institutions across the globe.  The international financial system has grown in size, breadth and complexity as markets became more integrated and as financial instruments multiplied and became more sophisticated.  One underlying force behind this transformation is the adoption of policy reforms in different countries that favored greater openness of domestic economy.  Another driving force consists of the technological advances made in the fields of telecommunications and information processing.  These two forces combined to substantially reduce transaction costs and build a global network of financial markets that transcends geographical boundaries, national borders and time zones.

What are the implications of this new environment to emerging economies?  On the one hand, the wave of reforms and innovations has led to increased access to foreign capital which helped propel emerging economies to higher growth rates.  On the other hand, the wave of change has also brought about periods of financial turbulence that spread rapidly across borders.  We do not have to look far back to recall the debilitating effects of the 1997 Asian financial crisis.

            The challenge is to be able to meaningfully take part in this increasingly globalized financial community while diminishing—if not completely avoiding—the adverse impact of financial crises.

Responding to global opportunities and  challenges

A key lesson from our experiences in weathering the Asian financial crisis is that banking sector soundness and financial diversity can help limit the effects of economic disturbances.  But how do we achieve this objective of soundness and diversity in the financial sector in an increasingly globalized environment?

You may be aware of our recent initiatives but let me share with you what we have done so far to advance the cause of extending the frontier of financial opportunities. 

Upgrading supervision practices

            One of the priorities of the BSP is the upgrading of its supervision capability.  If the supervisory system is to remain effective in fostering the safety and soundness of the country’s financial system, it must adjust to the changing structure of that system.

The on-site examination, off-site monitoring and analysis techniques of the BSP have been improved.  We are now adopting a forward-looking and risk-based framework.  This is more dynamic than the purely compliance-based and checklist-driven approach.  The bank examination process includes an assessment of the capability of banks to detect, evaluate and respond appropriately to their risk exposures.  Included is the consideration of the independent assessment of rating agencies in evaluating the risk carried by banks’ loan portfolios.  Equally important, we have also begun implementing consolidated supervision of financial conglomerates to better assess bank risks.  Furthermore a first-generation early warning system has been started to facilitate the evaluation of bank solvency. 

Upgrading prudential standards

Domestic standards have been brought closer to international best practices, in such areas as capitalization, connected lending, loan concentration, loan provisioning, data disclosure and qualifications of owners and managers.

A key initiative has been the passage of the General Banking Law 2000, which gives the BSP more flexibility in supervising the banking industry and upgrades the country’s banking laws to meet global standards.  The law also liberalizes foreign participation in domestic banks, provides stricter rules on DOSRI loans, adopts fit and proper principle in the appointment of senior bank officers and promotes greater transparency in bank practices.

In this connection, we have created a task force to ensure that policies and procedures are in line with the New General Banking Law.  Critical areas of implementation include the issuance of regulations implementing a risk-based capital adequacy standard, guidelines for bank closure and receivership, and the identification of unsafe and unsound practices.

Related to this successful advocacy program, the BSP continues to push for the amendment of the New Central Bank Act (R. A.No.7653).  These legislative measures aim to enhance the supervisory and enforcement powers of the BSP and further improve prudential standards for the banking system, among others.

One of the exciting developments in the banking industry is the advent of electronic banking.  As the volume of transactions involving this type of technology increases, the identification, assessment, management and control of the attendant risks should be properly evaluated.  Recognizing this, the BSP issued Circular No. 240 on 5 May 2000 outlining the requirements imposed on banks seeking to provide electronic banking services.  This is to ensure that banks that are planning to provide these services, have in place a risk management process that is adequate to assess, control and monitor associated risks.  It is instructive to note that the passage into law of the E-commerce Act last 14 June 2000 provides the legal framework that will facilitate the exchange of information and promote the security of electronic transactions.

Recently, we called off the last stage of the planned increase in capital requirements and extended the deadline of the 1999 capitalization requirements to end-2000.  This is to provide banks breathing space in their capital build-up program as the BSP remains flexible in the implementation of prudential regulations during this recovery period.  Banks will now be required to carry differing levels of capital in accordance with the risk level of their respective portfolios. 

Enhancing market discipline

To enhance market discipline we have supported greater disclosure and transparency among market players.  New regulations now require the inclusion of detailed information on non-performing loans and other risk assets, loan loss reserves, return on equity and insider (DOSRI) loans in banks’ quarterly disclosures.  The new public disclosure framework should improve the access of creditors, investors and depositors to the necessary information to assess risks properly.  More recently, the BSP has intensified its drive against money laundering.  Financial institutions have been required to establish and record the true identity of all their clients.  They have also been required to give special attention to all complex, and all unusual patterns of transactions which have no apparent or visible lawful purpose.

Establishing  sound infrastructure

The BSP is likewise a keen supporter of efforts to establish a sound financial infrastructure.  Key components of this financial infrastructure include accounting standards, legal systems that protect property rights and enforce contracts, bankruptcy provisions and sound payment and settlement arrangements.

Currently we are preparing for the eventual adoption of Real Time Gross Settlement System. This should augur well in eliminating payments risks and reducing transactions costs in the banking transactions. 

Banking excellence

While the BSP endeavors to create the appropriate regulatory and supervisory environment for the entire banking system, sound decisions at the individual bank level is indispensable to the creation of a sound and effective banking system in this rapidly changing environment.

To achieve excellence in this new environment, management must adopt mechanisms to safeguard the bank from unsound transactions and to warn management of vulnerabilites even before they reach critical levels.

I think these factors—appropriate risk management and innovativeness—are two of the key elements that will continue to define bank excellence in the new millennium. 

Concluding remarks

The quest for financial stability and bank excellence is a never ending task. The BSP will continue to be vigilant and will continue to work in addressing the perceived threats to the overall health and soundness of the financial system.

Let me therefore close my remarks by encouraging the institute to continue its close partnership with the regulatory authorities to help achieve excellence within individual banking institutions and soundness across the financial system.

Thank you.

(Note: Turnover Ceremonies and First General Membership Meeting, Bank Administration Institute (BAIPHIL), July 18, 2000 Shangri-La Hotel, Makati City)

Title: Monument More Enduring Than Bronze
Occasion: Citibank Reunion, Citibank's 99th Anniversary
Speaker: Governor Rafael Buenaventura
Transcription:
Thank you, Cathy, for the generous introduction.  I would like to assure you that despite the likelihood of salary reductions in the Government that you have been hearing about, I am not here to try to get back my old job in Citibank.

Kidding aside, I am most happy to be here at this reunion among friends and familiar faces, and be able to greet each other on this particular anniversary celebration of Citibank, our alma mater in more ways than one.  I assume that this reunion is the beginning of a year-long series of activities that will culminate in a big centennial celebration next year.  One hundred years is a long time and Citibank has all the good reasons to celebrate especially in the Philippines where it can very well make a legitimate claim for some credit in the country’s growth and development.

I would like to thank Cathy and her staff for giving me the honor of being your special guest at this reunion.

If you come to think of it, one does not need to organize a formal reunion to see a gathering of former Citibankers.  We are such a big family now that in any gathering of bankers there are bound to be a number of Citibank alumni present.  Each meeting of the Board of the Bankers Association of the Philippines, for example, can be a mini-reunion of sorts  However, we are careful not to always call attention to this fact.   In the Bangko Sentral, I hear that we ex-Citibankers there are referred to in jest as the “Citibank mafia.”

On the other hand, it should be with a certain amount of pride on the part of Citibank to see the names of its former officers associated often with important events.  Note the announcement in the newspapers last week about the Monetary Board approving the appointment of Equitable PCIBank as the depository bank of the Social Security System.  One can call that a Citibank family affair with the three chief executives involved in the arrangement being all ex-Citibankers.

If I remember correctly, the first Citibank alumni reunion took place in 1980 on the 78th anniversary of the bank.  I was Regional Treasurer based in Hong Kong at the time  This was a public relations project to correct the impression created in the newspapers that the fast turnover of Citibank officers in those days was the result of a personnel management problem.  That reunion showed that the officers left the bank not because of pique or resentment but because they were lured by higher pay and position to join other institutions.  This was the first time that the effectiveness of the Citibank training program came to the surface.  Citibank instantly became known as the “University of Banking” churning out officers who could go all the way up to the most senior positions in the institutions that they joined.  The idea of gathering the alumni to show how successful the people trained in Citibank have become was subsequently copied in other countries.  Whether one agrees with it or not, it became a spectacular way for Citibank to show its contribution to the development of managerial talent in a country.

The second major reunion in Manila took place on the occasion of my departure as Philippine CCO in 1985 to become the first Asian Division Executive in Europe.  By then, it was common knowledge that the frequent source of managerial talent for banks was Citibank.

I am sometimes asked to explain how this phenomenon came about.  I think it all started when top management in New York decided that Citibank grow 15% per annum.  The bank could do that only if it had a cadre of people to make it happen.  Conventional wisdom up to that point was that banking had to be learned over a period of years.  So young people became apprentices for 4 or 5 years before they could become an officer of a bank.  Citibank decided to put an end to that mindset.  Citibank said that anyone who had an MBA from a good school could be taught to become a manager in one year and be given a position of responsibility immediately.  The Citibank executive training program was really an experiment of giving responsibility to young people who had a good academic background but very little experience.

Looking back now, I believe that the Philippines was the testing ground to determine whether the executive training program worked well or not.NN Modesty aside, I think that all of the ladies and gentlemen in this room will agree that it did.

I can speak about my own experience.  I joined the Executive Training Program in the Philippines in 1965 and with me in that class were Xavier Loinaz, Bill Go and Teddy Montecillo.    George Vojta ran the program.  George was the same visionary who, as EVP in New York eventually, wrote Walter Wriston’s highly successful 10-year program that catapulted Citibank to a dominant position worldwide.

In 1971 I agreed to join the international staff and my first assignment was to take charge of a joint venture project with Fuji bank.  I was not quite 30 yet with only six years in the bank and the fellow from Fuji reporting to me was in his 40’s with some 20 years of experience.

There is no doubt in my mind that the good balance between the training program and the increasing amount of responsibility that came with every new assignment defined my personal development as a manager.  I stayed in Citibank until 1989, just a few months short of qualifying for membership in the Quarter Century Club.

And yet Citibank is to be admired not only for its training program.  Its history in the last 99 years, beginning with the acquisition of the Asian branches of the International Banking Corporation, which included those in Cebu and Binondo, is replete with sincere efforts to help in the economic development of the country.

Citibank is known to have pioneered in funding the development of export products and went on to help in the task of rebuilding industries and infrastructure after the Pacific War.  As Filipino entrepreneurs assumed positions of leadership in Philippine business, Citibank became a source of important financing for taking over companies established by the Americans.

The late governor Gregorio Licaros loved to tell the story when, just before Martial Law, the reserves of the Central Bank were down to one million dollars and the country had maturing obligations of two hundred million dollars in two months.  It was the Citibank country head, Rick Wheeler, who led the campaign to persuade other banks in New York to join the consortium to lend the money that the Philippines urgently needed.  The maturing loans were repaid and the Government paid off the new loans in five years.

I had my own chance to play a role in resolving a crucial issue during the restructuring of the Philippine debt after the Aquino assassination in 1983.  It was a delicate balancing act that I had to do.  I was expected not to pull a fast one on the Philippines but neither would I give away the family jewels, so to speak.  I left for Europe for my new assignment after the debt moratorium was put in place.  I can say now that, despite the recriminations that followed, Citibank tried its best to help the Philippines at that crucial time.

Citibank today is the only foreign bank with three office buildings in Metro Manila, a testament no doubt to its unbending commitment and confidence in the future of the Philippines.

Let me conclude by coming back to the reunion and saluting everyone here and those who, I am sure only for reasons of space, could not get to Cathy’s short list for the picture taking this morning.  And I choose to paraphrase Tony Ozaeta who spoke as president of the bankers association of the Philippines during the first alumni homecoming in 1980.  He said, addressing the alumni, that “(Your) achievements are in a manner the achievements of the institution that reared (you), a monument more enduring than bronze.”

Congratulations to Citibank on its 99th anniversary and good morning to all of you.

(Note: Citibank's 99th Anniversary, Citibank Reunion, July 13, 2001, Shangri-La Manila, Makati City)

Title: Anniversary Message
Occasion: 8th Year Founding Anniversary, Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas
Speaker: Governor Rafael Buenaventura
Transcription:
Today, as we celebrate the founding anniversary of the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas, we look back at how we as an organization braved the stormy weather of the past year since our last anniversary, and how we faced up to the difficult challenges to emerge a stronger institution.

The eighth year of the BSP saw us continuously working to fulfill our primary mandate of maintaining price stability conducive to balanced and sustained economic growth.  We faced serious shocks to the domestic economy, in the form of the rise in international oil prices to record levels and the volatility in the foreign exchange market, which saw the peso breach the P55 level against the dollar for the first time.  We had to deal with the financial impact of domestic political tensions, as the nation grappled with questions about political leadership and public governance.

It was a difficult time, to say the least, but the bank was able to rise to the challenge.  Indeed, where there are challenges, we do not see problems but opportunities.  In response to the emergent inflationary pressures and the narrowing interest differentials that were contributing to the volatile exchange rate, we pursued a tight monetary policy stance through a series of increases in our key policy interest rates in may and in September-October 2000.  The underlying objective of our actions at the time was to stabilize the economy.  And true enough, as the foreign exchange market started to stabilize, we gradually eased monetary policy to help create a more supportive environment for business activity.  This easing was continued with the resolution of the political crisis and the expectation of lower inflation.  Since December last year, the BSP has reduced its key policy rates by a total of 600 basis points.

We also set about strengthening further our banking system, first by working on the implementing rules of the General Banking Law of 2000, which was signed into law in may 2000.    Various BSP circulars were issued pertaining to foreign stockholdings, outsourcing, microfinance loans and risk-based capital adequacy standards.  At the same time, our examiners have also made the shift from a purely compliance-based and checklist-driven assessment of banks’ conditions to a forward-looking and risk-based framework.  These initiatives will help improve banks’ risk management along with their ability to efficiently intermediate funds, and enhance their effectiveness as transmission channels of monetary policy.

All these efforts have paid off in terms of improved fundamentals for our economy.  At present, we have low and stable inflation, a sound banking system, and improving economic activity.  The prospect of a benign inflation environment this year has enabled us to adopt an accommodative monetary policy to help stimulate investments and strengthen domestic demand.    Further monetary actions will continue to take into account the various risks to the inflation outlook so as not to jeopardize the stable, low inflation environment.

Meanwhile, on the homefront, we worked on the challenge of organizational renewal at the BSP and the task of improving ourselves as an institution.  An institution is only as strong as the set of personal values of its members.  Thus, we successfully launched our work attitude and values enhancement program, which sought to impart the set of positive values that all of us, officers and employees alike, should have as public servants.  We also saw to the needs of our own employees by providing various benefits and grants in the course of the year.  For example, we increased the food subsidy and medical insurance and provided a transportation allowance for the non-SSL exempt class.

We also marked another year of successful financial operations, which we are celebrating with contributions to the national coffers.  Over the past eight years, the Bangko Sentral has managed to remit more than P65 billion in dividends and taxes with an initial capitalization of only P10 billion.  This does not include our dividend remittances to the National Government of P2.1 billion, which we will be presenting to president Gloria Macapagal-Arroyo this Friday.  The funds should help build up government finances and help our fiscal authorities meet the fiscal targets for the year.

As we complete another year in the unfolding history of the BSP, I feel greatly encouraged by our performance in the past 12 months with respect to our mandate of safeguarding price stability and the health of the Philippine financial system.  Theodore Roosevelt once said that the best prize in life is the chance to work hard at work that is worth doing.  I believe that our pledged stewardship of the Philippine economy is of central value to our economic development.  The local and international business communities recognize the BSP’s efforts to keep prices low, the peso generally stable and interest rates reasonable as key elements in the performance of the Philippine economy.

We must always keep in mind, however, that what made all of this possible was the human element—the unique individual contributions of all our employees, from the top rung to the lowest level of the organizational ladder.  Our mission at the BSP, therefore, is one that we must all pursue singularly, with a firm commitment to constant self-improvement and self-renewal.  Let me, therefore, congratulate all of you, my colleagues at the Bangko Sentral, for your hard work and your commendable performance.

In the year ahead, we will again have our hands full.  Our preparations will continue for our planned shift to inflation targeting as a framework for monetary policy.  The shift to inflation targeting will increase the accountability of the central bank and raise transparency in the conduct of monetary policy.  It will thus help provide a credible and forward-looking policy framework that further strengthens our focus on price stability.

Last year, we worked hard for the passage of the amendments to the New Central Bank Act (R.A. No. 7653), but as you all know, we ran out of time in the last congress.  This was one of the most anticipated pieces of legislation for most of us here, since these amendments will help us create a better and more competitive working environment at the Bank and help us attract the best talent available.  More importantly, these measures will enhance our supervisory powers and operational independence, further improve prudential standards for the banking system, promote more competition in the banking sector.  This year, we will redouble our efforts to push for these amendments when the new Congress begins its session.

At the same time, we will also continue to push for further reforms in the banking system for improved risk management and more efficient financial intermediation.   The BSP also supports the global drive against money laundering, and will push for the passage of a comprehensive Anti-money Laundering Law.  This is in addition to the range of administrative measures that we have undertaken unilaterally to show our commitment to the global fight against money laundering.   Together, these measures are expected to avoid possible additional costs in our cross-border transactions and should have a beneficial impact on good governance.

In addition to all this, our April 2001 corporate planning conference list of agreements contains various initiatives aimed at enhancing the BSP’s image, improving corporate governance, and addressing human resource concerns.  It is going to be a busy year, indeed.

Looking back at my experience so far as BSP Governor, I realize that the life of a central banker is not for those who desire an easy life.  It is not for the timid, nor for the indolent.  But as a wise man once said, “Do not pray for easy lives.  Pray to be stronger men.  Do not pray for tasks equal to your powers.  Pray for powers equal to your tasks.  Then the doing of your work shall be no miracle, but you shall be the miracle.”

Maraming salamat at mabuhay po tayong lahat na bumubuo ng Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas.

  (Note: 8th Year Founding Anniversary, Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas, July 03, 2001, Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas Complex, Manila)

Title: The Role of the Philippine Banking Sector in the Promotion of Sustainable Development
Occasion: Launching & Signing of the BAP Statement on Environment and Sustainable Development
Speaker: Governor Rafael Buenaventura
Transcription:
Secretary Alvarez, Undersecretary Bernardo, Dr. Mapa, Mr. Leung, Ms. Macalincag, distinguished guests, colleagues in the financial community, co-workers in government, ladies and gentlemen, good afternoon.

One of the visions embodied in our medium-term development plan is an economic growth path that is sustainable across all generations of Filipinos.  This implies the protection of our environment and the efficient utilization of our natural resources in ways that would meet the needs of the present generation without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs. The realization of this vision is a collective responsibility which demands the commitment and cooperation of the entire spectrum of society—including the government, business and private individuals.

The Banking Sector and Sustainable Development

I commend the initiatives of the local banking community to contribute to the attainment of this vision. The signing of the Statement on Environment and Sustainable Development by the Bankers Association of the Philippines (BAP) is an explicit signal of the community’s firm commitment to environmental protection and the conservation of natural resources. Integrating such a commitment into a bank’s corporate philosophy is a very laudable move of the banking community for it bespeaks of corporate responsibility.

The Statement affirms the principles that good ecology is sound economics and that being pro-environment is pro-development.  Indeed, good environmental practices and a credible financial performance can go hand in hand. Integrating environmentally sound practices into daily banking operations and management systems can lead to reduction in costs and help maximize earnings. Specific programs including those that reduce energy and paper consumption, limit waste production, and promote recycling contribute to the efficiency of banks’ work processes. These initiatives can provide clear benefits to the bottom line of banks as well as promote environmental protection.

Beyond these company-specific environmental objectives, banks—as intermediaries of financial resources—are actually in a distinct position to influence businesses to play a major role in promoting sustainable development. Bankers can do this by including environmental criteria in their overall lending and investment strategy. Banks can, therefore, be more pro-active in supporting projects that are environmentally sound. There are new and expanding opportunities in environmental markets and services including those in cleaner technologies and eco-tourism which can yield both environmental and financial dividends.

Banks can also help propagate the environment ethic among their corporate-clients. A study of Burton Hamner, formerly of the Asian Institute of Management, suggests that companies are willing to adopt clean technology and invest in pollution prevention if they have an accurate picture of how these activities can help minimize costs in the long term. Banks can help in this area by identifying and advising corporations about the financial and economic costs of pollution and the advantages of adopting cleaner production technologies. This requires, however, that banks develop expertise on environmental cost and benefit analysis to complement their financial analysis in their role as financial advisers to projects with significant impact on the environment.

To push the principles embodied in the Statement a bit further, the banking sector can engage in a range of activities to foster private environmental investment. The banking sector can undertake information-sharing programs regarding best practices and effective environmental management tools so that bank customers themselves can strengthen their own capacity to reduce environmental risks. Furthermore, financial institutions can support more intensive collaborative efforts with a broader set of stakeholders regarding environmental concerns to increase the level of environmental awareness nation-wide.

The trend towards greater environmental activism is actually a global phenomenon. With the signing of this Statement, the local banking industry joins a growing international community of financial institutions that are engaged in activities to promote the integration of environmental concerns in the operations of financial institutions. This international effort has been spearheaded by the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) Financial Institutions Initiative. [1] Since 1992, more than 170 financial institutions from more than 40 countries have signed the UNEP Statement by Financial Institutions on the Environment and Sustainable Development. In fact, several Philippine banks are already among the signatories of this UNEP Statement.[2]

Concluding Remarks

This occasion marks an important step in the banking community’s effort to contribute to the drive for environmental protection and sustainable development. I believe that environmental issues will generate more attention and will become increasingly integrated with core business activities in the future. Thus, I challenge the banking community to translate these environmental commitments into practical actions on a sustained basis while working within the framework of market mechanisms. I am thus impressed that some members of the banking community have started to incorporate environmental concerns in their policies and have began to adopt environmental programs.
