I wish to congratulate the Bankers Association of the Philippines (BAP), the Chamber of Thrift Banks (CTB), and the Rural Bankers Association of the Philippines (RBAP) for initiating this activity for the environment. I would also like to thank the Development Bank of the Philippines (DBP) for hosting this affair and taking the lead in environmentalism among banks. This event emphasizes one social dimension of banking which is corporate responsibility and this should augur well for all the stakeholders of the Philippine financial community.

Thank you.


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

[1] http://unepfi.net

[2] Bank of the Philippine Islands, Development Bank of the Philippines, Global Business Bank, Land Bank of the Philippines, Metropolitan Bank and Trust Company, Philippine Bank of Communications, Planters Development Bank, Rizal Commercial Banking Corporation.

Title: Opening Statement
Place: BSP Institute, Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas
Occasion: Seminar Briefing for FOCAP Members
Speaker: Governor Rafael Buenaventura
Transcription:
It is indeed a pleasure to have with us today members of the Foreign Correspondents Association of the Philippines (FOCAP) as participants in this Briefing-Seminar on Key Central Banking Issues.  This is a welcome event for us at the Bangko Sentral, for it gives us the opportunity to discuss important issues with the foreign press, who are in the forefront of the efforts to bring the Philippines to the radar screens of investors and the global financial community.  It also provides a forum for a constructive exchange of views since this format has room for clarification and elucidation.  I am also glad to see the members of the press corps covering the BSP and the Department of Finance.

The presentations that we have prepared for this seminar-briefing focus on issues relating to monetary policy and banking that are of current interest.  I understand that you have been advised of the topics well in advance.  All the presentations will be made by key officials of the Bank so that you are able to have a reading of these issues from the most authoritative sources.

As an aside, we have indicated earlier that the rehabilitation of PNB would be one of the issues for discussion.  However, we have decided to present alternative issues instead, in deference to the PNB’s newly appointed Board of Directors that is now in the process of addressing the more problematic issues concerning the bank.  Once these issues are settled, we—in coordination with the PNB Board—will be glad to inform you of the results.

There will be three presentations today.  The first one, which will be presented by Deputy Governor Tetangco of the Banking Services Sector, Research and Treasury, will be on inflation targeting.  As you well know, inflation targeting will be our new framework for monetary policy.   By adopting it, we hope to improve further the transparency and consistency of monetary policy as well as the accountability of the Bangko Sentral to the price stability objective.  In turn, greater price stability is expected to promote the efficient functioning of markets and encourage longer term saving and investment.

The second topic, which will be presented by Deputy Governor Reyes of the Supervision and Examination Sector, will be on key banking reforms, particularly in the context of the Basel Agreements.  His presentation will deal with measures that are intended to improve the Bangko Sentral’s supervisory capabilities.  This upgrading includes the adoption of a more forward-looking and risk-based supervision framework and the implementation of a consolidated supervision of financial conglomerates.

The third presentation, which will be given by our General Counsel, Atty. de Zuñiga, will focus on the latest developments in the Government’s anti-money laundering campaign, particularly the proposed bill to be introduced in the next Congress.  This bill consolidates the salient features  of  related bills filed in the previous congress and reflects feedback from public consultations.  We consider the passage of this bill into law as a testament to our commitment to the fight against money laundering.

These selected presentations point to the Bangko Sentral’s continuing efforts to fulfill its primary mission of promoting price stability conducive to sustainable growth and of keeping the banking system sound and resilient amidst the challenges that it faces.

Let me also take this opportunity to inform you about the key results of my recent trips to Singapore and Basel, Switzerland.

In Singapore, where central bankers in the region gathered together for a two-day International Monetary Conference, the participants focused on the need to further strengthen the structural reforms that are being implemented in their respective economies, with a view to reducing their economies’ vulnerability to external shocks.   Participants also discussed the existing economic peer review process in the ASEAN and ways to improve this as well as the Currency Swap Arrangements among the ASEAN members, which were expanded to include China, Japan and South Korea, under what is known as the Chiang Mai Initiative.  These moves highlight the spirit of regional cooperation that promotes the pursuit of sustainable and prudent macroeconomic policies in each of the countries in the region.

In Basel, more than 100 central bankers from around the world met for the annual Shareholders’ Meeting of the Bank for International Settlements.   The meeting also underscored the need for closer ties among individual economies as a result of increasing globalization and the emerging uncertainties in the international economy.  Like the meeting in Singapore, this gathering also highlighted the need for greater cooperation among individual economies to improve their resiliency to external shocks.

The discussions in the two meetings confirm that the Philippines is on the right track in its steadfast implementation of a policy reform agenda aimed at fostering a vibrant domestic economy amidst the global headwinds.  At the same time, the results of the discussions confirm that there remains much to be done in terms of minimizing the external vulnerabilities of individual economies and of preparing them for greater regional and global integration.

With this note, I will end my remarks to give way to our presenters.  I certainly hope that this will be an interesting and fruitful seminar for all of us.

Thank you and good day.

 (Note: Seminar-Briefing for FOCAP Members, June 25, 2001, BSP Institute, Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas)

Title: Closing Address
Occasion: 5th SEACEN Course on IT Risk Management in Banking Supervision (Advanced Level)
Speaker: Governor Rafael Buenaventura
Transcription:
Good evening.  It is a pleasure to address this audience of banking supervisors participating in the 5th SEACEN course on it risk management in banking supervision.

The thrust of this training course is consistent with our efforts, here in the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas, to continually update our regulations and our expertise in banking supervision.

The rapid development of information and communication technologies has revolutionized the way business is being conducted all over the world.

As expected, banking institutions have been quick to take advantage of the new technologies in providing electronic banking services to their clients and in transacting with counterparties.

In the last two years, for instance, the use of mobile phones for messaging and the internet, has generated unprecedented interest worldwide.

It has spawned a new entertainment and business medium for both corporate and consumer users.  As reported in the May 31, 2001 issue of the Far Eastern Economic Review, 15 billion messages were sent in December 2000 globally; a five-fold increase over the previous December, according to the GMS association, a London-based wireless-industry group.

Indeed, Asia is now out-texting the rest of the world!  With the trial launch three weeks ago (May 31) of new mobiles by Japan’s mobile carrier, NTT Do Co Mo, the race is on in providing 3G (third generation) services, such as video conferencing and high-speed internet access, through mobile phones.

As regulators and examiners, we have to keep abreast with the developing technology particularly in internet banking and in mobile banking.  We need to understand them to be able to evaluate the risks that banks contend with in highly computerized environments --- in line with our mission to promote and maintain a stable and healthy banking system.

For our part, the Bangko Sentral has issued circulars specifically aimed at regulating the new trends in the banking industry.  We have guidelines for banks intending to offer electronic banking services as well as enhancements to approved electronic banking services.

I understand that this course gave you first hand exposure on information technology (IT) audit using the Federal Reserve Banks’ model and the latest regulations in the United States.

You also had briefings on risk issues and computer fraud arising from electronic banking and the risk analysis, prevention and contingency measures to address them.

You were also given a bird’s eye view on the latest developments and future trend of it in the financial sector so you can study their implications on banking supervision.

We thank the SEACEN Centre, its course officials and staff for setting up this specialized course.    We give special thanks to Mr. Cheong Kwok Yew, Director for Training and Administration, and Ms. Doris Wong, the Course Coordinator.

We also thank the Bangko Sentral officers and staff, particularly the members of the various committees and working groups for ensuring the smooth conduct of the course.

We are especially grateful to the excellent resource persons for sharing their expertise.    They are:

  • Mr. Bradley Beytien from the Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City

  • Mr. Tony Chew from the Monetary Authority of Singapore

  • Mr. Ang Swee Leong from Arthur Andersen & Co. – Malaysia

  • Ms. Bella Valdez from Sycip, Gorres, Velayo & Co. – Philippines, and

  • Mr. Teodoro Panganiban from the Union Bank of the Philippines.

Congratulations to the participants --- all 37 of you --- for completing the course!

We are confident that you are now better equipped for the tasks awaiting you in your respective central banks and monetary authorities.

Thank you and have a pleasant evening.

 

 (Note: Closing Ceremony, 5th SEACEN Course on IT Risk Management in banking Supervision (Advanced Level, June 20, 2001, Westin Philippine Plaza Hotel)

Title: Laying the Foundation for Higher Gear
Occasion: Annual National Convention, Rural Bankers Association of the Philippines
Speaker: Governor Rafael Buenaventura
Transcription:
A pleasant good afternoon to all of you.

I am very pleased and honored to again have this opportunity to address the rural banking community on the occasion of its National Convention.  I am quite encouraged by your choice of principal convention theme, “Rural Banks:  Moving to High Gear”, because it suggests to me a strong resolve and a readiness by the rural banking industry to engage whatever challenges head on and thus continue to be of service and relevance to our economy and your respective communities.

However, how effective we are in achieving our goals and in meeting our commitments is ultimately a function of our own preparation to take on the challenges.

Rural Banking System Today

How is the rural banking system today?  Much like the rest of the banking industry, the rural banking system is still struggling to fully recover from the impact of the Asian financial crisis and its subsequent fallout on the economy.

However, the rural banking system as a whole has proven to be quite resilient notwithstanding the higher number of bank closures in recent years.  Indeed, despite the tough banking environment, the rural banking system’s asset base still grew by a respectable 8.5 percent last year.  A major factor supporting asset growth was the continuous mobilization of deposits which increased by nearly 16 percent.  This compares very favorably with the less than 9 percent deposit growth in commercial banks.

I am also heartened to note that traditionally high capitalization ratios of around 16-17 percent of total assets have been maintained.  This is an important factor that secures public confidence.

But we must also accept that the system remains under stress.  This is clearly reflected in the high level of non-performing assets (consisting of non-performing loans and acquired assets) and in the relatively low industry profitability.

As of end-December 2000, the ratio of non-performing assets to total assets averaged about 20 percent for the industry.  This is far too high by any measure.

Not surprisingly, the large component of non-performing assets has created a drag on bank profitability and increased the cost of financial intermediation.  In the last three years, the average return on equity has remained stuck at only around 8.5 percent.

Given this overall picture, clearly the industry will be well advised to prioritize and to promote the basic improvement of asset quality among its membership.  Otherwise, this will be a severely limiting factor that could consign many banks into permanent low gear. 

Need for Action

For many rural banks, there is need to move quickly and aggressively to reduce the volume of non-performing assets and to accelerate the build up in loss provisions against non-performing assets.   As of end-December 2000, the total provisions represent only about a quarter of total non-performing assets, thus adding to the concern on underlying solvency.

The Bangko Sentral will soon be coming up with new proposals to induce banks to accelerate the build up in loss provisions especially on acquired assets which have rapidly accumulated.   At industry level, we hope that the RBAP will take a leading role in exploring viable options for orderly balance sheet clean-up that respond to the special needs of the rural banking industry without necessarily calling for the expediency of a government bail-out which will just be a non-starter given current fiscal realities.   For example, in commercial banks, we are aware that there are now initiatives to set up private asset management companies as a market-driven solution to this type of problem.

Admittedly, the short-term measures to mitigate bad assets will add to the pressure on rural banks but they may be our most pragmatic responses.  The alternative of simply waiting for better times to roll in to outgrow the problem may prove too little, too late and condemn a bank to mediocre performance for a long time.  That will probably be costlier in the long run for the banks’ stakeholders and for the economy.

On the other hand, banks that act decisively can expect faster recovery and thus be in a strategically advantageous position for a quick rebound as the economy recovers.

At present, the new administration is firmly committed to attaining a moderate but sustainable economic growth rate.  The Bangko Sentral will actively support that objective by keeping inflation low, interest rates reasonable, and the exchange rate relatively stable.  Already, interest rates today are at their lowest since the Asian financial crisis in 1997 and we have made significant progress in reducing exchange rate volatility. 

Further reform initiatives

Looking back at the experience, there is clearly a need to further strengthen the institutional capability of our banks to deal with risks, especially credit risks, in a disciplined manner that promotes financial safety and soundness without unreasonably hampering profitable operations.   After all, a healthy banking system must first of all be a profitable system.

In addressing these issues from a regulatory perspective, we are being guided by evolving international best practices particularly in the critical areas of institutional governance and transparency, risk-based capital, and risk management.   The common denominator of these initiatives is to promote institutional self-control rather than to impose external constraints and limits on business decisions.

In order to promote better bank governance, the monetary board recently approved Circular 283 which clearly defines the duties and responsibilities of the Banks’ Board of Director both collectively and as individuals.  It is based on the principle that the Banks’ good governance is the primary responsibility of the Board of Directors.  The new Circular amends Circular 130, issued in 1997 by expanding on the key duties and responsibilities in line with best international practice.    Among the new features, it calls for the Board to:   (1) conduct the affairs of the bank with high degree of integrity; (2) monitor, assess and control management performance; (3) adopt and maintain adequate risk management policy; (4) meet regularly; (5) keep individual directors and shareholders informed; and  (6) conduct regular performance assessments of all key personnel including the Board of Directors.    The Circular also aims to have a Board of Directors composed of competent and active members who can each contribute to the effective governance of the institution and the attainment of its objectives.

Moreover, there will be a follow-on Circular in the near future which would implement fit and proper tests for directors and officers as provided for in the new General Banking Law.  One of the requirements will be for all bank directors to undergo at least a one-day seminar where they will be given orientation on their duties and responsibilities and other related topics.  The same Circular will also operationalize the concept of independent director of which two must be present in the Board of Directors as provided for in the new General Banking Law.

We are now also reviewing the current rules on disclosures with the end in view of expanding the amount of relevant information now required to be regularly provided to the public.    The objective is to let the market have sufficient basis for making informed decisions on the financial performance and condition of a bank so that good bank behavior will be promoted.  It is increasingly clear that the lack of information to the public in the past has made it easier for bank management to misbehave.  It also placed too much burden on the already overstretched resources of bank supervisors.

Another initiative that Bangko Sentral will be pursuing is the strict implementation of risk management standards in our banks in the context of a risk-based examination approach.  For example, it is our experience that far too few of our banks have sufficient systems in place to systematically review their loan portfolio and assign proper risk classifications and provisions as may be warranted.  Many banks have come to rely on Bangko Sentral examiners to do this for them and this has hampered the efficient conduct of bank examinations.  Under risk-based examination, our examiners will now increasingly focus on the quality of a bank’s internal decision making processes rather than auditing its transactions.

And as you are now also probably aware, we also recently issued Circular No. 280 prescribing risk-based capital requirements.  Essentially, it is a standard that matches the bank’s capital against its risk-weighted assets and prescribes a minimum capitalization ratio of 10 percent.   This further reinforces our emphasis on proper deployment of the bank’s resources with due regard to the trade-off between risk and return. 

Microfinance Opportunities

We are complementing our new regulatory initiatives by recognizing the potential role of microfinance as a banking product that fits the reinforced risk management standards while allowing our banks especially rural banks to meet the credit needs of the enterprising poor.

In this regard, I would like to commend the RBAP for its proactive role in working with foreign donors and experts to mount a viable microfinance program in select rural banks in Mindanao.   I understand that because of its success, the new technology is now being propagated to other rural banks and other areas outside Mindanao.

On our part, the Bangko Sentral has rapidly responded to this new development by issuing implementing rules to allow collateral free microlending based on well-defined and proven standards.   We have also partially lifted the moratorium on the establishment of new banks to accommodate the formation of microfinance-oriented banks.   Finally, we have opened a rediscount window for microfinance loans of qualified banks to encourage the participation of existing banks.

We are strongly supporting legitimate microfinance programs because it delivers much needed credit to a segment that has long been denied adequate credit access.  It is a potentially powerful weapon to combat poverty.  At the same time, it is an opportunity for upgrading the credit management skills of our smaller banks and for introducing them to state-of-the-art but user-friendly information technology specifically adapted for credit risk management. 

Concluding remarks

Let me now conclude my presentation.

I strongly believe that our rural banking system will continue to play a very important role particularly in the delivery of banking services to our countryside and to economic groups that have the greatest need for economic opportunities.  Because of this, it is vital that you succeed.

However, success is not a birthright.  It is something that you need to constantly work for.  The business of banking has undergone profound change in the last couple years as competition has intensified, globalization became more pervasive and as financial market volatility has become more entrenched.   All of these require new approaches both in the way banking is conducted and the way it is regulated and supervised.  Rapidly, the margin for complacency is being eliminated for all of us.

I am confident, however, that the rural banking community will stay attuned to the new realities and that it will evolve new strategies and remake itself with the same determination and tenacity that has enabled it to hurdle so many challenges in the past.

Thank you and good day.

Title: Policy Thrusts and Prospects in an Uncertain Global Economic Environment
Occasion: General Assembly Meeting, Japanese Chamber of Commerce and Industry
Speaker: Governor Rafael Buenaventura
Transcription:
Introduction

Ladies and gentlemen, good evening.

It is a great pleasure to join this gathering of the officials and members of the Japanese Chamber of Commerce and Industry in the Philippines.  The Japanese business community has been an important partner of the Philippines in our drive to boost investments and create more employment opportunities.

The close economic ties of the Philippines with Japan are seen in the significant trading and investment relations between the two countries.  Japan is the third biggest market for Philippine exports, accounting for about 15 percent of Philippine goods sold abroad in 2000.  Also, imports from Japan accounted for almost 20 percent of total imports.  Furthermore, Japanese companies contributed more than US$1.8 billion in direct investments in the last 3 years, about 21 percent of the total foreign direct investment inflow during that period.[1]   In fact, for the first quarter of this year, this trend continued as several big Japanese corporations reportedly expanded their operations in the Philippines.[2]

One may observe that the trend for large Japanese corporations now is to look for alternative manufacturing bases which offer cheaper labor.  We believe, and I think most of you would agree,  that the Philippines enjoys certain key advantages as an alternative destination for investments.  The labor cost in the country remains relatively competitive.  More importantly, the Philippines offers a large pool of highly skilled professionals including engineers.  The Government has also been consistent in its policy of encouraging investments, providing various incentives to priority investment areas.

One advantage of the Philippines as an investment site, which we are trying to reinforce, is the relatively stable macroeconomic environment.  Another advantage is the sound and efficient domestic banking system.  These are areas which the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP) has an active participation in, and will be the focus of my talk in the next few minutes.  However, before focusing on the developments and issues in the monetary and banking sectors, I will first elaborate on the key elements of the domestic and international environment that policymakers and the private sector have to contend with. 

A Challenging Environment

We are all aware that the Philippines was subjected to episodes of domestic political tensions since late last year.  Increased political tension was experienced during the impeachment proceedings last year, the EDSA II People Power in January, the arrest of the former President in April, and the violent May 1st rally.  Depreciation pressures on the peso and decline in stock prices accompanied these events.  Nevertheless, the Philippines emerged with its democratic institutions intact and with the basic strength of its economy preserved.  We have undergone a peaceful transition of Government that has been upheld by the Supreme Court.  Even as some recent controversy has surfaced, the foundations for a stable political infrastructure—which is essential for the viability of long-term investment in the country—have been laid.  Moreover, the impact of the political disturbances on financial markets are temporary and this is reflected in the subsequent recovery of the peso-dollar rate and in the rebound in the performance of the Philippine Stock Exchange Composite Index.  The generally peaceful conduct of the recently concluded National Elections also galvanizes the strength of democratic institutions in the country.

While the domestic political environment continues to improve, we meet today at a time of great uncertainty for world economic growth.  This challenging external environment, highlighted by the slowing down of the U.S. and Japanese economies, looms as a dark cloud over the horizon for both developed and developing economies.  This development could have significant effect on the economic performance of Asian economies in view of the importance of the U.S. and Japanese markets as destinations for exports and as a source of investments.  Specifically, growth in the export sector could be expected to soften and the inflow of foreign investments could be subdued.   On the other hand, lower interest rates and growth prospects in developed economies could lead to a reallocation of capital portfolios.  Whether or not this will lead to strengthened capital inflows to particular economies will depend on the ability of those economies to demonstrate good track records in terms of attaining macroeconomic and financial stability, and to lay down, through appropriate structural reforms, the foundations for sustainable economic growth.  The Philippine Government is aware of this, and in response has strengthened its commitment to implementing sound and consistent macroeconomic policies as well as pursuing the necessary reform agenda.

Let me now focus on what the BSP is doing to contribute to macroeconomic stability and to the structural reform process. 

Monetary Developments and Policy Stance

The focus of monetary policy for this year will continue to be the maintenance of low inflation while providing sufficient liquidity to meet the country’s growth requirements.  Inflation averaged 6.8 percent during the first four months of 2001.  This is within the Government’s target of 6-7 percent for the whole year.  Moreover, expected improvements in supply conditions and stability in the foreign exchange market suggest that inflationary pressures will abate starting the second half of this year, and these increase our confidence that the inflation targets will be met. These favorable expectations have actually supported some flexibility in the conduct of monetary policy.    Benign inflation for the first quarter of the year, improving but still relatively weak domestic demand, the presence of spare capacity, and broad exchange rate stability justified monetary easing.    Since December 2000, the BSP has reduced policy rates by a total of 550 basis points. The overnight borrowing (RRP) and lending (RP) rates now stand at 9.5 percent and 11.75 percent, respectively, back to the levels a year ago.  The benchmark 91-day Treasury bill rate fell from an average of 12.23 percent in January 2001 to 9.90 percent in April, while average bank lending rates fell from a range of 16.46-18.23 percent to 13.49-15.11 percent during the same period.  From zero growth in January 2000, outstanding loans of commercial banks rose by 5.7 percent year-on-year in February 2001.  The decline in interest rates is expected to have a pro-growth bias as it would provide impetus for investment and consumption.

The BSP’s commitment to price stability will be enhanced further by the adoption of inflation targeting as the framework for monetary policy in the second half of 2001. By stabilizing prices, inflation targeting will encourage longer term saving and investment, and will deepen the role for longer-term financial intermediation.

With some volatility in most currencies of the region, we likewise reiterate our commitment to maintain a market-oriented foreign exchange rate policy under a freely floating exchange rate system.  Exchange rate determination will be left to market forces, with some scope for occasional actions to maintain orderly adjustment in the foreign exchange market. 

Banking sector developments and the reform process

The Philippines’ banking system remained fundamentally sound amidst the Asian financial crisis and the challenges that faced us last year and in more recent periods.  This resilience by the banking sector is demonstrated by several key indicators.

The banking system’s total resources increased on an annual basis by 18.6 percent, to P3.5 trillion in January 2001.  This represented a significant improvement over the 10.5 percent growth as of end-December 2000.

Asset quality remained manageable.  As of February 2001 the non-performing loan (NPL) ratio of commercial banks stood at 16.48 percent. The NPL ratio of commercial banks has been within the 14-16 percent range for about a year now.  However, the broad stability in the exchange rate and the decline in interest rates as well as the pick-up in bank lending activity are expected to have a favorable impact on banks’ NPL situation in the future.  It may also be noted that no public funds have been used in the Philippines to purchase non-performing assets or recapitalize financial institutions.

The banking system remained adequately capitalized.  As of end-December 2000, the average capital adequacy ratio reached 16.4 percent, well above the BSP statutory floor of 10.0 percent and the Bank for International Settlement’s (BIS) standard of 8.0 percent.

Preliminary data on the real estate exposure of commercial banks showed that the ratio of real estate loans to total loans declined slightly to 11.3 percent as of end-December 2000, from 11.6 percent at end-December 1999. The current ratio remained far below the 20 percent ceiling imposed by the BSP.

The credible performance of the banking sector in the past few years may be attributed to the wide-ranging reform measures started even two decades ago.  In fact, the BSP has continued to undertake steps to further strengthen the financial system in recent years.  Let me discuss briefly some of these recent policy actions.

The BSP has instituted major reforms in financial supervision and regulation.  The recently passed General Banking Law of 2000 (Republic Act No. 8791) provides the overarching framework for financial regulation.  Under this framework, financial reform efforts continued to be geared towards strengthening the banking system, improving transparency, putting in place internationally accepted standards relating to risk-based capital adequacy, and enhancing competition in the banking system.  An avenue for fostering competition is through the further liberalization of the ownership participation of foreign banks in the local banking system to 100 percent within seven years after the effectivity of the GBL 2000.  The BSP has tasked a committee to formulate the implementing rules of the new law.  So far, Circulars have been issued pertaining to foreign stockholdings, outsourcing of banking functions, guidelines on microfinance loans and the adoption of risk-based capital adequacy standards aligned with international norms.  Other areas being reviewed by the committee pertain to revised guidelines governing the composition of the board of directors of banks, the observance of the fit and proper rule on the management of banks to better protect depositors and the general public, and revised guidelines governing the single borrower’s limit.

To further improve risk management in the financial system, the BSP continued to institute regulatory changes:

The BSP has changed the focus of its supervision from a purely compliance-based and checklist-driven assessment of banks’ conditions to a forward-looking and risk-based framework.    The BSP has also begun to supervise financial conglomerates on a consolidated basis, including consolidation of limits on foreign currency exposures between banks and their affiliated foreign exchange corporations, and a consolidated approach to addressing bank solvency.

The BSP, in collaboration with the Bankers Association of the Philippines (BAP), is upgrading the existing payment system into a Real Time Gross Settlement System (RTGS) that will cover transactions in the equities, fixed income, money and foreign exchange markets.  Once fully operational, the RTGS would offer a powerful mechanism for limiting settlement risks.

In response to current trends towards increased use of the internet in banking, the BSP has laid down the requirements for banks seeking to provide e-banking services. This is to ensure that banks planning to provide these services have in place a risk management process that is adequate to assess, control and monitor associated risks.

To promote bigger-capitalized banks that can be better equipped to meet the demands of the new globalized environment, the BSP continues to encourage mergers and consolidations through the provision of incentives.  The policy also reduces moral hazard since owners have more of their wealth at stake.

In response to the global drive against money laundering, the BSP, since July 2000, has undertaken important actions on the matter. We have issued a number of Circulars in 2000 which bring the country’s regulatory regime on anti-money laundering closer to international standards.    These Circulars require banks to take reasonable means to determine the true identities of their clients and report suspicious transactions.  In addition the BSP continues to actively support initiatives—including legislation—aimed at enhancing the effectiveness of activities to curb money laundering activities.

On the legislative front, the reforms in the General Banking Law of 2000 will be complemented by the proposed amendments to the New Central Bank Act.  These amendments aim to enhance the BSP’s supervisory powers and operational independence, improve prudential standards and promote greater competition in the banking system. Key reforms would include the grant of authority to the BSP to conduct more frequent banking examinations and greater scope and strength of administrative sanctions. 

Concluding remarks

With the improvement in the domestic political environment, we see the uncertainty of the global economic environment as one of the major challenges for policymakers.  In response, we continue to enhance our commitment to fighting inflation and to pursue the needed financial sector reforms.  We believe this strategy would form the sound basis for a sustained non-inflationary growth and for continued viability of long-term investments in the country.  For this year, we expect the country’s GNP to expand by 4-4.5 percent and by another 4.9-5.4 percent next year. Meanwhile, inflation is seen to average 6-7 percent for the whole year and by 5-6 percent next year.

We have no doubt that the economy can again weather any challenge that external factors may pose for this year.  The prospects are favorable for long-term investments and I hope that all of you will continue to be our partners in our drive for strong economic growth.

Thank you and good evening.

Title: An Assessment of Philippine Compliance with International Standards in Banking
Occasion: "The Implementation of Financial Architecture in Asia - An ADB-FSF Seminar"
Speaker: Governor Rafael Buenaventura
Transcription:
I am deeply honored to participate in this seminar on the implementation of a strengthened financial architecture in Asia.

In the Philippines, particularly in the banking system, we have intensified our structural reform efforts in response to vulnerabilities highlighted by the Asian financial crisis.  These initiatives have significantly improved our compliance with the core principles for effective banking supervision as articulated by the BASLE Committee. 

Key Strengths of the Philippine Banking System

Even prior to the core principles, the Philippines already had in place a set of basic banking laws that establish a clear and reasonably effective legal framework for the supervision and regulation of the banking system.   We believe that this has been instrumental in somewhat mitigating the impact of the Asian financial crisis on the banking sector.

The General Banking Act, comprehensively updated and amended into the General Banking Law of 2000, is a key element of the legal framework that defines the chartering of Philippine banks, prescribes binding standards of prudent behavior, and defines their manner of supervision.

The General Banking Law is closely complemented by the Central Bank Act of 1993 which established an independent central bank, the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP), that has primary responsibility for both monetary policy and the supervision of the banking and financial system.      The independence of the BSP in discharging its responsibilities is guaranteed by no less than the Philippine constitution.

We also have a long-established deposit insurance system administered by the Philippine deposit insurance corporation (PDIC), patterned after the U.S. FDIC, that forms part of the safety net.  The PDIC supports the oversight of the safety and soundness of the banking system and plays a role in the orderly resolution of problem banks.

The supervisory framework defined by these basic laws and institutions provides US with the ability to readily uphold a critical mass of the BASLE core principles for effective banking supervision. 

Recent enhancements

As duly noted by the World Bank, we have been taking additional steps since 1997 to further upgrade our compliance with international banking standards.   These include:

Structural improvements:

Consolidation of the banking sector through incentives for mergers and acquisitions, restrictions on branch expansion, higher capital requirements, and greater foreign competition.

Better prudential regulation:

Implementation of risk-based capital requirements, tighter loan classification and provisioning rules, implementation of mark-to-market on securities portfolio, better consolidated reporting, tighter implementation of connected lending limits, limits on real estate exposure, and more conservative collateral valuation.

Improved supervision:  

Shift from checklist approach to measurement of risks, monitoring of top 200 borrowers, better on- and off-site supervision, higher monetary penalties, expanded powers for inspectors, improved and formal plans for prompt corrective actions, development of systemic contingency plans, and better coordination between BSP and PDIC.

Improved intelligence and transparency:  

Implementation of a basic early warning system as well as a bank performance rating system, and more comprehensive and timely industry analysis. 

Improved management of market risks:  

Better matching of foreign currency assets and liabilities, expanded liquidity cover against foreign currency liabilities, closure of regulatory loopholes on transactions of bank-affiliated FOREX corporations.

Improvements in corporate governance and disclosure:  

Accreditation of external auditors, specifications of duties and responsibilities of bank directors, fit and proper tests for directors and officers, reporting of suspicious transactions, “know your customer” rules, fuller disclosure of shareholders, quarterly publication of statement of condition and key financial indicators as well as non-performing loans, and related party lendings. 

Challenges ahead

Notwithstanding the significant progress to date on banking reforms, we remain acutely aware of remaining gaps that hamper our full compliance with the core principles.  These will be addressed, many in the context of new legislation.

A key legislative priority is the further strengthening of the legal framework for resolving distressed banks by providing, among others, the BSP and PDIC with sufficient powers to override consent of existing shareholders in cases of severe capital deficiency.  We are also seeking better protection for regulators from suits and other legal challenges in the exercise of their duties.    These would involve further amendments to basic banking laws particularly the general banking law and the charters of the BSP and the PDIC.

We are also working for a comprehensive law that will criminalize money laundering activities and facilitate the cooperation of banks and other financial institutions in related investigations.   To support anti-money laundering efforts and to strengthen the general ability of supervisors to monitor abuses in the banking system, we are likewise seeking a judicious dilution of current highly restrictive deposit secrecy laws to achieve a more reasonable balance between protecting the confidentiality of deposits and preventing the use of the banking system to hide criminal activities.   In particular, we favor allowing bank supervisors to look into suspicious deposit transactions strictly following a well-defined administrative process.

In addition to the preceding legislative priorities, the BSP will continue to push for other amendments to the BSP charter which we believe will further strengthen its institutional capacity to discharge its duties independently and effectively.  These include full exemption of BSP personnel from salary standardization and the exemption of BSP from taxation especially on its open market operations.  We are also seeking greater flexibility to impose higher monetary penalties when appropriate, to conduct consolidated supervision of banks and their non-bank subsidiaries and affiliates as well as their parents, to determine the frequency of on-site examinations, and to impose additional capital requirements on individual banks when warranted by specific risks.

In addition to legislative initiatives, we are emphasizing the training of bank examiners in risk-based examination.  We are also reviewing examination procedures accordingly.  To strengthen off-site surveillance, we are accelerating our shift to electronic reporting and are increasing our investment in electronic databases and computer-based analytical tools.

Finally, we are working closely with other regulators particularly the PDIC and Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) to further strengthen coordination in the supervision of banks and their non-bank affiliates.

Conclusion

The Philippines is firmly committed to strengthening its banking and financial system in response to the challenges of globalization by putting in place critical structural reforms and fully adopting a supervisory framework in accordance with best international practices.  We have already made significant progress.  We are determined to complete the task.

Thank you.

Title: Current Thrusts in Monetary Policy and Financial Supervision and Regulation
Occasion: Investors' Meeting - JP Morgan, 34th ADB Annual Meeting
Speaker: Governor Rafael Buenaventura
Transcription:
I.  Introduction

Ladies and gentlemen, good afternoon.

It is a great pleasure to address this investor meeting on the prospects and potentials of the Philippine economy.  My thanks go to JP Morgan for organizing this discussion, and I am quite sure that the informal and intimate atmosphere of our meeting is conducive to a frank discussion of issues.

This afternoon, my presentation will center on the monetary and financial sector.  Dr. Dante Canlas, Secretary General of the National Economic Development Authority, will meet with you tomorrow and talk about the Philippines’ general economic prospects, including the fiscal sector.     I will therefore:

  •   Discuss the stance of monetary policy in the light of current developments in the domestic and international environments;

  •    Then update you on the present state of the Philippine banking system, and go over the policy reforms that the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas has done to strengthen the financial system and prepare the system to meet the challenges presented by globalization; and finally,

  •    Present the policy reform agenda for the medium term.

The Philiipines was tested in both political and economic terms last year.  The political scenario was clouded by hostilities in Mindanao and by concerns about public governance, while economic challenges included rising world oil prices and the tightening of U.S. monetary policy, which included a weakening of the peso and other regional currencies.  Nevertheless,  the Philippines emerged with its democratic institutions intact and with the basic strength of its economy preserved.  It is worthy to note that a peaceful transition of government has been effected, the Supreme Court has upheld the constitutionality of the new government, and recent events have enhanced the credibility of the judicial system.  Even as some recent controversy has surfaced, the foundations for a stable political infrastructure - which is essential for the viability of long-term investment in the country - have been laid.  The impact of the May 1 disturbance is temporary: an indication of this is that financial markets improved the following day, with a 4.14 percent recovery in the Philippine Stock Exchange Composite Index and an appreciation of the exchange rate to P51.00/$ on 2 May, from P51.34/$ on 30 April 2001.  These reflect the business sector's support for continued stability of the government  

II.   Monetary policy considerations over the near term

An important challenge to the Philippines’ economic performance for this year comes from external developments —specifically, from the anticipated slowdown in the US and Japan.  This could impact disproportionately on the ASEAN economies, and on the information technology (IT) sector in particular, in view of the importance of the U.S. and Japanese markets as destinations for ASEAN exports.  However, I am sure that you have noted the considerable uncertainty with respect to the duration of the slowdown.   An IMF paper, for example, argues that there is a chance that recovery could start in the second half of 2001.

The impact on emerging market economies such as the Philippines is likely to be two-pronged.  Growth in the export sector could be expected to soften and the inflow of foreign investments could be subdued.  On the other hand, lower interest rates and growth prospects in developed economies could lead to a reallocation of capital portfolios.  Whether or not this will lead to strengthened capital inflows to particular economies will depend on the ability of those economies to demonstrate good track records in terms of attaining macroeconomic and financial stability, and to lay down, through appropriate structural reforms, the foundations for sustainable economic growth.  The Philippine government is aware of this, and in response has strengthened its commitment to the reform agenda.

The focus of monetary policy for this year will continue to fall on the maintenance of low inflation while providing sufficient liquidity to meet the country’s growth requirements.  Inflation averaged 6.8 percent during the first quarter of 2001.  This is within the Government’s target of 6-7 percent for the whole year.  Moreover, recent developments have suggested that inflationary pressures will abate starting the second half of this year, and these increase our confidence that the inflation targets will be met. These favorable expectations have actually supported some flexibility in the conduct of monetary policy.  Benign inflation for the first quarter of the year, improving but still relatively weak domestic demand, the presence of spare capacity, and broad exchange rate stability justified monetary easing.  Since December 2000, the BSP has reduced policy rates by a total of 550 basis points.  The overnight borrowing (RRP) and lending (RP) rates now stand at 9.5 percent and 11.75 percent, respectively, back to the levels a year ago.                The benchmark 91-day treasury bill rate fell from an average of 12.23 percent in January 2001 to 9.90 percent in April, while average bank lending rates fell from a range of 16.46-18.23 percent to 13.43-15.11 percent during the same period.  From zero growth in January 2000, outstanding loans of commercial banks rose by 5.9 percent year-on-year in February 2001.   Flexibility in monetary management will help support the attainment of the 4-4.5 percent growth target for GNP in 2001 and contribute to the prospects for investments.

The BSP’s commitment to price stability will be enhanced further by the adoption of inflation targeting as the framework for monetary policy in the second half of 2001. By stabilizing prices, inflation targeting will encourage longer term saving and investment, and will deepen the role for longer-term financial intermediation.

With the current volatility in most currencies of the region, we likewise reiterate our commitment to maintain a market-oriented foreign exchange rate policy under a freely floating exchange rate system.  Exchange rate determination will be left to market forces, with some scope for occasional actions to maintain orderly adjustment in the foreign exchange market. 

III.   State of the Philippine Banking System

Through the Asian financial crisis and the challenges that faced us last year and in more recent periods, the Philippines’ fundamentally sound financial system has served us in good stead.   A two-decade history of close supervision, sustained banking reforms, and implementation of timely pre-emptive measures have helped develop a financial system that is able to withstand transitory shocks arising from both domestic and external sources.  Key banking sector indicators reflect this:

  •   The banking system’s total resources increased on an annual basis by 18.6 percent, to P3.5 trillion in January 2001.  This represented a significant improvement over the 10.4 percent growth as of end-December 2000.

  •    Asset quality remained manageable.  As of end-2000, the non-performing loan (NPL) ratio of the banking system was 15.0 percent, higher than the 12.7 percent recorded at end-1999.  The NPL ratio of commercial banks stood at 16.5 percent in February 2001.  While the ratios have fallen faster in some of the other affected Asian economies, these declines have reflected largely the off-loading of NPLs to public restructuring agencies.  By contrast, no public funds have been used in the Philippines to purchase non-performing assets or re-capitalize financial institutions.

  •   The banking system remained adequately capitalized.  As of end-December 2000, the average capital adequacy ratio reached 16.4 percent, lower than the previous year’s 17.5 percent but well above the BSP statutory floor of 10.0 percent and the Bank for International Settlement’s (BIS) standard of 8.0 percent.  The decline in the capital adequacy ratio was attributable to the increase in the required valuation reserves.

  •    Preliminary data on the real estate exposure of commercial banks showed that the ratio of real estate loans to total loans declined slightly to 11.3 percent as of end-December 2000, from 11.6 percent at end-December 1999.  The current ratio remained far below the 20 percent ceiling imposed by the BSP.

In the face of the anticipated correction in international equity markets for 2001 and the subdued mood for foreign investment, the financial sector’s efficiency in fund intermediation and risk management would play a key role in determining how well the Philippine economy performs this year.   Let me, therefore, discuss some of the recent steps that the BSP has undertaken in order to further strengthen the financial system.

IV.    Reforms and policy directions

The BSP has instituted major reforms in financial supervision and regulation.  The recently passed General Banking Law of 2000 (Republic Act No. 8791) provides the overarching framework for financial regulation.  Under this framework, financial reform efforts continued to be geared towards strengthening the banking system, improving transparency, putting in place internationally accepted standards relating to risk-based capital adequacy, and enhancing competition in the banking system, including through further liberalizing the ownership participation of foreign banks in the local banking system to 100 percent within seven years after the effectivity of  the GBL 2000.    The BSP has tasked a committee to formulate the implementing rules of the new law.  So far, circulars have been issued pertaining to foreign stockholdings, outsourcing of banking functions, guidelines on microfinance loans and the adoption of risk-based capital adequacy standards aligned with international norms.  Other areas being reviewed by the committee pertain to revised guidelines governing the composition of the board of directors of banks, the observance of the fit and proper rule on the management of banks to better protect depositors and the general public, and revised guidelines governing the single borrower’s limit.

To further improve risk management in the financial system, the BSP continued to institute regulatory changes:

  •    The BSP has changed the focus of its supervision from a purely compliance-based and checklist-driven assessment of banks’ conditions to a forward-looking and risk-based framework.   The BSP has also begun to supervise financial conglomerates on a consolidated basis, including consolidation of limits on foreign currency exposures between banks and their affiliated foreign exchange corporations, and a consolidated approach to addressing bank solvency.

  •    The BSP, in collaboration with the Bankers Association of the Philippines (BAP), is upgrading the existing payment system into a Real Time Gross Settlement System (RTGS) that will cover transactions in the equities, fixed income, money and foreign exchange markets.  Once fully operational, the RTGS would offer a powerful mechanism for limiting settlement and systemic risks in the interbank settlement process.

  •    In response to current trends towards increased use of the internet in banking, the BSP has laid down the requirements for banks seeking to provide electronic banking services.  This is to ensure that banks planning to provide these services have in place a risk management process that is adequate to assess, control and monitor associated risks.

  •   To promote bigger-capitalized banks that can be better equipped to meet the demands of the new globalized environment, the BSP continues to encourage mergers and consolidations.  The policy also reduces moral hazard since owners have more of their wealth at stake.  The BSP offered incentives in support of this policy, including allowing banks to amortize their goodwill up to a maximum period of forty (40) years.  

In response to the global drive against money laundering, the BSP, since July 2000, has undertaken important actions on the matter, including new regulations and cooperative actions with the private sector.  Thus, the BSP required banks to report activities pertaining to large financial transactions and unusual patterns of transactions that have no apparent lawful purpose.  Banks and non-bank financial institutions were also required to take reasonable measures to establish and record the true identity of their clients. The coverage of anti-money laundering regulations was extended to offshore banking units.  An anti-money laundering working group from the Bankers Association of the Philippines and the BSP is currently preparing an operating manual for banks against money laundering.   Recognizing the importance of legislation, the BSP is advocating the passage of House Bill No. 5216, also known as the Anti-Racketeering Bill, which would make money laundering a crime in the country.   A proposed amendment to the BSP Charter would also allow the monetary board to inquire into deposit accounts of a suspicious nature.  These actions bring the country’s regulatory regime on anti-money laundering closer to international standards.

On the legislative front, the reforms in the General Banking Law of 2000 will be complemented by the proposed amendments to the New Central Bank Act.  These amendments aim to enhance the BSP's supervisory powers and operational independence, improve prudential standards and promote greater competition in the banking system.  Key reforms would include the grant of authority to the BSP to conduct more frequent banking examinations and greater scope and strength of administrative sanctions.

V.    Conclusion

I hope my presentation has convinced you that the Philippines not only has an active commitment to its structural reform program, but that the program has also been kept forward-looking and abreast of the latest developments.  With the improved political environment and the fundamental strength of the economy backed up by the government’s firm commitment to needed reforms, there is sound basis for a sustained non-inflationary growth and for continued viability of long-term investments in the country.  There is therefore no doubt that the economy can again weather any challenge that external factors may pose for this year.  Prospects are, therefore, favorable for long-term investments, and I am sure that this is an important consideration in your portfolio decisions.

Thank you and good afternoon.

 (Note: Investors' Meeting organized by JP Morgan, 34th  ADB Annual Meeting, May 8, 2001, Hilton Hawaii Village, Honolulu)

Title: Philippines: Monetary Sector, External Sector and the Financial System
Occasion: Country Presentation of the Philippine Panel, 34th ADB Annual Meeting
Speaker: Governor Rafael Buenaventura
Transcription:
Ladies and gentlemen, I am pleased to have the opportunity to be able to talk on two of the primary policy areas of the central bank of the Philippines:  Monetary Policy and the Banking System. 

Developments in the Monetary Sector

Inflation.   Inflation was relatively subdued.  In 2000, due to favorable weather conditions and the Central Bank’s resolve to keep monetary aggregates within programmed levels, the average inflation for 2000 was at 4.4 percent, well below the government’s full-year target of 5.0-6.0 percent.

During the first quarter of 2001, inflation averaged 6.8 percent, which was within the Government’s target of 6–7 percent for the whole year of 2001.

This year, inflation is expected to be relatively higher during the first semester due to the lagged effects of a weaker peso, higher petroleum prices and wage adjustments that happened in late 2000.   However, improvements in supply conditions and prospects for continued stability in the FOREX market are expected to contribute to a trend decline in  inflation in the second half, to around 5 percent by December.

Market and policy interest rates.   The 91-day T-bill rate averaged 9.9 percent in 2000, down from the 10.2 percent average in 1999.  However, the benchmark 91-day T-bill rate reached a peak of 16.7 percent in late 2000 (6 November auction) as the monetary stance was tightened.   Subsequently, the benchmark interest rate gradually declined as the Central Bank steadily eased its monetary stance due to the decline in political risk premium.

From December 2000 to  20 April 2001, the Central Bank reduced its policy rates by 550 basis points.  The overnight borrowing (RRP) and lending (RP) rates now stand at 9.5 percent and 11.75 percent.  They are back to the levels of a year ago.

Domestic liquidity and credit.  Domestic liquidity growth began to pick up in 2000, with m3 rising by an average of 12.1 percent during the year as economic growth strengthened.    Latest data shows that domestic liquidity grew by 12.8 percent in February 2001.

The expansion in domestic liquidity has been supported by increased bank lending.  From a zero growth in January 2000, outstanding loans of commercial banks rose by 5.9 percent in February 2001. 

Developments in the Foreign Exchange Market

The peso averaged P44.20/US$1 in 2000, depreciating by about 13 percent relative to the 1999 average peso-dollar rate.  The peso reached a high of about P55.00/US$1 at the height of the political crisis in mid-January.  However, since then the peso has strengthened steadily.  Of late, the movement of regional currencies, the emergence of corporate demand and some political tension have contributed to downward pressures on the peso, with the peso trading around P50- P51/US$  in April.

Developments in the External Sector

The gross international reserves of the country continues to provide a comfortable cushion to our external obligations.  As of end-March 2001 international reserves stood at US$14.7 billion which is about 4.4 months worth of imports of goods and services.

The external debt of the country also remains manageable at US$52.06 billion as of end-2000, with short-term obligations comprising only 11.0 percent of the total. 

Developments in the Banking Sector

The positive developments in the monetary and external sectors are complemented by the favorable performance of the banking system.

Capital adequacy.  The banking system is comfortably capitalized.  The banking system’s capital-to-risk assets ratio was 16.4 percent p/ as of December 2000, well above both the BIS standard of 8 percent and the statutory floor of 10 percent.  The successive increases in the minimum capitalization requirement of banks and the ongoing consolidation process helped Philippine banks maintain their relatively strong capital positions.

Quality of loan portfolio.  For commercial banks, their non-performing loan (NPL) ratio was at 16.0 percent in January 2001.  The NPL ratio of commercial banks has been within the 14-16 percent range for a year now.  However, the broad stability in the exchange rate and the decline in interest rates as well as the pick-up in bank lending activity are expected to have a favorable impact on banks’ NPL situation going forward.

Real estate exposure.   The exposure of commercial banks to the real estate sector continues to be moderate at 12.3 percent of total loans (as of end-September 2000).  This is well below the central bank’s ceiling of 20 percent. 

Central bank policy directions  As to the policy direction of the Central Bank... 

Monetary policy

The thrust of monetary policy will continue to be guided by the pursuit of the Central Bank’s primary mandate of maintaining price stability conducive to a balanced and sustained economic growth.  Expectations of a trend decline in inflation by the second half of this year and the stabilization of the financial markets gave the Central Bank scope to ease monetary conditions early this year.  As stated, the Central Bank reduced its key policy rates by a total of 550 basis points since last December.  The gradual relaxation of monetary policy should help establish a more supportive environment for business activity.

The Central Bank will continue to monitor and assess carefully the risk stemming from possible inflationary pressures.  Further Central Bank policy rate cuts will be calibrated vis-à-vis economic and financial developments, and would be considered carefully with a view to observing an appropriate differential with international interest rates.

To further improve the central bank’s capability to pursue its mandate of maintaining price stability, an inflation targeting framework will be adopted in the second half of this year.    Under this framework, government authorities will pre-announce the inflation target over a given time horizon.  If the target is not met, the central bank has to explain the reasons and spell out the measures that it will take to get back on track relative to the target.  This forward-looking framework is expected to help the central bank build its credibility by demonstrating consistent adherence to the price stability objective.  In the process, the framework will promote greater transparency in the conduct of monetary policy, thus facilitating more efficient markets, as well as greater accountability on the part of the monetary authorities. 

Exchange rate policy

The Central Bank will continue to support a floating exchange rate system, with some scope for occasional Central Bank action to smooth out sharp fluctuations and maintain orderly market conditions.  In this regard, the Central Bank continues to monitor developments in the foreign exchange market, with a view to determining the appropriate policy response. 

Banking sector policy

In the banking system, the Central Bank’s focus remains to be the promotion of a globally competitive banking system that is strong, sound and resilient as well as able to intermediate funds effectively and manage risks efficiently.

Legislative framework.  A key reform measure is the General Banking Law (GBL) of 2000 or R.A. No. 8791, which was passed last may 2000, now forms the basic legal fabric governing the banking system.  The law enhances the competitiveness of the banking sector, improves the prudential standards and strengthens the effectiveness of the central bank’s supervision over banks.  A number of circulars to implement some of the provisions of this new law have already been issued by the central bank including those pertaining to foreign stockholdings, outsourcing of banking functions, guidelines on microfinance loans and the adoption of risk-based capital adequacy standards aligned with international norms.

The reforms supported by the GBL 2000 will be complemented by the proposed amendments to the Charter of the Central Bank.  The amendments will reinforce the autonomy, authority and capacity of the Central Bank not only to regulate and supervise the banking system but also to more effectively implement monetary policy.  Key initiatives include the restoration of the tax-exempt status of the central bank; the relaxation of the deposit secrecy provision which would allow the monetary board to inquire into deposit accounts of a suspicious nature;  the grant of authority to the Central Bank to conduct more frequent banking examinations;  and the imposition of broader and more stringent administrative sanctions.

The Central Bank has also strengthened the efforts to combat money laundering activities.   We have issued a number of circulars in 2000 which bring the country’s regulatory regime on anti-money laundering closer to international standards.  These circulars require banks to take reasonable means to determine the true identities of their clients and report suspicious transactions.  In addition the Central Bank continues to actively support initiatives — including legislation — aimed at enhancing the effectiveness of activities to curb money laundering activities.

Supervisory and Regulatory Framework.  Aside from the changes in the country’s banking laws, an ongoing initiative by the Central Bank is the improvement of its supervisory framework in line with the evolving structure of the financial system.  This upgrading of capabilities would ensure that supervision will remain effective in fostering the safety and soundness of the country’s banking system.  An important step in this effort is the adoption of a more forward-looking and risk-based bank supervision framework.  This involves the re-orientation of the bank examination process towards improving the quality of decision processes rather than just compliance with rules and regulations.  Another dimension of the upgrading is the implementation of consolidated supervision of financial conglomerates. This approach facilitates a more comprehensive assessment of the risks involved in the banks’ activities.

The Central Bank has also started to improve the regulatory framework in anticipation of the expected growth of e-banking.  General guidelines for banks planning to offer e-banking services have been issued to ensure that they have rigorous internal controls and comprehensive risk management systems that can adequately take into account the risks involved in these new banking activities.  Existing rules and regulations are being reviewed continuously in order to align prudential standards with international best practices.

The Central Bank is also encouraging the restructuring of the local banking industry.   In a more globalized financial landscape, domestic banks need to mobilize sufficient capitalization and to strengthen risk management systems to compete in this challenging environment.  This strengthening can be assisted through mergers and acquisitions and through greater participation of foreign financial institutions.

In 1998, the World Bank granted a $300 million Banking Sector Reform Loan (BSRL) to the Philippines.  The BSRL was in support of structural reforms needed to help the banking system withstand difficulties faced by the Philippines during the regional financial crisis and build resistance against future shocks. The Philippine Government is on track with most of its reform commitments under the BSRL and has already drawn on part of the loan. One of the requirements for the release of the remaining tranches is the privatization of the Philippine National Bank (PNB).  Currently, the Government and the majority stockholders are developing measures to ensure the continuing viability of the bank.  They include various reforms in the bank’s structure and operations.  The steps being undertaken are preparatory to the eventual sale of the government’s equity either in a joint-sale or on its own.  Privatization is still the ultimate goal for PNB.

Market Infrastructure.   The Central Bank is also supporting the modernization of the market infrastructure for the financial system.  In line with this, a key initiative supported by the Central Bank is the upgrading of the existing payment system into a Real Time Gross Settlement System to enhance operational efficiency, reliability, speed and timeliness of payment transactions.  This will not only foster a more efficient banking system but also help develop the capital market.

Microfinance Loans.    The Central Bank is also extending support to the social development agenda of the government within the limits set by its charter.  In this regard, the Central Bank has released guidelines to govern the microfinance operations of banks.[1]   through this initiative, the Central Bank hopes to contribute to the efforts to bring more resources and opportunities to the marginalized sectors of our society.

Thank you and good day.


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

p/ Preliminary

[1] Last January, the Central Bank issued a circular on microfinancing loans to implement some of the provisions of the GBL. These provisions relate to the application of market-based interest rates by lending institutions to enable them to recover the financial and operational costs of their micro finance operations.  The Central Bank is also finalizing guidelines for the opening of a rediscount window for rural banks and cooperative banks engaged in microfinance. This facility will support small banks that have achieved efficiency in their microfinance operations, without sacrificing prudential standards.

Title: Sustaining Economic Recovery Through Sound Monetary Policy
Occasion: * 4th Monthly Business Meeting, Chamber of Real Estate & Builders' Association, Inc. (CREBA)
Speaker: Governor Rafael Buenaventura
Transcription:
Mr. Charlie Gorayeb, officers and members of the Chamber of Real Estate and Builders’ Associations, inc. (CREBA), distinguished guests, ladies and gentlemen, good morning:

I would like to begin by thanking CREBA for inviting me to its 4th  Monthly Business Meeting this year.  Occasions such as this one remind policymakers like myself about the importance of the dynamic and synergistic relationship between the government and the private sector in the efforts to sustain economic growth.

Introduction

Our shared task is to build a path to strong recovery and sustained non-inflationary growth.   As we gear up towards a more broad-based economic recovery in 2001, the role of the private sector becomes more important in providing the sustaining momentum for economic growth.  I speak in particular of the real estate sector as represented by groups such as CREBA with its large and influential membership.

The real estate sector is vital to the national economy as a prime mover of the housing sector.  Housing, as you know, has long been a priority program of the government both as a major component of social policy and an instrument for economic growth.  The role of housing as an essential channel for economic pump-priming is particularly important because of its impact on ancillary industries, which include the basic building materials sector and the construction sector.

On the other hand, the role of government, and the BSP in particular, in sustainable growth consists of providing a supportive economic environment for vigorous productive activity through sound and coherent macroeconomic policies.  I would like to discuss briefly with you this morning the BSP’s efforts in this regard and how they have affected the real estate and housing sector.

Ensuring a sustainable recovery

The BSP’s efforts to ensure a supportive macroeconomic environment have centered on preserving price stability, which is the BSP’s primary mandate, while also broadly supporting the economy’s output growth objective.  Ensuring a reasonably low level of inflation helps reduce the uncertainty in economic decision-making, so that individuals and businesses have a reliable basis for long-range decisions and plans.

Our efforts to keep inflation in check have so far been successful.  Actual inflation continues to be well on track relative to its projected path for this year, holding steady at 6.7 percent in March and averaging at 6.8 percent in the first quarter.  Latest readings on inflation also indicate a declining trend towards the end of the year.  This makes us confident that the inflation target of 6.0-7.0 percent for 2001 is well within reach.

The favorable inflation environment has also enabled us to provide broad support to the economy’s growth objectives. Over the last few months, the BSP has brought down interest rates through an accommodative monetary policy stance.  Beginning December 2000, key BSP policy rates were reduced by a cumulative 550 basis points.  This has led to the downtrend in market interest rates.  The 91-day Treasury bill rate, for example, has fallen from a high of 16.72 percent in November 2000, when political tensions were running high, to 9.855 percent at the latest auction on 23 April.  Similarly, banks’ lending rates have fallen to a range of 13.4-15.0 percent for the period 2-6 April 2001 compared to 18.3-20.1 percent in the first week of December. 

Benefits to the economy

Our policy actions have continued to pay off in terms of a healthier economic picture.    Recently, we have seen indications of stronger private demand in terms of rising power sales and faster growth in bank lending.  Meralco power sales rose by 9.4 percent year-on-year in February, up from the 6.3 percent increase registered in the previous month.  The total loan portfolio of our commercial banks has continued to grow steadily with a year-on-year increase of 7.8 percent in January.  With these positive indicators, we expect to see sustained economic activity this year, as quarterly GDP growth is expected to accelerate beginning in the second quarter to produce an average annual GDP growth of 3.8-4.3 percent for 2001.

The combination of subdued inflation, easing credit conditions and broad stability in the foreign exchange market should pave the way for a continued decline in interest rates in the remainder of 2001.  Lower domestic interest rates, together with improved financing conditions, should provide a boost not only to real estate and construction activity but also to the overall economy.  These conditions will allow domestic demand to take over the reins of growth while external demand remains weak due to the global economic slowdown.  Business confidence is part of the key to raising domestic demand and the best way for the government to boost private sector confidence is to reaffirm its abiding commitment to policy reforms.

In this regard, we realize as well that financing is vitally important to the key economic sectors such as real estate and housing. To this end, the BSP has continued to pursue reforms to create a stable, sound and globally competitive banking and financial system.  We believe that better financial intermediation will give freer rein to vigorous business activity.

Broad key measures in banking and financial reform include the implementation of the General Banking Law (GBL) of 2000 (R.A. No. 8791).  The GBL is aimed at strengthening and modernizing the basic legal framework for the banking system.  It is also expected to foster greater public confidence in the banking system through better supervisory and enforcement capability of the BSP, improved prudential and regulatory standards, and greater competition in the banking industry.  This will be complemented by proposed amendments to the Bangko Sentral Charter aimed at reinforcing the BSP’s autonomy, authority and capacity to both regulate the banking system and implement monetary policy more effectively.  Other initiatives include the improvement of the BSP’s supervisory framework (for example, through the adoption of forward-looking and risk-based bank supervision) and the strengthening of the local banking industry through consolidation and increased participation of foreign financial institutions.

The BSP is also supporting the development of our capital markets through the modernization of the market infrastructure of the financial system (via the upgrading of the existing payment system into a real time gross settlement system) and the promotion of the securitization of long-term deposits to help spur domestic savings and deepen the local capital market.
