The package of BSP initiatives also comprises specific issuances aimed at supporting the housing sector.  These include BSP Circular No. 211 (dated 29 September 1999), which established a BSP rediscounting window for the socialized and low-cost housing loan papers of qualified commercial, thrift and rural banks.  We also issued a Circular-letter (dated 23 November 1999) exempting loans to low- and middle-cost housing developers under the government’s National Shelter Program from the 20 percent aggregate limit on real estate loans of banks and from the reduction in the loan values of real estate collateral (from 70 percent to 60 percent of appraised value).  Meanwhile, BSP Circular No. 218 (dated 23 November 1999) exempted banks, in certain cases, from the requirement of hiring an independent appraisal company to appraise collateral to support loan restructuring.   These BSP issuances are part of the wider government initiatives to ensure the viability of the country’s housing program by lowering the cost of housing loans and facilitating better access to financing. 

Concluding remarks

The role of the BSP in ensuring broad-based and sustainable growth consists of providing a supportive economic environment in which businesses can thrive.  We do this through our unwavering commitment to sound macroeconomic policy and financial sector stability.

At the same time, our collective efforts toward sustainable growth require the crucial participation of the private sector.  This includes the real estate sector’s role in providing the impetus for key sectors such as housing.  I am pleased to note that CREBA continues to be at the forefront in this area.  As your president Mr. Charlie Gorayeb said, “creba has always been a partner of government in promoting its pro-poor programs, specifically, providing a roof for every Filipino.”    I hope your organization will continue to work with the government in pushing forward our common agenda for a sustainable economic future.

Thank you.

 (Note: 4th Monthly Business Meeting, Chamber of Real Estate and Builders' Associations, Inc. (CREBA), April 26, 2001, Hotel Inter-Continental, Makati City)

Title: Ensuring Sustainability of Economic Development
Occasion: 1st General Assembly
Speaker: Governor Rafael Buenaventura
Transcription:
I welcome this opportunity to discuss with you the ongoing reforms in the financial sector. These days political news tends to obscure the crucial work being done quietly away from the limelight. I hope to rectify this by sharing with you our recent initiatives and what we have charted to do further in the future. 

Prospects for 2000

By and large, Asia is now back on its feet. The region’s snap back from recession has been remarkable for both its speed and timing. For the Philippines, the favorable assessment by the recent IMF mission adds to expectations of an even stronger economy this year.

For example, real GNP growth is expected to easily hit the target range of 4.5–5.5 percent this year as industry and services continue to recover. Inflation is projected to average between 5 and 6 percent after reaching well below the target for 1999. In the external sector, a sizable projected current account surplus will help build up gross international reserves to $17.1 billion by yearend.  We are also moving closer to fiscal consolidation. Fiscal authorities are expecting a reduction in the consolidated public sector deficit from 3.4 percent of GNP in 1999 to 2.9 percent this year. First-quarter revenue collections suggest that the national government’s target deficit of P62.5 billion for 2000 can be achieved. 

Ensuring Sustainability

The immediate challenge now for Asian leaders is to sustain the cyclical upturn and translate it into robust long-term growth. This means stepping up reform efforts.

In the Philippines, financial reform initiatives have drawn heavily from the lessons of past crises. In addition, as former World Bank Chief Economist Joseph Stiglitz argued, we also need to reshape our methodology in favor of looking at the microfoundations, for instance, of bankruptcy and fear of default so that our analysis is more complete.  

Reform Initiatives

To do this, the Bangko Sentral has focused on strengthening governance, upgrading regulatory standards, and building up the BSP’s independence and capabilities as regulatory authority.

Let me cite some of the measures we have put in place.

Promoting better bank governance means improving transparency and raising the quality of bank management. Hence, we have required more detailed quarterly reporting from banks on NPLs, risk assets, return on equity and DOSRI loans. We also drew up guidelines on the duties of banks’ directors to improve the quality of management.

Improvements in regulatory standards involve introducing changes in the definition of non-performing loans and tighter requirements for loan classification and loan-loss provisioning to conform with international standards.

Upgrading the BSP’s supervisory capacity means using a more dynamic, forward-looking and risk-based approach to bank supervision. In this regard, we have conducted seminars and dialogue with foreign and local institutions to train and upgrade the skills of BSP personnel. 

Future Policy Thrusts

Needless to say, the work does not stop there.  Further banking reforms will have to deal with increasing sophistication in the financial environment.

The reforms that I have just outlined centered mainly on the banking system because the BSP’s authority is precisely built on that bedrock.  This is not to say, however, that we are neglecting the other crucial areas of financial reform.  We remain ever aware of the need to develop sources of long-term financing and of putting up the necessary infrastructure for developing the capital markets. In fact, reforms have already been proposed aimed at resolving issues on the taxation of financial transactions.

The BSP is also working closely with the BAP and the other financial associations on the establishment of best practices for (1) risk management, including credit risk rating, market risk process, propriety and compliance test; (2) accounting and valuation standards, such as marking-to-market and stress testing; (3) the origination and underwriting of securities; (4) trading and market making; and (5) trust and asset management. Appropriate working groups have been put in place in order to ensure that specific work programs are carried out within specific time tables. We are likewise working with the BAP in developing a market for fixed-income instruments (such as REPOs) and making the payment and settlement system more efficient through the real-time gross settlements (RTGS) project.    This is expected to be operational within the year. Supervisory authorities are also improving the monitoring of banks’ off-balance sheet transactions to obtain a more complete and accurate assessment of portfolio risk.

One crucial point in this long laundry list of planned measures is that they cannot be implemented without the proper macroeconomic environment. Therefore, the Bangko Sentral’s abiding commitment to price stability remains as crucial as ever to continued reform and the sustainability of economic growth. Stable price levels are a key ingredient to strong and sustainable growth, since they reduce uncertainty so that, to quote Alan Greenspan, “expectations of change do not become major factors in key economic decisions.”

Thus, the Bangko Sentral is planning to shift to inflation targeting as the framework for conducting monetary policy in 2001. Among other things, this involves determining and announcing an explicit inflation target, and making regular reports on the performance of monetary policy. This framework raises both the level of transparency in the conduct of monetary policy and the BSP’s accountability to the inflation goal.

In closing, I would like to reassure you of the Bangko Sentral’s unstinting commitment to financial reform and macroeconomic stability.  I think I can say, without being immodest, that our record largely speaks for itself. This country’s long history of financial reform largely helped shield it from the worst of the past crisis. We intend to continue and build on that tradition.

However, we cannot do it all on our own.  The task of upgrading the capabilities and practices of the financial system also requires the initiative of industry groups like mart, the BAP and other associations. I am therefore grateful for the invaluable cooperation and support extended to the BSP by the financial community. I hope our partnership will continue to prosper in the years to come.

Thank you and good evening.    

(Note: 1st General Assembly, MART, April 25, 2000, Hotel Intercontinental, Makati)

Title: Credit Management in the New Economy
Occasion: 25th National Credit Congress, Credit Management Association of the Philippines (CMAP)
Speaker: Governor Rafael Buenaventura
Transcription:
Introduction

I am very pleased to join this gathering of distinguished credit and finance executives of the member-companies of the credit management association of the Philippines.

The theme of this year’s national credit congress ----- credit management in the new economy ----- is a fairly broad canvass to work on and I am grateful for the flexibility you are giving me in choosing the specific issues to develop.

As credit professionals, i think we can all readily find common ground in taking a look anew at developments in our banking system which stands at the very heart of the national credit mechanism. 

The current situation

Nearly four years after the outbreak of the Asian financial crisis, many countries in the region including ourselves are still sorting out the mess.   Although we have fortunately managed to avoid the worst disruptions, we have not been immune from the crisis and its effects.

The banking system today continues to labor under the heavy burden of the bad credit decisions of yesterday.  The non-performing loan ratio, 16 percent for the commercial banking system as of end-January 2001, remains uncomfortably high.  In addition, the volume of acquired assets and rescheduled debt have also significantly increased.  There is little comfort that our overall asset quality situation is still significantly better than those in other crisis countries.    These developments have inevitably eroded bank profitability, eaten away at scarce bank capital and reduced appetite for new lending. 

What should be done?

Reversing the dangerous tide calls for resolute action by government and by the financial institutions. One cannot simply wish away the problems by assuming that we will be able to grow our way out of trouble.  That may be especially unrealistic at this point in light of the dimming economic outlook for our key trading partners, notably the united states and Japan, which would limit our own ability to rebound more quickly.  Indeed, in the ASEAN region, economic growth is forecasted to slow down to 3 percent this year.  In the Philippines, GDP growth is projected at around 4 percent.

Two things need to be done quickly.  First, we have to address the weakened balance sheet condition of some of our financial institutions by expediting both the clean up of bad assets and the replenishment of capital when necessary.  Second, we need to introduce genuine internal reforms in our institutions to improve credit decision-making processes and avoid future problems.

In light of fiscal realities and on moral hazard grounds, the government cannot be expected to shoulder the main burden of the balance sheet clean-up.  This must primarily be the responsibility of the concerned financial institutions and their owners.  But government can play a constructive and supportive role by, first of all, taking a more realistic view on the tax treatment of loan loss provisions along the lines of international best practice.  I am particularly referring to allowing the tax deductibility of specific loan loss provisions.

I believe there is also scope for meaningful government support by way of strategic enhancements to essentially market-driven mechanisms either to take out bank assets or to re-capitalize banks.  There are already existing models we can look at.

The Bangko Sentral has been playing a catalytic role in the clean-up process by forcing the issue on realistic valuation of loans and other assets through its regulations and enforcement actions.  Key initiatives include tightened policies on loan classification and provisioning, on marking-to-market of securities portfolio, and on asset appraisals.

We have also recently issued BSP circular 280 implementing the risk-based capital framework which would officially take effect on July 1 this year.

Under this framework, which is based on the basle capital accord, banks’ assets will be categorized into 4 risk buckets with risk weights of 0%, 20%, 50% and 100%, respectively.  Both on-balance and off-balance sheet assets are included.  Banks will need to maintain, on a daily basis, a minimum eligible capital level equivalent to at least 10 percent of total risk-weighted assets.  However, the definition of eligible capital is broader than the conventional concept since it includes so-called tier 2 or supplementary capital such as long-dated subordinated debt.  In addition, the minimum capital ratio has to be maintained on stand-alone basis by the bank and also on banking group-wide basis if it has financial subsidiaries.

By hardening the capital constraint, this is expected to affect in a fundamental way how banks allocate their scarce capital resources bearing in mind the relative risks of their asset choices.  The framework will also be evolving in the future in the direction of increasing sophistication of risk measurement which will put an even greater premium on the quality and discipline of credit management. 

Towards an improved credit process

A clean-up of the balance sheet is not enough.  More critically, we need to thoroughly reform our credit processes precisely to avoid the kind of headaches we face today that are ultimately extremely costly to the economy.

There is a basic need for better corporate governance in our credit institutions.  Banks are not the private reserve of their primary shareholders to be used as a ready source of cheap credit.    But all too often, this principle may have been honored in the breach.   At ground level, our bank examiners play a constant cat-and-mouse game with some of our banks in identifying so-called DOSRI lendings that are very imaginatively concealed.  When you analyze it, most of our recent bank failures and near-failures can ultimately be traced to insider abuse.

The Bangko Sentral is determined to raise the governance standards of our banks.  We will soon be issuing new regulations defining clearly the duties and responsibilities of the board of directors --- the body that should be primarily responsible for ensuring sound corporate governance. This would be backed-up by fit and proper rules on bank directors and officers, that include the rules for disqualification, as provided for in the New General Banking Law.

The GBL has also provided us the legal basis to issue strengthened regulations on DOSRI loans and the single borrowers limit.  Both regulations are also in the pipeline.

On a more general note, we need to recommit ourselves to sound credit management principles that we may have started to take for granted.  The monetary board has recently approved a proposal for the establishment of minimum standards for a comprehensive credit risk management system that should be consistent with international standards. This shall be done in consultation with the Bankers Association of the Philippines and other banking associations. This would lay down the basis for more rigorous credit assessment standards including the wide and consistent use of internal credit grading systems.

The development of a strong credit culture will also be assisted by the development of private providers of credit information like credit bureaus as well as local rating agencies. The Bangko Sentral recognizes the need to nurture these institutions as a means of fostering credit discipline as well as to expand access to credit especially of smaller enterprises based on performance rather than collateral.   In this regard, the Bangko Sentral is open to information sharing arrangements with legitimate institutions subject to certain safeguards as set out in a formal memorandum of agreement. 

A final note

To achieve excellence in the rapidly changing environment, sound credit decisions at your level is essential.  Management must adopt mechanisms to safeguard your institution from unsound transactions.  On our part, the BSP will adjust to the changing needs of the system by continuously improving the supervisory and regulatory framework.

I urge you to continue to work in partnership with us in achieving excellence within individual institutions and in attaining our quest for a stable, sound and globally competitive financial system.

Thank you and good day.

 (Note: 25th National Credit Congress, Credit Management Association of the Philippines (CMAP), April 20, 2001, Hotel Inter-Continental Hotel, Makati City)

Title: Welcome Remarks
Occasion: IMF-World Bank Seminar on Standard and Codes in the New Int'l Financial Architecture
Speaker: Governor Rafael Buenaventura
Transcription:
Mr. Charles Enoch, Ms. Lynn Aylward, Mr. Axel Peuker, distinguished guests and participants to the IMF-World Bank Seminar on Standards and Codes in the New International Financial Architecture, friends and colleagues, ladies and gentlemen, good morning:

Let me begin by thanking all of you for joining us here in this seminar.  We are very fortunate to have with us today three distinguished officials from the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the World Bank (WB) who will talk about current international initiatives in standards and codes for economic and financial areas such as statistics, the monetary and financial sector, the fiscal sector and corporate governance.

The need to establish international standards and codes for all countries should be clear to most of us here.  Our experience with macroeconomic crises in the past decade has heightened the need for a policy framework to minimize the effects—if not prevent altogether—these crises.  Good economic citizenship is an important part of macroeconomic crisis prevention, and good citizenship implies adherence to internationally accepted standards, principles, and guidelines of good practice for economic, financial, and business activities.  Adherence to these good practices helps ensure the proper functioning of not only individual domestic economies and financial systems but also the international financial system as a whole. Initiatives in these areas contribute to the collective good, and require the collaboration of both the public and private sectors.  One important initiative is the collaborative effort between the IMF and the World bank to monitor and assist various countries in the observance of international standards and codes. This effort includes, among other things, the Reports on the Observance of Standards and Codes (ROSCS), which are experimental case studies on individual countries’ observance of international standards.  The ROSCS and other recent developments in data standards, fiscal transparency, corporate governance, guideline concerning accounting and insolvency, are the subject of this morning’s presentations.

With its decades-long history of continuing economic reforms, the Philippines has already made good progress in observing the standards and codes of good economic citizenship.  Nevertheless, I believe today’s presentation and discussion will greatly help the country build further upon its track record.  I hope that this seminar will open up further discussion and cooperation in these areas to help the Philippines take further steps along the road to better economic citizenship.   Thank you and good morning.

 

(Note: IMF-World Bank Seminar on Standards and Codes in the New International Financial Architecture, April 19, 2001, Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas)

Title: Promoting the Growth and Stability of the Banking System
Place: Resident Lounge, Ayala Center, Makati City
Occasion: Monthly Membership Meeting, Australia-New Zealand Chamber of Commerce (Philippines)
Speaker: Governor Rafael Buenaventura
Transcription:
I.      Introduction

Mr. William f. Mason and Mr. Chris Ward, President and Executive Director, respectively, of the Australia-New Zealand Chamber of Commerce (Philippines), Inc.; friends, ladies and gentlemen, good evening.

It is my distinct pleasure to address this monthly membership meeting of the Australia-New Zealand Chamber of Commerce.  Together, our three countries share many common interests in the region, and the Australia-New Zealand chamber of commerce has contributed significantly to the promotion of these interests, be they in cultural, social or economic affairs.

My talk tonight will focus on the importance of promoting the growth and stability of the banking system in a globalized environment.  After experiencing a setback due to the Asian financial crisis, most of the affected economies in the region recovered rather quickly, and seemed poised for a take-off into sustainable growth.  However, recent uncertainty about the extent and duration of the slowdown in the U.S. economy, coupled with the fragile recovery in Japan, have underscored the importance of international developments on the region’s growth prospects. The increased mobility of cross-border capital flows that has accompanied globalization and the greater economic linkages among countries call attention to the crucial issue of the stability and efficiency of our financial systems.  This evening, I will, therefore,

First present briefly the important aspects of the current international environment that could bear on the performance of the economy for the coming year; and point out the role that a healthy financial sector plays in supporting sustainable growth;  

Then update you on the present state of the Philippine banking system;  

Next, go over the policy reforms that the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas has done in order to prepare the financial system to meet these challenges; and  

Finally, present the policy reform agenda in the medium term. 

II.   The Challenge from a Possible Global Economic Slowdown

The importance of implementing a structural reform program for the economy in general and the financial sector in particular is underscored by concerns about the near-term prospects of the global economy.   The anticipated slowdown in the U.S. and Japan could impact disproportionately on the ASEAN economies, and on the information technology (it) sector in particular, in view of the importance of the U.S. and Japanese markets as destinations for ASEAN exports.  Central forecasts of economic growth in the U.S. have fallen to 1.5–2.5 percent in 2001, from 3.5 percent in 2000, while structural weaknesses in the banking and corporate sectors are expected to hold down the growth of the Japanese economy to a little over 1.0 percent.  However, an IMF paper cites significant room for policy maneuver in both the fiscal and monetary areas in most advanced economies, with the exception of Japan, and, as a result, the paper argues that there is a chance that recovery could start in the second half of 2001.

What do these developments mean for emerging market economies?  Growth in the export sector could be expected to soften and the inflow of foreign investments could be subdued.  On the other hand, lower interest rates and growth prospects in developed economies could lead to a reallocation of capital portfolios.  Whether this will lead to strengthened capital inflows to particular economies or not will depend on the ability of those economies to demonstrate good track records in terms of attaining macroeconomic and financial stability, and to lay down, through appropriate structural reforms, the foundations for sustainable economic growth.  With regard to the financial system, the challenge is to sustain its growth and stability in the midst of these fast-moving global developments. Any disruption in the intermediation process of the financial system will inevitably have negative repercussions on the rest of the economy. As a result, the soundness of the banking system and the adequacy of the supervisory framework have generated considerable interest.    Allow me to discuss these with you in some detail. 

III.   State of the Philippine Banking System

The Philippines has emerged from a crisis-prone year with its democratic institutions intact and with the basic strength of its economy preserved.  Through this and through the Asian financial crisis, the Philippines’ fundamentally sound financial system has served us in good stead.  A two-decade history of close supervision, sustained banking reforms, and implementation of timely pre-emptive measures have helped develop a financial system that is able to withstand transitory shocks arising from both domestic and external sources.  Key banking sector indicators reflect this:

The banking system’s total resources increased by 10.4 percent in 2000, to P3.3 trillion.  

Asset quality remained manageable, despite a recent uptrend in non-performing loans as a result of the pass-through effects of higher interest rates and the depreciation of the peso.    As of end-2000, the non-performing loan (NPL) ratio of the banking system was 15.0 percent, higher than the 12.7 percent recorded at end-1999.  In particular, the NPL ratio of commercial banks improved to 16.0 percent in January 2001, after peaking at 16.3 percent in November 2000.  In comparison, the end-December 2000 NPL ratios were 17.7 percent for Thailand and 18.8 percent for Indonesia, and the end-January 2001 ratio was 9.4 percent for Malaysia.[1]  While the ratios have fallen faster in some of the other affected Asian economies, these declines have reflected largely the off-loading of NPLs to public restructuring agencies.  By contrast, no public funds have been used in the Philippines to purchase non-performing assets or recapitalize financial institutions.  

The banking system remained adequately capitalized during the year. As of end-December 2000, the average capital adequacy ratio reached 16.4 percent, lower than the previous year’s 17.5 percent but well above the BSP statutory floor of 10.0 percent and the Bank for International Settlement’s (BIS) standard of 8.0 percent.  The decline in the capital adequacy ratio was attributable to the increase in the required valuation reserves.  

While the real estate exposure of commercial banks rose slightly to 12.3 percent as of end-September 2000, from 11.6 percent in December 1999, the ratio remains far below the 20 percent ceiling imposed by the BSP.

In the face of the anticipated correction in international equity markets and the subdued mood for foreign investment, the financial sector’s efficiency in fund intermediation and risk management would play a key role in determining how well the Philippine economy performs this year.  Let me, therefore, discuss some of the recent steps that the BSP has undertaken in order to further strengthen the financial system. 

IV.    Reforms and Policy Directions

The BSP has instituted major reforms in financial supervision and regulation.  The overarching framework is provided by the recently passed General Banking Law of 2000 (Republic Act No. 8791).  Some of the more important features of the GBL  2000 include: (1) granting authority to the Monetary Board to require banks to adopt internationally accepted standards relating to risk-based capital adequacy;  (2) providing for stricter rules governing bank exposure to directors, officers, stockholders and related interests (DOSRI);  (3) strengthening current regulations with respect to transparency practices;  (4) adopting a fit-and-proper rule test for appointment of senior bank officials; (5) further liberalizing the ownership participation of foreign banks in the local banking system to 100 percent within seven years after the effectivity of the GBL 2000; and (6) granting authority to the BSP to regulate electronic banking.  The BSP has tasked a committee to formulate the implementing rules of the new law.  So far, circulars have been issued pertaining to foreign stockholdings, outsourcing of banking functions, guidelines on microfinance loans and the adoption of risk-based capital adequacy standards aligned with international norms.

The BSP also instituted regulatory changes so as to improve risk management in the financial system:

The BSP has changed the focus of its supervision from a purely compliance-based and checklist-driven assessment of banks’ conditions to a forward-looking and risk-based framework.  The BSP has also begun to supervise financial conglomerates on a consolidated basis, including consolidation of limits on foreign currency exposures between banks and their affiliated foreign exchange corporations.  

The definition of past due loans was tightened.[2]  

To promote sound risk management in large-value transactions, the BSP, in collaboration with the Bankers Association of the Philippines (BAP), is developing a Real Time Gross Settlement System (RTGS) that will cover transactions in the equities, fixed income, money and foreign exchange markets.  Once fully operational, the RTGS would offer a powerful mechanism for limiting settlement and systemic risks in the interbank settlement process.  

In response to current trends towards increased use of the internet in banking, the BSP has laid down the requirements for banks seeking to provide electronic banking services. This is to ensure that banks planning to provide these services have in place a risk management process that is adequate to assess, control and monitor associated risks.  

A policy of encouraging mergers and consolidations has been in place for some time.  This recognizes the fact that bigger-capitalized banks can withstand better the increased volatility of capital flows, and are, therefore, better equipped to meet the demands of the new globalized environment.  The policy also reduces moral hazard since owners have more of their wealth at stake.  The BSP offered incentives in support of this policy, including allowing banks to amortize their goodwill up to a maximum period of forty (40) years.

In addition to the foregoing measures, the BSP has adopted key reforms that strengthen the foundations for good governance in the financial system. Among other areas, these reforms address the need for:

Management integrity and adequacy of training and experience.  The BSP has provided guidelines governing the responsibilities of banks’ boards of directors and the election/appointment of bank directors and officers.  

Transparency and disclosure.  The BSP has instructed all banks to disclose publicly detailed quarterly information on their non-performing loans, classified loans and other risk assets, amount of general and specific loan-loss reserves, return on equity, and insider (DOSRI) loans. 

V.   Looking Ahead

Moving forward, a major plus factor for the Philippines is the greatly improved and stabilized political situation which has improved confidence.  In addition, fiscal authorities have committed to firmly address the fiscal deficit through a combination of expenditure restraint and—more importantly—improvements in tax collection efforts and administration. The outlook for inflation in 2001 is also favorable, with indications that inflationary pressures will abate starting the second half of this year, to average 6-7 percent in 2001.  It may be recalled that inflation remained steady at 6.7 percent in march relative to its month-ago rate.  These factors provide greater flexibility to the BSP to pursue its primary mandate of maintaining price stability for sustained economic recovery and growth.  The inflation-targeting framework—which the BSP plans to implement in the middle of 2001—embodies this commitment through its emphasis on transparency, accountability and a forward-looking perspective.  By stabilizing prices, inflation targeting will encourage longer term saving and investment, and will deepen the role for longer-term financial intermediation.    Flexibility in monetary management will also help support attainment of the 4-4.5 percent growth target for GNP.

On the legislative front, the reforms in the general banking law of 2000 will be complemented by the proposed amendments to the New Central Bank Act.  These amendments aim to enhance the BSP’s supervisory powers and operational independence, improve prudential standards and promote greater competition in the banking system.  Key reforms could include the relaxation of the deposit secrecy provision which would allow the monetary board to inquire into deposit accounts of suspicious nature; grant of authority to the BSP to conduct more frequent banking examinations; and greater scope and strength of administrative sanctions.

With respect to another area of recent concern, the BSP issued in 2000 a number of circulars which bring the country’s regulatory regime on anti-money laundering closer to international standards.  These circulars require banks to take reasonable means to determine the true identities of their clients and report suspicious transactions.  Recognizing the importance of legislation, the BSP is advocating the passage of House Bill No. 5216, also known as the Anti-racketeering Bill, which would make money laundering a crime in the country.  Moreover, the BSP is currently working with the Bankers association of the Philippines to come up with guidelines regarding a proposal that will give banks and regulators the right to examine foreign currency deposit unit accounts under certain conditions.

I hope that the foregoing discussion has gone some distance in convincing you of the vibrancy of the economic reform program in the Philippines and the continued strength of the banking system.  My invitation is for you to take part in the efforts of nation-building in the Philippines.  With the improved political environment and the fundamental strengths of the economy backed up by the government’s firm commitment to needed reforms, there is sound basis for a take-off into sustained non-inflationary growth and for continued viability of the long-term investments in the country.

Thank you and good night.

----------------------------------------------

[1] Data for other Asian economies come from the Asian Development Bank ASEAN Economic Outlook 2001 (April 2001).

[2] The entire outstanding balance of a loan/receivable would now be considered as past due when the total amount of arrearages reaches ten percent (10%) of the total loan receivable balance.

Title: Keynote Address
Occasion: E-Commerce Product Launch, Union Bank of the Philippines
Speaker: Governor Rafael Buenaventura
Transcription:
It is my pleasure to keynote this evening's event.  The importance of this event goes beyond the walls of Union Bank and its customers and partners as well as stakeholders. Its implications are quite far-reaching, extending to the way Philippine firms conduct business and the way consumers transact their dealings.  Dramatic changes are occurring in the structure of banking. The environment has become so dynamic largely because we continue to grapple with technological innovations and globalization brought about by increased interdependence of markets and financial flows.

Tonight, Union bank and partners Visa and Thyron are unveiling two e-banking products that will take e-commerce in the Philippines to the next stage of development and onward from there.  Chairman Ortiz had earlier outlined what merchant establishments can do with the payment gateway, and what consumers can do with Eon Visa Electron.

The main attraction is Union Bank's payment gateway, the Port.  This is the first time a payment gateway is being made available to Philippine merchants and retailers.  The implications —as we noted—are tremendous.  The Port expands the payment options and accessible markets of Philippine merchants.  Hence, Philippine merchants who otherwise could not sell locally and abroad through the internet—because they are not connected to an internet payment facility—can now link up with the Port and consummate the payment part of the transaction.  This is indeed a much welcome development, because it could enable more Philippine export sales through the internet by giving Philippine businesses an opportunity to break out in the world market as well as enabling existing exporters to expand their global reach.  Thus, the availability of this gateway facility will contribute significantly to today's efforts to boost exports and speed up the recovery process.  Exports remain as one of the country’s strong growth drivers. Not only the exports industry, but the retail trade industry as well stands to benefit from this development.  Last year, the Retail Trade Liberalization Act was passed, opening the industry to increased foreign competition.  With this internet payment facility, local entrepreneurs can compete more effectively with their foreign counterparts.

So, part of my advice to Unionbank is to tell their merchant customers that, because of this technology, borders are increasingly being rendered seamless, with the end-result that their markets can potentially expand to include the whole world.

On a more general level, this initiative is thus supportive of the government’s efforts to further promote both domestic absorption and exports in order to fire the engines of economic growth.

The Bangko Sentral is, therefore, quite pleased to see these banking innovations because they are good for the global competitiveness of Philippine business.  I normally order my books from amazon.com because they're reasonably priced and delivered fast.  If a Philippine supplier later on emerges that is price-competitive, operationally efficient and image-and-media-savvy enough to at least match the amazon.coms of the world, then I don't see any reason why you and I won't buy from that supplier.  As I scan the possibilities in the horizon, the payment gateway might help unlock the entrepreneurial talents and competitiveness of many Philippine businesses.

It is not impossible if the next logistics company to challenge UPS, DHL and Federal Express would be an enterprising Philippine outfit. This is not far-fetched given that Philippine entrepreneurs are quite adept at innovating, particularly those who understand the challenges presented by a wired world.  I must commend Union Bank and partners Thyron and Visa for taking the initiative.  In particular, I would like to commend Tito Ortiz for crusading e-commerce in the Philippines.  A crucial segment in e-commerce is, of course, the payment leg; otherwise e-commerce is not consummated.   What Union Bank is doing is providing the payment leg by bringing proven world-class technology into the Philippine market.  That is a clear, positive contribution to the evolution of the Philippine e-marketplace.   For our part as your central bank, I wish to give you my assurance that the Bangko Sentral under my watch remains accommodating and supportive of the ongoing evolution of e-commerce in the Philippines, which is led by the private sector, as should be the case.  Like the private sector, the Bangko Sentral is responding to the demands of e-commerce.  We have ongoing initiatives such as the Real Time Gross Settlement project, which is expected to enhance operational efficiency, reliability, speed and timeliness of payment transactions in the face of rapidly increasing volume and value of transactions.  The RTGS system, once in place, will offer a powerful mechanism for limiting settlement and systemic risks in the interbank settlement process, thus ensuring stability of the whole financial system.

Another initiative is in the form of interbank call loans, which are now electronically linked to the BSP's financial accounting system, among others.  However, as transactions involving this type of technology grow in volume and complexity, there is a need to identify, assess and manage the risks attendant to these transactions.  The BSP has already undertaken initial steps towards this direction.  It has issued some requirements to be imposed on banks seeking or already providing e-banking services to ensure that these banks have in place a risk management process that is adequate to assess, control, and monitor associated risks.

My challenge to union bank and other Philippine banks who are at the forefront of e-banking is this: make sure transaction security and integrity as well as client confidentiality are never compromised.  These are the non-negotiable items as far as Bangko Sentral is concerned.    E-commerce is a new and unfamiliar terrain to many of us, and we have to be very careful.

For sure we at the BSP are as vigilant as ever in monitoring and providing safeguards for the general public with respect to these banking innovations.

This is indeed an auspicious evening. Thank you and good evening.

 

(Note: E-Commerce Product Launch, Union Bank of the Philippines, March 29, 2001, Shangri-La Hotel, Makati City)

Title: Recent Developments in the Philippine Economy
Occasion: Philippine-American Chamber of Commerce Trade Mission, Makati Business Club
Speaker: Governor Rafael Buenaventura
Transcription:
I take great pleasure in joining the participants in this trade mission led by the Philippine American Chamber of Commerce, Inc.

Today, you have come at an auspicious time when the country is reviewing its directions and priorities in an effort to achieve faster economic recovery and a more conducive business environment.   I therefore welcome this opportunity to update you on the Philippine economic situation, particularly on developments in the monetary and banking system.

Real sector

Let me start with the real sector developments.

·         In the face of challenges from the domestic and international fronts last year, the Philippine economy managed to pull off a respectable performance.  Real GNP grew by 4.2 percent, well above the 3.7 percent posted in 1999.  The economic expansion was underpinned by a more balanced and broad-based growth among the major sectors of the economy.

·         This growth picture in 2000 continues to be validated by key advance indicators.  On the supply side, the production index has been on the rise both in value and in volume.  On the demand side, exports continue to grow although at a slower pace.  Power sales remain strong, while appliance sales have rebounded from a declining trend in 1999.  Commercial bank lending also continues to be favorable, showing a 7.8 percent growth in January this year, up from a negative 0.2 percent growth a year ago.  However, imports growth has remained low, and passenger car sales have declined in the first two months of the year.

Monetary sector

Notwithstanding the pick-up in economic activity last year, prices have remained generally stable.

·         Inflation averaged 4.4 percent last year, compared to the 6.7 percent recorded in 1999.    This was also well below the program range of 5-6 percent in 2000.  For the first two months of this year, inflation averaged 6.8 percent, well within the program range of 6-7 percent for whole year.

·         Moreover, benign inflation was achieved despite inflationary pressures from oil price and transport fare increases and the depreciation of the peso, which fed into wage adjustments.

·         Overall, in 2000, monetary policy was supportive of economic growth, despite some tightening episodes in May, September and October to smoothen out some instability in the financial market.  The calibrated adjustments in policy rates during these episodes were eventually offset by policy rate cuts since December as broad stability in the market eventually prevailed.   Since December last year, we have reduced our policy rates by 500 basis points.

·         As a result, interest rates have begun to ease toward the end of the year.  This was true both for the benchmark 91-day T-bill rate and the bank lending rates.

·         The easing of the monetary stance resulted in the expansion in domestic liquidity by 4.6 percent in 2000, and further to 12.2 percent in January this year.  This expansionary trend was reflected as increases in the public and private sector credits, with the bulk of bank loans going into manufacturing and other key sectors of the economy. 

Fiscal sector

·        In the fiscal sector, the fiscal position was a source of concern in 2000 as the National Government deficit exceeded the target for the year.  Nonetheless, it is helpful to note that the increasing use of domestic sources to finance the shortfall did not lead to a precipitate increase in market lending rates.

·        For this year, fiscal consolidation is a tall order that will require fiscal discipline on the part of the government.  Fiscal prudence is expected to be achieved through:  improvement in tax collections, improvement in tax administration, and rationalization of government expenditures.  

External sector

·        In the external sector, the current account posted a hefty surplus in 2000, owing to brisk exports and low import growth.  The overall balance of payments, however, showed a deficit due to a weaker financial account.

·        As of end-February 2001, our international reserves remained high at $14.2 billion, which is equivalent to 4.2 months of imports of goods and payments of services, and more than enough to cover our short-term obligations.

·        The country’s external debt remained manageable, with the bulk of total debt stock accounted for by medium and long-term liabilities.  Owing to this and good export numbers, the country’s debt service burden has also remained manageable at 12.5 percent compared to 17 percent, which was observed in the early 1990s.

·         Meanwhile, the peso started appreciating slightly toward the end of December 2000 on account of foreign exchange inflows and the progress in the political situation during the period.  But in early January this year, the peso was again subjected to some pressure owing to political uncertainties at that time.  However, following the change in administration in mid-January, the peso has since improved and stabilized.

The banking system

·         In the banking sector, our banking system has remained sound as evident in its steady level of resources and manageable banking ratios.

·         As of end-December 2000, total resources of the banking system reached P3.3 trillion, compared to P3.0 trillion a year ago.

·         The capital adequacy ratio of banks at 15.6 percent as of end-December 2000 was well above the 10 percent minimum requirement and the 8 percent international standard.

·         Meanwhile, the quality of commercial bank assets continued to be manageable.  As of end-December 2000, the NPL ratio of commercial banks fell to 15.1 percent from 16.3 percent a month ago.

·         In addition, our banks’ real estate exposure at 12.3 percent of total loan portfolio as of December 2000 was way below the 20 percent ceiling imposed by the BSP.

·         n general, our banking system remains healthy and resilient and continues to be an efficient transmission channel of monetary policy.

Outlook

·         Overall, if the economy’s performance last year is any indicator, we are moving toward a more broad-based growth, even as we strive to rise to the challenge of fiscal consolidation.    For this year, the government expects the economy to grow by 4.0-4.5 percent in terms of GNP and by 3.8-4.3 percent in terms of GDP.  Growth is expected to be underpinned by the continued strength of the services sector.  Meanwhile, inflation is expected to be in the range of 6.0-7.0 percent.

·         With the stabilization of the domestic political situation, business confidence has continued to improve.  One indication is the result of the business world-audit & surveys worldwide joint survey for the last couple of months, which showed a significant rise in the business confidence index.

External environment

·         In the external front, macroeconomic developments in the major industrial countries are expected to continue to exert a major influence on domestic economic developments.    Upside factors that are being monitored include:  the moderating trend in world oil prices and lower U.S. interest rates; while risk factors include a slower growth in the U.S. economy as well as potential weaknesses in the economies of Japan and the European Union.

The Philippines as an ideal investment site

·         In addition to the country’s sound macroeconomic performance, the positive economic outlook, and the supportive external environment that we have discussed earlier, one other factor that makes the Philippines an ideal investment site is its high-quality workforce.

·         As most of you would know, the country has a large pool of highly trained, English-speaking manpower.

·         In 1999, the PERC survey ranked the Filipino worker first in Asean and second in Asia in terms of quality, cost competitiveness and availability.

·         Around the same period, the Meta Group’s Cyber Atlas ranked the Philippines first among 47 countries in terms of availability of knowledge workers.  This was based on the country having more qualified IT engineers, more senior managers and higher enrollment in higher education.

Policy thrusts

·         I have given you some broad-brush strokes on the state of the Philippine economy.  With the recent change in administration and the return of business confidence, faster economic recovery is clearly underway.

·         For its part, the Bangko Sentral will continue to pursue its primary mandate of maintaining price stability conducive to a balanced and sustained growth of the economy.

·         One major policy thrust will be the implementation of the shift from monetary targeting to inflation targeting.  This is expected to improve further the transparency and consistency of monetary policy, and consequently its effectiveness.

·         In the banking sector, efforts to further strengthen and modernize the banking sector will continue to be pursued.  This will include: finalizing the rules and regulations implementing the General Banking Law of 2000; improving risk management and the payment and settlement infrastructure;  encouraging mergers and consolidations; pursuing amendments to the BSP charter;  and strengthening efforts to combat money laundering.

In closing, I wish to thank the organizers of this mission for the opportunity to present the current monetary and banking environment in the country.   I hope that the members of the mission will be able to spread the word about the more positive prospects now prevailing in the economy.

Thank you and good day.

 

(Note: Philippine American Chamber of Commerce Trade Mission, Makati Business Club, March 23, 2001, Hotel Inter-Continental, Makati City )

Title: Outlook for Monetary and Banking Policies in the Philippines
Occasion: Business Conference, The Economist Intelligence Unit (EIU)
Speaker: Governor Rafael Buenaventura
Transcription:
It is with great pleasure that I join this gathering of the top executives of multinational companies in the local business community.  Of late, I have attended a number of similar sessions with leaders of the business community and have had interesting discussions with them.  I am sure that we will also have productive exchange of views today.

The BSP has two major responsibilities under its charter. One, to provide policy direction in the areas of money, banking and credit. Two, to supervise the operations of banks and regulate finance companies and non-bank financial institutions performing quasi-banking functions.  Allow me then to provide you with a broad outline of the BSP’s policy thrust in these two areas. 

Monetary policy

The thrust of BSP monetary policy will continue to be guided by our primary mandate of maintaining price stability conducive to a balanced and sustained economic growth.  Monetary policy stance was generally accommodative for most of last year as inflation remained largely subdued.  However, there were tightening episodes, particularly in may and in September-October, in response to emerging inflationary pressures and the narrowing of interest differentials which contributed to volatility in the foreign exchange market.  These episodes were characterized by increases in our key policy rates as well as in liquidity reserve requirements.  However, as the foreign exchange market began to achieve stability in December, monetary policy was gradually eased.  Further boost in the stability of financial markets was achieved with the peaceful resolution of the recent political impasse.  Expectations of declining inflation and the stabilization of the financial markets have provided more room for easing of monetary conditions and helped establish a more supportive environment for business activity. Thus, this year saw the continued gradual relaxation of monetary policy.  Since December last year, the BSP has already reduced its key policy rates by a total of 450 basis points.

In the near term, the BSP sees some potential for further easing of the monetary policy stance.  Inflation for this year is expected to be relatively higher during the first semester due to the lagged effects of a weaker peso, oil price hikes and wage adjustments late last year. However, improvements in supply conditions and prospects for continued stability in the foreign exchange market are expected to lead to a downtrend in inflation in the second half.  This anticipated downtrend in inflation and the easing bias of the U.S. Fed will provide the BSP with greater latitude for further cuts in the BSP’s policy rates.  However, this has to be weighed alongside the need to maintain an appropriate interest rate differential to encourage investors to keep their peso- denominated assets.  There may also be downside risks that dictate a circumspect approach in further reducing policy rates.  As such, the BSP will continue to watch closely developments in the financial and fiscal sector and more importantly, the emerging inflationary scenario to guide its subsequent actions.

To further improve its capability to pursue its mandate of price stability, the BSP plans to formally shift to inflation targeting as the framework for conducting monetary policy by the middle of this year.

Under this framework, government authorities will pre-announce the inflation target over a given time horizon.  If the target is not met, the BSP will be required to explain the reasons and to spell out the measures that it will take to get back on track.  The framework, therefore will allow the Bangko Sentral to build its credibility by demonstrating consistent adherence to the inflation goal.  In the process, the framework will promote greater transparency in the conduct of monetary policy, thus facilitating more efficient markets, as well as greater accountability on the part of monetary authorities for its actions. 

Banking sector policy

In the banking system, the BSP’s focus remains the promotion of a stable, sound and globally competitive financial system.  The BSP envisions a banking system that is strong, sound and resilient as well as able to intermediate funds effectively and manage risks efficiently.

A key reform measure is the change in the legislative framework for the banking system.    The General Banking Law (GBL) of 2000 or R.A. No. 8791, which was passed last May 2000, now forms the basic legal fabric governing the banking system.  The law gives the BSP flexibility in supervising the banking industry and upgrades the country’s banking laws to meet global standards.  A number of Circulars to implement the provisions of this new law have already been issued by the BSP including those on the definition, classification, powers and scope of authorities of banks, outsourcing of banking functions, foreign stockholdings, and microfinancing loans.

The reforms supported by the GBL 2000 will be complemented by the proposed amendments to the Charter of the Bangko Sentral. These amendments are important if we are to reap the full benefits offered by the GBL. The amendments will reinforce the autonomy, authority and capacity of the BSP not only to regulate and supervise the banking system but also to more effectively implement monetary policy.  A specific amendment to the New Central Bank Act will among others relax existing barriers to the fight against money laundering.  We are proposing to Congress that the Monetary Board be allowed to look into deposits of more than P50 million in an individual account, provided that there is reasonable ground to believe that such an account is being used in relation to any fraud or irregularity.  This will effectively restore the authority of the Monetary Board under the old Central Bank Act, which was deleted under the New CB Act, to inquire into deposit accounts of a suspicious nature.

The BSP is also currently working with the BAP on guidelines that will give banks and regulators the right to examine FCDU accounts under certain conditions.  Under the plan, non- Philippine resident depositors will be asked to sign a voluntary waiver on secrecy upon opening an FCDU account in any Philippine-based bank.

To raise the level of awareness of the general public and the authorities concerned, the BSP and the BAP institute have sponsored and will continue to sponsor seminars on money laundering.

Related to this effort, the BSP is supporting the passage of a legislation which would, among others, make money laundering a crime in the country.

Aside from the changes in the country’s banking laws, an on-going initiative by the BSP is the improvement of its supervisory framework in line with the evolving structure of the financial system.  This upgrading of capabilities would ensure that supervision will remain effective in fostering the safety and soundness of the country’s banking system.  An important step in this effort is the adoption of a more forward-looking and risk based bank supervision framework.  This involves the re-orientation of the bank examination process towards quality of decision processes rather than just compliance with rules and regulation.  Another dimension of the upgrading is the implementation of consolidated supervision of financial conglomerates.  This approach facilitates a more comprehensive assessment of the risks involved in the banks’ activities.

The BSP is also in the middle of pursuing important changes in the regulatory framework for banks.  Regulatory standards are being aligned with international norms and internationally- accepted best practices.  Transparency, on the part of both market participants and regulators, is being emphasized to promote better bank governance and more effective market discipline.  The entire regulatory framework is in fact being reviewed to plug any remaining loopholes.  The regulatory gaps between banks and non-banks are being closed to avoid regulatory arbitrage activities.   The remaining regulatory loopholes on foreign exchange trading are likewise being addressed.

The BSP has also started to address the need to improve the regulatory framework with the introduction and anticipated growth of e-banking.  We have already issued general guidelines for those banks planning to offer e-banking services to ensure that banks have rigorous internal controls and comprehensive risk management systems that can adequately take into account the risks involved in these new banking activities.  The BSP will remain vigilant for developments in the banking community and innovations in technology so that we can finetune our policies accordingly.

The BSP is also encouraging the restructuring of the local banking industry.  In a more globalized financial landscape, we realize that domestic banks need to mobilize sufficient capitalization and to strengthen risk management systems to compete in a more challenging and globally integrated banking environment.  This strengthening can be assisted through mergers and acquisitions and through greater participation of foreign financial institutions.

The BSP is also supporting the modernization of the market infrastructure for the financial system.  In line with this, a key initiative supported by the BSP is the upgrading of the existing payment system into a Real Time Gross Settlement system to enhance operational efficiency, reliability, speed and timeliness of payment transactions. This will not only foster a more efficient banking system but also help develop the capital market.

Another initiative being supported by the BSP that can enhance the development of the domestic capital market is the plan to securitize long-term deposits.  The proposed scheme involves the pooling of funds deposited for at least five years into certificates of deposits that can be traded in the secondary market.  This scheme can help spur domestic savings and deepen the local capital market.

The BSP is also extending support to the social development agenda of the government within the limits set by its charter.  Last January, the BSP issued a Circular on microfinancing loans to implement some of the provisions of the GBL. These provisions relate to the application of market-based interest rates by lending institutions to enable them to recover the financial and operational costs of their micro finance operations.  This was complemented by the lifting of the moratorium on the licensing of new thrift and rural banks to allow the entry of microfinance-oriented banks.  The BSP is also finalizing guidelines for the opening of a rediscount window for rural banks and cooperative banks engaged in microfinance.  This facility will support small banks that have achieved efficiency in their microfinance operations, without sacrificing prudential standards.    Through this initiatives, the BSP hopes to contribute in the effort to bring more resources and opportunities to the marginalized sectors of our society. 

Conclusion

I have given you this morning an overview of the recent changes and future direction of BSP monetary and banking sector policies. The BSP has sought to maintain stable monetary conditions in the country.  It has also undertaken wide-ranging reform measures in recent years and we expect this process to continue as our economy develops and as the economic and financial environment evolves.  We expect that the initiatives that we have set to pursue will enhance our ability to help create an environment conducive to the expansion of productive activities of the private sector.  We hope that the business community will respond positively to our efforts and do its share in achieving a higher, more balanced and sustained growth path for our economy.

Thank you and good day.

(Note: Business Conference, The Economist Intelligence Unit (EIU), March 16, 2001, Mandarin Oriental Hotel, Makati City)

Title: Moving Forward with Monetary Policy in 2001
Occasion: Business Economics Club, University of Asia and the Pacific
Speaker: Governor Rafael Buenaventura
Transcription:
Ladies and gentlemen, good afternoon:

It is my great pleasure to join this distinguished gathering of business and economics professionals to talk about the prospects for monetary policy in 2001.  This is indeed a timely opportunity to discuss the Bangko Sentral’s conduct of monetary policy.   One of the fulcrums of sound and sustainable economic growth is price stability, and preserving price stability is the major challenge that confronts central bankers around the world.   The remark made by US Treasury Secretary Lawrence Summers that “Monetary policy is destiny” may be an exaggeration, but it carries a fair amount of truth in it.

This afternoon I would like to begin with a brief description of present monetary conditions, along with the Bangko Sentral’s recent policy actions.  I would then like to move on to the broader plan for monetary policy, which is to shift to an inflation targeting framework by the middle part of the year. 

Recent   economic   and   monetary   developments

Last year, as you know, was an eventful one for the Philippines, with pressures coming from both the domestic and international fronts.  The BSP’s monetary policy stance took a generally accommodative path for most of 2000.   However, there were some tightening episodes in May, September, and October in response to emerging inflationary pressures and the narrowing interest rate differentials that have contributed to some volatility in the foreign exchange market.    

The increases in policy rates and the liquidity reserve requirement in 2000 were calibrated carefully to address the underlying price pressures without unduly restricting the pace of economic recovery.  Thus, despite domestic and external shocks, the economy managed to register a respectable performance.  Real GNP growth strengthened to 4.2 percent in 2000 from 3.7 percent in 1999.   At the same time, inflation remained largely subdued despite pressures from supply-side shocks such as record-high world oil prices.  Average inflation for the year was recorded at 4.4 percent, well below the government’s target of 5-6 percent.

Overall economic activity continues to show signs of improvement, as indicated by leading indicators of supply and demand conditions.  For example, manufacturing production posted higher growth rates in both value and volume terms for the whole of 2000. Average capacity utilization likewise picked up slightly from 79.3 percent in December 1999 to 80.0 percent in December 2000.   Palay production also reached a record high of 12.4 million metric tons in 2000, which could translate into favorable food prices this year.  Growth in commercial bank lending has continued to expand, rising by 7.2 percent year-on-year at end-December 2000.   Similarly, Meralco power sales grew by 7.1 percent in 2000, compared to 0.6 percent in the previous year.   Appliance sales made a turnaround, rising by 7.2 percent last year following an 8.4 percent decline in 1999.  These favorable trends augur well for overall economic performance for the year.

At the same time, the recent stabilization of the domestic political situation and the peaceful change in political leadership have brought about renewed business confidence and restored stability in our financial markets.  This broad stability has provided room for the gradual easing of the BSP’s monetary policy stance.  The series of reductions in key policy interest rates in December, January and February amounting to a cumulative total of 400 basis points effectively reversed the increases in October 2000 and brought down policy rates back to their pre-crisis levels.  The resulting monetary easing should provide a supportive environment for business activity.

 Outlook   for   monetary   policy

What do we expect for monetary policy for the rest of the year? Since February 12, the monetary board has kept the BSP’s policy rates steady at 11.0 percent and 13.25 percent for the overnight RRP and RP rates, respectively.   The Monetary Board will, however, continue to review the BSP’s monetary policy settings, taking its cue from financial markets and other economic indicators before effecting further policy rate reductions.  The important precondition for rate cuts in the near term is that price pressures remain subdued so that monetary policy action does not jeopardize the low-inflation environment needed to foster investment and growth.

The overall direction for monetary policy in 2001 will thus depend on the assessment of the inflation path for the year.  Prevailing inflationary pressures remain relatively benign, and there are indications that cost-push influences may turn out to be weaker than previously expected.  For example, the Department of Agriculture has reported that the dry spell associated with the el niño weather phenomenon this year may be milder than previously expected.  This implies favorable food supply conditions which, in turn, would translate into stable food prices.

Nevertheless, some risks remain.  On the external front, the slowdown in the U.S. economy will have a significant impact on emerging economies like the Philippines which have close trade and financial linkages with the U.S.  Concerns over the U.S. slowdown could be amplified by continued weakness in the Japanese economy and slow recovery in the Euro area.    The prospect of lower foreign interest rates—as these countries try to rev up their economies —creates the risk of exchange rate volatility in emerging economies as interest rate differentials narrow.  There are also talks of a new round of oil production cuts, which could lead to higher crude oil prices and create cost-push inflationary pressures.  All these could pose a threat to the expected deceleration of domestic inflation in the second half of the year.  On the domestic front, the main risks to inflation could come from the large fiscal deficit, although the government has committed to make fiscal discipline a key plank in its economic program.  These risks highlight the need for greater vigilance on the part of monetary authorities to ensure that the price stability objective is achieved.  For the year, the government is targeting an average inflation rate of 6–7 percent. 

Moving  towards  inflation  targeting

Looking ahead, the BSP’s efforts are focused on preparing for the shift to inflation targeting.  As some of you may know, on January 24, 2000, the Monetary Board approved in principle the shift to inflation targeting as the framework for monetary policy.  Let me explain briefly the thinking that went behind the decision to adopt this framework.

Inflation targeting focuses mainly on price stability as the primary objective of monetary policy.  This approach has several basic features.  First, the central bank announces an explicit inflation target, which it commits to achieve over a suitable time horizon.  Second, monetary policy is forward-looking, since it is important for policy to react at an early stage to emerging inflationary risks.   Third, the commitment to an explicit inflation target improves the accountability of the central bank and raises transparency in the conduct of monetary policy, two common threads of good governance.  Increased accountability enhances the credibility of monetary policy, while greater transparency promotes the efficient functioning of financial markets which, in turn, leads to a stable and predictable macroeconomic environment.

Inflation targeting has attracted considerable attention over the past few years from central bankers, academics and other government policymakers.  Its growing appeal is based on two factors.  First, for many countries, financial liberalization in the past decades has led to the weakening of the relationship between money and prices, and also between broad money and operating targets such as base money and reserve money.  This has reduced the effectiveness of standard monetary aggregate targeting and prompted a search for an alternative policy framework.  Second, monetary authorities were encouraged by the success of the pioneer countries that have adopted inflation targeting.  Countries like Australia, Canada, Finland, Sweden, New Zealand, the United Kingdom, Israel and Chile moved from a high-inflation to a low-inflation environment and experienced higher output growth as well as reduced volatility in prices and output growth.  This strategy has also been adopted in developing economies, notably Brazil and, more recently, Thailand.

Inflation targeting in the Philippines is expected to help advance the cause of economic reform.  Specifically, by helping ensure price stability, inflation targeting creates a stable macro environment for continuing reforms.  Moreover, the basic preconditions of inflation targeting—the primacy of price stability objective as the objective of monetary policy and central bank independence—are already in place.  Republic Act (R.A.) 7653 or the New Central Bank Act (dated 3 July 1993) explicitly identifies price stability consistent with a balanced and sustainable economic growth as the primary objective of the Bangko Sentral.  The law specifically provides for the operational (or instrument) independence of the BSP.  This means that the BSP is free to choose its own instruments, such as open-market operations, in the conduct of monetary policy.  Central bank independence also implies fiscal independence, or the absence of fiscal dominance.    the BSP Charter provides for clear limits to any possible financial assistance of the BSP to the National Government.  Fiscal independence thus allows the BSP to pursue its main objective of price stability without being constrained by fiscal considerations.   Successful inflation targeting also requires a well-developed financial system, to ensure the effectiveness of the monetary transmission mechanism.  The Philippine financial system has a long history of reforms, which should further strengthen the foundations and enable it to be an efficient channel for monetary policy.

With the basic preconditions in place, the challenges of the shift to inflation targeting involve mainly the operational aspects of the new framework.  We began last year with a series of public hearings on inflation targeting to promote better public understanding of the directions of monetary policy.

Other important operational issues include the use of the headline inflation rate as the measure of inflation and core inflation as the operating target.  Headline inflation is widely known and easily understood by the public, but is also subject to supply-side shocks that are beyond the central bank’s control.  Thus, the BSP's announced targets would have to take into account the impact of supply-side shocks on inflation.   This can be addressed through the adoption of a target band for greater flexibility.  Meanwhile, core or underlying inflation makes a good operating target since it excludes volatile CPI components, such as food and energy, that are subject to short-run disturbances.  Thus, it is affected mainly by demand factors that can be influenced by monetary policy actions.  The National Statistics Office (NSO) currently does not publish a core inflation series, but work is now underway to construct an NSO definition of core inflation.

Effective inflation targeting also requires an accurate forward-looking assessment of inflation and output growth over the target horizon. This is to allow policy to react at a relatively early stage to emerging inflationary pressures.  To this end, the BSP is at work on further strengthening its econometric modeling and forecasting capabilities with the development of a long-term macroeconomic model to complement its current short-term inflation forecasting models. Lastly, measures to enhance BSP transparency include the adoption of annual inflation targets for the medium-term, publication of monetary board discussions pertaining to monetary policy, publication of a quarterly inflation report, and press releases on both policy actions and assessments of the monetary stance. 

Concluding  remarks

In conclusion, improving economic conditions have allowed monetary easing to reverse the temporary tightening in 2000.   This should help provide a supportive environment for economic growth objectives.  Nevertheless, the presence of upside risks to the inflation outlook requires policymakers to stand alert against threats to price stability.  In this regard, the shift to inflation targeting this year will help provide a credible and forward-looking framework that further strengthens the central bank’s focus on price stability.

In closing, I would like to offer some words from U.S. Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan, who said in a recent congressional testimony: “A central bank can best contribute to economic growth and rising standards of living by fostering a financial environment that promotes overall balance in the economy and price stability.”   In short, the chief importance of monetary policy is in creating the supportive economic conditions necessary for long-term sustainable development.  Through strategies such as inflation targeting, the central bank aims to contribute to broad macroeconomic stability through stable prices.  This is the abiding commitment of the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas.

Thank you and good afternoon.

 

(Note: Business Economics Club, University of Asia and the Pacific, March 07, 2001, UA&P, Pasig City)

Title: Opening Statement
Occasion: Breakfast Meeting, Foreign Correspondents Association of the Philippines (FOCAP)
Speaker: Governor Rafael Buenaventura
Transcription:
The year 2000 saw the economy challenged from several sides. On the external front, world oil prices shot up to record levels, leading to higher transport costs and higher wages.  A buoyant U.S. economy necessitated the tightening of U.S. monetary policy, which narrowed interest rate differentials and contributed to the generalized weakening of regional currencies.  These adverse global developments were compounded by uncertainties on the domestic front, particularly in the political arena. 

Recent economic developments

However, even in the face of domestic and international shocks, the economy managed to pull off a respectable performance.  The recovery that started in 1999 was sustained in 2000 as real GDP grew by 3.9 percent and real GNP rose by 4.2 percent. Growth was broad-based, and, in terms of expenditures, exports and personal consumption were the main drivers.  This moderate expansion in economic activity was realized amidst a benign inflation environment.  Favorable weather conditions—which kept food prices generally stable in 2000—and the BSP’s resolve to keep monetary aggregates within programmed levels helped keep inflation at bay.

Inflationary pressures were evident toward year-end due to the series of oil price and transport fare increases as well as the depreciation of the peso, which fed into wage adjustments.  However, due to good inflation numbers early on, the average inflation for 2000 remained low at 4.4 percent.  In January 2001, year-on-year inflation rose slightly to 6.9 percent but it decelerated to 6.7 percent in February, bringing the average inflation to 6.8 percent, within the government’s target of 6-7 percent for 2001.

Moderate inflation provided the flexibility to keep interest rates low and stable in 2000.    the 91-day t-bill rate averaged 9.9 percent in 2000, down from the 10.2 percent average in 1999.    At the latest auction, the benchmark T-bill rate averaged 10.3 percent. Mirroring the trend in the T-bill rates, bank lending rates have also begun to ease. Starting December, the BSP has also reduced its own policy rates, as the financial markets showed signs of stability and in response to the future outlook on inflation. Lower lending rates are expected to steer the economic recovery towards a sustained path.
