In the external sector, the current account posted a hefty surplus of US$7.6 billion for the first eleven months of 2000 due mainly to the strong performance of exports which outpaced the growth in imports.  The overall BOP position, however, recorded a deficit of US$918 million due to a weak capital and financial account.

Meanwhile, as of end-January 2001, the country’s gross international reserves (GIR) stood at $14.4 billion, equivalent to 4.2 months of imports of goods and services.

With the speedy and peaceful resolution of the political crisis, and with the Supreme Court ruling on the legitimacy of the Arroyo administration, the peso appreciated to P47.812 on 05 March 2001, the strongest daily average reached this year.

On the banking system, Philippine banks have been able to hold their ground amidst a challenging environment despite some stress here and there.  Capitalization is more than adequate relative to international standards and the statutory floor.  The banking system’s capital-to-risk assets ratio as of November 2000 was recorded at 16.4 percent.  The NPL ratio of commercial bank remains within the 15-16 percent range.  As of end-December 2000, it dropped to 15.10 percent from a peak of 16.26 percent in November 2000.  The real estate exposure of commercial banks also remains moderate at 12.3 percent of total loans (as of end-September 2000), well below the Bangko Sentral’s ceiling of 20 percent. 

Recent policy initiatives

On money laundering.    A number of BSP issuances during the year reflected the efforts and commitment of the BSP in the international fight against money laundering.  These efforts, however, have been circumscribed by the legal environment that the BSP has to work with.    nonetheless, several administrative measures have been undertaken by the BSP to bring the country’s regulatory regime on anti-money laundering closer to international standards. Among others, these measures included:  1) instructing FOREX corporations, which are affiliates or are subsidiaries of banks, to report details of all FOREX transactions;  2) requiring banks and non-banks to establish the true identity of their clients; 3)  requiring banks and non-banks to report suspicious transactions;  4) prohibiting banks from issuing cashier’s, manager’s or certified checks payable to cash or numbered accounts; and  5) requiring FOREX corporations that are subsidiaries or affiliates of banks, quasi-banks and non-bank financial intermediaries to demand supporting documents from residents buyers if FOREX in amounts of $10,000 or more.

In order to raise the awareness of the general public and the authorities concerned, the BSP and the BAP institute have and will continue to sponsor seminars on money laundering. In addition, the BSP and the BAP are currently working on guidelines for the proposal that will give banks and regulators the right to examine FCDU accounts under certain conditions.  Under the plan, non-Philippine resident depositors will be asked to sign a voluntary waiver on secrecy upon opening an FCDU account in any Philippine-based bank.  A number of initiatives are in place but these details may be discussed in the q&a portion.

On economic development.    The BSP has been supportive of the government’s social development objectives within the parameters set by its charter.  In particular, the BSP, in January 2001,  released a circular to implement the provisions of the General Banking Law of 2000 with respect to microfinancing loans.  These are small loans granted to the basic sectors, as defined in the social reform and poverty alleviation act of 1997 and other loans granted to the poor and low-income households for their microenterprises and small businesses.  The BSP is also finalizing plans to open a rediscount window for rural and cooperative banks which lend to microfinance activities.  This initiative is aimed at supporting rural and cooperative banks which have achieved efficiency in their microfinance activities, without sacrificing prudential standards.

In September 1999, the BSP approved the opening of a rediscount window for banking institutions providing financing for socialized and low-cost housing.  The measure supports the government’s efforts to pump prime the economy through the housing sector, thus, helping bridge the gap in the supply of affordable housing especially to the underprivileged.  

Policy thrusts

Going forward, the thrust of monetary policy will continue to be guided by the pursuit of the BSP’s primary mandate of maintaining price stability conducive to a balanced and sustained economic growth.  Towards this end, the shift to inflation targeting as the framework of monetary policy will be implemented.  This is expected to improve further the transparency and consistency of monetary policy as well as the accountability of monetary authorities to the price stability objective.

In the banking sector, the BSP will continue to improve its supervisory framework. This upgrading includes the adoption of a more forward-looking and risk-based bank supervision framework and the implementation of a consolidated supervision of financial conglomerates for a more comprehensive assessment of bank risks.  The BSP will also continue to support the ongoing restructuring of the banking system, with a view to developing regionally if not globally competitive banks.

Furthermore, the BSP will continue to work for the improvement in the legislative framework particularly the amendments to the BSP charter which, among others, will relax existing legal barriers to the fight against money laundering.  In particular, a proposed amendment will allow the Monetary Board to look into deposits of more than P50 million in an individual account, provided that there is reasonable ground to believe that such an account is being used in relation to any fraud or irregularity.  This effectively restores the authority of the Monetary Board under the Old Central Bank Act, which was deleted under the New CB Act, to inquire into a deposit account of a suspicious nature.

In closing, I wish to thank the organizers of this meeting for the opportunity given to me to share with you my views on the Philippine economy and the future policy thrusts of the BSP in the areas of money and banking.  Thank you.

(Note: Breakfast Meeting, Foreign Correspondents Association of the Philippines, March 7, 2001, Manila Hotel, Metro Manila)

Title: Opening Remarks
Occasion: 2001 BSP Monetary Conference
Speaker: Governor Rafael Buenaventura
Transcription:
Mr. George Pickering, Chief Representative for Asia and the Pacific, Bank for International Settlements; Mr. Chee Sung Lee, Division Chief, Monetary and Exchange Affairs Department, International Monetary Fund; Mr. Enoch Ch’ng, Senior Director, Monetary Authority of Singapore; Honorable Dante Canlas, Secretary of Socio-economic Planning; panel discussants, members of the Monetary Board; co-workers at the BSP; distinguished guests; ladies and gentlemen, good morning:

Let me begin by saying that I am deeply honored by the presence of many distinguished guests, and delighted by the attendance of friends and colleagues in the banking system, the business community, the academe and the government.  This monetary conference is the second in a series that the Bangko Sentral has organized.  In 1999, when the BSP held its first monetary conference, I was wearing a different hat.  I was invited to serve as one of the panel discussants on the topic, Inflation Targeting: An Alternative Way of Achieving Price Stability.  I was then the president of a commercial bank.

The theme of today’s conference—E-Banking:  Challenges and Opportunities for Central Banks—is indeed timely.    A barometer of the market’s perception of its importance is the number of participants here and the broad spectrum of society that they represent.  The exponential growth of the internet, which only a decade ago was limited largely to academic users, clearly shows that electronic technology has become very important to all of us.

Dramatic changes are occurring in central banking.  They are, in fact, happening even as we speak because the environment has become so dynamic.  In part, this is because we continue to grapple with globalization, which has brought about increased interdependence of markets and mobility of capital flows.

Admittedly, these changes are oftentimes hard to read but read them we must, so that we do not simply react to events that occur around us.  Instead, we must anticipate change.  It is in recognition of this that I have always subscribed to the notion that it is better to anticipate change rather than to have it forced upon you.

However, to be able to do so, one must first understand the nature of things. Central banks must, therefore, be at the forefront of efforts to discern—even anticipate—the implications of this technological revolution on their own operations.

There may be some nay-sayers, who have visions of a meltdown in information technology and its catastrophic effects on society. They will be, therefore, quite reluctant in recognizing the merits of e-banking. However, based on our experience with the Y2K millennium crossover, the largest danger that the year 2000 data change engendered came from the uncertain response of consumers and other market players rather than from any computer failures.  Moreover, it seems that this is no longer a question of whether we want to play the game—because this seems to be inevitable. Rather, the question is how prepared are we as we are drawn into the game.

The digital divide in technology puts a premium on knowledge.  It is imperative, therefore, that we learn as much as we can regarding information technology and e-banking. This conference will hopefully go some distance towards satisfying these imperatives.

The progress of e-banking will impact on monetary policy in various ways.  For instance, e-banking will bring about changes in the structure of the real economy and this will influence the conduct of monetary policy.  I.T.-induced changes to payment and settlement systems will also influence the effectiveness of monetary policy, and affect the central bank’s day-to-day operations.

E-banking will surely have an impact on financial stability.  As more and more people embrace e-banking, payment and settlement systems become more and more dependent on physical information systems such as computers and communication networks.  Thus, bottlenecks in such systems, caused by purely technical reasons—not economic or financial ones—could ignite unwanted chain reactions in the payment system that could cause serious financial disruption.  This would have important implications on the role of the central bank as the lender of last resort and as a repository of public confidence.

The coming of age of e-banking will necessitate regulatory changes congenial to technological change.  Invariably, we may have to rewrite the rules of the game to be in tune with the challenges of e-banking.  In fact, some steps have already been done in this direction.  On May 5, 2000, the BSP has issued a Circular requiring banks to seek prior approval before they can be allowed to provide e-banking services.  This will help ensure that these banks have the appropriate risk management systems accompanying their provision of e-banking services.

Meanwhile, increased private sector awareness of e-banking would prompt institutions to build up their capability to manage attendant risks, allowing them at the same time to maximize the resulting economic gains.  Greater interaction between the private sector and regulators in this kind of forum could also assist the central bank in formulating measures that are more responsive to the needs of market players.

On a more general plane, we hope that this conference will go some distance in advancing the cause of economic reform, as the country prepares to join in the growth trajectory of the third millennium.

We have an interesting day ahead of us as we discuss the issue of e-banking and how this will impact on its brick-and-mortar counterparts.  I look forward to a fruitful and rewarding conference.  Thank you and good morning to all of you.

(Note: 2001 BSP Monetary Conference, February 26, 2001, Westin Philippine Plaza)

Title: Closing Remarks
Occasion: Bank Analysis and Examination Training Program ADB-APEC Financial Regulators Training Initiative
Speaker: Governor Rafael Buenaventura
Transcription:
Mr. Norberto Nazareno, President of PDIC; Mr. Robert Porter, Consultant to ADB on Bank Supervision; Ms. Shamsad Akhtar, Manager, Financial Sector and Industry Division of ADB; distinguished guests, fellow workers of the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas, ladies and gentlemen, good afternoon.

First of all, I would like to personally commend the group which initiated the holding of this first “national” session of the APEC Bank Supervision Training Initiative.  This is the first group of participants to take part in active classroom training of this large-scale initiative, which is being supported by a wide group of international organizations as well as supervisory authorities of this region.

The course is intended to provide our examiners from BSP and PDIC with a fresh understanding of the issues considered in assessing a bank’s financial condition including assigning a camels rating.   Also included are information on the regulatory approach to assessing risk, definitions of financial terms, descriptions of common financial products and concepts, and the cause and effect relationships of financial strategies.

For the past five (5) days, the participants were subjected to an intense training on bank financial analysis, combined with some concepts for on-site examinations, particularly, on risk-focused examination process, and the camels rating system.

Let me tell you that the BSP, for its part, has been consistently aligning its policies and procedures, not only on supervision of banks, but also on its examination process, to international standards.  I’m sure the PDIC is also undertaking similar initiatives.

As early as November 1997, in order to avoid creating dangerous gaps in regulatory oversight, the BSP has adopted a consolidated approach to bank supervision as well as a risk-based examination approach.

The consolidated supervisory approach is deemed essential because of the growing complexity of banking organizations and their related interests.  On the other hand, the risk-based examination approach is most appropriate given the complexity of risks inherent in banking in a more liberalized and globalized economy.

In implementing a risk-based approach to examination, the BSP is shifting the examination focus to:

·         A review of the bank’s corporate governance and internal risk management system;  and

·         An appropriate level of transaction testing.

More than determining a bank’s financial condition and performance, examiners are required to assess the manner in which a bank identifies, measures, and manages risks.

Examination reports now include an evaluation of “bank-wide” risk management.  This is a significant departure from the segmented, unit-based examination approach. 

Existing supervisory processes and systems are also being modified to be more supportive of a pro-active stance in the supervision of banks. The modifications are aimed at enhancing our ability to identify, at an early stage, potential problems in individual banks and in the banking system as a whole through a more effective offsite surveillance system.

In fact, we have expanded our analytical range to have in place an early warning system that is more forward looking.   Aside from monitoring key historical trends and performance variables on an individual bank level and at an industry level, we have developed or are developing:

·         A set of statistical bank failure prediction models that can effectively guide and prioritize on-site bank examination;

·         A comprehensive bank performance reporting system that will facilitate ready analysis of individual bank performance trends, peer group analysis and overall industry trends; and

·         A corporate borrowing monitoring system that will facilitate a more complete evaluation of the quality of loan portfolio of banks.

These changes in BSP supervisory approaches and techniques would certainly require an enhanced set of skills that is supportive of a proactive stance in the supervision and examination of banks.

I truly hope that this training program has been beneficial to you as supervisors, as it has equipped you with the appropriate skills and expertise needed to successfully meet the demands of your challenging jobs.

Thank you and congratulations!

(Note: Bank Analysis and Examination Training Program, ADB-APEC Financial Regulators Training Initiative, BSP Institute, February 23, 2001)

Title: Key Emerging Economies Drive to Participate in the Global Markets - What Role for the Financial Services Industry in the Philippines
Occasion: Annual Governors' Meeting for Finance, World Economic Forum
Speaker: Governor Rafael Buenaventura
Transcription:
Introduction

Officers and members of the World Economic Forum, fellow central bankers and distinguished colleagues from the various finance ministries represented in this meeting, friends, ladies and gentlemen, good morning.

It is encouraging to see emerging economies and other countries dust themselves from the effects of the recent economic downturn.  But as they come out of the slump, these countries will again have to grapple with the forces of globalization brought about by the increased interdependence of markets.

While they continue to make headway toward full recovery, there is wide recognition in these countries of the need to go the full distance by ensuring that the recovery does not undercut the will to proceed with essential reforms. Even those economies which  are in the path of strong growth acknowledge the wisdom behind the phrase “Peacetime is the right time to get the army in shape”. 

Winds of Globalization

It cannot be denied that globalization has brought substantial benefits to countries that have opened up their financial systems.  These gains include the introduction of new sources of funds and instruments, which have enabled participants to earn the highest possible returns on their investments and to diversify risk. However, the increased mobility of funds has also heightened the risks associated  with the failure to address inappropriate policies, weaknesses in the financial system, problems in corporate and public governance and policy uncertainties that arise from inconsistencies among policy objectives.

Key emerging countries in particular are likely to face headwinds in maintaining growth. Hence, as we prepare ourselves to face the new risks emanating from continued participation in global capital markets, the subject of this special session becomes more urgent.

The Financial Services Industry

A prominent feature of the reform packages adopted in key emerging economies involves the liberalization of their financial systems. This has been achieved through the removal of financially repressive policies (such as directed credit schemes and interest rate controls) as well as the removal of barriers to the cross-border provision of financial services and to the establishment of foreign financial institutions.

While financial services are intangible, invisible, and non-storable, economists use some measures of financial intermediation to gauge the extent of financial deepening. In the Philippines, the financial intermediation ratio (defined as the ratio of M3 to GNP) rose from 0.28 in 1992 to 0.42 in 1997. While it dipped slightly to 0.41 in 1998, [1] preliminary estimates for 1999 place the ratio at 0.54.[2] Overall, the trend, which shows more efficient utilization of financial resources, is a testimony of the success of the reform efforts that have been painstakingly adopted in the past 10 years.

These measures have led to an increase in the magnitude of financial services transactions. Enhanced competition in the financial system has also led to a broadening of the range of financial products and services available to savers and investors, and to gains in allocative and internal efficiency. The latter, in turn, has contributed to lower financial intermediation cost that has had positive repercussions on the real sector of the economy.

Some emerging economies, in fact, have gained enough sophistication to make considerable inroads in supplying financial services internationally through cross-border trade, through the establishment of commercial presence abroad, and through the provision of financial services in the home country to international travelers and foreign residents.[3]  Other economies, the Philippines included, see the internationalization of their financial institutions as a long-term, but nevertheless, achievable goal in the march toward global economic integration.

The Role of the Financial Services Industry in the Global Integration Process

In such a setting, it is important to examine the role of the Philippine financial services industry in the process of global integration.

In sum, the industry should strive for flexibility in its capability to respond to changes in the economic environment, both domestic and external, and to the changing funding requirements of the country. This requires that borrowers as well as lenders are able to take into account uncertainty. A pragmatic view of the functioning of financial markets accepts the reality of uncertainty while improving upon the markets’ capability to manage risks. 

Upgrading risk management capabilities requires financial intermediaries to recognize and understand the increased risks associated with financial liberalization, such as credit risk, liquidity risk, exchange risk and interest rate risk. It requires them to design instruments that will allow borrowers and investors to spread and diversify their risks. Increasingly, this involves the use of hedging and  other risk management instruments such as commodity and financial futures, options and swaps, and other financing techniques.  

Financial innovation is not an arbitrary process, however. It is most evident in financial systems where competitive pressures have been allowed. To promote globally competitive and more efficient banks, monetary and financial authorities in the Philippines have encouraged mergers and consolidations in the banking system. Such consolidation will help banks take advantage of their collective experience, services and technological know-how.   

Complementary Institutional Reforms

However, in many countries, domestic financial institutions are unable to effectively manage capital flows because of the inappropriateness of institutional arrangements in integrating cross-border capital flows with financial policy decision-making.

Allow me  then to discuss what I think the  Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas’ role should be since it is a major participant in the development of the financial services industry in the Philippines.

Financial authorities generally have three interrelated objectives in promoting a sound financial system. First, they wish to ensure that financial markets  are efficient channels between savers and investors, and that these markets provide the financial services needed by the economy.  Second, they wish to ensure that financial markets are stable. And, third, they wish to ensure that adequate protection exists for investors and depositors.

In pursuing these objectives, Philippine authorities have put in place a policy environment where finance is used in the context of a voluntary market process for mobilizing and allocating resources rather than as a tool for implementing interventionist development strategies. Toward this end, the Philippines has adopted a largely open financial market policy. This is consistent with the view that an open financial market is necessary for effective market discipline.  

Several initiatives have also been taken in the microeconomic front to ensure that the supporting financial infrastructure promotes robust financial structures and contributes to lower barriers to cross-border capital flows. These measures include: ensuring an adequate capital base for financial institutions; providing for adequate information flow, credit appraisal and risk rating systems; ensuring efficient, safe and adequate clearing and settlement systems; developing appropriate and effective legal and accounting standards and framework; and strengthening prudential supervision and regulation.  

Conclusion

Whenever I am invited to a forum such as this, the talk invariably drifts into a discussion of the good template for the financial architecture for the future.  However, I do not feel comfortable with “one size fits all” prescriptions. I think that there is no single set of policies that is right for every country.  Hence, while the measures that I discussed may work for the Philippines, these may not necessarily apply to other emerging economies. I also think that reforms in the financial system will continue to be work-in-progress. 

Several things are clear though.  Emerging economies are in the midst of profound changes in their development process. Hence, without policy changes, financial systems will serve as a drag to the growth process. On the other hand, authorities’ high degree of policy commitment in effectively addressing macroeconomic imbalances and in implementing structural reforms in the financial sector will have a markedly uplifting effect on recovery and longer-term growth.

Thank you and good day.

-------------------------------

[1] M4 consists of M3 (as conventionally defined) and non-bank residents’ foreign currency deposits.
[2] For the period January-September
[3] Tamirasa, Natalia, 1999.  Trade in Financial Services and Capital Movements. IMF Working Paper 99/89.

Title: Philippines: Recent Economic Developments and Outlook
Occasion: MOPC Press Forum, Manila Overseas Press Club
Speaker: Governor Rafael Buenaventura
Transcription:
Mr. Juan P. Dayang, Chairman of the MOPC press forum, officers and members of MOPC, friends, ladies and gentlemen: good afternoon.

It is always a pleasure to break bread with the press, particularly members of the Manila Overseas Press Club. However, this day takes on a different dimension given the momentous events that have transpired in the past few days.

Amidst the challenging developments that took place last year, it has been easy to lose sight of the more basic bread-and-butter issues confronting our country. Today, I will put a different focus on these issues by talking about the state of the Philippine economy, particularly the monetary and banking sectors.

 Recent Economic Developments

 The year 2000 saw the economy challenged from all sides.

On the external front, world oil prices shot up at decade-high levels, and drove up transport costs and wages. The U.S. economy continued to heat up, calling for a tighter monetary stance, which narrowed interest rate differentials across regions and contributed to the weakening of their currencies.

On the domestic front, conflicts in Mindanao and issues about public governance contributed to business uncertainty that hindered the economy’s growth momentum.

Nevertheless, the economy continued to expand. During the first three quarters of 2000, real GNP grew by 4.5 percent, an improvement from the 3.1 percent recorded a year ago. Moreover, the expansion became broad-based, with manufacturing posting a recovery and agriculture and services maintaining their strength and resiliency.

The moderate expansion in economic activity was realized amidst a relatively benign inflation environment. Inflation for the whole year averaged 4.4 percent, well below the target of 5–6 percent.  This was also despite inflationary pressures coming from increases in oil prices and transport fares during the last half of the year.

Moderate inflation helped keep interest rates lower than 1999 levels. For instance, the 91-day T-bill rate averaged 9.861 percent, down from the 10.197 percent recorded in 1999.    This was despite the calibrated and temporary upward adjustments in the BSP policy rates starting in the middle of this year.  Recently, owing to the broad stability in the financial markets, we have started to gradually bring our policy rates down. Consequently, lending rates have begun to ease toward the end of 2000. Lower interest rates are needed to nurse the economy towards a sustainable growth path.

In the banking system, indicators remained positive and stable. Banks’ capital-to-risk assets ratio remained high at 16.6 percent as of September last year.  The non-performing loans ratio on the other hand, has stayed within the 15-16 percent range during the latter part of last year.

In the external sector, our current account continued to be in surplus at US$6.75 billion for the first ten months of 2000.  However, a weaker financial account resulted in an overall balance of payments deficit of US$950 million during the same period. Investments, however, continued to come in although at a slower pace.

The continued surplus in the current account contributed to the build up in our gross international reserves during the last quarter of the year.  As of end December 2000, the GIR level reached US$15 billion, enough to cover 4.45 months’ worth of imports of goods and payments of services.

Meanwhile, we have managed to trim our external debt from us$52.2 billion at end-June 2000 to us$51.8 billion as of September 2000.  As a result, and also due to good export numbers, our debt service burden has remained manageable.  For the first ten months of 2000, our debt service ratio was lower at 12.3 percent compared to the 17 percent observed in the early 1990s.

In the foreign exchange market, the peso was actually making some headway before the political crisis in October came to a head.  In fact, it started appreciating slightly toward the end of December 2000, largely on account of foreign exchange inflows and the progress in the impeachment process. However, last week saw mounting public protests over the recent impasse in the impeachment trial, which triggered overreactions from the market.  As a result, the peso-dollar rate exhibited substantial fluctuations from the normal trend.  While we regretted these adverse developments in the market, we have always held that these movements are temporary and would not permanently reverse the gains that we have made in stabilizing the peso.  This has been proven true—with the peso registering the largest ever one-day rally last Friday, as it closed at P47.50: US$1.00.  Today, the peso opened even stronger at P47.00 and has been trading at around the same level.

Finally, in the fiscal sector, the national government deficit reached P136.1 billion, exceeding the target for the year by P73.6 billion. Nonetheless, this has not resulted in substantial hikes in market lending rates. Moreover, the authorities remain fully aware of the need for fiscal consolidation and are taking steps to ensure maximum prudence in fiscal management. 

Policy Directions

For the year 2001, the Bangko Sentral will continue to pursue its primary mandate of maintaining price stability, both in the domestic and foreign exchange markets, in support of balanced and sustainable economic growth. In order for the Bangko Sentral to best serve this purpose, a shift from monetary targeting to inflation targeting as the framework for conducting monetary policy will be implemented by the middle of this year.

Under this new framework, government authorities will announce in advance the inflation target over a given time horizon.  If the target is not met, the Bangko Sentral is required to explain the reasons and to spell out the measures that it will take to get back to target. The framework, therefore, allows the Bangko Sentral to build its credibility by demonstrating consistent adherence to the inflation goal. This would help cement inflationary expectations. In the process, the framework also promotes greater transparency in the conduct of monetary policy, thus facilitating more efficient markets.

In the banking system, reforms to further strengthen the system will continue to be pursued, even as major policies have already been implemented over the past decade. In particular, major reforms are being implemented to prepare banks for greater international competition as a result of increasing market globalization and liberalization.  Hence, the reform agenda in the banking sector is a robust one going forward.

On the legislative front, rules and regulations to implement the new general banking law of 2000 are being formulated.  Guidelines already issued in the form of circulars include provisions on foreign stockholdings and electronic banking.  The reforms contained in the General Banking Law of 2000 will be complemented by proposed amendments to the BSP Charter. These amendments aim to enhance the BSP’s supervisory and operational independence, improve prudential standards and promote greater competition in the banking system.

To improve its monitoring capability, the BSP is developing a more integrated system of bank reporting.    This includes measures to reform the country’s settlements and payments system by developing a real-time gross settlements system, and the issuance of new reporting guidelines to simplify and rationalize bank reports.

During the year, the BSP has also continued to encourage bank mergers and consolidations to further strengthen the banking system. As of November 2000, a total of 21 banks have entered into such arrangements with both banks and non-bank financial institutions.  Despite these consolidations, studies have shown that the level of competition in the banking system remains healthy.

Outlook

Given the economy’s performance last year and the policy thrusts that have been envisioned for this year, government expects that in 2001, the economy will grow by 3.2-3.7 percent in terms of GNP.   This expected expansion is based on the strength of all sectors.    Meanwhile; inflation is expected to be in the range of 6-7 percent as a result of the pass-through effect of the exchange rate depreciation, higher oil prices and the adjustment in transport fares and wages.

In the external sector, the key factors that are expected to have a major impact on the economy include: interest rate movements and the extent of the slowdown of the U.S. economy, the extent of recovery of the Japanese economy, the growth momentum in Europe and the volatility of global financial markets.

On the domestic front, the primary task of government is to achieve fiscal consolidation and improve public governance. 

Conclusion

I have provided you an overview of the state of the economy.  With the presidential transition completed, we expect the economic recovery to gain further momentum.  As business confidence revives, we hope that the Philippines will be back in the radar screens of foreign investors.  This could re-launch us on a growth trajectory that would be more sustainable.  Let me state right away that these words are not due to the exuberance of the moment.  My views are based on the fact that our commitment to much-needed policy reforms has never faltered, and that there has never been any policy inertia, let alone any policy drift.  While conditions can turn tough in 2001 due to external factors such as the slowing U.S. economy, surprises can be on the upside, particularly as investors reassess and take a closer look at our economic fundamentals.

On the part of the Bangko Sentral, the commitment to maintain stability in the domestic and foreign markets will remain our primary concern.  At the same time, reforms in the banking system will continue to be pursued. In the process, we hope to provide the right macroeconomic environment that will be conducive to a sustainable recovery of the economy, and reduce its vulnerability to external shocks.

Thank you and good day.

 
(Note: Manila Overseas Press Club, MOPC Press Forum, January 22, 2001, Century park Hotel, Manila)

Title: Year 2000: A Tale of Two Stories
Occasion: Annual Reception of the Banking Community
Speaker: Governor Rafael Buenaventura
Transcription:
Year 2000 was both a challenging year and a fulfilling one. 

A challenging year

It was a challenging year because the economy was confronted by decade-high world oil prices compounded by tight U.S. monetary policy.  On one hand, the supply situation was squeezed by higher domestic oil prices leading to higher wages and transport costs.  On the other hand, the demand situation had to accommodate the need to keep the interest rate differential between foreign and domestic interest rates from further narrowing. 

As the U.S. continued to grow in 2000, most of the Asian regional currencies weakened against the U.S. dollar.  The peso also declined in exchange value but held its ground towards the end of the year, averaging about P44.13, even as imports showed some increase while the public sector foreign interest expense rose. 

It was a challenging year because of some political tension adding more pressure to the economic scenario.  What was needed at the time was some room for the economy to stabilize and for the market to realize that the problem was neither fundamental nor permanent. 

It was for these reasons that year 2000 was indeed a challenging year: the monetary authorities went into a cautious, but necessary, mode, adjusting the BSP’s policy interest rates a number of times to ensure that the price stability objective was upheld.  The BSP also provided some dollar liquidity in the system when required to ensure that legitimate dollar demand was served, and at the same time sought to plug any remaining loopholes in foreign exchange trading. 

A fulfilling year

Notwithstanding these twists and turns, year 2000 also proved to be a fulfilling one. 

The calibrated adjustment in interest rates did not stand in the way of economic growth.    Real GNP expanded by 4.5 percent in the first three quarters exceeding the year-ago performance of only 3.1 percent.  Real GDP improved by 4.2 percent against year-ago achievement of only 2.7 percent as growth came from all the sectors of agriculture, services and industry. 

The cause of price stability was served by the cautious monetary stance.  Eleven-month inflation rate averaged only 4.0 percent, well below the government’s inflation target range of 5-6 percent for 2000. 

Although the public sector finances turned out to be more than challenging, the increasing use of domestic financing did not lead to precipitate increase in market lending rates. In fact, domestic credit growth for both public and private sectors showed significant improvement in October, growing by close to 11 percent year on year with the bulk of bank loans going into manufacturing, wholesale and retail trade and business services.

The weak market confidence did not also dampen the external sector account.  The current account, owing chiefly to brisk exports, sustained its large surplus of more than US$6 billion for the first nine months of 2000 leading to a gross international reserves build-up to US$14.5 billion at end-November 2000.  External debt even dropped to US$51.85 billion at end-September 2000 from US$52.16 billion at end-June 2000. 

The banking system also held its ground against all the domestic and external shocks to its resiliency.  Its assets continued to climb, the capital to risk asset ratio remained high at more than 16.5 percent while asset quality was kept manageable with non-performing loans ratio declining from 15.7 percent in September to 15.6 percent in October. 

Prospects

Looking ahead, the main challenge to policymakers is to continue building upon the gains achieved thus far.  A sound macroeconomic environment requires the relentless pursuit of key structural reforms.  While we expect a moderate growth of output of about 3.2-3.7 percent in terms of GNP and a slightly higher inflation rate of about 6-7 percent, we are optimistic that these initial projections can be bettered by continued hard work by all. 

For our part, the monetary authorities will continue to focus on the medium-term outlook for inflation and financial markets rather than on the daily gyrations of key parameters.  This is the thrust of transparent inflation targeting framework.  We will continue to keep our ears tuned to international developments while sustaining our efforts to modernize the banking system. 

  (Note: Regular Membership Meeting, Rotary Club of Manila, January 4, 2001, Manila Hotel)

Title: he Philippine Economy: Recent Developments, Policy Directions and Outlook for 2001
Occasion: Regular Membership Meeting, Rotary Club of Manila
Speaker: Governor Rafael Buenaventura
Transcription:
I. Introduction

Mr. Sebastian B. Arrastia, President of the Rotary Club of Manila (RCM), officers and members of RCM, friends, ladies and gentlemen:  good afternoon.

It is a pleasure for me to be with you on the occasion of your first membership meeting for 2001.

During the past few months, political concerns have dominated the news, diverting public attention from other issues that matter in the long haul. Today, the fourth into the new year, I invite you to shift focus—to take stock of our country’s economic gains and appreciate the progress we have made in advancing the structural reform agenda as well as in laying the foundations for sustainable growth. I hope that after this talk, you will leave this hall convinced that, through our current challenges, we can face the new year ready to make the most of the opportunities that they present.

II. Recent economic developments

The year 2000 was indeed a challenging one.

Decade-high world oil prices squeezed supply, leading to higher transport costs and higher wages.  A buoyant U.S. economy necessitated the tightening of monetary policy, which narrowed interest rate differentials and contributed to the weakening of regional currencies.

Adverse global developments were compounded by uncertainty on the domestic front arising from, among other factors, the hostilities in the south and troubling questions about public governance.

Nonetheless, the past year was also a fulfilling one.

In the face of domestic and international shocks, the Philippine economy managed to pull off a respectable performance. During the first three quarters of 2000, real GNP grew by an average of 4.5 percent, well above the 3.1 percent for the comparable period in 1999.  Meanwhile, real GDP improved by 4.2 percent as against the year-ago achievement of only 2.7 percent. The economic expansion was underpinned by the resilience of services and agriculture and the recovery of industry, signaling the economy’s shift to a more balanced and broad-based growth path.

For the whole of 2000, real GNP is expected to grow by 4.2 percent, while GDP growth is estimated at 4.0 percent.  Growth is expected to ride on the continuing strength of agriculture, services and industry. On the demand side, stronger personal consumption and exports are expected to be the drivers for the economic expansion.

Notwithstanding the pick-up in economic activity last year, prices have remained generally stable.  The average inflation rate for the first 11 months of 2000 of 4.0 percent was well below the full-year target of 5.0-6.0 percent.  Moreover, it was achieved despite inflationary pressures from oil price and transport fare increases and the depreciation of the peso, which fed into wage adjustments.

Despite posting an uptrend starting October 2000, interest rates settled lower during the year, with the 91-day T-bill rate averaging 9.861 percent, compared to 10.197 percent in 1999. If you will recall, last year, we raised our policy rates three times—in May, September and October. Let me note in this regard, however, that the calibrated adjustments in interest rates appear to not have stood in the way of economic growth, particularly since we have started to gradually bring our policy rates down, owing to broad stability in the financial markets.     

As a result, lending rates started to ease toward the end of the year.  Domestic credits have started to go beyond single digit, with the bulk of bank loans going into manufacturing and other key economic sectors.

In the external sector, the current account continued to be in surplus at over US$6 billion for the first nine months of 2000, owing to brisk exports. However, a weaker financial account offset the gains in the current account, resulting in an overall balance-of-payments deficit of US$532 million during the period.

The robust current account position helped to build up gross international reserves (GIR) to $14.5 billion as of end-November 2000.  This GIR level is enough to cover 4.4 months’ worth of imports of goods and payments of services, and is more than enough to cover short-term obligations, twice-over.

The country’s external debt dropped to US$51.85 billion at end-September 2000 from US$52.16 billion at end-June 2000.  Owing to this and good export numbers, the country’s debt service burden has remained manageable.  For the period January-September 2000, the debt service ratio reached only 13.38 percent compared to 17.0 percent, which was observed in the early 1990s.

Meanwhile, the peso-dollar rate has, of late, been subject to substantial gyrations owing to the spate of bombings in the metropolis.  We note with regret that these adverse developments have reversed—temporarily, we hope—the gains we have made in stabilizing the peso.  It may be worth noting that, prior to these unfortunate events, the peso was making some headway, appreciating slightly toward the end of December, on account of foreign exchange inflows and the progress in the constitutional process.  The strengthening of the peso at the close of 2000 may also be attributed in no small part to the measures taken by the BSP toward this end.

The financial system remains stable and sound.  Total assets continued to climb; the capital-to-risk assets ratio remained high at 16.5 percent; while asset quality was kept manageable, with the non-performing loan ratio declining slightly from 15.73 percent in September 2000 to 15.56 percent in October.

In the fiscal sector, the task of consolidation remains a tall order.  For the period January-November 2000, the National Government incurred a deficit of P114.4 billion, exceeding the target for the period by P53.03 billion.  Nonetheless, it is helpful to note that the increasing use of domestic sources to finance the shortfall did not lead to a precipitate increase in market lending rates.  The authorities are fully aware of the need for prudence in fiscal management and are taking steps to ensure that the national coffers will provide ample support for this year’s budgetary needs.

Overall, if the economy’s performance last year is any indication, we are moving toward more broad-based—and thus sturdier and more sustainable—growth, even as we strive to rise to the challenge of fiscal consolidation. 

III. Policy directions, structural reforms and outlook for 2001

Policy directions

This year, the conduct of monetary policy will continue to focus on containing inflationary pressures while maintaining stability in the foreign exchange market.  This objective, we believe, will be best served by our shift from monetary targeting to inflation targeting as the framework for conducting monetary policy, by the middle of this year.

Under the inflation targeting framework, the Government will announce the inflation target that it is committed to achieve over a given target horizon.  In cases when the inflation targets are not achieved, the BSP will have to explain the reasons for the slip and the policy measures that it will need to adopt to bring inflation to target.  An indispensable ingredient, therefore, is the BSP’s accountability to the price stability objective.  Credibility is thus built on a record of adherence to the inflation target.  Such a framework enhances the transparency of monetary policy and, therefore, promotes the efficient functioning of markets. 

Structural reforms

Alongside efforts to provide a monetary policy environment conducive to the stability of the general price level, the BSP will continue to pursue reforms to strengthen the financial system.   While policies implemented over the past decade have had major positive results—made evident by the resiliency of the domestic financial system in the midst of the 1997 crisis—events over the past three years have highlighted that more needs to be done.

To prepare the financial system for the challenges posed by globalization, the BSP is implementing major reforms in financial regulation and legislation.  In particular, the BSP has sought to prepare the domestic banking system for the increased international competition brought on by globalization through the adoption of measures in the following areas:

Improving the legislative and regulatory framework

On the legislative front, the BSP has formed a committee to formulate the implementing rules of the new General Banking Law of 2000 or R.A. no. 8791.  The initial output of the committee involves the formulation of the guidelines for implementing provisions on foreign stockholdings, and the deferment by the Monetary Board of the implementation of the provision allowing banks to sell the financial products of their allied undertakings or of their investment house units.  These guidelines were issued under Circular No. 256 dated 15 August 2000.

The reforms introduced in the GBL 2000 will be complemented by the proposed amendments to the Charter of the BSP.  These measures aim to enhance the supervisory and enforcement powers of the BSP, further improve prudential standards for the banking system, intensify competition in the banking sector, and enhance the BSP’s independence. 

Strengthening prudential measures

To improve regulatory oversight and monitor bank compliance with the new guidelines, the BSP is developing a more integrated system for bank reporting and a more effective supervisory framework.  The significant developments in this area include:

-    Reform of the settlements and payments system.  Settlement risk will be reduced by developing a Real-time Gross Settlements system (RTGS), which will cover equities, fixed income, money, and foreign exchange markets and will effect final settlement on a continuous basis;

-    Development by the BSP of a risk assessment system in lieu of a checklist-driven approach to on-site bank examination; and

-    Implementation of a risk management program, which involves the adoption of the BAP’s foreign exchange manual and financial markets risk reference manual, and the holding of risk management courses for bank examiners. 

Encouraging bank mergers and Consolidations

The BSP also continues to encourage bank mergers and consolidations as a means of enhancing the strength of the financial system.  As of end-November 2000, a total of 21 banks, 15 of which were commercial banks, have entered into such arrangements with both banks and non-bank financial institutions.  Two more applications involving five banks are now pending.  Let me note at this point that, these consolidations notwithstanding, a BSP study finds that there is a healthy level of competition in the banking system, which is necessary for safeguarding the interests of depositors and borrowers as well as banks’ other stakeholders. 

Outlook

These policy thrusts and structural reform measures should help us consolidate and build upon our recent gains.  For 2001, the Government expects the economy to grow by  3.2-3.7 percent in terms of GNP and by 3.0-3.5 percent in terms of GDP.  Growth is expected to be underpinned by the continued strength of the services sector.  Meanwhile, agriculture and industry are also expected to post positive growth.

In the external sector, macroeconomic developments in the major industrial countries are expected to continue to exert a major influence on domestic economic developments.  Key factors that are being monitored include:  the prospects for lower interest rates and soft landing in the U.S., the strength of recovery of the Japanese economy, the momentum of growth in Europe, the volatility in global financial markets, and the divergence of major currency exchange rates from medium-term fundamentals.

On the domestic front, downside risks to the country’s growth momentum include the state of fiscal finances and the quality of public governance, particularly in the area of transparency and accountability.

Meanwhile, inflation is expected to be in the range of 6.0-7.0 percent. 

IV.  Conclusion

I have given you some broad-brush strokes on the state of the Philippine economy.    Recovery is clearly under way.  However, conditions can turn tougher this year.  We all know that the ongoing political exercise is an important factor.  We should allow it to take its course.  At the same time, it is important to recognize that part and parcel of the process of recovery is a strategy of economic reform that will give credibility to the country’s economic program, as well as greater clarity and coherence in overall economic management capabilities.

For its part, the BSP remains committed to the pursuit of structural reforms in the financial system.  We will also continue to provide a macroeconomic policy environment that is both conducive to growth and to the maintenance of price and exchange rate stability. Through these measures, we hope to improve the quality of the country’s economic recovery, thereby reducing its vulnerability to external shocks.  In the end, these efforts should put the Philippines on the path of sustainable growth.

Thank you and I wish you all a prosperous new year.

  (Note: Regular Membership Meeting, Rotary Club of Manila, January 4, 2001, Manila Hotel)

Title: Moving The Financial Markets Forward
Occasion: Joint General Membership Meeting ACI Philippines
Speaker: Governor Rafael Buenaventura
Transcription:
I.   Introduction

Officers and members of ACI Philippines, Money Market Association of the Philippines, Trust Officers Association of the Philippines; distinguished guests; ladies and gentlemen:

I am very pleased to be with you this evening on the occasion of your joint general membership meeting.  This is perhaps the biggest single group of financial market practitioners gathered in one place.

Together, your views and actions yield considerable influence on the economy.  I don’t think I am exaggerating if I say that foreign exchange and money markets move in large part on actions taken by people gathered in this hall.  This has been demonstrated in the past few weeks when the attention of most people has been focused on the peso exchange rate and interest rates.

Recent political concerns have dominated perceptions with respect to the Philippines.  As a result, both FX and money markets have been largely sentiment-driven, and long-term economic prospects have been relegated to the background.  Our job as economic managers is to see to it that through our current difficulties, the Philippines’ long-term economic promise remains intact.

In this respect, the BSP performs a dual role. First, as the country’s monetary authority, the BSP sees to it that monetary policy is supportive of its mandate of maintaining price stability conducive to sustainable economic growth. With price stability, long-term savings and investments are encouraged, which in turn leads to the growth and development of the financial market.  I realized that in a time of uncertainty such as this, a review of the so-called fundamentals of the economy becomes suspect; however, I submit that now is precisely the time when we should be vigilant and take great care that the fundamentals do not deteriorate in such a way that the long-term growth prospects are affected.  Second, as the regulator of the financial system, the BSP promotes the stability and soundness of the financial system, which is key to overall economic stability and growth.  I will therefore focus on the current thrusts of the BSP along these two main areas of responsibilities. 

II.    Helping the financial market move forward under a globalized environment:  Reforms and policy directions

Setting the right environment

 

international experience in central banking has shown that the greatest contribution of a central bank to sustainable growth lies in providing a stable price environment.  In many ways, the charter and monetary framework of the BSP incorporates the state-of-the-art in thinking about the proper role of a central bank. The process began with the 1986 Philippine Constitution, which guaranteed the independence of the BSP.   In 1993, the New Central Bank Act (R. A. No. 7653) then reorganized the Central Bank into the BSP, focused the bank’s mandate on the maintenance of price stability, changed the composition of the Monetary Board towards a private sector majority, and granted fiscal and administrative autonomy to the bank.  These developments will culminate in our shift to inflation targeting as the monetary policy framework beginning in 2001.

Under the inflation targeting framework, the BSP will announce explicit inflation targets to the public.  Inflation targeting thus provides a clearer assignment of the BSP’s accountability to the objective of promoting price stability and increases the transparency of monetary policy. 

            The shift to inflation targeting is important in view of the growing body of evidence that low inflation helps to promote growth and efficient resource allocation in the long run.  Controlling inflation will help us to avoid asset price bubbles, achieve lower interest rates in the long term, stabilize the exchange rate, and therefore help maintain the soundness of the financial system and overall macroeconomic stability. 

Improving the framework for the development of the financial sector 

While the preceding macroeconomic-oriented reforms are being implemented, the BSP is also adopting major reforms in financial regulation and legislation to address the concerns raised by globalization on the stability of the financial system.    The growth in the size and complexity of financial markets has brought about considerable benefits in terms of a broader menu of alternative sources of funds for investment and a shorter process of technological acquisition.

 

Theoretically, the diversification of funds sources that accompanies globalization should offer expanded opportunities for better risk management.  In practice, however, globalization has been characterized by volatility in capital flows to emerging markets, to the detriment of the performance of the real economy.

 

The government has adopted a multi-pronged approach to meeting these challenges.  In the case of the banking system, the BSP has sought to make banks more ready to face international competition, by improving the legislative and regulatory framework, by strengthening prudential measures, and by encouraging mergers and consolidations.  The main legislative framework is provided by the General Banking Law of 2000 (R.A. No. 8791, or GBL 2000), which supersedes the half-century old General Banking Act of 1949.   The reforms introduced in the GBL 2000 will be supported by the proposed amendments to the Charter of the BSP. 

General Banking Law of 2000.    Some of the more important features of the GBL 2000 include (1) granting authority to the Monetary Board to require banks to adopt internationally accepted standards relating to risk-based capital adequacy;  (2) providing for stricter rules governing bank exposure to directors, officers, stockholders and related interests (DOSRI); (3) further liberalizing the ownership participation of foreign banks in the local banking system to 100 percent within seven years after the effectivity of the GBL 2000, and (4) granting authority to the BSP to regulate electronic banking. 

To implement the provisions of the GBL 2000, the BSP has formed a committee to formulate the implementing rules of the new law.  The initial output of the committee involves the formulation of the guidelines for implementing section 11 of the GBL, which allows foreign individuals and non-bank corporations to own or control up to forty percent (40%) of the voting stock of a domestic bank, subject to certain conditions, and which also allows a Filipino individual and a domestic non-bank corporation to each own up to forty percent (40%) of the voting stock of a domestic bank, without any limits on the aggregate ownership by such individuals and corporations in a domestic bank.  These guidelines were issued under Circular No. 256 dated 15 August 2000. 

Amendments to the New Central Bank Act.    The BSP is also working for amendments to the New Central Bank Act (R. A. No. 7653).  Broadly speaking, these legislative measures aim to enhance the supervisory and enforcement powers of the BSP, further improve prudential standards for the banking system, intensify competition in the banking sector, and enhance the BSP’s independence.   The Senate version of the bill has been finalized, while the House version is set for second reading.  The new Speaker of the house has indicated that passage of the bill is included in the priority agenda of the house. 

Improving risk management.   To complement BSP circulars aimed at strengthening prudential regulations, the BSP and the BAP are taking the lead role in developing an informative framework for risk management standards which could be useful for banks in understanding risks and shaping their own risk management infrastructures.  Recently, a manual of current best practices in risk management has been released.   This documentation of international best practices is expected to help banks understand risks associated with banking activities.  Risks need to be better understood especially because they have begun to take different forms and are often off the balance sheets.  The manual can also serve as guide to banks in the process of developing their own risk management procedures which could be unique to their respective organizations.  Development of risk management manuals for specific products are currently in progress. 

In addition, a foreign exchange manual has also been developed and released to the banks for their guidance.  This manual institutionalizes a system of financial records, operational procedures and control mechanisms applicable to all operating units in a bank to account for foreign exchange transactions.  It also allows the banks to monitor its total currency exposure at any given time. 

Another risk management initiative in progress is the current effort to upgrade the existing payment system and develop it into a Real Rime Gross Settlement system.  This will enhance operational efficiency, reliability, speed, and timeliness of payment transactions in the face of the rapidly increasing volume and value of transactions.  The RTGS system once in place, will offer a powerful mechanism for limiting settlement and systemic risks in the interbank settlement process thus ensuring stability of the whole financial system.  This will also pave the way for the achievement of a delivery versus  payment system which should develop further the capital market. 

Upgrading BSP’s supervisory capability.   The BSP is continuously upgrading its supervisory capabilities in line with the changing structure of the financial system to ensure that supervision remains effective in fostering the safety and soundness of the country’s financial system.  This upgrading includes the adoption of a forward-looking and risk-based framework.  To operationalize this framework, we have developed our own risk assessment system. 

A first-generation early warning system has also been developed to facilitate the evaluation of bank solvency.  This will assist our supervisors in identifying possible weaknesses in individual banks even before they reach critical proportions.

We also continue to send our supervisors to various trainings abroad to sharpen their supervisory capabilities and to expose them to international best practices in supervision and risk-management techniques in other countries. 

Mergers and consolidations.   The BSP continues to support bank mergers and consolidations as a means of enhancing the strength of the financial system, and has extended a package of short-term incentives to support these consolidations.  In the future, we feel that the banking system would ideally consist of several major local and foreign banks accounting for the bulk of the total spectrum of the banking system.  The rest will be niche players, which will have a competitive advantage in dealing with specific groups of customers.   Mergers and consolidations actually complement the opening up of the banking sector to new foreign participants, inasmuch as both measures will increase the ability of the banking system to compete in the globalized environment.  Our assessment of the financial system indicates that the industry has enough room for mergers and consolidations while at the same time maintaining the effective competition that is beneficial to depositors and borrowers. 

III.   Conclusion

            I have given you today the broad contours of the financial reform efforts that are now underway.  We are committed to these reforms which we expect will ensure the resiliency of the financial system even through our current difficulties. Finding the right regulatory balance is always difficult.  While we need to encourage greater prudence in lending, regulation must not stifle competition and innovation in the financial markets.  In the end, however, we hope to be rewarded when we achieve greater competitiveness and efficiency in the Philippine financial system, an enhanced role of intermediation in ensuring broad-based, sustainable development, and a regulatory environment that is up to the challenges of the times.  We are quite sanguine about the future because of what we are undertaking today.  After all, “the best way to predict the future is to make it happen”.

Thank you and good night.

(Note: Joint General Membership Meeting, ACI Philippines, Money Market Association of the Philippines and Trust Officers Association of the Philippines, November 20, 2000, Hotel Intercontinental, Makati City)

Title: Providing Support to the Corporate Sector
Occasion: Luncheon Meeting, Federation of Philippine Industries, Inc. (FPI)
Speaker: Governor Rafael Buenaventura
Transcription:
Mr. Raul T. Concepcion, Mr. Antonio M.  Garcia, distinguished leaders of the business community, friends and colleagues, good afternoon: 

I am grateful for this chance to meet with you and discuss some of your concerns on the current economic situation. As leaders of the business community, I very much appreciate your ideas on how we can work together to boost the engines of economic activity. I also share your concerns on the potential impact on business activity of recent BSP policy measures.  This afternoon I would like to provide you with some perspective on these policy moves and also address some of the issues raised in your position paper.

The issues that you raised fall under three main headings: (1) the use of alternative measures to stabilize the exchange rate; (2) encouraging banks to restructure the loans of financially distressed businesses; and (3) the creation of a rescue fund for these companies.  I shall structure my comments accordingly. 

On using other monetary measures to stabilize the exchange rate

Let me clarify first the rationale for the BSP’s recent policy rate increases.  The Bangko Sentral’s decision to raise its policy interest rates was in response mainly to a volatile situation that is becoming a threat to the economy. The BSP took action in order to help stabilize the economic situation while the political concerns are being addressed.  Raising interest rates was not an easy choice to make, since the BSP has always been supportive of the economic recovery.  However, we believe that there is also a significant potential economic damage from a free fall in the peso, since it weakens consumer and business confidence, discourages investments and inhibits growth. 

Let me also make clear that the relatively high interest rates will not be there forever.  Our policy moves are intended to give time for the political situation to sort itself out. Thus, once the situation stabilizes, we will adjust our monetary policy stance to allow the recovery to proceed. I must also emphasize that in the last few months, the BSP has used policy tools other than interest rates to stabilize the exchange rate. For example, to alleviate demand pressure in the spot FOREX market, we expanded the coverage of the Currency Risk Protection Program (CRPP) to service the foreign exchange requirements of oil companies. We have also tightened the rules covering the foreign exchange units of banks by requiring them to submit documents for dollar sales of over US$10,000. This was intended to curb the speculative activities involving these FOREX corporations and also prevent possible money laundering. 

In addition, we do not expect the hike in interest rates to translate into an excessive increase in bank lending rates for the following reasons: 

»    There is still ample liquidity in the financial system;

»    Banks’ deposit rates have not gone up in the same proportion. Therefore, banks should not increase their lending rates excessively;

»    Commercial banks have entered into a gentleman’s agreement that puts a cap of 0-5 percentage points on the spread of bank lending rates over the yield on the 42-day cash management bills; and

»    Most important, the increase in BSP policy rates actually benefits the banks which place their funds with the BSP in the course of this open market operation. 

The BSP has also exempted thrift banks from the recent increase in liquidity reserves.    This is to encourage them to continue to provide credit to their target markets, which are the small and medium-sized enterprises and the housing sector.  At the same time, bank lending activity continues to improve.  Total outstanding loans of commercial banks grew by 4.4 percent year-on-year in august 2000.  Loans to the manufacturing sector have been rising for ten straight months since November 1999, with an annual growth of 11.3 percent in August. 

On restructuring the loans of financially distressed companies

The second set of proposals has to do with encouraging banks to restructure loans and be more liberal and flexible in extending credit.  Specific proposals call for relaxing the rules on the classification of restructured loans and on loan loss provisioning. Our sound banking system remains one of the bright areas of our economy, and maintaining the health of the system remains a priority of the BSP.  The rules on loan restructuring and loan provisioning were put in place precisely to ensure the soundness of the financial system. The stringent bank requirements and thorough scrutiny are part of the lessons of the Asian crisis, which underscored the importance of maintaining prudential standards. Relaxing these rules would go against established principles of sound banking regulation and financial supervision. Such an approach would strengthen the corporate sector at the expense of weakening the banking system. We must not forget that a strong economy requires a healthy banking system.

Moreover, as policymakers, one of our main tasks is to ensure the even-handed application of policy rules.  To extend preferential treatment to selected sectors implies an uneven application of policies and distorts the policy environment. 

Your position paper also calls for the BSP to take a lead role in evaluating rehabilitation proposals, since the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) and the courts may not be effective in this role. We have taken some crucial steps to address this issue. Secretary Jose Pardo and I have asked President Estrada to certify as urgent proposed House Bill No. 11867, also known as the Corporate Recovery Act (CRA). 

The Corporate Recovery Act is a comprehensive approach to addressing corporate financial distress.  It allows the long-overdue reform of our insolvency laws and provides for the remedy of rehabilitation for distressed companies. The CRA will benefit greatly our efforts in corporate restructuring by providing immediate remedies to troubled corporations, speeding up their recovery and putting them on a more solid financial footing. 

On the creation of a rescue fund

The third set of proposals is on the creation of a rescue fund for distressed but viable businesses. This set of proposals would have a potential impact on the fiscal budget, and would be best addressed by our fiscal authorities.  Let me say, however, that such a rescue fund should not become an added fiscal burden.  Of course, it is possible to arrange for external financing. However, if external funds will be used, stringent requirements should still apply in choosing the fund’s potential beneficiaries, which should be limited to well-managed companies with genuine liquidity problems.  Maintaining prudential standards and ensuring good corporate governance should remain a top priority at all times.

The idea of providing a rescue fund may result in what economists call a moral hazard problem and, over time, result in a weaker corporate sector.  The assurance of a government- funded bailout may be construed by some as carte blanche to spend unwisely and undertake potentially risky investments in the future, and eventually create bigger financial problems.  We have already seen how such an approach can have disastrous results, as in the case of Japan and Korea, whose banks remain mired in a sea of bad loans. 

On the proper role of government

I believe that government intervention should not be treated as a blanket solution to all our economic troubles. The government’s role is not to ensure the uniform survival of all enterprises, but rather to ensure a properly functioning, conducive business environment that will allow the fittest, most competitive companies to flourish.  This is the essence of free market competition. The ideal economic environment likewise includes a solid institutional framework for good corporate governance, to insure against corporate misdeeds. 

Policymakers should also focus on providing an enabling economic environment conducive to vigorous economic activity.  This implies prudent monetary and financial policies as well as a continuing commitment to vital economic reforms. 

Concluding remarks 

In closing, I would like to emphasize that the BSP’s responses to the FPI’s proposals are guided primarily by sound economic principles. We continue to be supportive of the corporate sector, but within the larger context of our main policy objectives of ensuring price stability and maintaining a sound banking system.  The key to restoring the confidence of banks to extend credit and maneuvering ourselves out of economic hardship lies in providing an enabling economic environment for sustained economic growth.  Asking banks to relax credit standards only invites future trouble in the form of more bad loans and corporate bankruptcies.  Corporate restructuring should not be done at the expense of prudential standards. 

At the same time, the Bangko Sentral is very much aware of the importance of bank financing for the working capital needs of Filipino companies.  For this reason, we will continue to review our regulatory framework to make them more responsive to prevailing business conditions.  The BSP will also continue its efforts to encourage bank lending activity as soon as market conditions permit.  In line with this, let me again emphasize that the relatively high interest rate policy is not going to be a permanent economic fixture.  We will continue to monitor the situation with a view to adjusting the monetary stance when the political situation improves.

The business community can be assured that the BSP’s policy actions will remain broadly supportive of our common objective of sustainable economic growth.

Thank you and good day.

(Note: Luncheon meeting, Federation of Philippine Industries, Inc. (FPI), November 6, 2000, Dusit Nikko Hotel, Makati City )

Title: The Near-Term prospects for the Philippine Economy
Occasion: European Union Embassies' Economic Counsellors Meeting
Speaker: Governor Rafael Buenaventura
Transcription:
Counsellor Jean-Philippe Quercy, counselors and officials of the European Union Embassies, distinguished guests, ladies and gentlemen, good morning:

It is a pleasure to have this opportunity to discuss with you the present economic situation of the Philippines and the outlook for the coming months. The European Union has significant economic ties with the Philippines, accounting for about 20 percent of Philippine exports as well as a substantial amount of foreign investment inflows into the country.  The EU has been a constant development partner whose confidence has been a continuing source of strength in times of difficulty.

You are all aware of the pressures currently facing the Philippines, and of the recent policy moves of the BSP in response to these pressures.  I am here today to provide you with some perspective about our recent policy actions.  My essential point is that the economy is facing pressures from various fronts, and the BSP’s recent policy moves were taken in order to help stabilize the economic situation while the political concerns are being addressed. 

Recent economic developments

The recent pressures on the Philippine economy have come from various sources.  On the external front, adverse shocks such as the oil price hikes and shortages, the middle east tension, and the political problems in Thailand and Indonesia, have weakened the peso along with the other currencies both in Asia and elsewhere.  On the domestic front, negative political developments such as allegations of high-level corruption have further clouded market sentiment toward the peso.    The resulting exchange rate depreciation and the lower level of confidence have created a situation that threatens our nascent economic recovery. 

Policy responses

BSP measures include increases in the BSP’s policy interest rates by a cumulative 500 basis points for the September-October period. The increases were intended to address the narrowing differential between foreign and domestic interest rates, which has partly caused the peso to weaken.  We also raised the liquidity reserve requirement for commercial banks by a total of 400 basis points in order to siphon off excess liquidity in the system, which we believe is being used for speculative activity against the peso.

To alleviate demand pressures in the FOREX market, we expanded the coverage of the Currency Risk Protection Program (CRPP) to service the FOREX requirements of oil companies.    More recently, we have tightened the rules covering the foreign exchange units of banks by requiring them to submit the necessary documents for dollar sales of over us$10,000.  This was intended to curb the speculative activities involving these FOREX corporations and also prevent money laundering.  This is not a form of exchange control.  What we want is to provide foreign exchange for legitimate and productive uses.
