The main result of all these policies is a significant tightening of monetary conditions, leading to higher interest rates. This was a difficult choice to make, given the importance of supporting economic recovery.  However, we believe that the potential damage from a currency free-fall is also very significant since it weakens confidence, discourages investments and inhibits growth.  Difficult situations require difficult measures, and inaction is no longer a practical alternative.

Let me emphasize, however, that the current high interest rate regime is intended to be only temporary.  Monetary authorities are very much aware of the serious adverse effects of high interest rates on the economy.  The series of actions are intended to give time for the political situation to be sorted out in an orderly manner.  I personally am hopeful that due process will prevail and allow an orderly resolution of the issues.  At the same time, there is enough reason to expect that in two or three months’ time, we will have a clearer outlook for the world oil market as well as the political tensions in the middle east and Asia.

As safeguard, monetary authorities have taken steps to help minimize the impact of the recent monetary tightening on lending rates.  For example, we have exempted the thrift banks from the higher liquidity reserve requirement, so as not to unduly constrain priority lending to small and medium-sized enterprises and the housing sector. Commercial banks have also entered into a “gentleman’s agreement” that puts a 0-5 percentage point spread over the yield on the 42-day cash management bills for their lending rate.

Let me again make clear that the relatively high interest rates are expected to be only temporary.  For the moment, we have put off further monetary policy actions but we will continue to closely monitor the situation and take any policy action that may be deemed necessary.  Once the situation stabilizes, we will adjust the stance of monetary policy to allow the recovery to flourish. 

Outlook for 2000 and 2001

In looking now at the months ahead, I think our expectations for sustained economic performance should be guided by an appreciation of the Philippines’ sound macro fundamentals.    So far this year, we have seen broader-based output growth, moderate inflation, a healthy external position with robust export growth, a fundamentally sound banking system. These economic gains have been due to an enabling policy environment borne of a steady commitment to vital economic reforms.

In the last few months, we have also continued to see positive trends in various leading indicators of economic activity.  For this reason, we expect sustained output growth in the second half of 2000. For the whole of 2000, GDP growth is expected to meet at least the lower end of the target of 4.0-5.0 percent.  Inflation is expected to build up in the remaining months of 2000 due to emerging inflationary pressures from exchange rate movements, oil price increases and wage adjustments.  However, these factors are expected to be offset in part by low food prices due to strong agriculture output growth and the timely importation of basic food products such as rice and sugar.  Thus, the 2000 average inflation target of 5.0-6.0 percent is well within reach. 

Concluding remarks

In closing, Philippine authorities have had to make some tough decisions in this very challenging economic and political environment. It must be underscored that our actions to stem a free fall of the peso have been balanced with the crucial goal of long-term sustainable growth.  The relatively high interest rates are intended only as a temporary measure. These policy moves are really meant to allow some time for the political situation to be clarified.

Let me make just one final point. The Philippines has faced tight situations before, in both the economic and political fronts. The difference now is that we have better established democratic institutions and a vastly improved policy environment.  I strongly believe that our established constitutional processes will allow the orderly resolution of current political concerns, and that we shall overcome such adversity in the end.

Thank you and good day.

(Note: Economic Counsellors Meeting, European Union Embassies, October 31, 2000, Embassy of France, Makati City )

Title: An Update on the Monetary Situation
Place: Canadian Chamber of Commerce, Shangri-La Hotel, Makati City
Speaker: Governor Rafael Buenaventura
Transcription:
It is always a pleasure to break bread with the officers and members of the Canadian Chamber of Commerce.  With the swiftly unfolding political and economic developments in our country, I welcome this opportunity to update you on the monetary situation, particularly the exchange rate and interest rates. 

Recent actions of the BSP

During the past few weeks, the Bangko Sentral has been implementing a package of measures aimed at stabilizing the foreign exchange market.  This package included the following:

»     The increase in the BSP’s policy rates by 100 basis points on September 11 and by another 400 basis points on October 13, partly to widen the interest differential between peso and dollar assets;

»     The increase in the liquidity reserves of commercial banks by a total of 400 basis points;

»     The expansion of the coverage of the currency risk protection program to include the requirements of oil companies; and

»     Just recently, the rationalization of the operations of FOREX corporations which are subsidiaries or affiliates of banks.  This latest measure is intended to:

»»    Further strengthen existing money laundering measures;

»»    Align our foreign exchange system which is very liberal, with those of other countries like Thailand and Indonesia; and

»»    Reduce the scope for speculative play by some market players who are sourcing their dollars from FOREX corporations.

Moreover, the minimum capital requirement of FOREX corporations has been increased to fifty million pesos.  Given the increasing volume of transactions of these corporations, this prudential measure has been deemed necessary.

Following this initial package of measures, the peso started to improve somewhat in the first week of October.  Nevertheless, it is important to point out that the peso is moving broadly in sync with other currencies.

Pressure points on the economy

Of late, however, the economy continues to face increasing pressure from several points, as indicated by the peso’s substantial weakening and its premium against the Thai baht, which had gone up considerably to about eight pesos from what it was in the early part of the year.  On the domestic front, negative political developments—such as the “jueteng” scandal, allegations of cronyism and unexplained wealth—have clouded the outlook on the peso.  On the external front, adverse shocks, including the oil price hikes and shortages, the middle east tension, and the political problems in Thailand and Indonesia, have further weakened the peso.  The confluence of these aggravating circumstances has created a volatile situation.  This could have adverse effects on the economy. 

Differentiating the economic sphere from the political arena

It is therefore important that to the extent possible, we differentiate the economic sphere from the political arena.  We should realize that amidst the current political noise, the substantial gains on the economic front have been unfortunately ignored.  These include good output numbers, subdued inflation, a favorable external position, and considerable progress in structural reforms.  These economic gains can be preserved, given that most leading indicators show the economy’s continuing recovery momentum.  It is also important to point out that, on the political side, democratic institutions are in place and that we have a constitutional process which should be followed in addressing outstanding political issues. The political turmoil is something expected of, and must be addressed within, a dynamic and democratic political system.

A delicate balancing act

One cannot overemphasize that a difficult situation requires tough and radical solutions, which may not necessarily sit well with the general public. During the past few weeks, we at the Bangko Sentral have had to make precisely such tough decisions.

The underlying premise of our strategy is that there is a need to stabilize the economy while a political solution is being worked out.  Stabilization involves, among others, siphoning liquidity that is being used by speculators to buy dollars, thus putting further pressure on the peso.   At the same time, measures to make peso assets more attractive are being implemented, including adjustments in the Bangko Sentral’s policy rates.

Basically, there are two hard choices available to us: (1) letting the peso go, or (2) raising interest rates.  Obviously these choices are akin to a razor-sharp, double-edged blade.  Hence, it is important that these should be handled carefully lest the economy suffer unnecessarily.  We believe, however, that there is a scope for taking the middle ground. 

The middle way

Let us first consider our options if we let the peso go.  Filipinos seem to be very sensitive to the peso-dollar rate.  This could be partly because there are about five million overseas Filipino workers with five million families to support.  These overseas workers maintain dollar accounts with banks and remit dollars to their families.  We have also a very strong export sector.  On the other side of the ledger, we also have to consider our imports as well as our external debt payments.  As a result, the exchange rate, rightly or wrongly, is seen by most people as a barometer of the economy’s condition. Thus, if the peso goes on a free fall, then we will be entering unchartered waters.

While it may be easy to say that the peso should bear all the brunt of adjustment, in a small, open economy like the Philippines this could have dire consequences.  The impact on markets will be almost immediate: oil price increases, transport fare adjustments, and wage hike petitions that go over and beyond productivity increases.  All of these could develop eventually into an inflationary spiral, which could undo most—if not all—of the gains that we have achieved thus far.

On the alternative choice of raising interest rates, it is important that we remain sensitive to its adverse effects on the real and financial sectors. High interest rates discourage investment and production.  High interest rates contribute to further corporate distress and in turn, affect asset quality.  This is the reason why we are monitoring the situation very closely with a view to reversing direction as soon as circumstances warrant.  Thus, we expect the current relatively high interest rate regime to be temporary.

This contingency measure is expected to buy us time.  Perhaps, within the next three months, the middle east situation as well as the political situation in Thailand and Indonesia would have stabilized.  And in our case, a clearer picture of our own political situation shall have emerged.

In fact, except for some extremists, most of us agree that our domestic political concerns can be addressed in an orderly manner, following established constitutional processes.  It is important that this is conveyed not only to ourselves but also to foreign investors.  I remain fully convinced that the constitutional process will prevail in the quick resolution of our current political problems.

 Moreover, let me stress that we do not expect the hike in interest rates to translate into a one-to-one increase in bank lending rates for the following reasons:

»     There is still ample liquidity in the system;

»      Banks’ deposit rates have not gone up in the same proportion. Banks, therefore, should not increase their lending rates excessively;

»     We recently arrived at a gentlemen’s agreement with banks to cap lending rates. The spread will be 0-5 percent over the cash management bills rate; and

»     We exempted the thrift banks from the recent increase in liquidity reserves. This is to encourage them to continue to provide credit to their target markets, which are the small and medium-sized enterprises and the housing sector.

In summary, let me be the first one to assure you that we at the Bangko Sentral are aware that monetary tools should not be used to address a non-monetary problem.  Nevertheless, the recent political developments have fed into the economic stream and this has driven the dynamics of our recent actions.

Let me also emphasize my view that the basis of the current high interest rate regime is not expected to continue.  Hence, this regime is not meant to be prolonged.  The interest rate situation will be reviewed continuously and interest rates will be adjusted accordingly as financial markets stabilize. 

Conclusion

Let me close by saying that our guiding strategy is to strike a balance and not take extreme measures that may cause permanent damage to the economy.  Not to do something at this point is tragic.  Remember that old adage: “If you don’t make up your mind, then your unmade mind will unmake you.”   You are all seasoned businessmen and interested followers of Philippine conditions, and I would be happy to hear your views.

     Thank you.

(Note: Canadian Chamber of Commerce, October 30, 2000, Shangri-La Hotel, Makati City )

Title: An Update on the Foreign Exchange Situation

(Note: Makati Business Club, October 26, 2000, Dusit Nikko Hotel, Makati City)

Title: Recent Developments and Directions for the Philippine Economy and Banking System
Occasion: Le Club Meeting
Speaker: Governor Rafael Buenaventura
Transcription:
I.  Introduction

It is a pleasure for me to speak before the regular forum of Le Club.  In its capacity as the French Chamber of Commerce in the Philippines, Le Club has certainly done much to foster not only French-Philippine economic relations but also understanding and mutual appreciation of our two cultures.  In an even broader sense, Le Club offers an important gateway for enhanced economic ties between the Philippines and the European Union, which now accounts for about 20 percent of Philippine exports.

This morning, I will argue that the recent economic and political developments have obscured the concrete structural reform measures that have been instituted, and the foundations that have been laid in order to support sustainable development.  The Philippines remains an excellent opportunity for investment.  In this connection, I will brief you on the latest developments in the Philippine economy in general and the banking system in particular.   It is my hope that at the end of our meeting, I would have presented the case for the Philippines.

II.    Assessments

What are some salient features of our recent economic performance?

Economic recovery more broad-based in 2000.    Industry expanded by 4.1 percent for the first semester of 2000, compared to only 0.3 percent for the whole of 1999.  Thus industry figures more importantly in this year’s growth, in contrast to last year, where growth was to a large extent due to an agricultural rebound.  The structure of economic growth is, therefore, shifting in such a way that growth is becoming more sustainable.  The Mindanao conflict has certainly made international headlines, but this is confined only to the central region of Mindanao, which contributes less than 3 percent to total domestic output.  Moreover, despite the recent pressures on the exchange rate and political concerns, advance indicators of economic activity have been registering generally positive trends:

  • Indices of the value and volume of manufacturing production increased year-on-year by 35.8 percent and 23.9 percent, respectively, in July 2000.
     
  • Meralco power sales and car industry sales are recovering and have risen by 8.2 percent and 13.7 percent for January-August, as opposed to contractions experienced during the same period in 1999.

Key monetary and financial variables also point to the sustainable growth of the economy.

  • The 5.0-6.0 percent annual target, and was achieved despite inflationary pressures from oil price and transport increases and wage adjustments. 
     
  • The treasury bill rate has experienced some upward pressure recently, but still stands at a manageable 9.892 percent as of the latest auction,[1]  while bank lending rates range from 12.27-15.22 percent. [2]  
     
  • As of end-June 2000, the total resources of the Philippine financial system had risen by 43.7 percent compared to the end-1996 or pre-crisis level.
     
  • Banks’ asset quality remains manageable· as of July 2000, the non-performing loan ratio of commercial banks stood at 15.26 percent.  A Goldman Sachs survey places the comparable June figures at 21.5 percent for Malaysia, 16.7 percent for Korea, and 39.7 percent for Thailand.  
     
  • Bank lending has shown consistent signs of recovery for several months now, with loans outstanding of commercial banks growing by 5.5 percent year-on-year as of July 2000.   In particular, bank lending to the manufacturing sector advanced by 15.3 percent year-on-year in July.

In the face of the foregoing positive developments, however, we realize that the current volatility in the foreign exchange represents one of the most serious challenges to the momentum of growth.

Current foreign exchange market pressure does not reflect long-term trend.  The pressure on the peso emanates from several factors: (1) narrowing of the differential between domestic and foreign interest rates due in large part to the rise in us interest rates since mid-1999; (2) the overall weakening sentiment on regional currencies; (3) an increase in corporate demand for dollars, arising from the pick-up in economic activity; and (4) negative market perception due to non-fundamental factors such as developments in Mindanao and in the political arena.

By contrast, measures of the impact of exchange rate movements on the international competitiveness of Philippine industry indicate that the current level of the peso has been out of line with long-term fundamentals.  Thus, the BSP views the current weakness of the peso as temporary, and not reflective of economic fundamentals.  We believe that, as the international financial markets calm down, as the prospects for additional interest rate increases by the US Fed are reduced, and as concerns about the domestic political situation are resolved, the market will realize that the foreign exchange rate has overadjusted and will correct itself.    Moreover, the BSP is carefully monitoring the pass-through effects of the peso weakness into the general price level.  Accordingly, the BSP’s approach has been to ensure an orderly adjustment in the foreign exchange market.

To this end, the BSP has adopted several policy measures, including:

-  Increases in the BSP’s policy rates in may and September 2000, with the cumulative increase reaching 225 basis points each for the BSP’s borrowing (RRP) and lending (RP) rates.  On top of this, the Monetary Board announced a 400 basis point increase in policy rates effective Friday, 13 October 2000.  These adjustments address the narrowing of the differential between domestic and foreign interest rates, which has helped to drive the peso weakening.  The adjustments in policy rates are also expected to stave off emerging inflationary pressures due to the impact of exchange rate movements on import prices and on wage settlements;

- Increases in banks’ and quasi-banks’ liquidity reserve requirement by two percentage points effective 13 October 2000, and by another two percentage points for commercial banks and one percentage point for thrift banks effective 20 October 2000; and

- Expansion of the coverage of the Currency Risk Protection Program (CRPP) to include the requirements of oil companies.  This will alleviate the strain on the spot market due to demand pressure from unhedged borrowers wanting to cover their future foreign exchange requirements due to fears of further peso depreciation.

In addition to the foregoing, the following aspects of the Philippine economy are supportive of an orderly foreign exchange adjustment:

  • A low rate of inflation.
  • A healthy trade position.
  • Robust export growth.
  • Improved maturity profile of our foreign debt.
  • Adequate international reserves.
  • Finally, a strong commitment to a floating exchange rate system.

III.    Reforms and policy directions

Globalization counts a lot of merits. It widens the opportunities for emerging markets such as the Philippines, but at the same time punishes policy mistakes much more quickly and more severely.  Today, therefore, requires that growth must be continuously nurtured, and the pace of reforms maintained and even accelerated.  To a large extent, these concerns will be addressed by recent reform measures which further opened up the economy to foreign investment.   Major foreign entrants are expected to come in the banking and retail sectors, with the recent enactment of the General Banking Law of 2000 and retail trade liberalization law, while the E-commerce Act and Regional Headquarters Law make a pitch to the technology industry and to multinationals seeking to enhance their presence in the region.

Mergers and consolidations.   We envision a future where there are, eventually, several major local banks and foreign banks accounting for the major portion of the total spectrum of the banking system.  The rest will be niche players, which will have a competitive advantage in dealing with specific groups of customers.  To achieve this end, the BSP continues to support bank consolidation, through the extension of a package of short-term incentives.   The policy of encouraging mergers and consolidations is actually complementary to that of opening up the banking sector to new foreign participants, inasmuch as both measures will increase the ability of the banking system to compete in the globalized environment.  To date, there have been a total of 9 mergers and consolidations involving 16 commercial banks, 1 thrift bank and 2 rural banks. Five more mergers have been approved in principle by the monetary board.

General Banking Law of 2000.    The recently passed general banking law of 2000 (R. A. No. 8791, or GBL 2000) supersedes the half-century old General Banking Act of 1949.  The GBL 2000 now forms the basic legal fabric governing the banking system, and is expected to further strengthen the banking sector by, among others, improving transparency, putting in place internationally accepted standards relating to risk-based capital adequacy, and enhancing competition, including through allowing foreign banks to acquire up to 100 percent of the voting stock of an existing bank within 7 years from the effectivity of the law.

Amendments to the New Central Bank Act.  The BSP is pushing for amendments to the New Central Bank Act (R. A.  No.  7653).  Broadly speaking, these legislative measures aim to enhance the supervisory and enforcement powers of the BSP, further improve prudential standards for the banking system, intensify competition in the banking sector, and enhance the BSP’s independence.

Improving risk management.   To improve regulatory oversight and monitor bank compliance with new guidelines, the BSP is developing a more integrated system for bank reporting.  Risk management will be enhanced further through the implementation of a risk-based approach to supervision.   Also, in line with the growing international awareness of the need for sound risk management in large-value fund transfer systems, the BSP and the BAP are also collaborating in upgrading the Settlements and Payments System into a Real Time Gross Settlements system (RTGS), which will cover equities, fixed income, money, and foreign exchange markets and will effect final settlement on a continuous basis.

IV. Conclusion

I have today sketched to you the financial reform efforts that are now underway, but I hope that this has gone some distance in convincing you of the Philippine government’s commitment to its reform agenda and of our continuing search for a regulatory environment that is up to the demands of the times.  Such reform agenda constitutes a key ingredient in the foundation for what we envision to be the banking landscape of the future—one that is characterized by bigger and more stable banks, with a regional orientation.  We recognize that the reform process necessary to achieve this vision will be long and arduous, but eventually, we hope to be rewarded in terms of the emergence of Filipino financial institutions with transnational reach.

Thank you and good day.

Title: ome Thoughts on the Prospects for Asian Economic Cooperation
Occasion: First International Conference on Asian Political Parties
Speaker: Governor Rafael Buenaventura
Transcription:
Leaders and representatives of the various Asian political parties, distinguished colleagues, friends, ladies and gentlemen, good morning: 

First of all, I would like to thank the organizers of this conference for inviting me to speak at this forum.  It shows vision on their part to establish a dialogue and a broad consensus on the long-term economic and political issues that will be of increasing significance for the Asian region in the coming decades.   But you can be assured that my thoughts on Asian cooperation will not border on the political; central bankers are an apolitical tribe but hopefully non-trivial. 

The outlook for Asia

Asia is becoming an increasingly dominant player in the global economy.   Already it accounts for about a third of the world GDP, about a quarter of world trade and more than half the world's international reserves.  The long-term economic outlook for the region has also remained largely undimmed by the crisis.  The factors that made east Asia a high-growth area in the past decade are basically intact, such as the presence of an increasingly educated workforce and high savings rates. 

At the same time, the increased trade flows among Asian economies have fostered economic cohesiveness and political cooperation among these countries.  Asia is, therefore, a force to reckon with, after North America and the Euro currency area. 

The result of this increased cohesion and growing economic strength is inexorably a serious determination to establish regional institutions geared to look after Asia’s needs.  Today I would like to offer some personal observations on the initiatives to promote economic cooperation, such as regional financing arrangements and a common Asian currency.  These two areas are part of the more dominant trend towards increased regional integration, and, therefore, deserve some amount of consideration. 

The case for regional cooperation and integration

Our collective experience with macroeconomic crises in the 1990s suggests the following: first, macroeconomic crises produce negative spillover effects that tend to affect entire regions; and second, most foreign institutional investors tend to indiscriminately lump emerging markets together instead of making country-specific analyses and investments.  Often, a weakness or attack in one currency will provoke a reassessment of the fundamentals of the other comparable countries in the same region.  Moreover, losses in one market may lead investors to pull out their funds in other regional markets.

These considerations, together with the presence of extensive intra-regional trade and investment linkages, provide the case for a “peer pressure” or “club spirit” that will promote the pursuit of sustainable and prudent macroeconomic policies in individual countries in the region.  In this area, soft forms of regional cooperation such as the exchange of economic information and best practices have proven invaluable and should continue to be encouraged.    Other, more substantive modes of cooperation may include regional training in finance and macroeconomics to upgrade the quality of both economic research and macro and financial management.

Over the years, there has been a growing determination to set up formal regional institutional arrangements in Asia.  This is due partly to the desire for a uniquely Asian institution that will have a focused mandate and will be responsive to the region’s needs. For example, the regional crisis has spurred interest in policies to promote greater regional economic stability.   Particular attention has been paid to, among other things, arrangements to ensure exchange rate stability and improved regional surveillance. 

The Regional Financing Arrangement

Asian central banks have shown the way in establishing the foundations for cooperation.   In 1977, the ASEAN Swap Arrangement (ASA) was established with five participating ASEAN countries to provide a short-term liquidity facility to help each participant meet temporary balance of payments difficulties.  The main idea was to provide a short-term financial safety net for countries in distress.

In May 2000, ASEAN finance ministers agreed, under the “Chiang Mai Initiative” to expand the ASA to include all ten ASEAN members and, in addition, provide a network of bilateral swap and repurchase arrangement facilities among ASEAN, China, Japan, and Korea (or what is known as ASEAN +3).  The Chiang Mai Initiative, therefore, expands the short- term financial safety to include all of ASEAN plus Japan, China and Korea.  This proposal was further threshed out in Brunei and discussions will likely culminate in Prague this month towards an expanded ASEAN Swap Arrangement.  It also provides for the possible creation of a regional surveillance system for East Asia.  Thus, by providing the basis for a regional support mechanism, the Chiang Mai Initiative may be considered a major step forward in the efforts to strengthen official financial cooperation in the Asian region.

Efforts to further develop the Chiang Mai arrangements into a longer-term scheme are embodied in the current plan for a Regional Financing Agreement (RFA).  The RFA is intended to complement existing international financing facilities by bridging the gap between short-term financial arrangements and medium-term schemes such as those of the IMF.  Proposals for the mechanisms and features of the RFA—such as funding source, conditionalities, and surveillance—are presently under evaluation by ASEAN. 

The prospects for an Asian common currency

Another factor spurring Asian economic cooperation is the continued expansion of regional arrangements in other parts of the world.  The recent successful launching of the Euro has prompted many Asian leaders to ask why Asia cannot work toward creating a common currency of its own.   In fact, Europe is increasingly seen as a model for the Asian region’s economic future, with a single currency and its own mechanism for responding to macroeconomic crises.

The idea for an Asian common currency was first proposed by the Philippines and Hong Kong.   The suggestion was for the creation of an Asian Currency Unit (ACU), analogous to the European Currency Unit (ECU) which was the precursor of the Euro.   Creating a synthetic currency like the ACU may be a viable route to monetary union in Asia in light of the absence of a single dominant currency or country.

The benefits of a single Asian currency are in the form of increased economic integration, higher levels of investment and trade, and lower transaction costs as a result of the elimination of multiple exchange rates and the convergence towards a single price for each good.  Lower transaction costs for businesses translate into increased efficiency in regional trade activity.  However, a single Asian currency essentially means a single monetary policy implemented by an independent Asian central bank.  This means that member countries will have to contend with the prospect of a loss of monetary autonomy under such an institution.    On the positive side, such an institution will also have a large amount of international reserves at its disposal, which will help deter speculative attacks against the common currency.

All these benefits are still well into the future tense.  This is because one of the main requirements for successful monetary union is that member economies should be on broadly similar cycles and have similar structures.  As you well know, the various economies of the Asian region are at very different stages of development, and operate under differing cultures and government regimes.  These economic disparities, therefore, may necessitate a lengthy period of time for allowing members to comply with the economic preconditions for currency union.  These preconditions include, among other things, economic convergence criteria, an interim exchange rate arrangement, rules for fiscal policy, a regional competition policy and labor market integration.  Needless to say, these things will take a long time to put together.  If the Euro is of any guide, we are looking at some fifty years of preparatory work towards a single currency area.  Thus, in view of the extensive preconditions for monetary integration, a currency union for Asia may be more of long-term priority for Asian leaders. 

Other barriers to regional cooperation

Other barriers to regional integration exist.  For example, most of the East Asian countries continue to view each other as economic or political rivals more than as potential partners.  Hong Kong and Singapore, for example, are competing to become the financial hub of east Asia.  Differences in political systems also underlie some rivalries. These contemporary differences have historical and cultural roots, and will tend to complicate any efforts toward integration, at least in the medium term.  He agenda should be topped by initiatives to establish common understanding of the key issues in this part of the world and our stakes in making this work for our respective countries and people. 

Concluding remarks

Asia is a force to reckon with in the world economy, one with impressive assets, increasing cohesiveness and bright economic prospects in the long term.  This cohesiveness and increasing strength have led to a growing determination to create uniquely Asian regional institutions.  Initiatives for increased regional cooperation are expected to produce benefits in the form of increased financial and economic stability.  Prospects for regional financial cooperation appear to be good in view of the initial achievements in the form of currency swap and repurchase arrangements. Efforts to create a single Asian currency are expected to be a long-term matter given the complex set of preconditions for monetary union.  Nevertheless, the successful example of Europe in this area provides some ground for optimism.

Another reason for optimism in the prospects of regional economic integration is the determination of Asian leaders to make it work.  Building long-term institutions in Asia requires firm political commitment.  For this reason, I am heartened that Asian leaders have venues like this one which would enable us to collectively chart our strategies for the future. The challenge for us all here will be to build on the commonalities and emerging ties of our countries and to overcome the diversities, many as they are, through diplomacy and understanding.

At the same time, there remains no substitute for putting one’s house in order.  No amount of regional cooperation will produce benefits as long as the fundamentals of individual countries remain unsound.  Addressing domestic weaknesses in the financial and corporate sectors should remain the foremost priority for Asian governments.

Our initiatives as Asian leaders may turn out to be one of the shaping forces of the world economy in the next few years.  My hope is that they will continue to be positive and visionary.  I am reminded of the words of dr. Robert Scalapino at the recent “Future of Asia” conference in Tokyo:  “Never forget that leadership is a critical element in this whole question of economic development and growth.”

Thank you very much.

 (Note: First International Conference on Asian Political Parties, September 19, 2000, Manila  Hotel)

Title: The Philippines: Recent Economic Development and Policy Thrusts
Place: Rotary Club of Makati, Makati City
Speaker: Governor Rafael Buenaventura
Transcription:
Introduction

Ladies and gentlemen, good morning.

It is indeed a great pleasure to be here and be able to join the officers and members of the rotary club of Makati in this forum.  I always look forward to this kind of interaction with the corporate leaders in business and industry in the country. 

Macroeconomic performance

I am sure that I have already met most of you in various fora this year and have heard me articulate on the positive outlook of the macroeconomy and the soundness of the banking system.   As we approach the last quarter of this year, we remain convinced that with the solid economic foundations, our economy will be able to hurdle domestic and external shocks and perform credibly not only this year but more importantly even in the medium-term.

In the past few days several important economic indicators were released that tend to affirm our optimism at the start of this year.  For the first semester of this year, real GNP showed an expansion of 4.0 percent.  This was above market expectations and higher than the 2.8 percent growth registered during the same period last year.  Overall growth was driven mainly by the stronger performance in industry and sustained expansion in services as well as in agriculture.

            Things are also going well on the inflation front.  Inflationary pressures have been quite subdued.  Inflation last month increased slightly at 4.6 percent.  This brings the average inflation for the first eight months of the year to 3.7 percent, well within our target for the year of 5.0 – 6.0 percent.  Inflation may continue to rise modestly towards year-end but we are confident that the whole year target will be achieved.

            The benign inflation numbers have contributed to the maintenance of a low interest rate regime which is needed to spur more productive activities in the economy.  For August the benchmark 91-day treasury bill rate averaged 8.926 percent only slightly higher than the 8.898 percent average in December 1999.

The exchange rate has been stable for the first four months of the year but has experienced some episodes of volatility and increased depreciation pressures since late may.    A large part of the depreciation pressures stemmed from the weakening of regional currencies, the increase in U.S. interest rates and the tensions in Mindanao.  With the resolution of the Mindanao crisis and the expectations of stable interest rates in the U.S., as well as the continued inflow of foreign exchange from our export receipts and OFW remittances we expect the peso to recover some of its value towards year-end.

            Our external position also continues to be solid.  Thanks to our exports, which saw robust growth of 11.5 percent for the first half of the year.  The remarkable export performance helped the current account register a surplus of US$2.45 billion for the first five months of 2000.    The overall balance of payments likewise registered a surplus US$397 million during the same period. 

Banking sector performance

Looking at the banking system, key indicators point to the system’s continuing soundness.

As of June 2000, the non-performing loan ratio of commercial banks stood at 14.65 percent.   A Goldman Sachs survey places the comparable June figures at 21.5 percent for Malaysia, 16.7 percent for Korea, and 39.7 percent for Thailand.  In the case of the Philippines, no public funds have been used to restructure the banks.

Philippine banks continue to be well-capitalized with the banking sector’s Capital Adequacy Ratio (CAR) recorded at 17.2 percent as of end-March 2000, higher than the end-1999 CAR for Malaysia (12.3 percent) and Thailand (15.2 percent). 

Policy thrusts

Going forward, BSP’s efforts will continue to focus on the maintenance of stable overall prices and of sound banking system.

To enhance our capability to achieve our primary mandate of price stability, we are shifting to an inflation targeting framework next year.  We believe that this framework is useful in conducting monetary policy in an increasingly liberalized and globalized financial environment.   Inflation targeting is expected to, among other things:

  • Manage inflation expectations, because of its forward-looking features;

  • Strengthen the BSP’s accountability and commitment to the price stability objective; and

  • Enhance transparency in the conduct of monetary policy.

We are also considering entering into a post program monitoring arrangement with the IMF without a  financial component after the existing standby arrangement expires at the end of this year.  The precautionary program will act as a seal of good housekeeping and further boost the credibility of our macroeconomic policies.

In the banking sector, the BSP will continue to push for measures supportive of a sound and healthy banking system.

An important recent legislative reform is the enactment of the General Banking Law of 2000.  This new law addresses the need to make our previous 50 year-old General Banking Act of 1949 more responsive to the needs of the new financial environment.  It provides the BSP more flexibility in supervising the banking industry and upgrades the country’s banking laws to meet global standards.  The law also liberalizes foreign participation in domestic banks, provides stricter rules on DOSRI loans, adopts the fit and proper test in the appointment of senior bank officers and promotes greater transparency in bank practices.  The passage of the general banking law will add more clout to the supervision and regulatory functions of the Bangko Sentral, allow the adoption of internationally accepted risk-based capital adequacy formula and enhance competition.

With the passage of the GBL 2000, an ongoing concern of the BSP right now is the operationalization of the provisions of the new law.   A task force to operationalize the GBL has been formed within the BSP. The implementing rules and regulations for the provisions of the GBL are expected to be completed by the end of the year.  New circulars are already being drafted while existing rules and regulations are being reviewed to align current policies with the new GBL.

A necessary legislative initiative to complement the general banking law of 2000 is the amendment to the New Central Bank Act.  The broad objectives of the amendments to the new central bank include:

  • Strengthening further the BSP’s regulatory oversight;

  • Aligning prudential standards with international norms;

  • Fostering greater competition; and

  • Enhancing the supervisory capability and independence of the Bangko Sentral.

One important proposed amendment to the New Central Bank Act is the restoration of the tax exempt status of the BSP.   We have been actively participating in congressional hearings to enlighten our legislators that exempting the BSP from taxes is not synonymous to the government losing money.  We have made the point that, exempting the BSP from taxes will not make the national government financial position worse-off.  This is because the loses in the form of taxes would be offset by the higher dividends and interest rebates that the BSP would be remitting to the national government.  We have also emphasized that BSP transactions are policy-driven and not aimed at earning any income for itself.

This fiscal autonomy of a central bank is not unique to the Philippines, it is practiced elsewhere.   Other central banks that enjoy tax exempt status include:  the Bank of Thailand, the Bank Negara Malaysia, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority, the Reserve Bank of New Zealand and the Reserve Bank of Australia.

To reiterate, tax exemption of the BSP does not necessarily imply a worsening of the government’s financial position but contributes to the effectiveness in the conduct of monetary policy.

            We are also closely watching the growth of the so-called electronic banking activities of domestic banks.  We foresee an expansion in the volume of such transactions in the future.          We encourage the adoption of these new delivery mechanisms in our domestic system to ensure that we keep in pace with the latest financial innovations.  However, such systems entail new risks which have to be clearly understood and accurately priced by our banks.  From a regulatory point of view, there is a need to identify, assess and manage these attendant risks.  The BSP has undertaken initial steps towards this direction.  We have issued some requirements to ensure that banks have in place a risk management process that is adequate to monitor, assess and control the associated risks.

Another current undertaking of the BSP is the development of a Real Time Gross Settlement System (RTGS).  This is expected to enhance operational efficiency, reliability, and timeliness of payment transactions in the face of the rapidly increasing volume and value of transactions.  This new system will limit settlement and systemic risks in the interbank settlement process thus ensuring the stability of the whole financial system.  This should be an initial step towards the eventual integration of our payment system with those of the rest of the region. 

Concluding remarks

            In closing, I would like to thank the officers and members of the Rotary Club of Makati for inviting me to this gathering and be able to share with you our views on recent economic developments and our future policy thrusts.  Once again, I solicit the support of our friends from the Rotary Club in pushing for these plans of the Bangko Sentral.   It takes time for these reform measures to be implemented and for these initiatives to take effect.  However, with close partnership between policymakers and the private sector, this process can be accelerated.    We are confident that as the reforms are implemented, these policy measures will eventually lead to sustained and faster growth for the economy.

  (Note: Rotary Club of Makati, September 6, 2000, Makati City )

Title: Confidence in the Financial System: How Do We Protect Our Investments?
Occasion: Joint MAP-PCCI-MBC Membership Meeting
Speaker: Governor Rafael Buenaventura
Transcription:
Introduction

I am delighted to be able to speak before the General Membership Meeting of the Management Association of the Philippines (MAP), held jointly with the Philippine Chamber of Commerce and Industry and the Makati Business Club.  I am sure that our discussion will be very fruitful for two very important reasons.   First, this joint gathering of three of the country’s most important business groups is rather rare.  Second, the organizers chose an excellent topic for discussion— for the issue of confidence in the financial system is crucial to the question of confidence in the rest of the economy, and, indeed, to the sustainability of our development agenda.

If the Philippines is to catch up with the rest of Asia, then there is no choice but to integrate with the global economy.  However, as the Asian financial crisis has demonstrated, globalization heightens demands on both the economy and on economic management.  The past decade has witnessed large fluctuations in external financing flows to emerging markets, and recent developments indicate that this volatility is likely to continue.  Continued strengthening of the financial sector is, therefore, an imperative.  A stable, competitive, and innovative financial sector will help greatly in sustaining and stabilizing the economy’s growth path by ensuring that financing flows efficiently towards its most productive uses.

The two important areas that impinge upon the financial system’s performance are: (1) the state of the overall macroeconomy, and (2) the authorities’ commitment to the structural reform program.  Accordingly, I shall look into these two areas in detail. 

The state of the economy

Economic recovery without sacrificing price stability.    A strong industrial sector recovery contributed greatly to our 3.45 percent real GNP growth for the first quarter of this year.   This contrasts with 1999, where the 3.6 percent whole year growth was to a large extent due to an agricultural rebound, and where industry expanded by only 0.3 percent.   The sectoral composition of GNP, therefore, argues in favor of a healthier and more sustainable growth compared to last year.

It is important to note that this recovery has been achieved without sacrificing broad stability in prices.   Inflation averaged 3.6 percent for the first seven months of this year, as against a full-year target of 5-6 percent.  Low inflation has also contributed to a trend decline in interest rates.   The 91-day treasury bill rate stood at 8.93 percent as of the latest auction on 21 August, while lending rates have been within the range 11.41-14.33 percent for August 2000.

External payments risk managed through prudent external debt and international reserve management.     Apart from a sound policy framework, the other aspect of macroeconomic management that has an important bearing on confidence in the financial system involves our ability to pay our foreign obligations on time.  Two ingredients are important in this respect—the BSP’s management of, first, the level and composition of our external debt, and second, our international reserve position.  We have improved significantly in both respects.  

Thus, although the end-march 2000 level of foreign debt increased by 7.8 percent over its year-ago level, the maturity profile of the debt has improved, with medium- and long-term loans accounting for 88.5 percent of the total at end-March 2000, compared to 85.0 percent for the year-ago level.    Furthermore, as of 10 August 2000, the GIR level has gone up to $15.455 billion, which is equivalent to 4.6 months of imports of goods and services.  This provides us an additional cushion of comfort against external shocks.

Finally, our commitment to a floating exchange rate system remains the best means of addressing foreign exchange risk, as this removes a one-way bet on the direction of exchange rate movements and ensures that the risk of exchange rate movements are borne by market players. 

The state of the banking system

At the threshold of the 21st century, the Philippine banking system stands resilient and dynamic.  Successive increases in the minimum capitalization requirement of banks and the consequent mergers and consolidations have resulted in bigger and better-capitalized banks.      The banking system is also moving toward greater transparency and improved corporate governance. Overall, key indicators point to the system’s continuing stability and growth.  As of June 2000, the non-performing loan ratio of commercial banks stood at 14.65 percent.  A Goldman Sachs survey places the comparable June figures at 21.5 percent for Malaysia, 16.7 percent for Korea, and 39.7 percent for Thailand.   The higher level of capitalization has also allowed Philippine banks to post a Capital Adequacy Ratio (CAR) of 17.2 percent as of end-March 2000, higher than the end-1999 CAR for Malaysia (12.3 percent) and Thailand (15.2 percent).

One important benefit of banking system soundness is that, to date, the liquidity assistance of the Bangko Sentral to distressed banks has been significantly lower compared to the levels extended by other Asian monetary authorities.  Also very importantly, no public funds have been used to bail out failed banks and financial institutions.  Restructuring of banks in the Philippines have involved mainly the consolidation of the banking industry.

Reforms and policy directions

All the foregoing statements should not be taken as implying in any way that we have become complacent about our growth prospects—far from it.  In fact, we recognize the recent existence of some negative market sentiment towards the Philippines.  We take this sentiment as a challenge for us to remain ever more committed to the pursuit of structural and social reform.    The reform agenda is a robust one going forward.  Key reforms have been and are currently being put in place to build the architecture necessary to equip the banking system for globalization.

General Banking Law.     The passage of the General Banking Law of 2000 (R.A. No. 8791) is expected to further strengthen the banking sector by, among others, improving transparency, putting in place internationally accepted standards relating to risk-based capital adequacy, and enhancing competition, including through allowing foreign banks to acquire up to 100 percent of the voting stock of an existing bank within 7 years from the effectivity of the law.

Amendment of the New Central Bank Act.    The BSP is pushing for amendments to the New Central Bank Act (R. A. No. 7653).    Broadly speaking, these legislative measures aim to enhance the supervisory and enforcement powers of the BSP, further improve prudential standards for the banking system and enhance the BSP’s independence.

Mergers and consolidations.    The BSP continues to support a liberal banking policy that promotes an environment conducive to the development of big, regionally—if not globally— competitive banking institutions.  This policy is actually complementary to that of opening up the banking sector to new foreign participants, inasmuch as both measures will increase the ability of the banking system to compete in the globalized environment.

In view of the large number of competitors in the commercial banking sector, we are confident that such mergers will not result in an oligopolistic banking industry.  The industry has enough room for mergers and consolidations without staving off the effective competition that is beneficial to depositors and borrowers.  Smaller banks will play a significant role as niche players, specializing in products that will give them competitive advantage in catering to specific customers.

            Enhancement of banks’ risk management capability.  We have repeatedly emphasized that the dramatic changes in the structure of banking and the increased risks associated with financial liberalization and globalization entail upgrading banks’ risk management capabilities. The significant developments in this area include:

·        Improvements in the financial infrastructure to ensure compliance with international best practices in supervision and risk management, including development by the BSP of a more integrated bank reporting system for monitoring bank compliance with new guidelines.

·        Reform of settlements and payments system.   The BSP and the BAP are collaborating in developing a Real Time Gross Settlements System (RTGS), which will cover equities, fixed income, money, and foreign exchange markets and will effect final settlement on a continuous basis;

·       Completion by the BSP of a first-generation early warning system for commercial banks, which will provide the BSP with advance indicators of bank solvency;

·       Development by the BSP of a risk assessment system in lieu of a checklist-driven approach to on-site bank examination.

            The BSP is also closely monitoring the proposed amendments by the BASLE Committee on Banking Supervision to the capital adequacy framework.  The proposed framework aims to eliminate the distortions caused by the existing capital framework and further promote systemic stability.  The features of this new framework will be incorporated into the implementing rules and regulations of the General Banking Law of 2000 that the BSP is formulating.

Increasing the transparency of the financial market.   Transparency is essential for market discipline, for proper market evaluation of risks, and for ensuring that these risks are correctly and promptly reflected in market prices.  Recent BSP measures meant to improve market transparency include requiring banks to post information on interest rates and to disclose the levels of non-performing loans, classified loans and other risk assets, and insider loans in their quarterly statements of condition.

Challenges ahead

            With the implementation of our economic reform agenda, we are confident of achieving our program targets.  For the year 2000, these targets include a GNP growth rate of 4.5-5.5 percent, an inflation rate of 5.0-6.0 percent, a current account balance of US$6.3 billion, and a foreign reserve position of US$16.1 billion by year-end. However, we must always bear in mind that global and regional stability is very much a work-in-progress.  Uneven growth and possible slowdown in certain major economies could still cause destabilizing aftershocks in Asia.   In connection with this, recent indications of a soft landing for the us economy are a welcome development.

            The key feature of globalization is that it confronts us with new combinations of both opportunities and risks.  Thus, a financial system that is attuned to the demands of the new environment must be responsive to both the opportunities and risks present in the market.            The key challenge is to find the appropriate level of prudential supervision that ensures the safety and soundness of the financial system, while at the same time balancing this consideration with the need to maximize the level of competition and efficiency in the provision of financial services.    As policies take hold and the confidence of the business sector builds up,  we can expect greater business receptivity to economic opportunities.  Such confidence is self-reinforcing, and the task for government is therefore to continue to build the foundations that will allow for a sustained economic take-off.

            Thank you and good day.

  (Note: Joint MAP-PCCI-MBC Membership Meeting, August 28, 2000, Hotel Intercontinental, Makati City )

Title: Shangri-La Hotel, Makati City
Place: The BSP and the ECCP: Partners in Promoting Philippine Development
Occasion: European Chamber of Commerce of the Philippines (ECCP)
Speaker: Governor Rafael Buenaventura
Transcription:
It is a pleasure to be invited to this luncheon meeting of the European Chamber of Commerce of the Philippines.

Indeed, it is an excellent opportunity to break bread with members of the umbrella organization for European businesses in the country and exchange views on the state of Philippine business and the economy.

Europe has been one of the Philippines’ strategic partners in the areas of trade and investment.  The annual flow of foreign equity investments in the country by European countries has grown steadily during the last ten years from US$30 million in 1990 to US$1.2 billion in 1999.  The yearly flow of European portfolio investments in the country also followed the same trend, rising from US$17 million in 1990 to US$4.7 billion in 1999.  For the first five months of this year, our balance of trade with the European bloc was positive at US$1.3 billion.  In 1999, we also enjoyed a balance of trade surplus with Europe amounting US$3.6 billion.  Europe is also an important destination region for our overseas workers, whose remittances from this area have been growing steadily.

As long-time trade and investment partners, most of you, I am sure, are no longer strangers to the intricacies of Philippine business.  What you need at this time, I think, is an update on the Philippine economy to keep you informed of key developments that may affect the cost and pace of doing business in the country.  They say that perception is key and this afternoon, I would like to share with you some  developments that would hopefully help you arrive at a more informed assessment of the Philippine economy.

One encouraging piece of news is that the economy has continued to expand.  In the first quarter of this year, real gross domestic product grew by 3.4 percent, way above the 0.7 percent growth posted during the comparable quarter in 1999. This growth was underpinned by the expansion in industry and services, indicating broad-based recovery. In particular, the manufacturing sector appears to be taking over the reins of growth, as it rose by 5.8 percent during the quarter relative to its level during the same period a year earlier.

It is also noteworthy that in contrast to the first quarter of 1999, when the public sector propelled overall growth, private sector activities were behind this year’s first quarter expansion, indicating more durable growth prospects.

There are other indicators that support this expansionary trend.  On the supply side, the value and volume of production indices for the first five months of this year posted positive growth rates, a reversal of the negative growth in 1999.  On the demand side, exports growth remained strong at 11.5 percent in the first six months of this year.    Meanwhile, import growth continues to be positive, indicating the underlying growth momentum  of the economy.  Car sales and power sales are also on the rise and these indicators attest to the strengthening of consumer confidence.

As the economy positions itself for further expansion, the macroeconomic environment remains fundamentally sound and conducive to doing business.  Inflation has remained low and stable at 3.6 percent during the first seven months of this year.  This has helped keep interest rates at steady and reasonable levels. Of late, the peso has followed a more stable path after its sentiment-driven weakening in the past few weeks.  We expect that this trend will continue as regional currency movements stabilize and the political turmoil in Mindanao subsides.  Our external payments position remains solid, reflecting a respectable current account surplus, high level of foreign reserves and an improving maturity structure of external debt.  Our banking system remains safe and sound and serves as an efficient channel for business and investment transactions.

This overall positive view of the economy’s fundamentals has been confirmed by various international research agencies.   For instance, Morgan Stanley found that the Philippine stands at a favorable position relative to some international investment benchmarks, including external debt as a percentage of exports, debt service ratio and reserve coverage.  Paine Webber, which came up with its ability to pay index, grouped the Philippines with south Korea, Thailand and Malaysia as the countries with the “lowest risk” in East Asia, indicating that it has a low prospect of default due to its sound financing position.

But the key event that confirmed the soundness and direction of the Philippine economic program was the endorsement by the international monetary fund last week of the findings of the fifth review of the country’s stand-by arrangement.  Not only did it pave the way for the release of US$314 million worth of financing for the country, but it also helped in bolstering the country’s international credit standing.  Meanwhile, the government remains  firm in strengthening its efforts at improving tax administration and holding back on non-essential expenditures with a view to keeping the fiscal program on track.

In addition to our fundamentally sound economy, our strategic location as a gateway to Asia and the superior quality of our manpower resources are some key positives that prospective investors would do well to consider in their fund allocation decisions.  The 1999 survey by the Hong Kong-based Political and Economic Risk Consulting Limited showed that Philippine labor was second only to India in Asia and ahead of ASEAN countries in terms of quality, cost competitiveness and availability.  In another report based on a new global cyber index called “Cyber Atlas” of the US-based Meta group, which measures the “technological vitality” of 47 countries, the Philippines ranked first in terms of available workers who are skilled in information technology.

Perhaps this competitive edge of our human resources could find some match with the European investors’ expertise and industrial strength not only in information technology but also in other related areas such as power, telecommunications, energy and even banking.  Any European-RP venture in this direction will continue to be supported by our firm commitment to structural reforms that have seen the passage in congress of such legislations as the electronic commerce law, the revised General Banking Act and the Regional Headquarters Law.   All of which aim to facilitate greater efficiency in business transactions in a globally integrated context.

On the part of the Bangko Sentral, continued prudence in monetary policy and in bank supervision will remain our primary thrusts to ensure a stable monetary and financial environment conducive for business and investment transactions in the country.

In closing, I wish to thank the officers and organizers of this meeting for the opportunity to address the ECCP members and share my views on the Philippine economy.   We have brought this Philippine story to the United States and it was received well.  Hopefully, members of this Chamber would be equally receptive to our story and signify their willingness to join the Philippines in a partnership to develop further the economy.   After all, prosperity shared is never diminished but grows into an even grander vision for all its beneficiaries.

Thank you and good day.

  (Note: Luncheon Meeting, European Chamber of Commerce of the Philippines (ECCP), August 7, 2000, Shangri-La Hotel, Makati City )

Title: Closing Address: SEACEN Workshop on Concepts and Measurements of Core Inflation and Inflation Forecasting
Speaker: Governor Rafael Buenaventura
Transcription:
Monetary Board member Vicente B. Valdepeñas, Jr., Dr. Subarjo Joyosumarto, officials and staff of the SEACEN Centre, distinguished guests, participants, my colleagues at the BSP, ladies and gentlemen, good evening:

Tonight we are concluding a very successful and productive SEACEN workshop.  Let me take this opportunity to thank all those who have made this event truly successful.  Our profound gratitude to the SEACEN Centre for co-sponsoring this workshop—SEACEN has been a historical partner in this type of regional cooperation; the resource persons for generously sharing their expertise—and without whom international flavour would have been wanting; the SEACEN member central banks for sparing their staff for a few days—there is no truth to the saying that those who attend seminars and workshops are those who are dispensable, our representation to this activity are some of our best staff;  and members of the Bangko Sentral preparatory committee who helped organize this event.  Your contributions to this event cannot be missed.

The subject of this workshop, measurements of core inflation and inflation forecasting, is very timely and useful to central bankers, particularly at this time when forward-looking and information-intensive methods of policy-making take a front seat over traditional methods that respond to what has already taken place.  I am positive that the workshop was able to shed light on a very critical goal of monetary policymaking—price stability. In a dynamic environment where traditional relationships among macro variables are beginning to, or have in fact weakened, particularly in periods of crises, it is pertinent for policy-makers to be equipped with the proper tools and techniques for monitoring and forecasting that one variable which is at the center of monetary management—the inflation rate.   A reasonable tracking of its future movements effectively enables monetary authorities to win half the battle of fighting inflation.  After all, nobody says this is easy.   This workshop was meant to help our respective research or economic forecasting departments.

The other half of the battle, of course, relies on the ability of those who actually shape policy to give the appropriate response in a timely manner.  A good prediction of inflation is particularly relevant to the BSP’s planned shift to inflation targeting as a monetary policy framework in 2001. I am positive that the participants from Indonesia have benefited in the same way since this country is also on the road to adopting inflation targeting as an alternative policy framework.

Equally important to a good prediction of inflation is a better understanding of that part of inflation which monetary authorities have some degree of control—underlying or core inflation.  It is true that the literature is far from achieving convergence to a single, acceptable measure of core inflation, but venues such as this provide us with a better understanding of this concept as well as options that are currently available for its measurement.

I have been informed that this workshop has been a fruitful learning experience for many of you.  It is my hope that whatever insight or even wisdom that you picked up in the past four days will be applied in your respective workplaces.

Also, I hope everybody took the opportunity to get to know one another on a more personal level.  I hope the acquaintances gained through the interaction among the participants in this workshop will go a long way.

The workshop proper ends here but I would like to encourage everyone to join the post-workshop activities which the Bangko Sentral has organized.  I have been advised that the members of the BSP preparatory committee will be taking you to Tagaytay highlands where one could have a picturesque view of the famous Taal volcano and lake.  We also invite you to enjoy the amenities there. Try your hand in the golf course, swimming pool, or perhaps just take a look at the gardens.  There are other sports facilities available.  Do enjoy the rest of your stay.

Thank you and good evening.

(Note: SEACEN Workshop on Concepts and Measurements of Core Inflation and Inflation Forecasting, July 7, 2000, Ilustrado, Intramuros, Manila)

Title: Keynote Speech
Occasion: Rural Bankers Association of the Philippines
Speaker: Governor Rafael Buenaventura
Transcription:
Mr. Ives Nisce, newly elected officers of the RBAP, distinguished colleagues, ladies and gentlemen, good evening:

I would like to start by congratulating the new officers of the RBAP for 2000-2001.  Rural banks are a key instrument in providing credit to the countryside as well as mobilizing domestic savings.  Because you are at the frontlines in providing financial services to the rural areas, you are a vital component of the domestic financial system.

In recent years, our experience with crisis conditions has shown the central value of maintaining a sound banking system. This has been one of the major tasks of the BSP since its inception, and progress in the same area has helped us weather the financial storm in 1997-1998. 

The banking system at present

Today, the fundamental strength and soundness of the banking system is shown by the continued growth of its assets to P2.96 trillion as of end-March 2000, and by its capital adequacy ratios which remain well above international standards.

The rural banking system also continues to grow apace.  Its branch network has more than doubled from 490 branches in 1993 to 1,068 as of end-March 2000. However, we need to address some weak areas.  Asset quality, for example, is less favorable compared to the overall banking system.   As of end-January 2000, the NPL ratio for rural banks was recorded at 19.6 percent compared to 13.65 percent for the entire banking system.  There have also been in recent months more than a few cases of liquidity problems among rural banks as well as reports of DOSRI-related abuses.

The BSP, of course, is quite willing to provide help to troubled rural banks. However, bank owners and managers should also do their part in ensuring the basic soundness of their respective institutions, so that these types of problems can be avoided altogether.

In short, there is a fair amount of room for improvement in our rural banking sector.    Strengthening the sector thus remains a top priority for regulators. 

Maintaining a sound banking system

Our continuing efforts to develop the banking system essentially focus on pushing forward key reform initiatives.  Let me spend a few minutes on some of these efforts. 

The General Banking Law

One crucial initiative is the recently signed General Banking Law (GBL) of 2000. The GBL is envisioned to enhance the BSP’s supervisory capability and enforcement powers, raise transparency and prudential standards as well as promote greater competition in the industry.

Most important, the General Banking Law also tightens the rules on exposure of all banks to DOSRI or insider lending. These tighter rules apply to all banks, rural banks included.  The GBL helps establish effective deterrents to unsound banking practices.  Addressing this issue is vitally important to preserving public confidence in the banking system.

I must firmly emphasize here that, in cases where enough evidence of unsound banking practices is found, authorities are fully committed to imposing appropriate penalties on the concerned parties.  This ensures that managers and owners will suffer the consequences of their misdeeds, so that they will not be repeated in the future.

We have already taken a major step in this direction recently by filing charges for DOSRI lending violations against officials of two failed commercial banks, a failed thrift bank and a failed rural bank.  These actions should make clear to everyone that violations of the law will not be tolerated.

Other banking reform priorities focus on improving the system for oversight and supervision of banks.

Expected to be passed later in 2000 are the proposed amendments to the New Central Bank Act (R.A. 7653).   Among other things, we are pushing for the inclusion of investment houses that offer investment banking services under BSP supervision.   This is so that the Bangko Sentral can monitor the activities of investment houses, specially those affiliated with banks.  We think this is a timely move in view of the recent liquidity problems of some investment houses involved in direct lending.

At the same time, the BSP remains flexible in implementing prudential measures to give banks breathing space, particularly in their capital build-up program.  We have already postponed the increase in the minimum capital requirements for all banks for 2000, and extended the compliance period for the 1999 capital requirements to end-2000.  This relieves the pressure on our banks so they can concentrate more on business strategy. 

Concluding remarks

All these efforts are aimed at further strengthening the banking system, by increasing transparency and improving governance. They are also aimed at ensuring that the banking system will have a talented and highly qualified pool of managers who are firmly committed to their fiduciary responsibilities to stakeholders.

I would therefore like to end by saying our goal of balanced, sustainable growth for the economy also requires a strong and stable partnership with the private sector, and I am glad that the future of rural banking rests on capable hands. I wish you success in all your activities in the coming year and beyond.

Thank you very much.

(Note: Induction of New Officers, Rural Bankers of the Philippines, July 4, 2000, Century Park Sheraton, Manila)

Title: The BSP in the New Millennium
Occasion: 7th Anniversary of the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas
Speaker: Governor Rafael Buenaventura
Transcription:
This is a special day for me.

This is the first time I will be presiding over the celebration of the BSP’s founding anniversary since I assumed the governorship last year.

And completing one year in room 501 seems eternal to me. Some had their baptism in water, others had their baptism in the spirit. I had my baptism of fire—the issue of interest rates raged last year, the Y2K changeover required tons of liquidity, one failed bank sent tremors through the banking system, the equities market was rocked with scandal, the exchange rate is playing up again.  Now my friends beat me occasionally in the fairways. This is one of the hazards of being a signatory to the country’s currency. But our collective efforts and teamwork at the BSP enabled us to overcome all of these obstacles.

During my first year in office, I have kept my faith in that wonderful adage, that the privilege to work is a gift, that power to work is a blessing, and that love of work is success.

As we mark the seventh anniversary of the BSP, let us consider this a rare opportunity to look back and assess our performance with respect to our mandate, the strategies we have adopted, and our broad record of contribution to the sustainability of economic growth. The BSP charter gifted us central bankers with the privilege to look after the macro objective of price stability and the health of the financial system.

This is a mandate we need to pursue without wavering, and we need to continue reinventing ourselves, so that we will not fall short of the sine qua non of our mandate. In this connection, let me congratulate you, my colleagues in the Bangko Sentral, for your excellent performance. 

Path breaking reforms in the financial system have been put in place in order to address the issue of the system’s stability and capacity to compete in the globalized setting. This includes the passage of the general banking law 2000, which gives the BSP more flexibility in supervising the banking industry, improving business practices, and upgrading the country’s banking laws to meet global standards. The Makati Business Club Executive Survey has again voted the Bangko Sentral, for the 8th time, as the number one performing government agency.

That is the blessing of work, and of working hard.

Looking forward, what is the major work agenda of the BSP?

First, pursuant to the Monetary Board approval, we will be shifting from monetary targeting to inflation targeting as the framework for monetary policy starting 2001. Under an inflation targeting framework, the BSP will give primary importance to the goal of price stability. We will announce inflation targets to the public and will explain how we intend to achieve them. We will then be accountable for the achievement of the inflation target. Such a framework highlights the importance of communication by the BSP of the rationale for its policy decisions to the public. Thus, inflation targeting offers greater transparency and accountability in the conduct of monetary policy. This, in turn, will help increase the credibility of the central bank over time.

The second thrust is the implementation of the General Banking Law of 2000. We have created a task force in order to ensure that policies and procedures are in line with the new general banking law.  Critical areas of implementation include the issuance of regulations implementing a risk-based capital adequacy standard, guidelines for bank closure and receivership, and the identification of unsafe and unsound practices.

Related to this successful advocacy program, the BSP is now pushing for the amendment of the New Central Bank Act (R.A. No. 7653).
