The continued stability of the peso and the fall in inflation starting in February 1999, have afforded the BSP enough flexibility in monetary management.

This flexibility enabled the BSP to reduce its policy interest rates several times by more than 400 basis points and its reserve requirements by five percentage points in 1999. These, in turn, provided strong support for the reduction in market interest rates, which have fallen to pre-crisis levels since May 1999. 

Flexible Fiscal Response 

On the fiscal side, the government continued to pump-prime the economy to boost domestic demand and enhance an early recovery. 

Endorsement From the IMF 

We also need to tell you that in march 1998, a two-year stand-by arrangement was agreed with the IMF, with $1.4 billion in available funds. This modest amount was in contrast to the huge rescue packages for the other crisis-hit economies in the region. So far, the country has drawn $755 million from the facility. While the facility ends this march, we have formally requested from the IMF an initial three-month extension of the standby arrangement to complete the reforms we have begun.

The Country’s Performance Exceeded Program Targets 

Most of the macroeconomic objectives of the program for 1999 were met. I refer to our over performance in output, inflation and the current account.

The economy’s performance was within the criteria set in the program. These criteria cover base money, net international reserves, short-term debt availments and BSP approvals of medium and long-term loans.

These favorable developments were confirmed in our recent discussions with the IMF. We wish to assure you that the Philippines remains committed to continue the reforms begun under this facility. 

III.  BSP Financial Highlights 

Let me now brief you on the Bangko Sentral operations. In sum, we were able to sustain a fairly sound financial condition during the last three years. 

Assets increased to P967 billion in December 1999 from P730 billion in 1998, or an expansion of 32 percent, while net worth increased by 7 percent to P75 billion. 

Net income for 1999 was P2.0 billion or a return on equity of 20 percent, given its paid-up capital of only P10 billion.

For 1999, the Bangko Sentral had paid p6.0 billion in taxes to the national government. As a result, total taxes paid to the national government since its tax-exemption status expired last July 1998 amounted to P14.7 billion. 

From July 1993 to June 1999, the Bangko Sentral has remitted to the national government P43.8 billion in dividends and interest rebates. Including taxes paid as of December 1999 of P14.7 billion, total funds transferred to the national government since July 1993 amounted to P58.5 billion, an amount higher than the total statutory capital of the BSP itself. 

IV.  OUTLOOK 

Looking forward, we do anticipate an acceleration of economic growth at a rate of 4.5-5.5 percent this year. 

Inflation is expected to average 6.0-7.0 percent for the whole year. For the first two months of this year, inflation averaged 2.8 percent. 

With falling inflation and a stable peso, interest rates are seen to remain relatively low this year, ranging from 9.5 to 10.5 percent. 

For the year, the current account is estimated to post a US$5.1 billion surplus, resulting in a US $2.8 billion surplus in our balance of payments. By end-2000, our foreign reserves are estimated to rise to US $17.4 billion. 

Economic Reforms to Continue 

In terms of our policies, most of the reforms initiated in 1999 will be continued. 

These include: the implementation of prudent fiscal and monetary policies; adoption of a liberal foreign exchange regime; liberalization and privatization of the banking and power sectors; proactive management of the external debt; and progressive development of the capital market. 

On the part of the Bangko Sentral, focus will be on the continuation of structural reforms to make the economy, in particular the banking system, more market-oriented. 

Towards this end, the Bangko Sentral will continue to encourage mergers in the banking system to promote big, globally competitive banks. We intend to further liberalize the banking environment by working for the entry of more foreign banks, possibly for a limited period. 

V.  CONCLUSION 

In closing, let me assure you that the Bangko Sentral will remain committed to its strategic role in promoting early and sustainable recovery of the economy. This role covers the objectives of: keeping prices low, the peso relatively stable, interest rates reasonable and the banking system safe and sound. 

As the new century dawns, we look forward to a gradual but sustained growth in the economy as government renews its commitment to continue the process of economic reforms.

Thank you very much.  

(Note: “The Philippines: Consolidating Economic Growth”, ABN-AMRO Investors’ Briefing, March 13, 2000, Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas)

Title: Fostering the Proper Environment in Developing the Philippine Capital Market
Occasion: 1st Annual Finance Asia-TRP Philippine Local Debt Conference, Thomson Ratings Philippines
Speaker: Governor Rafael Buenaventura
Transcription:
It gives me great pleasure to be invited to this First Annual Philippine Local Debt Conference under the auspices of Finance Asia and Thomson Ratings Philippines. Indeed, it is a privilege to address this first major gathering in the new millennium of the issuers, investors, regulators, underwriters and other key players in the Philippine capital market.

 

The BSP and the Philippine Capital Market

Let me assure you that the development of the local capital market has been the driving force of the government and the private sector since the opening of the manila stock exchange in 1927. Since then, numerous developments in the market had transpired. And since 1949, the Bangko Sentral has consistently implemented and supported measures to strengthen the market. In 1980 for instance, the then Central Bank of the Philippines instituted financial reforms that removed various distinctions among financial institutions. This introduced the modified universal banking concept that required higher levels of capitalization, thus increasing the capacity of banks to engage in long-term funding and to venture into such activities as underwriting, securities dealership and equity investments in allied and non-allied undertakings. During the same period, the Central Bank implemented a number of measures to increase the yield of debt instruments by eliminating administrative ceilings on interest rates.  In 1986, the government securities network was mobilized and the auction system for treasury issues was installed. These were essential not only in ensuring marketability in the primary market but also in developing a strong secondary market.

During the same period, the Central Bank adopted a phase-out policy with regard to central bank bills.  To avoid competition in the market, regular CB bills were withdrawn to give way to treasury issues as open market instruments. At the same time, the debt-to-equity conversion program was introduced, enabling the country to generate foreign equity investments that could help advance the cause of capital market development.

The Central Bank was also instrumental in the establishment of the Credit Information Bureau in 1982, which has provided vital credit information and helped reduce risks involved in investments in capital market instruments.

But it was the establishment of the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas in 1993 that gave the major boost to the development of the capital market in the country.  The establishment of a financially stronger and more policy independent Bangko Sentral spelled greater stability in the financial system. It ensured a firmer handle on price and exchange rate movements. These, in turn, provided the primary incentives for investors to go into long-term investments in the country and eventually benefit the capital market.

The financial restructuring of the Bangko Sentral also promoted the government securities market with the issuance by the National Government of P170 billion in special treasury bills to the New Central Monetary Authority.  This not only widened the Bangko Sentral’s open market flexibility but also increased the supply of treasury securities in the market.

The complete transfer of the Bangko Sentral’s fiscal functions to the Bureau of the Treasury in 1998 signaled the shift of the public debt management function to the Finance Department and the strengthening of the Bangko Sentral’s monetary policy independence.   These developments further ensured a more efficiently functioning capital market.  

Current Issues

Ladies and gentlemen, today, the Philippine capital market has gone a long way.    With the increasing globalization and deregulation of the financial system, the market is facing a different set of challenges in the new millennium.  A long-term yield curve has to be established; market infrastructure and mechanisms have to be put in place; and finally, various taxation issues have to be resolved. The country’s credit rating capability also needs to be improved.  

BSP’s Main Policy Thrusts

Against all these new challenges, the Bangko Sentral remains committed to fostering the proper environment in further developing the Philippine capital market.

In pursuing this goal, we have two major roles to play: one is to foster macroeconomic conditions conducive to the further development of the market and two, is to ensure the strength and stability of the financial system that will serve as an efficient channel for capital market transactions.

I am pleased to report to you that the Bangko Sentral has been doing its homework in fostering the appropriate macroeconomic conditions for capital market growth.  In carrying out its primary mandate of maintaining stable prices, the Bangko Sentral generates the most basic incentive that inspires investor confidence in the market. In 1999, the inflation rate exhibited a steady downtrend. From a high of 11.5 percent in January, it steadily declined to 4.3 percent in December, bringing the full year average for the year to 6.6 percent. The decline in inflation and maintenance of monetary aggregates at levels below program, as well as the relative stability in the foreign exchange market, provided the Bangko Sentral with some flexibility in substantially bringing down its key policy rates and in lowering reserve requirements against bank deposits.  These facilitated appropriate adjustments in the price of credit that eventually benefited the capital market. Inflationary expectations, the bane of capital market development, have thus been favorable.

To the extent that the Bangko Sentral gives more emphasis on indirect and market-based policy instruments such as open market operations, it influences the availability and rate of return on assets in the securities market.

In addition to its own measures, the Bangko Sentral also supports the undertakings of other government and private entities that seek to enhance the efficiency of the market.

Ensure a Strong Financial System

The second major role of the Bangko Sentral is to ensure the existence of a strong and stable financial system. In this area, the bank has also been doing a good job. This is one of the reasons why the Philippine economy was not severely affected by the Asian financial crisis. In 1999, the banking system continued to make significant inroads in containing the lingering effects of the regional crisis. Non-performing loans of commercial banks at 14.6 percent in November remained one of the lowest among crisis-affected nations even without the benefit of a systemic financial restructuring. Commercial banks’ capital adequacy ratio during the same period was recorded at 17.8 percent, well above the Bangko Sentral and international standards. During the year, we continued to promote an environment conducive to the development of big, globally competitive banks. To date, nine mergers involving twelve commercial banks, four thrift banks and two rural banks, have taken place. All these measures promoted the mobilization of more resources that will be made available to the market.

To promote quality and transparency in investor information, we have required banks to include additional key information in their regular reports, properly certified by accredited external auditors. We have also required banks to list in the Philippine Stock Exchange for greater transparency and regulatory oversight. Speaking of regulations, in 1998 we transferred to the Securities and Exchange Commission the regulatory power over most non-bank financial institutions without quasi-banking functions.  This is expected to facilitate greater consistency in the regulation of these institutions and allow the Bangko Sentral to concentrate on its core function of supervising banks.

In the area of clearing and settlements, the Bangko Sentral is poised to move into the real-time-gross-settlement arrangement within the year or early next year.

Complementary to these measures that we have implemented, we have also supported pending legislations in congress that are expected to foster greater competition, raise prudential standards to international norms and strengthen further the Bangko Sentral’s regulatory and supervisory capability. These include amendments to the General Banking Act and the New Central Bank Act. We also support the proposed revisions to the Revised Securities Act that will further strengthen the regulatory powers of the sec.  

Future Policy Thrusts

In closing, let me underscore that the development of the capital market is not an end in itself. It is only a means for mobilizing savings and channeling them into productive enterprises that would facilitate rather than disrupt economic growth and improve the standard of living of our people.

To achieve this objective, the Bangko Sentral is prepared to play its role and continue the following policy thrusts:

» Maintenance of price and exchange rate stability as the basic foundation for economic growth. We are gradually moving into inflation targeting as a framework for conducting monetary policy and further ensuring price stability.

» Strengthening further the financial system and other key institutions participating in the capital market. We shall intensify prudential regulation and advance the concept of competition through mergers and consolidation. We shall continue to monitor the health of the banking system through our macro and micro early warning systems.

» Promotion of greater transparency and timeliness in financial and corporate reporting. We shall put premium on greater disclosures to the market to avoid surprises and help solidify market confidence.  

The BSP will also continue to support measures to reduce taxation obstacles to capital market development and the improvement of the country’s credit rating capability. Toward this end, we support the activities of Thomson Rating Philippines and other existing and potential domestic rating agencies in the country. We welcome benchmarking exercises to ensure the appropriate direction of the market.

Conclusion

Finally, let us allow ourselves to be reminded by that Jewish girl, Anne Frank, who said: “How wonderful it is that nobody need to wait a single minute before starting to improve the world.” We shall not wait a single minute before we undertake our future moves to help improve the capital market. I hope that market participants shall not also wait a single minute to advance their own share that, together, we shall not have to wonder at the dynamics of change in the capital market, but we shall always be driven by the goal to do something positive for the market and necessarily, for all.

Thank you and good day.

 

(Note: Philippine Local Debt Conference, Thomson Ratings Philippines, February 17, 2000, Peninsula Hotel, Makati City)

Title: PHILIPPINE BANKS: THE LANDSCAPE BEYOND 2000
Occasion: Asian Banking Conference, Salomon Smith Barney
Speaker: Governor Rafael Buenaventura
Transcription:
INTRODUCTION

Ladies and gentlemen, good afternoon.

Allow me to say, first of all, that it is indeed a pleasure to speak at this forum. I understand this conference seeks to take stock and look ahead in the banking sector after the Asian crisis and into the new millennium. Let me say at the outset that I am putting myself above the fray on whether the new millennium has started this year or still has to start in 2001.

Levity aside, the region became the focus of grave investor concern during the recent financial turmoil. The crisis exposed fundamental weaknesses  in  Asian  financial  systems that   were masked by one of the longest periods of sustained economic growth in recent history. This growth was accompanied by large capital inflows that were encouraged by prevailing economic policies, including financial system and capital account liberalization.

Greater openness, however, implied that external shocks were more easily transmitted through the financial system, and from there, to the rest of the economy.  The increased mobility of funds also heightened the risks associated with inappropriate domestic policies and weaknesses in the financial system. Surges in capital inflows brought about excessive demand expansion, and their abrupt reversal following changes in investor sentiment caused destabilizing asset price volatility and demand contraction.  Maturity and currency mismatches exacerbated the weaknesses in domestic financial systems.


POLICY RESPONSES TO THE ASIAN FINANCIAL CRISIS

All of us are probably somewhat wiser now.  Dealing with the problems brought up by the crisis necessitated both broad, macroeconomic policy responses and the adoption of structural reforms, including in the banking system.

In the Philippines, the financial sector had gone through  several episodes of policy reform from the 1980s that included allowing greater role for market forces, higher bank capitalization and better bank supervision.  Thus, before the crisis, there was already a relatively high degree of market orientation in the financial system and the regulatory framework was being continuously improved.  When the crisis struck, a further program of reform was adopted aimed at improving disclosure, strengthening compliance and upgrading the quality of bank management.

Consequently, the Philippine financial system fared relatively well during the crisis.  The system’s strength was evident in the sustained rise in its total resources, compliance with prudential norms, and relatively good asset quality.  The NPL ratio of Philippine commercial banks reached 14.6 percent as of November 1999, one of the lowest in the region.  In the months ahead, the NPL ratio is expected to decline as the downtrend in interest rates and broad stability in the exchange rate are expected to increase the repayment capability of corporates.  Overall, banks have remained an efficient channel of monetary policy, an important element in our efforts to stabilize the macroeconomy.  

 

ECONOMIC PERFORMANCE

Post-crisis, macroeconomic conditions have improved considerably.  The Philippine economy grew by 3.6 percent in terms of GNP in 1999 and average inflation was kept at 6.6 percent. Lending rates are now even lower than pre-crisis levels. The country’s external payments position is comfortable—helped in large part by robust exports—and gross international reserves are at record-highs.

 

CHALLENGES OF GLOBALIZATION

In the period ahead, further reforms in the banking system will have to clearly deal with the challenges of increasing sophistication and globalization. I have always subscribed to the notion that it is better to anticipate change rather than to have it forced upon you.

The liberalization of the Philippine financial system has brought about significant benefits in terms of encouraging efficiency and competition, and allowing our banks to take advantage of international opportunities.  However, the events of the past years have demonstrated that such an environment has attendant risks.

We are ever mindful of this. Maintaining stability in a globalized environment requires enhanced prudence in financial intermediation by banks.  At the same time, we need to have stronger supervisory institutions.

In terms of future changes, we have submitted major banking reforms to the Philippine legislature. The proposed revisions seek to align our prudential standards with international norms, enhance competition in the banking sector, and strengthen the powers of the Monetary Board. The amendments will also enable the regulatory structure to adapt to the latest innovations in response to powerful changes occurring in banking technology. Electronic banking, including banking through the internet, will be placed under the authority of the BSP.

Upgrading risk management capabilities requires that financial intermediaries recognize and adequately deal with the increased risks associated with financial liberalization and globalization.  In this connection, improvements are being made in the financial infrastructure to comply with the best practices in risk management. The settlement and payments system is being reformed with a view to effecting final settlement on a continuous basis, via RTGs.  The system is now in the development stage and will cover equities, fixed income, money and FX markets.

Risk rating is also being introduced. Among other things, this will allow early identification of problems, improve credit risk management, provide basis for a portfolio management process and improve loan loss reserve methodology and support.

We have also started to use the first-generation early warning system for commercial banks that will give us an indication of banks’ solvency outlook well in advance.  To reinforce the system on a macro basis, we are also in the process of finalizing a set of leading indicators that will enable us to detect potential, system-wide currency and financial crises.

Financial innovation is an integral component in meeting the challenges posed by globalization.  It is not surprising that financial innovation is most evident in systems where the competitive spirit has been fostered. In the Philippines, monetary authorities have encouraged mergers and consolidations in the banking system to promote competitive and efficient banks. Such consolidation will help local banks take advantage of their collective experience, services, and technological know-how to extend the perimeters of their businesses, with a view to realizing gains in terms of expanded markets and enhanced expertise.  To-date, two mergers of commercial banks have been approved, and two more are in the final stages of the merger process.

On the number of surviving banks, I see four or five big domestic banks plus the foreign banks accounting for about 70-80 percent of the resources of the commercial banking system.  At present, roughly 57 percent of commercial banks’ assets are attributable to the top five domestic banks and Philippine branches of foreign banks.  In the end, the market, on its own, will determine the exact number of all banks.  While size will increase, appropriate prudential measures are expected to check any tendency of big banks toward excessive risk-taking.

Institutional changes also involve ongoing programs to upgrade our supervisory skills through intensified training of our personnel.  This is consistent with the shift in supervisory focus from a compliance-based and checklist-driven assessment of banks’ conditions to a forward-looking and risk-based approach. We are also promoting a culture of learning in our bank, through the exchange of best practices with local and foreign institutions, and through the conduct of dialogues.  These would help us obtain insights that would strengthen our appreciation of key issues and take the reform process forward.

Before I end, let me clarify that the new 90-day guideline on foreign capital lodged as peso time deposits is meant to limit the movement of speculative money in and out of the country. By doing this, we hope to minimize foreign exchange volatility, which should be good for the economy over the longer term.  The other objective of the new rules is to strengthen the monitoring of foreign investment flows in the Philippines.  They in no way presage the introduction of controls. We in the Philippines remain committed to market-oriented policies.

 

CONCLUSION

Recently, Alan Greenspan remarked that the challenge faced by U.S. Monetary Authorities involves fostering, as best as they can, the financial conditions that will allow the economic expansion to continue as long and as vigorously as possible.  We hope that someday we will be met with the same challenge in our home shores, and we hope that we will be up to the task.  Our commitment to a transparent and carefully formulated strategy to strengthen our banking system should serve us in good stead.

            Thank you and good day.  

(Note:  Asia Banking Conference, Salomon Smith Barney, 14-15 February 2000, Hong Kong)

Title: THE PHILIPPINES: GEARING UP FOR HIGHER GROWTH
Occasion: Presentation at the CSFB Meeting, Credit Issue First Boston
Speaker: Governor Rafael Buenaventura
Transcription:
I take great pleasure to be invited to this very prestigious organization to present the Philippine story. I always welcome the opportunity to touch base with the key players in the international capital markets like you who closely monitor our performance, policy actions and pronouncements because of the large stake that you have on these matters.

This morning allow me to walk you through the key developments in the Philippine economy and the direction where the economy is heading.  

Recent Economic Developments

We take pride in the fact that the Philippine economy made substantial progress in most economic fronts. Let me cite some of the macroeconomic indicators.

» Output performance better than expected

The Philippine economy staged a strong rebound during the first three quarters of 1999 as real GNP grew at a higher-than-expected rate of 3.0 percent from a 0.5-percent growth for the same period in 1998. The leading indicators of demand particularly from the external sector and the expansion in domestic credit are telling us that growth will continue through the last quarter of 1999.

» Prices have remained broadly stable

It must be emphasized that the economic expansion was achieved amidst a broadly stable price situation and a sustained fall in domestic interest rates. Notwithstanding inflationary pressures emanating from the series of oil price increases and the wage and transport fare hikes, the country’s inflation rate exhibited a steady downtrend during the year. From a high of 11.5 percent in January 1999, the inflation rate fell to 4.3 percent in December, bringing the 1999 inflation average to 6.6 percent.

» Domestic interest rates on the downtrend

Domestic interest rates continued their general downtrend for most of 1999. The benchmark 91-day t-bill rate declined from an average of 13.2 percent in January to almost 8.9 percent by December.

» Foreign exchange market broadly stable

There continues to be broad stability in the FOREX market, consistent with the country’s stable macro fundamentals and robust external payments position. Market price volatility has dropped significantly in 1999 relative to what it was in 1997 and 1998. This was due largely to the package of reforms implemented by the BSP to stabilize the FOREX market as well as its strong commitment to a floating rate system.

» External position remains strong

The rebound in the Philippine economy was supported by strong performance in the external sector: a strong export growth, and substantial capital inflows funded from foreign investments and proceeds from government international bond offerings. For the first 10 months of 1999, the BOP recorded a surplus of $3.4 billion, a dramatic improvement from the $1.4 billion recorded for the same period in 1998. In particular, the current account – buttressed by strong exports, which grew by 19 percent – has strengthened considerably, increasing nearly ninefold to $5.5 billion from January-October 1999 from $575 million for the same period in 1998.

Non-resident gross portfolio investments grew by over 170 percent for the first 10 months but due to some withdrawals, net portfolio investments grew by only 143 percent. 

» Gross international reserves (GIR) up to historic highs

As a result of our improved external payments position, we were able to build up our GIR to a record level of $15.02 billion by end-1999, equivalent to 4.3 months’ worth of imports of goods and services.  At this level, GIR is roughly two and a half times more than sufficient to cover the country’s total short-term external debt.

» External debt manageable

The Philippines’ outstanding external debt remains manageable at $48.1 billion as of end-June 1999, with the creditor and maturity profile improving. The share of short-term debt to total has declined from 15.0 percent in 1998 to 13.6 percent as of end-June 1999. Meanwhile, debt service burden as a ratio to exports of goods and services has dropped through the years: from 17.4 percent in 1994 to 13.7 percent from January-September 1999.

» Expansionary fiscal policy pump-primed the economy

On the fiscal side, the National Government overshot the fiscal target for 1999 due largely to pump-priming efforts aimed at rejuvenating demand.  The government expects that with the revival of economic growth, it can revert to fiscal consolidation by 2003, with the private sector taking over the reins of growth.

» Banking sector remains relatively strong

The resilience of the banking system has helped save us from the worst effects of the Asian financial crisis. This strength is evident in the sustained rise in the total resources, the strong capital base, healthy asset quality, and the continued broad compliance with prudential norms.

Operations in the first nine months of 1999 resulted in a modest expansion in the assets of the banking system.

Our banks continue to be adequately capitalized as reflected in their 18 percent networth to risk asset ratio as of end-September 1999.

Meanwhile, the non-performing loans ratio of commercial banks remains manageable at 14.6 percent as of end-November 1999.

Aided by the stricter provisioning requirements, banks have also built up their reserves against loan losses to adequate levels.

Banks’ exposure to the real estate sector remains moderate at 12.2 percent of total loan portfolio as of September 1999 from 10.6 percent in March 1997, well within the 20-percent ceiling prescribed by the BSP in mid-1997.

Overall, the banking system remains to be financially healthy and operationally sound and continues as an efficient channel of monetary policy.  

Performance Under the IMF Program

 

The economy’s performance remains broadly on track relative to the IMF performance criteria.

Monetary aggregates were below programmed ceilings for the first 11 months of the year. However, the monetary targets were exceeded by some margin in December due to the precautionary preparations for the Y2K changeover, but already liquidity in the system is going back to normal levels.

Net international reserves was maintained above the floor in 1999, while ceilings on medium- and long-term approvals of external borrowings remained below limits.

The National Government overshot its fiscal target for 1999 of P85.3 billion by over P26 billion. Fiscal transactions for 1999 resulted in a deficit of P111.7 billion.  

Challenges and Prospects

While the economy is well geared up for growth, certain challenges have to be addressed squarely to ensure a faster yet sustainable rate of growth.  We at the Bangko Sentral are conscious of the fact that global and regional stability is still a work-in-progress.    Uneven growth and possible slowdowns in key industrial economies, particularly the U.S. and Japan, could still cause destabilizing aftershocks in Asia. For this reason, efforts should continue to complete the needed structural reforms to address the remaining weaknesses.

In terms of monetary policy, the mix will continue to aim for a continued decline in inflation and broad stability in the exchange rate, while seeing to it that interest rates are reasonably low to support economic growth.

In the banking system, the thrust will be to deepen further banking reforms that carried the system through the Asian crisis. We will seek to foster greater competition, raise prudential standards to international norms, and strengthen further the Bangko Sentral’s regulatory oversight and supervisory capability.

Complementary to these, we have completed the first-generation early warning system for commercial banks that will allow us to predict the banks’ solvency outlook one year in advance. To reinforce the system on a macro basis, we are also in the process of finalizing a set of leading indicators that will allow us to detect in advance potential, system-wide currency and banking crises.  

New Reform Initiatives of the BSP

We are now exploring new initiatives for possible implementation this year. We are reviewing our policy on bank mergers and acquisitions to determine and assess its total impact on the banking system. Relatedly, the moratorium on the granting of new branch licenses is also being reviewed for possible relaxation in areas, which can still accommodate additional bank branches.

We are also looking into the practice of banks of using “off-balance sheet” transactions that add unnecessary risks into their portfolios and preparing guidelines that will discourage such risky practices.  

Outlook for 1999 and 2000

As policy reforms are implemented in the various sectors and as the global economic and financial conditions continue to improve, we see the improvements in the Philippine economy continuing and further strengthening this year. Inflation, having registered a rate well below the 7.0–8.0 percent target for 1999 at 6.6 percent, is targeted to average around 6.0-7.0 percent in 2000. On the balance of payments, a surplus of around $2.4 billion or 2.8 percent of GNP is projected for the current year compared to the estimated $3.8 billion surplus for 1999.    Gross International Reserves are expected to increase further to over $17 billion by end-2000.  

Concluding Remarks

Let me conclude my presentation by saying that while the economy tracks the path for higher economic growth, the Bangko Sentral is ever mindful of the tasks ahead. Indeed, after hurdling the initial challenges of stabilization, the new environment calls us to enlarge the place of our tent, lengthen our cords and strengthen our stakes (Isaiah 54:2). Bangko Sentral is therefore committed to the continuous review of its monetary and banking policies with a view to adapting to contemporary demands and to helping propel the economy toward self-sustaining growth.

Thank you and good day.  

(Note: Presentation during the Credit Suisse First Boston Meeting, 27 January 2000, Zurich, Switzerland)

Title: THE FINANCIAL EXECUTIVE: IN PURSUIT OF EXCELLENCE IN A GLOBAL SETTING FROM THE POINT OF VIEW OF A CENTRAL BANKER
Occasion: First General Membership Meeting, Financial Executives Institute of the Phils.,
Speaker: Governor Rafael Buenaventura
Transcription:
Distinguished officers and members of the Financial Executives Institute of the Philippines (FINEX), colleagues, guests, ladies and gentlemen, good afternoon.

First of all, allow me to congratulate the newly elected officers and members of the FINEX board. I am extremely glad for this opportunity to join you today in marking another year, the very first of the new millennium. Like you, my sincere hope is that it will prove to be a fruitful one for all of us.

I think it is very timely that for this year, FINEX will be driven by the theme “The Financial Executive: Pursuing Excellence in a Global Setting”. The pursuit of excellence demands that we prepare ourselves to manage the challenge of greater competition and an increased potential for risk even on a global scale. This should imply not only the adoption of international best practices but also, on a personal level, being a responsible and competent corporate citizen. Our common experience with globalization and increased financial integration in the last few years has shown that individual actions can have systemic consequences, that excessive risk-taking by individual players and disobedience to prudential regulations can lead to systemic collapse. This was one of the main lessons of the Asian financial crisis.

At the same time, there is also a need to address the weaknesses in the system that contributed to the Asian banking crisis. An ADB study pointed out that one of the root causes of the Asian debacle is inadequate bank governance that allowed excessive risk-taking by financial institutions. It is the realization of the benefits of good governance that prompted countries in the Asian region to work hard at instituting governance reforms. Therefore, this is a very timely occasion to discuss good governance with financial executives on whom the success of the reform effort greatly rests.  

A Call for Governance Reforms

Corporate governance refers to a set of rules that define the behavior of company managers while ensuring their accountability to stakeholders. Good governance, whether applied to banks or non-bank corporates, is essential for a well functioning economy as it provides incentives for management to act in ways that improve the firm’s financial position and assure shareholders of an adequate return. At the same time, good corporate governance helps create an environment conducive to the sustained growth of the industry. Good corporate governance always asks us in the face: “Is there a better way?”  

Elements of Good Governance in the Banking System

In my recent lecture at the Asian Institute of Management, I emphasized that good governance at the individual bank level hinges in part on the business practices adopted by the board of directors and management. In the same lecture, I outlined some of the key elements of a good governance system at the individual bank level, which are the following:

» Management with high integrity, adequate training and experience, which concerns all of you;

» A good internal information and control system to ensure that decisions affecting the rights and obligations of the bank are never made solely by one individual;

» Prudent credit approval procedures and risk limitation procedures; and

» Effective external and internal audit procedures to ensure that established policies and procedures are followed and special interests are not allowed to influence decisions.

At the same time, experiences in the past showed that there are factors by which the quality of corporate governance can be enhanced in the banking system.  Most important of these factors include:

» The existence of independent and effective bank supervisors, who ensure that prudential standards are adhered to;

» The requirement to list in the stock exchange, which promotes transparency and market discipline;

» An active merger and acquisitions market, which compels banks’ best behavior to avoid a takeover or merger; and

» Effective anti-corruption laws, which prevent, among other things, abuses in connected lending.

These are the four pillars of corporate governance in the banking system.  

BSP: GUARDIAN OF BANK GOVERNANCE  

An important ingredient that helped spare the country from the worst effects of the Asian crisis has been the relative strength of the Philippine banking system. This derives from the combination of a past history of banking reforms and the timely pre-emptive measures taken to address any potential financial sector weakness.

The reform efforts of the BSP took different dimensions, from tightening of minimum capital and bringing regulatory standards closer to international best practices to re-orienting bank supervision toward risk-based analysis and strengthening bank exit policies. Together with the other measures on provisioning, portfolio valuation, public disclosure, and consolidated bank supervision, the BSP has covered practically the whole range of critical policies in banking supervision.

As a result of these initiatives, Goldman Sachs in its recent cross-country study found that prudential standards in the Philippines remained strong and compared favorably with the standards used in the Asian region. Moreover, the performance of the Philippine banking system in terms of NPL, profitability and capital adequacy during the crisis was generally positive. These reflect in part the good governance structure existing in Philippine banks.  

Concluding Remarks

Let me conclude these remarks by saying that the banking system has undergone a substantial period of reform in the last decade to achieve the goal of strengthening the system itself, including through development of a culture of good corporate governance.

However, the caveat has to be mentioned: the reform effort is a continuing process as we try to keep pace with the demands of globalization and liberalization. Therefore, it will require the Bangko Sentral to maintain an activist stance in the reform program. This is evident in the range of proposed reforms submitted to the legislature as amendments to the General Banking Act and the New Central Bank Act.

There is a final caveat. Good governance in the banking system cannot be effected by the BSP alone. It also requires active participation of other sectors in the economy, particularly the corporate sector.

You as financial executives have the responsibility to raise the code of conduct in your chosen field and to pursue excellence in such endeavor. Let this goal be pursued by working towards and adhering to good corporate governance. Through our combined efforts, the challenges of the new global setting will indeed be much less daunting.

Thank you and good afternoon.    

(Note: First General Membership Meeting, Financial Executives Institute of the Philippines (FINEX), January 19, 2000, Hotel Intercontinental, Makati City)

Title: BSP Policy Thrusts for the New Millenium
Occasion: Luncheon Meeting, Rotary Club of Makati
Speaker: Governor Rafael Buenaventura
Transcription:
I take great pleasure in joining the officers and members of the premier Rotary Club in Makati today. While this club is the oldest and largest of the 29 Rotary Clubs in Makati, counting among your membership major professionals and corporate leaders in business and industry in the country, I am very confident your organization has maintained fresh and dynamic perspectives especially at this time of the new millennium.

Coming at the heels of a major revamp in the cabinet and the virtual end of the watch for the millennium bug, this meeting is a perfect opportunity to brief you about recent economic and financial developments and the new policy initiatives of the Bangko Sentral.  

Recent Developments

I start with key economic and financial developments in the past year.

The year 1999 saw the economies of the crisis-affected countries recover from the Asian financial crisis. Most economic indicators were looking up. Output growth expanded. Inflation continued to decline. Exports sustained their growth. Domestic demand began to pick up. As a result, market confidence started to return, allowing Asia to remain on top of the other emerging economies in other parts of the world.

We take pride in the fact that the Philippine economy made good progress in most economic fronts. Let us look at some of these key economic indicators.

Output growth has rebounded, with GNP growing at an average of 3.0 percent during the first three quarters of the year. We are also optimistic that growth will be higher in the last quarter given the very good leading indicators of growth. Inflation remained single-digit, averaging 6.6 percent for the whole year of 1999. Interest rates had trended down during the same period, even reaching pre-crisis levels.

In the external front, the exchange rate was relatively stable in 1999 compared to 1998. We continued to post positive gains in our external payments position, with our balance of payments recording a surplus of $3.8 billion. As a result, our gross international reserves continued to rise, posting a record level of $15.0 billion as of end-December last year. This is expected to boost further investor confidence and reduce our vulnerability to potential external shocks.

Turning to the banking system, Philippine banks remained financially healthy and operationally sound. In 1999, reforms focused on further strengthening the financial system in order to support economic recovery and to enhance its resiliency to domestic and external shocks. As a result, banks continued to be adequately capitalized as reflected in their 18 percent net worth to risk asset ratio as of end-September 1999. This ratio far exceeded the statutory requirement of 10 percent and the international standard of 8 percent.

As of end-September 1999, banks’ NPL ratio was recorded at 14.5 percent. This ratio compared favorably with those of our Asian neighbors, which ranged from 19 percent in Malaysia to 75 percent in Indonesia, already incorporating the impact of financial restructuring.

Moreover, as of end-June 1999, total exposure of commercial banks to the real estate sector was contained at 12.3 percent of their loan portfolio. This was well within the prescribed ceiling of 20 percent.

Overall, while there were some banks that failed in the aftermath of the Asian crisis, the banking system continued to be a sound and efficient channel of monetary policy. This was further confirmed during the millennium bug watch, when there were no major glitches that surfaced in the banking sector.  

Challenges and Prospects

Although the economy is now in a much better shape compared to a year ago, certain challenges have to be addressed squarely to ensure a faster yet sustainable rate of growth capable of attracting more foreign investments. We should keep in mind that global and regional stability is still a work-in-progress. Uneven growth and possible slowdowns in key industrial economies, particularly the U.S. and Japan, could still cause destabilizing aftershocks in Asia.  For this reason, efforts should continue to complete the needed structural reforms in the financial and corporate sectors, which are the main transmission lines of outside shocks in the economy. In particular, vital economic legislations related to these reforms will have to be passed and implemented as soon as possible. The fact that the Philippines was least affected by the crisis should challenge us to undertake even more significant policy and structural improvements to sustain our good economic fortune.

On the part of the Bangko Sentral, future policy actions will support the government’s thrust for a broad-based and sustainable economic recovery. This means Bangko Sentral will be working for a more efficient and competitive economy and a safer, stronger and globally-competitive banking system.

Our monetary policy mix will continue to aim for a continued decline in inflation and broad stability in the exchange rate, while seeing to it that interest rates are reasonably low to support economic growth. The exchange rate will remain market-determined and the build up in foreign exchange reserves will be pursued to the extent allowed by monetary and foreign exchange market conditions.

In the banking system, the thrust will be to deepen further banking reforms that carried the system through the Asian crisis. We will seek to foster greater competition, raise prudential standards to international norms, and strengthen further the Bangko Sentral’s regulatory oversight and supervisory capability.

While most of the changes are embodied in the proposed amendments to the General Banking Act and the New Central Bank Act, which we expect to pass Congress early this year, several policy initiatives have been implemented by the Bangko Sentral to support these major improvements in banking laws. To promote bigger and stronger banks capable of competing globally, we have encouraged bank mergers and consolidations by providing incentives and suspending the grant of new bank branch licenses. So far, three bank mergers have been completed, while several others are in various stages of negotiation.

At the same time, banks’ compliance to the phased increase in minimum capitalization was monitored closely and loan classification and provisioning requirements were tightened further to enhance the capability of banks to withstand shocks.

Complementary to these, we have completed the first-generation early warning system for commercial banks that will allow us to predict the banks’ solvency outlook one year in advance. To reinforce the system on a macro basis, we are also in the process of finalizing a set of leading indicators that will allow us to detect in advance potential, system-wide currency and banking crises.  

New Initiatives

We are now exploring new initiatives for possible implementation this year. We recognize that the economic and banking system blooms with more vigor after each pruning.

For one, we are reviewing our policy on bank mergers and acquisitions to determine and assess its total impact on the banking system. Relatedly, the moratorium on the granting of new branch licenses is also being reviewed for possible relaxation in areas, which can still accommodate additional bank branches. These initiatives are aimed at enhancing competition on a greater scale, even allowing existing banks with comprehensive networks to expand, to ensure that economies of scale and the benefit of efficiency are realized by surviving market players.

We are likewise reviewing the guidelines on FCDU licensing, with the end in view of making the banking system more resilient to external shocks. In particular, we will be looking at the capability of certain types of banks in handling FCDUs. In fact, we have instructed our technical staff to suggest ways of addressing the problems associated with indiscriminate traffic between the banks’ regular books and FCDU books. In particular, matters of taxation will be addressed to remove the distortionary aspects of maintaining the difference between regular and FCDU books.

We are also looking into the practice of banks of using “off balance sheet” transactions that add unnecessary risks into their portfolios. The Bangko Sentral is preparing guidelines that will discourage the use of such risky practices as “off balance sheet” repos and direct lending facilities. We are also looking at engineered swaps to see how arbitrage opportunities between peso and dollar deposits can be reduced.

 In order to monitor compliance by banks to the new guidelines, a more integrated bank reportorial system is also being developed.

 At the end of the day, all these new initiatives are meant to usher in an improved regulatory environment that emphasizes a higher level of competition based on stronger, more globalized banks. Indeed, the Philippine banking system is entering a new era of banking which we are glad to be a part of.

Conclusion

In closing, I would like to thank the officers and members of the Rotary Club of Makati for inviting me to this gathering and to be able to share with you some of our important plans for the new millennium. I solicit the support of our friends from the Rotary Club in pushing for these plans of the Bangko Sentral. Let me encourage our Rotarians that, paraphrasing Jimmy Carter in 1978, “If we fear making anyone mad, then we ultimately probe for the lowest common denominator of human achievement.”

Thank you and good day.  

(Note: Luncheon Meeting, Rotary Club of Makati, 18 January 2000, Hotel Intercontinental, Makati City)

Title: Building the Infrastructure for Effective Governance in the Banking System
Occasion: JBF Center Lecture Series, Asian Institute of Management
Speaker: Governor Rafael Buenaventura
Transcription:
Introduction:  The Analytics of Banking Governance

Ladies and gentlemen, good evening. I am deeply honored to be invited to deliver the first lecture in this year’s edition of the Jose B. Fernandez Center Lecture Series. I always welcome opportunities, such as tonight’s forum, to interact with practitioners in the financial system regarding relevant issues confronting our economy. The theme of tonight’s discussion is The Establishment of an Adequate Infrastructure for the Effective Governance in the Banking System.

Banks and other financial institutions by virtue of their deposit and borrowing functions are custodian of the country’s liquid reserves. As such, they play an important role in the efficient functioning of a modern economy. They constitute a system that serves as a pooling mechanism for savings and an efficient allocation device that channels these funds to the most productive economic activities. Any disruption in the intermediation process by the financial system will inevitably lead to negative effects on the whole economy. There is, therefore, strong public interest in the safety and liquidity of the banking system’s financial condition. As such, much attention has been devoted to the issue of building a strong and stable financial system.

In the recent Asian regional financial crisis, among the factors identified to be behind the collapse of some of the banking systems in the region has been the inadequacies in the corporate governance of banks. Its been said that one of the lessons from the 1997 Asian debacle is that good governance of banks is an essential element of a sound banking system.  Moreover, the financial sector has grown remarkably in recent years to even exceed the size of the real sector. As a result, a financial crisis can readily spill over to the real sector.  

Elements of Good Corporate Governance of Banks [1]

Corporate governance refers to the set of rules that define the relationships between shareholders, managers, creditors, government and other stakeholders and a set of mechanisms that help directly or indirectly to enforce these rules.[2] Good governance, whether applied to banks or non-bank corporates, is essential for a well functioning economy as it provides incentives for management to act in ways that raise the firm’s net present value and assure shareholders an adequate return.  At the same time, good corporate governance can help create an environment conducive to the sustained growth of the industry – in this case the banking system.

To be sure, a good governance structure in the banking system by itself cannot build a strong and stable financial system on its own.  It needs to be complemented by, among other things, similarly appropriate governance structures in the regulatory agencies and the general corporate sector.

Good governance at the individual bank level hinges in part on the business practices adopted by the board of directors and management. A competent management is the first line of defense against excessive risk taking by banks. Most bank failures can be attributed to inadequate management that allows the bank to acquire low quality assets and take inappropriate risk positions, and that fails to detect and resolve deterioration in existing assets and risk positions. Briefly, some of the key elements of a good governance system at the individual bank level are:

  • Management that possesses high integrity and has adequate training and experience;
  • Good internal information and control system to ensure that decisions affecting the rights and obligations of the bank never rest with just one individual;
  • Prudent credit approval procedures and risk limitation procedures; and
  • Effective external and internal audit procedures to ensure that established policies and procedures are followed and special interests are not allowed to influence decisions.

Let me focus on the elements of good corporate governance at the industry level.  Specifically, what are some of the factors that can contribute in the creation of an environment conducive to the adoption of good governance practice by banks?

1.   Independent and capable banking supervisors

A key element of good governance of the banking industry is the quality of governance of monetary authorities and bank supervision agencies as the regulators set an example for the industry and as they are able to effectively perform their responsibilities/functions/duties.

The importance of independence of bank supervisors has been emphasized in the Bank for International Settlements (BIS) paper entitled “Core Principles For Effective Banking Supervision” which states that “an effective system of banking supervision will have clear responsibilities and objectives for each agency involved in the supervision of banking organizations. Each such agency should possess operational independence and adequate resource.”  

2.   Adequate bank rating system

The traditional system of analyzing and rating the soundness of financial institutions used by regulators, supervisors, credit rating agencies or corporate analysts has been the camel methodology. Bank soundness is evaluated based on capital adequacy, asset quality, management capability, earnings potential and liquidity.    However, this methodology may not be able to fully cover the entire range of governance risks faced by banks. Thus, there is a need to augment the camel methodology to include explicitly governance as a risk factor. This can be done, for example, by taking a closer look at the board of directors in terms of independence, accountability, interlocking interests, integrity, experience and ability to assume their duties, among other things.  

3.   Active merger and consolidation market

A more dynamic industrial environment characterized by an active merger and acquisition market can also induce good governance in banks. The threat of a corporate takeover or a merger should provide an impetus for the adoption of appropriate governance practices. To facilitate merger and consolidation activities, issues such as the limits on foreign ownership of banks, existence of dual classes of shares and tax and accounting regulations hampering mergers should be addressed.  

4.   Effective anti-corruption framework

The campaign to improve governance practices in banks should be accompanied by an anti-corruption framework that is strictly enforced by the relevant agencies.    Banks are often a target of corruption activities such that bank collapse often blamed on some form corrupt practice.

One of the core principles for effective supervision of banks identified by the BIS relates to connected lending, a form of corruption in banks. The BIS core principles for effective banking supervision states that “in order to prevent abuses from connected lending, banking supervisors must have in place requirements that banks lend to related companies and individuals on an arm’s length basis such that extensions of credit are officially monitored, and that other appropriate steps are taken to control or mitigate the risks.”  

5.   Others

Other factors essential to the creation of an environment for the good governance of banks are: the codification of the fiduciary duties of care and loyalty and the liabilities of bank directors; the requirement for banks listed in the stock exchange to disclose their governance practices as part of their annual reports; and the promotion of education, training and information on governance and professional directorship.  

BSP Towards an Environment of Good Governance

How does the Philippines rate against these elements of good governance? In a number of regional conferences I have attended, the observation has been made that the Philippines has fared relatively better than some other countries during the financial crisis. It did not undergo a similar degree of capital outflows, banking sector distress and other forms of financial upheavals as was experienced by the other countries in the region.

An important ingredient to this performance has been the relative strength of its banking system which derives from the combination of past history of reforms in the banking system and the timely pre-emptive measures taken by the authorities to address any potential financial sector weakness. This effectively spared the Philippines from the wrenching adjustments that have had to be made.

Such reforms took different dimensions from tightening of minimum capital and bringing regulatory standards closer to international best practices to re-orienting bank supervision toward the analysis of risk and strengthening bank exit policies. Let me discuss some of the more important measures:  

Bank capital requirements

Minimum capital requirements for banks were raised through end-2000, with intermediate minimum levels for end-1998 and end-1999.  The larger banks have not encountered meeting the new requirements. In some cases, mergers have been resorted to.  

Marking to market  

The BSP has also required banks to start marking to market their trading securities portfolio so that significant changes in their market values are properly accounted for.    Accounting standards have been agreed upon with the BAP, and the relevant price benchmarks have been discussed with market operators.  

Transparency and disclosure  

To enhance transparency and market discipline, the BSP has instructed all banks to disclose publicly, whether listed in the stock exchange or not, detailed information on a quarterly basis, their non-performing loans, classified loans and other risk assets, amount of general and specific loan-loss reserves, return on equity, and insider (DOSRI) loans.  

Consolidated supervision 

We have also started to supervise financial conglomerates in a consolidated fashion in order to address bank solvency on a consolidated basis. Since legislative changes are needed to fully impose consolidated capital requirements and extend consolidated supervision of financial institutions to include their interests in non-financial ventures, the authorities have proposed an amendment of the GBA in this regard which is currently under consideration by Congress. The BSP has already begun to consolidate limits on foreign currency exposures between banks and their affiliated FCDUs.  

Supervisory methods  

The BSP has also changed the focus of its supervision activities from a purely compliance-based and check-list driven assessment of banks’ condition to a forward-looking and risk-based framework. Together with the change in emphasis towards a risk-based approach, significant improvements have taken place in the area of rating methodologies. In July 1998, “sensitivity to market risk(s) was added to arrive at a camels rating system”.  

Others  

Other reforms include the intensified bank monitoring of selected banks especially those in potential distress. The BSP has also adopted explicit procedures to be used when banks fail to reach certain thresholds of capital adequacy. External auditors of banks have been required to report to the BSP all matters that could adversely affect the financial condition of their clients, any serious irregularity that may jeopardize the interest of depositors and creditors, and any losses incurred which substantially reduce bank’s capital. Stricter provisioning regulations have also been put in place.

How have these actions by the regulators been perceived by the observers? An independent assessment made recently by Goldman Sachs found that prudential standards in the Philippines remained strong and compare favorably with the standards used in the Asian region.  Moreover, the performance of the Philippine banking system in terms of NPL, profitability and capital adequacy during the crisis was generally positive. These reflect in part the good governance structure existing in the Philippine banks.

Let me quote part of that report, “bank managements are generally seasoned and cautious, having gone through a decade of economic depression and political upheaval. We also regard the BSP as a more transparent and effective regulator among Asian banks, though continued closer, preemptive supervision of bank is vital. The BSP appears to be more vigilant in bank supervision, particularly in terms of related-party lending. It now conducts more off-site examinations and monitors banks’ FOREX activities on a daily basis.”  

Concluding Remarks

In the last decade, the banking system has undergone a substantial period of reform not only to build a culture of good corporate governance but also to achieve the broader goal of strengthening the banking system. However, the reform process is a continuing process as we try to keep pace with the demands of globalization and liberalization. Thus, the Bangko Sentral continues to take an activist stance in the reform efforts as evident in the range of proposed reforms that have been submitted to the legislature as amendments to the General Banking Act and the New Central Bank Act. The proposed revisions seek to achieve the following: further strengthen banking supervision; enhance competition in the banking sector; promote further the independence of the BSP, particularly its ability to effectively conduct monetary policy, and strengthen the framework for failure resolution to ensure the speedy settlement of potential problems in the banking system.

Finally, let me emphasize that good governance of the banking system may not work in isolation. It has to be accompanied by good governance in the major components of the economy, particularly the corporate sector. Given the concentrated ownership in some parts of the corporate sector as well as the cross shareholdings between banks and corporations, there is a need to address governance issues in both the banking and corporate sectors.

Let me close this lecture with the quote on good corporate governance….“Corporate governance is not rocket science. All its principles are derived from common principles of business ethics. Nevertheless, its importance should not be underplayed since the consequences can be costly or catastrophic in the worst case.  Being an intangible asset, good governance requires attention and investment of time, money and the need for recourse to sources of professional governance expertise and advice.”

Thank you and good evening.  

--------------------------

[1] This section is based largely on ‘The Corporate Governance of Banks: CAMEL-in-a-Cage” by Arvind Mathur and Jimmy Burhan of the Asian Development Bank.

[2] “A Consolidated Report on Corporate Governance and Financing in East Asia: Executive Summary”, Asian Development Bank, November 1999, p.1.

Title: Keynote Address
Occasion: BSP-IMF Conference on Framework for Monetary Policy in Post-Crisis Asia
Speaker: Governor Rafael Buenaventura
Transcription:
BSP Monetary Board members Vicente Valdepeñas, Jr. and Melito Salazar, Jr., Mr. Kunio Saito, Mr. Stefan Ingves and Mr. Yusuke Horiguchi of the International Monetary Fund, participants to the BSP-IMF conference on “Framework for Monetary Policy in Post-Crisis Asia:  Policy Options and Inflation Targeting” ,friends, ladies and gentlemen, good morning.

First of all, let me say that I deeply appreciate the efforts of the International Monetary Fund in mounting this conference in collaboration with the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas.    The BSP is honored to co-host this event which gathers some of the most seasoned practitioners in the field of monetary policy.

Belatedly perhaps, let me also welcome you all to Cebu, the Philippines’ Queen City of the South, known for its vibrant economy and colorful past. It was on the shores of Limasawa, a small island off Sugbu—now known as Cebu—that the Portuguese explorer, Fernando de Magallanes, landed in March 1521, after an arduous two-year voyage from Seville, Spain.    A month later, he would set foot on Sugbu itself, and learn that he had discovered not just two islands, but a group of islands, which would eventually be named Filipinas—or Philippines—in honor of Felipe, then king of Spain. This brief visit into the past helps to emphasize that crossroads are true not only in history but also in contemporary economic and financial interactions. And we are honored that this very important interaction among central bankers around the world is taking place in this historic island of Cebu.  

POSITIVE PROSPECTS AND CHALLENGES FOR THE REGION

As the title of this conference indicates, Asia is now on the mend: the region has emerged from two-and-a-half years of arduous maneuvering through rough waters. The foundations for broad-based economic recovery in the region are beginning to be laid.    Recent trends continue to support this view. Starting the second quarter of this year, there has been an upturn in domestic demand along with increased industrial activity, rising exports and an improving investment climate. Relative stability in international financial markets has also been restored. These factors bode well for the region’s growth prospects.  However, while affirming these positive prospects, let me stress that a lot of hard work lies ahead to ensure lasting economic growth.

This conference, which seeks to provide Asia’s central bankers the opportunity to discuss options for monetary policy regimes in an environment, which for most countries involves greater exchange rate flexibility is, therefore, timely. Choosing the appropriate monetary policy framework is crucial to preserving monetary stability, establishing stronger macroeconomic fundamentals and sustaining economic growth.   

THE ROLE OF THE MONETARY POLICY IN ECONOMIC GROWTH

As you well know, there has been a shift in the understanding of the role of monetary policy in the past two decades. Prior to the 1980s, monetary policy was seen as a vehicle for promoting economic development by supporting production and employment.    Thus, slightly higher inflation, on account of accommodative monetary policy, was considered permissible as it allowed for faster economic growth. This old view of the role of monetary policy assumed the existence of a trade-off between inflation, on the one hand, and employment and growth, on the other.

However, developments in the past twenty years or so have required a review of this paradigm. Accommodative monetary policy has almost always led to higher inflation without necessarily promoting economic growth. The link between expansionary monetary policy—hence higher inflation—and economic growth, if it existed at all, proved to be operative only in the short run. Thus, we saw the shift in the focus of monetary policy from the promotion of production and employment to maintaining price stability.

It is widely accepted in policy circles that price stability can be best achieved by constraining discretionary policy, which may give rise to an inflationary bias in the conduct of monetary policy. Discretionary policy, in turn, may be curbed through the adoption of a nominal anchor. Depending on the choice of a nominal anchor, monetary policy may follow one of four basic approaches: monetary targeting, interest-rate targeting, exchange rate targeting and inflation targeting.

Nobody but nobody can prescribe what is best for a particular economy except those who have a stake in public policy. And the choice will be a function of the behavior of that economy’s liquidity as it relates to prices, income and employment; the independence of its monetary authorities; and the extent of development of its financial system as a channel of monetary policy.   

THE CONDUCT OF MONETARY POLICY IN THE PHILIPPINES

As the Philippines’ central monetary authority, the BSP’s primary mandate is to maintain price stability conducive to a balanced and sustainable growth of the economy. In fulfilling this mission, the BSP is vested with policy independence by the Philippine constitution itself, as well as the BSP charter. Given this responsibility, how does the BSP conduct monetary policy?

The BSP currently follows a monetary targeting framework. Under this approach, the demand for money is estimated, given the government’s targets for inflation and output growth. The appropriate level of money supply is then chosen to match estimated money demand so as to bring about basic equilibrium in the money market. To attain the targeted level of money supply, the BSP manages the level of base money (BM), taking into account the link between base money and the money supply. This it does by employing a variety of monetary policy instruments.

Thus far, monetary targeting has worked for us. Since the establishment of the Bangko Sentral in 1993, various forms of inflationary pressures have challenged its task of maintaining price stability. Nevertheless, the BSP has managed to keep inflation within single-digit levels. I am fully aware, of course, of the other monetary frameworks, including inflation targeting.

The BSP’s efforts to ensure price stability has given it the flexibility to conduct monetary policy in support of the economic recovery. With inflation within target levels and monetary aggregates below programmed ceilings, adjustments have been made—in the BSP’s policy interest rates and the reserve requirements—to lower the cost of lending and to improve the availability of credit. This monetary stance has helped nurture the economic recovery. During the first three quarters of the year, the Philippines performed better than expected, with real GNP expanding by 3.0 percent compared to the programmed 1.9 percent. Growth was promoted in a low-inflation environment amidst generally stable foreign exchange market conditions, a sound external position and a healthy financial system.

However, successful monetary targeting has certain requisites. Foremost among these is a stable and predictable relationship between monetary and real sector variables.    We are well aware, however, that financial deregulation and liberalization have given rise to a new financial architecture and a continuously evolving array of financial products and services. These developments have caused large and frequent fluctuations in the velocity of money, thus weakening the link between monetary and real sector variables. In the Philippines, we have experienced this “de-linking” in at least two instances: first, when inflation remained low, even as monetary aggregates were breached, and second, when inflation continued to accelerate, while monetary aggregates were kept well within targets.

These experiences have led the BSP to explore other options for monetary policy, among them, inflation targeting. During the symposium commemorating the 50th anniversary of central banking in the Philippines, which was held in Manila last January, inflation targeting was one of the topics for discussion. Governor Donald Brash of the Reserve Bank of New Zealand presented the main paper and I was privileged to have been invited as one of the reactors. Let me discuss some of the points I raised in my reaction paper.

First, inflation here in the Philippines is affected, to a large extent, by non-monetary factors. In fact, food accounts for more than 50 percent of our CPI basket. Clearly, in our case, inflation cannot be addressed by monetary policy alone. Our experience has proven that inflation can be triggered by weather-related disturbances and structural factors such as weaknesses in the food distribution system.

Aside from non-monetary factors, another possible hindrance to the implementation of inflation targeting in the Philippines is the difficulty of formulating a forecasting framework with a very high degree of accuracy, and which is easily understood by the public.On the latter point, it is important to underscore that the effectiveness of monetary policy is strengthened if the goals and instruments of policy are known to the public and if the authorities can make a credible commitment to meeting them.

In addition, inflation targeting requires the strict accountability of the head of the central bank. Of course, holding a public official accountable for his performance is a basic tenet of public governance.  However, putting the job of the central bank governor on the line even when inflation is not necessarily driven by central bank policy is-in my view-quite harsh and would undermine stability in the monetary system.

And let me quickly add that when I advanced these points, I had not assumed the post at room 501 of the Executive Building of the Bangko Sentral.

Assuredly, there are varying views on the subject-which is why I look forward to the discussions ahead. I am certain we will leave this island of Cebu very much refreshed and imbued with new ideas. There is much to be learned from the experiences of our colleagues from across continents.    

REGIONAL COOPERATION

As I noted earlier, patterns of recovery are emerging in Asia, with the pace and magnitude of recovery stronger for some countries. Sustaining the recovery requires firm commitment on the part of the governments in the region to pursue structural reforms, as well as implement consistent macroeconomic policies. These twin thrusts will help ensure the soundness of the financial system and create a more robust macroeconomic environment, which will minimize the effects of any external shock on the domestic economy.

However, in an increasingly globalized economic environment, efforts on the national level are unlikely to be very effective in reducing the likelihood of the recurrence of a similar crisis. Regional collaboration is crucial. Cooperation is particularly needed in the areas of bank supervision, information exchange, surveillance and possibly, the establishment of a regional financing facility. There is need to improve bank supervision in the region by developing standards that adhere to international best practices and to foster information exchange among countries, by establishing accessible data banks on the financial system and developing high-quality, credible, and transparent reporting and disclosure standards.    There is also a need to sustain the surveillance process on the global and regional level.    Such a surveillance process enables us to anticipate the emergence of potential instability, and react in a timely fashion to limit the spread of contagion. There is likewise a need to examine the possibility of establishing a regional financing facility, which can help solve liquidity problems during speculative attacks, and help maintain stability in the region.  

CONCLUDING REMARKS 

Earlier, I said that information exchange is one area where regional cooperation can be enhanced. This conference provides a very important venue for this exchange, as it provides Asia’s central bankers and other policymakers the opportunity to discuss how some of the analytical developments, such as inflation targeting frameworks, might apply in Asia. The discussion will be all the richer as it draws on the experience of central banks from around the world that have adopted these frameworks. With the impressive list of participants, we can look forward to two-and-a-half more days of highly stimulating discussions.

In closing, let me invite you to the dinner, which I am hosting tonight at the beachfront of the hotel. For now, let us proceed to our lunch date.

Thank you and good day.
