(Note: “Framework for Monetary Policy in Post-Crisis Asia: Policy Options and Inflation Targeting”, 8-10 December 1999, Cebu City)

Title: Keynote Address - Euromoney
Occasion: 7th Annual Asia pacific Issuers and Investors Forum, Euromoney
Speaker: Governor Rafael Buenaventura
Transcription:
Introduction

Mr. Adrian H. Thomas, Conference Manager and Head of the Asian Division of Euromoney, distinguished participants to this Seventh Annual Asia Pacific Issuers and Investors Forum organized by Euromoney:

Let me begin by expressing my deep appreciation to the conference organizers for inviting me to keynote the Euromoney Investors Forum, which is the leading regional gathering for the capital markets in Asia. For more than two years now, developments in Asia have been the focus of grave investor concern. But I am sure that you will agree with me that the foundations for economic recovery in the region are now beginning to be laid, in almost all cases being accompanied by a painful restructuring and reform program.    Relative stability in international markets have been restored starting the second quarter of this year, and the International Monetary Fund has also projected a stronger growth in most Asian economies in the first year of the new millennium. The fundamentals of the Asian economies can be now be said to be better than at any time since the 1997 crisis.

The regional financial crisis has highlighted the importance of nurturing investor confidence in national policies. In particular, the key role played by transparency in policy formulation, and the timeliness and accuracy of financial and economic information has been underscored. This forum, therefore, is an important step in maintaining this confidence.

Please do not interpret my statements as indicating that we have become sanguine about our growth prospects.  In the Philippines, we are only too acutely aware that sustained recovery and sustainable growth requires continued hard work.  This is reflected in our commitment to our economic reform agenda. In the spirit of transparency, therefore, let me now provide you with greater detail about how we have coped with the crisis.  My focus will necessarily be on the Philippines, but you will find me drawing on issues of current regional concern.  

The Role of the BSP

At this point, let me underscore certain distinguishing features of the Philippine monetary system, which served it in good stead in weathering the Asian financial crisis.  As the Philippine central monetary authority, the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP) is mandated by the Philippine Constitution to provide policy directions in the areas of money, banking and credit; to supervise the banking system, and to regulate other financial institutions such as finance companies.  The BSP’s primary mission is to deliver price stability conducive to a balanced growth of the economy. The BSP enjoys policy independence in the pursuit of this mission. This is guaranteed not just by ordinary law but by the Philippine constitution itself.

The onset of the financial crisis in Asia has provided a major challenge to the bank’s adherence to this mission, and at times has subjected the bank to criticism and pressure to sacrifice this objective in the pursuit of short-term, more popular goals.  The BSP responded to this challenge by adjusting its monetary and financial policies and striking a delicate balance between restoring order in the foreign exchange market, containing inflationary pressures, and limiting the adverse impact of the crisis on the banking and corporate sectors. At no time was the BSP’s pursuit of its mission of delivering price stability compromised. This policy stance was rewarded by the containment of the annual inflation rate to single digit levels even at the height of the crisis. Belying dire predictions arising from the current increases in world oil prices, the general price level has remained broadly stable, with the inflation rate settling at 5.4 percent in October this year, for a year-to-date average of 7.2 percent.  

Economic Growth Performance and Prospects

With the economy recovering from the Asian financial storm and with improvement in weather conditions, the Philippines performed better than expected during the first three quarters of this year, with gross national product (GNP) expanding by 3.0 percent in real terms. The evidence is now clear that industry has begun to recover. Our growth prospects-especially in terms of our exports-have been helped in large part by the recent marked improvement in global economic and financial conditions. Of late, some concerns have been raised over the eventual demand slowdown of the US economy. However, with adept management especially by the U.S. Fed, we believe that if there is any slowdown at some point, it will be a soft landing. This could be offset by the strengthening economies of Japan and Europe, as well as of other Asian countries.

Our commitment to price stability has also paid off, in that the resulting low inflation rates have given monetary policy the necessary flexibility in supporting the economic recovery. Thus, sustained policy adjustments have been made to lower the cost of lending and to improve the availability of credit. The benchmark 91-day Treasury bill rate was 8.894 percent at the auction held this Monday [29 November 1999], much lower than the 15.3 percent average for 1998. Last November 3, we trimmed our overnight borrowing rate by 25 basis points to 8.75 percent.  We assure you that at no point will this compromise our inflation targets.  

Facing External Challenges

Focusing now on the external sector, risk management will be pursued through the maintenance of an adequate level of foreign exchange reserves and through careful management of our external debt position.

There continues to be broad stability in the foreign exchange market, with reduced market volatility in 1999 relative to 1997 and 1998. The improvement should continue as regional factors become more positive and as we continue to see a surplus in our external accounts. For the first ten months of 1999, the balance of payments posted a surplus of US$3.4 billion. This was a significant increase over the US$1.4 billion surplus recorded during the comparable period in 1998.  In particular, the current account-buttressed by strong exports-has strengthened considerably, registering a surplus of US$3.3 billion in the first eight months from a surplus of only US$14 million during the same period a year ago.

As a result, we have been able to build up our foreign exchange reserves to a record high of US$14.6 billion as of the end of October. This is equivalent to 4.2 months of imports of goods and payments of services, and is more than enough to cover our short-term external liabilities, even if these are doubled. Apart from being a precautionary measure-particularly against the volatile, short-term capital-our reserve build-up program is also a confidence-building measure.

And let me report to you that our external debt continues to be manageable. Total foreign indebtedness amounted to US$48.1 billion as of end-June 1999. While there has been some increase in the aggregate level, the maturity and creditor profiles have improved.  The share of short-term debt to total debt has declined from 16.4 percent as of end-1992 to 13.6 percent as of the end of the first half of 1999. Reflecting the judicious sourcing and utilization of foreign borrowings, the debt service burden has dropped through the years:  from 17.1 percent in 1992 to 13.5 percent for the first semester of 1999. This means that-dollar for dollar-we are using less resources to service our foreign obligations.

Financial Sector Reforms

The strength of the Philippine financial system effectively shielded the country from the worst impacts of the regional financial crisis. This strength is evident in the sustained rise in the total resources of the financial system, underpinned by higher deposits and a stronger capital base, as well as in the improvements in banks’ asset quality and compliance with several prudential norms.

Banks’ capital adequacy ratio was recorded at 17.6 percent as of end-June. This was well above the 8 percent standard of the bank for international settlements and the 10 percent statutory requirement. The real estate exposure of commercial banks dropped to 12.3 percent as of end-June 1999 from 13.1 percent as of end-December 1998. Meanwhile, the non-performing loans ratio of commercial banks remains manageable at 13.4 percent as of end-September 1999. Provisioning against loan losses is also adequate, with loan loss reserves equivalent to 5.1 percent of total loans as of end-August 1999.

The non-performing loan (NPL) situation is expected to improve as the economy gains further momentum, resulting in increased lending, and as the effects of lower interest rates and relatively stable exchange rates impact positively on the repayment capability of corporates. We have started to see some signs of recovery in bank lending. As of end-September, outstanding loans of commercial banks were still down from last year, but the contraction was miniscule, at 0.15 percent, compared to 3.4 percent in August and 4.8 percent in July. Moreover, outstanding loans registered a 1.1 percent growth on a month-on-month basis. This follows the 2.0 percent month-on-month increase in August, as well as the increases in June and July.

Some of the important factors that were responsible for the respectable performance of the banking system include: the long history of financial sector reforms, complemented by appropriate and timely implementation by the authorities of regulatory changes before and during the crisis and the vigilant and close supervision by the banks’ major stakeholders.  The relatively high equity ratios in Philippine commercial banks have ensured, through stakeholders’ rights, that these institutions are managed as sound and profitable entities.  Moreover, the management teams of Philippine banks have had prior experience in dealing with the crisis in the Philippine economy in the early 1980s.

We also realize the necessity of continuing the structural reform program. Thus, major reform packages have been submitted to the legislature as amendments to the General Banking Act and the New Central Bank Act. Broadly speaking, the proposed revisions seek to achieve the following: enhance prudential standards; enhance competition in the banking sector; and promote further the independence of the BSP, particularly its ability to effectively conduct monetary policy.  

Need for Regional Cooperation

In my earlier address before the east Asia economic summit, 1 enumerated certain measures that can be adopted at the regional level in order to reduce the chance of future occurrence of a crisis of this magnitude. Inasmuch as international investor opinion can go a long way towards their adoption, let me take the occasion of this forum to re-enumerate some of the main areas that I feel need to be addressed.

First, there is need to develop national standards in bank supervision that adhere to international best practices. Collaborative initiatives along this line would reduce systemic risks in global and regional financial markets. Key components of these efforts include the development of accessible data banks on the financial system and of high-quality, credible, and transparent reporting and disclosure standards. In recognition of the importance of these issues, the BSP has enlisted as one of the first of the IMF member countries to enlist in the IMF Special Data Dissemination System (SDDS). While significant progress in international cooperation has been achieved, this is too important a task to be left to national and international organizations alone. Active private sector participation is a requirement for success.

Second, the foundation of these efforts to achieve market transparency is the timeliness and accuracy of the data that countries provide the public. This is an important issue to be addressed, as the move to increase the accessibility and speed of availability of financial sector data must not be at the expense of accuracy of information. The risk is that greater openness in information might be attended to by greater volatility in financial markets. In this respect, international conferences such as this present gathering serve as important avenues for linking economic decision makers in the region, both from the government and private sectors. The challenge is therefore for us to utilize for a such as this to come up with concrete vehicles for government-private sector cooperation.

Third, it is also important to sustain the surveillance process both globally and regionally. On a global scale, multilateral institutions need to intensify such a process with the cooperative support of the member nations. In this part of the world, regional surveillance should continue under the umbrella of the Asean and the three partners such as China, Japan, and Korea. Peer review is a very useful mechanism of ensuring regional awareness of key developments and possible roadblocks to economic advance. Such a surveillance process indeed buys us time to anticipate the emergence of potential instability and the possibility of contagion.

Thank you and good day. 

----------------------------------------------- 

1 held in Singapore, 20 October 1999

Title: Monetary and Fiscal Policy: Looking Ahead
Occasion: Philippine Association of Hong Kong (PAHK) and Philippine Bankers Club of Hong Kong
Speaker: Governor Rafael Buenaventura
Transcription:
Chief executives, officers and members of the Philippine Association of Hong Kong (PAHK) and the Philippine Bankers Club of Hong Kong (PBHK), good afternoon:

Hong Kong is a very suitable place to discuss our country’s monetary and fiscal policies. This economic entrepot is a bastion of free market principles; and it therefore serves as a very good setting to present our essentially market-based monetary and fiscal policies. Our meeting this afternoon is also auspicious because we are at such a decisive juncture of the economic recovery of the Philippines when we begin to look ahead to the challenges of the new millennium.

But let me preface my remarks this afternoon cautioning you that I will be a one-handed speaker; I will focus on monetary policy and touch on, as necessary, — in passing — the acts of the fiscal authorities. Our responsibilities are sufficiently cut and dried that we can easily discern where one should end and the other should begin.  

Current Economic Policy 

Current macroeconomic policy aims to foster the recovery and shield against domestic and external shocks. We have had our learning curve flattened by our interesting experiences in the 1990s including the surge in foreign money in 1993-97, the Tequila effect of 1994-95 and the Tom Yang effect of 1997-99. We have kept the course in the two and a half years of the Asian financial crisis. Monetary policy, in particular, has tried to contain inflation while being flexible enough to enable lower interest rates and a stable exchange rate. Fiscal policy, on the other hand, continues to aim to stimulate demand through pump-priming without necessarily crowding out private investment. 

Recent Economic Results  

This overall approach produced very good results in 1999, with signs of returning stability and a reviving economy. Our first three quarter data show that growth has indeed rebounded as agriculture continued to perform strongly and manufacturing made a turnaround. Inflation was mostly tame because of ample food supply, and the ten-month average inflation rate of 7.2 percent is quite close to the full-year target of 7 percent. The foreign exchange market was relatively stable in the first three quarters thanks to strong capital inflows. Bank lending has improved, with a smaller rate of decline in September, and domestic demand strengthened, based on data on imports, car sales and power consumption.

The recovery was due partly to the accommodative policy adopted in the first semester, with measures to help bring down interest rates combined with fiscal pump-priming to stimulate demand. Monetary stance was afforded greater flexibility because of the subdued inflation trend and the stable foreign exchange market. Actual monetary growth was also significantly below our target ceilings. In a word, conditions were suitable for an easier stance of monetary policy.

In the first seven months of 1999, accommodative monetary policy brought down the Reverse Repurchase (RRP) rate to 9 percent in a series of 20 policy rate cuts. The reserve requirement for banks was also cut by a total of 5 percentage points to 12 percent. These measures enabled a decline in both the 91-day Treasury bill rate and bank lending rates. As a precautionary measure, the Bangko Sentral also kept base money and reserve money comfortably below the IMF program ceilings. 

Meanwhile, expansionary fiscal policy took the form of a P22-billion fiscal stimulus package featured under the 1999 budget. The package set aside some P14 billion for quick-gestating infrastructure projects and some P8 billion for the acceleration of back payments owed to government contractors.

It was not entirely smooth sailing, however. Steering the economic ship through the Charybdis waters of the Asian crisis would be everything but smooth. Our fiscal authorities also have to deal with revenue shortfalls that threatened the fiscal targets. To cope with this, policymakers resorted to virtual belt-tightening by cutting down on non-essential expenditures. Also, in July, in response to short-term foreign exchange volatility, the Bangko Sentral switched to a neutral monetary stance and kept policy rates steady. As external factors such as the weakening Thai baht put pressure on the peso, our neutral stance allowed us to closely study the impact of accommodative policy before deciding to relax the stance further. Since then, the currency market has re-stabilized, allowing us to make another 25-basis point cut in overnight RRP rates to 8.75 percent effective November 3.   Earlier, we adopted the two-tier approach in our interest rate policy with the end result of achieving lower interest payments of the Bangko Sentral to the banks. Our aim is to induce banks to lend out their excess liquid funds, instead of parking them in the overnight window of the Bangko Sentral. In this way we hope to sustain the improvement in credit growth. 

Given these recent economic developments and expected turn of events for the rest of the year and the next, we believe that at this point, our banks, while watching their bottomlines, would need to be more aggressive to protect their present market share of the credit market. We have reached the lowest point of the economic cycle, and the only way for the various indicators of demand is up. The banks, coming from the supply side, should therefore assume the leadership in optimism. It is up to them to break the economic stalemate. We are, therefore, encouraged by the trend in credit growth. More and more banks have started to open their doors to borrowers and investors. In due time, we should see the fruits of this positive trend.  

PRESENT AND FUTURE POLICY STANCE  

The question now is, what is our present stance? And looking ahead, do we need to modify our existing one?

To begin with, policy actions in the near future — such as the decision to further ease the monetary stance — will indeed depend on the final shape of the economic outlook and on prevailing market conditions. For this year, we are targeting an average inflation rate of 7 percent and a GNP growth rate of 3.5 to 4 percent. Both goals are well within reach. In 2000, we expect economic conditions to improve further as the recovery gets underway. GDP growth is expected to be stronger, reaching 4 to 5 percent for the year. Improved agriculture performance and a stable foreign exchange market will help temper inflation in 2000 to an average of 6 to 7 percent. There are a number of challenges, of course, and further stimulation may be required to help achieve our broad economic targets. Over the next few quarters, we will need to continue to nurture the industrial sector and make sure that the turnaround in manufacturing is sustained. We would also like to see bank lending strengthen further and convince our local banks to gradually ease their cautious lending stance. And most important, we should be able to sustain our actions to intensify our reform agenda in banking, in tax administration as well as in corporate and public governance.  The crisis has taught us to be humble for change.

The November rate cut reflects our belief that there is still some room for monetary easing, particularly since average inflation remains close to the year’s overall target.  Monetary policy will continue to support growth while keeping inflation at bay, but further relaxation will be done carefully, in order to sustain the stability of the currency.  To put it briefly, our monetary stance will remain cautious yet flexible. The art of monetary policy is essentially a juggling act; you try to keep several balls in the air all at once. We try to balance the objective of stimulating the economy with the goals of price stability and exchange rate stability. That means taking it one step at a time. This means we are not targeting all monetary goals at the same time. Our monetary instruments are limited.

Similarly, if we may speak about it, fiscal policy is also trying to balance the need to stimulate private demand with the goal of fiscal prudence. Hence the fiscal stimulus package was combined with some belt-tightening. Unfortunately, the target budget deficit of P85.3 billion this year may still be exceeded. Personally, however, I don’t think that should be the main concern. To my mind, at this early stage of economic recovery, we can afford to accommodate some deficits, at least temporarily, if it would also mean having increased economic activity. At any rate, fiscal pressures may begin to ease soon. Revenue collection is expected to improve as economic growth resumes normal levels. More importantly, because of the more favorable economic scenario, there will be less need for government pump-priming. Therefore, fiscal policy in 2000 will be slightly less expansionary compared to this year.  Instead, the main focus will be on fiscal consolidation.

As the economy continues to recover, authorities need to focus on sustainability in the long haul. For the fiscal sector, the main concern will be balancing the budget in the medium term, say within the next two or three years. There are two key strategies to do this. First is strengthening the revenue base by improving tax administration. Higher revenues will reduce the deficit and help pay for priority projects and programs. The fiscal authorities also plan to rationalize the investment incentive structure by narrowing down the list of tax and duty exemptions. The second fiscal strategy is expenditure control, or cutting down on non-essential spending. With these measures, authorities hope to narrow down the deficit to P62.5 billion in 2000 and hopefully reduce it to zero later on.

Ladies and gentlemen, I took the liberty of venturing onto fiscal ground. I wanted to put across at this important gathering the crucial role of a healthy fiscal sector to the conduct of an independent monetary policy. To the extent that the fiscal balance is in good shape, the Bangko Sentral can continue focusing on its primary mandate of keeping inflation low and the banking system robust. These are the basic elements of vibrant economic growth. Short of this scenario, however, we might also have to watch for a possible current account deficit and a weak currency. The curse of high interest rates could very well be again on our laundry list of priority concerns. At this point, we have fundamentally put this behind us. And the challenge therefore is to ensure that it stays behind us as we strengthen our path to economic recovery.  

THE CHALLENGES AHEAD  

Part of our job as policymakers is anticipating and responding to emerging issues on both the domestic and external front. On the home front, the major concern will be the potential inflationary pressure from rising oil prices and adjustments in wages and transport costs. Here there should be less concern since we expect that strong agricultural output will help keep down prices for the basic food items, which comprise about 55 percent of the CPI. This was what happened in the October inflation data. More important, greater competition is expected to water down the inflationary impact of higher petroleum prices, transport and wage adjustments. 

On the external front, we will need to watch for large fluctuations in the regional currency market.  Further adverse shifts in regional sentiment cannot be ruled out completely yet, and we must remain alert to instability in other Asian countries. Over the medium term, market expectations of rising foreign interest rates, particularly in the US, may prompt investors to reallocate their portfolio to foreign assets, thereby affecting short-term movements of the peso and limiting the extent to which interest rates can be brought down. 

The main lesson from these challenges that I have outlined to you is the importance of prudent but forward-looking policy that keeps a sharp eye on new developments. Monetary policy will continue to be cautious yet flexible, and fiscal policy, as we read it, will focus on consolidation. The basic overall thrust is the same: we will try to nurse the recovery but preserve stability and guard against potential shocks to the economy.

In the old days when trains ran on steam, the train engineer kept the train running smoothly by putting coal into the boiler. We have already managed to get the train going, and it is running steadily. We have done our part and will continue to do so. And let me add that I hope that you will come on board and join us as we push full steam ahead into the new millennium. And I assure you, the coalfed locomotive is only metaphorical; when you board the Philippine train, it will run on our people’s ingenuity and productivity and global competitiveness.  

Thank you and good afternoon.     

(Note: Philippine Association of Hong Kong (PAHK) and Philippine Bankers Club of Hong Kong (PBHK), 6 December 1999, Conrad Hilton Hotel, Hong Kong)

Title: THE PHILIPPINES: ECONOMIC RECOVERY WITH A STRONGER BANKING SYSTEM
Occasion: 3rd General Membership Meeting, MART-FOREX-TOAP
Speaker: Governor Rafael Buenaventura
Transcription:
INTRODUCTION 

Officers and members of the Money Market Association of the Philippines, the Foreign Exchange Association of the Philippines, and the Trust Officers Association of the Philippines, distinguished guests, friends, ladies and gentlemen, good evening.

It is not often that a speaker is able to address three organizations at the same time.   This three-in-one affair is also very convenient since it collapses what would have been three dinners into one, thus helping me keep my waistline in shape while requiring me to speak only once. This arrangement is also efficient since it cuts travel time and lessens the ordeal of going through Manila’s traffic jams. This gathering thus bespeaks good planning. Given this propitious start and the impressive roster of participants, this evening’s activity should be a stimulating and fruitful undertaking.

I am indeed honored to speak before major players in the country’s money, foreign exchange and capital markets. Developments since July 1997 have brought to the fore the importance of a stable currency market in the efficient functioning of the economy on the path to sustained growth. We are all painfully aware—on both the professional and personal levels—of the costs inflicted by currency attacks on Asia’s economic tigers. The Asian crisis also highlighted the importance of well-functioning money and capital markets in achieving broad-based economic growth. For instance, there is wide agreement with the view that one of the causes of the region-wide crisis is the underdevelopment of the capital market, which encouraged not only over-investment in the money and asset markets but also over-reliance on short-term bank resources. The resulting asset bubbles placed the countries’ financial systems at risk, some more so than others.

It is true that the Philippine financial system was relatively unscathed by the recent financial storm. Though sustaining some cuts and bruises here and there, the system remained essentially sound and unbowed, as prudential measures adopted much earlier supported the viability of the system. Thus, our financial system did not have to undertake the scale of restructuring that its counterparts in neighboring countries had—and for some time still, will have—to go through. Nor did the Philippine government—and thus the tax-paying public—have to pay the enormous costs associated with such a restructuring.

However, I have never been one for self-congratulations. Aside from a typical Filipino’s aversion to such a trait, I think it is a dangerous stance to have, since it could mean that you are letting your guard down. Let me assure you, therefore, that we are resolute in our commitment to further strengthen our financial system. This would help ensure that financial resources are efficiently intermediated, thus providing the wherewithal for our shared goal of sustained and strong economic growth.

Let me say that we are fortunate to have strong foundations to build on. Allow me then to give you a brief exposition on the Philippine economy.  

RECENT ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENTS 

The country’s recent economic performance bodes well for its prospects in the near term. During the first half of this year, output performance was better than expected, with the real gross national product (GNP) expanding by 2.9 percent. Growth was underpinned by the strong expansion of the agricultural sector and the renewed strength of the services sector. Moreover, the contraction in industry appears to have been arrested, with manufacturing in particular showing signs of resurgence. The improving economies of Japan and Europe as well as the recovery of many of the crisis-afflicted emerging countries in Asia should impact favorably on our growth prospects, even if the much-hailed strengthening of the U.S. economy should simmer down.

Consumer prices have remained broadly stable, with the inflation rate for October settling at 5.4 percent, for an average of 7.2 percent during the first ten months of the year.    We have been able to promote growth in a low-inflation environment by reducing interest rates to low and sustainable levels. Interest rates have been on a steady downtrend since the height of the financial crisis. The benchmark 91-day Treasury bill rate was 8.9 percent at the last auction (15 November), much lower than the 15.3 percent average for 1998.

There continues to be broad stability in the foreign exchange market, consistent with the country’s stable macroeconomic fundamentals and strong external payments position.    Market price volatility has dropped significantly in 1999 relative to what it was in 1997 and 1998. This was due in large part to the measures implemented by the authorities to stabilize the foreign exchange market as well as to the credibility of their commitment to the floating exchange rate system.

The external payments position is more than comfortable. Surpluses in both the current account and the overall balance of payments were recorded for the first seven months of the year. A robust export performance was a major factor behind this trend. Altogether, these developments have allowed the Bangko Sentral to further increase its foreign exchange reserves to US$14.6 billion as of end-October this year from only US$8.8 billion at end-1997. We see the build-up in our foreign reserves as both a precautionary and confidence-building measure, and we intend to add to these reserves some more by year-end.

Our external debt continues to be manageable. While the level of foreign indebtedness has risen to US$48.1 billion as of end-June 1999, its maturity profile has continued to improve.    The share of short-term debt to total debt has declined, and, dollar for dollar, we are using less resources to service our foreign obligations in 1999 relative to earlier years. All these developments lower the vulnerability of our external payments position to possible abrupt changes in the global financial environment.

The fiscal position bears close watching, though. It has been reported that the P85 billion programmed deficit for 1999 has already been exceeded in the first ten months.    However, let me cite three factors that could mollify your concern about the fiscal picture.    First, the government has observed that the financing for this year’s deficit had already been secured; thus there should be no undue pressure on domestic interest rates from this end.    Second, the government went into deficit spending deliberately to pump-prime the economy and provide the safety nets needed to cushion the social costs of the crisis. Third, it went into deficit spending with the intention that such a policy will have a limited shelf-life. The government expects that, with the revival of economic growth, fiscal consolidation can be realized starting mid-2002.  

MONETARY AND FINANCIAL SECTOR POLICIES 

In terms of our monetary policy stance, we will continue to promote growth in a low-inflation environment through the reduction in interest rates to low but sustainable levels.    Operationally, this means that we are committed to providing sufficient liquidity for the strengthening economy, which is expected to grow at around 3.5-4 percent this year.    Moreover, last November 3, we trimmed our overnight borrowing rate by 25 basis points to 8.75 percent. With inflation within the programmed level and monetary aggregates comfortably below program ceilings, we have adequate flexibility in monetary policy. We expect that the reduction in our overnight policy interest rate would create a more normal yield curve, and encourage more active bank lending activity, which is a necessary condition for the resurgence of economic growth. Having said all of these, it must also be pointed out that we will calibrate policy interest rates in the event of marked changes in the external interest rate environment, and significant shifts in domestic inflation and exchange rate conditions.

As a channel of monetary policy, the Philippine financial system remains sound and healthy. Not once during the crisis has there been any concern about a possible disruption of the financial intermediation process. The system’s strength is evident in the continued increase in its aggregate resources, the compliance with prudential norms, and the fact that while asset quality—though weakened somewhat—remains manageable and compares well with those of other countries in the region.

The quality of the loan portfolio of the country’s commercial banks improved significantly as of end-September as non-performing loans dropped to 13.4 percent of total outstanding loans from 14.4 percent in August. The sharp decline in the industry’s non-performing loans bolstered overall asset quality. This significant improvement in banks’ asset quality is expected to continue in the coming months as banks build up further their loan books and as bad loans are worked out.

This owes in large part to the sustained implementation of major financial reforms. The reform efforts included, among others, measures to improve the quality of bank management, increase capital requirements, improve bank asset quality, enhance transparency in the system, and align prudential rules with international norms.

Let me add that we continue to take an activist stance in these matters, in order to be attuned to the dynamic mode of financial markets. In particular, measures have been proposed to amend the general banking act and the new central bank act with a view to enabling the Monetary Board to adopt internationally accepted standards relating to risk-based capital requirements and to clearly define unsound banking practices, among other things. We also continue to focus on structural reforms that will make our banking system more market oriented. Towards this end, we have encouraged mergers and consolidations in the banking system to promote globally competitive and more efficient banks.

The prudential supervision of financial institutions is crucial in maintaining the safety and soundness of the financial system during normal times. But it is during periods of strong pressure on financial markets that the stability of the system is really put to the test. Just as financial systems under inadequate prudential supervision would tend to be more vulnerable to the adverse effects of a crisis, financial institutions in those jurisdictions where supervisory authorities have succeeded in implementing appropriate safeguards are likely to be affected less and come out of the crisis much better than poorly supervised financial institutions.  

TOWARDS BETTER RISK MANAGEMENT 

However, there is still much to be done in bringing about a smoothly functioning and strong financial system that can advance economic growth. In particular, a key lesson from the recent financial crisis is the importance of transparency in reforming financial institutions.    Greater transparency is expected to reduce problems arising from asymmetric information by ensuring the free flow of information to all market players so that risk can be borne by appropriate parties.

For this reason, I commend recent efforts to develop a system of risk rating of Philippine banks. This risk rating system can embody the application of the best financial theory in managing our banks and, in particular, in managing levels of risk and, therefore, capital requirements. In this task, cooperation and dialogue between the private sector, particularly the Bankers Association of the Philippines (BAP) and the Bangko Sentral is indispensable. Just last week, the BSP and the BAP organized a conference on risk ratings, and hopefully, the discussions there will go some distance in encouraging the BAP to take the lead in developing the risk rating concept for the Philippine banking system.

Going further, at the 29th Asean Banking Council meeting held last week, we proposed the establishment of an Asean-based credit-rating firm. As you know, banks in the region currently depend on US- or Europe-based risk evaluators, which may not be quite familiar with the region. By contrast, a region-based credit-rating firm would be more sensitive to the nature, characteristics and practices of regional banks, which have more or less comparable standards.

Moreover, for improved risk management, the BSP will start requiring foreign and local banks to renew their expanded derivatives licenses every year, commencing in the first quarter of next year at the earliest. With risks getting exponentially greater owing to the dynamic nature of the derivatives market, it is vital that banks with licenses pose no danger to the soundness of the banking system. The BSP is continuously reviewing current rules and would adopt additional regulations and guidelines concerning accounting, booking and evaluation of risks.

Y2K-RELATED LIQUIDITY MEASURES 

We are hoping that the Y2K crossover is going to be a smooth business-as-usual event, We have nevertheless set in place contingency measures in case these are needed. To provide assistance to banking institutions in relation to any Y2K-related liquidity problem, the Monetary Board of the Bangko Sentral has recently approved a menu of schemes which includes (1) the establishment of an Emergency Year 2000 loan facility, (2) the establishment of a special repurchase facility, (3) the lengthening of the period for compliance with the reserve position, and (4) the lowering of the reserve requirement on inter-bank loans from one percent to zero percent.

The Emergency Year 2000 loan facility, meanwhile, is intended to provide temporary back-up assistance to banks in the event that they are unable to obtain funding from the market to meet any unusual increase in liquidity demand during the millennium changeover. It is believed that the very availability of a special Y2K financing facility could be a reassuring factor to help forestall potential liquidity problems. This facility is consistent with the relevant provisions of R.A. No. 7653, which state that the Bangko Sentral can provide liquidity to the banking system in periods of national and/or local emergency which directly threaten monetary and banking stability. Availments under this facility is allowed from 1 December 1999 to 31 January 2000. The pre-qualification period to gain quick-disbursing access to this facility has been set for the period on or before 26 November.

The special repurchase facility shall be open during the period 15 December 1999-15 January 2000 for qualified borrowers. Acceptable collateral for availments under this facility includes peso-denominated government securities (under a relaxed valuation schedule) and selected foreign currency-denominated government securities. The relaxed valuation will allow banks to borrow greater amount from this facility.

The Monetary Board also approved the lengthening of the compliance period for reserve position to cover the reserve period 17 December 1999 – 6 January 2000. The objective of this policy measure is to spread out the time required for banks to cover their reserves, thus reducing the pressure on interest rates. Meanwhile, the reserve requirement of interbank loans was also reduced from one percent to zero percent, consistent with the broad policy thrust of the Bangko Sentral to reduce banks’ intermediation cost and bring down interest rates. Moreover, the policy will not significantly affect liquidity since interbank transactions involve only a transfer of funds among banks.

The Monetary Board emphasized that all these privileges, accommodations and facilities will be made available to ease whatever liquidity pressure may be occasioned by the millennium crossover. Proceeds of availments are not, therefore, to be used for speculative investments.  

CONCLUSION  

The mood is cautiously upbeat for the Philippines. There is much to look forward to, but also much to be prepared for. Our increasing integration with the world economy has provided numerous and major benefits to the country. Yet, it also entails new set of challenges. The ability of the financial system to efficiently intermediate funds, always a concern, assumes greater importance as flows through the system increase with globalization and growth.    Against such a backdrop, I believe that the best posture that can be adopted is to be aware of the opportunities and the challenges, and to be prepared to always grasp the opportunities and turn challenges into yet new opportunities. The past two years and a half of the Asian crisis were both challenges and opportunities for us; we did not let go of the opportunities to strengthen our macroeconomy and the banking sector, yet the difficult times also forced us precisely to undertake measures that would help us avoid another of those crisis episodes.

This underscores the synergy between the government and the private sector in developing and strengthening of financial markets. This evening’s gathering provides another opportunity for you in the private sector to explore the possibilities by which this collaboration can be further enhanced, in support of our common vision of sustained economic development where free enterprise can thrive.

Thank you and good evening.  

 

(Note: 3rd General Membership Meeting of the Money Market Association of the Philippines (MART) held jointly with the Foreign Exchange Association of the Philippines (FOREX) and Trust Officers Association of the Philippines (TOAP), 22 November 1999, Hotel Intercontinental, Makati City)

Title: The Bangko Sentral and the International Capital Market
Place: ABN-AMRO Bank, Shagri-La Hotel, Makati City
Occasion: Signing Ceremony for the US$400M BSP Syndicated Credit Facility
Speaker: Governor Rafael Buenaventura
Transcription:
I am very pleased to see the successful completion of this joint undertaking today.    For the record, the Bangko Sentral has tapped the international debt market only five times since its establishment in July 1993. During my term, the first issuance was made in August 1999, involving 8.5% notes worth US$300 million. But I consider this one as a milestone because it is the first facility to be arranged under my watch.

The strong response of our lending investors to our latest fund raising exercise is much appreciated. This is more than indicated by the over-subscription in commitments that resulted in the increase in the facility amount from the initial US$250 million to US $400 million. I must also say that I am satisfied with the terms covering the facility. This underscores investor confidence in the continued soundness and resiliency of the Philippine economy. That this is the case has been validated by the consistent and steady credit ratings that we received from major rating agencies even at the height of the Asian financial crisis when most of our Asian neighbors suffered downgrades.

Indeed, I consider this positive investor response as an encouragement to the Bangko Sentral to continue in its present policy direction and to keep on working to provide the most appropriate environment for the sustained recovery of the economy.

And I am pleased to say that our efforts are now bearing very good fruit. The key economic indicators speak for themselves. Real GNP has rebounded. Inflation has been reduced from double to single digit levels, despite the recent hike in the prices of oil products. Interest rates are down and remain reasonable. Bank lending is picking up and the banking system continues to be healthy and strong. The exchange rate remains broadly stable. Our exports are soaring, our bop is sustaining a huge surplus and as a result, our international reserves are breaking record levels.

I must therefore say that the greatest compliment of the market is to lend us the rope when we feel that it is still long enough. This is one of those good ironies surrounding the decisions of countries to borrow.

Ladies and gentlemen, I assure you that the proceeds of this facility will be put to good use to enable the Bangko Sentral to keep the monetary and banking environment conducive to doing business in the country.

In closing, I would like to extend my thanks to the joint coordinating arrangers and to all those who collaborated with us in completing this undertaking.

Thank you and good day.    

 

(Note: Signing Ceremony for the US$400M BSP Syndicated Credit Facility, ABN-AMRO Bank, 19 November 1999, Shangri-La Hotel, Makati City)

Title: Banking Reform and the Role of the Thrift Banking Industry
Occasion: Signing Ceremony for the US$400M BSP Syndicated Credit Facility
Speaker: Governor Rafael Buenaventura
Transcription:
Mr. Dionisio C. Ong, president of the Chamber of Thrift Banks, officers and members of the chamber, distinguished guests, ladies and gentlemen, a pleasant day!

First of all, thank you for this opportunity to be in touch with you again. We at the Bangko Sentral always appreciate having a close and active communication with the banking community.

On the occasion, let me try to assess where we are now on the banking reform process and what that may imply for the thrift banking industry.

Recent developments

As you are well aware, the entire banking community, including the thrift banking industry, underwent significant stress during the 1997-1998 Asian financial crisis. Those effects continue to linger despite recent signs of economic recovery.

Fortunately, our banking system has been quite resilient. It is now in the process of consolidation that will provide a strong basis for renewed growth once the economy fully recovers.

Looking at the thrift banking industry as a whole, I think we should take heart in some recent improvements.

As of end-June 1999, total resources of thrift banks already recorded a 4.4 percent annual growth. Although modest, this still represents a complete turnaround from the 5.8 percent decline previously.

It is also a pleasant surprise to note that the total number of thrift bank offices actually showed a net increase of 22 offices between June 1998 and June 1999.

Total deposits likewise increased by 3.8 percent and profitability was restored as the combined loss of P 224 million a year ago was turned around into a net income of P 990 million as of end-June 1999.

In terms of loan quality, there are clear signs that at least the situation has stabilized.    The industry NPL ratio stood at 16.7 percent, almost the same as last year’s. Loan loss coverage also improved significantly to about 34 percent from just 23 percent last year and is now roughly at par with commercial banks. Nevertheless, overall asset quality remains a problem as evidenced by the steady increase in acquired assets.

Thrift banks also enjoyed high capitalization levels relative to risk assets equivalent to almost 21 percent. This compares with the 10 percent statutory requirement.

However, the aggregate story conceals some very real problems especially affecting a handful of problem banks and the relatively smaller thrift banks that have experienced a declining asset and deposit base, operating losses and capital deficiencies in today’s tough banking environment.

But the flip-side to this is the fact that many thrift banks are actually on very sound and solid financial footing. Yes, the critical core of the thrift banking system is fundamentally healthy.

For the record, as of end-June 1999, 74 out of the 120 operating thrift banks have already complied with the latest prescribed minimum capitalization requirements. Right now, these are P 250 million for thrift banks based in metro manila and P40 million for those based outside metro manila. And by December 2000, these go up further to P400 million and P 64 million respectively.

Of the 46 banks still unable to meet the new standards so far, 22 intend to convert into rural banks. These thrift banks are mostly based outside metro manila. The remaining banks are either negotiating for merger and/or acquisition or have submitted a capital build-up plan based on commitments from shareholders to infuse new capital.  

The Changing Banking Environment

Let me now stand back to look at the evolving overall financial environment and try to situate the thrift banking industry within that.

One of the most important lessons of the Asian financial crisis is the need to promote and maintain a sound financial system if economic growth is to be sustainable.

On this basis, we have intensified our own financial reforms, even if that may be painful in the short-run, to ensure that our financial system remains competitive and efficient and so that it will continue to retain investors’ confidence.

We are hoping that the reform process would pave the way for an even more resilient and effective banking system complemented by a vigorous domestic capital market. Together these can more fully meet the complex and enormous financing needs of our developing economy.

Within the banking industry, the reforms are taking deep root. Already, it has spurred unprecedented changes that are changing the face of Philippine banking.

In the commercial banking industry, which will continue to be the core of the banking industry, we are steadily moving to a scenario of fewer but more financially powerful main banks that are better able to compete in a world of more open borders. That logic is the most compelling driving force behind the current wave of bank mergers and acquisitions.

The Bangko Sentral certainly welcomes this development and we have been actively promoting it through our regulatory policies.

However, this is not to say that there will be no place in the evolving financial firmament for smaller banks especially thrift banks. Ideally, what will emerge is a backbone of big banks whose services will be well complemented by smaller specialist players that can more effectively cover important niche markets that have their own unique needs. Important niches for example include consumer lending, housing loans, small business loans, agri-business loans, as well as niches based on specific geographic markets. This is a role that the thrift banking industry should be able to play very well especially given certain regulatory advantages that are already existing.

 In fact, many players have already identified this opportunity. Looking at the thrift banking industry today, many large domestic and even foreign banks as well as other financial service organizations have already established their own thrift banking subsidiaries as part of broader corporate strategy to service a wide range of client markets. At present, there are 18 such thrift bank subsidiaries representing just 15 percent of the number of thrift banks but they already account for more than 40 percent of total banking offices and about half of the total resources of the entire thrift banking industry.

 For the rest of the thrift banking industry, composed of smaller and independent banks, you will need more than ever to carefully define your place in the market and muster the necessary resources to compete effectively and survive.

 In a sense, the Bangko Sentral’s increased minimum capitalization requirement, apart from the prudential aspects, concretely reinforces the market signal that may have been missed by some players. As a result, marginal banks must now decide in accordance with the set time frame whether to merge or be acquired, to put up more capital, or to compete in another more appropriate division.

Admittedly, these may not be very easy choices especially for banks that have long been used to an easy and quiet life. But it is no longer realistic nor constructive to think of banking life that way. Whether we like or not, the business of banking has changed irreversibly and you must step up to meet your clients’ higher expectations for greater safety, for better returns, and for more choices.

As far as the Bangko Sentral is concerned, it is vitally important that we are able to shape our own banking policies in line with the public’s expectations. This has been our primary guide in instituting various reforms that promote financial strength, better management, greater transparency and more accountability. And you can expect that we will continue to move in this direction.  

A Commitment to Monetary Stability

Let me conclude my speech today with another critical lesson learned from the Asian financial crisis. And this is the importance of ensuring basic macroeconomic stability in protecting the health of the financial system.

We all know how destabilizing very high interest rates and a large peso depreciation can be to the banking system and to the whole economy. For this reason, we are determined to act pro-actively on monetary policy to ensure continuous monetary and price stability even if sometimes this involves nudging up interest rates a little bit.

This is the duty of an independent central bank.

We are of course well aware that the economy is currently in a fragile state of recovery. For this reason, it is vitally important that we all cooperate to ensure the sustainability of the fiscal position and support government’s efforts to keep the fiscal deficit within reasonable levels.

This is the key to lower interest rates that are sustainable. It is also the critical battle that will determine our credibility and our ability to keep the delicate financial balance.

Thank you and good day.  

(Note: General Membership Luncheon Meeting, Chamber of Thrift Banks, 18 November 1999, Shangri-La Hotel, Makati City)

Title: Commitment to Banking Reforms: A Pillar of Asian Recovery
Place: New World Renaissance Hotel, Makati City
Occasion: 29th ASEAN Banking Council Meeting, ASEAN Banking Council
Speaker: Governor Rafael Buenaventura
Transcription:
Introduction

Mr. Secretary General Tay Kay Chye, distinguished officers and members of the ASEAN Banking Council, honored guests, ladies and gentlemen:

At the onset, I would like to congratulate the council for its many accomplishments.    Judging from the steady increase in its membership, it continues to demonstrate its vitality and relevance in a period of sweeping change in ASEAN banking.

I am glad to note the presence of the new members representing Laos and Cambodia.    I understand that preparations are also underway so that Myanmar will be represented in the next council meeting. When this happens, the council shall have all the banking associations of the Ten (10) ASEAN nations at the turn of the century.

This provides the council a golden opportunity to further enhance cooperation among member banking associations to promote faster regional growth in a globalized environment. 

The Tasks at Hand

The Asian financial crisis may be abating but greater challenges still lie ahead as the globalization of banking markets gathers a new momentum in the third millennium. The greatest challenge is in making banks evolve along with the society it serves. Doing so would ensure that they remain efficient and relevant catalysts for growth.

A decisive follow-through on banking and corporate reforms is crucial for sustained recovery. Structural weaknesses which were brought to the fore by the Asian crisis should not remain unresolved as these would only impede recovery prospects and could lead to a repeat of the recent regional experience. 

Asia Poised for a Resumption of Rapid Growth

The probability of putting Asia back on a fast-growth track is high considering the following factors:

(1) The general socio-political stability prevailing in the region;

(2) The limited inflationary pressures which were different from those seen in Latin America in the 1980s;

(3 The continued savings mobilization despite the economic slack;

(4) The enhanced ability of our banks to capture these savings;

(5) The strength of government balance sheets in absorbing their banking system’s losses; and

(6) The obvious commitment and courage of governments in reforming and restructuring the region’s financial architecture.

Our prospects are made even brighter with the improving trends of currencies, interest rates, a recovery of confidence in banking systems, and improved liquidity in the financial system of the member countries. 

Policy Directions for the Philippine Banking System

In the Philippines, we are continuing to build upon the many banking reform initiatives that have been started even before the Asian financial crisis struck. Our main goal is to promote a sound, stable and globally competitive financial system anchored on prudent risk management practices.

Our major thrust in this regard is two-pronged. First, we are strengthening the legislative framework; and second, we are adopting internationally accepted practices into our supervisory processes.

The major legislative reforms are to be effected mainly through the amendment of both the General Banking Act and the New Central Bank act. The major changes involve:

»    Providing the legal basis for the consolidated supervision of banks;

»    Lifting the restriction on Bangko Sentral’s authority to examine banks on-site which is presently limited to only once every 12 months;

»     Providing legal protection to supervisors in the conduct of their duties;

»    Further strengthening the framework for failure resolution and ensuring speedy settlement of potential problems;

»    Raising fines and penalties for non-compliance with prescribed prudential requirements, as well as adopting a mechanism for prompt corrective action; and

»    Clarifying conditions for access to the BSP’s lender-of-last resort facility.

The proposed amendments will further enhance the Bangko Sentral’s independence. The monetary board will have the necessary authority to adopt internationally accepted standards of banking operations, including those related to capital adequacy requirements.

The creation of stronger and globally competitive institutions anchored on sound risk management practices shall be facilitated through the progressive increase in minimum capitalization and encouragement of bank consolidations.

We are also promoting greater efficiency through competition. In this regard, we are considering allowing the entry of more foreign banks, especially through the acquisition of weak and undercapitalized banks, through appropriate changes in legislation.

We need banks which have the expertise in intermediating large volume of funds as well as in responding to the growing demands of their clients. Furthermore, we need banks that can offer superior financial advice and services. We need banks that have the capability to operate confidently and efficiently across borders. 

Complementary Reforms

In addition to the restructuring of the banking sector, we have also embarked on the broadening and deepening reforms in the domestic capital market. The reforms involve the strengthening of the regulatory framework for securities and the strengthening of the debt resolution process.

The taxation framework on financial transactions and instruments are also currently under review to ease the tax burden of financial intermediation and to promote a more level playing field. Consequently, these should facilitate the introduction of new financial instruments for trading and investments and the development of institutions that will harness savings and channel them into investments.

Capital market reforms are essential in reducing our reliance on the banking system for financing development. Our experience during the recent regional crisis showed us clearly the danger of this over reliance. 

Outlook for the Economy

As the Philippine economy continues to make progress under its economic and financial program, the country’s banking sector is expected to perform even better in the near future.

The first semester economic performance has so far been encouraging.

Our real gross national product exceeded expectations as it expanded by 2.9 percent in the first half of 1999 from the 0.1 percent growth in 1998.

We continue to keep inflation under control. Inflation rate settled at 5.7 percent in September, for an average of 7.4 percent during the first three quarters of the year.

We have also been successful in stabilizing the peso. The volatility of the exchange rate was lessened in 1999 compared to that of 1997 and 1998.

We have also continued to sustain prudent monetary management to provide sufficient liquidity to the economy. The benchmark 91-day treasury bill rate is currently at around 8.8 percent. This is much lower than the 15.3 percent average for 1998.

We have a relatively strong balance of payments. As a result of the robust growth in export averaging 14.7, the surplus in current account rose to US$2.5 billion from a deficit of US$111 million for the same period last year. The balance of payments surplus was US$ 2.8 billion during the first seven months of 1999. Consequently, our gross international reserves are again back at all-time high levels.

Finally, we managed to maintain the stability and promote growth of the Philippine financial system during and after the crisis. The steady improvement in bank asset quality, capital adequacy ratio, liquidity and profitability manifest its strength. 

Concluding Remarks

As a final note, let me call on the support of your council in vigorously promoting the restructuring of the Asian banking and financial system. Your steadfast commitment for continuous reforms of banking sectors will be the single most important contribution to regional prosperity.

Thank you and more power to your future undertakings!

 

(Note: 29th ASEAN Banking Council Meeting,13 November 1999, New World Renaissance Hotel, Makati City)

Title: The Bangko Sentral and the Banking System
Occasion: Induction of Officers and Board of Trustees, Clearing Officers Club
Speaker: Governor Rafael Buenaventura
Transcription:
It gives me great pleasure to be invited to the Induction of the Officers and Board of Trustees of the Clearing Officers Club, Inc. Indeed, occasions like this always evoke new beginnings and great expectations. At the same time, they remind us of new challenges and of course, whether one welcomes them or not, additional responsibilities.

I can say these with conviction because four months ago, I was precisely in the same situation. When I took my oath in Malacañang as the new Bangko Sentral Governor last July, it was a new beginning for me. From international banking with Citibank and domestic banking with PCIBank, I have made that important changeover from the supervised to the supervisor.  And I can assure you at this point that I find the change in my career very exciting. I am quite familiar with the script and the subtext of our market players on the other side of the fence. I’ve been there.

Yet having said that, in the four months that I have chaired the Monetary Board, what I realized most of all is the awesome responsibility of having to pull the levers of monetary policy with the full recognition of their implications on both markets and people. When I accepted the mantle of leadership from Governor Singson, he has intimated to me this truth, but it is only now that I am beginning to appreciate every grain of monetary policy. And so, during the last couple of months, I learned the hard truth behind the goal of preserving the policy independence of the Bangko Sentral. The episode was the period when interest rates were plummeting beyond those levels consistent with market fundamentals, while the peso was weakening because of adverse shifts in regional conditions.

On the issue of interest rate, the BSP maintained the importance of keeping such price variable market-determined. We dread the day when market players would refuse to touch financial instruments of savings and investments whether public or private, knowing that they scarcely reflect market sentiments. On the issue of the exchange rate, your monetary authorities kept their hands off the market even as the peso hovered around P41 to a dollar.    We believed, and we were proved correct by events, that the pressures on the currency were regional and temporary. Thus, not long after, the weakness of the peso diminished, consistent with our strong balance of payments.

Thus today, I encourage the Clearing Officers Club of the Philippines to maintain the pure ideals of your organization.

The clearing officers club was organized to promote professionalism among its members. This is done thru intensive study of established bank clearing procedures and functions. In the process, you are fulfilling a key role in the overall intermediation function of the banking system. When the clearing of checks is not efficiently done, the banking system suffers. We all know that the backbone of the banking system is the integrity and efficiency of the payment and settlement system. It is the link that connects the banks with one another and the banks with the public. Everyday, thousands of checks worth billions of pesos are drawn and cleared through the banking system. It is your main responsibility to ensure that the transactions underlying these checks are correctly accounted for on a timely basis. This is your call, this is your mandate. On this you will be challenged and will be expected to perform.

On the part of the Bangko Sentral, we fully support the activities of your organization.    In fact, in case of checks drawn within Metro Manila, the clearing office is right in the BSP complex. The Bangko Sentral, in cooperation with the bankers association of the Philippines and the Philippine Clearing House Corporation, has also been working to build up the electronic capability of our payment system. Of course, this is not only in preparation for the Y2K compliance of the banking system, but also for the long-term goal of enhancing the payment system in the Philippines. Financial intermediation can only be as effective as the completion of the whole financial settlement loop.

Focusing on the Y2K issue, let me advise you that the Bangko Sentral is addressing this not only in terms of its externally-supported systems but also of its in-house maintained systems. As regulator of the banking industry, the BSP is also devoting significant efforts and resources to ensure the Y2K preparedness of the Philippine banking system. It monitors the banks’ Y2K readiness by conducting on site verification of their Y2K efforts. To enhance monitoring, a banking industry year 2000 task force was created, headed by the BSP, and composed of representatives from the bankers association of the Philippines, the Chamber of Thrift Banks and the Rural Bankers Association of the Philippines. Close coordination is also being maintained with the Presidential Commission on Year 2000 Compliance and other regulatory bodies, including other banking supervisory authorities around the globe to address cross-border Y2K issues.

And so, in closing, I would say that the Bangko Sentral and the COCI are not really completely distinct and separate entities. We have common goals that keep us connected.    The most important and basic of which is to keep the banking system efficient and effective channel of monetary policy.

I challenge you today, as I was challenged before, to muster your collective spirit to uphold the pure ideals of your organization. You can never be wrong when you pursue your mandated goals.

Congratulations to the new officers and the members of the Board of Trustees of the Clearing Officers Club, Inc.

Thank you.

(Note: Induction of Officers and Board of Trustees, Clearing Officers Club, Inc., 2 November 1999, Mandarin Oriental Hotel, Makati City)

Title: The BSP's Short-and Medium-Term Plans
Occasion: Silver Anniversary, Bank Marketing Association of the Philippines
Speaker: Governor Rafael Buenaventura
Transcription:
Distinguished officers and members of the Bank Marketing Association of the Philippines, honored guests, ladies and gentlemen:

Let me first congratulate the members of the association on your silver anniversary. It gives me great pleasure to celebrate this special occasion with you and share some of my thoughts on the Philippine banking industry.

It is a recognized fact that a sound financial system is one of the main pillars of a strong and healthy economy. In the Philippines, the banking industry is presently the single most influential player in the financial system and its importance has been clearly manifested in recent times. The Asian financial crisis that started in 1997 is a strong testimony to this.    Many of our neighbors were severely affected by the crisis, owing in large part, to weaknesses in their respective financial systems. 

THE STATE OF THE BANKING SYSTEM

Our banking system has played a key role in insulating the country from the more serious problems that confronted other countries in the region. This is not to say that the industry has not been adversely affected by the crisis, as I’m sure all of you are aware.    However, many indicators are encouraging and signal a gradual return to normalcy.

For instance, the expansion of the total resources of the banking system slowed down from an average of 28 percent during the preceding five years to only 1 percent in 1998. By mid-1999, however, bank assets stood at P2.86 trillion, slightly up by 1.3 percent over figures for end-1998.

Bank earnings declined starting 1997. From 16.3% in 1996, return on equity dropped to 5.8% in 1998 and further to 1.8% in March 1999.

The dramatic rise in non-performing loans (NPLs) is probably the most telling indicator of the impact of the crisis on the financial sector. From 2.8 percent in December 1996, NPLs of commercial banks in relation to total loan portfolio surged to 14.3 percent in July 1999. Still, the situation remains manageable as the level is moderate compared to others in the region. With the recent uptick in business activity such as the 6.1 percent year-on-year growth in imports in august 1999, the NPL ratio is expected to gradually decline as companies recover and improve their capability to meet their obligations to banks and other financial institutions. Banks are also expected to expand their lending operations as positive developments continue.

Bank capitalization has remained adequate. At end-June 1999, the capital-to-risk assets ratio of commercial banks stood at 17.6 percent, way above the prescribed minimum of 10 percent and the international benchmark of 8 percent.

Commercial bank exposures to the real estate sector of 12.3 percent as of June 1999 is way below the 20 percent limit which the Bangko Sentral imposed even before the crisis started. The ratio likewise compares favorably with most Asian countries.

Finally, while there were bank failures, these were isolated cases. The combined assets of these banks represented less than half a percent of total resources of the system while their loans were no more than 0.6 percent of the system’s total exposure.

The relative resiliency of our banking system vis-à-vis its counterparts in the region could be traced to the numerous prudential measures implemented by the Bangko Sentral before and during the height of the Asian crisis. These included: imposition of a lower ceiling on real estate lending; introduction of the general loan loss provisioning; stricter definition of past due loans; higher minimum capital requirements; shift to risk-based approach in bank examination and greater transparency in reporting banks’ lending and borrowing operations.

The Philippine banking system thus remains safe and sound. But there is no room for complacency or reform fatigue. The globalization of the financial and capital markets presents important challenges that need to be addressed. At the same time, it offers new windows of opportunity just waiting to be recognized and tapped.  

POLICY DIRECTIONS FOR THE BANKING SYSTEM

Our top priority then is to ensure continued stability in the financial system by promoting stronger and globally competitive institutions anchored on sound risk management practices. We intend to do this by continuing to pursue a program of structural reforms in the banking system. Our major thrusts in this regard are two-pronged: first, we are strengthening the legislative framework; and second, we are adopting internationally accepted practices into our supervisory processes.

The approach aims at enhancing Bangko Sentral’s supervisory and enforcement powers; improving prudential standards for the banking system; fostering greater competition and competitiveness of banks; and promoting further the independence of the Bangko Sentral, particularly its ability to deal with threats to the overall stability of the financial system.

We have proposed to congress amendments to both the General Banking Act and the New Central Bank Act. These include making explicit the power of the BSP to issue and revoke banking licenses, promulgate more objective guidelines and additional penalties for unsafe and unsound practices, and require periodic submission and publication of financial reports.  

The proposed legislative amendments also seek to:

»Provide the legal basis for the consolidated supervision of banks;

»Lift the restriction on BSP’s authority to examine banks on-site which is presently limited to only once every 12 months;

»Provide legal protection to supervisors in the conduct of their duties;

»Further strengthen the framework for failure resolution to ensure speedy settlement of potential problems;

»Raise fines and penalties for non-compliance with prescribed prudential requirements, as well as adopt a mechanism for prompt corrective action for such non-compliance; and

»Clarify conditions for access to the BSP’s lender-of-last resort facility.

The foregoing changes will give the monetary board the authority to adopt internationally-accepted standards on banking operations, including those related to capital adequacy requirements. Other proposals involve the strengthening of provisions on insider loans, limits for borrowings and allied and non-allied investments of banks.

Moreover, BSP guidelines will focus on ensuring more competent bank management, greater transparency, reduced moral hazard and more effective bank regulation and supervision.

To promote greater competition within the industry, we are seeking to allow the entry of more foreign banks within a limited time period. At the same time, we are proposing that foreign investors be allowed to own 100 percent of local banks. Mechanisms will be put in place to ensure that local banks maintain dominance of our banking sector.

A major feature of the reform initiatives undertaken even prior to the Asian crisis was the progressive increase in minimum capitalization and encouragement of mergers and consolidations.  The increase in bank capitalization is being implemented on a phased approach over a three-year time frame from 1998 to the year 2000. We believe that a strong capital position provides cushion against adverse shocks. It also results in lower cost of funds due to the improvement in the bank’s credit standing. Here, I would like to point that while our banks are among the highly capitalized in the region, most of them remain relatively small by regional standards.

Given the rapid pace of globalization, we need to have forward-looking banks with the expertise to intermediate large volume of funds and to respond to the growing demands of their clients. We need banks that can offer superior financial advice and services with the capability to operate confidently and efficiently across borders.

Consolidation will enable banks to harness with greater efficiency their collective experiences, expertise and technological know-how. These are the overriding considerations for encouraging bank mergers and consolidations for which we have offered short-term incentives.   I’m confident that this will lead to the emergence of Philippine banks with regional and eventually, transnational reach.  

COMPLEMENTARY REFORMS

The restructuring of the banking industry, however, needs to be complemented by a broadening and deepening of reforms in the domestic capital market. While the banking sector is the dominant player in the Philippine financial system, there is danger in relying excessively on this sector for financing as the recent regional crisis so vividly showed us.  

Thus, the BSP, in coordination with the SEC, the Department of Finance, private institutions such as the Philippine Stock Exchange and business organizations will continue to vigorously push measures to develop the local capital market. These include the introduction of new financial instruments for trading and investments and the development of institutions that will harness savings and channel them into investments. In addition, the Bangko Sentral supports the further lowering of over-all credit costs to stimulate investment, e.g., through the progressive lowering and eventual abolition of the gross receipts tax on banks and financial institutions.  

SUMMARY
